questions.explanation: Recovery has to replay WAL from the last checkpoint's redo point, so checkpoints limit how much needs replaying, and WAL before that point can be removed (unless replicas or archiving still need it). Durability comes from flushing commit records, not from checkpoints.

questions.prompt: In what order does ARIES run its recovery phases after a crash?
options: Analysis, Undo, Redo
Analysis, Redo, Undo
Redo, Undo, Analysis
Undo, Redo, Analysis
questions.explanation: Analysis rebuilds the dirty page and active transaction tables from the last checkpoint, Redo repeats history to restore the state at the crash, and Undo rolls back transactions that never committed.

questions.prompt: During its redo phase, ARIES reapplies updates from ALL transactions, including those that will be rolled back. Why?
options: Because undo can't run without a checkpoint
To restore the exact database state at the crash so that undo, driven by LSNs and log records, can correctly roll back the losers
To find out which transactions committed
To compress the log
questions.explanation: This 'repeating history' makes page state match the log, so undo can safely reverse loser updates, including partial rollbacks already in the log. Analysis, not redo, determines which transactions committed.

questions.prompt: What role do compensation log records (CLRs) play in ARIES?
options: They mark the start of a checkpoint
They record each undo action, are redo-only, and point to the next record to undo, so a crash during recovery never undoes the same change twice
They log index splits for replication
They store checksums for torn-page detection
questions.explanation: Each undo writes a CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips past what has already been undone. If recovery crashes and restarts, redo replays the CLRs and undo continues from where it stopped, which bounds the work and avoids double undo.

questions.prompt: A buffer manager may write uncommitted dirty pages to disk (steal) and doesn't force committed pages to disk at commit (no-force). What must recovery support?
options: Only undo
Both undo (for stolen uncommitted changes) and redo (for committed changes not yet on disk)
Only redo
Neither, because the log is enough
questions.explanation: Steal puts loser changes on disk, which need undo. No-force can leave winner changes missing from disk, which need redo. ARIES is designed for steal/no-force because it gives the buffer manager the most freedom.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a team sets synchronous_commit = off for a high-volume event table. What risk are they accepting?
options: A crash can lose the most recent commits that were acknowledged but not yet flushed to WAL, while the database stays consistent
Table corruption after a crash
Transactions may see uncommitted data
Replicas will diverge permanently
questions.explanation: With synchronous_commit off, COMMIT returns before the WAL flush. A crash may lose a short window of transactions (up to about three times wal_writer_delay), but WAL ordering keeps the database consistent. It doesn't change isolation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about checkpoints in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: A transaction becomes durable only when the next checkpoint completes
More frequent checkpoints shorten crash recovery
WAL before the latest checkpoint's redo point can be recycled unless replication or archiving still needs it
More frequent checkpoints increase write I/O, partly because of more full-page writes after each checkpoint
questions.explanation: Checkpoint frequency trades recovery time against I/O: the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs a full page image. Durability comes from the commit record's WAL flush, not from checkpoints.

questions.prompt: Which features in PostgreSQL are built on the write-ahead log? Select all that apply.
options: Deciding row visibility for MVCC snapshots
Streaming physical replication
Logical decoding for change data capture
Query plan caching
Crash recovery
Point-in-time recovery from a base backup plus archived WAL
questions.explanation: The WAL is replayed for recovery, shipped to standbys, archived for PITR, and decoded for logical replication and CDC. Plan caching is per session, and visibility is decided from tuple xmin/xmax plus the commit log, not by reading WAL.

questions.prompt: In ARIES redo, a logged update is reapplied to a page only if the page's pageLSN is lower than the log record's LSN.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: pageLSN records the last update applied to the page. If it's already ≥ the record's LSN, the change is on disk and redo skips it. That makes redo idempotent.

questions.prompt: Why do teams put a pooler like PgBouncer in front of PostgreSQL when they run many app instances?
options: PgBouncer shards writes across replicas
PostgreSQL caps clients at 10 connections
PgBouncer caches query results
PostgreSQL forks a backend process per connection, so thousands of client connections waste memory and hit max_connections
questions.explanation: Each PostgreSQL connection is a separate process with its own memory and setup cost, so many mostly-idle connections are expensive. PgBouncer multiplexes clients onto a small server pool. It doesn't cache results or shard.

questions.prompt: In PgBouncer transaction pooling mode, when is a server connection assigned to a client?
options: For the duration of one transaction, then returned to the pool
Only for write statements
For the client's whole session
For a single statement only
questions.explanation: In transaction mode the client gets a server connection from BEGIN (or an implicit single-statement transaction) until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Session mode pins the connection for the whole session; statement mode releases it after every statement.

questions.prompt: Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, which of these behaves correctly?
options: SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '2s' inside a BEGIN ... COMMIT block
SET search_path = tenant_a, run once after connecting
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42), released at the end of the request
LISTEN orders_channel, to receive notifications later
questions.explanation: SET LOCAL lasts only for the current transaction, which is exactly the unit PgBouncer pins. A session-level SET, LISTEN or session advisory lock stays on whichever server connection you used, which may then go to a different client.

questions.prompt: 20 Node instances each create a node-postgres Pool with max: 20 against a PostgreSQL server with max_connections = 100. What happens at peak, and what is a sound fix?
options: Raise max_connections to 10000
Node shares one pool across instances automatically
Up to 400 connections are attempted and many fail; add PgBouncer in transaction mode and/or shrink per-instance pools so the total fits
PostgreSQL queues the extra 300 connections internally
questions.explanation: Pools are per process, so the total demand is instances × max. PostgreSQL rejects connections beyond max_connections ('too many clients'). A shared pooler or smaller pools keep the backend count sane; a huge max_connections wastes memory and adds contention.

questions.prompt: On an 8-core PostgreSQL server, a team raises the pooler's server pool from 50 to 500 connections, expecting more throughput. What usually happens?
options: Throughput rises roughly 10x
Throughput stays flat or drops, because extra active backends add context switching and lock contention without more CPU or disk
Queries become serializable
PgBouncer refuses pools larger than the core count
questions.explanation: Throughput peaks with a fairly small number of active connections, on the order of a few times the core count depending on I/O. Past that point, queuing in the pooler beats contention inside the database.

questions.prompt: A Node service checks out a client with `const client = await pool.connect()` but forgets client.release() on an error path. What symptom appears over time?
options: The pool silently opens unlimited extra connections
The pool runs out of clients, and new requests hang waiting for a connection
PostgreSQL kills the connections at once
Queries return stale data
questions.explanation: Clients that are never released stay checked out forever. Once all max clients have leaked, pool.connect() and pool.query() wait, indefinitely by default unless connectionTimeoutMillis is set. Use try/finally to always release.

questions.prompt: A handler runs BEGIN, updates an order, calls a payment provider over HTTP (2-5 seconds), then COMMITs. Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, pool waits climb under load. What is the best fix?
options: Switch PgBouncer to session mode
Disable transactions for this handler
Raise default_pool_size until waits stop
Move the HTTP call outside the transaction and keep transactions short
questions.explanation: The server connection is pinned for the whole transaction, including the slow network call, so a few requests starve the pool and also hold row locks. Session mode pins even longer, and a bigger pool just pushes contention into the database.

questions.prompt: Which PgBouncer pooling mode does not allow multi-statement transactions at all?
options: Statement
Session
Transaction
Replication
questions.explanation: Statement mode returns the server connection after every statement, so a multi-statement transaction would span connections. PgBouncer therefore refuses them. Transaction mode supports them by pinning for the whole transaction.

questions.prompt: Why is PgBouncer transaction pooling attractive for a serverless Node app on PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: Many short-lived function instances each open connections
Client connections to PgBouncer are cheap compared with PostgreSQL backends
It makes session-level advisory locks safe across invocations
It keeps the number of PostgreSQL backend processes small
It makes each individual query execute faster on the server
questions.explanation: Serverless scales to many instances, and the pooler absorbs their connections and multiplexes them onto a small pool of backends. It doesn't make session state safe (it breaks it) and doesn't speed up execution itself.

questions.prompt: Which features break or misbehave behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode? Select all that apply.
options: Several statements inside one BEGIN ... COMMIT
Temporary tables expected to survive across transactions
A long-lived LISTEN for NOTIFY events
SET LOCAL inside a transaction
Session-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock)
Session-level SET (without LOCAL)
questions.explanation: Anything stored on the server session leaks to, or disappears for, other clients when the connection is reassigned after a transaction. SET LOCAL and statements within a single transaction stay on one pinned connection, so they're fine.

questions.prompt: PgBouncer in transaction mode lets many client connections share a much smaller number of PostgreSQL server connections.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That's its main purpose. Because clients only hold a server connection during a transaction, thousands of mostly-idle clients can share tens of backends.

questions.prompt: What choice does the CAP theorem actually force on a distributed data store?
options: Pick any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance at design time, permanently
Choose between ACID and BASE transactions
Choose between low latency and high throughput
While a network partition is happening, choose between consistency (linearizable answers) and availability (every non-failed node answers)
questions.explanation: Partitions can't be avoided in a real network, so the real choice is what to do during one: refuse or delay some requests (CP), or answer with possibly stale data (AP). The 'pick two' slogan is misleading because P isn't optional.

questions.prompt: PACELC extends CAP. What does the 'ELC' part describe?
options: Else (no partition), the system trades Latency against Consistency
Every Leader Commits
Errors, Logs and Checkpoints
Eventual Leader Consensus
questions.explanation: PACELC: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. It captures that even in normal operation, waiting for replicas to agree costs latency.

questions.prompt: A 5-node etcd cluster is partitioned into a group of 3 and a group of 2. A client connected to the 2-node side tries to write a key. What happens?
options: Both sides elect leaders and accept writes
The write succeeds on the 2-node side and is merged later
The write fails or times out, because the minority side can't reach a quorum; consistency wins over availability
The write is accepted and then rejected after the partition heals
questions.explanation: etcd is a CP system built on Raft: only a majority (3 of 5) can commit. The minority side can't make progress on writes, which avoids split-brain. Accept-and-merge behaviour describes AP systems.

questions.prompt: A Cassandra cluster uses consistency level ONE for reads and writes. A network partition splits the data centre in two. What happens to writes on both sides?
options: Both sides keep accepting writes to their reachable replicas, and conflicts are reconciled later (by last-write-wins timestamps)
Writes are queued on the client
All writes are rejected until the partition heals
Only the larger side accepts writes
questions.explanation: With ONE, any reachable replica can acknowledge, so both sides stay available (AP) and diverge; LWW timestamps and repair converge them later. Majority-only writes would need QUORUM.

questions.prompt: A geo-distributed database waits for a cross-region quorum before acknowledging every write, even when the network is healthy. In PACELC terms, what is it choosing?
options: PA/EL
Consistency over latency when there is no partition (EC)
Latency over consistency (EL)
Availability over consistency during partitions
questions.explanation: Paying a cross-region round-trip on every write in normal operation means favouring consistency over latency, the EC half. Systems like Spanner are usually classified PC/EC; default Dynamo-style stores are PA/EL.

questions.prompt: A vendor markets its multi-node replicated database as 'CA: consistent and available, no trade-offs'. What is the best interview critique?
options: CA means the system uses consensus
CA systems give up durability
CA is the ideal choice and is common
Across a network, partitions will happen; when one does, the system must give up C or A, so 'CA' only really describes a single-node system
questions.explanation: You can't choose to have no partitions. A 'CA' distributed system just hasn't specified its partition behaviour, which in practice is either errors (C) or divergence (A). A single node, where partitions don't apply, is the only honest CA.

questions.prompt: A database serves reads from asynchronous followers, so a read right after an acknowledged write can return the old value. Is it 'consistent' in the CAP sense?
options: Yes, if the follower is in the same region
Yes, as long as there is no partition
No: CAP consistency means linearizability, so once a write completes, every later read must see it or something newer
Yes, because the follower eventually catches up
questions.explanation: CAP's C is a strong guarantee: a single up-to-date copy as far as clients can tell. Stale follower reads break it even without a partition. Eventual catch-up is eventual consistency, a weaker model.

questions.prompt: With replication factor 3 in Cassandra, a team switches latency-sensitive reads from QUORUM to ONE while keeping QUORUM writes. What is the effect?
options: Writes become eventually consistent
Reads get faster, but may return stale data, because 1 + 2 is not greater than 3
Reads become strongly consistent
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: Reading from one replica cuts latency (an EL choice), but read and write sets no longer have to overlap, so a read can miss the newest write. Write behaviour is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which of these are typically classified as CP (they refuse requests rather than return possibly stale data during a partition)? Select all that apply.
options: Cassandra with consistency level ONE
DNS
Apache ZooKeeper
etcd
questions.explanation: etcd and ZooKeeper use majority-quorum replication, so a minority partition stops serving writes (and linearizable reads). Cassandra at ONE and DNS's cached, eventually consistent records keep answering, which is AP behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PACELC are true? Select all that apply.
options: It says the latency-versus-consistency trade-off only exists during partitions
Synchronous cross-region replication raises write latency in exchange for consistency
It extends CAP to cover the trade-off during normal operation, not just during partitions
A PA/EL system may return stale reads even when there is no partition
questions.explanation: PACELC's point is that the Else case (no partition) still forces latency-versus-consistency choices; that's why PA/EL systems serve stale reads in healthy conditions. The last option inverts the theorem.

questions.prompt: In the CAP theorem, 'availability' means every request received by a non-failing node gets a non-error response, even if that response may not reflect the latest write.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That is the formal definition in CAP: every non-failed node must respond, and the response needn't be up to date. It's stricter than uptime SLAs, which allow some nodes to refuse requests.

questions.prompt: What are the two phases of the two-phase commit (2PC) protocol?
options: Prepare, where participants vote yes or no; then commit or abort, where the coordinator broadcasts the decision
Lock acquisition, then lock release
Leader election, then log replication
Read, then validate
questions.explanation: In 2PC the coordinator asks every participant to prepare. Only if all vote yes does it send commit; otherwise it sends abort. Growing and shrinking lock phases belong to two-phase locking, a different protocol.

questions.prompt: In 2PC, what must a participant do before voting 'yes' in the prepare phase?
options: Commit its local changes
Release all its locks
Durably record that it is prepared (and its changes), so it can commit even after a crash
Ask the other participants how they voted
questions.explanation: A yes vote is a promise to commit if told to, so the participant must survive a crash in the prepared state, keeping its changes and locks. Committing or releasing locks before the decision would break atomicity.

questions.prompt: In 2PC, all participants have voted yes, and the coordinator crashes before sending its decision. What state are the participants in?
options: They abort automatically after a timeout
They are 'in doubt': blocked, holding locks, until the coordinator recovers and reports the outcome
They elect a new coordinator and vote again
They commit automatically after a timeout
questions.explanation: A prepared participant can't decide alone: the coordinator might have logged commit, or abort, before crashing. So it blocks with its locks held. This is 2PC's classic blocking problem; acting unilaterally could break atomicity.

questions.prompt: In 2PC, three participants vote yes and one votes no. What does the coordinator do?
options: Sends abort to all participants
Commits on the three yes participants
Commits if a majority voted yes
Retries the prepare phase on the no participant until it votes yes
questions.explanation: 2PC requires unanimous yes votes. A single no (or a timeout during prepare) means global abort. Majority voting is consensus, not atomic commit.

questions.prompt: Why must the 2PC coordinator durably log its commit decision BEFORE sending commit messages?
options: Because participants read the coordinator's log directly
To release the participants' locks sooner
So that after a crash it can tell in-doubt participants the same outcome, instead of possibly deciding differently
To make the participants' writes durable
questions.explanation: If the coordinator sent commit to some participants and crashed without logging, it might abort on recovery, leaving some committed and some aborted. Logging the decision first makes it the single source of truth. It doesn't make participant writes durable; their own prepare records do that.

questions.prompt: With max_prepared_transactions > 0, an app uses PostgreSQL's PREPARE TRANSACTION for 2PC. The coordinator dies and never sends COMMIT PREPARED. What is the operational risk?
options: PostgreSQL commits the transaction automatically after an hour
The orphaned prepared transaction keeps its locks and holds back VACUUM's xmin horizon indefinitely, even across restarts, until someone resolves it
PostgreSQL rolls it back on the next restart
Only the coordinator's session is affected
questions.explanation: Prepared transactions survive restarts and are never resolved automatically. They block conflicting writers and stop dead-tuple cleanup. Monitor pg_prepared_xacts and resolve them with COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED.

questions.prompt: Why do microservice architectures rarely use 2PC across services' databases?
options: It needs a SERIALIZABLE isolation level
2PC can't guarantee atomicity
It couples every service's availability and latency to all the others, holds locks across network round trips, can block on coordinator failure, and many brokers and APIs don't support it
2PC only works with NoSQL databases
questions.explanation: 2PC is atomic, but at the cost of blocking and tight coupling, which conflicts with independent deployability and availability. Sagas with the outbox pattern are the usual alternative. 2PC doesn't require SERIALIZABLE.

questions.prompt: Three-phase commit (3PC) adds a pre-commit phase to reduce blocking. Why isn't it widely used in practice?
options: It only works for read-only transactions
It needs more participants than 2PC
It requires global clocks
Its non-blocking guarantee assumes bounded network delays; under real partitions it can still reach inconsistent outcomes
questions.explanation: 3PC is non-blocking only under a synchronous model with bounded delays and fail-stop crashes. Real networks partition and delay messages, so 3PC can let both sides decide differently. Systems that need fault tolerance replicate the coordinator with consensus instead.

questions.prompt: Which are inherent costs of two-phase commit? Select all that apply.
options: Participants hold locks from prepare until they learn the decision
A participant may abort on its own after voting yes
The transaction can only succeed if every participant is up and reachable
It guarantees participants never block
At least two message round trips between coordinator and participants before commit completes
questions.explanation: Extra round trips, locks held across the protocol, and availability limited by the weakest participant are 2PC's costs. Blocking is exactly its weakness, and a yes vote takes away the right to abort unilaterally.

questions.prompt: Which approaches genuinely reduce the impact of a 2PC coordinator failure? Select all that apply.
options: Add more participants so a majority vote decides
A cooperative termination protocol: in-doubt participants ask the others whether any of them already knows the outcome or never voted yes
Lower the participants' lock timeouts so they release locks sooner
Replicate the coordinator's decision log with a consensus protocol (as Spanner does with Paxos groups)
questions.explanation: Consensus-replicated coordinators survive individual crashes, and cooperative termination resolves some in-doubt cases (it can't help if all are prepared and nobody heard the decision). Releasing locks breaks the prepared promise, and majority voting is not atomic commit.

questions.prompt: In 2PC, a participant that has voted 'yes' may safely abort on its own if it hasn't heard from the coordinator within a timeout.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: After voting yes, the coordinator might already have decided commit and told others. Aborting alone could leave the transaction committed on some nodes and aborted on others. Before voting, a timeout-abort is safe; after voting, it isn't.

questions.prompt: What is a saga in the context of distributed transactions?
options: A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it if a later step fails
A two-phase commit with retries
A long-lived database lock held across services
A replicated log shared between microservices
questions.explanation: Each step commits locally and publishes progress; on failure, compensations for completed steps run in reverse. There's no global lock or atomic commit. That's the point, and also the main trade-off.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an orchestrated saga from a choreographed one?
options: In orchestration a central coordinator tells each service what to do next; in choreography each service reacts to the others' events with no central controller
Orchestration uses 2PC; choreography uses compensation
Choreography only works with synchronous HTTP
Orchestration can't compensate
questions.explanation: An orchestrator (often a workflow engine or state machine) owns the flow and the saga state. In choreography the flow emerges from event subscriptions. Both compensate, and neither uses 2PC.

questions.prompt: An order saga runs: 1) reserve inventory, 2) charge payment, 3) book shipping. Step 3 fails permanently. What should happen?
options: Roll back all three local database transactions with ROLLBACK
Retry step 1
Leave the payment and reservation in place and alert support
Run the compensations in reverse: refund the payment, then release the inventory reservation
questions.explanation: Steps 1 and 2 already committed locally, so they can't be rolled back with ROLLBACK. They need semantic compensations, usually in reverse order. Leaving them creates charged-but-unshipped orders.

questions.prompt: While a saga is in progress, another request sees inventory reserved for an order whose payment later fails. Which saga weakness is this, and what is a common countermeasure?
options: Lack of durability; enable synchronous replication
Lack of atomicity; use 2PC for that step
Lack of isolation; use a semantic lock such as a PENDING status that other flows respect
A clock skew problem; use NTP
questions.explanation: Sagas give up isolation: intermediate commits are visible. Countermeasures include semantic locks or status flags, commutative updates, re-reading values before acting, and ordering steps to reduce risk. Durability and clocks aren't the issue here.

questions.prompt: Saga steps and compensations are triggered by messages from a broker with at-least-once delivery. What property must the compensation 'refund payment P' have?
options: It must be idempotent and retryable, so a duplicate message doesn't refund twice and a failure can be retried
It must run exactly once, which the broker guarantees
It must hold a lock on the order until the saga ends
It must run inside the original payment transaction
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen, and compensations can't be allowed to fail permanently. Idempotency keys (for example refund keyed by payment id) make repeats harmless. Brokers rarely guarantee exactly-once end-to-end processing.

questions.prompt: A signup saga includes sending a welcome email, which can't be undone. Where should that step go?
options: First, so the user is informed early
In parallel with all other steps
In the middle, with a compensating 'ignore previous email' message
After the pivot: once every step that can fail has succeeded, as a retryable final step
questions.explanation: Irreversible actions belong after the point of no return, and the steps after it should be retriable until they succeed, so they're never compensated. Sending first risks emailing users whose signup later fails, and follow-up 'ignore' emails are a poor compensation.

questions.prompt: A service must update its orders table AND publish an OrderCreated event for the next saga step. Which pattern avoids the dual-write problem?
options: Publish the event first, then write the row
Transactional outbox: insert the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the order, and have a relay publish it
Use a distributed lock around both writes
Write the row, then publish the event in a finally block
questions.explanation: The outbox makes the state change and the intent to publish atomic in one database. A relay (polling or CDC) publishes at least once. The other orderings can still crash between the two writes, and a lock doesn't make two systems commit atomically.

questions.prompt: A team's choreographed saga has grown to eight services reacting to each other's events, and nobody can tell where a given order is stuck. Which change best addresses this?
options: Make every service call the next one synchronously over HTTP
Remove compensations
Add more event types
Switch to an orchestrator that owns the flow and persists each saga's state
questions.explanation: Choreography spreads the flow logic across services, which gets hard to trace and change as steps grow. An orchestrator centralizes sequencing, timeouts and state, so 'where is order X' becomes a lookup. Synchronous chains add coupling and cascading failures.

questions.prompt: Which are valid saga compensations? Select all that apply.
options: Issue ROLLBACK on the payment service's already-committed transaction
Release seats that were reserved
Refund a payment that was charged
DELETE the payment row so the charge appears never to have happened
Cancel a shipment request that was created
questions.explanation: Compensations are new business actions that offset earlier ones, leaving an audit trail. Deleting history hides a real side effect (the card was charged), and committed transactions can't be rolled back.

questions.prompt: Which statements about sagas are true? Select all that apply.
options: An orchestrator should persist saga state so it can resume after a crash
A compensation may not restore the exact prior state (an email already sent stays sent)
They hold locks across all services until the final step commits
They don't provide isolation: other transactions can see intermediate states
questions.explanation: Sagas trade isolation and exact undo for availability and loose coupling, and durable orchestration state is needed for recovery. They deliberately avoid cross-service locks; that's how they differ from 2PC.

questions.prompt: A saga's compensating transaction undoes a step by rolling back that step's original database transaction.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: By the time compensation runs, the step's local transaction has long since committed. A compensation is a new transaction that semantically reverses it, such as a refund or a release.

questions.prompt: Under the transactional outbox pattern, a downstream consumer may receive the same event more than once, so it should process events idempotently.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The relay can crash after publishing but before marking the outbox row as sent, and then republish it. Outbox delivery is at-least-once, so consumers should deduplicate, for example by event id.

questions.prompt: Why do practical consensus protocols like Raft (and Multi-Paxos) elect a single leader?
options: So one node orders all log entries, avoiding conflicting proposals and making replication simple and efficient
To avoid needing a majority
Because followers can't store data
So reads never need network calls
questions.explanation: A stable leader serializes client commands into one log and replicates it, avoiding repeated proposal conflicts. A majority is still needed to commit and to elect the leader.

questions.prompt: A Raft cluster has 5 nodes. How many node failures can it tolerate while still committing writes?
questions.explanation: Commits need a majority, which is 3 of 5. Losing 2 leaves 3, still a majority; losing 3 leaves 2, which can't commit. In general, 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures.

questions.prompt: Why are consensus clusters usually sized at an odd number of nodes, such as 3 or 5, rather than 4?
options: A 4-node cluster needs 3 for a majority, so it tolerates only 1 failure, the same as 3 nodes, while adding cost and latency
Raft rejects even-sized clusters
Even clusters can't elect a leader
Odd clusters avoid clock skew
questions.explanation: The majority for 4 is 3, so one failure is the limit, just like a 3-node cluster, with an extra machine to run and a larger quorum to wait for. Raft does work with even sizes; it's just inefficient.

questions.prompt: In Raft, why are election timeouts randomized (for example 150-300 ms)?
options: To spread network load
To let the leader commit faster
So followers rarely time out at the same moment, which makes split votes and repeated failed elections unlikely
To keep logs in sync
questions.explanation: If all followers became candidates together, the votes would split and no one would win. Randomization usually lets one node time out first, ask for votes and win. It has nothing to do with log replication speed.

questions.prompt: A Raft leader of a 5-node cluster is partitioned with one follower; the other 3 nodes elect a new leader. What happens to writes the old leader accepts during the partition?
options: The new leader copies them when the partition heals
Both leaders commit, and the newer timestamp wins
They commit on the old side and merge later
They can't commit (no majority); when the partition heals, the old leader sees the higher term, steps down, and those uncommitted entries are overwritten
questions.explanation: Committing needs 3 of 5 acknowledgements, and the old leader's side has only 2, so clients never get a success. On reconnect, the higher term forces it to follower, and its log is truncated to match the new leader's. That's how Raft avoids split-brain.

questions.prompt: In Raft, a voter refuses to vote for a candidate whose log is less up-to-date than its own (comparing last log term, then index). What does this guarantee?
options: Any elected leader already holds every committed entry, so committed data is never lost
Elections finish in one round
Followers never need to truncate their logs
Terms never increase
questions.explanation: A committed entry is on a majority, and a winner needs votes from a majority, so at least one voter has the entry and will refuse a candidate without it. This is the leader completeness property. Elections can still need several rounds.

questions.prompt: A Raft leader answers reads straight from its local state machine, without contacting anyone. In what situation can this return stale data?
options: Only when followers are slow
Only when snapshots are being taken
When the node has been deposed by a newer leader during a partition but doesn't know it yet; linearizable reads need a ReadIndex quorum check or a lease
Never: the leader always has the latest data
questions.explanation: A partitioned old leader may still believe it leads while a new leader commits writes. Confirming leadership with a heartbeat round (ReadIndex), or relying on a clock-bounded lease, prevents stale reads.

questions.prompt: The FLP impossibility result says no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash. How do Raft and Paxos cope in practice?
options: They assume no node ever crashes
They stay safe always, and use timeouts so they make progress whenever the network is stable enough (partial synchrony)
They give up safety under partitions
They use synchronized atomic clocks
questions.explanation: Raft and Paxos never violate safety (agreement), but may stall during bad periods. Timeouts and leader election make progress likely once message delays settle. They never trade away safety; liveness is what is conditional.

questions.prompt: Which of these systems use the Raft consensus algorithm internally? Select all that apply.
options: Memcached
etcd
HashiCorp Consul
CockroachDB
questions.explanation: etcd (and Kubernetes through it), Consul and CockroachDB (per-range Raft groups) all use Raft. Memcached has no replication or consensus at all. (ZooKeeper uses its own ZAB protocol, not Raft.)

questions.prompt: Which statements about Raft terms are true? Select all that apply.
options: Every term always has exactly one leader
A node that sees a message with a higher term updates its term and becomes a follower
Terms only increase
Each term has at most one leader
questions.explanation: Terms act as a logical clock. A term may end with no leader at all if the vote splits, which is why 'exactly one' is wrong, but never with two. Seeing a higher term makes stale leaders and candidates step down.

questions.prompt: A 3-node Raft cluster with 2 nodes down can still accept writes if the remaining node was the leader.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Committing needs a majority (2 of 3). A lone leader can append to its own log but can't commit, so clients don't get success. It also loses leadership once it can't confirm a quorum.

questions.prompt: With asynchronous leader-follower replication, the leader acknowledges a commit and then crashes before the follower receives the change. The follower is promoted. What happens to that commit?
options: It is replayed from the follower's WAL
The promotion waits until the old leader returns
It is lost, even though the client was told it succeeded
The new leader fetches it from the client
questions.explanation: Async replication acknowledges before followers have the change, so failover can drop acknowledged writes. Synchronous or quorum replication closes that gap at the cost of commit latency. The follower never received the WAL, so it can't replay it.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL primary has exactly one synchronous standby, configured with synchronous_commit = on. The standby goes down. What happens to writes on the primary?
options: They continue normally in async mode
The primary shuts down
Commits hang, waiting for a standby acknowledgement that never comes, until a standby returns or the config changes
The primary rejects writes with an error immediately
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL doesn't fall back to async on its own. Commits wait indefinitely for the named synchronous standby. That's why setups use several candidates or quorum lists such as ANY 1 (s1, s2).

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a team sets synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)'. What does this give them?
options: Commits are fully async
s1 always takes priority, and s2 is ignored
Commits wait for both standbys
Commits wait for at least one of s1 or s2, so either standby can be down without blocking writes
questions.explanation: Quorum-based sync replication needs acknowledgements from any 1 of the listed standbys, so every commit is on at least two machines while one standby failure is tolerated. FIRST 1 (s1, s2) would be priority-based instead.

questions.prompt: A multi-leader setup accepts writes in us-east and eu-west. Two users edit the same document title in each region within the same second. What must the system handle?
options: A write conflict, resolved by last-write-wins, merge logic or CRDTs, or by routing each record to a single home region
Replication lag only, which resolves itself
Nothing: multi-leader replication serializes writes globally
A deadlock between the regions
questions.explanation: Each leader commits locally and replicates asynchronously, so concurrent edits produce conflicting versions that some rule must reconcile. Avoiding conflicts by giving each record a home region is common. There's no global serialization, which is the whole trade-off.

questions.prompt: In a Dynamo-style leaderless store, a replica is briefly down, so another node stores the write on its behalf and forwards it when the replica returns. What is this called?
options: Log shipping
Read repair
Hinted handoff
Anti-entropy with Merkle trees
questions.explanation: Hinted handoff keeps writes available during short outages by parking them with a hint. Read repair fixes stale replicas when they're read, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy reconciles replicas in the background.

questions.prompt: After failover, the old primary comes back online, still believes it is the leader, and accepts writes alongside the new primary. What is this, and what prevents it?
options: A hot partition; reshard
Write skew; use SERIALIZABLE isolation
Split-brain; fence the old leader (STONITH, revoked network access or storage, or epoch/fencing tokens the storage layer checks)
Replication lag; add read replicas
questions.explanation: Two leaders accepting writes diverge and lose data. Fencing guarantees the deposed leader can't act: it's powered off, cut off, or its stale epoch is rejected downstream. Isolation levels only work within a single leader.

questions.prompt: A multi-leader system resolves conflicts with last-write-wins using each node's wall-clock timestamp. One node's clock runs 2 seconds fast. What is the risk?
options: That node's writes win conflicts they should lose, so other nodes' genuinely later writes are silently dropped
Replication stops
Writes from that node are rejected
Nothing, because NTP corrects it instantly
questions.explanation: LWW trusts timestamps, so a skewed clock makes stale writes look newer and data is lost with no error. NTP narrows skew but doesn't eliminate it. Logical clocks or version vectors detect concurrency rather than guessing an order.

questions.prompt: Why does statement-based replication break with statements like UPDATE t SET token = random() or INSERT ... VALUES (now())?
options: These statements are always rejected by the leader
Replicas can't parse functions
They need SERIALIZABLE isolation
Nondeterministic functions evaluate differently on each replica, so the data diverges; row-based (logical) replication ships the resulting values instead
questions.explanation: Re-executing a statement only reproduces state if it's deterministic. Random values, the current time, auto-increment races and triggers can all diverge. That's why MySQL defaults to row-based binlogs and PostgreSQL ships WAL or logical row changes.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of multi-leader replication across regions? Select all that apply.
options: The system tolerates the loss of an entire region more gracefully
Each region can keep accepting writes during an inter-region network partition
It's simpler to operate than single-leader replication
Write conflicts can't happen
Users write to a nearby leader with low latency
questions.explanation: Local writes, partition tolerance and regional fault tolerance are why teams accept multi-leader's costs: conflicts that must be resolved, plus more complex operations and reasoning.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL with a synchronous standby configured, which statements about synchronous_commit levels are true? Select all that apply.
options: off makes commits wait for the standby but skip the primary's own flush
on waits until the standby has flushed the commit's WAL to durable storage
local waits only for the primary's own WAL flush
remote_apply waits until the standby has applied the commit, so reads on that standby see it
questions.explanation: The levels progress: local (primary flush), remote_write (standby wrote to the OS), on (standby flushed), remote_apply (standby replayed). off doesn't even wait for the primary's local flush, and it never waits for standbys.

questions.prompt: Synchronous replication to one standby means a commit is acknowledged only after at least two machines have durably recorded it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With synchronous_commit = on and one sync standby, the primary flushes locally and waits for the standby's flush acknowledgement, so losing one machine doesn't lose acknowledged commits. The cost is a network round trip on every commit.

questions.prompt: A users table is hash-sharded on user_id. What is the main downside of hash sharding compared with range sharding?
options: Point lookups by user_id hit every shard
Range queries on the shard key (for example user_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000) must go to every shard
Data spreads unevenly across shards
It can't use more than 16 shards
questions.explanation: Hashing destroys key order: it spreads load evenly, but adjacent keys land on different shards, so range scans fan out. Point lookups go to exactly one shard, which is hashing's strength.

questions.prompt: An events table is range-sharded by created_at. Writes slow down even though there are 10 shards. What is the likely cause?
options: Timestamps hash poorly
Every new insert has the latest timestamp, so all writes hit the shard holding the newest range (a hot shard)
The shards are unbalanced in total size
Range sharding doesn't support inserts
questions.explanation: Monotonically increasing keys always fall in the last range, so one shard takes the whole write load while the others sit idle. Fixes include hashing, prefixing the key with a bucket, or a different shard key.

questions.prompt: A cache cluster places keys with hash(key) % N. Growing from 4 to 5 nodes causes a huge spike in misses. Why, and what reduces the impact?
options: Hash functions change with N; use MD5
The cluster needs an odd number of nodes
The new node is cold; pre-warm it and the problem disappears
Modulo hashing remaps most keys when N changes; consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of them
questions.explanation: With modulo placement, about 80% of keys change owner going from 4 to 5 nodes, so nearly the whole cache misses at once. Consistent hashing (or fixed slots, as in Redis Cluster's 16,384 hash slots) moves only the slices the new node takes over.

questions.prompt: What is a key trade-off of directory-based (lookup-table) sharding?
options: It forces every query to hit all shards
It's very flexible, because any key can be moved by editing the mapping, but the directory becomes a critical dependency that must be highly available and heavily cached
It can't move individual keys between shards
It only works with hash keys
questions.explanation: A directory allows custom placement (for example moving one big tenant) and smooth rebalancing, but every request depends on the mapping. It has to be replicated, cached and kept consistent during moves.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS shards by tenant_id. Most tenants are tiny, but one enterprise tenant generates 40% of traffic and overloads its shard. What is a sound approach?
options: Switch to sharding by row id across all tenants
Rate-limit that tenant permanently
Add read replicas to every shard equally
Keep tenant_id as the shard key, and move the large tenant to dedicated shards or sub-shard it by a second key, using a directory mapping
questions.explanation: Sharding by tenant keeps each tenant's queries on one shard, which is worth preserving. Outliers get special placement (a dedicated shard, or splitting by tenant plus another key). Sharding by row id would turn every tenant query into scatter-gather.

questions.prompt: A social app shards posts and likes by user_id. A celebrity's new post receives millions of likes per minute, overloading one shard. Which mitigation targets the hot key directly?
options: Split the hot counter into N sub-keys (likes:post:1..N) spread across shards, and sum them on read or periodically
Use a larger connection pool
Switch to range sharding by user_id
Increase the number of shards
questions.explanation: More shards don't help when a single key is hot: it still maps to one shard. Splitting that key's writes across sub-keys (salting) spreads the load, at the cost of aggregating on read. Caching helps the read side.

questions.prompt: You need to move data online from 4 shards to 8 with no downtime. Which sequence is the most robust?
options: Stop writes, copy everything, update the routing, resume
Copy a snapshot to the new shards, stream ongoing changes (CDC or double writes) until caught up, verify, switch reads and then writes per range, then clean up the old copies
Change the routing to 8 shards first, then copy the data in the background
Copy a snapshot, then delete the old shards
questions.explanation: Online resharding is backfill plus change capture plus verified, gradual cutover, so nothing is lost and rollback is possible. Switching routing before data arrives serves missing data, and stopping writes is downtime.

questions.prompt: Orders are sharded by customer_id. A new admin dashboard lists 'latest 50 orders across all customers'. What does each request cost, and what is a common mitigation?
options: A single cross-shard JOIN, cheap with indexes
It's impossible with sharding
A scatter-gather query to every shard plus a merge; mitigate with a separate denormalized read model or index (for example via CDC into a search store)
One shard query, since order ids are global
questions.explanation: Queries that don't include the shard key must fan out, and latency is set by the slowest shard. For non-shard-key access patterns, maintain a secondary read model fed asynchronously, rather than slowing down the primary shards.

questions.prompt: Which NEW challenges does sharding a relational database introduce? Select all that apply.
options: Transactions that span shards need 2PC or sagas
Single-row lookups by shard key must be broadcast to all shards
Rebalancing data when shards are added or become hot
Generating globally unique ids without a single sequence
Joins between data on different shards become expensive or happen in the application
questions.explanation: Sharding gives up single-node atomicity, sequences and joins, and adds rebalancing work. Lookups by shard key are the case sharding handles best: they route to exactly one shard.

questions.prompt: Which statements about consistent hashing with virtual nodes are true? Select all that apply.
options: Many virtual nodes per server smooth out uneven key distribution
Servers with more capacity can be given more virtual nodes
A newly added server takes small slices from many existing servers instead of one big chunk from a single neighbour
It eliminates hot keys, because each key is spread across many virtual nodes
questions.explanation: Virtual nodes balance load and make rebalancing incremental and weighted. A single key still hashes to one position, and therefore one server, so hot keys need separate techniques such as splitting or caching.

questions.prompt: With range sharding on a monotonically increasing key such as an auto-increment id, new inserts spread evenly across all shards.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every new id is larger than the last, so all inserts land in the final range, on one hot shard. Hash sharding or a non-monotonic key (for example a random UUID or a bucket prefix) spreads the writes.

questions.prompt: A user saves their profile (written to the primary), is redirected to their profile page (read from a replica), and sees the old values. What is happening?
options: The browser cached the old page
The write failed
Replication lag: the replica hasn't replayed the write yet
The replica rejected the write
questions.explanation: Async replicas trail the primary by milliseconds to seconds, so a read immediately after a write can miss it. This is the classic read-your-writes violation. Replicas don't accept writes in the first place.

questions.prompt: Which approach gives a user read-your-writes consistency when reads normally go to replicas?
options: Increase the replicas' cache size
Add more replicas
After a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary for a short window (or until a replica has caught up past the write)
Read from a random replica each time
questions.explanation: Pinning recent writers to the primary, or to a replica known to be past their write, ensures they see their own changes, while everyone else still reads from replicas. More replicas don't reduce lag.

questions.prompt: A user refreshes a feed twice: the first load shows a new comment, the second (served by a different, more-lagged replica) doesn't. Which guarantee is violated, and how do you fix it?
options: Linearizability; use 2PC
Causal consistency; use synchronous replication everywhere
Monotonic reads; pin each user (session) to the same replica, for example by hashing the user id
Read-your-writes; route to the primary
questions.explanation: Monotonic reads means a user never sees time go backwards. Different replicas lag by different amounts, so sticky replica selection solves it. This user didn't write the comment, so read-your-writes isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL streaming replication, which is a correct way to observe replica lag?
options: Check the replica's max_connections
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_locks on the replica
Query pg_stat_replication on the primary (for example replay_lag), or compute now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on the standby
Compare the table row counts on both servers
questions.explanation: pg_stat_replication reports per-standby write, flush and replay lag (as times and LSNs). On the standby, the last replayed transaction timestamp gives an approximate lag, which overstates it when the primary is idle. Row counts are expensive and misleading.

questions.prompt: After a write, the app records the primary's pg_current_wal_lsn(). On a later read, how can it decide whether a PostgreSQL replica is fresh enough?
options: Compare transaction ids directly
Check whether the replica's pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() is ≥ the saved LSN; if not, read from the primary or wait
Check whether the replica's clock is ahead of the write time
Ask the replica to run VACUUM first
questions.explanation: Comparing LSNs is precise: once the replica has replayed past the write's LSN, it reflects the write. Clock comparisons suffer from skew, and transaction ids don't indicate replay progress.

questions.prompt: A long analytics query on a PostgreSQL hot standby fails with 'canceling statement due to conflict with recovery'. Which fix keeps the query running, and what does it cost?
options: Turn on hot_standby_feedback; the primary keeps rows the query still needs, which can bloat tables on the primary
Set hot_standby = off; reads stop working
Use synchronous_commit = remote_apply; writes get slower
Increase work_mem; queries use more RAM
questions.explanation: WAL replay wants to remove rows the standby query still sees, so PostgreSQL cancels the query. hot_standby_feedback stops the primary from vacuuming those rows (risking bloat). Raising max_standby_streaming_delay instead lets replay pause, which increases lag.

questions.prompt: A write-heavy PostgreSQL primary is at 90% CPU from INSERTs and UPDATEs. A teammate proposes adding three read replicas. What is the main flaw?
options: Replicas can't serve reads
Replicas make writes slower by locking tables
Every replica must replay all the writes, and writes still go to the primary, so read replicas don't scale write throughput
PostgreSQL limits clusters to two replicas
questions.explanation: Read replicas offload reads only. A write bottleneck needs batching, query or index tuning, partitioning or sharding. Async replicas don't lock the primary.

questions.prompt: A checkout service reads stock from a replica, and if stock > 0 sends UPDATE stock = stock - 1 to the primary. Under load, it oversells. What's the correct fix?
options: Do the check and the decrement atomically on the primary, for example UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock > 0, and check the affected row count
Increase the replica's resources to reduce lag
Read from two replicas and take the minimum
Add a cache in front of the replica
questions.explanation: Decisions that guard writes must use current data, and a lagging replica (plus the gap between read and write) causes oversell. An atomic conditional update on the primary is correct whatever the lag. Less lag only shrinks the race window.

questions.prompt: Which are reasonable strategies for coping with replication lag in an app that reads from replicas? Select all that apply.
options: Send correctness-critical reads (such as checks before writes) to the primary
Add more replicas to reduce lag
Keep each user on the same replica for monotonic reads
Raise cache TTLs in front of the replicas
Show optimistic UI updates for the user's own changes
questions.explanation: Routing critical reads, sticky sessions and optimistic UI handle lag rather than wishing it away. More replicas don't make replay faster, and longer cache TTLs add even more staleness.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL streaming replication, which of these can cause replica lag to grow? Select all that apply.
options: Limited network bandwidth between primary and replica
The replica's disk I/O is under-provisioned compared with the primary's
A large bulk load or migration on the primary generates a burst of WAL
The primary uses synchronous_commit = on without any synchronous standbys
Long queries on the replica pause WAL replay (for example max_standby_streaming_delay = -1)
questions.explanation: Lag comes from WAL being produced faster than the replica can receive and replay it: slow replica I/O, paused replay, WAL bursts and thin network links. synchronous_commit = on without sync standbys only waits for the local flush, so it doesn't affect the replica.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL physical streaming replication, you can create an extra index on a hot standby to speed up its reporting queries.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A physical standby is a read-only, block-level copy of the primary, so no DDL is allowed on it. Reporting-specific indexes need to exist on the primary, or you use logical replication to a separate, writable database.

questions.prompt: Two worker processes append order records to the same CSV file at the same time, and some lines come out interleaved or missing. Which DBMS capability directly addresses this?
options: Data independence between schema levels
A declarative query language for reports
Normalisation to remove redundant columns
Concurrency control through transactions and locking
questions.explanation: A DBMS isolates concurrent writers (locks or MVCC) so each insert is applied whole and none are lost. Normalisation reduces redundancy but does nothing to coordinate simultaneous writes.

questions.prompt: A customer's address is copied into the billing, shipping and CRM files. Support updates it only in the CRM file. What file-system problem is this, and how does a DBMS typically prevent it?
options: Data isolation; the DBMS encrypts each file separately
Redundancy causing inconsistency; store the address once and reference it
Atomicity failure; the DBMS writes all three files in a transaction
Security leak; the DBMS restricts who can read the CRM file
questions.explanation: Duplicated data drifts apart when only one copy is updated. A shared, normalised schema stores the fact once and other tables reference it. Writing three copies atomically would still keep redundant data around.

questions.prompt: A file-based banking script debits account A in one file, then crashes before crediting account B in another file. How does a DBMS prevent this half-finished state?
options: It locks both files so no other process can read them
It replicates both files to a standby server before writing
It validates balances with CHECK constraints after the crash
It logs changes (write-ahead log) and rolls back uncommitted transactions on recovery
questions.explanation: Atomicity comes from logging: on restart the DBMS undoes changes from transactions that never committed, so the debit disappears too. Replication copies the broken state as well, and CHECK constraints can't tell that a transfer was half done.

questions.prompt: In a file-based system, every new business report ("orders over ₹5,000 last month by city") needs a developer to write and deploy a new program. Which DBMS feature removes that bottleneck?
options: Storing every table in its own file on disk
A declarative query language such as SQL for ad-hoc queries
Role-based access control for analysts
Automatic backups taken on a schedule
questions.explanation: With SQL you describe what you want and the optimiser works out how to get it, so new questions don't need new access code. Backups and access control matter, but they don't make data easier to query.

questions.prompt: A video platform stores multi-GB video files. Which design is generally better than putting the raw video bytes in PostgreSQL rows?
options: Split each video into 1 KB rows so the DBMS can index every chunk
Store videos in object storage and keep metadata and object keys in the DBMS
Store the video in a bytea column and stream it from SQL queries
Keep videos in a JSONB column encoded as base64
questions.explanation: Large, immutable, sequentially read blobs fit object storage and CDNs. The DBMS adds value for the queryable, transactional metadata. Huge bytea or base64 values bloat the database, backups and replication without adding anything useful.

questions.prompt: Three different apps write to a shared employees file and each should reject a negative salary. Why is a DBMS CHECK constraint better than validating in each app?
options: CHECK constraints also encrypt the salary column
The rule is enforced centrally for every writer, including new and buggy ones
CHECK constraints run faster than any application code
Applications are not allowed to validate data once a DBMS is used
questions.explanation: An integrity rule declared in the schema applies to every insert and update, whichever app or ad-hoc script sends it. Validating in the app is still good for user feedback, but it can be skipped or implemented inconsistently.

questions.prompt: Support agents should see only tickets for their own region, and never the customers' card_last4 column. Why is this hard with plain files and easier with a DBMS like PostgreSQL?
options: File permissions apply per file, while a DBMS can grant per column and filter rows with row-level security
File systems cannot store more than one region's data in one file
A DBMS encrypts every column automatically so agents can't read it
Files cannot be read by more than one user at a time
questions.explanation: OS permissions are essentially all-or-nothing per file. PostgreSQL supports column-level GRANTs and row-level security policies that filter rows per user. It does not automatically encrypt columns.

questions.prompt: Which file-system problems does a DBMS address by design? Select all that apply.
options: The need to take backups at all
Partial updates left behind after a crash
Lost updates from concurrent writers
Inconsistency caused by uncontrolled redundancy
Reads that are slower than a raw sequential file read
questions.explanation: Central schemas, concurrency control and atomic recovery fix the first three. A DBMS still needs backups (corruption, bad deletes, disasters), and a raw sequential file scan can be faster than going through a DBMS.

questions.prompt: Which are real costs or trade-offs of adopting a DBMS instead of flat files? Select all that apply.
options: Inability to store binary data of any kind
Higher risk of losing committed data on crash
Per-operation overhead that a tiny embedded workload may not need
Operational work such as tuning, upgrades and monitoring
Schema changes that need coordinated migrations
questions.explanation: A DBMS adds operational load, query and transaction overhead, and migration discipline. It can store binary data (e.g. bytea), and durability of committed data after a crash is one of its main strengths, not a weakness.

questions.prompt: SQLite is a DBMS even though it keeps an entire database in a single ordinary file.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: What makes it a DBMS is the software layer: SQL, transactions, constraints and indexing. Where the bytes live doesn't matter. SQLite provides ACID transactions over one file.

questions.prompt: Using a DBMS eliminates all data redundancy.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A DBMS controls redundancy rather than removing it. Indexes, replicas, materialised views and deliberate denormalisation all duplicate data, but the DBMS keeps those copies consistent or managed.

questions.prompt: What are the three levels of the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture?
options: Logical, relational, physical
External, conceptual, internal
Client, server, storage
Presentation, business, data
questions.explanation: External schemas are per-user views, the conceptual schema is the whole logical model (tables, constraints), and the internal schema is physical storage. Presentation/business/data is the three-tier application architecture, a different concept.

questions.prompt: A DBA adds a B-tree index on orders(created_at). No application query changes, but reports run faster. Which property does this show?
options: Logical data independence
Physical data independence
View serializability
Referential integrity
questions.explanation: Indexes belong to the internal (physical) level. Changing them without touching the conceptual schema or queries is physical data independence. Logical independence is about changing the conceptual schema (tables or columns) without breaking external views.

questions.prompt: You split `users` into `users` and `user_profiles`, then create a view named after the old table with the same columns so read queries keep working. Which property does this provide?
options: Physical data independence
Transaction isolation
Logical data independence
Entity integrity
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema changed, and the view (external level) hides the change from applications. That is logical data independence. Physical independence would cover storage changes such as indexes or tablespaces.

questions.prompt: A DBA moves a large table to a tablespace on faster SSDs. Which schema level changes?
options: External
Conceptual
All three levels
Internal
questions.explanation: Where and how data is stored is the internal schema. Table definitions (conceptual) and views (external) are unchanged, so applications don't notice.

questions.prompt: Why is logical data independence generally harder to achieve than physical data independence?
options: Physical changes always require downtime while logical ones don't
Applications depend directly on the logical structure, and views can't hide every change
Only the internal level has a mapping to the level above it
Logical changes are made by developers, who don't use views
questions.explanation: Queries name tables and columns, so removing a column or changing its meaning can break them, and compatibility views may be read-only. Physical changes sit under a stable logical interface. Both levels have mappings.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which object most directly implements an external schema for a reporting team?
options: A view exposing only the columns and rows they need
A B-tree index on the reporting columns
A WAL archive
A tablespace
questions.explanation: External schemas are tailored user views of the data, which SQL views (plus grants) provide. Tablespaces, indexes and WAL are all internal-level storage concerns.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, the compatibility view `users` is defined as a JOIN of `accounts` and `user_profiles`. Old code runs `UPDATE users SET bio = 'x' WHERE id = 1`. What happens?
options: It updates both base tables in one implicit transaction
PostgreSQL rewrites it to update user_profiles automatically
It errors unless you add an INSTEAD OF trigger (or rule) on the view
It silently updates nothing and reports UPDATE 0
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL automatically makes only simple single-table views updatable. A view over a join can't be updated unless an INSTEAD OF trigger tells PostgreSQL how to apply the change. This is a common limit of logical data independence.

questions.prompt: Which changes are internal-level (physical) changes that shouldn't require changing application SQL? Select all that apply.
options: Adding a B-tree index
Dropping a column
Renaming a column
Moving a table to another tablespace
Changing a table's fillfactor
questions.explanation: Indexes, page fill settings and tablespaces only affect storage and access paths. Renaming or dropping a column changes the conceptual schema, and queries that reference it break.

questions.prompt: Which practices help applications survive conceptual-schema changes (better logical data independence)? Select all that apply.
options: Listing columns explicitly instead of SELECT *
Letting several services query each other's tables directly
Giving consumers views or an API instead of raw tables
Expand-and-contract migrations (add new, backfill, then remove old)
Reading result columns by ordinal position
questions.explanation: Explicit columns, stable interfaces and staged migrations keep consumers working while the schema changes. Relying on column positions or sharing tables between services ties every consumer to the current shape of the tables.

questions.prompt: Physical data independence means you can change how data is stored (files, indexes, storage devices) without rewriting application queries.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That is the definition: the conceptual/internal mapping absorbs storage changes, so queries written against tables keep working.

questions.prompt: The conceptual schema describes how records are laid out in pages and blocks on disk.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Page and block layout is the internal schema. The conceptual schema describes entities, attributes, relationships and constraints for the whole database, independent of storage.

questions.prompt: An Employee entity has date_of_birth, and age is always computed from it. In ER terms, what is age?
options: A composite attribute
A derived attribute
A key attribute
A multivalued attribute
questions.explanation: A derived attribute's value is computed from other stored attributes (shown as a dashed ellipse). Composite means it has sub-parts, which age doesn't.

questions.prompt: A Customer's address consists of street, city and pincode. What kind of attribute is address?
options: Multivalued
Simple
Derived
Composite
questions.explanation: A composite attribute can be split into meaningful sub-attributes. It would be multivalued only if a customer could have several addresses.

questions.prompt: A student can have any number of phone numbers. How is this attribute classified, and how is it usually mapped to tables?
options: Derived; computed from the contacts table at query time
Composite; phone1, phone2 and phone3 columns
Simple; one comma-separated text column
Multivalued; a separate student_phones(student_id, phone) table
questions.explanation: Several values of the same attribute per entity is multivalued, and the standard mapping is a child table keyed by (owner id, value). Fixed phone1..3 columns cap the count and leave NULLs.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to add an `age` integer column next to `date_of_birth` in the users table. What is the main problem?
options: Age changes every year, so the stored value goes stale unless something keeps updating it
Integers can't store ages above 127
It creates a composite key that slows down inserts
PostgreSQL forbids two date-related columns in one table
questions.explanation: Storing a derived, time-dependent value creates an inconsistency risk: it's correct only on the day it was written. Compute it at query time (e.g. in a view) from date_of_birth. A PostgreSQL integer easily holds any age.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16 you try `age int GENERATED ALWAYS AS (date_part('year', age(current_date, dob))) STORED`. What happens?
options: It works but is only recomputed when the row is read
It fails because generation expressions must be immutable, and current_date isn't
It fails because generated columns can't be integers
It works and is recomputed automatically every day
questions.explanation: Stored generated columns are computed on write and must use only immutable functions. current_date changes over time, so PostgreSQL rejects it. Compute age in a view or at query time instead.

questions.prompt: Posts store tags as a single text column like 'node,sql,redis'. Finding all posts tagged 'sql' is slow and sometimes matches 'nosql'. What is the underlying modelling mistake?
options: The column needs a CHECK constraint on its length
Tags should be a derived attribute computed from the post body
A multivalued attribute was packed into one non-atomic column instead of a separate table
Tags should be a composite attribute split into tag1, tag2, tag3
questions.explanation: Tags are multivalued. Packing them into a string breaks atomicity, which forces LIKE scans with false matches. A post_tags(post_id, tag_id) table gives exact, indexable lookups. Fixed tag1..3 columns just move the problem.

questions.prompt: Should Department be an attribute of Employee or its own entity, when departments have a budget and a manager and are shared by many employees?
options: An attribute, because each employee belongs to one department
Its own entity, because it has its own attributes and is shared
A derived attribute computed from the manager
A multivalued attribute of Employee
questions.explanation: Once something has properties of its own and many instances refer to it, model it as an entity linked by a relationship. As an attribute, the budget and manager would be repeated on every employee row.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you store a product's multivalued category_ids as an integer[] array instead of a junction table. What is a real trade-off?
options: Arrays are not allowed in tables that have a primary key
A GIN index supports containment queries, but elements can't have foreign key constraints
Arrays are limited to 10 elements per row
Arrays can't be indexed, so every lookup is a full scan
questions.explanation: GIN indexes make queries like `category_ids @> '{5}'` fast, but PostgreSQL has no per-element foreign keys, so deleted categories can leave dangling ids. A junction table keeps referential integrity.

questions.prompt: Which of these are typically derived attributes? Select all that apply.
options: A department's employee count
A person's age, from date of birth
A customer's email address
A product's SKU
An order's total, from its line items
questions.explanation: Totals, ages and counts can be computed from other stored data. Email and SKU are base facts that nothing else determines. Teams sometimes store derived values for speed, but then they must be kept in sync.

questions.prompt: Which designs let you filter customers by city efficiently in PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: A flattened address_city column with a B-tree index
A JSONB address with an expression index on (address->>'city')
One free-text address column queried with LIKE '%Pune%'
A separate addresses table with an indexed city column
questions.explanation: Flattening, normalising and an expression index on JSONB all give an indexable city value. A leading-wildcard LIKE on free text can't use a B-tree index and also matches 'Pune' anywhere in the address, such as street names.

questions.prompt: In Chen notation, a multivalued attribute is drawn as a double ellipse and a derived attribute as a dashed ellipse.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: These are the standard Chen ER conventions. Key attributes are underlined, and composite attributes branch into their component ellipses.

questions.prompt: Students enrol in many courses and each course has many students. How is this relationship represented in tables?
options: A student_id column in courses
A course_id column in students
An array of course ids in students with no constraints
A junction table enrollments(student_id, course_id)
questions.explanation: Many-to-many needs a separate relation whose rows pair one student with one course, with both foreign keys. A single FK column on either side can hold only one value per row.

questions.prompt: "Every employee must belong to a department" is total participation of Employee in WorksIn. How is it usually enforced when employees.dept_id is the FK?
options: Add ON DELETE CASCADE to departments
Make employees.dept_id NOT NULL
Make departments.id a composite key
Add a UNIQUE constraint on employees.dept_id
questions.explanation: Total participation means no employee can exist without a department, so the FK must not be NULL. UNIQUE would wrongly limit each department to one employee.

questions.prompt: Users and passports are 1:1. Every passport belongs to a user, but most users don't have a passport. Where should the foreign key go?
options: A junction table with no constraints
Both tables, each referencing the other
passports.user_id NOT NULL UNIQUE
users.passport_id, nullable
questions.explanation: Putting the FK on the side with total participation avoids NULLs, and UNIQUE keeps it 1:1. A nullable users.passport_id works but leaves NULL on most rows. Mutual FKs complicate inserts and deletes.

questions.prompt: "A supplier supplies a part to a project" relates Supplier, Part and Project together in one fact. What is the degree of this relationship?
options: Unary
Quaternary
Ternary
Binary
questions.explanation: Three entity sets take part in each relationship instance, so it is ternary (degree 3). Degree counts participating entity sets, not cardinality.

questions.prompt: Why can't the ternary Supplies(supplier, part, project) generally be replaced by three binary relationships (supplier–part, part–project, supplier–project)?
options: Three binary tables always use more storage than one ternary table
Binary relationships can't have foreign keys
The binaries lose which supplier supplied which part to which project
ER diagrams don't allow more than two binary relationships per entity
questions.explanation: If S1 supplies P1 (to some project), P1 goes to J1 and S1 supplies J1, it doesn't follow that S1 supplied P1 to J1. Joining the binaries can create spurious combinations. Storage size isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: Each employee may have a manager, who is also an employee. How is this recursive (unary) relationship mapped?
options: A nullable manager_id column in employees referencing employees(id)
A CHECK constraint listing valid manager ids
A composite primary key (id, manager_id)
A separate managers table copying employee columns
questions.explanation: A self-referencing FK models a 1:N recursive relationship. It's nullable because the top manager has none. A copied managers table duplicates people who are both employee and manager.

questions.prompt: Rule: every department must have at least one employee, with FK employees.dept_id → departments.id. How can PostgreSQL enforce this side of the participation?
options: A plain FK can't; use a deferred constraint trigger (or app logic) checked at commit
Make departments.id NOT NULL
Add UNIQUE to employees.dept_id
Add ON DELETE RESTRICT to employees.dept_id
questions.explanation: FKs enforce 'the child points to an existing parent', not 'the parent has at least one child'. You need a check that runs after both rows exist, such as a DEFERRABLE constraint trigger. RESTRICT only stops deleting referenced departments.

questions.prompt: Which of these relationships need their own junction table when mapped to relations? Select all that apply.
options: User–Profile (one-to-one)
User–Orders (one-to-many)
