Students–Courses (many-to-many)
Supplier–Part–Project (ternary)
Actors–Movies (many-to-many)
questions.explanation: M:N and ternary relationships can't fit in one FK column, so they get their own table. 1:N puts the FK on the many side, and 1:1 puts a unique FK on one side.

questions.prompt: The Enrolls relationship has an attribute `grade`. Which statements about placing relationship attributes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: For M:N, it must go in the student table
For 1:N, it can move to the table on the N side
For M:N, the attribute goes in the junction table
For 1:1, it can go in either participating table
questions.explanation: A grade belongs to a (student, course) pair, so in M:N it lives with the pair. In 1:N each N-side row has at most one partner, and in 1:1 either side works. The student table would need one grade column per course.

questions.prompt: A one-to-many relationship is implemented by putting the foreign key in the table on the 'many' side.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each many-side row references its single parent (e.g. orders.user_id). Putting it on the 'one' side would need multiple values per row.

questions.prompt: If an entity has total participation in a relationship, the relationship must be one-to-one.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Participation (must every instance take part?) and cardinality (how many partners?) are independent. Every order must have a customer (total), but a customer can have many orders (1:N).

questions.prompt: What defines a weak entity set?
options: It has no key of its own and is identified by its owner's key plus a partial key
Its rows are deleted automatically after a timeout
It has no attributes other than a foreign key
It participates in only one relationship
questions.explanation: A weak entity depends on an identifying (owner) entity. Its discriminator is unique only within one owner. It can have other attributes; what's missing is a key of its own.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best example of a weak entity?
options: A Room numbered 101, unique only within its Building
A Country identified by its ISO code
A Product identified by a global SKU
A User identified by a UUID
questions.explanation: Room 101 exists in many buildings, so a room is identified only together with its building. The others have globally unique identifiers and are strong entities.

questions.prompt: How do you map the weak entity OrderLine(line_no, qty), owned by Order(id), to a table?
options: order_lines(id SERIAL PK, qty), with line_no stored in orders
order_lines(line_no PK, qty) with no reference to orders
Add line_no and qty columns directly to the orders table
order_lines(order_id FK, line_no, qty) with PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
questions.explanation: The weak entity's key is the owner's key plus its partial key, and the owner FK usually has ON DELETE CASCADE. line_no alone repeats across orders, so it can't be the primary key on its own.

questions.prompt: A designer notices Car and Truck share registration_no, make and model, so creates a Vehicle superclass. What is this process called?
options: Generalization
Specialization
Normalization
Aggregation
questions.explanation: Generalization is bottom-up: common features of existing entity sets are pulled into a superclass. Specialization is top-down: starting from Vehicle and defining subclasses.

questions.prompt: A Person can be both a Student and an Employee at the same university. What constraint applies to this specialization?
options: Weak
Partial and disjoint
Overlapping
Disjoint
questions.explanation: Overlapping means one superclass instance can belong to several subclasses. Disjoint would force each person to be either a student or an employee, not both.

questions.prompt: Payment has subtypes Card and UPI, each with 2–3 extra columns, and most queries list all payments together. Which mapping fits best?
options: One database per subtype
A separate table per subtype with no shared parent table
An EAV table of (payment_id, attribute_name, value)
Single table: payments with a type column and nullable subtype columns
questions.explanation: With few subtype columns and many cross-type queries, one table avoids joins and UNIONs. Use CHECK constraints to tie subtype columns to the type. Per-subtype tables make 'list all payments' a UNION, and EAV loses typing and constraints.

questions.prompt: You map a Vehicle hierarchy as concrete table-per-subclass (cars and trucks tables, no vehicles table). What problem appears when a `rentals` table must reference any vehicle?
options: PostgreSQL limits each database to one table per entity type
A single foreign key can't reference either table, and ids may collide across them
Cars and trucks can't have primary keys
Queries on cars alone become slower than with a single table
questions.explanation: An FK targets exactly one table, so 'any vehicle' needs nullable FKs to both tables or a polymorphic id with no integrity. Separate sequences can also issue the same id twice. A parent vehicles table (class-table mapping) solves this.

questions.prompt: Which statements about weak entities are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It can exist without an owner entity
The weak entity has total participation in its identifying relationship
Its table's primary key includes the owner's primary key
Its partial key (discriminator) is drawn with a dashed underline
It can't have attributes besides the partial key
questions.explanation: A weak entity always needs its owner, the discriminator gets a dashed underline in Chen notation, and the mapped primary key is (owner key, discriminator). It can have any number of other attributes.

questions.prompt: Single-table mapping in PostgreSQL: vehicles(kind, seats, payload_tons, …). Business rule: every vehicle is exactly a car or a truck (total, disjoint). Which constraints help enforce it? Select all that apply.
options: kind NOT NULL with CHECK (kind IN ('car', 'truck'))
A foreign key from a cars table to vehicles
A UNIQUE constraint on the kind column
A CHECK requiring seats only for cars and payload_tons only for trucks
questions.explanation: A non-null discriminator restricted to the two subtypes enforces total and disjoint, and a per-kind CHECK keeps the subtype columns consistent. An FK from cars doesn't force every vehicle to have a subtype, and UNIQUE on kind would allow only one car.

questions.prompt: Specialization is the top-down process of defining subclasses of an entity set based on distinguishing characteristics.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Specialization starts from a general entity (Employee) and defines subclasses (Engineer, Manager). Generalization goes the other way, bottom-up.

questions.prompt: In an overlapping specialization, each superclass instance belongs to at most one subclass.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: 'At most one subclass' describes a disjoint specialization. Overlapping lets an instance belong to several subclasses, such as a person who is both a student and an employee.

questions.prompt: How is a strong entity set with simple attributes mapped to the relational model?
options: A view over the tables of related entities
One table per attribute, joined by a shared id
A table with one column per simple attribute and the entity key as the primary key
A single JSON column holding all attributes
questions.explanation: Each strong entity becomes a relation whose columns are its simple (or flattened composite) attributes, with the key as primary key. One table per attribute is a needlessly fragmented design.

questions.prompt: How is the M:N relationship Authors–Books mapped?
options: book_authors(author_id FK, book_id FK) with PRIMARY KEY (author_id, book_id)
A book_ids text column in authors
Merge authors and books into one table
A nullable author_id column in books
questions.explanation: M:N becomes its own relation with FKs to both sides, and the pair is the key so duplicate links are impossible. A single author_id in books supports only one author per book.

questions.prompt: Customer 1:N Order has a relationship attribute placed_via ('web' or 'app'). Where does placed_via go in the tables?
options: In the orders table, next to customer_id
In a lookup table keyed by customer
In a separate customer_orders junction table only
In the customers table
questions.explanation: In 1:N, each order relates to exactly one customer, so the relationship's attributes move to the N side along with the FK. In the customers table there would be one value per customer instead of one per order.

questions.prompt: Employee has a multivalued attribute skills. What is the standard mapping?
options: A comma-separated skills column
skill1, skill2 and skill3 columns in employees
A skills table with employee_name as primary key
employee_skills(employee_id FK, skill) with PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, skill)
questions.explanation: Each value becomes a row in a child table keyed by owner plus value, which allows any number of skills and prevents duplicates. Numbered columns cap the count and make 'who has SQL?' a multi-column search.

questions.prompt: The ER model shows Order.total as a derived attribute (sum of line items). What is the usual default when mapping to tables?
options: Store it in a separate totals table keyed by total
Don't store it; compute it in queries or a view, and denormalise only if measurements show the need
Represent it as a multivalued attribute table
Always store it as a column updated by the app
questions.explanation: Derived values are normally computed to avoid inconsistency. Storing one is a deliberate denormalisation for performance that then needs triggers or careful updates. Storing it by default invites drift.

questions.prompt: Person and PersonDetails are 1:1 with total participation on both sides, and they are always read together. What mapping is usually best?
options: A junction table linking person and details ids
Two tables with no foreign key, joined on name
Two tables, each with a foreign key to the other
Merge them into a single table
questions.explanation: When every person has exactly one details row and they're read together, a separate table adds a join and mutual-FK insert problems for no benefit. Splitting only makes sense for very wide, rarely read, or differently secured columns.

questions.prompt: A ternary relationship Supplies(supplier, part, project) has the constraint that each (project, part) pair has exactly one supplier. What should the primary key of the supplies table be?
options: (supplier_id)
(supplier_id, part_id, project_id)
(project_id, part_id)
A surrogate id with no other unique constraint
questions.explanation: The constraint says (project, part) determines the supplier, so that pair is the minimal key. Using all three columns would allow two suppliers for the same pair. A bare surrogate id enforces nothing.

questions.prompt: Users can follow other users (M:N recursive relationship). Which table design is correct?
options: follows(follower_id FK→users, followee_id FK→users) with PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
follows(user_id PK, followed_user_id)
A followers int[] column in users with no constraints
A follow_count column in users
questions.explanation: A recursive M:N relationship is still M:N: a junction table with two FKs to the same table, with the pair as key. Optionally add CHECK (follower_id <> followee_id). Making user_id the PK would let each user follow only one person.

questions.prompt: Mapping Student M:N Course with relationship attribute grade. Which columns belong in the enrollments table? Select all that apply.
options: student_name
course_title
grade
course_id (FK to courses)
student_id (FK to students)
questions.explanation: The junction table holds both keys plus attributes of the relationship itself. course_title and student_name describe the entities and already live in their own tables; copying them here causes update anomalies.

questions.prompt: users 1:1 profiles is mapped with a profiles.user_id column, and every profile must belong to a user. Which constraints are needed to enforce this faithfully? Select all that apply.
options: FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
An extra index on users.id
CHECK (user_id > 0)
NOT NULL on profiles.user_id
UNIQUE (or PRIMARY KEY) on profiles.user_id
questions.explanation: The FK makes it reference a real user, UNIQUE stops one user having two profiles (which would make it 1:N), and NOT NULL forces each profile to have an owner. users.id is already indexed as the PK, and a positivity check adds nothing.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you can map an M:N relationship as an integer[] column of foreign ids in one table and still have the database enforce referential integrity for each element.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL has no foreign keys on array elements, so deleted parents leave dangling ids unless you add triggers. A junction table with real FKs is the standard mapping.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. What is the closure A+?
options: {A, B}
{A, B, C}
{A, B, C, D}
questions.explanation: Start with {A}; A → B adds B, B → C adds C, C → D adds D. Closure keeps applying FDs until nothing new is added, so stopping at {A, B} forgets that derived attributes can trigger further FDs.

questions.prompt: With F = {A → B, C → D, AD → E}, what is {A, D}+?
options: {A, B, C, D, E}
{A, D, E}
{A, B, D}
{A, B, D, E}
questions.explanation: From {A, D}: A → B adds B, AD → E adds E. Nothing derives C, so C → D never helps. {A, B, C, D, E} wrongly assumes C can be reached.

questions.prompt: From A → B you conclude AC → BC. Which Armstrong axiom did you use?
options: Augmentation
Transitivity
Reflexivity
Decomposition
questions.explanation: Augmentation says that if X → Y then XZ → YZ for any Z; here Z = C. Transitivity chains X → Y and Y → Z, and decomposition is a derived rule that splits a right-hand side.

questions.prompt: From A → BC you conclude A → B. Which inference rule is this?
options: Augmentation
Union
Decomposition
Pseudotransitivity
questions.explanation: Decomposition (derivable from reflexivity and transitivity) splits a right-hand side: A → BC gives A → B and A → C. Union is the reverse direction, combining A → B and A → C into A → BC.

questions.prompt: F contains only AB → C. Which of these is NOT implied by F?
options: AB → AC
AB → C
ABD → C
A → C
questions.explanation: Knowing A and B together determines C does not mean A alone does; you cannot shrink a left-hand side without other FDs. ABD → C follows by augmentation, and AB → AC by augmentation plus decomposition.

questions.prompt: In an employees table, what does the functional dependency emp_id → dept_id mean?
options: Each dept_id maps to exactly one emp_id
Any two rows with the same emp_id must have the same dept_id
dept_id values are unique across the table
Every department has exactly one employee
questions.explanation: X → Y means rows that agree on X must agree on Y. It says nothing about the reverse direction, so a department can still have many employees (dept_id does not determine emp_id).

questions.prompt: What is a minimal (canonical) cover of F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}?
options: {A → B, B → C}
{AB → C, A → B}
{A → B, A → C, B → C}
{A → BC, B → C}
questions.explanation: Split A → BC into A → B and A → C, and remove the duplicate A → B. AB → C reduces to A → C because A alone determines C. A → C is then redundant through A → B and B → C, leaving {A → B, B → C}.

questions.prompt: A relation instance over (A, B, C) has rows (1, x, p), (1, x, q), (2, y, p). Which FDs does this instance violate? Select all that apply.
options: C → A
A → B
A → C
B → A
B → C
questions.explanation: A = 1 maps to C = p and q, B = x maps to C = p and q, and C = p maps to A = 1 and 2, so those three fail. A → B and B → A hold here. An instance can disprove an FD but never prove it holds for all data.

questions.prompt: Given F = {A → B, B → C}, which FDs can be derived? Select all that apply.
options: AD → CD
C → A
A → C
B → A
AC → B
questions.explanation: A → C by transitivity; AC → B by augmenting A → B with C and decomposing; AD → CD by augmenting A → C with D. Nothing lets you go backwards from C or B to A, so C → A and B → A are not implied.

questions.prompt: An FD X → Y is trivial when Y is a subset of X.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Trivial FDs like AB → A hold in every relation because of reflexivity, so they carry no information about the data. Normal-form definitions care only about non-trivial FDs.

questions.prompt: If X+ contains every attribute of R, then X is a candidate key of R.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: X+ = R makes X a superkey. It is a candidate key only if it is also minimal, meaning no proper subset of X has a closure equal to R.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. What are the candidate keys?
options: {A, B}
questions.explanation: A never appears on a right-hand side, so it must be in every key, and A+ = ABCD, so {A} alone is a key. B+ = BCD misses A, so B is not a key.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E}. What are the candidate keys?
options: {A, C}
{A, B, C}
questions.explanation: A and C never appear on a right-hand side, so every key contains both. {A, C}+ = A, C, B, D, E covers R, so AC is the only candidate key. BC+ = BCDE is missing A. ABC is a superkey but not minimal.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → A}. What are the candidate keys?
options: {A, B, C}
Only {A}
{A, B}
questions.explanation: The FDs form a cycle, so each single attribute determines the other two: A+ = B+ = C+ = ABC. All three are minimal, so there are three candidate keys.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. What are the candidate keys?
options: {A, B}
questions.explanation: B is never on a right-hand side, so it is in every key, and B+ = B. AB+ = ABCD; BC+: C → D, D → A, giving ABCD; BD+: D → A, AB → C, giving ABCD. CD+ = ACD lacks B.

questions.prompt: Why must an attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any FD be part of every candidate key?
options: Because no other attributes can determine it, so it can only be in a closure if it is in the starting set
Because it is always the primary key
Because such attributes are always unique
Because closure algorithms process left-hand sides first
questions.explanation: Closure only adds attributes that appear on some right-hand side. An attribute never on the right can only be in X+ if it is in X, so every key must contain it. This shortcut prunes the search a lot.

questions.prompt: For R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E}, whose only candidate key is {A, C}, which attributes are prime?
options: All five attributes
{A, B, C}
{B, D, E}
{A, C}
questions.explanation: An attribute is prime if it belongs to at least one candidate key. With AC the only key, only A and C are prime. This matters for 3NF, which allows a non-superkey determinant only when the dependent attribute is prime.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) has {A} as its only candidate key. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.explanation: Every superset of a key is a superkey, and here those are the only ones: A plus any subset of {B, C, D}, which is 2^3 = 8. 16 would count every subset of R, including those without A.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}. Which are candidate keys? Select all that apply.
options: {C, D}
{B, C}
{B, D}
questions.explanation: A+: BC, then D, then E, so all. E+: A, so all. BC+: D, then E, then A, so all. CD+: E, then A, then B, so all. Their single-attribute subsets fail (B+ = BD, C+ = C, D+ = D). BD+ = BD never reaches C.

questions.prompt: Which statements about keys are true? Select all that apply.
options: A relation can have several candidate keys
Every candidate key is a superkey
A candidate key can contain a proper subset that is also a superkey
The primary key is one candidate key chosen by the designer
questions.explanation: Candidate keys are minimal superkeys, so none can contain a smaller superkey. A table such as users(id, email) has two candidate keys and you pick one as primary; the other usually becomes a UNIQUE constraint.

questions.prompt: If an attribute appears on the right-hand side of some FD but never on any left-hand side, it is not part of any candidate key.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: If such an attribute X were in key K, then K minus X still reaches every attribute (X is never needed on a left side), including some Y with Y → X, so it also derives X. K would then not be minimal. So X can be left out of every key search.

questions.prompt: Adding any extra attribute to a candidate key produces another candidate key.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Adding an attribute gives a superkey that is no longer minimal, so it is not a candidate key. Minimality is the whole difference between a candidate key and a superkey.

questions.prompt: contacts(id, name, phone_numbers) stores values like '555-0101,555-0102' in phone_numbers. Which normal form does this violate first?
options: 3NF
BCNF
1NF
2NF
questions.explanation: 1NF requires atomic values, with no repeating groups packed into one column. A comma-separated list cannot be indexed, constrained or joined properly. Move phones into a contact_phones(contact_id, phone) table.

questions.prompt: enrollments(student_id, course_id, student_name, grade) has key (student_id, course_id) and student_id → student_name. Which normal form is violated?
options: 3NF only, through a transitive dependency
None; it is in BCNF
1NF, because student_name repeats
2NF, because student_name depends on only part of the key
questions.explanation: A non-prime attribute that depends on a proper subset of a composite key is a partial dependency, which 2NF forbids. Repeated values alone do not break 1NF; 1NF is about atomic values.

questions.prompt: employees(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name) has key emp_id, emp_id → dept_id and dept_id → dept_name. What is the highest normal form it satisfies?
options: 2NF
3NF
1NF only
BCNF
questions.explanation: With a single-attribute key there are no partial dependencies, so it is in 2NF. dept_name depends on the key only through dept_id (a transitive dependency on a non-key attribute), which breaks 3NF.

questions.prompt: teaching(student, course, instructor) has FDs {student, course} → instructor and instructor → course. The keys are (student, course) and (student, instructor). What is its highest normal form?
options: 3NF
1NF
2NF
BCNF
questions.explanation: instructor → course has a determinant that is not a superkey, so BCNF fails. 3NF allows it because course is prime (part of the key (student, course)). This is the classic 3NF-but-not-BCNF example.

questions.prompt: Which kind of relation is always in BCNF, whatever its FDs?
options: Any relation with a surrogate primary key
Any relation with exactly two attributes
Any relation in 3NF with a composite key
Any relation with no NULL values
questions.explanation: With two attributes, every non-trivial FD is A → B or B → A, and its left side is then a key of the two-column relation. A surrogate key does not remove FDs among the other columns, so such tables can still violate 3NF.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares 3NF and BCNF decomposition?
options: BCNF can always preserve dependencies, but 3NF may be lossy
Neither can guarantee a lossless join
3NF can always be lossless and dependency-preserving; BCNF can always be lossless but may lose dependencies
Both can always be made lossless and dependency-preserving
questions.explanation: 3NF synthesis guarantees both properties. BCNF decomposition is always lossless but sometimes has to split an FD across tables (as in the student/course/instructor example), which is the main reason designers sometimes stop at 3NF.

questions.prompt: A table is in 1NF and its primary key is a single column. What can you say about 2NF?
options: It is automatically in 2NF
2NF depends on whether the key is a surrogate
It cannot be in 2NF without a composite key
It is in 2NF only if it has no transitive dependencies
questions.explanation: 2NF forbids non-prime attributes depending on part of a candidate key. A single-column key has no proper non-empty part, so there are no partial dependencies on it, assuming no other composite candidate key. Transitive dependencies are a 3NF matter.

questions.prompt: order_lines(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name, customer_id, customer_city) has key (order_id, product_id) and FDs order_id → customer_id, customer_id → customer_city, product_id → product_name. Which problems exist? Select all that apply.
options: qty's dependency on (order_id, product_id) violates 2NF
product_name depends on part of the key (2NF violation)
customer_city depends on the key only through customer_id (3NF issue)
customer_id depends on part of the key (2NF violation)
questions.explanation: product_id → product_name and order_id → customer_id are partial dependencies, and customer_id → customer_city is transitive. qty depends on the whole key, which is exactly what every normal form wants. Split into orders, customers, products and order_lines.

questions.prompt: Which relations are in BCNF? Select all that apply.
options: R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C (key A)
R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B
R(A, B, C) with A → BC only
R(A, B) with A → B
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every non-trivial FD's left side to be a superkey. In the second relation B → C has non-key B; in the fourth, C → B has non-key C (keys are AB and AC). Two-attribute relations and a single key-based FD are fine.

questions.prompt: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey; 3NF adds an exception for prime dependents. Anything that passes the stricter BCNF test passes 3NF, but not the other way round.

questions.prompt: A relation in 3NF can never contain redundancy caused by functional dependencies.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: 3NF-but-not-BCNF relations still repeat data: in teaching(student, course, instructor) with instructor → course, the instructor-course pairing repeats for every student. Only BCNF removes all FD-based redundancy.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong when a decomposition is lossy?
options: Some original rows can no longer be stored
The fragments take more disk space than the original
Joining the fragments back gives extra (spurious) rows, so the original relation cannot be recovered
Foreign keys between the fragments cannot be declared
questions.explanation: "Lossy" loses information, not rows: the natural join returns a superset of the original with spurious tuples, and you can no longer tell which rows were real. Every original row is still inside the join.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C) has F = {A → B}. Which decomposition is lossless?
options: (A, B) and (A, C)
(A, C) and (B, C)
(A, B) and (C)
(A, B) and (B, C)
questions.explanation: A binary decomposition is lossless if the common attributes form a superkey of one fragment. The fragments share A, and A → B makes A a key of (A, B). Sharing only B or only C determines neither fragment, and no shared attribute gives a cross product.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a decomposition to be dependency-preserving?
options: The join of the fragments reproduces R exactly
Each fragment keeps the original primary key
No FD of R mentions attributes from two fragments
Every FD can be derived from the FDs that hold within individual fragments, so it can be enforced without joins
questions.explanation: Preservation means the union of the projected FDs implies F, so checking each table locally enforces every rule. Reproducing R exactly is losslessness, a separate property.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C) has F = {A → B, B → C} and is decomposed into (A, B) and (A, C). Which is true?
options: Lossy but dependency-preserving
Lossless and dependency-preserving
Lossless but not dependency-preserving
Lossy and not dependency-preserving
questions.explanation: The fragments share A, which is a key of (A, B), so the decomposition is lossless. The projected FDs are A → B and A → C, which do not imply B → C, so that rule now needs a join to check. (A, B) and (B, C) would be both lossless and preserving.

questions.prompt: teaching(student, course, instructor) with instructor → course is decomposed into BCNF as (instructor, course) and (student, instructor). What is the practical consequence?
options: instructor → course is lost
{student, course} → instructor can no longer be enforced by a key on one table; it needs a join-based check or trigger
Both tables need composite foreign keys to each other
The decomposition is lossy, so enrollments are corrupted
questions.explanation: The decomposition is lossless (instructor is a key of the first fragment), but student and course no longer sit in the same table, so "one instructor per student per course" cannot be a simple UNIQUE constraint. instructor → course is preserved in the first fragment.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C) holds the rows (1, x, p) and (2, x, q). It is decomposed into (A, B) and (B, C). How many rows does the natural join of the two fragments return?
questions.explanation: The fragments are {(1, x), (2, x)} and {(x, p), (x, q)}. Joining on B = x pairs every left row with every right row: 2 x 2 = 4, including the spurious rows (1, x, q) and (2, x, p).

questions.prompt: How are losslessness and dependency preservation related?
options: They are independent: a decomposition can have either, both or neither
Dependency preservation implies losslessness
Losslessness implies dependency preservation
They are two names for the same property
questions.explanation: (A, B) and (A, C) under {A → B, B → C} is lossless but not preserving, while (A, B) and (C) under {A → B} preserves A → B but is lossy. Designers want both, and 3NF synthesis guarantees both.

questions.prompt: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, C → D} (key AC). Which decompositions are lossless? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: (A, B)/(A, C, D) share A, a key of (A, B). For the three-way split, join (A, C) with (A, B) on A, then with (C, D) on C, a key of (C, D). Sharing nothing gives a cross product, and sharing only B determines neither fragment.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: 3NF synthesis from a minimal cover always preserves dependencies
Every lossless decomposition preserves dependencies
The standard BCNF decomposition algorithm always produces a lossless decomposition
A decomposition can preserve every FD and still be lossy
questions.explanation: Splitting on a violating X → Y keeps X as a key of one fragment, so the BCNF algorithm is lossless, and 3NF synthesis creates a table per FD, so it preserves them. The two properties are independent, so a lossless split can drop an FD and a preserving split can be lossy.

questions.prompt: Joining the fragments of a lossy decomposition returns fewer rows than the original relation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It returns more rows: every original row is still produced, plus spurious combinations. The information lost is which rows were real, not the rows themselves.

questions.prompt: In a dependency-preserving decomposition, every original FD can be enforced by checking each fragment on its own, without joins.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That is the point of preservation: the projected FDs imply all of F, so local constraints (keys and UNIQUE constraints per table) are enough. Without it, some FD needs a join-based check, usually a trigger.

questions.prompt: enrollments(student_id, course_id, course_title, instructor) repeats a course's instructor on every enrollment. The instructor changes, and a script updates only some rows. Which anomaly is this?
options: Phantom read
Update anomaly
Insert anomaly
Delete anomaly
questions.explanation: A fact stored in many rows must be changed in all of them; missing one leaves contradictory data. A phantom read is a concurrency phenomenon between transactions, not a schema-design anomaly.

questions.prompt: In enrollments(student_id, course_id, course_title, instructor) with key (student_id, course_id), you cannot record a new course until a student enrolls. Which anomaly is this?
options: Delete anomaly
Insert anomaly
Update anomaly
Lost update
questions.explanation: Course facts can only be stored inside an enrollment row, and a NULL student_id is not allowed in the key, so a course with no students cannot be stored. A courses table removes this.

questions.prompt: In the same enrollments table, the last student drops course C42. What else is lost?
options: The course's title and instructor, because they existed only in that row
The primary-key index on the table
The student's other enrollments
Nothing; the course stays in the system catalog
questions.explanation: This is a delete anomaly: removing one fact (an enrollment) also removes an unrelated fact (the course details). The student's other enrollment rows are separate rows and are untouched.

questions.prompt: Which redesign of enrollments(student_id, course_id, course_title, instructor) removes the insert, update and delete anomalies?
options: Add a surrogate id column to enrollments
Store course_title and instructor as a jsonb column in enrollments
Add a UNIQUE index on (course_id, instructor)
courses(course_id, course_title, instructor) plus enrollments(student_id, course_id)
questions.explanation: Course facts depend only on course_id, so they get their own table, stored once. A surrogate key or jsonb leaves the repetition in place, and that unique index would wrongly limit each course to one enrollment row.

questions.prompt: A MongoDB posts collection embeds author.name in each post for fast reads. An author changes their display name. What is the core issue, and the usual mitigation?
options: An update anomaly: copies go stale; either update all posts in a background job and accept a window of inconsistency, or store only author_id and look the name up
An insert anomaly; use $setOnInsert
No anomaly, because MongoDB updates embedded copies automatically
A delete anomaly; use a TTL index
questions.explanation: Embedding duplicates a fact that changes, so a rename must fan out to every copy, which is classic update-anomaly risk. MongoDB has no automatic propagation. Teams accept eventual consistency or reference the author instead.

questions.prompt: In FD terms, what is the root cause of insert, update and delete anomalies?
options: Nullable columns
Using too many indexes
Composite primary keys
Non-trivial FDs whose left-hand side is not a superkey, so one fact repeats across many rows
questions.explanation: If X → Y and X is not a key, the X-to-Y fact repeats on every row with that X value, which causes all three anomalies. BCNF removes exactly these FDs. Composite keys are fine when every FD's left side is a superkey.

questions.prompt: orders stores shipping_email copied from the customer when the order is placed. Later the customer changes their email. Is the old email on past orders an update anomaly?
options: Yes; past orders must be updated to the new email
No; it records a historical fact (where that order was sent), which is a different fact from the customer's current email
Yes; it violates 1NF
No, but only because emails are not part of any key
questions.explanation: Anomalies come from storing the same fact twice. "Email used for this order" is a separate, immutable fact, like a price at purchase time, so copying it is correct modelling. Rewriting it would corrupt order history.

questions.prompt: products(product_id, name, price, supplier_id, supplier_address) repeats supplier data per product. Which observations are symptoms of an update anomaly specifically? Select all that apply.
options: Changing a supplier's address needs an UPDATE touching hundreds of rows
A new supplier cannot be stored until they have a product
Deleting a supplier's last product loses their address
The same supplier shows different addresses on different product rows
questions.explanation: Update anomalies are about changing a repeated fact: inconsistent copies and multi-row updates. Being unable to add a supplier without a product is an insert anomaly, and losing the address with the last product is a delete anomaly.

questions.prompt: Which statements about anomalies and normalization are true? Select all that apply.
options: Normalization trades anomaly-prone writes for more joins on reads
A BCNF schema has no anomalies caused by functional dependencies
Using surrogate keys on every table eliminates update anomalies
A BCNF relation can still have redundancy from multivalued dependencies, which 4NF addresses
questions.explanation: BCNF removes FD redundancy, and independent multi-valued facts (an employee's skills and languages in one table) need 4NF. A surrogate key does not remove FDs among the other columns, so the repetition and its anomalies remain.

questions.prompt: A delete anomaly occurs when removing one fact unintentionally removes another, unrelated fact.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For example, deleting an employee who is the only member of a department also loses the department's name and location when both live in one table.

questions.prompt: Adding a UNIQUE index on the repeated column of a denormalized table fixes its update anomalies.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A repeated value appears in many rows by design, so a UNIQUE index would simply reject valid data. Update anomalies are fixed by storing the fact once (decomposition), not by indexing.

questions.prompt: A feed shows each post's comment count, and COUNT(*) per post is now the top query. Reads outnumber writes 100:1. What is a reasonable denormalization?
options: Drop the comments table's foreign key to speed up inserts
Add posts.comment_count, kept up to date in the same transaction as comment inserts and deletes
Store comments as a jsonb array inside posts
Cache the whole feed page forever in the CDN
questions.explanation: A counter column turns an aggregate into a column read, and updating it in the same transaction keeps it consistent. Embedding all comments makes rows huge and contended, and dropping the FK sacrifices integrity for no read gain.

questions.prompt: After adding posts.comment_count, a viral post gets thousands of comments per second and comment inserts start timing out. What is the most likely cause?
options: Autovacuum is disabled on comments
The comments table needs a larger fillfactor
Every insert UPDATEs the same posts row, so they queue on its row lock
COUNT(*) is still being run on every insert
questions.explanation: A shared counter is a hot row: concurrent transactions serialize on its row lock. Mitigations include sharded counters (N rows summed on read), batching increments asynchronously, or accepting an approximate count.

questions.prompt: A three-table join on PostgreSQL is slow and a teammate proposes copying columns to avoid it. What should you do first?
options: Raise max_connections
Denormalize right away, because joins are always slow
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and check for missing indexes on the join and filter columns
Move the tables to MongoDB
questions.explanation: Most slow joins come from missing foreign-key indexes or bad plans, which are cheap to fix. Denormalization adds lasting consistency costs, so it should follow measurement. More connections do not make one query faster.

questions.prompt: A monthly finance report aggregates 3 years of orders and may be up to a day stale. Which option denormalizes with the least ongoing complexity?
options: Duplicating customer and product columns into orders
A separate read replica running the raw aggregate
A materialized view of monthly totals refreshed nightly
Triggers updating per-month totals on every order write
questions.explanation: A nightly refresh fits the staleness budget, and the database recomputes the whole result, so there is no drift. Triggers add write overhead for freshness nobody needs, and a replica still runs the expensive aggregate each time.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest candidate for denormalization?
options: A password hash copied into a sessions table
A user's current email, read on most pages and changed occasionally
A country name looked up from a 250-row table that never changes, shown on every order list
A rarely read audit field that changes on every request
questions.explanation: Data that is read constantly and practically never changes has almost no consistency cost when copied. Copying mutable data like emails creates update work, copying fast-changing data multiplies writes, and copying secrets widens exposure.

questions.prompt: A chat service copies author_name into each of 50M message rows to avoid a join. What is the main cost when a user renames themselves?
options: Write amplification and a window of inconsistency: every message by that user must be rewritten, usually in a background job
Foreign keys stop working on the copied column
None; the copy is a historical snapshot
The messages table must be locked for the whole rename
questions.explanation: If the UI must show the current name, the copy is a cache of mutable data: renames fan out to many rows, and readers see a mix of old and new until the job finishes. It is only a snapshot if the product wants the name at send time.

questions.prompt: Why are data-warehouse star schemas deliberately denormalized (wide dimension tables)?
options: Workloads are read-heavy scans loaded in batches, so fewer joins matter more than update anomalies
Normalization is impossible for large tables
Warehouses do not support joins
Denormalized tables use less storage
questions.explanation: Analytics queries scan and aggregate, and data arrives through controlled ETL rather than ad-hoc updates, so anomaly risk is low and fewer joins pay off. Denormalized data usually takes more storage, not less.

questions.prompt: Which are legitimate signals to consider denormalizing? Select all that apply.
options: After proper indexing, profiling shows p95 latency dominated by a multi-join on a hot read path
The team feels normal forms are academic
A table has more than 10 columns
Reads vastly outnumber writes for the data you would copy
questions.explanation: Denormalize for measured read bottlenecks where the copied data is read far more often than it changes. Opinion and column counts are not performance evidence.

questions.prompt: Which risks does denormalization introduce? Select all that apply.
options: Harder schema changes, because the same data lives in several places
Lower total storage use
Write amplification, because one logical change touches many rows
Drift between copies when one update path is missed
questions.explanation: Copies must be kept in sync, which costs writes and creates drift and migration risk. Denormalization usually increases storage, since the same values are stored more than once.

questions.prompt: Denormalization generally makes writes faster, because each write touches fewer tables.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Denormalization speeds up reads at the cost of writes: every change to the copied fact must update every copy, often in more rows or more tables. Normalized schemas write each fact once.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED column can only reference columns of the same row, so it cannot maintain a cross-table aggregate like a comment count.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Generation expressions must be immutable and may not use subqueries or other rows. Cross-table aggregates need triggers, application code or a materialized view.

questions.prompt: A social app needs queries like 'friends of my friends who also follow topic X', several hops deep, with low latency. Which database family fits most naturally?
options: Key-value store
Graph database
Time-series database
Wide-column store
questions.explanation: Graph databases store relationships as first-class edges, so each hop costs roughly in proportion to the neighbours visited, not the table size. Key-value and wide-column stores would need many round trips or heavy denormalization for multi-hop traversals.

questions.prompt: An IoT platform stores millions of sensor readings per minute, queries by time range, downsamples old data to hourly averages, and drops raw data after 30 days. Which database family is the most natural fit?
options: Graph database
Time-series database
Key-value cache
Document database
questions.explanation: Time-series databases are built for append-heavy timestamped data, with time-partitioned storage, compression, downsampling and retention policies. A document store can hold the data, but you'd build those features yourself.

questions.prompt: An auth service needs to look up session data by session id on every request, with automatic expiry after 30 minutes. Which store fits best?
options: Key-value store with TTL support, such as Redis
Graph database
Columnar analytics warehouse
Wide-column store with secondary indexes
questions.explanation: This is a single-key lookup with expiry, which is exactly what in-memory key-value stores with TTL do well. A warehouse is built for scans, not millisecond point reads.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce catalog has products whose attributes vary widely by category (laptops have CPU and RAM, shirts have size and fabric) and are read as a whole. Which model fits most naturally?
options: Document database storing each product as one document
Graph database with one node per attribute
Key-value store with one key per attribute
Time-series database
questions.explanation: Documents hold nested, varying attributes per record and return the whole product in one read. One key per attribute turns each product page into many lookups and loses atomic updates of a product.

questions.prompt: Cassandra and similar wide-column stores use LSM trees (commit log, memtable, SSTables, compaction). What is the main trade-off of this design?
options: Reads are always one disk seek, but writes need a global lock
Writes are cheap sequential appends, but reads may have to check several SSTables, and compaction uses background I/O
Writes are slow because every write updates a B-tree in place
Data can't be deleted
questions.explanation: LSM trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted files, which makes writes fast. Reads may merge several files (bloom filters help), and compaction rewrites data in the background. In-place B-tree updates are the opposite design.

questions.prompt: Why does a graph database usually beat a relational database on a 6-hop traversal over a large social graph?
options: Each hop follows stored adjacency directly, instead of an index-backed join whose cost grows with table size
Graph databases keep all data in RAM
Graph databases avoid disk I/O by compressing edges
Relational databases can't express recursive queries
questions.explanation: Graph engines traverse from a node to its neighbours through stored adjacency, so cost tracks the visited subgraph. In SQL each hop is another join (or a recursive CTE iteration) through indexes on large tables. SQL can express it (WITH RECURSIVE), so the second option is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly sets a purpose-built time-series database apart from a general-purpose document store?
options: Support for JSON values
Built-in retention policies, downsampling and time-chunked columnar compression
Horizontal sharding
Secondary indexes
questions.explanation: Automatic retention, continuous aggregates or downsampling, and compression tuned for timestamped series are the defining features. JSON, secondary indexes and sharding exist in many general-purpose stores.

questions.prompt: Which workloads are a good fit for a key-value store? Select all that apply.
options: A shopping cart looked up by user id
Caching rendered pages by URL
Finding all users in a given city with no secondary index
Ad-hoc reports joining orders, customers and products
Per-user rate-limit counters
questions.explanation: Key-value stores excel when every access is by a known key. Ad-hoc joins and lookups by non-key attributes need query flexibility or indexes that a pure key-value store doesn't provide.

questions.prompt: Which statements about wide-column stores such as Cassandra are true? Select all that apply.
options: Querying by a non-key column is as cheap as querying by the partition key
They store data column by column like analytics warehouses, which makes them ideal for large aggregations
Rows within a partition are stored sorted by clustering columns
Joins between tables are not supported by the query language
Tables are usually designed around specific query patterns, often one table per query
questions.explanation: In Cassandra a partition key picks the node and clustering columns order rows within it; there are no joins, so you denormalize per query. 'Wide-column' doesn't mean columnar OLAP storage, and non-key filters need indexes or ALLOW FILTERING scans.

questions.prompt: 'Wide-column' databases like Cassandra are columnar analytics stores in the same category as ClickHouse or Redshift.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Cassandra stores rows grouped by partition key, optimized for high write throughput and key-based reads. Columnar warehouses store each column contiguously for fast scans and aggregations. The names sound alike, but the designs differ.

questions.prompt: A key-value store generally can't efficiently answer 'find all values where field X equals Y' unless you maintain your own index keys for that query.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A pure key-value store only knows keys, so querying by value means a full scan unless you write extra index entries yourself (for example a set per city). That's why access patterns have to be designed up front.

questions.prompt: In MongoDB, a blog post has at most about 10 short comments, always displayed with the post and rarely queried on their own. How should comments be modelled?
options: One collection per post
Embed the comments as an array in the post document
Store comments in a separate collection, joined with $lookup on every read
Store each comment in Redis
questions.explanation: A small, bounded set of children that is always read with the parent is the classic case for embedding: one read and atomic updates. $lookup on every read adds cost for no benefit at this size.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum size of a single BSON document in MongoDB?
options: 16 MB
64 MB
1 MB
4 MB
questions.explanation: MongoDB documents are capped at 16 MB, which limits how much you can embed. Larger files belong in GridFS or object storage, and unbounded child lists belong in their own collection.

questions.prompt: A MongoDB user document embeds an `activity` array, and a new entry is pushed on every page view, forever. What is the problem?
options: MongoDB doesn't allow $push on nested fields
Arrays can't be indexed
Reads of the user become eventually consistent
The array grows without bound: documents bloat, every read loads it, and it can eventually hit the 16 MB limit
questions.explanation: Unbounded arrays are a well-known anti-pattern: document size and write cost keep growing, and the hard limit is eventually reached. Store activity in its own collection (perhaps bucketed by time) that references the user. Arrays can be indexed (multikey).

questions.prompt: An orders collection stores customerId plus a copy of the customer's name and shipping address at order time (the extended reference pattern). Why?
options: The order page renders without a $lookup, and the copy records the address as it was when the order was placed
MongoDB forbids storing references alone
To avoid needing an index on customerId
So that changing a customer's address updates past orders automatically
questions.explanation: Duplicating a few stable or point-in-time fields saves a join on hot reads, and for orders the snapshot is actually correct historically. It does not update automatically; that's the trade-off, and here it's the desired behaviour.

questions.prompt: Every post document embeds the author's name and avatar URL. Authors change avatars occasionally, and some have 50,000 posts. What is the main cost of this design?
options: An avatar change must update every post by that author (a large fan-out write), or older posts show stale data
The 16 MB limit is reached quickly
Posts can't be indexed by author
Reading a post needs a multi-document transaction
questions.explanation: Duplication speeds up reads but turns one profile change into many writes, or forces you to accept staleness. It's fine when changes are rare and slight staleness is acceptable; otherwise reference the author and fetch or cache the profile.

questions.prompt: An order and its line items must be updated together atomically, and they are always read together. Why does embedding the line items in the order document help?
options: Embedding makes reads eventually consistent
MongoDB doesn't support transactions
Single-document writes are atomic, so order and items change together without a multi-document transaction
Embedded arrays are cached in RAM
questions.explanation: Any write to one document is atomic in MongoDB. Embedding data that must change together avoids the extra latency and complexity of a multi-document transaction. MongoDB does support those, so the second option is wrong.

questions.prompt: Each sensor in a MongoDB collection writes one reading per second. The team switches from one document per reading to one document per sensor per hour, holding an array of up to 3,600 readings (the bucket pattern). What do they gain?
options: Automatic downsampling
Strong consistency across shards
Far fewer documents and index entries, with each hour's data read in one fetch
Unlimited document size
questions.explanation: Bucketing groups many small readings into bounded documents, shrinking index size and document overhead and making time-range reads cheap. The bucket is bounded, so it stays far from 16 MB. MongoDB's native time-series collections apply a similar idea internally.

questions.prompt: Which signals suggest REFERENCING a child entity in its own collection rather than embedding it? Select all that apply.
options: The same child is shared by many parents
Children are always read together with the parent
Children are often queried or updated on their own
There are a fixed, small number of children per parent
The number of children can grow without bound
questions.explanation: Unbounded growth, independent access and many-to-many sharing all favour separate documents. Always reading together and small fixed cardinality are the classic reasons to embed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about MongoDB's $lookup stage are true? Select all that apply.
options: Heavy $lookup use on hot read paths can be a sign the schema should embed or denormalize
It is an aggregation pipeline stage
It can be used inside a find() query filter
It performs a left outer join, adding an array of matching documents
An index on the foreign collection's join field makes it much cheaper
questions.explanation: $lookup is an aggregation stage with left-outer-join semantics, and it benefits greatly from an index on foreignField. Frequent joins on hot paths often mean the data model fights the access pattern. It isn't available in find() filters.

questions.prompt: In MongoDB, an update that modifies several fields of one document is atomic even without a transaction.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: MongoDB guarantees atomicity at the single-document level, including embedded arrays and subdocuments. Transactions are only needed when several documents must change together.

questions.prompt: Because MongoDB is schemaless, data modelling decisions like embed versus reference can easily be changed later without migrating existing documents.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The schema is implicit, not absent. Moving from embedded to referenced data (or the reverse) means rewriting existing documents and changing every query that relies on the shape. Model around access patterns from the start.

questions.prompt: In MongoDB, a query is find({ status: 'active', age: { $gt: 30 } }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }). Following the Equality-Sort-Range rule, which compound index is best?
options: { status: 1, age: 1, createdAt: -1 }
{ createdAt: -1, age: 1, status: 1 }
{ age: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }
{ status: 1, createdAt: -1, age: 1 }
questions.explanation: Equality fields first narrow to one index range, the sort field next keeps results in index order (no in-memory sort), and range fields last. Putting age before createdAt would force a blocking sort.

questions.prompt: explain('executionStats') for a slow MongoDB query shows a winning plan stage of COLLSCAN. What does that mean?
options: No suitable index was used, so every document in the collection was scanned
The query ran across all shards
The query used a covered index
The result came from the plan cache
questions.explanation: COLLSCAN means a full collection scan. Compare totalDocsExamined with nReturned and add an index matching the filter and sort. An index scan shows up as IXSCAN.

questions.prompt: A MongoDB collection has the compound index { a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 }. Which query can NOT use it efficiently as a prefix?
options: find({ a: 5 })
find({ a: 5, b: 2 })
find({ b: 2, c: 3 })
questions.explanation: Compound indexes support queries on a leading prefix of their keys: a, then a+b, then a+b+c. A filter on b and c without a can't seek into the index, because entries are ordered by a first.

questions.prompt: An aggregation pipeline starts with $unwind on a large array, then $group, then $match on status. How can it be made much cheaper?
options: Move $match on status to the start so it can use an index and shrink the input before $unwind
Replace $group with $project
Use allowDiskUse to speed it up
Add $sort at the end
questions.explanation: Filtering first lets the pipeline use an index and cuts the documents flowing into the expensive $unwind and $group stages. (The optimizer may move some stages itself, but writing $match early is the reliable rule.) allowDiskUse avoids memory errors; it doesn't speed things up.

questions.prompt: A developer runs a multi-document transaction against a local standalone mongod and gets an error. Why?
options: Transactions only work on documents under 1 MB
Transactions must be enabled per collection
Transactions need MongoDB Atlas
Multi-document transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster; a single-node replica set is enough for development
questions.explanation: MongoDB transactions depend on replica set machinery (the oplog), so a standalone server rejects them. Running mongod as a one-member replica set is the usual dev setup. They work on self-hosted deployments too, not just Atlas.

questions.prompt: A MongoDB transaction fails with an error labelled TransientTransactionError. What should the application do?
options: Retry only the commit
Retry the entire transaction from the start
Treat the data as corrupted and alert
Ignore it, because the transaction committed
questions.explanation: TransientTransactionError (for example a write conflict or a primary step-down) means the whole transaction can safely be re-run. UnknownTransactionCommitResult is the label that calls for retrying just the commit. The driver's withTransaction helper handles both.

questions.prompt: In MongoDB, a team tries to create the compound index { tags: 1, categories: 1 }, where both fields are arrays in the same documents. What happens?
options: MongoDB indexes only the first element of each array
MongoDB refuses to index documents where both fields are arrays ('cannot index parallel arrays')
The index builds normally as a multikey index
The index is created but ignored by the planner
questions.explanation: A compound multikey index may have at most one array-valued field per document, because indexing the cross product of two arrays could explode. Inserting or indexing such documents fails. Use separate indexes, or restructure the data.

questions.prompt: A MongoDB query uses index { email: 1 } with projection { email: 1 }, but explain still shows a FETCH stage. What is the most likely reason?
options: The collection is sharded
email isn't unique
The index is multikey
The projection includes _id by default, and _id isn't in the index, so documents must be fetched
questions.explanation: A covered query needs every projected field to be in the index. _id is returned unless excluded, so use { email: 1, _id: 0 } to get a pure IXSCAN. Uniqueness has nothing to do with coverage.

questions.prompt: Which statements about MongoDB TTL indexes are true? Select all that apply.
options: Documents are deleted at the exact second they expire
A TTL index on a field holding a string like '2025-01-01' expires those documents normally
A background task removes expired documents about every 60 seconds, so documents can outlive their expiry briefly
A TTL index is a single-field index on a date field with expireAfterSeconds
questions.explanation: TTL deletion runs periodically, roughly every minute, and can lag under load, so don't rely on exact timing. The field must be a BSON Date (or an array of Dates); documents with strings or other types in it never expire.

questions.prompt: Which statements about MongoDB multi-document transactions are true? Select all that apply.
options: They add overhead, so modelling data to need only single-document atomicity is still preferred where practical
They have no time limit by default
They work on a standalone mongod
Writes inside the transaction aren't visible outside it until it commits
Reads inside a transaction see a consistent snapshot
questions.explanation: Transactions provide snapshot reads and all-or-nothing visibility, but they cost latency and resources, so MongoDB recommends schemas that mostly need single-document atomicity. They need a replica set or sharded cluster and abort after transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds (60s by default).

questions.prompt: In MongoDB, the index { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 } can serve find({ userId: 7 }).sort({ createdAt: 1 }) without an in-memory sort.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With equality on userId, the matching entries are ordered by createdAt descending, and MongoDB can walk the index backwards to get ascending order. Indexes can be traversed in either direction.

questions.prompt: A game needs a real-time leaderboard with 'top 10 players' and 'what is my rank?' queries. Which Redis data structure fits?
options: List
Sorted set (ZADD, ZREVRANGE, ZREVRANK)
Set
Hash
questions.explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score, with O(log N) updates and fast range and rank queries. A plain set has no ordering, and a list would need a full re-sort on every score change.

questions.prompt: Why are concurrent INCR calls on the same Redis key safe without extra locking?
options: Redis runs each command atomically, executing commands one at a time on its main thread
Redis takes a row lock per key
Redis serializes keys to disk first
INCR uses compare-and-swap retries in the client
questions.explanation: Commands execute one at a time on the main thread (I/O threads in Redis 6+ only handle network reads and writes), so each command is atomic. A client-side GET-then-SET would not be atomic, because other commands can run in between.

questions.prompt: A fixed-window rate limiter runs INCR key and then, if the result is 1, sends EXPIRE key 60 as a separate command. What is the bug?
options: The limit check should come before INCR
INCR isn't atomic
If the process dies between INCR and EXPIRE, the key never expires and the user is blocked forever
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero
questions.explanation: The two calls aren't atomic together. A crash or timeout after INCR leaves a counter with no TTL. Use a Lua script, a MULTI block, or SET key 0 EX 60 NX followed by INCR, so the TTL is always set.

questions.prompt: A Redis lock is acquired with SET lock:job <random-token> NX PX 30000. Why release it with a Lua script that deletes the key only if its value equals your token, instead of a plain DEL?
options: Lua scripts make the lock survive restarts
DEL can't delete keys with a TTL
If your lock already expired and another client took it, a plain DEL would delete THEIR lock
DEL is slower than Lua
questions.explanation: A long GC pause or slow job can outlive the TTL. Checking the token atomically ensures you only release a lock you still own. Even then, protect critical resources with fencing tokens, because expiry-based locks can't stop a paused holder from acting late.

questions.prompt: An admin script runs KEYS user:* on a production Redis with 50 million keys, and latency spikes for every client. Why, and what should it use?
options: KEYS is O(N) and blocks the single command thread until it finishes; use SCAN with MATCH to iterate incrementally
KEYS flushes the cache; use FLUSHDB instead
KEYS only works on replicas; use MONITOR
KEYS forces an AOF rewrite; use INFO instead
questions.explanation: KEYS walks the whole keyspace in one blocking command, stalling everything else. SCAN returns a cursor and small batches, so other commands run in between, at the cost of possibly seeing keys more than once.

questions.prompt: A Node service caches a hot product in Redis with a 60s TTL. Every 60s, latency spikes as thousands of requests miss at once and all query PostgreSQL. Which mitigation directly targets this?
options: Switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lru
Increase the TTL to 24 hours with no other change
Let only one request rebuild the value (a lock or single-flight) while others serve the stale value, and add TTL jitter or early refresh
Raise maxmemory
questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede. Coalescing rebuilds to one caller and refreshing before expiry stop the herd; jitter avoids synchronized expiries across keys. A longer TTL only makes the stampedes rarer and the data staler; memory settings don't help.

questions.prompt: A notification service must not lose events if a consumer is down for a few minutes, and several workers should share the load. Why choose Redis Streams over Pub/Sub?
options: Pub/Sub messages expire after one second
Pub/Sub can't deliver to more than one subscriber
Streams store messages and support consumer groups with acknowledgements (XACK) and pending-entry tracking; Pub/Sub drops messages for subscribers that aren't connected
Streams are faster than Pub/Sub for every workload
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: offline subscribers miss messages. Streams append to a log that consumers read from by ID, and consumer groups split work and track unacknowledged entries for redelivery. Pub/Sub does fan out to many subscribers.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Redis maxmemory-policy are true? Select all that apply.
options: The default policy is allkeys-lru
Under noeviction, write commands that need more memory return errors once the limit is reached
allkeys-lfu evicts the least frequently used keys across the whole keyspace
volatile-* policies only consider keys that have a TTL
questions.explanation: The default is noeviction, which is a common surprise when Redis is used as a cache and writes start failing. Set allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache. volatile-* policies ignore keys without TTLs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Redis persistence are true? Select all that apply.
options: AOF with appendfsync everysec can lose about one second of writes on a crash
appendfsync always is the most durable AOF setting and the slowest
With RDB snapshots only, a crash can lose all writes since the last snapshot
Taking an RDB snapshot has no cost regardless of dataset size
questions.explanation: Durability depends on configuration: RDB is point-in-time, AOF everysec risks about one second, and always fsyncs every write. RDB snapshots fork the process, and copy-on-write can use a lot of extra memory and latency on large, write-heavy datasets.

questions.prompt: If one command inside a Redis MULTI/EXEC block fails at runtime (for example INCR on a string value), Redis rolls back the commands that already ran in that block.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Redis transactions guarantee the commands run together without interleaving, but there is no rollback. A failing command returns an error and the others still apply. Only queue-time errors, such as syntax errors, abort the whole EXEC.

questions.prompt: A Redis HyperLogLog can estimate the number of unique visitors using a small, fixed amount of memory per key, at the cost of a small approximation error.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog uses at most about 12 KB per key, with a standard error around 0.81%, regardless of how many items are added. A Set gives exact counts, but its memory grows with every unique member.

questions.prompt: In DynamoDB (or Cassandra), what do the partition key and the sort key (clustering key) each do?
options: Both are hashed together to choose a node
The sort key chooses the node; the partition key orders items
The partition key decides which partition stores the item; the sort key orders items within that partition and enables range queries
The partition key must be unique per table; the sort key is optional metadata
questions.explanation: The partition key is hashed to place data, and all items with that key live together, ordered by sort key. That makes 'all orders for customer X between dates A and B' a single efficient query. The partition key alone doesn't have to be unique when a sort key exists.

questions.prompt: In DynamoDB, what is the key difference between Query and Scan?
options: Query needs an equality condition on the partition key and reads only that partition; Scan reads the entire table
Scan is faster because it reads in parallel
They cost the same, but Scan supports filters
Query can only return one item
questions.explanation: Query targets one partition key value (optionally a sort-key range), so its cost scales with the result. Scan reads every item and consumes capacity for all of them, even ones a filter later drops. Parallel scan only spreads that cost out.

questions.prompt: An events table in DynamoDB uses the current date ('2025-10-03') as its partition key. Under heavy write load, requests are throttled even though table capacity looks ample. Why, and what is a common fix?
options: Sort keys are missing; add one
Dates aren't valid partition keys; use numbers
DynamoDB limits tables to one write per second per day
All of today's writes hit one partition (a hot partition); add a random or computed suffix (write sharding) or use a higher-cardinality key
questions.explanation: Throughput is limited per partition, so a low-cardinality key that funnels all writes to one value hits that partition's limit. Spreading writes across date#0 to date#N, and querying all suffixes when reading, distributes the load.

questions.prompt: A single-table DynamoDB design stores items like PK='CUSTOMER#123', SK='ORDER#2025-10-01#987'. How do you fetch all orders for customer 123, newest first?
options: GetItem with PK only
Scan with a filter on PK
Query SK = 'ORDER#' across all partitions
Query PK = 'CUSTOMER#123' AND begins_with(SK, 'ORDER#'), with ScanIndexForward = false
questions.explanation: Putting the date in the sort key keeps orders sorted by date within the customer's partition, and ScanIndexForward=false reverses the order. GetItem needs the full primary key, and a key condition always requires partition-key equality.

questions.prompt: In DynamoDB, you need 'all orders with status = SHIPPED', but the table's partition key is customerId. What is the idiomatic approach?
options: Change the table's partition key in place
Create a local secondary index on status after the table exists
Create a global secondary index (GSI) keyed on status (sharded if it's low cardinality), knowing that GSI reads are eventually consistent
Scan the table with a FilterExpression
questions.explanation: A GSI re-partitions the data by another attribute and can be added at any time; it's updated asynchronously. LSIs must be defined at table creation and keep the same partition key, and a table's primary key can't be changed in place. A low-cardinality key like status can itself become hot, so it may need sharding.

questions.prompt: In Cassandra, a query filters on a column that isn't part of the primary key, and the server refuses unless ALLOW FILTERING is added. What is the right fix for a frequent production query?
options: Create another table, partitioned by that column, holding a denormalized copy of the data the query needs
Run the query at consistency level ALL
Raise the read timeout
Add ALLOW FILTERING, which is just a performance hint
questions.explanation: ALLOW FILTERING makes Cassandra scan many partitions and discard rows, which gets slower as data grows. The Cassandra way is query-first modelling: one table per access pattern, written together (for example with a logged batch). Consistency level doesn't change how much is scanned.

questions.prompt: A Cassandra table uses PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, ts), and sensors report every second for years. Reads and compaction for old sensors get slower and slower. What is the problem, and the usual fix?
options: Increase the replication factor
Cassandra can't store timestamps; use bigint
ts should be the partition key
Partitions grow without bound; bucket the partition key by time, for example PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)
questions.explanation: Every reading for a sensor lands in one partition, which keeps growing. Huge partitions hurt reads, repairs and compaction. A compound partition key with a time bucket bounds partition size, and queries then hit one bucket per day. Making ts the partition key would scatter related rows and break range scans.

questions.prompt: Which statements about DynamoDB secondary indexes are true? Select all that apply.
options: A global secondary index (GSI) supports strongly consistent reads
An LSI uses the same partition key as the base table, with a different sort key
A GSI can only be created when the table is created
A GSI can use a different partition key from the base table
A local secondary index (LSI) must be defined when the table is created
questions.explanation: LSIs share the base partition key, must be declared at table creation, and allow strongly consistent reads. GSIs choose any key, can be added or removed later, and only offer eventually consistent reads.

questions.prompt: A Cassandra keyspace has replication factor 3. Which statements about consistency levels are true? Select all that apply.
options: QUORUM writes plus QUORUM reads always overlap on at least one replica (2 + 2 > 3)
ONE writes plus QUORUM reads guarantee reading the latest write
ONE writes plus ONE reads can return stale data
Writes at ALL fail if any one replica is down
questions.explanation: The R + W > N rule guarantees overlap: 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, but 1 + 2 = 3 isn't greater than 3, so a QUORUM read can miss the single replica that took the write. ALL needs every replica, so it trades availability for consistency.

questions.prompt: In DynamoDB, a FilterExpression on a Query reduces the read capacity consumed, because filtered-out items are never read.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Filters are applied after items are read, so you pay for everything the key condition matched. To read less, push the condition into the key (a sort-key condition) or use an index.

questions.prompt: A DynamoDB item can be at most 400 KB, so large blobs are usually stored in S3 with a pointer kept in the item.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: DynamoDB's item size limit is 400 KB, counting attribute names and values. Storing large payloads in object storage and keeping metadata plus the S3 key in DynamoDB is the standard pattern.

questions.prompt: A fintech ledger needs multi-row transactions, foreign keys, CHECK constraints and ad-hoc reporting by finance analysts. Which default choice is strongest?
options: A graph database
DynamoDB with single-table design
A relational database such as PostgreSQL
Redis with AOF persistence
questions.explanation: Strong invariants, multi-entity atomicity and flexible SQL reporting are exactly where relational databases shine. DynamoDB can do transactions, but ad-hoc analytics and constraint enforcement would mostly be on you.

questions.prompt: A service has a few well-known access patterns (get by key, list by owner), needs predictable single-digit-millisecond latency at very large scale, and the team wants minimal operations work. What fits best?
options: A managed key-value or document store such as DynamoDB, modelled around those access patterns
A columnar data warehouse
A single PostgreSQL instance
A graph database
questions.explanation: Known patterns plus massive scale plus low operations work is DynamoDB's sweet spot. A single PostgreSQL node may also work at moderate scale, but horizontal scaling and operations become your problem at very large scale. Warehouses aren't built for low-latency point reads.

questions.prompt: An early-stage startup's data is relational (users, teams, projects, permissions), and its query needs change weekly. Some entities have flexible custom fields. What's the pragmatic choice?
options: Cassandra, to be ready for scale
One MongoDB collection per entity, joined with $lookup everywhere
Redis as the primary database
PostgreSQL, with JSONB columns for the flexible custom fields
questions.explanation: When access patterns are unknown and the data is relational, SQL's ad-hoc queries and constraints keep options open, and JSONB (indexable with GIN) covers the flexible parts. Cassandra needs query patterns fixed up front, which works against fast-changing requirements.

questions.prompt: A teammate argues for MongoDB 'because we won't need schema migrations'. What is the strongest counterpoint?
options: MongoDB requires DDL for every collection
MongoDB can't add fields to existing documents
The schema still exists in application code; changing document shapes still needs code that handles old and new shapes, or a backfill
Schemaless databases forbid indexes
questions.explanation: 'Schemaless' means schema-on-read: the database won't stop shape drift, so the app must handle every version or you migrate data anyway. MongoDB can enforce structure with JSON Schema validation if you want it.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL products table has a JSONB attrs column, and queries like WHERE attrs @> '{"color": "red"}' are slow. What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Move attrs to a separate MongoDB database
Cast attrs to text and use LIKE
Create a B-tree index on attrs
Create a GIN index on attrs
questions.explanation: GIN indexes support JSONB containment (@>) and key-existence operators. A B-tree on the whole JSONB value only helps equality on the entire document. This is a common reason PostgreSQL can cover document-style needs.

questions.prompt: In a design interview you're storing billions of chat messages, almost always read as 'latest N messages in conversation C', with very high write volume. Which data model fits best?
options: A graph database with one edge per message
Redis lists as the system of record
