questions.prompt: Bitmap indexes are usually a poor fit for unique columns such as a primary key, because each distinct value would need its own almost-empty bitmap.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With n distinct values you'd have n bitmaps, each with a single set bit. Compression helps, but a B-tree is the natural structure for unique keys.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL supports CREATE INDEX ... USING bitmap to create persistent bitmap indexes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's built-in index types are btree, hash, gist, spgist, gin and brin. Its 'bitmap' plans are built at query time from those indexes. Persistent bitmap indexes exist in engines like Oracle.

questions.prompt: What is a partial index?
options: An index on only the first few characters of a text column
An index that only includes rows matching a WHERE predicate given at creation
An index on some, but not all, partitions of a table
An index that is only partly loaded into memory
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX ... WHERE predicate indexes only the qualifying rows, so it is smaller and cheaper to maintain. A prefix index (MySQL's col(10)) is a different feature.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you create CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)). Which query can use it?
options: WHERE upper(email) = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM'
WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'
WHERE email = 'ana@example.com'
WHERE email ILIKE 'ana@example.com'
questions.explanation: An expression index is only used when the query contains the same expression. Plain email, ILIKE and upper(email) are different expressions, so the planner can't match them to lower(email).

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'. Which query can use this index?
options: WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
WHERE status IN ('pending', 'paid') AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
WHERE status <> 'paid' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
questions.explanation: The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE implies the index predicate. Only status = 'pending' guarantees that; the other queries may need rows the index doesn't contain.

questions.prompt: A users table uses soft deletes (deleted_at). Emails must be unique among active users only, so a deleted email can be registered again. Which PostgreSQL index enforces this?
options: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email, deleted_at)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
CREATE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email)
questions.explanation: A unique partial index enforces uniqueness only among rows matching its predicate, i.e. active users. (email, deleted_at) doesn't work: NULLs are distinct by default, so two active rows with the same email would both be allowed.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a query runs as a prepared statement: WHERE status = $1 AND created_at > $2. A partial index exists WHERE status = 'pending'. When a generic plan is used, the index is never chosen, even for $1 = 'pending'. Why?
options: Prepared statements always use sequential scans
The statistics for partial indexes are only read for literal queries
Partial indexes are disabled for prepared statements
Generic plans are made without parameter values, so the planner can't prove the query matches the index predicate
questions.explanation: Predicate matching happens at plan time. A generic plan has to work for any $1, so it can't assume status = 'pending'. Custom plans (with values known) can use the index, or you can put the literal in the SQL.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX ON events ((created_at::date)) fails when created_at is timestamptz. Why?
options: The expression needs an extra pair of parentheses
Converting timestamptz to date depends on the TimeZone setting, so the expression isn't IMMUTABLE
Expression indexes can't contain casts
date columns can't be indexed with a B-tree
questions.explanation: Index expressions must give the same result for the same input forever. The calendar date of a timestamptz depends on the session time zone, so the cast is only STABLE. A fixed zone, as in (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date, is immutable.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL you create CREATE INDEX ON docs ((data->>'customerId')) on a jsonb column. Which query can use it?
options: WHERE data->>'customerId' = '42'
WHERE data @> '{"customerId": "42"}'
WHERE data ? 'customerId'
WHERE data->'customerId' = '42'::jsonb
questions.explanation: A B-tree expression index matches only the exact expression data->>'customerId'. Containment (@>) and key-exists (?) need a GIN index, and data->'customerId' returns jsonb, which is a different expression from ->> (text).

questions.prompt: What are benefits of a partial index compared with a full index on the same columns? Select all that apply.
options: It is smaller, so more of it stays cached
Rows outside the predicate add no index maintenance on write
It can enforce uniqueness within just a subset of rows
Any query on the indexed columns can use it, whatever its WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Indexing only the interesting subset cuts size and write cost and allows per-subset uniqueness. A partial index can only be used when the query's WHERE implies the index predicate.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, given CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)), which queries can use the index? Select all that apply.
options: WHERE lower(email) IN ('ana@example.com', 'bo@example.com')
WHERE upper(email) = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM'
WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'
WHERE email = 'Ana@Example.com'
questions.explanation: Both equality and IN (= ANY) on the same expression match the index. Plain email or upper(email) are different expressions; the planner won't infer that they relate to lower(email).

questions.prompt: A partial index can only be used by a query whose WHERE clause implies the index's predicate.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Otherwise the query might need rows the index doesn't contain, and the results would be wrong. PostgreSQL proves the implication at plan time from the query text.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, an expression index on lower(email) is used automatically for WHERE email ILIKE 'ana@example.com'.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: ILIKE is a different operator on a different expression, so the planner can't match it to lower(email). Rewrite the query as lower(email) = lower($1), or use the citext type.

questions.prompt: A transfer debits account A and credits account B in one transaction. The server crashes after the debit but before COMMIT. Which ACID property guarantees A isn't left debited after recovery?
options: Isolation
Consistency
Atomicity
Durability
questions.explanation: Atomicity means all or nothing: an uncommitted transaction's effects are discarded on recovery. Durability protects committed work, which this transfer never reached.

questions.prompt: How do most relational databases make committed transactions durable without writing every modified data page at commit time?
options: They flush the write-ahead log (WAL) to disk at commit and replay it after a crash
They write each change to two tables at once
They rely on the OS to write pages eventually
They keep committed data in memory until the next restart
questions.explanation: Appending a compact WAL record and fsyncing it is cheap and sequential. After a crash, replaying the log rebuilds any data pages that hadn't been written yet. Relying on the OS without fsync can lose committed data.

questions.prompt: Which ACID property depends most on the application, rather than being provided entirely by the database?
options: Isolation
Durability
Atomicity
Consistency
questions.explanation: The database enforces declared constraints, but business invariants (e.g. 'stock never goes negative across orders') are only kept if the application's transactions are written correctly. Atomicity, isolation and durability are engine mechanisms.

questions.prompt: What does the Isolation property promise in its strongest form?
options: A transaction's changes are invisible forever until a DBA approves them
No two transactions can ever read the same row
Each transaction runs on its own server
Concurrent transactions produce the same result as if they had run one at a time in some order
questions.explanation: Full isolation is serializability. Weaker levels such as READ COMMITTED trade some anomalies for concurrency. Isolation doesn't stop concurrent reads of the same row.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a team sets synchronous_commit = off to speed up writes. Which guarantee have they weakened?
options: Isolation: other sessions can see uncommitted data
Atomicity: transactions may now be partially applied
Consistency: constraints are no longer checked
Durability: a crash can lose the most recent commits, but the database stays consistent
questions.explanation: COMMIT returns before the WAL is flushed, so a crash can lose a short window of acknowledged transactions. There is no corruption or partial transaction, so atomicity, consistency and isolation are intact.

questions.prompt: How does PostgreSQL undo the rows inserted by a transaction that aborts?
options: It keeps inserted rows in a temporary table until COMMIT
It rewrites the affected pages from a backup copy
It replays an undo log that deletes each inserted row
It marks the transaction as aborted in the commit log, so its row versions are invisible; VACUUM removes them later
questions.explanation: With MVCC, row visibility depends on whether the creating transaction committed. Rollback just records the abort, which is instant; the dead tuples are cleaned up later. InnoDB, by contrast, uses undo logs.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this node-postgres transaction code?
options: COMMIT must be sent before the UPDATEs
balance - 100 isn't valid SQL
pool.query may use a different connection for each call, so the statements aren't in one transaction
UPDATE statements can't run inside BEGIN/COMMIT
questions.explanation: A transaction belongs to a single connection. Each pool.query can check out a different client, so BEGIN and the UPDATEs may land on different sessions. Use const client = await pool.connect() and run all statements on that client, releasing it in finally.

questions.prompt: Which practices provide durability for committed transactions? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledging the commit once changes are in the in-memory buffer pool
Writing with the OS but never calling fsync
Flushing the WAL to disk before acknowledging the commit
Waiting for a synchronous standby to confirm before acknowledging
questions.explanation: Durability needs the commit to survive a crash before the client is told it succeeded: a flushed log, or a confirmed copy on another machine. Memory and unsynced OS buffers are lost on a crash or power failure.

questions.prompt: A money transfer is implemented as two separate autocommit UPDATE statements (debit, then credit). Which failures can leave money missing? Select all that apply.
options: The application crashes between the two statements
The connection drops after the debit
The credit fails a CHECK constraint after the debit has committed
Both statements succeed
questions.explanation: In autocommit mode each statement commits on its own, so any failure after the first leaves the debit applied. Wrapping both in one transaction makes them atomic. If both succeed, the transfer is complete.

questions.prompt: Atomicity is the ACID property that stops other transactions from seeing a transaction's partial results while it runs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Hiding intermediate state from concurrent transactions is Isolation. Atomicity is about the final outcome: all of the transaction's changes apply, or none do.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, if a statement inside a transaction block fails, the transaction becomes aborted and later statements are rejected until ROLLBACK, unless a savepoint is used.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL reports 'current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block'. Rolling back to a SAVEPOINT recovers from the error without abandoning the whole transaction.

questions.prompt: What is a serial schedule?
options: One that is equivalent to some serial order
One where transactions run in order of their IDs
One where every transaction runs completely before the next begins, with no interleaving
One where only reads are interleaved
questions.explanation: Serial means no interleaving at all. A schedule that is merely equivalent to a serial one is called serializable, which is the useful concurrency target.

questions.prompt: What makes an interleaved schedule serializable?
options: No two transactions touch the same data item
Its effect is equivalent to some serial execution of the same transactions
It runs under READ COMMITTED
Its transactions all commit successfully
questions.explanation: Serializability is defined by equivalence to some serial order. Transactions can share data and still be serializable, and committing successfully says nothing about equivalence.

questions.prompt: Which pair of operations conflicts?
options: W1(A) and W2(B)
R1(A) and W2(A)
R1(A) and W1(A)
R1(A) and R2(A)
questions.explanation: Operations conflict when they come from different transactions, touch the same item, and at least one is a write. Two reads never conflict, different items don't conflict, and operations of the same transaction aren't counted as conflicts.

questions.prompt: Is the schedule R1(A), R2(A), W1(A), W2(A) conflict-serializable?
options: No, it has conflicts in both directions (T1 before T2 and T2 before T1), which form a cycle
No, because two transactions read A at the same time
Yes, it is equivalent to T2 then T1
Yes, it is equivalent to T1 then T2
questions.explanation: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2; R2(A) before W1(A) gives T2 → T1. That cycle means no serial order matches. This is the classic lost-update interleaving. Concurrent reads alone are harmless.

questions.prompt: How should the schedule R1(A), W2(A), W1(A), W3(A) be classified?
options: View-serializable but not conflict-serializable
Conflict-serializable but not view-serializable
Neither conflict- nor view-serializable
Conflict-serializable and view-serializable
questions.explanation: Conflicts R1(A)→W2(A) and W2(A)→W1(A) form a cycle, so it isn't conflict-serializable. It is view-equivalent to T1, T2, T3: T1 reads the initial A and T3 writes the final A. Blind writes make this possible. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable, so the last option can't happen.

questions.prompt: Why do databases use conflict serializability, rather than view serializability, as their practical correctness target?
options: View serializability only applies to read-only transactions
Conflict serializability accepts strictly more schedules
Testing view serializability is NP-complete, while conflict serializability can be checked or guaranteed cheaply (e.g. with precedence graphs or 2PL)
View serializability allows dirty reads
questions.explanation: View serializability accepts a few more schedules (those with blind writes), but deciding it is NP-complete. Conflict serializability is a slightly stricter but cheaply enforceable subset. It accepts fewer schedules, not more.

questions.prompt: How many distinct serial schedules exist for 3 transactions?
questions.explanation: A serial schedule is an ordering of whole transactions, so there are 3! = 6. A serializable schedule only needs to match one of them.

questions.prompt: Which statements about schedules are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Every conflict-serializable schedule is also view-serializable
Every serial schedule is conflict-serializable
A schedule that interleaves operations can never be serializable
Every view-serializable schedule is also conflict-serializable
questions.explanation: Conflict serializability is a subset of view serializability, and serial schedules trivially satisfy both. The reverse inclusion fails (blind writes), and interleaved schedules are often serializable; that's the point of concurrency control.

questions.prompt: Which pairs of adjacent operations from different transactions can be swapped without changing the schedule's conflict equivalence? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Non-conflicting pairs (two reads, or operations on different items) can be swapped. A write followed by a read or write on the same item changes what is read or what the final value is, so those can't be reordered.

questions.prompt: A serializable schedule must produce the same result as running the transactions serially in the order they started.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Equivalence to any serial order is enough, not specifically start order. Requiring real-time order is a stronger property (strict serializability).

questions.prompt: Two schedules are conflict-equivalent if one can be turned into the other by repeatedly swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Such swaps preserve the order of every conflicting pair, which is exactly what conflict equivalence requires. A schedule is conflict-serializable if swaps can turn it into a serial schedule.

questions.prompt: In a precedence (serialization) graph, when is there an edge Ti → Tj?
options: When Tj commits before Ti
When Ti started before Tj
When an operation of Ti conflicts with, and comes before, an operation of Tj
When Ti and Tj read the same item
questions.explanation: Nodes are transactions and edges record the order of conflicting operations. Start time and commit order don't create edges, and two reads don't conflict.

questions.prompt: When is a schedule conflict-serializable, according to its precedence graph?
options: When every node has at most one outgoing edge
When the graph has no edges
When the graph is fully connected
When the graph is acyclic
questions.explanation: Acyclic means the conflict order can be laid out as a single sequence (a topological order). The graph can have plenty of edges; only cycles break serializability.

questions.prompt: In a schedule, W1(A) is followed later by R2(A). Which edge does this add to the precedence graph?
options: Edges in both directions
No edge, because a read is involved
T2 → T1
T1 → T2
questions.explanation: The conflicting operation of T1 comes first, so the edge points from T1 to T2: T2 must come after T1 in any equivalent serial order. Write-read pairs do conflict.

questions.prompt: Is the schedule R1(A), W2(A), R3(B), W1(B), R2(C), W3(C) conflict-serializable?
options: Yes, equivalent to T3, T1, T2
No: T1 and T3 both access B
Yes, equivalent to T1, T2, T3
No: the edges T1 → T2, T3 → T1 and T2 → T3 form a cycle
questions.explanation: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2; R3(B) before W1(B) gives T3 → T1; R2(C) before W3(C) gives T2 → T3. T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 is a cycle. Accessing the same item is fine; the cycle is what matters.

questions.prompt: A precedence graph has the edges T2 → T1, T2 → T3 and T3 → T1. Which serial order is equivalent?
questions.explanation: Topologically sort: T2 has no incoming edges so it goes first, then T3 (which must precede T1), then T1. T2, T1, T3 violates T3 → T1.

questions.prompt: A precedence graph contains a cycle. What can you conclude?
options: The schedule is not serializable in any sense
The schedule will deadlock
The schedule is not conflict-serializable, but it might still be view-serializable
One transaction must have aborted
questions.explanation: A cycle rules out conflict serializability only. Schedules with blind writes can be view-serializable despite a cycle. A precedence graph is not a wait-for graph, so it says nothing about deadlock.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI). Which pattern does it watch for to decide when to abort a transaction?
options: Any write-write conflict, which it always resolves by aborting the reader
Two consecutive read-write anti-dependency edges among concurrent transactions (a 'dangerous structure')
Any two transactions that read the same row
Transactions that run longer than statement_timeout
questions.explanation: Every non-serializable snapshot-isolation execution contains a pivot transaction with an incoming and outgoing rw-antidependency. SSI tracks these and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure. It may abort some safe transactions too, but never misses a real anomaly.

questions.prompt: A precedence graph has only the edges T1 → T3 and T2 → T3. Which serial orders are conflict-equivalent to the schedule? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Any topological order works: T3 must come after both T1 and T2, while T1 and T2 can be in either order. Putting T3 before T2 violates T2 → T3.

questions.prompt: Which pairs of operations (in this order, from different transactions) add an edge to the precedence graph? Select all that apply.
options: W1(X) then R2(X)
W1(X) then W2(X)
W1(X) then W2(Y)
R1(X) then W2(X)
R1(X) then R2(X)
questions.explanation: Read-write, write-write and write-read on the same item all conflict. Two reads don't, and writes to different items don't.

questions.prompt: A precedence graph only gets edges for pairs where both operations are writes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Any conflicting pair counts: read-write and write-read as well as write-write, as long as they are on the same item and from different transactions.

questions.prompt: If a precedence graph is acyclic, any topological order of it gives a serial schedule that is conflict-equivalent to the original.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every topological order respects every edge, i.e. every conflicting pair's order, which is exactly conflict equivalence. When several orders exist, all of them are valid.

questions.prompt: When is a schedule recoverable?
options: When all writes are logged
When no transaction reads data written by another
When, if Tj reads data written by Ti, Ti commits before Tj commits
When every transaction can be restarted after a crash
questions.explanation: Recoverability ensures a transaction never commits based on data that might still be rolled back. Forbidding all such reads is the stronger cascadeless property, and logging alone doesn't decide this.

questions.prompt: What is a cascading rollback?
options: Rolling back several statements in one transaction
Aborting Ti forces aborting every transaction that read Ti's uncommitted writes, and so on
Rolling back to a savepoint, then to an earlier one
Undoing a schema migration and all later migrations
questions.explanation: If Tj read Ti's dirty data and Ti aborts, Tj's work is based on values that never existed, so Tj must abort too, and anything that read from Tj as well. Cascadeless schedules prevent this.

questions.prompt: Classify the schedule W1(A), R2(A), C2, A1 (T2 commits, then T1 aborts).
options: Cascadeless but not strict
Not recoverable
Strict
Recoverable but not cascadeless
questions.explanation: T2 read T1's uncommitted write and committed before T1 finished. When T1 aborts, T2's committed result depends on a value that was rolled back, and a committed transaction can't be undone.

questions.prompt: Classify the schedule W1(A), R2(A), C1, C2.
options: Not recoverable
Strict
Cascadeless
Recoverable but not cascadeless
questions.explanation: T2 reads T1's uncommitted A, so it isn't cascadeless (if T1 had aborted, T2 would have to abort too). But T1 commits before T2, so it is recoverable.

questions.prompt: Why do database engines prefer strict schedules (no reading or overwriting an item until its last writer has committed or aborted)?
options: They allow more concurrency than any other class
Undo can simply restore before-images, because no other transaction has read or overwritten the uncommitted value
They remove the need for a write-ahead log
They make deadlocks impossible
questions.explanation: With strictness, rolling back just restores the old value without affecting anyone else. Strict 2PL provides it but can still deadlock, and recovery still needs logging. Strict schedules allow less concurrency, not more.

questions.prompt: Which locking protocol guarantees strict (and therefore cascadeless) schedules?
options: Optimistic locking with version numbers
Basic two-phase locking
Strict two-phase locking, holding exclusive locks until commit or abort
Releasing every lock right after each statement
questions.explanation: Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but can release write locks before commit, letting others read dirty data and causing cascading aborts. Holding exclusive locks until the end prevents that.

questions.prompt: Which relationship between these schedule classes is correct?
options: Recoverable ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ strict
Cascadeless ⊂ strict ⊂ recoverable
The three classes are unrelated
Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable
questions.explanation: Every strict schedule is cascadeless (no dirty reads), and every cascadeless schedule is recoverable (you can't commit on dirty data you never read). Each step adds restrictions.

questions.prompt: Which schedules are cascadeless? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Cascadeless means no transaction reads uncommitted data. Only the second schedule reads T1's write before C1. The last one is cascadeless (no reads at all) but not strict, because T2 overwrites T1's uncommitted A.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED (MVCC), which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Two transactions can both overwrite the same row without either waiting (dirty writes)
Transactions never read uncommitted data, so reads don't create cascading aborts
Lost updates from read-modify-write in application code are fully prevented
One transaction aborting never forces another to abort because the second read its data
questions.explanation: Snapshots only include committed versions, so there are no dirty reads and no cascading aborts. Row-level write locks prevent dirty writes. Lost updates from read-then-write in the app are still possible at READ COMMITTED.

questions.prompt: Every cascadeless schedule is also recoverable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: If transactions only read committed data, no transaction can commit while depending on an uncommitted one, which is the recoverability condition.

questions.prompt: A recoverable schedule never requires cascading rollbacks.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Recoverable only orders the commits. A transaction can still read dirty data, and if the writer aborts, the reader must abort too. Avoiding cascades needs the stronger cascadeless property.

questions.prompt: What is a dirty read?
options: Reading from a replica that is behind the primary
Reading the same row twice and getting different committed values
Reading data written by a transaction that hasn't committed yet
Reading a row that has been deleted and vacuumed
questions.explanation: If the writer later rolls back, the reader acted on data that never officially existed. Getting different committed values on re-read is a non-repeatable read, and replica lag is a replication issue, not an isolation anomaly.

questions.prompt: Within one transaction, running SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open' twice returns a higher count the second time, because another transaction inserted and committed a new open ticket. What is this anomaly called?
options: Phantom read
Write skew
Dirty read
Lost update
questions.explanation: A phantom is a change in the set of rows matching a predicate, caused by inserts or deletes. A non-repeatable read is an existing row's value changing, and the new row here was committed, so it isn't a dirty read.

questions.prompt: Two requests each read a balance of 100 and write back balance + 10, so the final balance is 110 instead of 120. Which change fixes it most simply at READ COMMITTED?
options: Use a single statement: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = $1
Wrap both reads in a longer transaction
Read the balance from a replica
Add an index on accounts.id
questions.explanation: This is a lost update caused by read-modify-write in the application. An atomic UPDATE computes from the current committed value while holding the row lock, so concurrent increments serialize. A longer transaction at READ COMMITTED doesn't stop it.

questions.prompt: Two on-call doctors each check that at least two doctors are on call, then each sets themselves off call, in separate transactions. Both commit and nobody is on call. What is this anomaly?
options: Write skew
Lost update
Non-repeatable read
Dirty read
questions.explanation: Each transaction read the same set, then updated a different row based on it, breaking an invariant across rows. It isn't a lost update because they wrote different rows, so snapshot isolation's write-write conflict check doesn't catch it.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't snapshot isolation (e.g. PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ) prevent write skew?
options: Write skew only happens with deletes
Snapshot isolation allows dirty reads
It doesn't take snapshots for UPDATE statements
It only detects conflicts when two transactions write the same row, and in write skew they write different rows
questions.explanation: Under snapshot isolation, two concurrent transactions that write the same row conflict and one fails. Write skew updates disjoint rows, so no conflict is detected. SERIALIZABLE (SSI) or explicit locking of the rows read is needed.

questions.prompt: An app uses optimistic concurrency: UPDATE docs SET body = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3. The update reports 0 rows affected. What does that mean?
options: The database is out of disk space
The row was locked, so the update was queued
The UPDATE succeeded but the count wasn't returned
Another transaction changed the row (or deleted it) since it was read, so the client should reload and retry or report a conflict
questions.explanation: The version predicate only matches if no one else has updated the row since it was read. Zero rows means the expected version is gone. Lock waits block; they don't return 0 rows.

questions.prompt: Using the SQL standard's definitions, what is the lowest isolation level that prevents non-repeatable reads?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
READ COMMITTED
questions.explanation: The standard defines READ COMMITTED as preventing dirty reads, REPEATABLE READ as also preventing non-repeatable reads, and SERIALIZABLE as also preventing phantoms. Real engines can be stronger than the standard requires.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED, which approaches prevent a lost update on a counter? Select all that apply.
options: A version column checked in the UPDATE's WHERE clause
Plain SELECT, compute the value in the app, then UPDATE t SET n = $computed
UPDATE t SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = $1
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing and writing the new value
questions.explanation: The atomic update and FOR UPDATE both serialize on the row lock, and the version check detects a concurrent change. A plain read followed by an absolute write lets two transactions read the same old value and overwrite each other.

questions.prompt: Which scenarios are examples of write skew? Select all that apply.
options: Two transactions both read a counter as 5 and both write 6
A transaction reads another's uncommitted row
Two users each check that a room is free for 2–3pm, then each insert an overlapping booking
Two doctors each go off call after checking that another doctor is still on call
questions.explanation: Write skew is when each transaction checks a condition on shared data and then writes something different, breaking the condition together. The booking case is phantom-driven write skew. The counter is a lost update (same row), and the last is a dirty read.

questions.prompt: A lost update involves two transactions writing the same row, while write skew involves transactions writing different rows based on a shared read.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That's the key distinction, and it explains why snapshot isolation stops lost updates (a write-write conflict on the same row) but not write skew.

questions.prompt: Phantom reads can only be caused by deleted rows, never by inserted rows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Phantoms come from any change to the set of rows matching a predicate. Inserts that newly match are the classic case; deletes and updates that move rows into or out of the predicate count too.

questions.prompt: What are the default transaction isolation levels in PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB?
options: PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED; InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ
Both default to SERIALIZABLE
PostgreSQL: REPEATABLE READ; InnoDB: READ COMMITTED
Both default to READ COMMITTED
questions.explanation: This difference catches teams porting code between the two: a read that is repeatable in MySQL by default can return changed values in PostgreSQL by default.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what happens if you set a transaction to READ UNCOMMITTED?
options: It behaves exactly like READ COMMITTED
It behaves like SERIALIZABLE
It is rejected with an error
It can see other transactions' uncommitted changes
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL accepts the level but treats it as READ COMMITTED; its MVCC design never exposes uncommitted row versions. The standard allows an implementation to be stricter than required.

questions.prompt: MySQL InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ: transaction A runs SELECT balance FROM acct WHERE id = 1 and sees 100. B then sets the balance to 50 and commits. A runs UPDATE acct SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1 and commits. What is the final balance?
options: 40, because UPDATE in InnoDB reads the latest committed row version
90, because A's update uses its snapshot value 100
A's update fails with a serialization error
50, because A's update is silently ignored
questions.explanation: In InnoDB, plain SELECTs read the snapshot, but UPDATE (like locking reads) uses the latest committed version: 50 − 10 = 40. PostgreSQL at REPEATABLE READ would instead fail A with a serialization error.

questions.prompt: In MySQL InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ, transaction A runs SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE. Transaction B tries to INSERT a row with id = 15 and blocks. Why?
options: B's insert is waiting for an auto-increment lock
InnoDB locks the whole table for any FOR UPDATE
A holds next-key (record + gap) locks on the scanned range, which block inserts into it
REPEATABLE READ blocks all inserts until A commits
questions.explanation: Next-key locks cover index records and the gaps between them, which prevents phantoms for locking reads. Only the scanned range is locked, not the whole table, and inserts elsewhere proceed.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service runs critical transactions at SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL and occasionally gets errors with SQLSTATE 40001 under load. What is the correct handling?
options: Lower the isolation level to READ COMMITTED to remove the errors
Retry only the statement that failed, within the same transaction
Ignore the error, since the data was committed anyway
Retry the whole transaction from the beginning, ideally with backoff and a retry limit
questions.explanation: 40001 is a serialization failure: the transaction was aborted and nothing was committed. Re-running it from the start (including its reads) is the expected pattern. Retrying one statement can't work because the transaction is already aborted.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ?
options: It locks every row read until commit
It allows non-repeatable reads but not phantoms
It equals SERIALIZABLE
It is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but write skew is possible
questions.explanation: Each transaction sees one snapshot taken at its first query, so re-reads and predicate queries are stable (stronger than the SQL standard requires). Write skew is still possible; only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) catches it.

questions.prompt: How do you run a single PostgreSQL transaction at SERIALIZABLE without changing the session default?
options: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
Add FOR SERIALIZABLE after each SELECT
SET GLOBAL transaction_isolation = 'SERIALIZABLE'
ALTER DATABASE ... SET default_transaction_isolation once
questions.explanation: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL ... (or SET TRANSACTION as the first statement) applies to just that transaction. SET GLOBAL is MySQL syntax, and ALTER DATABASE changes the default for every new session.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL's isolation levels are correct? Select all that apply.
options: REPEATABLE READ can still allow write skew
SERIALIZABLE works by taking table-level locks on everything it reads
SERIALIZABLE may abort transactions with serialization failures that the app must retry
REPEATABLE READ prevents phantom reads in practice
questions.explanation: Snapshot-based REPEATABLE READ is stable for predicates but misses write skew. SERIALIZABLE uses SSI with non-blocking predicate (SIRead) locks and aborts transactions on dangerous patterns instead of blocking with table locks.

questions.prompt: Which statements about MySQL InnoDB isolation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: READ COMMITTED mostly turns off gap locking for searches and index scans
At REPEATABLE READ, any concurrent update to a row you read causes a serialization error, as in PostgreSQL
At REPEATABLE READ, the snapshot is created at the first consistent read, not at BEGIN (unless WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT is used)
At SERIALIZABLE with autocommit off, plain SELECTs are implicitly turned into locking reads (FOR SHARE)
questions.explanation: InnoDB's SERIALIZABLE uses shared locks, its snapshot starts at the first read, and READ COMMITTED keeps gap locks only for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks. InnoDB REPEATABLE READ doesn't raise serialization errors; updates just apply to the latest version.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL maps READ UNCOMMITTED to READ COMMITTED, so dirty reads never happen. MySQL InnoDB's READ UNCOMMITTED does allow them.

questions.prompt: In MySQL InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ, two plain SELECTs in the same transaction see the same snapshot even if other transactions commit changes between them.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Consistent (non-locking) reads use the snapshot from the first read. Locking reads and DML, however, see the latest committed data, which is a common source of surprises.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Each element is first included, then excluded, and subsets are recorded only at the leaves. 'Include' branches run first, so the full set comes first and the empty set last, which is why there's a trailing comma: 2^3 = 8 results. The ordering ,1,2,3,… comes from a BFS-style or bitmask enumeration.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: res stores four references to the same path array, and after backtracking that array is empty, so every entry prints []. This is the most common backtracking bug. Push a snapshot instead: res.push([...path]). The count is still 4: [], [0], [0,1], [1].

questions.prompt: In the choose / explore / un-choose template, why must you undo the choice (e.g. path.pop()) after the recursive call?
options: Because JavaScript arrays can't grow past the recursion depth
To prevent the recursion from running forever
Because the path is shared, mutable state; undoing restores it so the next sibling branch starts from the same prefix
To free memory immediately
questions.explanation: All branches share one path array or used-set for efficiency. If you don't undo, a sibling branch inherits elements from the previous branch and produces wrong combinations. The alternative is to copy the state per call (immutable), which costs more memory.

questions.prompt: 'Permutations II' must generate unique permutations of [1, 1, 2]. After sorting, which skip condition prevents duplicates?
options: Skip i if the path already contains nums[i]
Skip i if nums[i] === nums[i + 1]
Skip i if used[i], or if i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]
Skip i if i > start
questions.explanation: Equal values must be used in a fixed order: the second 1 can only be placed if the first 1 is already in the path. That rule blocks identical permutations that differ only in which copy came first. Checking whether the path contains the value would never allow both 1s.

questions.prompt: What's the time complexity of generating all permutations of n distinct elements, copying each one into the result?
options: O(n · n!)
O(n!) with no extra factor
questions.explanation: There are n! permutations, and copying each one costs O(n), so the output alone is O(n · n!). O(2^n) counts subsets, a different problem. Saying O(n!) drops the copy cost, which interviewers usually expect you to mention.

questions.prompt: In N-Queens, how do you check in O(1) whether placing a queen at (r, c) is safe?
options: Keep sets of used columns, of r - c (one diagonal direction) and of r + c (the other); a square is safe if none contains its value
Keep a set of used rows only
Check only the cell directly above
Scan the whole board each time
questions.explanation: Placing one queen per row handles rows. Cells on the same diagonal share r - c, and cells on the same anti-diagonal share r + c. Three sets make each check O(1) instead of an O(n) scan, and you must remove the entries when backtracking.

questions.prompt: Combination Sum (each candidate can be reused) returns both [2,3,2] and [3,2,2] as separate answers. What's the bug?
options: Candidates weren't sorted
The recursion uses i + 1, which forbids reuse
The target check is <= instead of ===
Each recursive call loops from index 0 instead of from the current index, so the same multiset is built in different orders
questions.explanation: To produce combinations rather than permutations, pass a start index and loop from it: bt(i, remaining - c[i]) allows reuse while never going back to earlier candidates. Sorting helps pruning but doesn't prevent reorderings. Using i + 1 would forbid reuse, a different bug.

questions.prompt: For backtracking over positive integer candidates (as in Combination Sum), which pruning techniques are valid? Select all that apply.
options: Sort the candidates and break out of the loop once a candidate exceeds the remaining target
Check constraints before recursing, rather than at the leaf
Sorting is required for correctness in every backtracking problem
Memoize on the current path's contents to reduce the number of permutations that must be output
Skip a candidate equal to the previous one at the same depth when the input has duplicates
questions.explanation: Breaking early works because the candidates are sorted and positive, so every later one is also too big. Same-depth duplicate skipping and early constraint checks cut whole subtrees. When you must output every permutation, memoization can't reduce the output size, and sorting is only needed by some prunings.

questions.prompt: Which problems are typically solved with backtracking? Select all that apply.
options: Sudoku solver
Word Search (does a word exist as a path in a letter grid?)
Generate all valid parentheses strings of n pairs
Fewest moves in an unweighted grid
Length of the longest common subsequence
questions.explanation: Each of the first three builds a candidate step by step and abandons it as soon as a constraint fails. Fewest moves is a BFS problem, and LCS length has overlapping subproblems that DP solves in O(nm), where backtracking would be exponential.

questions.prompt: Generate Parentheses can prune by adding ')' only when the number of ')' placed so far is less than the number of '('.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Together with adding '(' only while fewer than n have been placed, this guarantees every prefix is valid, so the recursion never builds an invalid string. The number of results is the n-th Catalan number.

questions.prompt: With good pruning, a backtracking algorithm is guaranteed to run in polynomial time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Pruning shrinks the search tree in practice, but the worst case usually stays exponential (N-Queens, Sudoku, subset sum). And if the problem asks you to list all solutions, the output itself can be exponential in size.

questions.prompt: A road network has 100,000 intersections and 250,000 roads. Which representation fits best?
options: An edge list scanned on every neighbour lookup
A matrix of booleans packed into a string
Adjacency list (e.g. Map from node to neighbour array): O(V + E) memory
Adjacency matrix: 10^10 cells
questions.explanation: The graph is sparse (E is far smaller than V^2), so an adjacency list stores only the real edges, about 350k entries, and iterates a node's neighbours in O(degree). A matrix would need 10^10 cells. Scanning an edge list makes every neighbour lookup O(E).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: abcd bad 8
abcd bad 4
abcd abd 4
abdc bad 4
questions.explanation: A Map iterates keys in insertion order: a, b, c, d. c's neighbours are added in edge order: b (from b-c), a (from a-c), d (from c-d). size counts nodes (4), not directed entries; each undirected edge appears in two lists, so the lists contain 8 entries in total.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: fill([]) puts the same array object in every slot, so pushing to g[0] changes all of them. Use Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) to get independent arrays. This bug silently connects every node to every neighbour.

questions.prompt: Why is a Map often preferable to a plain object for an adjacency list keyed by node id?
options: Maps sort their keys automatically
Maps are always faster for every operation
Objects can't hold arrays as values
Map keeps key types (1 and '1' are different keys), has no inherited prototype keys, and has an O(1) size property
questions.explanation: Object keys are converted to strings, and integer-like keys are reordered ahead of the others. Maps keep keys as given (numbers, objects), iterate in insertion order and avoid prototype keys like 'constructor'. Maps don't sort, and objects can hold arrays fine.

questions.prompt: Your algorithm frequently asks 'is there an edge u to v?' on a large sparse graph stored as a Map of arrays. What change makes that check O(1) on average?
options: Store neighbours in a Set per node (Map<node, Set<node>>)
Sort each neighbour array and binary search, which is O(1)
Convert to an adjacency matrix regardless of size
Cache the result of the last query
questions.explanation: Set.has is O(1) on average, compared with Array.includes at O(degree). A binary search is O(log degree), not O(1). A matrix gives O(1) but needs O(V^2) memory, which a large sparse graph can't afford.

questions.prompt: A grid BFS stores visited cells with `visited.add([r, c])` and checks `visited.has([nr, nc])`, but it never terminates on some inputs. Why?
options: has() is O(n), which looks like an infinite loop
The Set grows past its maximum size
Arrays are compared by reference, so each new [r, c] literal is a different key and has() is always false; use a string like `${r},${c}` or a number like r * cols + c
Sets can't store arrays
questions.explanation: Set and Map use SameValueZero equality, which for objects means identity. Two different [1,2] arrays are different keys, so no cell ever counts as visited and cells get revisited endlessly. Encoding the coordinates as a primitive fixes it.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra on an undirected road map returns Infinity for some towns that are clearly reachable. The adjacency list is built with `g.get(u).push([v, w])` for each road. What's the most likely bug?
options: The priority queue should be a max-heap
Each road was added in one direction only; undirected edges must also push [u, w] into v's list
Dijkstra doesn't support undirected graphs
Weights must be integers
questions.explanation: Pushing only u to v makes the graph directed, so a town reachable only by traversing some road from v to u looks unreachable. Undirected edges must be stored in both lists. Dijkstra works on undirected graphs with non-negative weights.

questions.prompt: When is an adjacency matrix preferable to an adjacency list? Select all that apply.
options: Iterating the neighbours of low-degree nodes quickly
Small V where O(1) edge-existence checks matter
Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest paths, which works over a V × V table anyway
A sparse graph with 10^6 vertices
Dense graphs where E is close to V^2
questions.explanation: A matrix costs O(V^2) memory, which is reasonable when the graph is dense or small and buys O(1) edge checks. Floyd-Warshall needs a V × V table anyway. For 10^6 vertices it would need about 10^12 cells, and finding a node's neighbours means scanning a whole row, O(V).

questions.prompt: You build an adjacency list for nodes 0..n-1 from an edge list. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) creates an independent array per node
In an undirected graph, the sum of all list lengths equals E
Isolated nodes keep empty lists and must still be visited when counting connected components
For a directed edge u to v, only g[u] gets v
questions.explanation: The factory callback creates a fresh array each time. Components are counted by looping over all n nodes, so isolated nodes count as components of size 1. A directed edge belongs in one list only. In an undirected graph each edge appears in two lists, so the total is 2E.

questions.prompt: Iterating a Map with for...of visits its entries in the order the keys were first inserted.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Maps guarantee insertion order, and re-setting an existing key doesn't move it. That makes graph traversals over a Map deterministic. Plain objects instead put integer-like keys first, in numeric order.

questions.prompt: For an undirected graph stored as adjacency lists, the total length of all the lists equals the number of edges E.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Each undirected edge {u, v} appears in both u's list and v's list, so the total is 2E (the handshake lemma: the degrees sum to 2E). For a directed graph the total is E.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The islands are the 2×2 block at the top left, the single cell (1,3), the single cell (2,2), and the pair (3,3)-(3,4). (1,3) and (2,2) touch only diagonally, and the DFS moves in 4 directions only, so they're separate islands. With diagonal moves, (1,3), (2,2) and the pair would merge into one island, giving 2.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The wall at (1,1) forces the path down the left column and along the bottom row: (2,2) is 4 steps away and (1,2) is 5, reached by stepping up from (2,2). (0,2) is a wall and stays -1. BFS assigns each cell its shortest distance the first time it reaches it.

questions.prompt: In BFS, why mark a node as visited when it's enqueued rather than when it's dequeued?
options: Marking at dequeue gives wrong distances
It doesn't matter in any case
Marking at enqueue stops the same node from being added to the queue several times by different neighbours, which wastes time and memory
Marking at enqueue makes BFS behave like DFS
questions.explanation: If you mark only when dequeuing, a node with many already-discovered neighbours can be enqueued once per neighbour, so the queue can grow towards O(E) duplicates. Distances stay correct for unweighted BFS, but you lose the clean O(V) queue bound.

questions.prompt: 'Rotting oranges': every minute, rotten oranges rot their 4 neighbours. How do you compute the time until all oranges are rotten?
options: Run a BFS from each rotten orange separately and take the maximum
Multi-source BFS: put all rotten oranges in the queue at time 0 and expand level by level
Run Dijkstra from the top-left cell
DFS from the first fresh orange
questions.explanation: Starting the BFS from all sources at once gives each cell its distance to the nearest rotten orange in one O(R·C) pass. Separate BFS runs cost O(k·R·C) and still need a minimum per cell, not a maximum. If any fresh orange is never reached, the answer is -1.

questions.prompt: A recursive flood fill works on small tests but crashes in Node on a 1000×1000 grid that is all land. What's the cause and fix?
options: The recursion depth can reach about 10^6 and overflow the call stack; use an explicit stack or a BFS queue
The grid is too large for memory; use a Uint8Array
JS strings can't be mutated; convert rows to arrays
Recursion visits cells twice; add a visited set
questions.explanation: DFS on a snake-like or full grid can go about R·C calls deep, and V8's stack overflows after roughly 10k calls (depending on frame size) with a RangeError. An iterative version keeps the stack on the heap. The grid itself (10^6 cells) fits easily in memory.

questions.prompt: Edges have weight 0 or 1 only. What's the most efficient shortest-path approach?
options: 0-1 BFS with a deque: push the neighbour to the front for a 0-weight edge and to the back for a 1-weight edge, giving O(V + E)
Plain BFS, ignoring weights
DFS with memoization
Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: The deque keeps nodes in non-decreasing distance order without a heap, so this is Dijkstra in O(V + E). Plain BFS treats 0-weight edges as cost 1 and gets wrong answers. Bellman-Ford is O(VE).

questions.prompt: 'Shortest path in a grid with obstacle elimination' lets you remove up to k obstacles. Why is a visited[r][c] array alone wrong?
options: It uses too much memory
visited should be cleared after each level
Reaching a cell with more eliminations left is a different, better state; marking the cell visited on the first arrival can block a path that arrives later with more eliminations remaining
BFS can't handle obstacles
questions.explanation: The BFS state is (r, c, remaining eliminations). Track visited per state, or keep the best remaining count per cell and revisit only if the new arrival has more left. Otherwise an early arrival that has used up its eliminations hides a better route.

questions.prompt: Which cycle-detection approaches are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Directed graph: report a cycle whenever DFS reaches any already-visited node
Undirected graph: DFS that reports a cycle when it finds a visited neighbour other than the parent it came from
Directed graph: DFS with three states (unvisited, on the current path, done), reporting a cycle on reaching a node that's on the current path
Undirected graph: union-find, reporting a cycle when an edge joins two nodes already in the same set
questions.explanation: In a directed graph, reaching a node that's already finished (a cross or forward edge) is not a cycle; only a back edge to a node on the current path is. The parent check, the three-state DFS and union-find are the standard correct methods.

questions.prompt: Which tasks need BFS (rather than plain DFS) to get the answer directly? Select all that apply.
options: Distance from every cell to its nearest 0 in a binary matrix
Counting connected components
Checking whether any path exists between two nodes
Word Ladder: the minimum number of transformations
Fewest moves to reach the exit of an unweighted maze
questions.explanation: Minimum steps in an unweighted graph come from BFS's level-by-level order, and 'distance to nearest 0' is a multi-source BFS. Component counting and plain reachability only need every reachable node visited, so DFS works equally well.

questions.prompt: Flood fill on a grid of V cells runs in O(V) time when each cell is marked visited the first time it's reached.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Each cell is processed at most once and checks a constant 4 (or 8) neighbours, so the total is O(V). Without marking, cells get revisited, the work can blow up, and on cyclic regions the fill never terminates.

questions.prompt: In a DFS over an undirected graph, finding an already-visited neighbour always means there is a cycle.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. In an undirected graph, the node you just came from is always a visited neighbour, because the edge is stored in both directions. A cycle exists only if a visited neighbour other than the parent is found. With parallel edges, track the edge id instead of the parent node.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 0 is the only node with in-degree 0. Removing it frees 1 and 2, enqueued in adjacency order. 3 needs both 1 and 2 to be processed before its in-degree reaches 0. 0,2,1,3 is also a valid topological order, but this code's FIFO queue produces 0,1,2,3.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: ok 4
cycle 1
cycle 2
cycle 0
questions.explanation: 1 and 2 form a cycle, so after 0 is removed node 1 still has in-degree 1 (from 2) and never enters the queue. Node 3 depends on 2 and is stuck too. Only 0 is output. An output shorter than n is how Kahn's algorithm detects a cycle.

questions.prompt: In 'Course Schedule', when is it impossible to finish all courses?
options: When the prerequisite graph contains a directed cycle
When the graph is disconnected
When a course has no prerequisites
When some course has more than two prerequisites
questions.explanation: A topological order exists if and only if the directed graph is acyclic. A cycle means courses wait on each other forever. A disconnected graph is fine: each part is ordered independently. The number of prerequisites per course doesn't matter.

questions.prompt: In DFS-based topological sort, when is a node added to the output, and what's done with the output at the end?
options: After all its descendants are finished (post-order); reverse the list at the end
Before visiting its neighbours; reverse the list at the end
When its in-degree becomes 0; output as is
When it's first visited; output as is
questions.explanation: A node finishes only after everything reachable from it has finished, so its dependents are already in the list. Reversing the finish order puts every node before its dependents. Recording nodes on first visit (preorder) can place a node before one of its prerequisites.

questions.prompt: prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means 'take b before a'. A solution builds edges a to b and prints an order where courses appear before their prerequisites. What's wrong?
options: The edges are reversed; they should go b to a (prerequisite to dependent), otherwise the topological order comes out backwards
Kahn's algorithm can't handle this input format
In-degrees should be counted on the source node
The queue should be a stack
questions.explanation: Edges must point from what comes first to what depends on it. With reversed edges the algorithm still detects cycles correctly, since reversing every edge keeps cycles, but the order is backwards. Using a stack instead of a queue gives another valid order, not a fix.

questions.prompt: You need the lexicographically smallest valid topological order of a DAG with numbered nodes. What change to Kahn's algorithm achieves it?
options: Sort the final output
Replace the FIFO queue with a min-heap, so the smallest available node is taken each time: O((V + E) log V)
Run DFS from the smallest node first
Process nodes in reverse numeric order
questions.explanation: At each step, taking the smallest node whose prerequisites are all done is the greedy choice that gives the smallest sequence. Sorting the final output breaks the dependency order. Running DFS from the smallest node doesn't guarantee the smallest overall sequence.

questions.prompt: In 'Alien Dictionary', the word list contains 'abc' immediately followed by 'ab'. What should the algorithm do?
options: Return '' (invalid input), because a longer word can't come before its own prefix in a sorted dictionary
Ignore the pair because no characters differ
Add the edge c to b
Swap the two words and continue
questions.explanation: Comparing adjacent words gives no differing character, yet the longer word comes first, which no letter ordering allows. Skipping the pair silently accepts invalid input, and it's a classic hidden test case. When adjacent words do differ, the first differing character pair gives one edge.

questions.prompt: Which tasks are solved by topological sorting? Select all that apply.
options: Ordering build steps or jobs that depend on each other
Detecting a cycle in an undirected graph via in-degrees
Deciding the order to recompute spreadsheet cells after an edit
Shortest paths in an undirected weighted graph
Choosing an install order for packages with dependencies
questions.explanation: Dependency graphs with directed 'must come before' edges are exactly what topological sort orders. Undirected shortest paths need Dijkstra, and in-degree is a directed-graph idea; undirected cycles are found with DFS (skipping the parent) or union-find.

questions.prompt: 'Parallel courses': any number of courses can be taken per semester once their prerequisites are done. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Kahn's algorithm requires an undirected graph
The minimum number of semesters equals the number of vertices on the longest path in the DAG
Running Kahn's algorithm level by level (one BFS layer per semester) gives that number
A DFS topological sort without an 'on the current path' state can silently produce an order on a cyclic graph
questions.explanation: Each layer of Kahn's BFS is one semester, and the number of layers equals the longest dependency chain. A plain visited-set DFS can't distinguish back edges, so it outputs an order even when a cycle exists. Kahn's algorithm works on directed graphs; in-degree has no meaning for undirected ones.

questions.prompt: A DAG can have more than one valid topological order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Whenever two nodes don't depend on each other, either can come first. In the diamond 0 to {1, 2} to 3, both 0,1,2,3 and 0,2,1,3 are valid. The order is unique only if consecutive nodes in it are always joined by an edge (a Hamiltonian path).

questions.prompt: DFS-based topological sort outputs nodes in the order they're first discovered (preorder).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. It uses reverse post-order, the order in which nodes finish, reversed. Preorder can list a node before one of its prerequisites when DFS reaches it through another branch. For edges A to C, B to C and B to A, DFS from A gives preorder A, C, B, but B must come before A.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: true,true,true,false 3
true,true,true,true 2
true,true,true,false 2
true,true,false,false 4
questions.explanation: The first three unions merge different sets: {0,1,2} and {3,4}, with 5 alone. union(0, 2) finds that both have the same root and returns false; in 'redundant connection' that edge is the one closing a cycle. Each successful union removes one component: 6 - 3 = 3.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The chain is 4 to 3 to 2 to 1 to 0. Recursive path compression points every node on the path directly at the root as the recursion returns, not just the starting node. Later finds on any of them take one hop.

questions.prompt: 'Redundant connection': a tree with one extra edge is given as an edge list. How does union-find identify the extra edge?
options: The edge whose endpoints have the highest combined rank
The edge whose endpoints are both leaves
The edge that's processed last
Process the edges in order; the first edge whose endpoints already have the same root closes a cycle
questions.explanation: If find(u) === find(v), u and v are already connected, so adding the edge creates a cycle. Processing in input order returns the cycle edge that appears last in the input, which is what the problem asks for. Ranks and leaves are irrelevant here.

questions.prompt: With both path compression and union by rank (or size), what's the amortized cost per operation?
options: O(1) worst case for every operation
O(√n)
O(log n)
O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, at most about 4 for any practical n
questions.explanation: Tarjan's analysis gives O(α(n)) amortized, which is effectively constant. It isn't O(1) worst case: a single find before compression can still traverse a path of length O(log n) (with union by rank). Either optimization alone gives O(log n).

questions.prompt: Why use union by rank or size, rather than always attaching the first root under the second?
options: Without it, a sequence of unions can build a chain of height O(n), making find O(n) until path compression flattens it
It's needed to count components
It lets union-find support deleting an edge
It makes union return the right boolean
questions.explanation: Attaching the smaller or shallower tree under the larger keeps the height O(log n), because a node's depth grows only when its tree at least doubles in size. Naive unions like union(1,0), union(2,1), … build a long chain. Component counting works either way.

questions.prompt: In a graph where edges are only ever removed, you must answer 'are u and v connected?' after each removal. Why is plain union-find awkward, and what's the common trick?
options: Union-find is too slow; use a heap
Union-find can't split sets; process the operations offline in reverse, so removals become additions (unions), and answer the queries backwards
Union-find only works on trees
Union-find can't store edges; use BFS each time
questions.explanation: Union-find supports merging but not splitting. If all operations are known in advance, reversing time turns deletions into unions, which it handles well. Running BFS after each deletion costs O(V + E) per query, which is usually too slow.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with this union?
options: find must be called after the assignment
It should return true when the roots are equal
It re-parents node a instead of a's root, so a's old set isn't merged and a is detached from it
It should set parent[b] = a
questions.explanation: Union must link the roots: parent[find(a)] = find(b). Setting parent[a] moves only a into b's tree, while the rest of a's set keeps its old root, so connectivity becomes wrong. Swapping a and b has the same problem.

questions.prompt: Which problems fit union-find? Select all that apply.
options: Topological ordering of a DAG
Detecting the redundant edge in an undirected graph
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree
Shortest path in an unweighted graph
Number of connected components as edges arrive one by one
questions.explanation: Union-find answers connectivity questions under merges, which covers incremental components, Kruskal's 'would this edge form a cycle?' check and redundant edges. It records which set a node belongs to, not distances or directions, so shortest paths and topological order need BFS or DFS.

questions.prompt: Which statements about union-find complexity are correct? Select all that apply.
options: With path compression, every find is O(1) worst case
Path compression alone gives O(log n) amortized per operation
Using both gives O(α(n)) amortized
Union by rank alone keeps tree height O(log n), so find is O(log n) worst case
questions.explanation: Each optimization alone gives logarithmic bounds, and together they give the inverse-Ackermann bound. Compression is amortized: the first find on a long path still walks the whole path, then flattens it for later calls.

questions.prompt: Union-find can tell you whether two nodes are connected, but it can't by itself return the path between them.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The parent pointers form trees that have nothing to do with the graph's actual edges, especially after path compression. To get a path you need BFS or DFS on the adjacency list.

questions.prompt: Union by rank requires rank to equal each tree's exact height, so ranks must be recomputed whenever path compression shortens a tree.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Rank is only an upper bound on height. Path compression lowers actual heights but leaves ranks alone, and the O(α(n)) analysis assumes exactly that. Recomputing heights would cost extra and gain nothing. Union by size is an equivalent alternative.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: A to C costs 1, and A to C to B costs 3, which beats the direct 4. Then B to D costs 3 + 1 = 4, which beats C to D at 6. The stale [4, 'B'] entry is skipped by the d > dist[u] check (lazy deletion). The sorted array stands in for a heap here.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Each edge is [weight, u, v]. Kruskal takes them in weight order: 1 (0-1), 2 (2-3), 3 (1-2, joining the two parts), then skips 4 and 5 because they would form cycles. A spanning tree on 4 nodes always has V - 1 = 3 edges, here with total weight 6.

questions.prompt: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm return wrong answers when some edge weights are negative?
options: The heap can't store negative numbers
It always runs forever on negative edges
It finalizes a node when it's popped, assuming no shorter path can appear later, but a later negative edge can make a shorter path to an already-settled node
Negative weights make the graph disconnected
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's correctness relies on path costs never decreasing as edges are added, which negative edges break. A node popped with distance 5 might later be reachable for 3 through a negative edge. Without a negative cycle it doesn't loop forever; it just returns wrong distances.

questions.prompt: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle reachable from the source?
options: By checking for any negative edge weight
By running Dijkstra twice and comparing
By detecting that the priority queue grows past V entries
After V - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge, it runs one more round; if any distance still decreases, a negative cycle exists
questions.explanation: A shortest simple path has at most V - 1 edges, so V - 1 rounds are enough when no negative cycle exists. If a V-th round still improves something, some path keeps getting cheaper, which means a negative cycle. Negative edges alone are allowed. Total time O(V·E).

questions.prompt: What's the time complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap and lazy deletion, on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O(V · E)
O(E)
O((V + E) log V)
questions.explanation: Each edge can push one heap entry and each push or pop costs O(log E), which is O(log V) since E ≤ V^2. That gives O((V + E) log V). O(V^2) is the array-based version without a heap, which is better only for very dense graphs. O(V·E) is Bellman-Ford.

questions.prompt: 'Cheapest flights within K stops' is solved with Bellman-Ford limited to K + 1 rounds. Why does each round relax from a copy of the previous round's distances?
options: Because JS arrays can't be updated during iteration
To avoid mutating the input
To detect negative cycles
So each round extends paths by at most one edge; relaxing in place could chain several edges in one round and exceed the stop limit
questions.explanation: Relaxing in place can use a distance updated earlier in the same round, chaining two or more flights into one round. Reading from the previous round's snapshot caps round i at i edges. Plain Dijkstra on cost alone ignores the stop limit too.

questions.prompt: You need a minimum spanning tree for a dense graph (E close to V^2) given as an adjacency matrix with V = 5,000. Which choice is most natural?
options: Bellman-Ford
BFS spanning tree
Prim's O(V^2) array version: no heap, scanning for the closest vertex each step, which suits a matrix
Kruskal, because sorting E ≈ 25 million edges is cheap
questions.explanation: Array-based Prim does V steps of an O(V) scan, about 25 million operations, without building or sorting an edge list. Kruskal must sort about 25M edges, O(E log E), which is slower. A BFS tree ignores weights, and Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths, not spanning trees.

questions.prompt: Which statements about minimum spanning trees are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An MST of a connected graph with V nodes has V edges
Kruskal's algorithm finds minimum spanning arborescences in directed graphs
If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique
Cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST
An MST minimizes total edge weight, but the MST path between two nodes isn't necessarily their shortest path
questions.explanation: The cut property justifies both Prim and Kruskal, and distinct weights make the MST unique. Minimizing total weight doesn't minimize each pairwise distance. Directed graphs need Chu-Liu/Edmonds, and a spanning tree has exactly V - 1 edges.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm-to-scenario pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Negative edge weights: Dijkstra with lazy deletion
Unweighted shortest path: BFS
Negative edge weights, no negative cycle: Bellman-Ford
All-pairs shortest paths on a small dense graph: Floyd-Warshall
Non-negative weights, single source: Dijkstra
questions.explanation: BFS handles unit weights, Dijkstra non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford negative edges (and detects negative cycles), and Floyd-Warshall runs in O(V^3) for all pairs. Lazy deletion is only a heap trick; it doesn't fix Dijkstra's assumption that weights are non-negative.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm computes correct shortest paths when edge weights are zero or positive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Zero-weight edges are allowed: the algorithm only needs weights to be non-negative, so path costs never decrease as you extend a path. That's what makes finalizing the smallest-distance node safe. Negative edges break this.

questions.prompt: Prim's and Dijkstra's algorithms use the same priority key: a vertex's total distance from the start node.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The code looks almost the same, but Prim keys each vertex by the weight of the single cheapest edge connecting it to the current tree, while Dijkstra keys it by the total path distance from the source. Mixing the two up is a common interview mistake.

questions.prompt: Linear search scans an unsorted array of n items for a target. What are its best-case and worst-case running times?
options: Best Θ(1), worst Θ(n)
Best Θ(1), worst Θ(n log n)
Best Θ(log n), worst Θ(n)
Best Θ(n), worst Θ(n)
questions.explanation: If the target is the first element the search stops after one comparison (Θ(1)); if it is last or missing, all n items are checked (Θ(n)). Saying the best case is Θ(n) confuses 'the loop can run n times' with 'it always does'.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log^2 n)
questions.explanation: The outer loop runs n times; the inner loop doubles j each time, so it runs about log2 n times. n × log n = O(n log n). It's not O(n^2) because the inner loop is not linear in n.

questions.prompt: A quicksort implementation always picks the last element as the pivot. It is given an array that is already sorted. What happens?
options: It runs in Θ(n log n) because quicksort is n log n on average
It runs in Θ(n) because no swaps are needed
It degrades to Θ(n^2) because every partition is maximally unbalanced
It runs in Θ(log n) because the pivot is always the maximum
questions.explanation: With the last element as pivot on sorted input, each partition splits off just one element, giving n + (n-1) + ... = Θ(n^2). The 'average' n log n assumes random-ish pivots; sorted input is exactly this pivot rule's worst case.

questions.prompt: An algorithm's exact cost is T(n) = 3n^2 + 100·n·log n + 5. Which is the tightest correct description?
options: Θ(n^3), as an upper bound
Θ(n log n), because the 100 coefficient dominates
Θ(100 n log n + 3n^2)
questions.explanation: For large n the n^2 term outgrows n log n regardless of constant factors, so T(n) = Θ(n^2). The 100 coefficient only matters for small n, and Θ notation drops constants and lower-order terms.

questions.prompt: Which statement about insertion sort's running time is correct?
options: It is Θ(n log n) on average, like merge sort
Its best case is Θ(1) when the array is already sorted
It is Θ(n^2) on every input because it has two nested loops
Its worst case is Θ(n^2) and its best case (already sorted) is Θ(n)
questions.explanation: On sorted input the inner loop exits immediately for each element, giving Θ(n); reverse-sorted input forces Θ(n^2) shifts. Nested loops don't imply Θ(n^2) on every input. Even the best case must look at all n elements, so it can't be Θ(1).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs 0+1+2+3+4 = n(n-1)/2 = 10 times. That is still Θ(n^2): halving the work of a full n×n loop changes the constant, not the growth rate. 15 would be n(n+1)/2, which counts j <= i.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 (128 stops the loop), so 7 iterations, which is about ceil(log2 100). Loops that multiply the counter are logarithmic, not linear.

questions.prompt: Which statements about asymptotic notation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An O(n log n) algorithm can be slower than an O(n^2) one for small inputs
Big-Θ gives a tight bound: the function is bounded above and below by the same growth rate
Big-O keeps constant factors, so O(2n) and O(n) are different classes
Any algorithm that must read its whole input is Ω(n)
Big-O can only be used to describe an algorithm's worst case
questions.explanation: Θ is a tight bound; constants hidden by Big-O can make an asymptotically better algorithm slower at small n; reading n items is a lower bound. Big-O is just an upper bound and can describe best, average or worst case. It drops constants, so O(2n) = O(n).

questions.prompt: Which of these functions are O(n^2)? Select all that apply.
options: n^2 log n
n log n
questions.explanation: Big-O is an upper bound, so anything growing no faster than n^2 qualifies: 5n^2+3n, n log n and 1000n. n^2 log n grows faster than n^2 by a log factor, and 2^n is exponential.

questions.prompt: A hash table with average-case O(1) lookup guarantees that every single lookup finishes in constant time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Average case is about typical inputs; with many collisions (bad hash function or adversarial keys) a lookup can degrade to O(n) for chaining. The guarantee is about the expected cost, not every operation.

questions.prompt: A function that loops over an array of length n and then, separately (not nested), loops over another array of length m runs in O(n + m) time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Sequential loops add their costs: O(n) + O(m) = O(n + m). Only nesting multiplies them (O(n·m)). Collapsing it to O(n) is wrong unless you know m is bounded by n.

questions.prompt: You reverse an array in place by swapping arr[i] and arr[n-1-i] with two indices. What is the auxiliary space complexity?
options: O(n), because the array has n elements
O(n/2), because only half the elements are swapped
O(log n)
