questions.explanation: Auxiliary space counts extra memory beyond the input. Two indices and a temp variable are constant. The input array itself is O(n) but isn't counted as extra space for an in-place algorithm.

questions.prompt: What is the space complexity of this function, including the call stack?
options: O(n), because n stack frames are live at the deepest point
O(log n)
O(1), since no new arrays are created
questions.explanation: Each call waits for the next, so n frames are on the stack at once: O(n) space. 'No new arrays' misses the call stack, and JavaScript engines such as V8 do not perform tail-call optimisation.

questions.prompt: A dynamic array grows by adding a fixed 10 slots each time it fills up, instead of doubling. What is the total cost of n pushes?
options: O(n) total, because 10 is a constant
O(n^2) total, amortised O(n) per push
O(n) total, amortised O(1) per push
O(n log n) total
questions.explanation: Each resize copies all current elements: 10 + 20 + 30 + ... up to n is about n^2/20 copies, which is O(n^2). Amortised O(1) needs geometric growth (×1.5, ×2) so copy costs form a geometric series summing to O(n).

questions.prompt: In a 'does any pair sum to target?' problem, the interviewer says memory is extremely tight but the array may be modified. Which approach fits best?
options: Store every value in a Set: O(n) time, O(n) space
Build a frequency Map: O(n) time, O(1) space
Check all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Sort in place, then two pointers: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space (ignoring sort internals)
questions.explanation: Sorting in place plus two pointers trades some time for minimal extra memory. The Set approach is faster but uses O(n) space. Brute force needs only O(1) space, not O(n), but is slower, and a frequency map is O(n) space, not O(1).

questions.prompt: How does amortised analysis differ from average-case analysis?
options: Amortised analysis bounds the total cost of any sequence of operations, with no probability involved
Amortised analysis only applies to recursive algorithms
Amortised analysis averages over random inputs; average case averages over a sequence
They are the same thing with different names
questions.explanation: Amortised O(1) push means any sequence of n pushes costs O(n) total, a worst-case guarantee over the sequence. Average-case analysis assumes a distribution over inputs. Swapping the two definitions is the common mix-up.

questions.prompt: This simulates a doubling dynamic array. What does it print?
questions.explanation: Resizes happen when len is 1, 2, 4 and 8, copying 1+2+4+8 = 15 elements and ending at capacity 16. Total copies stay under n, which is why push is amortised O(1).

questions.prompt: What does this print (max recursion depth, then total calls)?
questions.explanation: Calls total 2^(n+1) - 1 = 31 (exponential time), but only one root-to-leaf path is on the stack at once, so the max depth is n + 1 = 5 (linear space). Time and space of recursion are governed by different things.

questions.prompt: Which of these allocate O(n) extra memory for an array of length n? Select all that apply.
options: arr.reverse()
arr.slice()
[...arr].reverse()
new Set(arr)
Swapping elements with two index pointers
questions.explanation: slice, spread and new Set all build a new collection of up to n entries. arr.reverse() mutates in place, and two-pointer swapping uses O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Which statements about amortised O(1) push on a doubling array are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An individual push can cost O(n) when it triggers a resize
It means each push is O(1) with high probability
The bound holds for every sequence of n pushes, not just on average over random inputs
Growing by a factor of 1.5 instead of 2 still gives amortised O(1)
questions.explanation: A resize push copies everything (O(n)), but the total over n pushes is O(n) for any sequence. Any constant growth factor above 1 gives a geometric series. There is no probability in amortised analysis.

questions.prompt: An algorithm with O(1) space complexity uses no memory at all beyond its input.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: O(1) space means the extra memory doesn't grow with n. It can still use a fixed number of variables, counters or even a fixed-size 26-slot array.

questions.prompt: A standard top-down merge sort on arrays needs O(n) auxiliary space for merging.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Merging two sorted halves into a temporary buffer needs O(n) extra space (plus O(log n) stack). That's the usual trade-off versus heap sort, which sorts in O(1) extra space but isn't stable.

questions.prompt: A BFS uses a plain array as its queue. On a graph with n nodes, what's the cost of the queue operations and the usual fix?
options: O(n log n), because shift is logarithmic
O(n^2) worst case, because shift re-indexes the array; use a head index instead of shift
O(n) total; shift is O(1) like pop
O(n^2), and the only fix is a linked-list library
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.shift moves every remaining element down, so n shifts can cost O(n^2). Keeping a `head` index (read queue[head++]) makes dequeue O(1). You don't need a library for this.

questions.prompt: You need to keep the items of array `a` (length n) that also appear in array `b` (length m). Which approach is asymptotically best?
options: Sort both and use includes: O(n log n)
a.filter(x => b.indexOf(x) !== -1): O(n log m)
const s = new Set(b); a.filter(x => s.has(x)): O(n + m) expected
a.filter(x => b.includes(x)): O(n + m)
questions.explanation: Building a Set is O(m) and each has() is expected O(1), giving O(n + m). includes and indexOf are linear scans, so the filter versions are O(n·m), not O(n + m) or O(n log m).

questions.prompt: What does the ECMAScript spec (since ES2019) together with V8's implementation guarantee about Array.prototype.sort?
options: O(n) for numeric arrays because it uses radix sort
Unstable, O(n^2) worst case (V8 uses quicksort)
Stable only for arrays shorter than 10 elements
Stable, O(n log n) worst case (V8 uses TimSort)
questions.explanation: ES2019 requires sort to be stable, and V8 switched to TimSort, which is O(n log n) worst case and O(n) on already-sorted runs. The old V8 behaviour (insertion sort for short arrays, quicksort otherwise) was unstable.

questions.prompt: A hot request path checks `Object.keys(cache).length > 1000` on a plain-object cache with k keys. What does that cost per call?
options: O(k), because it builds an array of all keys
O(1), objects track their size
O(1) amortised, because V8 caches the keys array
O(log k)
questions.explanation: Object.keys allocates and fills a new array of all k keys on every call, so it's O(k) time and memory. A Map exposes `.size` in O(1), which is one reason to prefer Map for caches.

questions.prompt: What is the expected time complexity of deduplicating an array with `[...new Set(arr)]`?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: Each insertion into the Set is expected O(1) and spreading it back out is O(n), so the total is O(n) expected. O(n log n) would be the sort-then-dedupe approach.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this code for an array of n users?
options: O(n^2), because each step copies the whole accumulator
O(n), reduce visits each element once
O(n log n)
O(1) amortised per user
questions.explanation: Spreading `acc` copies all keys collected so far, so step i costs O(i) and the total is O(n^2). Mutating the accumulator (acc[u.id] = u; return acc) or using a Map makes it O(n). Looping once doesn't make it O(n) if each step is O(n).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so '100' < '25' < '9'. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numeric order. The complexity is still O(n log n); only the order is surprising.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: bdca
dbca
dbac
bdac
questions.explanation: Sort is stable, so items with equal keys keep their original relative order: b before d (k = 1), a before c (k = 2), giving 'bdac'. Stability is what lets you sort by a secondary key first and the primary key second.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations are O(1) (amortised or expected) in a modern engine such as V8? Select all that apply.
options: arr.shift()
arr.push(x)
map.get(key)
arr.includes(x)
arr.pop()
arr.length
questions.explanation: push is amortised O(1), pop and length are O(1), and Map.get is expected O(1). shift re-indexes the remaining elements and includes scans linearly, so both are O(n).

questions.prompt: Which of these are O(n) in the size of the array? Select all that apply.
options: arr.splice(0, 1)
new Set(arr)
arr.at(-1)
arr.slice()
arr.concat(other) (counting the copy of arr)
questions.explanation: slice and concat copy elements, new Set inserts every element, and removing from the front with splice shifts everything left. at(-1) is a direct index access, which is O(1).

questions.prompt: arr.pop() is O(n) because the engine has to re-index the remaining elements.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: pop removes the last element, so no other indices change: it's O(1). Re-indexing happens with shift and unshift at the front, which is why those are O(n).

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks you to reverse a string in place in JavaScript. What's the right response?
options: Swap str[i] and str[n-1-i] with two pointers
JS strings are immutable, so convert to an array, reverse it, and join (O(n) extra space)
Use str.replace with a regex to swap characters in place
Use str.reverse(), which mutates the string
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable: assigning str[i] is silently ignored (or throws in strict mode). Two-pointer swapping is the right idea on a character array, not on a string. There's no String.prototype.reverse.

questions.prompt: Move all zeros in an array to the end, keeping the order of the non-zero elements, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Which approach works?
options: Filter non-zeros into a new array and append zeros
Sort with a comparator that puts zeros last
Use a write index: copy each non-zero to arr[write++], then fill the rest with zeros
splice out each zero and push a zero at the end
questions.explanation: One pass with a write pointer compacts the non-zeros in order, then the tail is zero-filled: O(n) time, O(1) space. splice in a loop is O(n^2), sorting is O(n log n), and filter uses O(n) extra space.

questions.prompt: How do you rotate an array right by k positions in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Call arr.unshift(arr.pop()) k times
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k % n elements, then reverse the rest
Sort the array by (index + k) % n
Copy into a new array at index (i + k) % n
questions.explanation: The triple-reverse trick is in place and touches each element a constant number of times. unshift is O(n) per call (O(n·k) overall), and copying to a new array is O(n) space. Remember k %= n for k > n.

questions.prompt: Sort an array containing only 0s, 1s and 2s in a single pass with O(1) extra space. Which technique is this?
options: Counting sort with a Map
Merge sort
Binary search for each boundary
Dutch national flag: low, mid and high pointers
questions.explanation: Dutch national flag keeps [0, low) as 0s, [low, mid) as 1s and (high, end] as 2s, swapping as mid advances. That's one pass in place. Counting sort is also O(n) but needs two passes.

questions.prompt: This is supposed to remove every even number from the array in place. What's wrong?
options: After a splice, the next element slides into index i and gets skipped
splice can't be used inside a for loop
Nothing: splice handles index shifting
It runs forever because arr.length changes
questions.explanation: Removing at i shifts the next element into i, then i++ skips it, so consecutive evens survive. Iterate backwards or use a write pointer. It also costs O(n^2) because each splice is O(n). It terminates since the length shrinks.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Reversing the whole array gives 7..1; reversing the first 3 gives 5,6,7; reversing the rest gives 1,2,3,4. Result: a right rotation by 3. 4,5,6,7,1,2,3 would be a left rotation.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Kadane's algorithm restarts the running sum whenever extending it is worse than starting fresh. The best subarray is [4, -1, 2, 1] = 6, found in one O(n) pass.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 'l' has char code 108, and 108 - 97 = 11; it appears twice, so counts[11] is 2, and the first index holding 2 is also 11. A 26-slot array is a common O(1)-space alternative to a Map for lowercase letters.

questions.prompt: Which of these array methods mutate the original array? Select all that apply.
options: slice()
sort()
concat()
toSorted()
splice()
reverse()
questions.explanation: sort, splice and reverse change the array in place. toSorted (ES2023), slice and concat return new arrays. Mixing these up causes bugs when you sort an input the caller still relies on.

questions.prompt: nums1 has length m + n, with m sorted values followed by n empty slots; nums2 has n sorted values. You merge nums2 into nums1 in place. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Filling from the back avoids overwriting nums1 values that haven't been compared yet
Filling from the front works without shifting elements
It needs O(m + n) extra space for a temporary buffer
The merge runs in O(m + n) time
questions.explanation: Writing the largest remaining value into the last free slot never clobbers unread data, so the merge is O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space. Filling from the front would overwrite nums1's own values unless you shift them, which is O(m·n).

questions.prompt: In JavaScript, `let s = 'cat'; s[0] = 'b';` changes s to 'bat'.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable primitives. The assignment is silently ignored in sloppy mode and throws a TypeError in strict mode. Build a new string or work on an array of characters instead.

questions.prompt: Count the subarrays whose sum equals k in an array that may contain negative numbers. Which approach is O(n)?
options: Running prefix sum plus a Map counting how often each prefix sum has occurred
A sliding window that shrinks when the sum exceeds k
Sort the array, then use two pointers
Binary search on the prefix-sum array
questions.explanation: A subarray (i, j] sums to k exactly when P[j] - P[i] = k, so at each j you add the count of earlier prefixes equal to P[j] - k. A sliding window needs non-negative values, and sorting destroys contiguity.

questions.prompt: You build P with P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + arr[i]. What is the sum of arr[l..r] inclusive?
options: P[r] - P[l]
questions.explanation: P[r + 1] is the sum of arr[0..r] and P[l] is the sum of arr[0..l-1]; subtracting leaves arr[l..r]. P[r] - P[l] drops arr[r]: the classic off-by-one.

questions.prompt: Why does the shrink-when-too-big sliding window fail for 'longest subarray with sum k' when the array has negative numbers, while prefix sums still work?
options: With negatives, the window sum isn't monotonic, so shrinking or growing doesn't reliably move it toward k
Prefix sums sort the array first, which removes negatives
Negative numbers overflow the window sum
Sliding windows can't handle arrays longer than k
questions.explanation: A window relies on 'adding increases the sum, removing decreases it'. Negatives break that, so a window you discarded might have become valid. Prefix sums with a Map of first occurrences check every start point implicitly without that assumption.

questions.prompt: With a 2D prefix sum S where S[i + 1][j + 1] is the sum of grid[0..i][0..j], what is the sum of the rectangle (r1, c1) to (r2, c2) inclusive?
questions.explanation: Take the big rectangle, subtract the strip above and the strip to the left, then add back the top-left corner that was subtracted twice (inclusion–exclusion). Subtracting the corner a third time, or using unshifted indices, gives wrong sums.

questions.prompt: An array of 10^5 values gets interleaved point updates and range-sum queries, about 10^5 of each. Why is a plain prefix-sum array a poor fit?
options: Range queries become O(n) once any update happens
Prefix sums can't answer range queries on numbers larger than 2^31
Each update forces an O(n) rebuild of the prefix array, so a Fenwick tree or segment tree (O(log n) per op) fits better
Prefix sums need the array to be sorted after each update
questions.explanation: Changing arr[i] changes every P[j] for j > i, which is O(n) per update and about 10^10 operations here. A Fenwick or segment tree supports both updates and queries in O(log n). Queries on a prefix array would still be O(1) if it were rebuilt.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: arr[2..5] = 4 + 1 + 5 + 9 = 19. P[6] = 23 and P[2] = 4, so 23 - 4 = 19. Using P[r] - P[l] would give 10 and drop the 9.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Prefix sums run 1, 3, 6, 3, 6. The matches are [1,2], [3], [1,2,3,-3], [3,-3,3] and the final [3], so 5. Seeding the map with {0: 1} is what counts subarrays that start at index 0.

questions.prompt: This applies range increments with a difference array. What does it print?
questions.explanation: Each update marks +v at l and -v at r + 1; a prefix sum then rebuilds the values: [1, 3, 3, 7, 2]. Index 3 gets 2 + 5 = 7, and index 4 only gets the +2. This makes each range update O(1).

questions.prompt: Which problems are naturally solved with prefix sums (possibly plus a hash map)? Select all that apply.
options: Finding the running median of a data stream
Longest substring without repeating characters
Many range-sum queries on a static array
Counting subarrays with sum exactly k
Finding a pivot index where left sum equals right sum
questions.explanation: Range sums, subarray-sum counting and pivot index all reduce to differences of prefix sums. A running median needs two heaps, and longest unique substring is a sliding window with a set or map.

questions.prompt: Which statements about prefix techniques are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Range products via prefix products and division break when the array contains zeros
Using a prefix array of length n + 1 with P[0] = 0 removes the special case for ranges starting at index 0
Prefix sums require the input to be sorted
Prefix XOR answers range-XOR queries, because x ^ x = 0
questions.explanation: Any invertible associative operation works (XOR undoes itself); division can't undo a zero; the leading 0 sentinel simplifies indexing. Prefix sums work on any order: sorting would change which elements are contiguous.

questions.prompt: After one element of the underlying array changes, a prefix-sum array still answers range sums correctly in O(1) without being rebuilt.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every P[j] after the changed index is now stale, so you must update O(n) entries. For frequent updates, use a Fenwick tree or segment tree.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this naive recursive function?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each call branches into two more and the same subproblems are recomputed repeatedly, so the call tree grows exponentially (about φ^n, bounded by O(2^n)). O(n) is what you get only after memoizing or tabulating.

questions.prompt: You add a Map-based memo to recursive Fibonacci so each fib(k) is computed once. What are the time and extra space costs for fib(n)?
options: O(n) time, O(n) space
O(n) time, O(1) space
O(2^n) time, O(n) space
O(log n) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each of the n states is computed once with O(1) work, giving O(n) time. Space is O(n) for the memo plus O(n) recursion depth. O(1) space needs the bottom-up rolling-variable version, not memoization.

questions.prompt: A memoized top-down solution works for n = 5,000 but throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` for n = 200,000. The bottom-up version of the same recurrence works. Why?
options: The memo Map has a maximum size and stops caching beyond it
Memoized results are garbage-collected before they are reused
Bottom-up DP uses a different recurrence that needs fewer states
Recursion depth grows with n and exceeds V8's call stack limit
questions.explanation: Top-down recursion goes about n frames deep before hitting a base case, and V8's stack holds only on the order of 10k frames. Tabulation loops in a single frame. The memo Map is not the problem; Maps can hold millions of entries.

questions.prompt: You space-optimised an LCS table down to two rows and it returns the correct length. Now the interviewer asks you to also return the subsequence itself. What is the core problem?
options: Backtracking needs the full table (or extra work like Hirschberg's) to retrace choices
You must re-run the DP with the strings swapped to recover the characters
The subsequence can only be recovered from a top-down memoized version
Two rows give the wrong length once strings exceed 1,000 characters
questions.explanation: Reconstruction walks back through earlier rows to see which transition produced each cell; a rolling array has discarded them. You either keep the O(mn) table or use divide-and-conquer (Hirschberg) to rebuild it in linear space. The length itself stays correct.

questions.prompt: Which pair of properties makes a problem a good fit for dynamic programming?
options: Independent halves that share no subproblems
A monotonic predicate over the answer space
A greedy-choice property and sorted input
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
questions.explanation: DP pays off when subproblems repeat (so caching helps) and the optimum is built from optimal sub-answers. Independent halves with no sharing is plain divide and conquer (e.g. merge sort), where memoization gains nothing.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: fib(10) is one call, and each fib(k) for k = 2..10 makes exactly two child calls (fib(k-2) is a memo hit or base case), so 1 + 9×2 = 19 calls. 177 is the call count without memoization.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The table starts with dp[0] = dp[1] = 1 and fills indices 2..5 inclusive, so it has 6 entries: 1,1,2,3,5,8. Stopping at 5 entries is the off-by-one you get if the loop used i < n.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine advantages of bottom-up tabulation over top-down memoization? Select all that apply.
options: You never need to work out an evaluation order for states
Computes only the states reachable from the final answer
Makes rolling-array space optimisation straightforward
Avoids per-call function overhead and Map lookups
No risk of exceeding the recursion depth limit
questions.explanation: Loops avoid stack limits and call overhead, and a fixed iteration order lets you discard old rows. Computing only reachable states and not needing an explicit order are advantages of memoization, not tabulation.

questions.prompt: Which of these mistakes break a memoized recursive solution, either giving wrong answers or losing the caching? Select all that apply.
options: Keys are strings like `${i},${j}` in a shared Map
The memo object is created inside the recursive function
The Map lives in a closure shared by all recursive calls
The cache key omits a parameter that affects the result
Lookups use `memo[k] || solve(k)` when 0 is a valid answer
questions.explanation: A key missing a parameter merges different states (wrong answers); a memo created per call is never reused; `||` treats a cached 0 as a miss and recomputes it. String keys in a shared closure Map are a normal, correct pattern.

questions.prompt: Memoizing naive recursive Fibonacci reduces its time complexity from exponential to linear.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With memoization each fib(k) for k ≤ n is computed once with constant extra work, so the exponential call tree collapses to O(n) distinct calls.

questions.prompt: A top-down memoized solution always computes at least as many subproblems as filling the full bottom-up table.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Memoization computes only the states actually reachable from the starting call, which can be far fewer than the full table (e.g. sparse knapsack capacities). Tabulation usually fills every cell whether needed or not.

questions.prompt: In House Robber (no two adjacent houses), let dp[i] be the best total using houses 0..i. Which recurrence is correct?
options: dp[i] = dp[i-2] + nums[i]
dp[i] = dp[i-1] + nums[i]
dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])
dp[i] = max(dp[i-2], dp[i-1] + nums[i])
questions.explanation: Either skip house i (keep dp[i-1]) or rob it and add to the best total ending two houses back (dp[i-2] + nums[i]). Adding nums[i] to dp[i-1] could rob two adjacent houses.

questions.prompt: You can climb 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to climb exactly 4 steps?
questions.explanation: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] + dp[i-3] with dp[0] = 1: dp[1] = 1, dp[2] = 2, dp[3] = 4, dp[4] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. 5 is the answer if only steps of 1 and 2 were allowed.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the classic LIS DP where dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all j < i with a[j] < a[i]?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: For each i you scan every earlier j, giving about n²/2 comparisons, so O(n²). O(n log n) needs the different patience-sorting approach with binary search over a tails array.

questions.prompt: In House Robber II the houses form a circle, so the first and last are adjacent. What is the standard approach?
options: Rob every other house starting from whichever end is larger
Run linear House Robber on the array doubled to length 2n
Run the linear version on nums[1..n-1] and on nums[0..n-2], take the max
Run the linear version once and subtract min(first, last) from the result
questions.explanation: At most one of the first and last house can be robbed, so solve the two linear subproblems that exclude one of them and take the better one. Subtracting min(first, last) doesn't work because the optimum may not include either end.

questions.prompt: In the O(n log n) LIS algorithm that keeps a `tails` array and binary-searches each element into it, what does tails[k] represent?
options: The smallest tail value of any increasing subsequence of length k+1
The largest value seen so far at position k of the input
The k-th element of one actual longest increasing subsequence
The number of increasing subsequences that end at index k
questions.explanation: tails[k] holds the smallest possible ending value for an increasing subsequence of length k+1, which keeps future extensions as easy as possible. Its length equals the LIS length, but the array itself is often not a real subsequence of the input.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: [2,7,9,3,1] → 2 + 9 + 1 = 12. [2,1,1,2] → rob the two ends for 4; the alternating-index sums are only 3, which is why greedy even/odd picking fails here.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 3 → [3]; 10 → [3,10]; 2 replaces 3 → [2,10]; 1 replaces 2 → [1,10]; 20 appends → [1,10,20]. The length 3 is the correct LIS length, but 1,10,20 is not a real subsequence (1 comes after 10 in the input).

questions.prompt: Which of these problems are naturally solved with a 1-D DP whose state is a single index or amount? Select all that apply.
options: Number of ways to decode a digit string
Climbing stairs with steps of 1 or 2
Longest common subsequence of two strings
Finding the k-th smallest element of an array
Minimum number of coins to make an amount
questions.explanation: Stairs and decode-ways index by position, and coin change indexes by amount, so all three are 1-D. LCS needs a state for a position in each string (2-D), and k-th smallest is a selection problem (quickselect or heap), not DP.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Longest Increasing Subsequence problem are correct? Select all that apply.
options: For strictly increasing, replace the first tail ≥ x; for non-decreasing, the first tail > x
It can be solved in O(n log n) with binary search over a tails array
The final tails array is always one valid LIS of the input
Greedily taking each next element larger than the last always finds the LIS
questions.explanation: Binary search gives O(n log n), and the lower-bound vs upper-bound choice decides whether equal values can extend a sequence. tails is not necessarily a real subsequence, and greedy fails on inputs like [1, 100, 2, 3].

questions.prompt: The number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time follows the Fibonacci sequence.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) with ways(0) = ways(1) = 1, which is the Fibonacci recurrence shifted by one index.

questions.prompt: In House Robber, taking either all even-indexed or all odd-indexed houses (whichever sums higher) always gives the optimal total.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Counterexample: [2, 1, 1, 2]. Even indices give 3 and odd indices give 3, but robbing houses 0 and 3 gives 4. The optimum can skip two houses in a row, which only the DP explores.

questions.prompt: A robot starts at the top-left of a 3×3 grid and can only move right or down. How many distinct paths reach the bottom-right cell?
questions.explanation: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] with the first row and column set to 1 gives 1,1,1 / 1,2,3 / 1,3,6. Equivalently C(4,2) = 6: choose which 2 of the 4 moves go down.

questions.prompt: In the LCS table, dp[i][j] is the LCS length of a[0..i) and b[0..j). If a[i-1] !== b[j-1], what is dp[i][j]?
options: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
questions.explanation: When the last characters differ, at least one of them isn't in the LCS, so drop one or the other and take the better result. dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 is the case where the characters match.

questions.prompt: In edit distance, when a[i-1] !== b[j-1], dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]). Which term represents replacing a[i-1] with b[j-1]?
options: dp[i][j-1]
dp[i-1][j]
dp[i][j]
questions.explanation: A replacement consumes one character from each string, so it moves diagonally from dp[i-1][j-1]. dp[i-1][j] is deleting a[i-1], and dp[i][j-1] is inserting b[j-1].

questions.prompt: Coin change counting with coins [1, 2] and amount 3. Looping coins in the outer loop and amounts in the inner loop gives 2. What do you get if amounts are the outer loop and coins the inner loop?
options: 3, because it counts ordered sequences like 1+2 and 2+1 separately
2, because loop order never affects the count
4, because the base case dp[0] = 1 is counted twice
1, because each amount is updated only once per coin
questions.explanation: Coins-outer counts combinations (each multiset once): {1,1,1}, {1,2}. Amount-outer lets every coin be the last step at every amount, so it counts permutations: 1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1 = 3. Picking the wrong order is a classic interview bug.

questions.prompt: 0/1 knapsack DP runs in O(n·W) where W is the capacity. Why is it called pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial?
options: W is a numeric value; its input size is log W bits, so n·W is exponential in input size
Its running time depends on the number of distinct item weights
The table needs O(2^n) memory unless it is space-optimised
It only runs in polynomial time when all weights are powers of two
questions.explanation: Complexity is measured against input length. Writing W takes about log₂W bits, so doubling the bit length squares W and the runtime. With W around 10^12 the DP is unusable even though n is small.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The LCS of ABCBDAB and BDCABA has length 4 (e.g. BCBA or BDAB). abc and def share no characters, so the answer is 0.

questions.prompt: This code tries to initialise a 3×3 DP table. What does it print?
questions.explanation: fill() puts the same inner array reference in every row, so writing grid[0][0] changes all three rows. Use Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => new Array(3).fill(0)) to create independent rows.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: horse → ros takes 3 edits (replace h with r, delete r, delete e). From an empty string, the loop never runs and prev[3] = 3 from the base row: insert all three characters.

questions.prompt: Which of these base cases are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Edit distance: dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j
0/1 knapsack max value: dp[0][w] = Infinity for every w
Unique grid paths (no obstacles): first row and first column are all 1
LCS: dp[0][j] = 0 and dp[i][0] = 0
Edit distance: dp[0][0] = 1
questions.explanation: Turning a prefix into an empty string takes i deletions, an empty string shares nothing, and border cells have one path. With no items the knapsack value is 0, not Infinity, and dp[0][0] for edit distance is 0 edits.

questions.prompt: Which of these 1-D space optimisations produce correct results? Select all that apply.
options: 0/1 knapsack value with one array, capacity iterated low to high
LCS length using two rows (previous and current)
Unbounded knapsack value with one array, capacity iterated low to high
Edit distance with one row, overwriting without saving the old diagonal
0/1 knapsack value with one array, capacity iterated high to low
questions.explanation: Going high to low in 0/1 knapsack reads only last round's values, so each item is used once. Low to high reuses the item, which is right for unbounded knapsack and wrong for 0/1. Edit distance needs the old dp[i-1][j-1] saved before you overwrite it.

questions.prompt: The edit distance between strings of lengths m and n is always at least |m − n|.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Replacements keep the length the same, so the length gap can only be closed by at least |m − n| insertions or deletions. It is also at most max(m, n).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 5 = 101 and 3 = 011, so AND = 001 (1), OR = 111 (7), XOR = 110 (6). ~5 flips all 32 bits, giving -(5 + 1) = -6 in two's complement, not -5.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: >>> 0 reinterprets the 32 bits as unsigned, so -1 becomes 4294967295. >> is arithmetic and copies the sign bit, so -1 >> 1 stays -1. -8 is 0xFFFFFFF8; shifting it right by 28 with zero fill leaves 0xF = 15.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 1 << 31 sets the sign bit, so it's -2147483648; >>> 0 reads it as unsigned 2147483648. Shift counts are taken mod 32, so 1 << 32 is 1 << 0 = 1. 2**32 | 0 converts to int32, which wraps 2^32 to 0.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly checks whether an integer n is a power of two?
questions.explanation: A power of two has exactly one set bit, and n - 1 clears it while setting all lower bits, so n & (n - 1) is 0. The n > 0 guard is needed because 0 & -1 is also 0. (n & -n) isolates the lowest set bit; it's 1 only for odd numbers.

questions.prompt: How many times does this loop body run?
options: Once per set (1) bit in n
log2(n) times rounded up
Once per bit up to the highest set bit
Always 32 times
questions.explanation: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit each iteration (Brian Kernighan's trick), so the loop runs popcount(n) times. A loop that checks bits one by one with >>> 1 would run up to the highest set bit.

questions.prompt: Every number in an array appears exactly twice except one. Which approach finds the single number in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Sort the array and compare neighbours
Sum the elements and divide by two
XOR all elements together
Count occurrences in a Map
questions.explanation: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative, so pairs cancel and the unique value remains. Sorting is O(n log n), and a Map needs O(n) space.

questions.prompt: This subset-enumeration loop works for n = 20 but runs zero iterations for n = 31. Why?
options: Numbers above 2^30 lose precision in IEEE-754 doubles
The shift count 31 is masked to 0, so the bound becomes 1
1 << 31 is -2147483648, so mask < (1 << n) is false at once
V8 caps loops at 2^30 iterations to prevent hangs
questions.explanation: Shifts produce signed 32-bit results, and 1 << 31 sets the sign bit, giving a negative bound. Doubles represent 2^31 exactly, and only counts of 32 or more wrap. Use 2 ** n as the bound (or BigInt), although 2^31 iterations is too many anyway.

questions.prompt: What does `x & -x` compute for a positive 32-bit integer x, and where is it commonly used?
options: The number of trailing zeros of x; used in hashing
The absolute value of x; used for branch-free abs
The highest set bit of x; used in heap indexing
The lowest set bit of x; used in Fenwick (binary indexed) trees
questions.explanation: -x is ~x + 1, which flips every bit above the lowest set bit, so the AND keeps only that bit (e.g. 12 & -12 = 4). Fenwick trees use it to step between nodes. It returns the bit's value, not the count of trailing zeros.

questions.prompt: You need a bitmask of 64 boolean flags in JavaScript. Which approaches work correctly? Select all that apply.
options: A single Number with `mask | (1 << k)` for k up to 63
BigInt masks with `mask | (1n << BigInt(k))`
Two Number values holding the high and low 32 bits
A Uint32Array of length 2 indexed by k >>> 5
A single Number using `2 ** k` and the & operator
questions.explanation: BigInt bitwise ops have arbitrary width, and splitting into two 32-bit words works with ordinary operators. On a Number, & and | truncate to 32 bits and shift counts wrap mod 32, so flags above bit 31 are lost.

questions.prompt: Which expressions correctly test whether bit k (0 ≤ k ≤ 31) of a 32-bit integer x is set? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Shifting bit k down then & 1 works with either shift (sign-filled high bits are masked away). Comparing with !== 0 also works. > 0 fails for k = 31 because the result is negative, and modulo only checks low bits.

questions.prompt: For every finite number x in JavaScript, `~~x` gives the same result as `Math.trunc(x)`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: ~~ goes through ToInt32, so it agrees with Math.trunc only within the signed 32-bit range. For example, ~~3e9 is -1294967296, while Math.trunc(3e9) is 3000000000.

questions.prompt: Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6. Taking the largest coin first gives 4 + 1 + 1. What is the optimal number of coins, and which approach guarantees it?
options: 2 (3 + 3), found by DP over amounts 0..6
3 (3 + 1 + 1 + 1), found by backtracking
3, and largest-coin greedy is optimal here
2 (4 + 2), found by greedy after sorting
questions.explanation: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) gives dp[6] = 2 via 3 + 3. Greedy is optimal only for canonical coin systems like [1, 5, 10, 25]; with arbitrary denominations it can miss the optimum.

questions.prompt: "Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters." Which technique fits best?
options: Binary search on the answer length
2-D DP over (start, end) pairs
Backtracking over all substrings
Sliding window with a last-seen index map
questions.explanation: A contiguous window that grows on the right and jumps its left edge past the last duplicate solves it in O(n). A DP over (start, end) pairs is O(n²) and gains nothing, because the window's validity changes monotonically.

questions.prompt: "Return every subset of nums whose sum equals target." Why is backtracking a better fit than DP here?
options: Backtracking always runs in polynomial time with pruning
DP tables are limited to 2-D in JavaScript
The output itself can be exponential, so you must enumerate anyway
DP cannot handle negative numbers in nums
questions.explanation: When you must list every solution, the output can have up to 2^n subsets and no caching avoids producing them. DP shines when you need a count, a yes/no answer or an optimum. Pruning helps backtracking but doesn't make it polynomial.

questions.prompt: "Given meeting intervals, find the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings you can attend." Which approach is correct and simplest?
options: Greedy: sort by start time and pick the earliest-starting meeting each time
Greedy: pick the shortest meetings first until none fit
Greedy: sort by end time and pick each meeting that starts after the last end
DP over every subset of meetings, keeping the largest valid one
questions.explanation: Picking the earliest finishing meeting leaves the most room for the rest, and an exchange argument proves it optimal (O(n log n)). Earliest start fails when one long early meeting blocks several short ones; shortest-first also has counterexamples.

questions.prompt: "Can this array (n = 200, each value 1..100) be split into two subsets with equal sums?" What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Sort and greedily assign each value to the smaller side
Try all 2^200 subsets with early termination
Two pointers on the sorted array
Subset-sum DP over reachable sums up to total/2
questions.explanation: The total is at most 20,000, so a boolean DP over sums up to 10,000 costs about 200 × 10,000 operations, which is cheap. Greedy balancing fails (e.g. [3,3,2,2,2]), and brute force over 2^200 subsets is hopeless.

questions.prompt: "Minimum number of moves from S to E in a grid maze, moving in 4 directions." A candidate writes dp[r][c] = 1 + min(neighbours). What is the flaw, and what should they use?
options: The grid needs memoization by direction; use 3-D DP
4-way moves create cycles, so there's no fill order; use BFS
Nothing; DP fills the grid row by row correctly
DP works but needs O(n^3) time; use DFS instead
questions.explanation: DP needs subproblems that form a DAG. With moves in all four directions, cells depend on each other in cycles, so no fill order works. BFS finds unweighted shortest paths in O(rows × cols). DFS doesn't give shortest paths.

questions.prompt: "Find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray (values may be negative)." Which pattern fits?
options: Sliding window that shrinks whenever the sum becomes negative and never resets
Sort the array and sum the largest positive values
Kadane's algorithm: best sum ending at i = max(a[i], best ending at i-1 + a[i])
Prefix sums with a hash map of seen sums
questions.explanation: Kadane's is a 1-D DP with O(1) space: either extend the previous run or start fresh at i. Sorting breaks contiguity. A prefix-sum map solves 'subarray sums to k', not 'maximum sum'.

questions.prompt: Which problem phrasings are typical signals that DP is the right tool? Select all that apply.
options: "How many ways are there to ..."
"Minimum cost to reach the end, choosing at each step ..."
"Find the k-th largest element ..."
"Return all valid combinations that ..."
"Length of the longest subsequence such that ..."
questions.explanation: Counting, min/max over a sequence of choices, and longest-subsequence questions usually have overlapping subproblems. Listing all combinations calls for backtracking, and k-th largest calls for a heap or quickselect.

questions.prompt: For which of these problems is a greedy algorithm provably optimal, so DP is unnecessary? Select all that apply.
options: Coin change with arbitrary denominations
Huffman coding by merging the two least frequent
Fractional knapsack by value/weight ratio
Activity selection by earliest finish time
0/1 knapsack by value/weight ratio
questions.explanation: Activity selection, fractional knapsack and Huffman all have greedy-choice proofs. 0/1 knapsack by ratio fails because items can't be split (a high-ratio small item can block a better fit), and arbitrary coin sets break greedy.

questions.prompt: If a recursive solution never calls itself twice with the same arguments (e.g. generating all permutations), adding memoization won't improve its asymptotic running time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Memoization only saves time when subproblems repeat. With no overlap every cache lookup misses, so you pay for memory without saving any work.

questions.prompt: Any problem with optimal substructure should be solved with DP rather than a greedy algorithm.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Optimal substructure is necessary for both DP and greedy. Dijkstra's algorithm and MST algorithms have it and also have a greedy-choice property, so greedy is correct and faster. DP is needed when a locally best choice can be wrong.

questions.prompt: You count occurrences with a plain object: `counts[x] = (counts[x] ?? 0) + 1` over the array [1, '1', 1]. What ends up in counts?
options: A TypeError, because the keys have mixed types
{ 1: 3 }, with a numeric key
{ 1: 2, '1': 1 }, because number and string keys stay distinct
{ '1': 3 }, because object keys are coerced to strings
questions.explanation: Plain-object property keys are strings (or symbols), so 1 and '1' are the same key and the count is 3. A Map keeps 1 and '1' distinct because it compares keys with SameValueZero.

questions.prompt: A function counts words from user-submitted text into `const counts = {}`. A user submits the word '__proto__'. What's the risk and the cleanest fix?
options: No risk: '__proto__' is stored like any other key
It deletes all existing keys; call Object.freeze(counts) first
It throws a SyntaxError; wrap the loop in try/catch
Assigning counts['__proto__'] hits the prototype setter instead of storing a count; use a Map or Object.create(null)
questions.explanation: On a normal object, '__proto__' is an accessor inherited from Object.prototype, so the count is never stored and can corrupt lookups. Map or a null-prototype object has no inherited keys. Freezing would just make the counts unwritable.

questions.prompt: You want to attach computed metadata to request objects without stopping them from being garbage collected once the request ends. Which structure fits?
options: A WeakMap keyed by the request object
A plain object keyed by the request
A Map keyed by the request object
An array of [request, metadata] pairs
questions.explanation: WeakMap holds its keys weakly, so when nothing else references the request, the entry can be collected. A Map keeps the request alive for as long as the Map lives (a leak), and a plain object would turn the key into the string '[object Object]'.

questions.prompt: In what order does Object.keys return the own string keys of a plain object?
options: Unspecified: it depends on the engine's hash function
Integer-like keys in ascending numeric order first, then the other string keys in insertion order
Alphabetical order
Strictly in insertion order
questions.explanation: The spec defines OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys: array-index-like keys ascending, then strings in creation order (then symbols, which Object.keys skips). Map, in contrast, iterates in pure insertion order for every key type.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 1 x
2 undefined
1 y
2 x
questions.explanation: Both object keys are converted to the string '[object Object]', so the second assignment overwrites the first: one key, value 'y'. Use a Map (or WeakMap) when keys are objects.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 2 num
2 str
1 str
1 num
questions.explanation: Map compares keys with SameValueZero, so the number 1 and the string '1' are different keys: size 2, and get(1) returns 'num'. A plain object would merge them into the single key '1'.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
const o = { b: 1, 2: 1, a: 1, 1: 1 };
console.log(Object.keys(o).join(','));
questions.explanation: Integer-like keys come first in ascending order (1, 2), then string keys in insertion order (b, a). Code that depends on 'insertion order' of a plain object breaks as soon as keys look like numbers.

questions.prompt: You replace a plain-object cache with a Map. Which behaviour changes should you expect? Select all that apply.
options: Keys 1 and '1' are now distinct entries
JSON.stringify(cache) now produces '{}' unless you convert the entries first
cache.size replaces Object.keys(cache).length and is O(1)
cache['k'] = v still adds an entry that cache.get('k') returns
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify ignores Map entries, size is a direct property, and keys aren't coerced to strings. Bracket assignment on a Map sets an ordinary object property, not a Map entry, so get('k') returns undefined.

questions.prompt: Which statements about WeakMap are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An entry can be garbage collected once its key object is unreachable elsewhere
Using a string as a key throws a TypeError
You can't iterate over its entries
It has a .size property, like Map
questions.explanation: WeakMap keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols), so primitives like strings throw. Because entries can vanish at any GC, WeakMap is not iterable and has no size.

questions.prompt: `'toString' in {}` evaluates to true, which is one reason the `in` operator is unreliable for membership checks on a plain-object hash table.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `in` walks the prototype chain, and toString is inherited from Object.prototype. Use Object.hasOwn(obj, key), a null-prototype object, or Map.prototype.has.

questions.prompt: Map compares object keys structurally, so m.get({ id: 1 }) finds an entry that was set with a different { id: 1 } literal.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Object keys are compared by reference identity. Two separate literals are different objects, so get returns undefined. To key by value, derive a primitive key such as the id or a canonical string.

questions.prompt: To check whether two strings of length n are anagrams, why is counting characters usually preferred over sorting both?
options: Sorting can't handle Unicode at all
Sorting fails on repeated characters
Counting is O(n) while sorting is O(n log n)
Counting uses less memory than sorting in every case
questions.explanation: One pass to increment counts and one to decrement them is O(n) versus O(n log n) for sorting. Sorting handles repeats fine. Counting uses O(k) space for k distinct characters, which isn't always smaller.

questions.prompt: What's the standard O(n) approach to find the first non-repeating character in a string?
options: Count frequencies in one pass, then scan the string again and return the first character with count 1
Use a Set and return the first character added
For each character, scan the rest of the string for a duplicate
Sort the string and pick the first unique character
questions.explanation: Two passes give O(n): build counts, then walk the original order. The nested scan is O(n^2), and sorting loses the original order, so you can't tell which unique character came first.

questions.prompt: Return the k most frequent elements of an array of n items in O(n) time. Which approach achieves this?
options: Insert every element into a max-heap and pop k times
Sort the array and scan runs
Count with a Map, then bucket the values by frequency (index 1..n) and read buckets from the highest
Count with a Map, then sort entries by count: O(n)
questions.explanation: Frequencies lie between 1 and n, so a bucket array indexed by frequency avoids comparison sorting: O(n). Sorting the entries is O(m log m) for m distinct values, not O(n). A size-k min-heap gives O(n log k), also not linear.

questions.prompt: When grouping anagrams of lowercase words, which grouping key is valid and avoids sorting each word?
options: A string encoding the 26 letter counts, e.g. counts.join('#')
The first and last characters
The sum of the character codes
The word's length
questions.explanation: A 26-count signature is identical exactly when two words are anagrams, and building it is O(k) per word. Code sums collide ('ad' and 'bc' both sum to 197). Length and first/last letters are far too coarse.

questions.prompt: An element appears more than n/2 times in an array. Which algorithm finds it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Sorting and taking the middle element
A frequency Map
Boyer–Moore majority vote
Binary search on the value range
questions.explanation: Boyer–Moore keeps one candidate and a counter, incrementing on matches and decrementing otherwise; the majority survives. A Map is O(n) time but O(n) space, and sorting is O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: s 4
s 5
i 5
i 4
questions.explanation: The counts are m:1, i:4, s:4, p:2. Map iterates in insertion order (m, i, s, p), and the strict > keeps the first character to reach 4, which is 'i'. Using >= would return 's'. Tie-breaking rules matter in frequency questions.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: undefined undefined
NaN NaN
questions.explanation: The first increment computes undefined + 1, which is NaN, and NaN + 1 stays NaN. Initialise with (counts[c] ?? 0) + 1 or (counts[c] || 0) + 1.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: true true true
true false true
false false true
true false false
questions.explanation: 'baa' supplies two a's and a b, so 'aab' works. 'ab' has only one 'a', so 'aa' fails. An empty note needs nothing, so it's true. Decrementing counts as you consume them is the core move.

questions.prompt: When can a fixed array of 26 counters replace a Map for character frequencies? Select the statements that are correct. Select all that apply.
options: When the input may contain arbitrary Unicode such as emoji
It gives O(1) extra space with respect to the input length
Comparing two such signatures costs a constant 26 steps, independent of n
When the input is guaranteed to be lowercase a–z
questions.explanation: A fixed alphabet maps each character to an index, giving constant space and constant-time signature comparison. Arbitrary Unicode has far too many possible characters (and surrogate pairs), so a Map is needed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about checking whether two strings are anagrams are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Comparing lengths first allows an early return
Comparing the sums of character codes is a valid check
If any count goes negative while decrementing for the second string, they aren't anagrams
Sorting both strings and comparing also works, in O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Different lengths can't be anagrams; a negative count means the second string has an extra character; sorting is a correct but slower check. Code sums collide (e.g. 'ad' and 'bc'), so a matching sum proves nothing.

questions.prompt: Frequency counting with a Map always uses O(1) extra space, because the set of possible values is finite.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A Map uses O(k) space for k distinct values, which can be O(n) for numbers or arbitrary strings. It's only O(1) when the alphabet is fixed and small, like 26 lowercase letters.

questions.prompt: In two-sum on a sorted array with lo at the start and hi at the end, the current sum is less than the target. What should you do and why?
options: Decrement hi, because the sum needs to change
Increment lo, because that is the only move that can increase the sum
Restart with lo + 1 and hi = n - 1
Move both pointers inward
questions.explanation: The array is sorted, so moving lo right can only increase the sum, while moving hi left can only decrease it. Each step discards a value that can't be part of any answer, giving O(n).

questions.prompt: To remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the count of unique values, what does the slow/fast pointer approach do?
options: Swap duplicates to the end with opposite-end pointers
Use splice whenever two neighbours are equal
fast scans; when nums[fast] differs from nums[slow], increment slow and copy; return slow + 1
Build a Set and copy it back into the array
questions.explanation: slow marks the end of the unique prefix; fast finds the next new value. That's one pass with O(1) space. splice is O(n) per call, and a Set uses O(n) extra memory.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the standard 3Sum solution (sort, then for each i run two pointers on the rest)?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Sorting is O(n log n), then each of n anchors runs an O(n) two-pointer scan: O(n^2) total. The sort doesn't dominate. Brute force over all triples would be O(n^3).

questions.prompt: In 'container with most water' (heights with lo/hi pointers at both ends), why do you always move the pointer at the shorter line?
options: The area is limited by the shorter line, so keeping it while shrinking the width can't beat the current area
Moving the shorter line guarantees the next area is larger
Moving the taller line always increases the area
It's arbitrary; either pointer works
questions.explanation: With the shorter line fixed, every narrower container has smaller width and height at most that short line, so none can beat the current area. That line is safe to discard. Moving it doesn't guarantee a bigger area; it's just the only move that might find one.

questions.prompt: You move a slow pointer one node and a fast pointer two nodes at a time through a singly linked list until fast reaches the end. Where is slow?
options: At the head
At a node chosen at random
At (or next to) the middle node
At the last node
questions.explanation: fast covers twice the distance, so when it reaches the end, slow has covered half: the middle (which middle you get for even lengths depends on the loop condition). The same fast/slow idea detects cycles in Floyd's algorithm.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: false true
false false
true false
true true
questions.explanation: Skipping non-alphanumerics and comparing case-insensitively, the first string reads 'amanaplanacanalpanama', a palindrome. 'raceacar' isn't. Two pointers do this in O(n) with no cleaned copy.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: slow ends at index 4, so there are 5 unique values, 0,1,2,3,4, in the prefix. Elements after the prefix are leftovers and don't matter.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The largest square is at one of the two ends, so you fill the output from the back: 100, 16, 9, 1, 0, which reads 0,1,9,16,100. That's O(n), versus O(n log n) for squaring and then sorting.

questions.prompt: Which statements about two-pointer techniques are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Opposite-end pointers find a pair sum in an unsorted array just as well
Same-direction (slow/fast) pointers suit in-place compaction such as removing duplicates
Opposite-end two-sum relies on the array being sorted
Sorting first to enable two pointers costs O(n log n) and loses the original indices
questions.explanation: Pointer moves are only safe when sorted order tells you which direction changes the sum. If you need original indices (as in classic two-sum), sorting loses them unless you sort index pairs, so a hash map is often better there.

questions.prompt: In sorted 3Sum (find unique triples summing to 0), which steps are correct for avoiding duplicates or pruning? Select all that apply.
options: Break out of the outer loop once nums[i] > 0
Skip index i when nums[i] === nums[i - 1]
Set hi = n - 1 once before the outer loop and never reset it
After recording a triple, advance lo and hi past equal neighbouring values
questions.explanation: Skipping equal anchors and equal lo/hi values prevents duplicate triples. Once nums[i] > 0, every later value is positive, so no triple can sum to 0. hi must be reset to n - 1 for each new i.

questions.prompt: On an already sorted array, the opposite-end two-pointer pair-sum check runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each step moves one pointer inward, so there are at most n - 1 steps, and only two indices are stored. If the array isn't sorted yet, add O(n log n) for sorting.

questions.prompt: To find the maximum sum of any k consecutive elements, what does the fixed-size sliding window do at each step?
options: Sort the window and take the top k
Recompute the sum of the k elements from scratch
Binary search for the best starting index
Add the element entering the window and subtract the one leaving it
questions.explanation: Updating the running sum by +entering and -leaving is O(1) per step, so O(n) overall. Recomputing every window is O(n·k).

questions.prompt: In 'longest substring without repeating characters', you store each character's last index. When you see a repeat, why must you set left = Math.max(left, last.get(c) + 1) rather than just last.get(c) + 1?
options: Math.max makes the loop O(n) instead of O(n^2)
To avoid an off-by-one at the end of the string
The stored index may be left of the current window; without max, left can jump backwards and re-admit duplicates
It's only needed for strings with uppercase letters
questions.explanation: In 'abba', when the final 'a' arrives, its old index 0 is already outside the window [2, 2]. Setting left = 1 would move the window backwards and count 'bba'. max keeps left monotonic. Complexity is O(n) either way.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the standard minimum-window-substring solution, with s of length m and t of length n?
options: O(m log m)
O(m · n)
O(m + n)
questions.explanation: Counting t is O(n). Then right and left each move forward at most m times, and validity is tracked with a 'formed' counter in O(1), so the total is O(m + n). Re-checking all of t's counts on each step would add a factor.

questions.prompt: What property must a problem have for a variable-size 'expand right, shrink left' window to be correct?
options: The answer must be at most k
All values must be distinct
Validity must be monotonic: if a window is valid, its sub-windows are too (or expanding never fixes an invalid window)
The input must be sorted
questions.explanation: Shrinking from the left only makes sense if discarded start positions can never lead to a better answer, which needs monotonic validity. Examples: 'at most k distinct', or sums of non-negative numbers. Sortedness isn't required; the window keeps order.

questions.prompt: Which technique computes the maximum of every window of size k in O(n) total?
options: Recomputing Math.max over each window
A max-heap of the window's elements
Sorting each window
A monotonic deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back
questions.explanation: The deque drops indices that left the window and pops smaller values from the back, since they can never be a future max. Each index is pushed and popped at most once: O(n). A heap gives O(n log k).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The window sums are 8, 7, 9 and 6, so the best is 9, from [5, 1, 3]. Each slide is a single add and subtract.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 'abc', 'wke' and 'ab' (or 'ba') are the longest unique substrings, with lengths 3, 3 and 2. 'pwke' isn't contiguous, so the answer isn't 4.

questions.prompt: This version has a bug (no Math.max on left). What does it print?
questions.explanation: At r = 3 ('a'), left jumps back from 2 to 1, so the window 'bba' (length 3) is counted even though it repeats 'b'. The correct answer is 2. Keeping left monotonic with Math.max fixes it.

questions.prompt: Which problems are a good fit for a sliding window? Select all that apply.
options: Counting subarrays with sum exactly k when values can be negative
Maximum average of any subarray of length k
Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
Smallest subarray with sum ≥ S when all values are positive
Finding the k-th largest element of the whole array
questions.explanation: These have contiguous windows with monotonic validity or a fixed size. With negative values, the sum isn't monotonic, so use prefix sums plus a map. The k-th largest isn't a contiguous-window problem; use a heap or quickselect.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the minimum-window-substring algorithm are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Once the window is valid, shrink from the left while it stays valid to find the minimum
After finding a valid window, reset the window to empty and start again from right + 1
Track how many required characters are currently satisfied, so validity is checked in O(1)
Counts in the 'need' map may go negative to record surplus characters
questions.explanation: A 'formed' counter avoids re-scanning t, shrinking finds the minimum for each right edge, and negative counts mark extra copies. Resetting the window throws away valid overlap and can miss answers or become O(m^2).

questions.prompt: A variable-size sliding window with an inner while loop that shrinks the left edge is O(n^2) in the worst case, because the loops are nested.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: left only moves forward and never passes right, so across the whole run it advances at most n times. Total work is O(n) amortised. Nested loops don't automatically mean O(n^2).

questions.prompt: A recursive function in Node.js has no reachable base case for some inputs. What happens when it's called with one of those inputs?
options: Node automatically converts it into a loop
It returns undefined after 10,000 calls
It throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
It loops forever, like a while(true)
questions.explanation: Each call pushes a frame until the V8 stack limit is hit, then a RangeError is thrown. It doesn't hang like an infinite loop, and V8 doesn't do tail-call elimination.

questions.prompt: You write a tail-recursive sum over a 1,000,000-element list in Node.js. Why does it still overflow the stack?
options: Tail calls only work in strict mode
The list is too large for memory
Tail recursion only works with arrow functions
V8 (and so Node) doesn't implement proper tail calls, so each call still adds a frame; convert to a loop
questions.explanation: ES2015 specified proper tail calls, but only Safari's JavaScriptCore ships them. V8 doesn't, even in strict mode. For deep recursion in Node, use iteration or an explicit stack.

questions.prompt: For naive recursive fib(n), what are the time and the maximum stack depth?
options: Time O(2^n), depth O(2^n)
Time O(n), depth O(n)
Time O(n^2), depth O(log n)
Time O(2^n) (more precisely about φ^n), depth O(n)
questions.explanation: The recursion tree has exponentially many nodes, but at any moment only one root-to-leaf path is on the stack, and that path is at most n long. Space follows depth, not total calls.

questions.prompt: A recursive algorithm splits the input in half, recurses on both halves, and does O(n) work to combine them: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). What's its complexity?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: The recursion tree has log n levels, each doing O(n) total work, so O(n log n). That's merge sort. T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) would give binary search's O(log n).

questions.prompt: This fast-power function is meant to run in O(log n). What is its actual time complexity?
options: O(n log n)
O(n), because the two recursive calls double the work at each halving
O(log n), because n halves each time
questions.explanation: Calling pow(x, n/2) twice gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1), which is O(n): the tree has about n nodes. Storing half = pow(x, n/2) once and returning half * half restores O(log n).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
in 1

in 2
out 2
in 1
out 1

in 2
in 1
out 1
out 2

in 2
in 1
out 2
out 1
questions.explanation: Code before the recursive call runs on the way down (2, then 1); code after it runs as frames unwind, innermost first (1, then 2). This pre/post order is the same shape as DFS pre-order and post-order.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: fib(6) = 8. The number of calls satisfies C(n) = C(n-1) + C(n-2) + 1, which gives 25 for n = 6 (2·fib(7) - 1). It grows exponentially, which is why memoization matters.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 6 abc cab
9 abc ccc
6 abc cba
3 abc cba
questions.explanation: Each first-character choice is followed by all permutations of the rest: abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba. That's 3! = 6, ending in 'cba'. The tree has n! leaves, so time is O(n · n!).

questions.prompt: Which statements about recursion and the call stack in JavaScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Memoizing recursive fib reduces its maximum recursion depth to O(1)
The maximum recursion depth determines the stack space used
Each call gets its own frame with its own parameters and local variables
A stack overflow in Node surfaces as a RangeError that try/catch can catch
questions.explanation: Frames are per call, stack space follows depth, and V8 throws a catchable RangeError on overflow. Memoization cuts the number of calls to O(n), but the first top-down descent is still n frames deep.

questions.prompt: Which changes turn naive exponential fib(n) into linear time? Select all that apply.
options: Compute bottom-up with a loop that keeps the last two values
Recurse with accumulators, e.g. fib(n, a = 0, b = 1) calling fib(n - 1, b, a + b)
Memoize results in a Map keyed by n
Add an extra base case for n === 2
questions.explanation: Memoization, bottom-up iteration and the accumulator version each compute every subproblem once: O(n). An extra base case only trims the leaves; the tree stays exponential.

questions.prompt: Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively by managing an explicit stack.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Recursion uses the call stack implicitly. Pushing the same state (arguments and where to resume) onto your own stack reproduces it, which is how you avoid stack overflow on deep inputs in Node.

questions.prompt: In a 0-indexed array-backed binary heap, what are the parent and child indices of node i?
options: parent = (i + 1) >> 1; children = 2i - 1 and 2i
parent = i >> 1; children = 2i and 2i + 1
parent = (i - 1) >> 1; children = 2i + 1 and 2i + 2
parent = i - 1; children = i + 1 and i + 2
questions.explanation: With the root at index 0, the children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, so parent = floor((i-1)/2). The i>>1 / 2i / 2i+1 formulas are for 1-indexed heaps; mixing the two conventions is a classic off-by-one bug.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 3 sifts up past 5, giving [3,5,8]. Then 1 lands at index 3, swaps with 5 at index 1, then with 3 at index 0, giving [1,3,8,5]. A heap is only partially ordered: each parent is <= its children, and the array is not sorted.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The first pop moves the last element (5) to the root and sifts it down past the smaller child 3: [3,5,8]. The second pop moves 8 to the root and sifts it below 5: [5,8]. Values come out in sorted order (1, 3), and the array stays a valid heap after each pop.

questions.prompt: Building a heap from an unsorted array of n items: what's the cost of the bottom-up heapify (sift down from index n/2 - 1 to 0) compared with n successive pushes?
options: Both are O(n log n)
Heapify is O(n); n pushes are O(n log n) in the worst case
Both are O(n)
Heapify is O(n log n); n pushes are O(n)
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance; summing the heights gives O(n) total. Pushing one element at a time can make each new element sift up O(log n) levels, giving O(n log n) in the worst case. Heapify is the standard way to build a heap from existing data.

questions.prompt: What's the bug in this pop()?
options: When the heap has one element, pop() removes it and then writes it back to a[0], so the heap never empties
It returns the maximum instead of the minimum
siftDown should start at the last index, not 0
Destructuring is needed to swap correctly
questions.explanation: With one element, a.pop() returns that element, the array becomes empty, and a[0] = ... puts it right back, so size stays 1 forever. On an empty heap it writes undefined into a[0]. Guard with `if (this.a.length)` after popping the last element, as correct implementations do.

questions.prompt: A job scheduler uses a binary min-heap ordered by priority. Two jobs with equal priority must run in submission (FIFO) order. What's the right fix?
options: Nothing; binary heaps are stable
Store a monotonically increasing sequence number with each job and compare by (priority, seq)
Sort the heap array after every push
Use a max-heap instead
questions.explanation: Heaps aren't stable: sift operations reorder equal keys unpredictably. Breaking ties with an insertion counter makes the ordering total, so equal priorities come out FIFO. Sorting after every push would cost O(n log n) per operation and defeat the purpose of a heap.

questions.prompt: In siftDown for a min-heap, why must the node swap with the smaller of its two children rather than, say, always the left child?
options: The right child might be undefined
Swapping with the left child is slower because of cache misses
Because siftDown must keep the array fully sorted
If the larger child moved up, it would sit above its smaller sibling, violating the heap property
questions.explanation: The child that moves up becomes the parent of the other child. Only the smaller child can be a valid parent of its sibling. Always taking the left child breaks the invariant whenever the right child is smaller. Bounds checks deal with a missing right child.

questions.prompt: Which operation costs on a binary heap of n elements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Heapify an unsorted array: O(n)
Push: O(log n)
Peek at the min (min-heap): O(1)
Search for an arbitrary value: O(log n)
Pop the min: O(1)
questions.explanation: The min sits at index 0, push sifts up one path of length log n, and bottom-up heapify is O(n). A heap doesn't order siblings, so finding an arbitrary value is O(n). Pop must sift down after moving the last element to the root, which is O(log n).

questions.prompt: Which arrays are valid 0-indexed min-heaps? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Check each parent i against its children 2i+1 and 2i+2. [2,1,3] fails at the root (1 < 2). [1,5,2,6,4] fails at index 1 (child 4 < 5). In [0,4,1,7,9,2], index 2 (value 1) has child 2 at index 5, which is fine. Siblings don't need to be in order.

questions.prompt: Any array sorted in ascending order is a valid min-heap.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Children 2i+1 and 2i+2 always come after i in the array, so in a sorted array every parent is <= its children. The reverse doesn't hold: most valid heaps aren't sorted.

questions.prompt: Once all insertions are finished, the array inside a binary min-heap is in sorted order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A heap only guarantees parent <= children; siblings and cousins can be in any order (e.g. [1,3,2]). To get sorted output you pop repeatedly, which is O(n log n) heap sort.

questions.prompt: A solution using `new MinPriorityQueue()` passes on LeetCode, but throws `ReferenceError: MinPriorityQueue is not defined` in a plain Node.js interview pad. Why?
options: Node 22 renamed it to PriorityQueue
It only exists in TypeScript
It must be imported from 'node:collections'
It comes from the third-party @datastructures-js/priority-queue package that LeetCode's JS runtime provides; neither JavaScript nor Node.js has a built-in priority queue
questions.explanation: LeetCode adds this library to its JS environment, but ECMAScript and Node.js ship no heap or priority queue, and there is no 'node:collections' module. In interviews, be ready to write a small MinHeap yourself or ask whether a library is allowed.

questions.prompt: You use a comparator-based priority queue (`new PriorityQueue(compare)`) for tasks. It should pop the earliest deadline first, breaking ties by the smallest id. Which comparator is correct?
options: (a, b) => a.deadline - b.deadline && a.id - b.id
(a, b) => a.deadline < b.deadline
(a, b) => b.deadline - a.deadline || b.id - a.id
(a, b) => a.deadline - b.deadline || a.id - b.id
questions.explanation: Like a sort comparator, a negative result means a comes out first, and `||` falls through to the id only when deadlines are equal. A boolean comparator never returns a negative number, the reversed version pops the latest deadline, and `&&` returns 0 whenever deadlines differ.

questions.prompt: With a comparator-based priority queue holding plain numbers, which comparator makes it behave as a max-heap?
options: (a, b) => b - a
(a, b) => a > b
(a, b) => Math.max(a, b)
(a, b) => a - b
questions.explanation: b - a is negative when a > b, so larger values rank first and the max is dequeued first. a - b gives a min-heap. Math.max returns one of the values rather than an ordering, and a boolean comparator never signals 'a first'.

questions.prompt: A submission written for one major version of @datastructures-js/priority-queue does `sum += pq.dequeue()`, and sum turns into a string like '0[object Object]'. What's the most likely cause?
options: Numbers are stored as strings inside the queue
The installed version's dequeue() returns a wrapper object (e.g. { element, priority }) rather than the raw element, so you need .element
dequeue() returned undefined because the queue was empty
The comparator returned NaN
questions.explanation: Adding an object to 0 converts it to a string ('[object Object]') and concatenates, which matches the symptom. Older major versions returned { element, priority } wrappers, newer ones return the element itself. An empty queue would give NaN or 'undefined', not '[object Object]'. Check which API version you're on.

questions.prompt: Your LeetCode Dijkstra uses a library priority queue that has no O(log n) decrease-key. What's the standard approach?
options: Push a new [dist, node] entry whenever a distance improves, and skip popped entries whose dist is greater than the best known for that node
Give up on Dijkstra and use BFS
Use a plain array and scan it for the minimum, since that's faster
Rebuild the queue every time a distance improves
questions.explanation: Lazy deletion leaves stale entries in the heap and throws them away when they're popped. The heap can grow to O(E) entries, so the total is O((V + E) log E), which is fine in practice. Rebuilding the queue on every update costs O(n) each time, and BFS ignores edge weights.

questions.prompt: A priority queue pops elements in the order this comparator sorts them. What does this code print (the pop order)?
questions.explanation: Lower p comes first, so ids 2 and 4 (p = 1) come before 1 and 3. The tie-breaker b.id - a.id puts the larger id first, so 4 before 2 and 3 before 1. Get the tie-breaker direction wrong and you get 2,4,1,3.

questions.prompt: What are the typical time complexities of enqueue, dequeue and front (peek) in a binary-heap priority queue such as @datastructures-js/priority-queue?
options: O(n), O(log n), O(1)
O(log n), O(log n), O(1)
O(log n), O(n), O(log n)
questions.explanation: A binary heap sifts one element along a single root-to-leaf path on enqueue and dequeue, which is O(log n), and peeking reads the root in O(1). No comparison-based priority queue can make both insert and extract-min O(1), because that would let you sort faster than O(n log n).

questions.prompt: Which are good practices when using a library priority queue in LeetCode JavaScript submissions? Select all that apply.
options: Assume dequeue() returns the same shape in every library version
Add a tie-breaker when the order of equal priorities affects the answer
