Know how to write your own heap, since interview environments may not provide the library
Call toArray() each iteration to peek at the minimum
Make the comparator return a negative, zero or positive number, not a boolean
questions.explanation: Correct comparators, deterministic tie-breaks and being able to code a heap yourself all hold up across environments. API shapes changed between major versions, so check them. toArray() copies the elements (O(n) or more), while front() peeks in O(1).

questions.prompt: In which of these problems is a priority queue the natural tool? Select all that apply.
options: Two Sum
Dijkstra's shortest paths with non-negative weights
Valid parentheses
Merge k sorted lists
Meeting rooms II (minimum number of rooms)
questions.explanation: Merging k lists repeatedly takes the smallest head, meeting rooms track the earliest-ending meeting, and Dijkstra pops the closest unsettled node. All three need a repeated min. Two Sum uses a hash map, and parentheses use a stack.

questions.prompt: JavaScript (ES2024) and Node.js 22 provide a built-in PriorityQueue class in the global scope.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. There's no heap or priority queue in the language or the Node standard library. LeetCode provides one through a preinstalled third-party package; elsewhere you install a library or implement a binary heap (about 30 lines).

questions.prompt: In a comparator-based priority queue, the comparator `(a, b) => a.cost - b.cost` makes the element with the smallest cost come out first.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. These priority queues follow Array.prototype.sort conventions: a negative result means a comes first, so a smaller cost is dequeued earlier. Flip it to b.cost - a.cost for largest-first.

questions.prompt: To find the k largest values in a large array, which heap do you keep and at what size?
options: A min-heap of all n elements, then pop k times
A max-heap capped at k, popping the max when size exceeds k
A max-heap of all n elements, then pop k times
A min-heap capped at k: push each value and pop the min when size exceeds k; its root ends up as the k-th largest
questions.explanation: The min-heap's root is the weakest of the current top k, so evicting it whenever the size exceeds k keeps the k largest, in O(n log k) time and O(k) space. A max-heap capped at k would evict the largest values, the opposite of what you want.

questions.prompt: 'Top K frequent elements': after counting frequencies in a Map, how can you beat O(n log k)?
options: Binary search over frequencies
Bucket sort: an array indexed by frequency (0..n) holding lists of values, then scan from the highest bucket down until k values are collected, O(n)
Sort the Map entries by frequency
Use a balanced BST keyed by value
questions.explanation: No frequency can exceed n, so frequencies can index an array of buckets. Filling the buckets and scanning them from the top is linear. Sorting the entries is O(m log m) for m distinct values, which is no better than the heap approach.

questions.prompt: Which statement about quickselect for the k-th largest element is correct?
options: It's O(log n) because it halves the array each step
It needs O(n) extra memory to partition
It runs in O(n log n) like quicksort
Its average time is O(n), its worst case is O(n^2), and it only recurses into the side that contains the k-th position
questions.explanation: Unlike quicksort, quickselect recurses into one side only, so the expected work is n + n/2 + … = O(n). Bad pivots can still give O(n^2), and random pivots make that unlikely. Partitioning works in place, so no extra O(n) memory is needed.

questions.prompt: 'Kth largest element in a stream': add(x) is called millions of times and must return the current k-th largest each time. What's the best design?
options: Keep a max-heap of all values and pop k times on each add
Keep all values in an array and sort on every add
Recompute with quickselect on each add
Keep a min-heap of size k; on add, push and pop if the size exceeds k, then return the root, giving O(log k) per add and O(k) memory
questions.explanation: Only the top k values can ever be the answer, so a size-k min-heap keeps exactly those, and its root is the k-th largest. Memory stays O(k) however long the stream runs. Sorting, quickselect or popping from a full heap all redo O(n)-scale work on every call.

questions.prompt: You need the exact top 100 most frequent URLs in a 1 TB log on one machine with 8 GB of RAM. Which approach works?
options: Sample 1% of the lines and count those
Use a count-min sketch and report its top 100
Load all URLs into a Map and sort it
Hash-partition the URLs into many files so every occurrence of a URL lands in the same file, count each file in memory, keep a top-100 per file, then merge the per-file results
questions.explanation: Hash partitioning guarantees each URL's full count is in exactly one partition, so per-partition counts are exact and the global top 100 is among the per-partition winners. A count-min sketch and sampling give approximate answers, and a single Map won't fit in 8 GB.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: This simulates a size-k min-heap: after each push, the smallest value is evicted once there are more than k. The two largest values, 5 and 6, survive, and the root (5) is the 2nd largest. A real heap does each step in O(log k) instead of sorting.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: abc
abd
bac
acb
questions.explanation: The counts are a:3, b:2, c:1, d:1. Sorting by count descending puts a then b first, and the alphabetical tie-break puts c before d, so the top 3 are 'abc'. Without a tie-breaker, the c/d order would depend on Map insertion order, which happens to be the same here.

questions.prompt: Which approaches correctly find the k closest points to the origin? Select all that apply.
options: A max-heap of size k keyed by distance, evicting the farthest when size exceeds k: O(n log k)
Sort all points by distance and take the first k: O(n log n)
BFS outward from the origin
Quickselect on distance: O(n) average
A min-heap of size k keyed by distance, popping the min when size exceeds k
questions.explanation: To keep the k smallest distances, evict the largest, which needs a max-heap. A capped min-heap would throw away the closest points. Quickselect and full sorting are also correct, with different costs. The points aren't a graph, so BFS doesn't apply.

questions.prompt: Which statements about choosing a top-K approach are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A size-k heap needs O(n) extra memory
When k is close to n, simply sorting can be as good as a heap
Quickselect needs all elements in memory and reorders the array in place
A size-k heap works on streams where you can't hold all n elements
Quickselect returns the top k elements in sorted order
questions.explanation: Heaps need only O(k) memory and handle one element at a time, which suits streams. Quickselect is an in-place, all-in-memory partition. With k ≈ n, O(n log k) ≈ O(n log n). Quickselect leaves the top k unsorted, and the heap uses O(k), not O(n), memory.

questions.prompt: To find the k smallest elements, keep a min-heap capped at size k and pop its minimum whenever the size exceeds k.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Popping the min evicts the smallest element, the opposite of what you want. For the k smallest, use a max-heap capped at k and evict its maximum. Remember it this way: the heap's root should be the element you're most willing to throw away.

questions.prompt: Heapifying all n elements into a max-heap in O(n) and then popping k times costs O(n + k log n), which can beat O(n log k) when k is small.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Bottom-up heapify is O(n), and each pop is O(log n). For n = 10^6 and k = 10 that's about 10^6 + 200 operations, versus about 3.3 × 10^6 for the capped heap. The trade-off is O(n) memory and needing all the data up front.

questions.prompt: A trie stores W words. What's the time to insert or look up a word of length L?
options: O(L), independent of W
O(L * W)
O(W)
O(log W)
questions.explanation: Each character follows one child link, so the cost depends only on the word's length, not on how many words are stored. A sorted array with binary search would cost O(L log W) string comparisons.

questions.prompt: Why does a trie node need an explicit `isEnd` flag instead of treating every leaf as the end of a word?
options: Without it, deletion would be O(n^2)
A word can be a prefix of another (e.g. 'app' and 'apple'), so its last node has children but is still the end of a word
Leaves can't hold values in JavaScript objects
isEnd makes lookups O(1)
questions.explanation: After inserting 'apple' and 'app', the node for 'app' has a child 'l', so it isn't a leaf, yet 'app' is a word. Without the flag, search('app') would wrongly return false, or 'appl' would wrongly count as a word.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: false false true false
true false false false
true true true false
true false true false
questions.explanation: 'app' was inserted, so its node has the '$' end marker. The node for 'appl' exists but has no marker, so search returns false while startsWith returns true. 'apples' runs off the trie after 'apple', so #walk returns null and the result falls back to false.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 3 2 1 undefined
questions.explanation: Each node counts how many inserted words pass through it. 'ca' is a prefix of car, cart and cat (3); 'car' of car and cart (2); 'd' of dog (1). A missing prefix returns 0 through the explicit guard. This gives prefix counts in O(|p|).

questions.prompt: How do you delete a word from a trie without breaking other words?
options: Clear the end marker on the last node, then remove nodes bottom-up only while a node has no children and isn't the end of another word
Just clear the end marker; nodes can never be removed safely
Delete every node on the word's path
Rebuild the trie without that word
questions.explanation: Removing the whole path would delete shared prefixes, like 'app' when deleting 'apple'. Clearing only the marker is correct but leaves dead nodes behind. The usual approach is a recursive delete that prunes childless, non-terminal nodes on the way back up.

questions.prompt: 'Word Search II' asks which of 10,000 words appear in a letter grid. Why is a trie of the words much faster than running a separate DFS for each word?
options: A trie makes each DFS step O(1) instead of O(L)
One DFS from each cell checks all words at once, and it stops as soon as the current path isn't a prefix of any word
It lets you sort the grid first
It removes the need to track visited cells
questions.explanation: Walking the trie in step with the DFS shares the work across every word with the same prefix, and a missing child prunes the path immediately. Removing found words or pruning empty trie nodes speeds it up further. You still need visited tracking to avoid reusing a cell.

questions.prompt: HTTP routers such as find-my-way (used by Fastify) store routes in a radix tree rather than a plain character trie. What's the main benefit?
options: Radix trees keep routes in insertion order
They use hashing, so lookups are O(1)
Radix trees support regular expressions natively
Chains of single-child nodes are merged into one edge labelled with a string, so there are fewer nodes and fewer hops per lookup
questions.explanation: Route paths share long literal segments ('/api/v1/users'). A radix (compressed) tree stores each run as a single edge, which cuts memory use and pointer hops. Lookups are still proportional to the path length, and parameter matching is handled as special nodes, not native regex.

questions.prompt: Which tasks are a good fit for a trie? Select all that apply.
options: Range-sum queries over an integer array
Longest common prefix of a set of strings
Longest-prefix match for IP routing (binary trie over address bits)
Shortest path between two cities
Autocomplete suggestions for a typed prefix
questions.explanation: Tries index by prefix, so prefix lookups, common prefixes and longest-prefix matching follow directly. Range sums need prefix-sum arrays or Fenwick or segment trees, and shortest paths need graph algorithms.

questions.prompt: In 'design add and search words', search may contain '.', which matches any letter. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Searches with many dots can visit far more than L nodes
addWord remains O(L)
At a '.', the search must branch into every child node (DFS)
Search is always O(L), even with dots
questions.explanation: A wildcard can't choose one edge, so the search tries every child, and the worst case grows with the number of nodes at each wildcard depth (up to 26^dots paths). Insertion is unaffected. Only searches without dots are guaranteed O(L).

questions.prompt: Checking whether any stored word starts with prefix p takes O(|p|) in a trie, regardless of how many words are stored.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. You follow |p| child links and check that the final node exists. Listing every completion is a different matter: it costs extra time proportional to the size of the subtree under that node.

questions.prompt: A trie always uses less memory than storing the same words in a Set.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Tries save space only when words share prefixes. Each node is an object or Map with real overhead in JS, so words with few shared prefixes (such as random IDs) can use far more memory in a trie than as strings in a Set. Radix trees reduce, but don't eliminate, that overhead.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Sorted by start: [1,3],[2,6],[6,7],[8,10],[15,18]. [2,6] overlaps, giving [1,6]; [6,7] touches it (6 <= 6), giving [1,7]; [8,10] starts after 7, so it stays separate. Whether touching intervals merge depends on <= versus <, so make sure you know which the problem expects.

questions.prompt: Why does the standard interval-merge algorithm sort by start time first?
options: So the output comes out sorted by end time
To make the algorithm O(n) overall
So any interval that overlaps the merged block will come next, and a single pass that compares with the last merged interval is enough
Sorting by start is required for stability
questions.explanation: Once intervals are sorted by start, if the next one doesn't overlap the current merged block, no later one can either, because they start even later. That allows one O(n) pass after the O(n log n) sort, so the total is O(n log n), not O(n).

questions.prompt: A merge-intervals solution uses `last[1] = en` instead of `last[1] = Math.max(last[1], en)` when intervals overlap. Which input breaks it?
questions.explanation: [2,3] lies inside [1,10]. Assigning en shrinks the merged block to [1,3], and then [4,8] becomes a separate interval, so the result is [[1,3],[4,8]] instead of [[1,10]]. Non-overlapping, chained or single intervals never take the buggy branch in a harmful way.

questions.prompt: 'Non-overlapping intervals' asks for the fewest removals that leave no overlaps. The greedy keeps intervals sorted by which key?
options: Start time descending
Length, keeping the shortest first
Start time, keeping the earliest start
End time, keeping the interval that finishes first
questions.explanation: Choosing the interval that ends earliest leaves the most room for the rest, which maximizes how many you can keep, and removals = n minus kept. Sorting by start fails on one long early interval covering several short ones. Shortest-first fails too: a short interval can overlap two compatible ones.

questions.prompt: How does the exchange argument show that 'pick the interval with the earliest end' is optimal for activity selection?
options: By dynamic programming over end times

Take any optimal solution and replace its first interval with the earliest-ending one; that creates no conflict because it ends no later, so an optimal solution exists that starts with the greedy choice, and induction finishes the proof
By showing the greedy choice is always the longest interval
By trying every subset and comparing
questions.explanation: The exchange argument transforms an optimal solution into one that agrees with the greedy choice without making it worse, then repeats the argument on the remaining subproblem. That's the standard way to justify a greedy algorithm in an interview. Brute force or DP can confirm the result but aren't the argument.

questions.prompt: Meeting rooms II uses a sweep line over events (+1 at each start, -1 at each end). Meetings are half-open [start, end). When a start and an end share a timestamp, how must ties be ordered?
options: Process them in input order
Starts before ends
Ends before starts, so a meeting ending at 5 frees its room for one starting at 5
The order doesn't matter
questions.explanation: With [1,5) and [5,8) only one room is needed. Processing the end (-1) first drops the count before the new start (+1). Processing starts first would briefly count 2 and overstate the answer. Sorting by (time, delta) with delta -1 before +1 does this.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: At most two meetings overlap in the first input, so 2. In the second, the tie-break processes -1 before +1 at time 5, so the meetings don't overlap: 1. In the third, all three overlap during [3,4): 3. The peak of the running count is the number of rooms needed.

questions.prompt: Which problems does a greedy algorithm (with the right sort key) solve optimally? Select all that apply.
options: 0/1 knapsack by value-to-weight ratio
Minimum arrows to burst balloons (sort by end)
Jump Game: can you reach the last index (track the farthest reachable index)
Maximum number of non-overlapping activities (sort by end)
Coin change with arbitrary denominations, taking the largest coin first
questions.explanation: The first three have a provable greedy-choice property. The ratio greedy is optimal only for fractional knapsack; 0/1 knapsack needs DP. Largest-coin-first fails for coins like {1,3,4} with target 6: greedy gives 4+1+1, while 3+3 is optimal.

questions.prompt: Which statements about 'insert interval' (insert into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals, merging where needed) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: One O(n) pass is enough
Overlapping intervals merge into the new one using min of starts and max of ends
Intervals that end before the new start are copied unchanged
The whole list must be re-sorted in O(n log n)
Binary search makes the whole operation O(log n)
questions.explanation: The input is already sorted, so you copy the intervals that end before the new one, merge the overlapping run, and copy the rest, all in O(n). Re-sorting is unnecessary. Binary search can find the overlap boundaries in O(log n), but building the output is still O(n).

questions.prompt: Greedy coin change (always take the largest coin that fits) gives the minimum number of coins for every set of denominations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. It works for canonical systems such as US coins, but for {1,3,4} and target 6 greedy picks 4+1+1 (3 coins) while 3+3 needs only 2. The general problem needs DP. Interviewers like this case for testing whether you can argue a greedy is correct rather than assume it.

questions.prompt: For 'minimum arrows to burst balloons', sorting balloons by end coordinate and shooting at the end of the first balloon not yet burst is optimal.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Some arrow must hit the balloon that ends first, and shooting at its end point also hits every balloon that starts at or before that point, as much as any single arrow could. It's the same exchange argument as activity selection.

questions.prompt: Why do many linked-list implementations start with a dummy (sentinel) head node?
options: It makes the list doubly linked without extra pointers
It speeds up random access to the middle of the list
It lets the garbage collector free nodes sooner
It removes special cases for inserting or deleting at the front, since every real node then has a predecessor
questions.explanation: With a sentinel, the 'previous node' always exists, so deleting the first real node is the same code path as deleting any other (prev.next = prev.next.next). It does nothing for random access, which stays O(n), and has no effect on garbage collection.

questions.prompt: An LRU cache combines a Map (key to node) with a doubly linked list. Why doubly rather than singly linked?
options: Map entries can only reference doubly linked nodes
Given a node from the Map, it can be unlinked in O(1) using its prev pointer; a singly linked list must search for the predecessor in O(n)
Doubly linked lists use less memory per node
It keeps keys sorted for range queries
questions.explanation: On a cache hit you jump straight to the node through the Map and move it to the front. Unlinking requires changing the predecessor's next pointer, which a prev pointer gives you in O(1). A singly linked list would have to walk from the head. The trade-off is one extra pointer per node, so more memory, not less.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Each unshift creates a new head that points to the old head, so the last value inserted is first: 3->2->1, and size counts three insertions. Inserting at the head is O(1); keeping insertion order would need a tail pointer.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with this `remove(val)` method on a singly linked list with a `head` field and no sentinel?
options: It never checks the head node itself, and it throws a TypeError on an empty list
It leaks the removed node because it doesn't set node.next = null
It runs in O(n^2) because of the nested property access
It removes every matching node instead of the first one
questions.explanation: The loop only ever inspects cur.next, so a match at the head is never removed. When head is null, reading cur.next throws. A sentinel head, or an explicit head check, fixes both. Removed nodes become unreachable and are garbage collected, so there's no leak.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list class's `remove(node)` fixes the prev/next pointers but never updates `this.tail` when the removed node is the tail. After removing the tail and then calling `push(x)`, what happens?
options: Nothing; push walks from head to find the real last node
push throws because tail is null
x replaces the head node
x is linked after the removed node, so a traversal from head never reaches it
questions.explanation: push typically does tail.next = node and node.prev = tail. A stale tail still points at the detached node, so x hangs off a node that is no longer reachable from head. The list silently loses data and its size goes out of sync. tail isn't null, so nothing throws.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: ca abc c
cba ac c
ca ac undefined
ca ac c
questions.explanation: Unlinking b points a.next at c and c.prev at a, so both directions skip b: forward 'ac', backward 'ca'. b's own pointers are untouched, so b.next is still c. That's harmless here, but a stale pointer can be a bug if someone keeps using b.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of `get(i)` (the value at index i) in a singly linked list of n nodes?
options: O(log n)
O(i), which is O(n) in the worst case
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: There is no index arithmetic: you follow next pointers i times from the head. Arrays give O(1) access because elements sit at computable addresses. A doubly linked list can start from whichever end is closer, but the worst case is still O(n).

questions.prompt: When is a linked list a better choice than a plain JavaScript array? Select all that apply.
options: A FIFO queue that must dequeue from the front in O(1) without index tricks
Removing an arbitrary node in O(1) when you already hold a reference to it (e.g. an LRU cache)
Tight loops where CPU cache-friendly iteration matters most
Moving a run of nodes between lists in O(1) when you hold its ends
Frequent random access by index
questions.explanation: Linked lists are good at O(1) splicing around nodes you already hold. They are bad at indexing (O(n)), and their scattered nodes iterate more slowly than contiguous arrays because of cache misses. That's why arrays win most 'just iterate' workloads in practice.

questions.prompt: You insert node x after node p in a doubly linked list, where p is not the tail. Which assignments are required? Select all that apply.
options: x.prev = p
p.prev = x
p.next = x (done after p.next.prev is updated)
p.next.prev = x
x.next = p.next
head = x
questions.explanation: x needs both of its links, and both neighbours must point back at x. Order matters: update p.next.prev before overwriting p.next, or you lose the reference to the old successor. p.prev and head are unaffected by inserting after p.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript, a node removed from a linked list must be explicitly freed, or it will leak memory.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. JS is garbage collected: once nothing references the node it is reclaimed. Leaks happen only if something still holds it, such as a stale Map entry or a forgotten tail pointer. Setting node.next = null can help in rare cases, but there's no free().

questions.prompt: With both head and tail pointers, a singly linked list can append in O(1), but removing the tail still takes O(n).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Appending only touches tail.next and tail. Removing the tail means the new tail is its predecessor, and a singly linked list can only find that by walking from the head. That's why deques and LRU caches use doubly linked lists.

questions.prompt: In Floyd's cycle detection (slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2), why must the pointers meet if there's a cycle?
options: Fast eventually laps the whole list and resets to head
Slow stops moving once it enters the cycle
Once both are in the cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 each step, so it reaches 0 instead of jumping over it
The cycle length is always even
questions.explanation: Inside the cycle, fast gains one node per step, so the distance from fast back to slow decreases by 1 every iteration and hits 0. Fast can't skip over slow. Nothing depends on the cycle length being even.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Reversal reuses the same nodes. r is the old tail and walks 4321. h still points at node 1, which is now the last node with next = null, so it prints just '1'. Expecting h to still read 1234 assumes a copy was made.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: With `while (f && f.next)`, slow stops at the exact middle of an odd-length list and at the second of the two middles of an even-length list (3 for [1,2,3,4]). To get the first middle, loop on `f.next && f.next.next` instead.

questions.prompt: After Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet inside a cycle, you reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time. Why do they next meet at the cycle's entry node?
options: Because slow has traversed the cycle exactly once
Because the distance from head to the entry is congruent (mod cycle length) to the distance from the meeting point forward to the entry
Because the cycle length equals the tail length
Because the meeting point is always the node just before the entry
questions.explanation: If the tail has length μ and the cycle length L, then at the meeting point 2(μ + k) ≡ μ + k (mod L), so μ + k ≡ 0 and the meeting point is μ steps (mod L) short of the entry. Walking μ steps from head and from the meeting point lands both on the entry. The tail and cycle lengths needn't be equal.

questions.prompt: To remove the n-th node from the end in one pass, fast is advanced n steps, then fast and slow move together. Why start both at a dummy node before head?
options: It's required for lists with an even length
It prevents fast from ever becoming null
If the node to remove is the head itself, slow still has a predecessor to unlink from, so there's no special case
It makes the algorithm O(1) instead of O(n)
questions.explanation: Removal needs the node before the target. When n equals the list length, the target is head, which has no real predecessor; the dummy provides one, and you return dummy.next. The algorithm is O(L) either way.

questions.prompt: A palindrome-list check finds the middle, reverses the second half in place, compares the halves, and returns. In code review, what's the most valid concern?
options: It mutates the caller's list; it should reverse the second half back before returning, or document the side effect
It's O(n^2) because reversal is O(n) per comparison
It fails for odd-length lists because the middle node is compared with itself
It needs O(n) extra space for the reversed half
questions.explanation: The point of the trick is O(1) extra space, but it rewires the input. Other code holding the list now sees it broken after the midpoint. Restoring the half (one more O(n) reversal) fixes that. The time is O(n), and odd lengths work if the middle is skipped.

questions.prompt: A recursive linked-list reversal works in tests but fails in production on a 200,000-node list in Node.js. What's the most likely error?
options: An infinite loop because recursion revisits nodes
Out-of-memory in the heap because each node is copied
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, since V8 doesn't do tail-call optimization
questions.explanation: Recursion depth equals the list length, and V8 doesn't eliminate tail calls, so roughly 10k+ frames (depending on frame size) overflow the stack. The iterative three-pointer version uses O(1) space. Nodes aren't copied, so heap memory isn't the problem.

questions.prompt: Which problems are typically solved with fast/slow pointers? Select all that apply.
options: Merging two sorted linked lists
Happy number (does repeated digit-square-sum reach 1?)
Finding the duplicate in an array of n+1 values in 1..n without modifying it, using O(1) space
Detecting a cycle in a linked list
Finding the middle node in one pass
questions.explanation: The duplicate-number problem treats i → nums[i] as a linked list with a cycle, and happy numbers either reach 1 or cycle; Floyd finds both in O(1) space. Merging two sorted lists uses two pointers, one in each list, but not a fast/slow pair.

questions.prompt: Which statements about iterative in-place reversal of a singly linked list are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It returns the old tail as the new head
It requires a doubly linked list
Afterwards the old head pointer still lets you traverse the whole reversed list
It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space
You must save head.next before overwriting head.next
questions.explanation: Three pointers (prev, cur, next) make it O(n) time and O(1) space. Without saving next first you lose the rest of the list. The old head becomes the tail, so traversing from it shows a single node. Only next pointers are needed, so no doubly linked list.

questions.prompt: Floyd's algorithm only works if fast moves exactly 2 steps; if fast moved 3 steps per iteration, the pointers could miss each other forever in some cycles.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Both start at head, so after t steps they're at positions t and 3t. Once t is at least the tail length, they coincide whenever the cycle length divides 2t, e.g. when t is a multiple of the cycle length. Step 2 is standard because it does the least work and keeps the cycle-entry proof simple.

questions.prompt: Floyd's cycle detection uses O(1) extra space, whereas detecting a cycle with a Set of visited nodes uses O(n).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Floyd's needs only two pointers. The Set approach stores every node it visits until it sees a repeat, so it uses O(n) memory. Both run in O(n) time; interviewers often ask for the O(1)-space version as a follow-up.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The position of the visit relative to the two recursive calls decides the order. Preorder visits the node first (1,2,4,5,3), inorder between its subtrees (4,2,5,1,3), postorder after both (4,5,2,3,1). 12345 is level order, not preorder.

questions.prompt: This 'iterative preorder' pushes the left child before the right. What does it print?
questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO, so the last child pushed is visited first. Pushing left then right visits the right subtree first, giving root-right-left: 1,3,2,5,4. For real preorder, push the right child first. Reversing this root-right-left order is a common trick for postorder.

questions.prompt: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits keys in ascending order?
options: Preorder
Level order
Postorder
Inorder
questions.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree (all smaller keys), then the node, then the right subtree (all larger keys), so a BST comes out sorted. Preorder lists the root first, which is useful for copying or serializing the tree but isn't sorted.

questions.prompt: In iterative inorder traversal (`while (cur || stack.length)`), after popping a node and visiting it, what should the loop do next?
options: Set cur = node.right, so the next iteration pushes that subtree's left spine
Push the node's left child
Push both children, right first
Set cur = null and pop again
questions.explanation: The pattern is: push the whole left spine, pop and visit, then move to the right child and repeat. The left subtree has already been handled by the time you pop. Pushing both children turns it into preorder-style processing.

questions.prompt: You must compute each node's subtree height (or free a tree bottom-up). Which traversal fits naturally?
options: Postorder, because both children's results are available before their parent is processed
Preorder, because the root is processed first
Inorder, because it visits nodes in sorted order
Level order, because it processes nodes by depth
questions.explanation: Height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), so the children must be finished first, which is what postorder guarantees. Preorder processes the parent before its children are known. Level order runs top-down, which is backwards for this.

questions.prompt: Morris inorder traversal achieves O(1) extra space. What's its main trade-off?
options: It temporarily rewires right pointers to inorder predecessors, so the tree is mutated during the walk and is unsafe for concurrent readers
It runs in O(n log n) time
It only works on complete binary trees
It visits nodes in a different order from recursive inorder
questions.explanation: Morris threads the predecessor's right pointer back to the current node to find its way back up, then removes the thread. It's still O(n) time and produces normal inorder, but the tree is modified mid-traversal, which breaks shared or read-only structures.

questions.prompt: What's the extra-space complexity of recursive inorder traversal on a balanced tree versus a completely skewed tree (n nodes)?
options: O(n) and O(n)
O(1) and O(1)
O(log n) and O(n)
O(log n) and O(log n)
questions.explanation: Stack depth equals tree height h: about log n when balanced and n when skewed (a linked list in disguise). This is why deep, unbalanced trees can overflow the call stack in Node, and an explicit stack (stored on the heap) is safer.

questions.prompt: Assuming all values are distinct, which pairs of traversal sequences determine a unique binary tree? Select all that apply.
options: Level order + inorder
Preorder + inorder
Level order alone
Inorder alone
Postorder + inorder
questions.explanation: Inorder tells you which values fall left and right of a root, and preorder, postorder or level order tells you which value is the root. Inorder alone can't tell different shapes apart, and level order alone doesn't record which child slots are empty.

questions.prompt: Which tree problems are naturally solved with a postorder (children first) traversal? Select all that apply.
options: Checking whether a tree is height-balanced
Printing BST keys in ascending order
Height of a tree
Diameter of a binary tree
Serializing a tree so it can be rebuilt by reading tokens left to right
questions.explanation: Height, diameter and balance all combine results from the left and right subtrees, so the children must be finished first. Sorted output is inorder. Serialization is usually preorder with null markers, because the root must come first for left-to-right rebuilding.

questions.prompt: Reversing a root-right-left traversal produces a postorder (left-right-root) traversal.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Reversing root-right-left gives left-right-root, which is postorder. That's why a simple iterative postorder runs a modified preorder (pushing the left child before the right) and reverses the output, avoiding the trickier single-stack postorder bookkeeping.

questions.prompt: When all values are distinct, preorder and postorder sequences together always determine a unique binary tree.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A root with only a left child and a root with only a right child have the same preorder (root, child) and the same postorder (child, root). Preorder plus postorder is only enough for full binary trees, where every node has 0 or 2 children.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Each loop iteration replaces q with all children of the current level, so the levels are [1], [2,3], [4,5]. Nodes 4 and 5 have different parents but the same depth, so they share a level. Building a fresh array per level avoids the O(n) cost of shift().

questions.prompt: In queue-based level order, why do we read `const size = queue.length` at the start of each level and loop exactly `size` times?
options: To process the level from right to left
Because queue.length is expensive to read inside the loop
To avoid an infinite loop when the tree has a cycle
So that only the nodes of the current level are processed, while children enqueued during the loop wait for the next level
questions.explanation: Children are appended to the same queue while you dequeue, so the queue length keeps changing. Fixing the count at the start draws the boundary between levels, which you need for per-level output, averages and right-side view. Trees have no cycles, so that isn't the reason.

questions.prompt: 'Binary tree right side view' returns the nodes visible from the right. With level-order BFS, which node do you record per level?
options: The last node dequeued in each level (children enqueued left before right)
The rightmost leaf of the whole tree
The first node dequeued in each level
The node with the largest value in each level
questions.explanation: If children are enqueued left then right, the last node in each level is the rightmost one, even if it's a left child because there's no right sibling. Choosing the largest value is a different problem (largest value in each row).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Zigzag reverses only the output of every second level; the traversal itself stays left to right. Level 0 prints 1, level 1 prints reversed (3,2), level 2 goes back to left to right (4,5). reverse() mutates vals, which is safe because vals is a fresh array.

questions.prompt: To find the minimum depth of a very unbalanced binary tree (a deep left chain, plus a leaf at depth 2 on the right), why is BFS preferable to DFS?
options: BFS can stop at the first leaf it dequeues, which is the shallowest, without exploring the deep chain
BFS avoids recursion, which is the only source of cost
DFS can't compute minimum depth correctly
BFS uses less memory in all cases
questions.explanation: Level order reaches leaves in order of depth, so the first leaf found is the answer and BFS stops there. A plain DFS must explore every path, including the deep chain, to be sure. DFS is still correct, just slower here, and BFS can use more memory on wide trees.

questions.prompt: For a complete binary tree with about 1,000,000 nodes, compare the peak extra memory of BFS (queue) and recursive DFS (call stack).
options: BFS about 20 entries; DFS about 500,000 frames
Both about 20 entries
Both about 1,000,000 entries
BFS about 500,000 entries (the last level); DFS about 20 frames (the height)
questions.explanation: BFS holds a whole level, and the last level of a complete tree contains about half the nodes. DFS only holds the current root-to-node path, about log2(10^6) ≈ 20 frames. For a skewed tree the comparison flips: the queue stays tiny and DFS depth becomes n.

questions.prompt: In a perfect binary tree, you must set each node's `next` pointer to its right neighbour on the same level using O(1) extra space (no queue). What's the key idea?
options: Store each level in an array and link neighbours
Do an inorder traversal and link consecutive nodes
Walk each level using the next pointers already set on that level, and wire the level below: node.left.next = node.right; node.right.next = node.next?.left
Use recursion, since the call stack doesn't count as extra space
questions.explanation: Once a level is linked, it acts as a linked list you can walk without a queue, and from it you connect the children, including across parents through node.next. Recursion uses O(h) stack, and an array per level is O(width) space, so neither meets the constraint.

questions.prompt: Which problems are naturally solved with level-order BFS on a binary tree? Select all that apply.
options: Lowest common ancestor in a BST
k-th smallest key in a BST
Largest value in each row
Minimum depth of the tree
Average value of the nodes on each level
questions.explanation: Per-level aggregates and 'first leaf by depth' fit BFS directly. The k-th smallest key is an inorder walk that stops early, and LCA in a BST is a single root-to-node walk using key comparisons.

questions.prompt: Which statements about level-order BFS on a binary tree with n nodes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Using an array as a stack (pop) instead of a queue still yields level order
Nodes are dequeued in non-decreasing order of depth
Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, so time is O(n)
Peak queue size is proportional to the tree's maximum width
It requires parent pointers on every node
questions.explanation: FIFO order makes BFS process depth d entirely before depth d+1, the queue holds at most about one level plus part of the next, and the total work is O(n). Parent pointers aren't needed. Swapping the queue for a stack turns the traversal into DFS.

questions.prompt: A binary tree is complete if and only if, in a BFS that also enqueues null children, no non-null node appears after the first null.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A complete tree fills every level left to right with no gaps, so in level order the nulls must all come after the real nodes. A real node after a null means there's a gap, so the tree isn't complete.

questions.prompt: Level-order traversal of a binary search tree outputs its keys in sorted order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Level order lists the root first, though it's usually somewhere in the middle of the sorted order. For the BST 2(1,3), level order gives 2,1,3. Only inorder produces sorted output.

questions.prompt: You insert the keys 1, 2, 3, …, 10,000 in order into a plain (unbalanced) BST, then search for 10,000. What's the cost of that search?
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: Inserting sorted keys makes every new node a right child, so the tree degenerates into a chain of height n, and a search costs O(h) = O(n). O(log n) only holds for balanced trees, which is why AVL and red-black trees exist.

questions.prompt: Deleting a BST node that has two children: what's the standard approach?
options: Rebuild the whole tree from an inorder traversal
Delete the node and attach both subtrees to its parent
Replace its key with its inorder successor (the minimum of the right subtree), then delete that successor, which has at most a right child
Replace it with its left child and re-insert the right subtree
questions.explanation: The inorder successor is the smallest key greater than the node, so putting it in the node's place preserves BST order. The successor has no left child (otherwise that child would be smaller), so deleting it is the easy case. A parent can't take two extra subtrees in one child slot.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Inserting the median first (4, then 2 and 6, and so on) builds a perfect tree of height 3. Sorted insertion turns every node into a right child, giving a chain of height 7. Same keys, different shape: a BST's shape depends on insertion order.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 4 7 null
3 7 null
3 7 undefined
3 6 null
questions.explanation: Iterative inorder visits keys in ascending order and stops at the k-th visit: the 3rd is 3 and the 7th is 7. For k = 8 the traversal ends first and the function returns its explicit null. Stopping early makes this O(h + k) rather than O(n).

questions.prompt: What's the efficient way to find the lowest common ancestor of nodes p and q in a BST?
options: Do a level-order BFS and return the first node that is an ancestor of both
Walk from the root: go left if both keys are smaller than the node, right if both are larger, and otherwise the current node is the LCA
Return the parent of whichever node is deeper
Find both root-to-node paths with DFS and compare them
questions.explanation: BST order tells you which side each key is on. The first node where p and q split (or which equals one of them) is the LCA, found in O(h) with O(1) space. Path comparison works for any binary tree but doesn't use BST order.

questions.prompt: In a BST without parent pointers, node x has no right child. Where is its inorder successor?
options: It's the nearest ancestor of x whose left subtree contains x (found by walking down from the root)
There's no successor; x must be the maximum
It's x's left child
It's the leftmost node of the whole tree
questions.explanation: With no right subtree, the next larger key is the first ancestor you reached by going left. Walking from the root, record a candidate each time you go left. If x has a right child, the successor is the leftmost node of that subtree instead. x is the maximum only if no such ancestor exists.

questions.prompt: You need floor(x), the largest key ≤ x, in a BST. Which walk is correct?
options: If node.v > x go right; otherwise record node.v and go left
Do an inorder traversal and return the first key ≥ x
Go left until null and return the last key seen
If node.v === x return it; if node.v > x go left; otherwise record node.v as a candidate and go right
questions.explanation: A key greater than x can't be the floor, so go left. A key smaller than x is a candidate, but a larger valid one might be in its right subtree, so record it and go right. This is O(h). Returning the first key ≥ x computes the ceiling, not the floor.

questions.prompt: Which properties hold for every valid BST with distinct keys? Select all that apply.
options: The minimum key is in the leftmost node (keep following left children)
Inorder traversal is strictly increasing
Level-order traversal is sorted
Every key in the left subtree of a node is smaller than that node's key
The height is O(log n)
questions.explanation: BST order applies to entire subtrees, which gives sorted inorder output and a leftmost minimum. Height is only O(log n) for balanced trees; sorted insertion gives height n. Level order isn't sorted.

questions.prompt: For 'sum of BST keys in the range [lo, hi]', which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: You must visit every node, because a BST doesn't store subtree sums
If node.v < lo, the left subtree can be skipped entirely
With pruning, the work is roughly O(h + k), where k is the number of keys in range
If node.v > hi, the right subtree can be skipped entirely
questions.explanation: Everything in the left subtree is smaller than a node already below lo, so it can be skipped; the same goes for the right subtree above hi. Pruning means you only walk the two boundary paths plus the in-range nodes, so visiting every node is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: When deleting a node with two children, replacing it with its inorder predecessor (the maximum of the left subtree) also keeps the tree a valid BST.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The predecessor is larger than everything else in the left subtree and smaller than everything in the right subtree, so it fits in the deleted node's place. Using the successor instead is symmetric; some implementations alternate between the two to limit skew.

questions.prompt: Inserting the same set of keys into a BST in a different order always produces the same tree shape.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The first key becomes the root and every later key follows comparisons down from there, so order decides the shape. [2,1,3] gives a balanced tree, while [1,2,3] gives a right-leaning chain. The inorder sequence is the same in both cases.

questions.prompt: You implement a stack on a JavaScript array. Why should push/pop operate on the end of the array rather than using unshift/shift on the front?
options: push/pop at the end are amortized O(1), while unshift/shift must re-index every remaining element (O(n))
unshift/shift are faster but are not guaranteed to preserve insertion order
Arrays only allow removal from the end; shift is deprecated in Node 22
push/pop at the end avoid garbage collection entirely, so memory never grows
questions.explanation: Working at the end touches one slot, so push/pop are amortized O(1). unshift/shift move every other element to a new index, so they are O(n). shift is not deprecated and it keeps order fine; the problem is cost, not correctness.

questions.prompt: For 'next greater element to the right', a monotonic stack of indices is used. Which invariant does the stack maintain while scanning left to right?
options: Values at the stacked indices are non-increasing from bottom to top; each is still waiting for a greater value
Values at the stacked indices are strictly increasing from bottom to top
The stack holds indices sorted by index descending, ignoring values
The stack always holds exactly the last k indices seen, like a sliding window
questions.explanation: When a larger value arrives it pops every smaller waiting index (that value is their answer), so the indices left on the stack have non-increasing values. An increasing stack is the one used for 'next smaller element', the mirror problem.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function for an array of length n?
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the inner while loop does at most n pops across the whole run: O(n) total. The nested loop makes O(n^2) look plausible, but that ignores this amortized bound.

questions.prompt: In the monotonic-stack solution to 'largest rectangle in a histogram', why do many implementations append a bar of height 0 at the end of the input?
options: To mark the end so the stack can be reused for the next test case
To make the input length even so the midpoint is well defined
To force every remaining bar on the stack to be popped, so its rectangle area gets computed
To avoid a division by zero when computing widths
questions.explanation: A bar's area is computed when it is popped, which happens when a shorter bar appears. A final height-0 sentinel is shorter than everything, so it flushes the stack. Without it, bars still on the stack at the end would never be measured unless you add a separate cleanup loop.

questions.prompt: A 'daily temperatures' solution (days until a strictly warmer day) pops the stack while `temps[i] >= temps[stack.at(-1)]`. What goes wrong?
options: A day followed by a day of equal temperature is wrongly answered with that day, though it isn't warmer
Nothing; >= and > give identical results for this problem
It becomes O(n^2) because equal values are pushed twice
It throws on an empty stack because >= skips the length check
questions.explanation: With >=, an equal temperature pops the earlier day and records it as the answer, but the problem asks for a strictly warmer day. Using > keeps equal days on the stack until a truly warmer one arrives. Complexity is still O(n) either way.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: false false false
true false true
true true false
true false false
questions.explanation: '([]{})' matches every closer with the right opener and empties the stack. In '(]' the ']' pops '(' which isn't '['. '((' never fails a match, but two openers remain, so the final length check returns false. Forgetting that final check is the classic bug.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: At index 2, value 2 pops index 1 (value 1), but 2 is not > 2, so index 0 waits. At index 3, value 4 pops indices 2 and 0. Value 3 at index 4 pops nothing, so 4 and 3 keep -1. The answer is 4,2,4,-1,-1: the equal 2 is not 'greater'.

questions.prompt: Which of these problems are classic monotonic-stack problems? Select all that apply.
options: Largest rectangle in a histogram
Daily temperatures (days until a warmer day)
Shortest path in an unweighted grid
Median of a data stream
Online stock span (consecutive previous days with price <= today)
questions.explanation: Daily temperatures, stock span and histogram rectangle all need the nearest greater or smaller element on one side, which is exactly what a monotonic stack finds in O(n). A stream median uses two heaps, and an unweighted shortest path uses BFS with a queue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about using a JavaScript array as a stack are correct? Select all that apply.
options: push() returns the element that was pushed
pop() is O(n) because remaining elements are re-indexed
arr.at(-1) reads the top element without removing it
pop() on an empty array returns undefined instead of throwing
questions.explanation: pop() on an empty array returns undefined (so check length if undefined is a valid value), and at(-1) peeks at the last element. push() returns the new length, not the element, and pop() removes the last slot without moving anything, so it's O(1).

questions.prompt: A monotonic-stack algorithm can run in O(n) total time even though it contains a while loop nested inside a for loop.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The total work of the inner loop is bounded by the number of pops, and each element is popped at most once. That's an amortized argument: one iteration of the outer loop may pop many elements, but the total over the whole run is at most n.

questions.prompt: Evaluating a postfix (Reverse Polish) expression such as `3 4 + 2 *` needs a queue, because operands must be consumed in the order they appeared.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. RPN evaluation uses a stack: push numbers, and for each operator pop the two most recent operands (the right operand first), apply it, and push the result. The operator always applies to the most recent values, which is LIFO, not FIFO.

questions.prompt: A BFS over a graph with 1,000,000 nodes uses `queue.shift()` to dequeue and runs far slower than expected. What's the most likely reason?
options: Arrays over 65,536 elements switch to a slower dictionary mode on every push
BFS is inherently O(n^2), so the slowdown is expected
shift() can re-index the remaining elements, making each dequeue O(n) and the BFS close to O(n^2)
shift() returns elements in LIFO order, so BFS explores depth-first
questions.explanation: Removing from the front of an array shifts every remaining element, so a dequeue can cost O(n) and a full BFS can approach O(n^2). shift() does remove the first element (FIFO), so the visit order is correct; the problem is speed. Use a head index or a linked list instead.

questions.prompt: A queue is implemented as an array plus a `head` index: enqueue pushes, dequeue returns `items[head++]`. What is the main downside of this design for a long-running service?
options: Dequeue becomes O(log n) as head grows
It returns items in LIFO order once head passes the middle
Dequeued slots are never released, so memory grows until you compact (e.g. slice when head passes half the length)
It cannot store undefined or null values
questions.explanation: Both operations stay O(1), but the array keeps references to items already dequeued, so memory grows without bound. A common fix is to drop the consumed prefix once head exceeds half the array. FIFO order is correct the whole time.

questions.prompt: In a queue made of two stacks (`in` and `out`), dequeue moves all of `in` into `out` only when `out` is empty. Why is dequeue O(1) amortized?
options: Because JavaScript's pop() is O(1) even when it moves many elements
Because each element is moved from in to out at most once, so total transfer work over n operations is O(n)
Because the transfer only happens when in holds a single element
Because out is kept sorted, so lookups are O(1)
questions.explanation: Every element is pushed onto in once, moved to out once, and popped from out once: a constant number of steps per element. A single dequeue can cost O(n) when it triggers a transfer, but averaged over a sequence of operations it is O(1).

questions.prompt: You build a FIFO queue on a singly linked list with head and tail pointers. Which assignment of operations keeps both enqueue and dequeue O(1)?
options: Enqueue at head, dequeue at tail
Enqueue at tail, dequeue at head
Enqueue and dequeue both at head
Either end works equally well for both operations
questions.explanation: Appending at the tail and removing at the head are both O(1). Removing the tail of a singly linked list requires finding its predecessor, which is O(n), so 'enqueue at head, dequeue at tail' makes dequeue slow. Using the same end for both would make it a stack.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer has capacity 5, `head = 3` (index of the oldest item) and `count = 4`. At which index does the next enqueue write?
questions.explanation: The write index is (head + count) % capacity = (3 + 4) % 5 = 2. The items occupy indices 3, 4, 0 and 1, so 2 is the only free slot. 7 is what you get if you forget the modulo wrap.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: After three pushes and one shift (which removes 1), head = 1. Pushing 4 makes the array [1,2,3,4]. The next shift returns 2 and moves head to 2, so size = 4 - 2 = 2. Size must subtract head; using the array length alone would report 4.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: b a c
a b c
a b undefined
a c b
questions.explanation: The first deq moves b and a into outS (a ends up on top) and returns a. 'c' goes into inS. The next deq pops b from outS, which isn't empty yet. Only when outS is empty does c get transferred and popped. FIFO order is preserved: a b c.

questions.prompt: Which implementation gives worst-case (not just amortized) O(1) for both enqueue and dequeue?
options: Two-stack queue
Array where enqueue uses unshift and dequeue uses pop
Singly linked list with head and tail pointers
Array with push/shift
questions.explanation: A linked list with head and tail pointers does constant work on every operation. The two-stack queue is only amortized O(1) because a transfer can cost O(n). Both array options use shift or unshift, which re-index the array and are O(n).

questions.prompt: Which of these dequeue strategies avoid O(n) work per dequeue on large queues? Select all that apply.
options: arr.shift() on a plain array
Singly linked list with head and tail
Two-stack queue (amortized)
Array plus a head index (items[head++])
arr.splice(0, 1)
questions.explanation: A head index and a linked list are O(1) per dequeue, and two stacks are O(1) amortized. splice(0, 1) and shift() both remove from the front, so the engine may have to move every remaining element, making them O(n).

questions.prompt: The ECMAScript spec guarantees that Array.prototype.shift is O(1) for arrays of any size, so it's safe to use in large BFS queues.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The spec defines shift as moving every element down one index and gives no performance guarantee. Engines sometimes optimize it, but you can't rely on that for large or long-lived arrays. Use a head index, a linked list or a ring buffer.

questions.prompt: A circular buffer that doubles its capacity when full can support amortized O(1) push and pop at both ends, making it a good deque.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With head and tail indices that wrap modulo the capacity, adding or removing at either end is O(1). When the buffer is full, copying into a buffer twice the size costs O(n) occasionally, but that is amortized O(1) per operation, the same argument as dynamic arrays.

questions.prompt:
Given a sorted array `a` and target `t`, this loop runs with `lo = 0, hi = a.length`:
`while (lo < hi) { const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1; if (a[mid] < t) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid; }`
What does `lo` hold when it ends?
options: The first index where a[i] > t, or a.length if none
The first index where a[i] >= t, or a.length if none
The index of t if present, otherwise -1
The last index where a[i] <= t, or -1 if none
questions.explanation: This is lower bound: everything left of lo is < t, and everything from hi onward is >= t. When they meet, lo is the first index with a[i] >= t, or a.length if every element is smaller. Changing < to <= turns it into upper bound (first index > t).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The first 2 is at index 1 (lower bound). The first element > 2 is the 5 at index 4 (upper bound), so the 2s span [1, 4) and there are 4 - 1 = 3 of them. 9 is larger than everything, so lower bound returns a.length = 5, not -1.

questions.prompt: This search for the largest x with ok(x) true sometimes hangs. Why?
options: The loop should be `lo <= hi`; with `<` it exits too early
ok() is called too often, making the search O(n)
hi = mid - 1 can make hi negative, which >> mishandles
When hi = lo + 1, mid rounds down to lo; if ok(lo) holds, lo = mid changes nothing and the loop never ends. Use mid = (lo + hi + 1) >> 1
questions.explanation: When the update is lo = mid, mid must round up or the range can stop shrinking. With hi = lo + 1, a floor mid equals lo, and if ok(lo) is true nothing changes. Switching to `<=` doesn't help: it changes the termination condition, not the rounding.

questions.prompt: 'Koko eating bananas' finds the minimum speed k to finish all piles within h hours. Which property makes binary search over k valid?
options: The piles are sorted
Feasibility is monotonic: if speed k finishes in time, every speed greater than k also does
The answer is always one of the pile sizes
Total time is a linear function of k
questions.explanation: Binary search on the answer needs a predicate that is false up to some threshold and true after it. Hours needed, sum of ceil(pile/k), never increases as k grows, so feasibility is monotonic. The piles don't need to be sorted, and the answer need not equal any pile size.

questions.prompt: 'Ship packages within D days' binary searches capacity between max(weights) and sum(weights). Each feasibility check is a greedy pass over n packages. What's the total time complexity (S = sum of weights)?
options: O(n log S)
O(n log n)
O(S log n)
O(n * S)
questions.explanation: The search range has at most S values, so there are O(log S) iterations, and each runs an O(n) greedy check: O(n log S). O(n * S) is what you'd get by trying every capacity linearly.

questions.prompt: You binary search sqrt(x) on doubles to about 1e-9 precision. Which loop is guaranteed to terminate for any positive double x, including x = 1e18?
options: `while (hi - lo > 1e-9)` halving the interval
`while (lo <= hi)` with lo = mid + 1 / hi = mid - 1
A fixed number of iterations (e.g. 100) halving [lo, hi]
`while (lo !== hi)` halving the interval
questions.explanation: For x = 1e18 the answer is near 1e9, where adjacent doubles are about 1e-7 apart. hi - lo can never drop below 1e-9, so that loop spins forever, and lo !== hi can stall the same way. ±1 updates skip real values. A fixed iteration count always ends and converges to full precision.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Comparing a[mid] with a[hi] shows which half holds the rotation point. If a[mid] > a[hi], the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to its left. The unrotated [1,2,3] correctly returns 1. Comparing with a[lo] instead gets the unrotated case wrong.

questions.prompt: Which of these are naturally solved with binary search on the answer? Select all that apply.
options: Shortest path between two nodes in a weighted graph
Counting distinct values in an unsorted array
Minimum number of days to make m bouquets
Minimum eating speed to finish piles within h hours
Split an array into m parts minimizing the largest part sum
questions.explanation: Each of the first three asks for the smallest value whose feasibility test (a greedy O(n) check) is monotonic. Counting distinct values uses a Set, and weighted shortest paths need Dijkstra-style algorithms; neither has a monotonic 'is answer >= x' predicate to search over.

questions.prompt: Which statements about binary search are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It can find a minimum in a rotated sorted array or a peak in an unsorted array in O(log n)
It needs a predicate that is monotonic over the search space, not necessarily a fully sorted array
On a linked list it still runs in O(log n) because only log n comparisons are made
If each predicate check costs O(n), the whole search costs O(n log range)
questions.explanation: Binary search needs a yes/no boundary, which rotated arrays and slope-based peak finding both have. On a linked list each comparison is cheap, but reaching the middle node takes O(n) steps, so the total is O(n) or worse. Expensive checks multiply the log factor.

questions.prompt: `(lo + hi) >> 1` is safe for every JavaScript array index because JS numbers are 64-bit floats.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. >> converts its operand to a 32-bit signed integer, so if lo + hi exceeds 2^31 - 1 the result goes negative. Array lengths can reach 2^32 - 1. Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2) or lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1) avoids this; the float representation doesn't help once >> is applied.

questions.prompt: A peak element (strictly greater than its neighbours, with out-of-bounds counting as -Infinity) can be found in O(log n) in an unsorted array by always moving toward the larger neighbour of mid.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. If a[mid] < a[mid + 1], a peak must exist to the right, because the values either keep rising to the boundary or turn down somewhere. So you can discard the left half. The array doesn't need to be sorted, only to have this local slope property.

questions.prompt: A log file of 10 million timestamps is almost sorted: each entry is at most a few positions away from where it belongs. Which simple algorithm handles this especially well?
options: Insertion sort
Selection sort
Quicksort with the first element as pivot
Heap sort
questions.explanation: Insertion sort runs in O(n + inversions), and with each item only a few places off that is close to O(n). Selection sort is always O(n^2). Quicksort with a first-element pivot degrades towards O(n^2) on nearly sorted input. Heap sort is O(n log n) no matter how sorted the input is.

questions.prompt: You need to sort 20 million exam scores that are integers from 0 to 100. Which approach is asymptotically best?
options: Insertion sort, since many values repeat
Merge sort, O(n log n)
Quicksort with a random pivot, O(n log n) expected
Counting sort, O(n + k) with k = 101
questions.explanation: With only 101 possible keys, counting sort counts occurrences and writes them back in O(n + k), effectively linear. The O(n log n) lower bound only applies to comparison sorts. Insertion sort is still O(n^2) on random order, duplicates or not.

questions.prompt: A hand-written quicksort that always picks the first element as pivot suddenly takes seconds on a 50,000-element input that is already sorted. Why?
options: Every partition is maximally unbalanced (0 and n-1 elements), giving O(n^2) time and O(n) recursion depth
Already-sorted arrays trigger V8 deoptimization of the comparator
Quicksort requires the input to be shuffled to be correct
Sorted input causes stack overflow only in JavaScript
questions.explanation: With the minimum as pivot every partition is empty on one side, so each level removes only one element: O(n^2) comparisons and recursion depth n. The output is still correct; only performance breaks. Random or median-of-three pivots avoid this.

questions.prompt: In this merge step, which change would make merge sort unstable?
options: Using out.push instead of preallocating out
Splitting the array at Math.floor(n / 2) instead of Math.ceil(n / 2)
Changing `<=` to `<`, so ties take from the right half first
Copying the rest of left before the rest of right after the loop
questions.explanation: Stability means equal keys keep their original order. Elements of the left half came first, so on a tie the left element must be taken. With `<`, a tie takes the right element first and reverses equal keys. The split point and copying the leftover tails don't affect stability.

questions.prompt: V8 implements Array.prototype.sort with TimSort. Which combination of properties best explains that choice?
options: It's stable (required by ES2019), O(n log n) worst case, and close to O(n) on input with long sorted runs
It's the only algorithm that works with custom comparators
It's unstable but has the lowest constant factors on random data
It's in-place with O(1) extra memory and O(n) worst case
questions.explanation: ES2019 requires sort to be stable. TimSort is a stable merge/insertion hybrid with an O(n log n) worst case that detects existing runs, so real-world partly sorted data sorts quickly. It is not O(1) memory (merging needs a buffer), and any comparison sort can take a comparator.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort makes one shift per inversion (a pair that is out of order). [3,1,2] has 2 inversions, (3,1) and (3,2); sorted input has 0; [3,2,1] has 3. This is why it is O(n + inversions): fast on nearly sorted data and O(n^2) on reversed data.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The counts are two 0s, one 1, one 2 and two 3s, so count = [2,1,1,2]. Writing each value out count times gives 001233. This simple version only works for plain integers; to sort records stably by key, you take prefix sums of the counts and place items from the end.

questions.prompt: Which of these sorting algorithms are stable as typically implemented? Select all that apply.
options: Merge sort
Counting sort using prefix sums
Heap sort
In-place quicksort (Lomuto or Hoare partition)
Insertion sort
questions.explanation: Merge sort (taking from the left on ties), insertion sort (shifting only strictly greater elements) and prefix-sum counting sort all keep equal keys in order. Heap sort and in-place quicksort swap elements over long distances, so equal keys can swap places.

questions.prompt: Which algorithms sort an array using O(1) or O(log n) extra space? Select all that apply.
options: Heap sort
Counting sort with a key range k much larger than n
Quicksort that recurses on the smaller partition first
Standard top-down merge sort on arrays
Insertion sort
questions.explanation: Heap sort and insertion sort are in-place with O(1) extra space. Quicksort that recurses on the smaller side keeps the stack at O(log n). Array merge sort needs an O(n) buffer, and counting sort needs O(k) for its counts, which is large when the key range is wide.

questions.prompt: No comparison-based sort can beat Θ(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, yet counting sort can sort n integers in [0, k) in O(n + k).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A comparison sort must tell apart n! orderings, which needs about log2(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons. Counting sort never compares elements; it uses their values as array indices, so that lower bound doesn't apply. It's only practical when k is not much larger than n.

questions.prompt: Choosing the quicksort pivot uniformly at random makes quicksort's worst-case running time O(n log n).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A random pivot makes the expected time O(n log n) on every input and makes adversarial inputs unlikely, but an unlucky sequence of pivots can still produce O(n^2). Guaranteeing O(n log n) needs something like introsort (falling back to heap sort) or median-of-medians.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code: console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort().join(','));
questions.explanation: Without a comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so '1' < '10' < '100' < '9'. For numeric order you need `(a, b) => a - b`. This is one of the most common JS sorting bugs.

questions.prompt: Why is `arr.sort((a, b) => a > b)` a broken numeric comparator?
options: It sorts in descending order instead of ascending
It returns booleans that coerce to 1 or 0, never a negative number, so 'a should come first' is indistinguishable from 'equal' and the result depends on the engine
Booleans cause a TypeError in strict mode
It works correctly but is slower than a - b
questions.explanation: A comparator must return negative, zero or positive. true/false become 1/0, so the engine is never told that a comes before b, and the comparator isn't consistent. Depending on array length and engine, it may happen to work on small inputs and silently fail on others. It does not throw.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
RangeError
1,2,3

TypeError
1,2,3
questions.explanation: Subtracting two BigInts gives a BigInt, and sort converts the comparator's result with ToNumber, which throws a TypeError for BigInt. Comparing with < and > and returning plain numbers works for BigInt, mixed-precision values and anything else that's ordered.

questions.prompt: In a Node 22 service you need a numerically sorted copy of `prices` without mutating the original array. Which is correct?
options: prices.sort((a, b) => a - b), since sort returns a new array
[...prices].sort(), since spreading makes elements compare numerically
prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)
Array.from(prices).reverse().sort()
questions.explanation: toSorted (ES2023, available in Node 20+) returns a new sorted array and leaves the original untouched. sort mutates in place and returns the same array. Spreading copies the array, but without a comparator the copy still sorts as strings.

questions.prompt: Sort employees by department ascending (A to Z), then by salary descending within a department. Which comparator does that?
options: (a, b) => b.salary - a.salary || a.dept.localeCompare(b.dept)
(a, b) => a.dept > b.dept || a.salary < b.salary
(a, b) => a.dept.localeCompare(b.dept) || b.salary - a.salary
(a, b) => a.dept.localeCompare(b.dept) && b.salary - a.salary
questions.explanation: `||` falls through to the second key only when the first comparison returns 0 (same department). `&&` returns 0 whenever departments differ. The boolean version never returns negative numbers. Swapping the key order sorts by salary first, which is the wrong priority.

questions.prompt: In Node 22, users are sorted by name, then sorted again with `(a, b) => a.age - b.age`. What's guaranteed about users who have the same age?
options: They are grouped, but their order changes between runs
Nothing; their order is implementation-defined
They stay in name order, because Array.prototype.sort is stable since ES2019
They are reversed relative to name order
questions.explanation: Since ES2019 the spec requires a stable sort, so elements that compare equal keep their previous relative order. Sorting by the secondary key first and the primary key second therefore yields a correct multi-key sort. Before ES2019, V8 used an unstable quicksort for long arrays.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
const a = ['b', 'B', 'a', 'A'];
console.log(a.toSorted().join(''), a.toSorted((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y, 'en')).join(''));
options: aAbB ABab
abAB aAbB
ABab aAbB
ABab AaBb
questions.explanation: The default sort compares UTF-16 code units, and all uppercase letters (65-90) come before lowercase (97-122): ABab. localeCompare with 'en' uses ICU collation, which orders by letter first and puts lowercase before uppercase on ties: aAbB. Use localeCompare or Intl.Collator for human-facing order.

questions.prompt: Code shuffles a playlist with `songs.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5)`. What's the best review comment?
options: Fine, it's an unbiased O(n log n) shuffle
It's correct, but should use 0.5 - Math.random() to avoid bias
It throws because comparators must be pure
The comparator is inconsistent, so the result is implementation-defined and not uniformly random; use a Fisher-Yates shuffle
questions.explanation: The comparator gives random answers for the same pair, which the spec calls inconsistent, so the resulting order is implementation-defined and in practice biased. Fisher-Yates (swap i with a random j <= i, from the end) is O(n) and uniform. Flipping the sign doesn't fix anything.

questions.prompt: Which comparators sort an array of finite numbers in ascending order? Select all that apply.
options: (a, b) => Math.sign(a - b)
(a, b) => a > b
(a, b) => b - a
(a, b) => a - b
questions.explanation: The first three all return a negative number when a < b, zero when equal, and a positive number when a > b. `a > b` returns booleans and never a negative value, so it's broken. `b - a` is a valid comparator, but for descending order.

questions.prompt: Which statements about sorting dates in JavaScript are correct? Select all that apply.
options: `(a, b) => a - b` works for Date objects because subtraction converts them to millisecond timestamps
ISO-8601 date strings ('YYYY-MM-DD') sort chronologically with plain string comparison
Calling sort() with no comparator on Date objects sorts them chronologically
`(a, b) => (a > b ? 1 : -1)` is a consistent comparator for Dates
questions.explanation: Date - Date gives numbers, and zero-padded ISO strings compare lexicographically in date order. Default sort converts Dates to strings like 'Mon Jan 01 ...', which puts weekday names in alphabetical order. The ternary comparator never returns 0, so it reports equal dates as different, which is inconsistent.

questions.prompt: Array.prototype.sort places undefined elements at the end of the array without ever passing them to the comparator.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The spec's sort algorithm moves undefined values to the end (with holes after them) and calls the comparator only for the other elements. So a comparator doesn't need to handle undefined, but null and NaN are passed to it and must be handled.
