questions.prompt: An ad click aggregator must report clicks per ad for each non-overlapping 1-minute bucket (12:00-12:01, 12:01-12:02, ...). Which window type fits?
options: Session window with a 1-minute inactivity gap
Sliding window of 1 minute that advances every 10 seconds
Tumbling window of 1 minute
A single global window triggered every minute
questions.explanation: Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping, so each click lands in exactly one minute bucket. A sliding/hopping window overlaps, so one click would be counted in several windows.

questions.prompt: Mobile clients buffer clicks offline and deliver them up to 3 minutes late. Billing must attribute each click to the minute it actually happened. What should the aggregation job use?
options: Processing-time windows, since late data averages out over a day
Event-time windows with a watermark that tolerates about 3 minutes of lateness
Hold every window open indefinitely until no more data can arrive
Windows keyed on the time the event reached the stream processor
questions.explanation: Event-time windows assign clicks by when they occurred; a watermark with allowed lateness lets windows close once late data is unlikely. Processing-time windows would put late clicks into the wrong minute, which matters for billing.

questions.prompt: In a stream processor such as Apache Flink, what does a watermark with timestamp 12:05:00 assert?
options: The consumer has committed Kafka offsets for everything produced before 12:05:00
All events up to wall-clock time 12:05:00 on the worker have been processed
A checkpoint containing state as of 12:05:00 has completed
No more events with event time earlier than 12:05:00 are expected, so windows ending by then may fire
questions.explanation: A watermark is a (heuristic) statement about event-time progress: events older than it are not expected, so windows ending at or before it can emit. It is unrelated to wall-clock time, offsets or checkpoints.

questions.prompt: A Flink job reads clicks from Kafka, computes per-minute counts, and inserts rows into a SQL table. After a crash and restore from the last checkpoint, some minutes appear twice in the table. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Event time was used; switch to processing time so replayed events fall into new windows
Kafka auto-commit was disabled; enable it so offsets are committed on every poll
The checkpoint interval is too short; increase it so fewer checkpoints are replayed
The sink is not idempotent or transactional; upsert keyed by (ad_id, window_start) or use a two-phase-commit sink
questions.explanation: Restoring from a checkpoint replays input since that checkpoint, so windows can be emitted again. Exactly-once end to end needs an idempotent (upsert) or transactional sink. Enabling Kafka auto-commit would bypass Flink's checkpointed offsets and can lose data.

questions.prompt: What is the main operational criticism of the Lambda architecture that the Kappa architecture addresses?
options: Lambda cannot store raw events, so historical recomputation is impossible
Lambda cannot serve low-latency queries because everything goes through batch jobs
The same business logic has to be built and kept consistent in two separate systems, a batch layer and a speed layer
Lambda requires exactly-once delivery from the message broker to work at all
questions.explanation: Lambda runs a batch layer and a speed layer whose outputs are merged, so the same logic lives in two codebases that must agree. Kappa uses one streaming pipeline and reprocesses by replaying the log. Lambda does serve low latency through its speed layer.

questions.prompt: In a Kappa architecture you fix a bug in the click-aggregation logic and need to recompute the last 30 days. How is this normally done?
options: Restore the job from its latest checkpoint so recent windows are recomputed
Start the fixed job as a new consumer from the start of the retained log, write to a new table, and switch readers once it catches up
Edit the aggregate rows in place with SQL updates that apply the correction
Run a nightly batch job over a data warehouse copy and merge it with the stream output
questions.explanation: Kappa reprocessing replays the immutable log (which must retain at least 30 days) through the corrected job into a fresh output, then cuts over. Restoring the latest checkpoint only replays a few minutes and would keep the old bug for older windows.

questions.prompt: A viral ad sends 40% of all clicks to one ad_id, overloading the single task that owns that key. Which mitigation works best?
options: Add more Kafka partitions so the hot key spreads across more consumers
Switch the job from event time to processing time to reduce buffering
Increase the window size so the hot key emits fewer results
Salt the key into N sub-keys (ad_id#0..N-1), pre-aggregate in parallel, then merge the partial counts in a second stage
questions.explanation: Salting spreads one hot key across many tasks and a second stage combines partial sums, which works because counts are associative. More partitions don't help: one key still hashes to one partition and one task.

questions.prompt: Which statements about session windows are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Their length is determined by gaps in activity rather than a fixed size
Their start and end times are known as soon as the first event arrives
Two sessions for the same key can merge when a late event fills the gap between them
They suit analytics like 'clicks per user visit'
questions.explanation: Session windows close after an inactivity gap, so their bounds depend on the data and can merge when a late event bridges two sessions. Because they are data-driven, the end time is not known when the first event arrives.

questions.prompt: An ad click aggregator must produce accurate billing counts and a real-time dashboard. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Deduplicate clicks by click_id within a bounded time window before counting
Use processing-time windows for billing because they are simpler to operate
Keep raw click events in durable storage such as object storage for audits and recomputation
Periodically reconcile streaming results against a batch recomputation over stored raw events
questions.explanation: Dedup, reconciliation and keeping raw events are standard for money-related counts. Processing-time windows attribute late clicks to the wrong period, which is unacceptable for billing even if fine for a rough dashboard.

questions.prompt: A hopping (sliding) window of size 10 minutes that advances every 1 minute assigns each event to 10 windows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each event belongs to size / slide = 10 / 1 = 10 overlapping windows. This is why sliding windows cost more state and output than tumbling windows of the same size.

questions.prompt: In a Kappa architecture, reprocessing historical data is impossible, so a separate batch layer is still required.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Kappa reprocesses by replaying the retained log through a new version of the streaming job. The batch layer is exactly what Kappa removes; the requirement is long enough log retention (or tiered storage).

questions.prompt: In Redis, which command adds 50 points to player:42 in the sorted set 'leaderboard', creating the member if it doesn't exist?
options: ZINCRBY leaderboard 50 player:42
HINCRBY leaderboard player:42 50
ZADD leaderboard NX 50 player:42
INCRBY leaderboard:player:42 50
questions.explanation: ZINCRBY increments a member's score in a sorted set and creates it if missing. ZADD with NX only adds new members and never updates existing scores, so it would ignore the increment for returning players.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of ZINCRBY on a Redis sorted set with N members?
options: O(N log N)
O(N)
O(log N)
questions.explanation: Sorted sets use a skip list plus a hash table, so updating a score and repositioning the member is O(log N). The O(1) hash lookup finds the member, but the reorder in the skip list is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: Scores are 'higher is better'. Which Redis command returns player:42's 0-based rank where rank 0 is the top scorer?
options: ZCOUNT leaderboard player:42 +inf
ZREVRANK leaderboard player:42
ZSCORE leaderboard player:42
ZRANK leaderboard player:42
questions.explanation: ZREVRANK ranks from highest to lowest score. ZRANK ranks ascending, so it would give 0 to the lowest scorer; ZSCORE returns the score, not the rank.

questions.prompt: Which command returns the top 10 players with their scores, highest first (Redis 6.2+)?
options: ZREVRANK leaderboard 0 9
ZRANGEBYSCORE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE leaderboard 0 10 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE leaderboard 0 9 REV WITHSCORES
questions.explanation: ZRANGE with REV and index range 0..9 returns the 10 highest-scored members (ZREVRANGE does the same in older versions). '0 10' is inclusive and returns 11 members in ascending order; ZRANGEBYSCORE 0 9 filters by score values, not positions.

questions.prompt: Two players have equal scores, and the one who reached the score first should rank higher. How do you implement this with a Redis sorted set?
options: Store timestamps in a separate hash; ZRANGE reads it when scores are equal
Encode a tiebreaker into the score, e.g. points * 10^10 + (MAX_TS - achievedAtSeconds), keeping values within 2^53
Nothing extra: Redis breaks ties by insertion time automatically
Use ZADD GT so the earlier score cannot be overwritten
questions.explanation: Redis orders equal scores lexicographically by member name, not by time, so the tiebreak must be folded into the score. Scores are doubles, so the composite must stay below 2^53 to remain exact.

questions.prompt: A Count-Min Sketch counts search-query frequencies with only non-negative increments. What kind of error can its estimates have?
options: Only underestimates, because collisions cancel out
Errors in both directions, symmetric around the true count
Exact counts for frequent items and zero for rare ones
Only overestimates, because hash collisions add other items' counts
questions.explanation: Each counter cell collects the counts of every item hashing to it, and the estimate is the minimum over rows, so it can only be equal to or above the true count. It never underestimates with non-negative updates.

questions.prompt: A leaderboard is sharded across 8 Redis nodes by user id (one sorted set per shard). How do you get the exact global top 100?
options: Fetch the top 100 from every shard and merge the 800 candidates, keeping the best 100
Fetch the top 13 from each shard (100/8, rounded up) and merge them
Write every score to one key and read from its replicas to spread load
Run ZUNIONSTORE across the 8 keys on the cluster and read the result
questions.explanation: Any user in the global top 100 must be in the top 100 of their own shard, so the union of per-shard top-100s contains the answer. Taking 13 per shard fails if one shard holds most top players; ZUNIONSTORE fails across hash slots in Redis Cluster.

questions.prompt: Which are valid techniques for finding approximate top-K heavy hitters in a very high-volume stream with bounded memory? Select all that apply.
options: The Space-Saving (or Misra-Gries) algorithm with a fixed number of counters
A Count-Min Sketch combined with a min-heap of the current K best items
A Bloom filter that reports how many times each item was inserted
A HyperLogLog per item to estimate how often each item occurs
questions.explanation: CMS plus a heap and Space-Saving/Misra-Gries are classic bounded-memory frequency algorithms. HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements, not frequencies, and a Bloom filter only answers membership.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Redis sorted sets are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Members are unique; adding an existing member updates its score
They are backed only by a hash table, so every range query scans all members
Scores are double-precision floats, so integers above 2^53 can lose precision
ZRANGEBYSCORE costs O(log N + M), where M is the number of returned elements
questions.explanation: Sorted sets combine a hash table (member to score) with a skip list ordered by score, which is why range queries are O(log N + M). Scores are IEEE-754 doubles, so very large integers are not exact.

questions.prompt: Running ZINCRBY for a member that is not yet in the sorted set creates it with the increment as its score.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: ZINCRBY treats a missing member as having score 0, so it is created with the increment. That makes it safe for the first score event of a new player.

questions.prompt: When any item can appear on any server, merging each server's local top-K list always yields the exact global top-K.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: An item ranked K+1 on every server never appears in any local list, yet its combined count could be the global #1. Merging local top-K lists is only exact when each item's full count lives on a single server, for example when partitioned by item key.

questions.prompt: A Node service schedules a daily email job with node-cron and runs on 3 replicas. Users get the email three times. What is the right fix?
options: Increase the job's retry count so failed replicas stop retrying
Configure each replica to run the job at a different minute
Add random jitter to the cron start time on each replica
Make sure only one executor runs each scheduled run, e.g. via a lease in a shared store or a single scheduler service
questions.explanation: Every replica runs its own in-process cron, so the job fires once per replica. You need coordination (a lease or a dedicated scheduler) so one run is claimed by one worker. Jitter or staggered minutes still runs it three times.

questions.prompt: Why should a worker's claim on a scheduled job be a lease with an expiry rather than a lock with no TTL?
options: Leases guarantee that each job runs exactly once
Leases are faster to acquire than locks in every database
If the worker crashes, the claim expires and another worker can take the job
Locks without TTL cannot be shared across machines
questions.explanation: A crashed holder never releases a TTL-less lock, so the job is stuck forever. A lease frees itself after expiry. It does not guarantee exactly-once: a slow holder may still be running when the lease passes to someone else.

questions.prompt: Worker A holds a job lease, then hits a 40-second GC pause. The lease expires, worker B takes it and writes results. A wakes up and writes stale results. What prevents A's write?
options: Use a longer lease TTL so pauses never exceed it
Have A check that it still holds the lease right before writing
Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token with each lease and have storage reject writes with an older token
Acquire the lease with Redis SET NX instead of a database row
questions.explanation: With fencing tokens, the storage itself refuses writes from an older lease holder, which closes the race. Checking the lease before writing still leaves a gap between the check and the write in which A can pause again.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, several workers poll a jobs table for due jobs. Which approach lets them claim different rows concurrently without blocking each other?
options: LOCK TABLE jobs IN EXCLUSIVE MODE before every poll
SELECT due rows, then UPDATE them to 'running' without any row lock
SELECT ... FOR SHARE on the due rows, then mark them 'running'
SELECT ... ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction, then mark them 'running'
questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks the selected rows and makes other workers skip them instead of waiting, so each worker gets a different batch. FOR SHARE lets several workers lock the same row, so two of them can claim it.

questions.prompt: A scheduled job calls a flaky third-party API. Which retry policy is most appropriate?
options: Retry immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
Exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count, then a dead-letter queue
Retry every second forever with a fixed delay
Never retry; let the next scheduled run pick up the work
questions.explanation: Backoff with jitter avoids hammering a struggling dependency and prevents synchronized retry storms; a cap plus a DLQ keeps permanent failures visible. Tight loops or fixed infinite retries amplify outages.

questions.prompt: A scheduler was down for 6 hours. An hourly job that rolls up billing for 'the previous hour' missed 6 runs. What should happen on recovery?
options: Fire the job 6 times concurrently with no identifiers
Create one run per missed scheduled time, keyed by (job_id, scheduled_for), so each hour is processed once
Skip the missed runs; the next scheduled run will catch up
Run once now, covering only the most recent hour
questions.explanation: Each hourly window must be processed, and keying runs by their scheduled time makes the backfill idempotent if recovery itself is retried. Running once covers only one hour; untracked concurrent runs can't be deduplicated.

questions.prompt: Why must scheduled jobs be idempotent even when you use leases?
options: Idempotent jobs run faster because the database caches them
Leases require idempotent jobs to be stored in a queue
Cron expressions can trigger twice within the same minute
Execution is effectively at-least-once: a crash or lease expiry can re-run a job that partly or fully completed
questions.explanation: A worker can finish the side effect and crash before marking the run done; the lease expires and another worker repeats it. Idempotency (unique keys, upserts) makes that repeat harmless. Cron itself fires once per matching minute.

questions.prompt: You are designing a distributed job scheduler. Which practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Compute next_run_at with explicit time zones so DST changes are handled deliberately
Store job definitions and next_run_at durably, with an index on next_run_at for polling
Keep the schedule only in the leader's memory to avoid database load
Have long-running workers heartbeat to extend their leases
questions.explanation: Durable, indexed schedules, lease heartbeats and explicit time-zone handling are standard. A schedule held only in the leader's memory is lost when the leader fails, which defeats the point of a distributed scheduler.

questions.prompt: Jobs are scheduled in local time in America/New_York. Which DST-related statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A job at 01:30 local time may run twice on the fall-back day because that hour repeats
A job scheduled at 12:00 UTC shifts by an hour in UTC terms when DST starts
Scheduling in UTC avoids gaps and repeats, but the job's local wall-clock time moves by an hour across seasons
A job at 02:30 local time may be skipped on the spring-forward day because that time does not exist
questions.explanation: In the US, clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00 in spring (02:30 doesn't exist) and from 02:00 back to 01:00 in autumn (01:00-01:59 happens twice). UTC has no DST, so a UTC schedule never shifts in UTC; it only shifts relative to local time.

questions.prompt: A Redis lock taken with SET key value NX PX 30000 guarantees mutual exclusion even if the holder pauses for longer than 30 seconds.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: After 30 seconds the key expires and another client can acquire it while the paused holder still believes it owns the lock. Safety then needs fencing tokens or idempotent side effects.

questions.prompt: With visibility timeouts (as in Amazon SQS), a message whose processing takes longer than the timeout can be delivered to another consumer while the first is still working on it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: When the visibility timeout expires without a delete, the message becomes visible again and can be received by another consumer. Long jobs should extend the timeout (ChangeMessageVisibility) and be idempotent.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes Prometheus's default collection model?
options: Agents push metrics to the server over UDP
The server scrapes HTTP /metrics endpoints of discovered targets at a fixed interval
The server tails application log files and parses metrics from them
Services write samples directly into the server's TSDB files
questions.explanation: Prometheus pulls: it discovers targets and scrapes their /metrics endpoints on an interval. Push-style UDP ingestion is the StatsD model, not Prometheus's default.

questions.prompt: A batch job runs for 20 seconds and Prometheus scrapes every 30 seconds. The job's metrics rarely show up. What is the standard fix?
options: Increase Prometheus retention so the samples are kept longer
Push the job's final metrics to a Pushgateway (or an OTLP collector) before it exits
Lower the scrape interval to 1 second for all targets
Use counters instead of gauges so values accumulate
questions.explanation: A pull model can't scrape a process that is gone. Short-lived jobs push to an intermediary that Prometheus then scrapes. A 1-second interval across all targets multiplies load and still races the job's exit.

questions.prompt: What is a genuine advantage of the pull model over push for metrics collection?
options: It works more easily for targets behind NAT or firewalls
It needs no service discovery because targets announce themselves
A failed scrape tells the server the target is down, and the server controls its own ingestion rate
It gives lower latency for very short-lived processes
questions.explanation: With pull, a failed scrape sets up=0, giving built-in health detection, and the server decides how much it ingests. Working behind NAT is a push advantage, and pull does require service discovery.

questions.prompt: A team adds a user_id label to http_requests_total and Prometheus memory usage explodes. Why?
options: Adding labels doubles the scrape frequency for that metric
Every unique label combination is a separate time series, and user_id makes the series count huge
Labels are stored as strings inside each sample, making every sample larger
Counters with labels force histogram buckets to be recomputed
questions.explanation: Series count is the product of label value counts; millions of user ids create millions of series, each with its own in-memory index and chunk. Unbounded values like user ids belong in logs or traces, not metric labels.

questions.prompt: Why do time-series databases such as Facebook's Gorilla and Prometheus compress samples so well (often around 1-2 bytes per sample)?
options: Only changed values are stored, indexed in a B-tree
Duplicate samples are hashed and removed across all series
Each sample is gzipped individually before being written
Regular timestamps give near-zero delta-of-deltas, and similar consecutive values XOR to few significant bits
questions.explanation: Delta-of-delta encoding turns evenly spaced timestamps into mostly zeros, and XOR-ing consecutive floats leaves few meaningful bits when values change slowly. Per-sample gzip would add overhead rather than remove it.

questions.prompt: You downsample raw 10-second p99 latency into 5-minute points by averaging the p99 values. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong, but it loses the original timestamps
Percentiles cannot be correctly averaged or re-aggregated; keep histogram bucket counts or sketches and compute p99 from the merged distribution
Downsampling must always use the median instead of the mean
You should take the max of the p99 values, which gives the exact 5-minute p99
questions.explanation: The p99 of a combined period is not the mean of sub-period p99s, especially with uneven traffic. Mergeable structures (histograms, t-digest, DDSketch) allow correct percentiles after rollup. The max of p99s is an upper bound, not the exact value.

questions.prompt: A metrics platform keeps raw data for 15 days, 5-minute rollups for 90 days and 1-hour rollups for 2 years. What is the main reason?
options: Rollups make old data more accurate than the raw samples
Cut storage and long-range query cost while keeping full detail for recent data
It speeds up writes, since raw samples are rejected after 15 days
Counters can only be stored after being rolled up
questions.explanation: Most queries over months only need coarse resolution, so rollups shrink storage and make dashboards spanning a year fast. Rollups lose detail; they never make data more accurate.

questions.prompt: Which per-bucket rollups can be correctly combined into coarser buckets later? Select all that apply.
options: Sum and count (so the average can be derived)
The plain mean of bucket averages when buckets have different sample counts
The 95th percentile of each bucket's 95th percentile
Minimum and maximum
questions.explanation: Sum, count, min and max are mergeable: combining them gives the exact value for the larger bucket. An unweighted mean of averages is biased when sample counts differ, and percentiles of percentiles are not the true percentile.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Prometheus counters and rate() are correct? Select all that apply.
options: rate() needs at least two samples in the range window to return a value
Apply sum() before rate(), i.e. rate(sum(x)), to get correct totals across instances
Counters only go up, except when they reset to zero, e.g. on process restart
rate() detects counter resets and compensates for them
questions.explanation: rate() handles resets per series and needs two or more samples. You must rate first and then sum, sum(rate(x[5m])), because summing raw counters hides the individual resets and produces bogus spikes.

questions.prompt: In a pure push model, the monitoring backend cannot easily distinguish a dead service from one that simply has nothing to report.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Missing pushes are ambiguous: the service may be down, partitioned or idle. Push setups add heartbeats or absence alerts; pull gets a failed scrape as an explicit signal.

questions.prompt: Time-series databases are typically optimized for frequent random in-place updates of historical data points.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: TSDBs are optimized for append-mostly writes of recent data and range reads over time, storing samples in immutable compressed blocks. Rewriting old points is rare and expensive.

questions.prompt: Discord's Cassandra message schema partitioned by (channel_id, bucket), where bucket is a fixed time window. Why add the bucket?
options: To spread a single message across several nodes
To let Cassandra sort messages alphabetically
To enable cross-channel joins
To bound partition size, so a busy, long-lived channel doesn't grow one partition forever
questions.explanation: With channel_id alone, an active channel's partition would grow without limit, and huge partitions hurt Cassandra reads and compaction. Discord's 2017 post describes a static ~10-day bucket in the partition key, with message_id as the clustering key. Cassandra has no joins.

questions.prompt: According to Discord's 2017 engineering post, why did they move message storage off MongoDB?
options: Licensing costs became too high
MongoDB had no replication
The data and indexes no longer fit in RAM, and latencies became unpredictable
MongoDB couldn't store Unicode emoji
questions.explanation: Discord began with a single MongoDB replica set. As messages grew into the billions, the working set outgrew memory and latency became erratic, so they chose Cassandra for scalable, predictable write-heavy storage. Replication and Unicode weren't the issues.

questions.prompt: Which problems did Discord's 2023 post cite with their large Cassandra cluster?
options: Inability to replicate across datacenters
Message IDs colliding across channels
Hot partitions, JVM garbage-collection pauses and compaction backlogs causing latency spikes and on-call toil
Lack of secondary indexes and SQL joins
questions.explanation: Busy channels concentrated reads on single partitions, GC pauses caused latency spikes, and compaction falling behind made reads worse. Operators spent a lot of time nursing the cluster. Multi-DC replication is a Cassandra strength, and Snowflake IDs don't collide.

questions.prompt: Discord placed Rust 'data services' between the API and the database. What key technique did they use to protect hot partitions?
options: Batching writes into daily files
Caching every message in Redis permanently
Rejecting reads for channels with more than 1,000 members
Request coalescing: concurrent identical reads share a single database query
questions.explanation: When a big announcement goes out, thousands of clients request the same channel's messages at once. Coalescing collapses them into one DB query whose result is fanned back out. Routing by channel (consistent hashing) sends those requests to the same instance so coalescing works.

questions.prompt: Why was ScyllaDB attractive to Discord as a Cassandra replacement?
options: It's a document database with flexible schemas
It's written in C++ with no garbage collector, uses a shard-per-core design, and is compatible with Cassandra's query language and drivers
It provides strict serializable transactions across all rows
It stores data only in memory
questions.explanation: Scylla reimplements Cassandra's data model and CQL in C++ (Seastar), so there are no JVM GC pauses, and each core owns a shard. Discord could keep its data model while getting more predictable latency. It is a wide-column store, not a document DB or an in-memory one.

questions.prompt: In Cassandra-style stores, a channel where users deleted millions of messages becomes very slow to read. Why?
options: Deletes trigger a full cluster repair on every read
Deletes write tombstones, and reads must scan past them until compaction purges them after the grace period
Deleted rows are moved to a separate slow table
Deleted data is decrypted on every read
questions.explanation: A delete is a write of a tombstone marker. Reads that cross a range full of tombstones must process them all, which costs CPU, memory and GC, until compaction drops them after gc_grace_seconds. Discord's 2017 post describes hitting exactly this.

questions.prompt: Discord uses Snowflake-style message IDs as the clustering key. What does that buy them?
options: IDs guarantee no two channels ever have messages in the same millisecond
IDs are time-ordered, so sorting by message_id gives chronological order without a separate timestamp sort
IDs are encrypted, so message content stays private
IDs can be guessed by clients, which avoids an extra round trip
questions.explanation: Snowflake IDs put a timestamp in the high bits, so clustering on message_id stores messages chronologically within a partition and 'latest N messages' is a cheap ordered slice. Encryption and uniqueness across channels aren't what the ordering provides.

questions.prompt: Which outcomes did Discord report after migrating messages from Cassandra to ScyllaDB? Select all that apply.
options: p99 read latency became lower and much more stable
All writes moved to strongly consistent Paxos transactions
Messages were moved into PostgreSQL
The cluster went from 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB nodes
questions.explanation: Discord's 2023 post reports 177 to 72 nodes, and p99 reads dropping from roughly 40–125 ms to about 15 ms. The data stayed in a Cassandra-compatible wide-column store with the same consistency model. There was no Paxos-everywhere change and no move to Postgres.

questions.prompt: How did Discord's data-service layer reduce load on hot message partitions? Select all that apply.
options: Requests for the same channel were routed to the same data-service instance via consistent hashing
Clients were made to poll less often by increasing app timeouts
A single channel's messages were scattered randomly across all nodes
Concurrent identical reads were coalesced into one database query
questions.explanation: Channel-affinity routing concentrates duplicate requests where they can be merged, and coalescing merges them. Randomly scattering a channel would break range reads, and the fix was server-side, not a client polling change.

questions.prompt: ScyllaDB is a JVM-based fork of Cassandra that relies on a carefully tuned garbage collector for low latency.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. ScyllaDB is a C++ reimplementation built on the Seastar framework. It has no JVM or GC, which is a major reason Discord saw steadier tail latency than with Cassandra.

questions.prompt: In Discord's Cassandra message store, a user editing a message while another deletes it could leave a row holding only the primary key and the edited text, so Discord had to detect and clean up such rows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Every Cassandra write is an upsert resolved last-write-wins per column, so the edit re-created the text column after the delete. Writing the whole message on edit could resurrect deleted messages, so Discord instead treated a null author_id (a required column) as corrupt and deleted the row ('How Discord Stores Billions of Messages', 2017).

questions.prompt: What does Netflix's Chaos Monkey do?
options: Randomly terminates production instances so teams must build services that tolerate instance loss
Injects bugs into code before deployment
Shuts down whole AWS regions every day
Load-tests services with synthetic traffic in staging
questions.explanation: Chaos Monkey kills instances during business hours, so instance failure becomes routine and services must be stateless and redundant. Region-level evacuation tests are Chaos Kong, a separate and much rarer exercise.

questions.prompt: How does Netflix Open Connect get content onto its edge appliances?
options: It proactively pre-positions content during off-peak hours, based on predicted popularity in each location
It fetches each title from AWS the first time a subscriber requests it
Subscribers' devices share segments peer-to-peer
ISPs upload titles themselves from DVDs
questions.explanation: Netflix knows its catalog and can forecast demand, so Open Connect Appliances are filled overnight during a 'fill window', when ISP links are quiet. Peak-hour streaming then comes from local disk instead of cache misses, unlike a pull-through CDN.

questions.prompt: Why are ISPs willing to host Netflix Open Connect Appliances in their networks?
options: The appliances also serve as the ISP's DNS resolvers
Regulators require it
Netflix provides the appliances at no charge, and serving locally cuts the ISP's upstream transit traffic
ISPs earn a fee per gigabyte streamed
questions.explanation: Netflix ships OCAs to qualifying ISPs for free. Because a large share of evening traffic is Netflix, serving it inside the ISP saves expensive transit and improves quality for subscribers, which benefits both sides.

questions.prompt: When a Netflix member opens the app, browses and presses Play, which part is served from AWS and which from Open Connect?
options: Browsing, recommendations, auth and playback steering run in AWS; video bytes come from Open Connect appliances
Everything is served from AWS
Browsing comes from Open Connect and video from AWS
Everything is served from Open Connect
questions.explanation: The control plane (UI APIs, personalization, licensing, choosing which OCAs to use) lives in AWS. Once playback starts, the client streams from OCA URLs it was given. This separates the compute-heavy logic from the bandwidth-heavy delivery.

questions.prompt: What problem was Netflix's Hystrix library designed to solve in its microservice architecture?
options: Encrypting traffic between services
Cascading failures: it wrapped remote calls with timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks
Service discovery
Distributed tracing of requests
questions.explanation: A slow dependency can exhaust a caller's threads and spread the outage. Hystrix isolated each dependency, failed fast when its circuit opened, and served fallbacks. Discovery was Eureka's job. Hystrix has been in maintenance mode since 2018, and the patterns live on in libraries like Resilience4j.

questions.prompt: What does Netflix's Chaos Kong exercise validate?
options: That new code passes unit tests
That database backups can be restored
That traffic can be evacuated from an entire AWS region to the remaining regions without a major member impact
That a single container can restart cleanly
questions.explanation: Netflix runs active-active across multiple AWS regions. Chaos Kong simulates losing a whole region and shifts its traffic to the others, proving capacity and failover work before a real regional outage. Instance-level failure is Chaos Monkey's domain.

questions.prompt: Which event Netflix has publicly described pushed it to move from its own datacenter to AWS?
options: An AWS sales promotion
A DDoS attack on its streaming launch day
A fire in its primary datacenter
A major database corruption in 2008 that stopped it from shipping DVDs for three days
questions.explanation: The 2008 corruption showed the risk of vertically scaled single points of failure. Netflix chose horizontally scalable, distributed systems in the cloud and completed the migration in early 2016.

questions.prompt: Match Netflix OSS components to their roles. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Hystrix: latency and fault tolerance (circuit breakers)
Zuul: edge gateway/router for incoming requests
Kafka: created at Netflix for chaos experiments
Chaos Monkey: load balancer for streaming traffic
Eureka: service discovery registry
questions.explanation: Eureka, Zuul and Hystrix were core Netflix OSS pieces. Chaos Monkey kills instances rather than balancing load, and Kafka was created at LinkedIn (Netflix uses it heavily for its data pipeline).

questions.prompt: Why does Netflix run chaos experiments in production instead of only in staging? Select all that apply.
options: Netflix runs no pre-production testing at all
Staging can't faithfully reproduce real traffic, data, configuration and dependency behavior
It builds confidence that the actual system people use tolerates failure
Production experiments need no blast-radius controls because failures never reach members
questions.explanation: The principle is to experiment on the real system, since that's where emergent failures hide. Netflix still limits blast radius carefully (ChAP routes only a small share of traffic into experiments) and still does pre-production testing.

questions.prompt: Netflix serves the majority of its streaming video bytes directly from AWS EC2 instances.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Video is served from Netflix's own Open Connect CDN appliances in ISPs and internet exchanges. AWS hosts the control plane: APIs, personalization, encoding pipelines and steering.

questions.prompt: Netflix's Chaos Automation Platform (ChAP) limits blast radius by routing a small slice of traffic into a control group and an experiment group and comparing their metrics.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. ChAP injects failures (e.g. latency or errors from a dependency) only for the experiment cohort and stops automatically if key metrics such as stream starts degrade. That makes production chaos safe enough to run continuously.

questions.prompt: Your server's POST /v1/payment_intents call to Stripe times out and you don't know whether it succeeded. What does Stripe recommend?
options: Retry with a new Idempotency-Key so it's treated as fresh
Retry the same request with the same Idempotency-Key header
Never retry payment calls
List recent payments and guess which one is yours
questions.explanation: Reusing the key makes the retry safe: if the first attempt went through, Stripe returns the saved result instead of creating a second payment. A new key would create a duplicate.

questions.prompt: You retry a Stripe request using the same idempotency key but change the amount. What happens?
options: Stripe creates a second object linked to the first
Stripe returns an error because the parameters don't match the original request for that key
Stripe silently returns the original result
Stripe processes the new amount and replaces the old result
questions.explanation: Stripe's idempotency layer compares incoming parameters with the original request and errors on a mismatch, which protects against accidental key reuse. Silently returning the original would hide a client bug.

questions.prompt: Per Stripe's docs, the first request with an idempotency key started executing and returned a 500 error. You retry with the same key. What do you get?
options: A 404 because failed requests aren't stored
A fresh attempt that may succeed
The same saved 500 result
A 409 telling you to use a new key
questions.explanation: Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request that began executing, whether it succeeded or failed, including 500s, and replays them. Results aren't saved when the request failed validation or conflicted with a concurrent request, so those can be retried with the same key.

questions.prompt: How should a Stripe client generate idempotency keys?
options: Generate a random V4 UUID (or similarly high-entropy value) per logical operation, and reuse it for that operation's retries
Use an incrementing integer that resets on deploy
Use the current Unix timestamp in seconds
Use the customer's email address
questions.explanation: Stripe suggests V4 UUIDs or other random strings with enough entropy to avoid collisions. Timestamps and counters collide across processes or after restarts, and an email would merge unrelated payments for the same customer.

questions.prompt: How does Stripe's date-based API versioning work for an account?
options: The account is pinned to the API version current at its first request; upgrades are opt-in, and a Stripe-Version header can override per request
Old versions are switched off every month
Every account is upgraded automatically on each release
Clients must send a version in the URL path, such as /v37/charges
questions.explanation: Stripe pins each account to a dated version (e.g. 2024-06-20) and internally transforms responses back to older shapes, so breaking changes never surprise existing integrations. The '/v1' in URLs is a stable prefix, not the evolving version.

questions.prompt: Stripe's guidance on network retries is to use exponential backoff with jitter. Why the jitter?
options: It makes requests harder to fingerprint
It spreads retries from many clients over time so they don't hit the server in synchronized waves
It's required by TLS
It shortens the total time to give up
questions.explanation: After an incident, clients that all failed at the same moment would retry at the same moments under pure exponential backoff, so their retries arrive together in bursts. Random jitter desynchronizes them and lets the service recover.

questions.prompt: Stripe list endpoints paginate with `starting_after=<object id>` instead of page numbers or offsets. Why?
options: Object IDs are smaller than integers
Offsets aren't supported by HTTP
It lets clients jump to any random page
Cursors are stable when new objects are inserted and don't require skipping N rows on every page
questions.explanation: With offsets, inserts shift items between pages (causing duplicates or gaps), and deep offsets get slower. Keying on the last seen ID is stable and index-friendly. Random page jumps are exactly what cursors give up.

questions.prompt: Which statements match Stripe's documented idempotency behavior? Select all that apply.
options: Keys may be removed automatically once they are at least 24 hours old
Keys never expire, so a key from last year still replays its result
Stripe generates the key and returns it in the first response
No result is saved if the request failed validation before the endpoint began executing
Sending a key on GET or DELETE has no effect, since those are already idempotent
questions.explanation: Those three come straight from Stripe's docs. Keys can be pruned after 24 hours, so they're meant for retry windows rather than permanent deduplication, and the client generates the key so it exists before the first attempt.

questions.prompt: Stripe object IDs carry type prefixes such as `cus_`, `pi_` and `ch_`. What are the benefits? Select all that apply.
options: The prefix guarantees global ordering across object types
The prefix encodes the account's secret key
The API can return a clearer error when an ID of the wrong type is passed
Humans can tell the object type at a glance in logs and support tickets
questions.explanation: Stripe has written about prefixed IDs as a developer-experience feature: they're self-describing for debugging and make wrong-type mistakes easy to spot. They carry no secrets and impose no ordering.

questions.prompt: With Stripe, a second request using the same idempotency key while the first is still executing is rejected rather than executed a second time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Stripe returns an idempotency error for a concurrent request with an in-use key, and saves no result for it, so the client can retry later and get the original outcome. This closes the race a simple check-then-insert would leave open.

questions.prompt: Stripe's versioning requires every client to send the newest version header, and old versions stop working with each release.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Accounts stay pinned to their version until they choose to upgrade. Stripe maintains backward-compatibility transforms so integrations written years ago keep working.

questions.prompt: Uber open-sourced H3, a hexagonal hierarchical spatial index. What is the main advantage of hexagons for its marketplace analysis?
options: All six neighbors share an edge and are equidistant from the center, which makes neighbor and gradient analysis uniform
Hexagon IDs are human-readable street addresses
Hexagons nest perfectly inside larger hexagons
Hexagons need no special handling anywhere on the globe
questions.explanation: Squares have neighbors at two different distances (edge versus corner), and triangles at three. Hexagons have one, which simplifies smoothing and k-ring aggregation for supply, demand and pricing. H3 children only approximately nest, and 12 pentagons per resolution need special handling.

questions.prompt: Uber's Ringpop, used in its Node.js dispatch services, provided what capability?
options: Application-layer sharding via consistent hashing, with SWIM-based gossip for cluster membership
A geospatial index built on quadtrees
A message queue replacing Kafka
Real-time map tile rendering
questions.explanation: Ringpop let a cluster of Node.js processes agree on membership (SWIM gossip) and route each key, such as a geo cell or rider, to its owner on a hash ring, forwarding requests when needed. It wasn't a spatial index or a queue.

questions.prompt: In Uber's 2015 talks on its dispatch system, which spatial library was described for dividing the map into cells to shard supply?
options: Elasticsearch geo_point
PostGIS R-trees
Geohash strings in MySQL
Google's S2 geometry library
questions.explanation: The dispatch rewrite talks describe using S2 cells (from projecting the sphere onto a cube) as shard keys for supply. H3 came later and became Uber's open-source standard for hexagonal analysis such as pricing.

questions.prompt: In H3, how does a cell relate to the next finer resolution?
options: Resolutions are independent with no parent/child relationship
Each cell has 32 children, like geohash
Each cell is split into exactly 4 children that tile it perfectly
Each cell has about 7 children (aperture 7) that only approximately cover the parent
questions.explanation: H3 uses aperture 7: each hexagon has about 7 children, each with roughly one-seventh of the area. Because hexagons can't be divided exactly into smaller hexagons, children only approximately fill the parent. Four children is quadtree or S2 behavior, and 32 is geohash.

questions.prompt: Why use consistent hashing (as Ringpop does) rather than `hash(key) % N` to assign cells to dispatch nodes?
options: It guarantees a perfectly even load
It keeps keys sorted by geography
It needs no hash function
When a node joins or leaves, only about 1/N of keys move instead of almost all of them
questions.explanation: With modulo, changing N remaps nearly every key and causes a storm of state movement. A hash ring moves only the keys adjacent to the changed node. Even load still needs virtual nodes, and hashing doesn't preserve geographic order.

questions.prompt: Why does representing an H3 cell as a 64-bit integer matter for large-scale data pipelines?
options: It makes cells compact, fast-to-compare keys for joins, group-bys and hash partitioning
It makes cells exactly equal in area
It means only 64 cells exist
It encrypts location data
questions.explanation: An H3 index packs resolution and cell digits into one 64-bit value, so 'aggregate trips per hexagon' becomes a cheap integer group-by or join. It isn't encryption, there are billions of cells at fine resolutions, and areas vary slightly.

questions.prompt: Uber has described using H3 to bucket supply and demand for dynamic pricing. Why bucket by hexagon instead of raw GPS points?
options: Aggregating into cells gives stable local counts to compare supply against demand and to smooth across neighbors
Hexagons hide all location data from the pricing team
GPS points can't be stored in databases
Pricing must be identical across a whole city
questions.explanation: Pricing needs per-area ratios, such as open requests versus idle drivers. Discrete cells turn noisy point data into counts that can be computed, cached and smoothed over k-rings. The point is local variation, not city-wide uniformity.

questions.prompt: Which statements about H3 are true? Select all that apply.
options: Each resolution includes exactly 12 pentagons
A cell index fits in a 64-bit integer
Child cells nest perfectly inside their parent
It has 16 resolutions (0 through 15)
It uses square cells for simpler math
questions.explanation: H3 projects onto an icosahedron, giving 16 resolutions with 12 pentagons each (topology requires them), and indexes fit in 64 bits. Hexagons can't be split exactly into smaller hexagons, so nesting is approximate, and the cells are hexagons by design.

questions.prompt: Ringpop used the SWIM protocol for membership. Which properties make SWIM suitable for large clusters? Select all that apply.
options: It requires a ZooKeeper ensemble to run
Membership changes spread epidemically by piggybacking on probe messages
Every node always has an identical, strongly consistent view of membership
Each node probes only a few random peers per period, so message load per node stays roughly constant as the cluster grows
Failure detection doesn't depend on a central coordinator
questions.explanation: SWIM's randomized probing, indirect pings and gossip dissemination scale well with no central service. The trade-off is that membership views are only eventually consistent, so nodes can briefly disagree, which is why it doesn't need ZooKeeper.

questions.prompt: H3 was created and open-sourced by Uber.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Uber open-sourced H3 in 2018. It's now widely used beyond Uber for geospatial analytics, with bindings in many languages and support in several databases.

questions.prompt: A grid can tile the whole sphere using only hexagons at every resolution, so H3 contains no other cell shapes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A sphere can't be tiled by hexagons alone. H3 places 12 pentagons at each resolution (at the icosahedron's vertices, mostly over oceans), and code doing neighbor traversal must handle them.

questions.prompt: Instagram's 2012 'Sharding & IDs' post describes a 64-bit ID layout. What is it?
options: 64 bits from a central auto-increment counter
41 bits timestamp, 10 bits machine ID, 12 bits sequence
32 bits timestamp, 32 bits random
41 bits milliseconds since a custom epoch, 13 bits logical shard ID, 10 bits per-shard sequence
questions.explanation: Instagram's IDs are 41 bits of time, 13 bits of logical shard (up to 8,192) and 10 bits of sequence. The 41/10/12 split is Twitter Snowflake's (timestamp, worker, sequence), the most common confusion.

questions.prompt: Why did Instagram want IDs that sort roughly by creation time?
options: So 'newest first' queries can sort or range-scan on the primary key without a separate timestamp index
So IDs are easier to memorize
To hide how many photos exist
Because PostgreSQL requires sorted primary keys
questions.explanation: Feeds and profiles are time-ordered, so time-prefixed IDs make ORDER BY id DESC equivalent to newest-first and keep inserts at the right edge of the B-tree. Postgres doesn't require sorted keys, and time-prefixed IDs actually reveal timing.

questions.prompt: Instagram created thousands of logical shards mapped onto far fewer physical database servers. What does that design enable?
options: Avoiding any routing logic in the application
Rebalancing by moving whole logical shards to new machines, without rehashing data or changing IDs
Making each logical shard exactly the same size
Cross-shard joins in a single SQL query
questions.explanation: A shard's ID never changes, only the logical-to-physical mapping. When a server fills up, some logical shards (PostgreSQL schemas) move to a new server. Picking a large logical count up front avoids painful resharding later. Joins across shards still aren't possible.

questions.prompt: With Instagram's 10-bit per-shard sequence, how many IDs can one logical shard generate in a single millisecond?
questions.explanation: 10 bits give 2^10 = 1,024 values per shard per millisecond (the sequence is taken mod 1024). 4,096 is Snowflake's 12-bit sequence, and 8,192 is Instagram's 13-bit shard space.

questions.prompt: Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys a poor fit for a write-heavy, time-ordered table in a B-tree database?
options: UUIDs can collide frequently
Random values insert all over the index, causing page splits and poor cache locality, and they don't sort by time
Databases cannot index 128-bit values
UUIDs must be generated by a central server
questions.explanation: Random keys land on random leaf pages, so the working set is the whole index and inserts fragment it. They're also twice the size of a 64-bit ID and give no time ordering. Collisions are vanishingly rare, and UUIDs are generated anywhere.

questions.prompt: Given Instagram's layout (41-bit time | 13-bit shard | 10-bit sequence), which expression extracts the shard ID from a BigInt id?
options: id >> 23n
(id >> 10n) & 0x1FFFn
(id >> 13n) & 0x3FFn
id & 0x3FFn
questions.explanation: Shift right by 10 to drop the sequence, then mask 13 bits (0x1FFF = 8191) to remove the timestamp. `id & 0x3FF` is the sequence, and `id >> 23n` is the timestamp. Embedding the shard lets any service route by ID with no lookup table.

questions.prompt: Facebook's TAO (USENIX ATC 2013) serves the social graph. Which description fits it?
options: A strongly consistent SQL database replacing MySQL
A geographically distributed, read-optimized caching layer over sharded MySQL that exposes objects and associations
A key-value store for photos and videos
A message queue for news feed fan-out
questions.explanation: TAO models the graph as objects (nodes) and associations (typed edges), caches them in tiers of leader and follower caches, and persists to sharded MySQL. It favors read throughput with eventual consistency across regions. Photos live in blob storage (Haystack, f4).

questions.prompt: Which statements about Snowflake-style time-prefixed 64-bit IDs are true? Select all that apply.
options: IDs from different shards or workers are strictly increasing across the whole system
A 41-bit millisecond timestamp covers roughly 69 years from the chosen epoch
Each ID needs a round trip to a central coordinator
If a server's clock moves backwards, the generator can produce duplicate or out-of-order IDs unless it guards against it
questions.explanation: 2^41 ms ≈ 2.2 trillion ms ≈ 69.7 years, and clock regressions are a known hazard (generators wait or refuse to issue IDs). Ordering across generators is only approximate (k-sorted), and the whole point is generating IDs locally without coordination.

questions.prompt: Which drawbacks did Instagram cite for the ID-generation alternatives it rejected? Select all that apply.
options: UUIDs are 128 bits and don't sort naturally by time
PostgreSQL had no way to run logic that generates IDs inside the database
Flickr-style ticket databases add a dedicated write path that can become a bottleneck
Snowflake added moving parts: running a separate ID service plus ZooKeeper
questions.explanation: Instagram considered UUIDs, Snowflake and ticket DBs, then generated IDs inside PostgreSQL itself using a PL/pgSQL function per shard schema. So Postgres could clearly do it, which is the scheme they shipped.

questions.prompt: In Instagram's design, each logical shard was implemented as a PostgreSQL schema.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Each logical shard was a Postgres schema containing the sharded tables and its own ID-generation function. Moving a schema to another physical server rebalances data without changing any IDs.

questions.prompt: Instagram's 2012 scheme generated IDs in a separate application service that the web tier called before each insert.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. IDs were generated inside each PostgreSQL shard by a PL/pgSQL function used as the column default. Avoiding a separate ID service was a deliberate goal.

questions.prompt: WhatsApp famously handled huge numbers of connections per server with a small team. Which runtime underpinned its chat servers?
options: Erlang on the BEAM VM (running on FreeBSD)
Go with goroutines
Java with Netty
Node.js on Linux
questions.explanation: WhatsApp built on Erlang (originally on an ejabberd/XMPP foundation) on FreeBSD. BEAM's lightweight processes, one per connection, plus heavy OS tuning enabled millions of connections per box.

questions.prompt: In Slack's real-time messaging architecture (2023 engineering post), what is the split between Gateway Servers and Channel Servers?
options: Both are stateless HTTP API servers
Gateway Servers store messages, and Channel Servers render the UI
Channel Servers hold WebSockets, and Gateway Servers write to MySQL
Gateway Servers hold client WebSocket connections and subscribe to channels, while Channel Servers own channels (via consistent hashing) and fan messages out to subscribed gateways
questions.explanation: Gateways are the connection tier near users. Each channel is owned by one Channel Server on a consistent-hash ring, which pushes new messages to every gateway that has subscribers for that channel. Messages are persisted through the web API and database, not by these servers.

questions.prompt: Why did Slack build Flannel, an application-level edge cache?
options: To replace MySQL as the system of record
Booting a client in a large team required a huge payload of every user and channel; Flannel let clients lazy-load only the data they needed
To cache images and file uploads
To provide end-to-end encryption
questions.explanation: Slack's original rtm.start returned the whole team's users and channels, which grew enormous for big organizations. Flannel sits near clients, holds team metadata and serves it on demand, cutting connect time and load on the backend.

questions.prompt: Slack originally sharded MySQL by workspace. Per its post on adopting Vitess, what was the main problem?
options: Workspaces were too small to shard
MySQL couldn't store emoji reactions
Very large enterprise workspaces outgrew a single shard and created hot spots, and finer-grained keys like channel were needed
Sharding forced every query to fan out to all shards
questions.explanation: Per-workspace shards were simple, but one huge customer could saturate a shard. Vitess let Slack shard by other keys (e.g. channel ID) while keeping MySQL. The issue was too-coarse tenancy, not fan-out.

questions.prompt: A chat app must not lose messages when a recipient's phone is offline. Which delivery design fits?
options: Broadcast to all devices globally and let them filter
Store-and-forward: persist the message server-side, push it when the device reconnects, and remove or mark it once the client acknowledges
Ask the sender to resend every few minutes until it works
Deliver only to currently connected clients and drop the rest
questions.explanation: The server keeps undelivered messages and uses client acks (with message IDs for dedup on retry) to know when delivery happened. WhatsApp documents that messages are deleted from its servers once delivered. Dropping or relying on sender retries loses messages.

questions.prompt: A message is posted to a channel with 50,000 members. How do architectures like Slack's fan it out efficiently?
options: Email each member
Have every member poll the channel every second
Insert one row per member into a per-user inbox table before replying
Send it once to the channel's owner server, which pushes one copy per subscribed gateway; each gateway delivers to its local connections
questions.explanation: Fan-out happens in memory over the connection tier: one hop to the channel owner, one per gateway, then local sockets. The message is stored once. Per-member inbox writes (fan-out-on-write) would mean 50,000 DB writes per message.

questions.prompt: WhatsApp's messages are 'deleted from our servers once delivered'. Which property does that store-and-forward model rely on?
options: Messages are sent peer-to-peer without servers
The server must permanently archive chat history for search
The server needs a reliable delivery acknowledgment from the recipient's device before it discards the message
Recipients must be online when the message is sent
questions.explanation: The server is a transient relay: it holds the message until the recipient's device confirms receipt, then drops it. History lives on devices (and optional user backups). Without reliable acks, deleting would lose messages.

questions.prompt: Which presence (online/away) designs scale to millions of users? Select all that apply.
options: Writing every heartbeat to the primary relational database
Heartbeats that refresh a TTL, so a missed heartbeat expires the user to offline
Broadcasting every presence change to every user in a huge workspace
Sending presence updates only to clients that are currently viewing or subscribed to that user
questions.explanation: TTL-based liveness avoids explicit logout handling, and interest-based subscription keeps fan-out proportional to what users actually see. Broadcasting is O(N²) traffic in big orgs, and persisting heartbeats floods the DB with throwaway writes.

questions.prompt: How do chat systems typically give users a consistent message order within a conversation? Select all that apply.
options: Every message across all channels globally is placed in one total order
Clients trust their own device clocks for ordering
A single owner per channel assigns increasing sequence numbers or server timestamps
Clients order by that server-assigned value and can detect gaps to request missing messages
questions.explanation: Per-conversation ordering from a single owner is cheap and is all users can perceive. Sequence numbers also make gaps detectable after reconnects. Global total order is unnecessary and costly, and device clocks drift.

questions.prompt: WhatsApp engineers publicly reported more than 2 million concurrent TCP connections on a single server in 2012.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. WhatsApp's January 2012 blog post ('1 million is so 2011') reported over 2 million connections on one FreeBSD server running Erlang, after kernel and BEAM tuning.

questions.prompt: With end-to-end encryption, the chat server can still read message contents to build server-side search indexes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. In E2EE (e.g. WhatsApp's Signal Protocol, rolled out in 2016) only endpoints hold the keys, and the server relays ciphertext. Search must happen on-device, which is a real product trade-off.

questions.prompt: In Shopify's pods architecture, what is a pod?
options: A Kubernetes pod running one Rails process
A fully isolated set of datastores (e.g. MySQL, Redis, Memcached) that holds a subset of shops
A group of microservices owned by one team
A CDN edge location
questions.explanation: Shopify partitions by shop: each shop lives in exactly one pod, and the pod has its own datastores. The name has nothing to do with Kubernetes pods, a common confusion in interviews.

questions.prompt: Why do pods help Shopify survive flash sales (e.g. a celebrity product drop)?
options: A hot shop can only saturate its own pod's datastores, so merchants in other pods are unaffected
Pods queue all writes until the sale ends
Pods cache every checkout page at the CDN
Pods automatically give each shop unlimited database capacity
questions.explanation: Pods limit blast radius: noisy-neighbor effects from one merchant's spike stay inside one pod. A single shop's write capacity is still bounded by its pod, which is why checkout throttling exists too.

questions.prompt: A request for `some-shop.myshopify.com` arrives. How does Shopify get it to the correct pod's data?
options: The shop ID is hashed modulo the number of pods on every request
DNS returns a different IP per pod and clients cache it forever
Every pod receives every request and ignores the ones it doesn't own
Software in the load balancers (Shopify calls it Sorting Hat) matches the request to its pod, adds a header and forwards it; app servers use that header to talk only to that pod's datastores
questions.explanation: Shopify's pods post (2018) describes Sorting Hat matching every request to a pod with a list of rules, tagging it with a header and forwarding it. App servers are shared, but each request touches only one pod's datastores. An explicit shop-to-pod mapping, unlike hashing by pod count, lets shops move between pods; broadcasting would break isolation.

questions.prompt: One pod becomes overloaded because a few shops grew huge. How does Shopify rebalance?
options: Move individual shops to another pod online, using a binlog-based migration tool (Ghostferry) with a brief cutover
Rehash every shop to a new pod count
Split each shop's tables across several pods
Ask merchants to export and re-import their data
questions.explanation: Shopify open-sourced Ghostferry, which copies a shop's rows and tails the MySQL binlog to keep them in sync, then performs a short cutover and updates the routing table. Shops are the unit of movement and never split across pods.

questions.prompt: Since a shop's data never spans pods, what is the main cost of the pod model?
options: Every request needs two-phase commit
Single-shop queries become distributed transactions
Shops can't have more than one product
Queries spanning many shops (platform-wide analytics, reporting) can't run against one database and go to separate data pipelines or warehouses
questions.explanation: Tenant-based partitioning makes in-shop work local and transactional, but cross-tenant queries need a separate system that aggregates data from all pods. Single-shop queries are the easy case.

questions.prompt: Shopify's core commerce application is well known for which architectural choice?
options: A Java EE application server cluster
A large Ruby on Rails modular monolith with enforced component boundaries
A serverless architecture built entirely on functions
Thousands of independently deployed microservices from day one
questions.explanation: Shopify has written extensively about deconstructing its monolith into components inside one Rails codebase (tooling such as Packwerk enforces boundaries) rather than splitting into microservices. Pods scale the data layer beneath that app.

questions.prompt: During a flash sale, checkout requests for one shop exceed what its pod's database can handle. What is the right protective pattern?
options: Let all requests through and rely on database autoscaling
Disable inventory checks so writes are cheaper
Throttle or queue checkouts at the edge and admit buyers at a rate the pod can sustain
Temporarily move the shop into every pod at once
questions.explanation: Admission control in front of checkout (Shopify has written about scriptable load balancers for this) keeps the pod healthy and gives buyers a fair queue. Databases don't scale up instantly, and skipping inventory checks causes overselling.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine properties or trade-offs of Shopify's pods? Select all that apply.
options: A single shop's writes automatically scale across all pods
Capacity grows by adding more pods
A failure or overload in one pod has a limited blast radius
A single very hot shop is still bounded by its one pod's capacity
Pods remove the need for any request routing
questions.explanation: Isolation and horizontal growth are the benefits, and the per-shop ceiling is the inherent limit, mitigated by throttling and moving big shops to roomier pods. Shops don't span pods, and routing to the right pod is essential.

questions.prompt: Compared with sharding every table by a hash of its row ID, why is partitioning by tenant (shop) a good fit for Shopify? Select all that apply.
options: Most requests touch only one shop, so they hit a single pod
Uneven tenant sizes mean big shops may need moving to keep pods balanced
All of one shop's data is colocated, so joins and transactions within a shop stay local
Every request must fan out to all pods to find a shop's rows
questions.explanation: Commerce requests are naturally scoped to a shop, so tenant colocation keeps them on one pod with local transactions. The flip side is skew between tenants. Fan-out would happen with row-hash sharding, not tenant-based routing.

questions.prompt: In Shopify's pods model, one shop's data is deliberately split across several pods to spread its load.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A shop lives entirely in one pod. That keeps queries and transactions local and makes isolation possible. Rebalancing moves whole shops rather than splitting them.

questions.prompt: Shopify's pods are an instance of cell-based architecture: self-contained units that each serve a subset of customers and contain failures.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Cells (pods) partition customers into independent units with their own data stores, behind a thin routing layer. The same pattern appears at AWS and Slack as a way to cap blast radius and scale by adding cells.

questions.prompt: What was Discord primarily optimizing for in its Cassandra → ScyllaDB migration?
options: Predictable tail latency and less operational toil at trillions of messages
Supporting SQL joins across channels
Stronger transactional consistency for messages
Cheaper object storage for attachments
questions.explanation: GC pauses, hot partitions and compaction pain drove the move. The data model and consistency stayed essentially the same. The gain was steadier p99s and far fewer firefights, with fewer nodes.

questions.prompt: What were Netflix's main goals in building Open Connect rather than relying only on commercial CDNs?
options: Hosting its recommendation engine
Stronger DRM for its content
Avoiding AWS for its control plane
Lower delivery cost and better streaming quality by serving video from inside ISP networks
questions.explanation: At Netflix's traffic share, an owned CDN with predictive overnight fill and placement inside ISPs cuts transit costs and keeps bitrates high at peak. DRM and recommendations aren't delivery problems, and the control plane stayed in AWS.

questions.prompt: Stripe's idempotency-key design optimizes first and foremost for:
options: Letting clients skip authentication on retries
Correctness under retries: a network failure should never cause a double charge
Minimizing API latency
Reducing storage costs
questions.explanation: Payments can't tolerate duplicates, and networks fail ambiguously. Idempotency keys make retries safe, which matters far more than a little extra latency or storage. Authentication is still required on every request.

questions.prompt: Instagram's 2012 ID scheme optimized for which combination?
options: Encryption and anonymity of creation time
Time-sortable 64-bit IDs generated inside the existing database, with no new service to operate
Human-readable IDs and alphabetical sorting
Strict global monotonicity and a single coordinator
questions.explanation: With a small team, Instagram wanted no extra moving parts. Generating Snowflake-like IDs in PostgreSQL per shard gave sortability and shard routing without running ZooKeeper or an ID service. Global strict ordering was explicitly not required.

questions.prompt: In an HLD interview you mention Shopify's pods. What makes that reference strong rather than name-dropping?
options: Claiming the design must copy Shopify exactly
Reciting the exact number of pods Shopify runs
Mentioning as many companies as possible in one answer
Naming the constraint (spiky, tenant-scoped load and noisy neighbors), explaining how pods address it, and saying whether your system shares that constraint
questions.explanation: Interviewers want reasoning: what problem forced the design, what it costs (no cross-tenant queries, per-tenant ceilings), and whether it fits the problem in front of you. Trivia and copying signal pattern-matching without understanding.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of company and primary bottleneck it designed around is correct?
options: Discord: payment double-charges; Stripe: chat fan-out
Netflix: bandwidth delivery at peak; Uber: real-time geospatial matching of supply and demand
Slack: ID generation; Netflix: ledger reconciliation
Shopify: video transcoding; Instagram: driver dispatch
questions.explanation: Netflix's dominant cost and quality driver is moving video bytes at peak, and Uber's is matching moving drivers to riders in real time. The other pairings swap companies with problems that belong to someone else.

questions.prompt: Discord's request coalescing, Netflix's off-peak pre-positioning and CDN origin shields share which underlying idea?
options: Removing duplicate or ill-timed work from the hot path before it reaches the scarce resource
Writing every request synchronously to the system of record
Using strong consistency everywhere
Replacing caches with bigger databases
questions.explanation: Each technique protects a bottleneck (DB partition, peak-hour links, origin) by merging identical requests or moving work to a cheaper time or tier. They're about load shaping, not consistency or bigger databases.

questions.prompt: Which of these are primarily techniques for limiting blast radius? Select all that apply.
options: Shopify's pods (shop-level cells)
Stripe's date-based API versioning
Netflix's multi-region setup validated by Chaos Kong evacuations
Circuit breakers and bulkheads as in Netflix's Hystrix
Instagram's time-sortable IDs
questions.explanation: Cells, regional failover and dependency isolation all contain failures. Time-sortable IDs solve ordering and sharding, and API versioning protects integrations from breaking changes rather than isolating runtime failures.

questions.prompt: Which are examples of a company building its own infrastructure because off-the-shelf options didn't fit its scale or problem? Select all that apply.
options: Instagram writing a new database engine to replace PostgreSQL
Uber creating the H3 hexagonal index
Netflix building the Open Connect CDN
Discord writing Rust data services in front of its database
questions.explanation: Netflix, Uber and Discord each built bespoke components for a specific bottleneck. Instagram did the opposite: it kept PostgreSQL and added sharding and ID generation on top, which is a good example of choosing boring technology.

questions.prompt: The lesson of Discord's move to ScyllaDB is that Cassandra is a bad choice for any chat system.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Cassandra served Discord well from billions to trillions of messages. Its JVM-related latency and operational costs only became decisive at that scale. Case studies teach context-dependent trade-offs, not universal verdicts.

questions.prompt: Instagram (PostgreSQL), Shopify (MySQL) and Slack (MySQL via Vitess) all kept a relational database as their system of record and scaled it by sharding rather than replacing it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Each kept relational guarantees and mature tooling and added partitioning (logical shards, pods, Vitess keyspaces) on top. It's a recurring pattern: shard what you know before adopting something exotic.

questions.prompt: You need to route /api/* to one backend pool and /static/* to another, based on the HTTP path. Which kind of load balancer can do this?
options: An L4 load balancer, because it sees the TCP port
Only a DNS-based load balancer using SRV records
Either one, since both see the destination IP
An L7 load balancer, because it parses the HTTP request
questions.explanation: Path-based routing requires reading the HTTP request line, which only an L7 (application-layer) balancer does. An L4 balancer works on IP/port tuples and never inspects the HTTP payload, so the port alone can't distinguish /api from /static.

questions.prompt: Requests to your service vary wildly in cost: some take 5 ms, some take 2 s. Round-robin is leaving some backends overloaded while others idle. Which algorithm is the best fit?
options: Weighted round-robin with static weights
Random selection with no weighting
Least outstanding requests (least connections)
IP hash so each client sticks to one backend
questions.explanation: Least-connections/least-outstanding-requests adapts to actual in-flight work, so slow requests naturally steer new traffic elsewhere. Static weighted round-robin only helps when backends differ in capacity, not when request costs vary unpredictably.

questions.prompt: Your health check hits GET /health, which also queries the shared database. During a brief DB slowdown, the LB marks every backend unhealthy and the site goes fully down. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the health check interval from 5 s to 60 s
Keep the liveness check local and handle dependency failures in-app
Remove health checks and rely on client retries instead
Make /health check the DB with a longer timeout only
questions.explanation: A health check that depends on a shared dependency turns a partial outage into a total one: every node fails at once and the LB has nowhere to send traffic. Keep the LB check about the instance itself and degrade gracefully on DB errors. A longer interval only delays the same cascade.

questions.prompt: An L4 load balancer is placed in front of servers that hold long-lived WebSocket connections. After adding two new servers, they receive almost no traffic for hours. Why?
options: The new servers failed health checks because of TLS
Round-robin skips servers that were added after startup
Existing connections stay pinned; only new connections get rebalanced
L4 balancers cannot forward WebSocket traffic at all
