questions.explanation: Balancing happens per connection. Long-lived connections stay on their original server until they close, so new capacity only fills as clients reconnect. Fixes include connection draining or periodic reconnects. L4 balancers forward WebSockets fine since they're just TCP.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason teams pick an L4 load balancer over an L7 one for a high-throughput service?
options: It supports cookie-based sticky sessions natively
Lower latency and overhead since it doesn't parse or terminate HTTP
It can retry failed HTTP requests on another backend
It can rewrite headers and add request IDs
questions.explanation: L4 balancers forward packets/connections without parsing application data, so they are cheaper and faster per request. Cookie stickiness, HTTP retries and header rewriting all need HTTP awareness, which is L7.

questions.prompt: You use IP-hash load balancing for session stickiness. Most of your traffic comes from a few large corporate NATs. What problem will you most likely see?
options: Health checks will stop working for hashed backends
A few backends get a disproportionate share of the load
Sessions will be lost on every request
TLS handshakes will fail because the IP changes
questions.explanation: Many users behind one NAT share a source IP, so IP hashing sends all of them to the same backend, creating hot spots. Sessions are kept, not lost, which is exactly what makes the load skew stick.

questions.prompt: A backend is removed from the pool during a deploy, and in-flight requests to it fail with 502s. Which LB feature prevents this?
options: Switching from least-connections to round-robin
Enabling HTTP keep-alive between LB and backend
Active health checks with a shorter interval
Connection draining (deregistration delay)
questions.explanation: Connection draining stops sending new requests to the instance but lets in-flight ones finish before it's removed. Faster health checks only detect failure sooner; they don't protect requests already in progress.

questions.prompt: Which capabilities generally require an L7 (HTTP-aware) load balancer rather than L4? Select all that apply.
options: Routing by Host header to different services
Cookie-based session affinity
Distributing TCP connections across backends
Retrying an idempotent GET on another backend after a 503
Preserving the client's source IP via direct server return
questions.explanation: Host routing, cookie affinity and HTTP-level retries all need the balancer to parse HTTP. Spreading TCP connections is the core L4 job, and direct server return is an L4 technique where responses bypass the balancer.

questions.prompt: A backend is flapping: it passes and fails health checks every few seconds. Which settings help avoid sending traffic to it while it's unstable? Select all that apply.
options: Use passive health checks (outlier detection) based on real errors
Remove the health check timeout entirely
Eject outliers for a cool-down period that grows on repeat failures
Lower the unhealthy threshold to a single successful check
Require several consecutive successes before marking it healthy
questions.explanation: Healthy/unhealthy thresholds add hysteresis, outlier detection reacts to real failing traffic, and growing ejection periods stop fast flip-flopping. Re-admitting after one success makes flapping worse, and no timeout means a hung backend is never detected.

questions.prompt: An L7 load balancer that terminates TLS can inspect HTTP headers and route on them, but the connection from the LB to the backend is a separate connection.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Terminating TLS lets the L7 balancer read the HTTP request, and it then opens (or reuses) its own connection to the backend, optionally re-encrypting. That's why the backend sees the LB's IP and needs X-Forwarded-For for the client IP.

questions.prompt: Power of two random choices (pick two random backends, send to the less loaded one) performs much worse than plain random selection when the balancer's load information is slightly stale.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Power of two choices is popular precisely because it gets most of the benefit of least-loaded selection while being robust to stale data. Always picking the single least-loaded backend with stale info is what causes herding, where everyone piles onto the same node.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility best distinguishes an API gateway from a plain reverse proxy?
options: Enforcing API concerns like auth, rate limits and API keys per route
Terminating TLS connections from clients
Hiding backend server IPs from the internet
Forwarding client requests to backend servers
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy forwards requests, hides backends and often terminates TLS. An API gateway adds API-level cross-cutting policy such as authentication, per-client rate limiting, quotas and request transformation. Forwarding and TLS termination are common to both.

questions.prompt: Behind Nginx, your Node.js (Express) app logs every request as coming from 10.0.0.5, so per-user rate limiting doesn't work. What is the correct fix?
options: Rate limit on the User-Agent header instead
Have Nginx set X-Forwarded-For and configure Express 'trust proxy' for it
Read req.socket.remoteAddress instead of req.ip
Trust whatever X-Forwarded-For value the client sends
questions.explanation: The proxy is the TCP peer, so the socket address is always the proxy. Nginx should append the client IP to X-Forwarded-For and Express should trust only that proxy hop. Trusting arbitrary client-supplied X-Forwarded-For lets attackers spoof IPs and dodge rate limits.

questions.prompt: A mobile app needs data from 5 microservices to render one screen, causing 5 round trips over a slow network. Which gateway pattern addresses this?
options: Request aggregation / Backend-for-Frontend at the gateway
Sticky sessions at the gateway
Response caching with a 1-hour TTL
Circuit breaker on each microservice call
questions.explanation: A BFF or aggregating gateway makes the 5 calls over the fast internal network and returns one combined response, cutting mobile round trips. Circuit breakers improve resilience, not round-trip count, and long TTL caching would serve stale personalised data.

questions.prompt: Every request passes through a single API gateway cluster. What is the most important risk to plan for?
options: It makes TLS impossible between internal services
It forces all services to use the same programming language
It prevents services from being deployed independently
It becomes a shared failure point and bottleneck for all traffic
questions.explanation: A gateway on the critical path is a shared dependency: misconfiguration, overload or a bad deploy takes down everything. Run it redundantly, keep business logic out of it and deploy it carefully. It does not constrain service languages or independent deploys.

questions.prompt: A team starts putting order-validation rules and pricing logic into the API gateway's plugins to 'avoid duplicating code'. What is the main problem?
options: It makes TLS termination slower
Business logic in the gateway couples teams and makes it a deploy bottleneck
Gateways strip request bodies before plugins run
Gateways cannot run custom code at all
questions.explanation: Gateways should hold cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limits, routing). Domain logic there couples every team to one shared component, so changes need gateway deploys and failures spread widely. Most gateways can run custom plugins, which is why this anti-pattern happens.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a forward proxy rather than a reverse proxy?
options: A CDN edge serving your site's assets
An API gateway validating JWTs
A corporate proxy that employees' browsers use to reach the internet
Nginx in front of three app servers
questions.explanation: A forward proxy acts for clients reaching arbitrary servers; a reverse proxy acts for servers, receiving client traffic for them. Nginx in front of app servers, CDN edges and API gateways all sit in front of servers, so they're reverse proxies.

questions.prompt: Your gateway retries any failed upstream call up to 3 times. During a backend slowdown, traffic to the backend jumps about 4x and it falls over completely. What is the best mitigation?
options: Disable timeouts so requests never fail and need retries
Increase the retry count so more requests eventually succeed
Move retries from the gateway into every client instead
Use a retry budget with backoff and jitter, and retry only idempotent calls
questions.explanation: Unbounded retries amplify load exactly when the backend is struggling (a retry storm). A retry budget caps extra traffic, backoff with jitter spreads it out, and limiting retries to idempotent calls avoids duplicate side effects. Moving retries to clients still multiplies load.

questions.prompt: Which concerns are reasonable to centralise in an API gateway? Select all that apply.
options: Per-API-key rate limiting and quotas
Validating JWTs and rejecting unauthenticated calls
Request/response logging and correlation IDs
Deciding whether an order can be refunded
Calculating discounts for a shopping cart
questions.explanation: Auth checks, rate limits and logging/tracing are cross-cutting and apply to many services, which is what gateways are for. Discount calculation and refund eligibility are domain rules that belong in the owning service.

questions.prompt: Nginx is a reverse proxy in front of a Node.js app. Which benefits does this setup commonly provide? Select all that apply.
options: Automatically making the Node app's database queries faster
Buffering slow clients so Node isn't tied up by slow uploads
Serving static files without hitting Node
Guaranteeing exactly-once processing of POST requests
TLS termination and HTTP/2 handling at the edge
questions.explanation: Reverse proxies buffer slow clients, serve static assets efficiently and terminate TLS/HTTP/2. They have no effect on DB query speed, and they can't guarantee exactly-once POST handling; that needs idempotency keys in the app.

questions.prompt: Using a service mesh sidecar (like Envoy) for service-to-service traffic removes any need for an API gateway at the edge.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A mesh handles east-west (internal) traffic: mTLS, retries, internal routing. The edge gateway handles north-south traffic from external clients: public auth, API keys, quotas, public routing. Many systems run both.

questions.prompt: If the gateway authenticates a JWT and forwards the request, backend services that are reachable directly on the internal network should still not blindly trust identity headers like X-User-Id from any caller.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. If anything else on the network can reach the service, a forged X-User-Id header bypasses the gateway's check. Use network policy, mTLS or a signed internal token so services can verify the caller really is the gateway.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a pull CDN and a push CDN?
options: Push CDNs fetch from origin on each request; pull CDNs never contact origin
Pull CDNs require you to manage TTLs; push CDNs ignore Cache-Control
Pull CDNs only serve video; push CDNs only serve images
Pull CDNs fetch from origin on a cache miss; push CDNs get content uploaded ahead of time
questions.explanation: A pull CDN lazily fetches from origin when an edge misses, then caches it. A push CDN has you upload content to the CDN in advance. Neither is limited by media type, and both respect expiry settings in some form.

questions.prompt: Your CDN hit ratio for product images is only 20%. URLs look like /img/123.jpg?utm_source=email&session=abc. What is the most likely cause?
options: The origin is sending Content-Type: image/jpeg
The CDN is configured as push instead of pull
The images are too large for the edge cache
Tracking and session query params are part of the cache key
questions.explanation: If the full query string is in the cache key, each unique utm/session value creates a separate cache entry, so almost every request misses. Strip irrelevant params from the cache key. Content-Type headers don't affect hit ratio.

questions.prompt: You deploy a new app.js and want users to get it immediately while still caching assets for a year. What's the standard approach?
options: Set Cache-Control: no-cache on app.js
Set a 60-second TTL on all JavaScript files
Use content-hashed filenames (app.3f9a1c.js) with long max-age and immutable
Purge the whole CDN on every deploy
questions.explanation: Fingerprinted filenames make each version a new URL, so it can be cached forever while the HTML points to the new name right away. Full purges are slow and cause an origin load spike; short TTLs give up most of the caching benefit.

questions.prompt: After a full CDN purge, your origin's CPU spikes to 100% and latency climbs. What's happening and what helps most?
options: Every edge misses at once; use origin shield and request collapsing
The purge invalidated TLS certificates at the edges
The CDN switched to push mode; switch back to pull
Purges disable gzip; re-enable compression at origin
questions.explanation: A purge empties every edge, so hundreds of POPs miss together and hammer origin. An origin shield (a middle cache tier) and request collapsing (one origin fetch per object, others wait) shrink that fan-in. Purges don't affect compression or certificates.

questions.prompt: An API returns different JSON for logged-in users, and you put a CDN in front of it. Some users report seeing another user's account data. What's the most likely misconfiguration?
options: The origin returned Cache-Control: private
The CDN's TTL was set too short
The CDN used HTTP/2 to talk to origin
The CDN cached personalised responses under a key without the user identity
questions.explanation: If personalised responses are cached under a URL-only key, the first user's response is served to everyone. Mark them Cache-Control: private/no-store, or bypass the cache for authenticated requests. Cache-Control: private would have prevented this, not caused it.

questions.prompt: Which header lets an origin give the CDN a different TTL than browsers, for example 1 day at the edge but 60 s in the browser?
options: ETag
Last-Modified
Expires
Cache-Control: s-maxage
questions.explanation: s-maxage applies only to shared caches (CDNs and proxies) and overrides max-age for them, so browsers keep the shorter max-age. Expires is an absolute date for all caches; ETag and Last-Modified are for revalidation, not TTL.

questions.prompt: A news site wants pages cached at the edge, but when an article is corrected, the fix must appear within seconds. Which design fits best?
options: Push all articles to the CDN once a day
No caching for article pages at all
Long edge TTL plus tag/surrogate-key purge triggered by the CMS on edit
Rely on a 24-hour TTL and ask readers to hard refresh
questions.explanation: Tag-based (surrogate key) purges let the CMS invalidate exactly the affected pages within seconds while keeping long TTLs for everything else. Disabling caching gives up the CDN benefit, and a daily push or long TTL can't meet a seconds-level requirement.

questions.prompt: Which practices improve CDN cache hit ratio? Select all that apply.
options: Using an origin shield tier between edges and origin
Adding Vary: User-Agent to all responses
Normalising or removing irrelevant query parameters from the cache key
Setting a unique Set-Cookie on every static asset response
Serving stale content while revalidating in the background
questions.explanation: Cleaner cache keys, a shield tier and stale-while-revalidate all increase hits. Vary: User-Agent splits the cache across thousands of UA strings, and many CDNs won't cache responses that set cookies.

questions.prompt: Which kinds of content are good candidates for a push CDN rather than a pull CDN? Select all that apply.
options: A small site whose assets rarely change and are known in advance
A large game patch released at a known time to millions of users
A video library prepared before a launch event
Per-user dashboard JSON
Search results generated per query
questions.explanation: Push suits content known ahead of time, especially big files with a predictable surge, so edges are warm before demand arrives. Per-user and per-query responses are dynamic and unbounded, so they can't be pre-uploaded.

questions.prompt: Using a CDN reduces latency for users mainly because the edge server is geographically closer, cutting round-trip time for TCP/TLS handshakes and data transfer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Edges terminate connections near the user, so the handshakes and data transfer cover a short distance, and cache hits never travel to origin at all. Even misses benefit, since the edge often keeps warm connections to origin.

questions.prompt: A CDN purge request takes effect at all edge locations worldwide instantly and atomically, so no user can get the old version after the purge API returns.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Purges propagate to many POPs and take from milliseconds to minutes depending on the provider, and browsers may still hold their own copies. That's why versioned URLs are preferred for things that must change atomically.

questions.prompt: In the cache-aside pattern, who is responsible for loading data into the cache on a miss?
options: The application reads the DB and writes the result to the cache
The database pushes changes into the cache
A background job preloads every key at startup
The cache itself fetches from the DB automatically
questions.explanation: In cache-aside (lazy loading) the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the DB and populates the cache. When the cache loads from the DB itself, that's read-through.

questions.prompt: With cache-aside, a service updates a user row in the DB and then updates the cache with the new value. Two concurrent updates sometimes leave the cache permanently stale. What's the usual fix?
options: Update the cache first, then the DB
Write to the cache twice to be safe
Increase the cache TTL
Delete (invalidate) the cache key after the DB write instead of setting it
questions.explanation: With two writers, their DB writes and cache sets can interleave so the cache ends up with the older value forever. Deleting the key after the DB write makes the next read reload fresh data. A short TTL as a safety net also helps; a longer TTL makes it worse.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of write-back (write-behind) caching?
options: Every write is slower because it waits for the database
Reads always miss because writes skip the cache
Data acknowledged to the client can be lost if the cache fails before flushing
It cannot be used with key-value stores
questions.explanation: Write-back acknowledges the write once it's in the cache and flushes to the DB later, so a cache crash can lose acknowledged writes. Slower writes is the trade-off of write-through, the opposite pattern.

questions.prompt: A product catalog is read thousands of times per second and edited a few times a day. Edits must show up within about a second. Which approach fits best?
options: Write-around with a 24-hour TTL
Write-back caching with hourly flushes
No cache; scale the DB with read replicas only
Cache-aside with invalidation on edit plus a TTL as a safety net
questions.explanation: Read-heavy, rarely changed data is the classic cache-aside case. Invalidating on edit gives near-immediate freshness and the TTL limits damage from a missed invalidation. Write-around with a 24 h TTL would serve stale data for up to a day.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes write-through caching?
options: Writes go to the cache and the DB synchronously before acknowledging
Writes go to the cache only; the DB is a read-only replica
Writes go to the cache and are flushed to the DB asynchronously
Writes go only to the DB; the cache is filled on the next read
questions.explanation: Write-through updates cache and store in the same write path, so the cache stays consistent at the cost of write latency. Writing only to the DB is write-around; asynchronous flushing is write-back.

questions.prompt: You use cache-aside. The DB write succeeds but the following cache DELETE fails because of a network blip. What's the consequence and a reasonable mitigation?
options: The stale value persists until TTL; retry the delete or invalidate via change data capture
Nothing; the cache detects DB changes on its own
Reads fail with errors until the cache restarts
The DB write is rolled back automatically
questions.explanation: Cache and DB aren't updated atomically, so a failed delete leaves stale data until the TTL expires. Mitigations: retry invalidation (e.g. via an outbox), drive invalidation from the DB's change stream/CDC, and always set a TTL. Caches don't watch the DB by themselves.

questions.prompt: A system logs millions of view-count increments per minute and can tolerate losing a few seconds of counts on a crash. Which strategy is most suitable?
options: Cache-aside: invalidate the counter key on every increment
Write-through: update Redis and the DB on every increment
Write-back: increment in Redis and flush aggregates to the DB periodically
No cache: run UPDATE ... SET views = views + 1 for each view
questions.explanation: High-frequency writes where small loss is acceptable suit write-back: batching turns millions of DB writes into a few. Write-through or per-view UPDATEs would hammer the DB, and invalidating on every increment defeats the cache.

questions.prompt: Which statements about read-through vs cache-aside are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Both can serve stale data unless writes invalidate or update the cache
Cache-aside keeps the application in control of what gets cached
Cache-aside requires the cache to understand the database schema
In read-through, the cache layer loads missing data from the store
Read-through means writes are never needed to keep data fresh
questions.explanation: Read-through puts the loading logic in the cache layer; cache-aside keeps it in the app. Both need a write-side strategy (invalidate, update or TTL) or they go stale. Read-through doesn't remove that need, and in cache-aside the cache knows nothing about the schema.

questions.prompt: You use write-through caching for user profiles. Which issues should you still plan for? Select all that apply.
options: Higher write latency because both writes happen in the request path
Automatic cross-region consistency with no extra work
Caching data that is written but never read (cache pollution)
Partial failure where the DB write succeeds but the cache write fails
Reads of profiles that were cached never hitting the cache
questions.explanation: Write-through adds write latency, caches everything written (even never-read data), and still faces partial failures between two systems. Reads of cached data do hit the cache, and it gives no cross-region consistency by itself.

questions.prompt: Write-around caching (write only to the DB, populate the cache on read) helps avoid filling the cache with data that is written once and rarely read.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Write-around skips the cache on writes, so only data that is actually read gets cached. The trade-off is that the first read after a write is always a miss.

questions.prompt: If you delete the cache key before writing to the DB (instead of after), cache-aside can no longer serve stale data under concurrent reads.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A concurrent reader can miss right after the delete, read the old DB value and re-cache it before the write commits, leaving stale data. That's why people delete after the write, sometimes with a delayed second delete.

questions.prompt: A popular cache key with a 5-minute TTL expires, and within a second 2,000 requests miss and all query the DB, which slows to a crawl. What is this called?
options: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
Cache pollution
Cache penetration
Write amplification
questions.explanation: A stampede is many concurrent misses on the same key all rebuilding it at once. Cache penetration is repeated lookups for keys that don't exist at all, which also bypass the cache but for a different reason.

questions.prompt: Which technique most directly prevents a stampede on a single expensive key?
options: Increase the cache's memory size
Let only one request rebuild the key (lock or single-flight) while others wait or get stale data
Lower the TTL so the key is refreshed more often
Switch the eviction policy from LRU to LFU
questions.explanation: Request coalescing (a mutex, SET NX lock or in-process single-flight) means one caller recomputes and the rest wait or get the stale value. More memory or a different eviction policy doesn't stop many simultaneous misses on an expired key.

questions.prompt: Your cache holds a small set of items accessed constantly, plus a nightly batch job that scans millions of keys once. After each batch run the hit rate collapses. Which eviction policy is most resistant to this?
options: TTL-only expiry with no size limit
LRU, because recently scanned items are evicted first
FIFO, because it ignores access patterns
LFU, because frequently used items outrank one-time scans
questions.explanation: A one-off scan touches each key once. Under LRU those keys look 'recent' and push out the real hot set. LFU ranks by frequency, so the hot items survive. FIFO also evicts the hot set, and no size limit just runs out of memory.

questions.prompt: You cache 10,000 keys at deploy time, all with TTL = 3600 s. Exactly an hour later, the DB gets a burst of load. What's the simplest fix?
options: Store all keys in a single hash
Add jitter to TTLs (e.g. 3600 s ± 10%)
Shorten the TTL to 60 s
Use LRU instead of TTL
questions.explanation: Keys written together with the same TTL expire together (synchronized expiry). Random jitter spreads expiries out. A shorter TTL just causes the burst more often, and LRU is a capacity policy, not a freshness one.

questions.prompt: One Redis key (a celebrity's profile) gets 200k reads/s and saturates one Redis Cluster node while others are idle. What's the most effective fix?
options: Switch the maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lfu
Change the key's TTL to 1 second
Add more nodes to the cluster
Replicate the hot key: cache it in-process or as N suffixed copies spread across nodes
questions.explanation: A single key lives on one slot, so adding nodes doesn't split its traffic. Local in-process caching or N copies (key#1..key#N, read a random one) spreads load. A shorter TTL or a different eviction policy doesn't change where the key lives.

questions.prompt: Attackers request random product IDs that don't exist. Each lookup misses the cache and hits the DB. What's a standard defence?
options: Cache negative results briefly and/or use a Bloom filter of valid IDs
Shard the database by product ID
Switch from LRU to LFU eviction
Use a longer TTL on existing products
questions.explanation: This is cache penetration. Caching 'not found' with a short TTL, or checking a Bloom filter of existing IDs before the DB, stops the misses reaching the DB. TTLs and eviction policies only affect keys that exist.

questions.prompt: Probabilistic early expiration (e.g. the XFetch algorithm) helps prevent stampedes by:
options: Doubling the TTL every time a key is accessed
Having requests randomly recompute a value shortly before its TTL ends, with rising probability
Refusing all reads while a key is being recomputed
Evicting keys with the lowest access count first
questions.explanation: Each reader near expiry has a small, increasing chance of refreshing early, so one request usually rebuilds the value before it expires and no herd forms. It doesn't change TTLs or eviction order, and it doesn't block reads.

questions.prompt: Which strategies help with a stampede on a hot key that is expensive to compute? Select all that apply.
options: Disable the cache for that key during peak hours
Serve the stale value while one worker refreshes it in the background
Refresh the key proactively before it expires
Use a distributed lock (e.g. Redis SET key val NX PX) so one worker recomputes
Give all keys the same TTL so they're easy to reason about
questions.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate, a recompute lock and proactive refresh all stop many callers recomputing at once. Identical TTLs cause synchronized expiry, and turning off the cache sends every request to the backend.

questions.prompt: In Redis 7, which maxmemory-policy values may evict keys that have no TTL set? Select all that apply.
options: volatile-ttl
allkeys-lru
allkeys-random
volatile-lru
allkeys-lfu
questions.explanation: allkeys-* policies consider every key. volatile-* policies only evict keys with an expiry set, so if no keys have TTLs they behave like noeviction and writes fail with OOM errors once memory is full.

questions.prompt: LRU evicts the item that hasn't been accessed for the longest time, regardless of how many times it was accessed before that.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. LRU only looks at recency. An item accessed 10,000 times an hour ago is evicted before one accessed once a second ago. LFU is the policy that weighs access frequency.

questions.prompt: Redis implements exact LRU, tracking a full ordered list of every key by access time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Redis uses approximated LRU/LFU: it samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the best candidate among them. This saves the memory a full linked list over all keys would need.

questions.prompt: Which Redis persistence option gives the smallest window of data loss on a crash with reasonable performance?
options: AOF with appendfsync everysec
AOF with appendfsync no
RDB snapshots every 5 minutes
No persistence with replicas only
questions.explanation: AOF with fsync every second loses at most about one second of writes and is the common default for durability. RDB every 5 minutes can lose up to 5 minutes, and appendfsync no leaves flushing to the OS, often about 30 s.

questions.prompt: How does Redis Cluster decide which node stores a key?
options: Consistent hashing on the full key using virtual nodes
Round-robin across masters as keys are written
CRC16(key) mod 16384 gives a hash slot; each master owns a range of slots
The client chooses any node and Redis replicates to all of them
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster has 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384 (or the hash tag in {}), and slots are assigned to masters. It's not a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, though moving slots gives similar rebalancing.

questions.prompt: In Redis Cluster, MGET user:1:name user:2:name fails with a CROSSSLOT error. How do you make related keys land in the same slot?
options: Run the command against a replica instead of the master
Use a longer key prefix like user:
Use hash tags, e.g. {user:1}:name and {user:1}:email
Set cluster-require-full-coverage no
questions.explanation: Only the substring inside {} is hashed, so keys sharing a hash tag map to the same slot and allow multi-key commands. A shared prefix outside braces doesn't affect hashing, and the coverage setting is about availability, not slots.

questions.prompt: What problem does Redis Sentinel solve?
options: Load balancing reads evenly across replicas automatically
Persisting data to disk
Sharding data across multiple masters
Monitoring a master and promoting a replica on failure, then telling clients the new master
questions.explanation: Sentinel provides monitoring, automatic failover and service discovery for a single master/replica set. It doesn't shard; that's Redis Cluster. Persistence is RDB/AOF.

questions.prompt: A Redis master acknowledges a write, then crashes before replicating it. Sentinel promotes a replica. What happens to that write?
options: It's recovered from the new master's AOF
It's lost, because replication is asynchronous
The client gets an error retroactively
Sentinel replays it from its own log
questions.explanation: Redis replication is asynchronous by default, so acknowledged writes not yet on the replica are lost on failover. WAIT can reduce the risk but doesn't make Redis strongly consistent. Sentinel doesn't store data.

questions.prompt: Redis is running BGSAVE on a 20 GB dataset with a heavy write load, and memory usage nearly doubles. Why?
options: Replicas send their data back to the master during BGSAVE
fork() uses copy-on-write; pages modified during the snapshot get duplicated
BGSAVE loads a second copy of the dataset from disk
AOF rewrite and RDB both store data in memory twice
questions.explanation: BGSAVE forks a child that shares memory pages with the parent. Each page the parent writes during the snapshot is copied, so heavy writes can approach 2x memory. Leave headroom and keep Transparent Huge Pages disabled.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, a Redis master is cut off from the majority, which promotes a new master. Clients on the minority side keep writing to the old master. Which setting limits how long those writes are accepted?
options: maxmemory-policy noeviction
min-replicas-to-write with min-replicas-max-lag
appendfsync always
cluster-node-timeout set to 0
questions.explanation: min-replicas-to-write makes the master refuse writes when it can't reach enough replicas within the allowed lag, so an isolated old master stops accepting writes that would later be thrown away. fsync settings protect against crashes, not split brain.

questions.prompt: Which statements about RDB vs AOF in Redis 7 are correct? Select all that apply.
options: RDB guarantees no data loss between snapshots
AOF with fsync always can never slow down writes
RDB files are compact and fast to load on restart
You can enable both, and Redis uses AOF on restart when it's enabled
AOF records write operations and can be rewritten to compact it
questions.explanation: RDB is a compact point-in-time snapshot that loads fast; AOF logs writes and is compacted by rewrite. With both on, Redis loads the AOF because it's more complete. RDB loses everything since the last snapshot, and fsync always is the slowest mode.

questions.prompt: Your team uses Redis as a distributed lock for payment processing. Which concerns are valid? Select all that apply.
options: Use fencing tokens checked by the downstream resource for correctness
SET key value NX PX is atomic, so it's safe from all failure modes
Redis locks never need an expiry because clients always release them
A GC pause can let the lock expire while the holder still thinks it holds it
Async replication means a lock can be lost on failover, so two holders are possible
questions.explanation: Failover can drop a lock and process pauses can outlive the TTL, so correctness-critical locks need fencing tokens. SET NX PX is atomic on one node but doesn't survive these failures, and a lock without expiry is held forever if the client crashes.

questions.prompt: Redis executes commands on a single main thread, so one slow command like KEYS * on a large dataset blocks all other clients.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Redis 6+ can use I/O threads for network reads and writes, but commands still run one at a time on the main thread. Use SCAN instead of KEYS, and avoid huge O(N) commands in production.

questions.prompt: Redis Cluster supports multi-key transactions across keys stored on different masters.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Multi-key commands, MULTI/EXEC and Lua scripts in Redis Cluster must touch keys in the same hash slot. Use hash tags to co-locate keys that need to be updated together.

questions.prompt: A network partition splits a replicated key-value store. The store is designed as CP under CAP. What must it do for clients on the side that cannot reach a quorum?
options: Reject or block those requests until the partition heals
Serve possibly stale reads and buffer writes locally
Accept writes on both sides and merge them with last-write-wins
Silently drop partition tolerance and keep serving
questions.explanation: A CP system preserves linearizability during a partition, so nodes that cannot coordinate with a quorum must refuse or block requests. Serving stale reads or accepting divergent writes is the AP choice, not CP.

questions.prompt: Under PACELC, how is Apache Cassandra with its default tunable settings (e.g. consistency level ONE) usually classified?
options: PC/EL
PA/EC
PA/EL
PC/EC
questions.explanation: With low consistency levels Cassandra stays available during partitions (PA) and, in normal operation, favours low latency over consistency (EL). PC/EC describes systems like Spanner that pay latency to stay consistent.

questions.prompt: An architect proposes a 'CA' multi-node database: consistent and available, but not partition tolerant. Why do most engineers reject this framing for a distributed system?
options: CAP forbids consistency and availability even when there is no partition
Partition tolerance only matters for systems spanning multiple cloud regions
CA systems exist but are always slower than CP systems in practice
Partitions are not optional: networks drop packets, so you only choose behaviour when one happens
questions.explanation: In a real network partitions will happen, so 'P' is not something you can give up; the real choice is C or A during a partition. CAP says nothing restricting C and A when there is no partition, which is why PACELC adds the latency-vs-consistency axis.

questions.prompt: Cassandra cluster, RF=3, client uses QUORUM for reads and writes. A partition leaves one replica plus the client on one side and two replicas on the other. What does the client experience?
options: Reads and writes succeed but may return stale data
Reads succeed from the local replica, writes fail
Writes succeed via hinted handoff and reads fail
Requests fail with an unavailable error since 2 of 3 replicas are unreachable
questions.explanation: QUORUM needs 2 of 3 replicas; the client can reach only one, so operations fail. Choosing QUORUM/QUORUM makes those operations behave CP. Hinted handoff stores hints but does not count toward the QUORUM consistency level.

questions.prompt: In the CAP theorem, what does the 'C' (consistency) formally refer to?
options: Linearizability: every read sees the most recent completed write
Each client sees its own writes within a session
The 'C' in ACID: transactions keep the database's constraints valid
Eventual convergence of all replicas once writes stop
questions.explanation: Gilbert and Lynch's proof defines CAP consistency as linearizability (atomic, single-copy semantics). ACID consistency is about application invariants, which is a different concept that happens to share the name.

questions.prompt: Google Spanner uses TrueTime and waits out clock uncertainty before acknowledging commits. Under PACELC, which classification fits Spanner best?
options: PA/EC
PA/EL
PC/EC
PC/EL
questions.explanation: Spanner gives up availability on the minority side of a partition (PC) and pays extra latency (commit wait, Paxos round trips) for external consistency in normal operation (EC). EL would mean trading consistency for latency, which Spanner does not do.

questions.prompt: A team says their PostgreSQL setup is 'CP' because it has a single primary. However, they route all reads to an async streaming replica. During a partition between primary and replica, what is true?
options: Replica reads keep succeeding but can be stale, so reads are effectively AP
Reads fail because PostgreSQL blocks replicas that lose the primary
Reads stay linearizable because the replica stops applying WAL
The replica automatically forwards reads to the primary
questions.explanation: A hot standby keeps serving reads when it loses its primary, returning data as of its last replayed WAL. That is available-but-stale behaviour. CP/AP is a property of each operation path, not of 'having a primary'.

questions.prompt: Why is PACELC considered more useful than CAP alone when choosing a datastore? Select all that apply.
options: It proves that CA systems are achievable with enough redundancy
It captures the latency vs consistency trade-off that exists even without partitions
Partitions are relatively rare, so the 'else' branch describes most day-to-day behaviour
It removes the need for consensus protocols in strongly consistent systems
questions.explanation: PACELC adds: Else (no partition), choose Latency or Consistency. Since partitions are uncommon, that branch describes most operation. It does not make CA possible, and strong consistency still needs coordination such as consensus.

questions.prompt: An AP, Dynamo-style shopping-cart store accepts writes on both sides of a partition. Which mechanisms does it need to converge once the partition heals? Select all that apply.
options: A single global leader through which every write must pass
Anti-entropy such as read repair or Merkle-tree comparison between replicas
A conflict resolution strategy such as CRDTs, application merge, or LWW
Two-phase commit across all replicas for every write
questions.explanation: Divergent replicas must detect differences (anti-entropy, read repair) and resolve concurrent updates (merge, CRDTs, LWW). 2PC or a single leader would block writes during partitions, which contradicts the AP design.

questions.prompt: In CAP, 'availability' means every request received by a non-failing node gets a non-error response, even if it does not reflect the latest write.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That is the formal definition used in the CAP proof. Note it does not mean 'fast' or 'high uptime percentage'; a response that is slow but eventual still counts, and staleness is allowed.

questions.prompt: When a partition occurs, a CP system such as etcd becomes unavailable to every client in the cluster.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Only the minority side loses availability. The side holding a majority can still elect a leader and serve linearizable reads and writes, so clients that can reach it keep working.

questions.prompt: A user posts a comment, the page reloads, and the comment is missing; a second reload shows it. The DB uses async read replicas. Which guarantee was violated?
options: Monotonic writes
Linearizable compare-and-set
Read-your-writes
Writes-follow-reads
questions.explanation: Read-your-writes says a client always sees its own prior writes. The reload hit a lagging replica. Monotonic writes is about a client's writes being applied in order, which is not the symptom here.

questions.prompt: In a social feed, users sometimes see a reply before the post it answers. Which consistency model, at minimum, would prevent this without requiring full linearizability?
options: Monotonic reads
Read-your-writes
Causal consistency
Eventual consistency
questions.explanation: The reply causally depends on the post, and causal consistency ensures causally related writes are seen in order by everyone. Monotonic reads only stops a single reader going backwards in time; it does not order two different writes.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows an order as 'shipped', then on the next refresh shows 'paid' again. Requests are load-balanced across replicas with different lag. Which fix targets this directly?
options: Pin each user session to one replica, or send a replication position with reads
Increase the replica count so lag averages out
Use a vector clock on every row
Switch to last-write-wins conflict resolution
questions.explanation: This is a monotonic-reads violation: the user read from a fresher replica, then a staler one. Sticky routing or requiring replicas to be at least at the last-seen position fixes it. More replicas makes the variance worse, not better.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between linearizability and serializability?
options: Linearizability is a real-time guarantee on single objects; serializability orders whole transactions without real-time constraints
Serializability respects real-time order; linearizability does not
Linearizability applies only to transactions spanning multiple objects
They are synonyms used by different database vendors
questions.explanation: Serializability says transactions behave as if run in some serial order, which may not match wall-clock order. Linearizability says single operations take effect at a point between invocation and response. Strict serializability combines both.

questions.prompt: With async PostgreSQL replicas, what is a practical way to give users read-your-writes without sending all reads to the primary?
options: Record the commit LSN of the user's last write and read from a replica only if it has replayed past it
Disable the replica's query cache
Retry each read on a different replica until the value changes
Set the replicas to synchronous_commit = off
questions.explanation: Tracking the write's WAL position (e.g. pg_current_wal_lsn after commit) and checking pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() on the replica ensures it has the user's write; otherwise fall back to the primary. Retrying until the value changes cannot know which value is correct.

questions.prompt: A Dynamo-style store has N=3, W=2, R=2, with sloppy quorums and hinted handoff enabled. Why can a read still miss an acknowledged write?
options: R + W must exceed 2N for overlap
Hinted handoff deletes the original write after delivery
The write may have landed on fallback nodes outside the key's home replicas, so the read quorum doesn't overlap it
Quorum reads always go to the coordinator's local disk only
questions.explanation: R + W > N only guarantees overlap if both quorums use the same N home nodes. Sloppy quorums let writes go to stand-in nodes during failures, breaking that overlap until hints are handed back.

questions.prompt: What does eventual consistency actually guarantee?
options: Reads are never more than a few seconds stale
Clients always see their own writes
If no new writes occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same value
Writes are applied in the same order on every replica
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency is a liveness guarantee about convergence only; it gives no bound on staleness and no session guarantees. A 'few seconds' bound is an SLA some systems add, not part of the model.

questions.prompt: Which of these are client-centric session guarantees often layered on top of eventual consistency? Select all that apply.
options: Writes-follow-reads
Monotonic reads
Serializability
Monotonic writes
Total order broadcast
Read-your-writes
questions.explanation: The four session guarantees (from the Bayou work) are read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads; together they give causal consistency per session. Serializability is a transaction isolation level and total order broadcast is a messaging primitive.

questions.prompt: In MongoDB 7, which choices give causal consistency guarantees within a client session that also hold across primary failover? Select all that apply.
options: Use readConcern "majority" together with writeConcern "majority"
Use writeConcern { w: 0 } so writes are faster to replicate
Use readConcern "local" with w: 1, which is equally safe during failover
Use a causally consistent client session (causalConsistency: true)
questions.explanation: MongoDB documents that causal guarantees hold in all cases only when a causally consistent session uses majority read and write concerns. With w: 1 or readConcern local, a rollback after failover can break them; w: 0 is unacknowledged.

questions.prompt: Linearizable operations typically cost extra latency because each operation must coordinate with a leader or a quorum.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: To ensure a read sees the latest write, the system must confirm with a leader or majority, adding network round trips (and cross-region latency if replicas are far apart). This is the 'EC' cost in PACELC.

questions.prompt: Causal consistency requires every replica to apply all writes, including concurrent ones, in a single identical total order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Causal consistency only orders writes that are causally related. Concurrent writes may be seen in different orders by different replicas; a single total order is a stronger property (sequential consistency or linearizability).

questions.prompt: In Raft, a leader receives an AppendEntries response carrying a higher term than its own. What does it do?
options: Forces the sender to truncate its log
Ignores it, since only leaders may change terms
Starts a new election immediately with its old term
Steps down to follower and adopts the higher term
questions.explanation: Terms act as a logical clock. Any node that sees a higher term updates its term and becomes a follower; that is how stale leaders are deposed. Forcing truncation is something a valid current leader does to followers, not to a node with a higher term.

questions.prompt: A Raft cluster has 5 voting members. How many simultaneous node failures can it tolerate while still committing writes?
questions.explanation: Commits need a majority: 3 of 5. With 2 nodes down, 3 remain and can still form a majority. With 3 down only 2 remain, which isn't enough. In general a cluster tolerates floor((n-1)/2) failures.

questions.prompt: Why does Raft use randomized election timeouts (e.g. 150–300 ms)?
options: To compensate for clock skew between servers
To make it unlikely that several followers become candidates at once and split the vote
To ensure the leader with the newest log always times out first
To spread disk writes evenly across nodes
questions.explanation: If all followers timed out together they would all vote for themselves and nobody would win a majority, repeatedly. Randomization usually lets one node time out first and win. Log freshness is enforced by the voting rule, not by timeouts.

questions.prompt: Node A's log ends with (term 5, index 10). Candidate B's log ends with (term 4, index 15). B requests A's vote in term 6. What does A do?
options: Denies the vote because A's last log term is higher, so A's log is more up to date
Denies the vote because candidates must have the same last index
Grants the vote because B's term 6 is higher than 5
Grants the vote because B's log is longer
questions.explanation: Raft compares the last entry's term first and only uses index as a tie-breaker. A's last term 5 beats B's 4, so B's log is less up to date and A refuses. Length only matters when last terms are equal.

questions.prompt: A new Raft leader sees an entry from an earlier term already stored on a majority of nodes. Why can't it mark that entry committed just by counting replicas?
options: The leader must first wait for every follower to acknowledge it
A future leader could still overwrite it; it only becomes safely committed once an entry from the current term is replicated to a majority
Entries from earlier terms must be re-proposed by a client before they can commit
Raft forbids leaders from replicating earlier-term entries at all
questions.explanation: The Raft paper (Figure 8) shows an old-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten by another leader. Leaders commit old entries indirectly by committing a current-term entry, which is why many implementations append a no-op on election.

questions.prompt: A Raft-based store serves reads directly from the leader's local state with no extra checks. Under what scenario can a client read stale data?
options: When a follower's disk is slower than the leader's
When two clients read the same key concurrently
When the snapshot interval is too long
When the leader has been partitioned and replaced, but doesn't yet know it's deposed
questions.explanation: An isolated old leader still thinks it leads and may serve reads while a new leader commits newer writes. Linearizable reads need ReadIndex (confirm leadership with a heartbeat quorum) or carefully bounded leader leases.

questions.prompt: A team plans a 4-node etcd cluster 'for extra safety' instead of 3 nodes. What is the effect on fault tolerance?
options: It tolerates the same single failure, but needs 3 votes per commit instead of 2
It tolerates 2 failures instead of 1
It tolerates 1 failure but commits become faster
It can no longer elect a leader because of ties
questions.explanation: Majority of 4 is 3, so losing 2 nodes stops writes, the same as a 3-node cluster losing 2. You add cost and replication latency for no gain, which is why odd cluster sizes are recommended. Ties are resolved by re-elections, so it still works.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a committed Raft log entry are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It is committed as soon as the leader writes it to its own disk
It will be present in the log of every future leader
It is committed only once every follower has acknowledged it
The current-term leader has replicated it to a majority of servers
questions.explanation: Majority replication by the current leader commits an entry, and the election restriction ensures any future leader has it (Leader Completeness). Writing to the leader's disk alone isn't enough, and waiting for all followers would let a single slow node block progress.

questions.prompt: A 5-node Raft cluster partitions: old leader L plus one follower on one side, three nodes on the other. Which are true? Select all that apply.
options: After healing, L's uncommitted entries may be overwritten
L cannot commit new entries because it can't reach a majority
The three-node side can elect a new leader in a higher term
Clients writing to L receive success, causing split-brain
questions.explanation: L can append but never commit without 3 acks, so it shouldn't acknowledge client writes. The majority side elects a new leader; on reconnection L sees the higher term, steps down and has its conflicting uncommitted entries replaced.

questions.prompt: Raft followers accept AppendEntries from any node claiming to be leader, regardless of the term in the request.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Followers reject AppendEntries carrying a term lower than their current term. This stops a stale, deposed leader from changing logs after a new election.

questions.prompt: In Raft, log entries flow only from the leader to followers, never from followers to the leader.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Raft's strong-leader design simplifies reasoning: the leader's log is authoritative and followers are made to match it. Leader election makes sure the new leader already has all committed entries, so nothing needs to flow back.

questions.prompt: Why should a distributed lock stored in Redis always have an expiry (TTL)?
options: If the holder crashes without releasing, the lock would otherwise be held forever
Redis rejects keys without TTLs when maxmemory is set
TTLs let several clients share the lock safely
TTLs make the lock linearizable across replicas
questions.explanation: Without a TTL, a crashed or partitioned holder leaves the lock stuck and everyone else waits forever. TTLs trade that liveness problem for a safety risk (expiry while still working), which is why fencing matters.

questions.prompt: Clients acquire a lock with SET lock:job <random-uuid> NX PX 30000. Why must release check that the value equals the client's own uuid (atomically, e.g. in Lua) before deleting?
options: If the lock expired and another client took it, a plain DEL would remove their lock
Redis requires a value check for keys set with NX
It makes acquiring the lock faster under contention
DEL is not supported on keys with a TTL
questions.explanation: If client A runs past the TTL, B acquires the lock; A then calling DEL would release B's lock and let a third client in. Compare-and-delete must be one atomic Lua script, since a separate GET then DEL can race.

questions.prompt: Client A holds a lock with a 10 s TTL, then hits a 15 s stop-the-world GC pause. Meanwhile B acquires the lock and writes to storage. A resumes and writes too. What prevents A's stale write?
options: A fencing token: a number that increases with each lock grant, which storage checks to reject older ones
Checking the lock key exists right before writing
Running the lock on a Redis replica set
A longer TTL, e.g. 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Any TTL can be exceeded by a pause, and 'check then write' still races with the pause in between. Fencing moves the check into the storage layer: B's higher token was already seen, so A's lower token is rejected.

questions.prompt: A storage service enforces fencing tokens. It has accepted a write with token 34. What should it do with a write carrying token 33?
options: Reject it, because a newer lock holder has already written
Accept it only if the lock key still exists in Redis
Queue it until token 35 arrives
Accept it, since 33 was issued legitimately
questions.explanation: Fencing tokens are monotonic. Once storage has seen 34, any write with a lower token comes from a holder whose lock has since been superseded. Checking Redis at write time just re-introduces the race.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures Martin Kleppmann's main critique of Redlock for correctness-critical locks?
options: It works only with Redis Cluster, not standalone instances
It cannot be implemented in Lua
It needs five Redis nodes, which is too expensive
It relies on bounded clock drift, pauses and network delay, and provides no fencing token
questions.explanation: Redlock's safety depends on timing assumptions that real systems violate (GC pauses, clock jumps, delayed packets), and it doesn't produce monotonic tokens storage could check. Cost is a secondary concern and not the core argument.

questions.prompt: What does an etcd-based lock offer that a single-instance Redis SET NX lock does not?
options: No need for any expiry or session
Raft-replicated linearizable state, plus key revisions that can serve as fencing tokens
Automatic retries of the critical section on failure
Lower latency per acquire
questions.explanation: etcd stores the lock key via Raft, so it survives a node failure without losing the lock, and every write gets a monotonic revision usable as a fencing token. Locks are still tied to a lease with a TTL, and etcd is usually slower than Redis.

questions.prompt: A lock only stops two workers from regenerating the same cached report (duplicate work is wasteful, not harmful). Which choice is most reasonable?
options: Use a ZooKeeper cluster with fencing tokens on the cache
A single Redis SET NX PX lock is fine; occasional double work is acceptable
Use Redlock across five independent Redis masters
Use 2PC between the workers
questions.explanation: Kleppmann distinguishes efficiency locks from correctness locks. When a rare double execution costs only CPU, a simple Redis lock is enough; heavier coordination like ZooKeeper with fencing is warranted only when correctness depends on mutual exclusion.

questions.prompt: Which practices are correct when implementing a Redis-based lock? Select all that apply.
options: Store a unique random value per acquisition
Release with an atomic compare-and-delete Lua script
Pick a TTL comfortably above the expected critical section, and renew it for long work
Release with a plain DEL to keep things simple
Acquire with SETNX and then set EXPIRE in a separate command
questions.explanation: Unique values plus compare-and-delete stop you releasing someone else's lock; sensible TTLs with renewal limit premature expiry. SETNX followed by EXPIRE isn't atomic: a crash between them leaves a lock with no TTL. Use SET key val NX PX instead.

questions.prompt: Which events can let two clients both believe they hold a lock in a single-primary Redis setup with async replication? Select all that apply.
options: Release uses an atomic Lua compare-and-delete
The holder pauses (GC, VM migration) for longer than the TTL
Each client uses a unique random lock value
The primary fails before replicating the lock key, and the promoted replica doesn't have it
questions.explanation: Async replication can lose an acknowledged lock key on failover, and a long pause lets the TTL expire while the holder still thinks it owns the lock. Unique values and compare-and-delete are safeguards; they don't create double ownership.

questions.prompt: A lock with a TTL alone guarantees mutual exclusion even if the holder pauses for longer than the TTL.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Once the TTL passes, another client can acquire the lock while the paused holder still thinks it owns it. TTLs prevent deadlock but cannot guarantee safety; fencing tokens checked by the resource close that gap.

questions.prompt: The ZooKeeper lock recipe uses ephemeral sequential znodes, with each waiter watching only its immediate predecessor to avoid a herd effect.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each client creates an ephemeral sequential node; the lowest number holds the lock. Watching only the predecessor means a release wakes one client, not all. Ephemeral nodes vanish when the session dies, releasing the lock automatically.

questions.prompt: In two-phase commit, the coordinator crashes after all participants vote YES but before sending the decision. What happens to the participants?
options: They elect a new coordinator and roll back
They abort automatically after a short timeout
They stay blocked, holding locks, until the coordinator's decision is known
They commit automatically because everyone voted YES
questions.explanation: A participant that voted YES has promised to commit if told to and can't decide alone: aborting might contradict a commit others already got. This blocking is 2PC's main weakness. Committing alone is unsafe too, since the coordinator might have decided abort.

questions.prompt: In a saga, the 'charge card' step succeeded but 'create shipment' failed permanently. What does the compensating action for the payment step usually look like?
options: A database ROLLBACK of the payment row
Deleting the payment record from the ledger
A refund: a new business operation that semantically undoes the charge
Retrying shipment creation forever
questions.explanation: Saga steps are already committed local transactions, so they can't be rolled back. Compensation is a new forward operation such as a refund or cancellation. Deleting ledger rows destroys the audit trail and doesn't move money back.

questions.prompt: An order flow has 7 steps with conditional branches (fraud check, split shipments, partial refunds). Which saga coordination style is usually easier to reason about?
options: 2PC across all seven services
Choreography: every service reacts to the others' events
A single shared database table that every service polls
Orchestration: a central state machine that issues commands and tracks progress
questions.explanation: With many steps and branches, choreography spreads the flow across services and makes it hard to trace or change. An orchestrator keeps the flow explicit and visible. Choreography works well for short, linear flows with few participants.

questions.prompt: Sagas lack isolation: another request can see an order whose payment is done but inventory isn't reserved yet. Which countermeasure is commonly used?
options: Make every step synchronous over HTTP
Use a longer message retention period
A semantic lock: mark the record as PENDING and have other operations respect that status
Raise the DB isolation level to SERIALIZABLE in every service
questions.explanation: Each local transaction commits on its own, so DB isolation levels don't span the saga. An application-level PENDING flag (semantic lock) signals the record is mid-saga. Synchronous HTTP still exposes intermediate state between calls.

questions.prompt: When ordering saga steps, where should the 'pivot' transaction (the go/no-go step that can't be compensated) go?
options: Anywhere, because order does not matter in sagas
Last, after every retriable step
First, so failures are detected as early as possible
After the compensatable steps and before the steps that are retried until they succeed
questions.explanation: The usual structure is compensatable steps, then the pivot, then retriable steps. Before the pivot, failures are undone with compensations; after it, the saga must go forward, so later steps must be retriable until they succeed.

questions.prompt: A saga's compensation 'refund payment' fails because the payment provider is down. What is the correct design response?
options: Mark the saga as failed and stop; the customer can contact support
Roll back the orchestrator's database to before the saga started
Run the original charge again to cancel it out
Retry the compensation idempotently with backoff until it succeeds, escalating to an operator if it keeps failing
questions.explanation: Compensations must eventually succeed, so they should be idempotent (e.g. keyed by saga id) and retried, with alerts and manual handling for stuck cases. Giving up leaves the system inconsistent, and rolling back the orchestrator's DB doesn't undo external effects.

questions.prompt: Why is XA/2PC rarely used across microservices that own separate databases and call each other over HTTP?
options: 2PC only works with exactly two participants
2PC cannot guarantee atomicity
HTTP has no way to carry transaction ids
Every participant must support prepare/commit, locks are held across network round trips, and a coordinator outage blocks everyone
questions.explanation: 2PC couples availability and latency: resources stay locked during the protocol and a coordinator failure blocks participants. Many datastores and brokers don't support XA at all. The 'two' in 2PC refers to phases, not participants.

questions.prompt: Which statements about two-phase commit are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It provides atomic commit across multiple resources
It never blocks, even if the coordinator fails
A participant that voted YES cannot abort unilaterally
The transaction commits only if every participant votes YES
questions.explanation: 2PC gives atomicity: everyone commits or nobody does. YES voters are bound to the coordinator's decision. That same rule is what makes it block when the coordinator fails after collecting votes.

questions.prompt: You're designing an orchestrated order saga: reserve inventory → charge card → create shipment. Which are good design choices? Select all that apply.
options: Show the order as PENDING until the saga completes
Send an idempotency key with each step's command so retries are safe
Persist saga state so the orchestrator can resume after a crash
Wrap all three remote calls in one database transaction in the orchestrator
questions.explanation: Durable saga state, idempotent steps and visible pending states are core saga practices. A local DB transaction in the orchestrator can't roll back calls already made to other services, so it gives a false sense of atomicity.

questions.prompt: A saga provides isolation equivalent to a serializable database transaction.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Sagas are ACD without I: each step commits locally and is visible immediately, so other operations can see intermediate states. Countermeasures such as semantic locks reduce, but don't remove, the resulting anomalies.

questions.prompt: In 2PC, once the coordinator has durably logged a COMMIT decision, it must eventually deliver COMMIT to every participant, even after crashing and recovering.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The logged decision is the point of no return. On recovery the coordinator reads its log and resends COMMIT to all participants (which must apply it idempotently). Switching to abort then would break atomicity.

questions.prompt: A mobile client calls POST /payments with an Idempotency-Key header, times out, and retries with the same key. The first attempt actually succeeded. What should the server do?
options: Ignore the header and rely on the client not retrying
Process the payment again, since POST is not idempotent
Return the stored response from the first attempt without charging again
Return 409 Conflict so the client knows it was a duplicate
questions.explanation: The point of an idempotency key is that a retry gets the same result as the original without repeating side effects. Returning 409 would make the client think the payment failed or is unknown, even though it succeeded.

questions.prompt: Two identical requests with the same idempotency key arrive at the same time on different servers. Both check 'key exists?', see no, and charge the card. What's the fix?
options: Add a random delay before processing
Check the key twice before processing
Atomically insert the key in an 'in progress' state, relying on a unique constraint, before doing work; the loser waits or gets 409
Cache the key in each server's memory
questions.explanation: Check-then-act is a race. Claiming the key with an atomic insert (unique index or SET NX) means only one request proceeds, and the other can return 409 or wait for the stored result. Per-server memory doesn't help across instances.

questions.prompt: Interviewers often say 'exactly-once delivery is impossible'. What do systems that advertise 'exactly-once' actually provide?
options: Exactly-once processing: at-least-once delivery plus deduplication or idempotent effects
Networks that never lose or duplicate packets
At-most-once delivery with very reliable hardware
A guarantee that the broker never redelivers anything
questions.explanation: Over an unreliable network a sender can't tell whether a lost ack means the message was lost or processed, so it must retry and duplicates are possible. 'Exactly-once' means the effect happens once, using dedup or idempotency. At-most-once just accepts loss.

questions.prompt: A consumer reads a message, updates Postgres, then commits its Kafka offset. It crashes between the DB commit and the offset commit. How do you make reprocessing harmless?
options: Commit the offset before writing to Postgres
Store a processed-message id (or offset) in the same Postgres transaction and skip messages already recorded
Increase session.timeout.ms so crashes are rarer
Use acks=all on the producer
questions.explanation: Recording the message id or partition/offset atomically with the side effect makes redelivery detectable, so the effect happens once. Committing the offset first just switches to at-most-once (data loss on crash), and producer acks don't affect consumer processing.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent according to the HTTP semantics specification (RFC 9110)?
options: GET
PUT
POST
DELETE
questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE as idempotent. POST isn't, which is why APIs add idempotency keys to POST endpoints that create resources or move money.

questions.prompt: A client retries POST /payments with the same Idempotency-Key, but the body now has amount 50 instead of 30. What is the safest server behaviour?
options: Reject the request with an error, since the key was used with different parameters
Charge the 20 difference
Process the new 50 payment and overwrite the stored response
Replay the original 30 response silently
questions.explanation: Reusing a key with different parameters usually means a client bug. Silently replaying hides it, and processing breaks idempotency. Stripe, for example, returns an error when a key is reused with different parameters. Store a hash of the request to detect this.

questions.prompt: What does Kafka's exactly-once semantics (idempotent producer + transactions) cover?
options: Any side effect a consumer performs, including HTTP calls
Only messages smaller than one batch
Read-process-write pipelines where input offsets and output records are committed atomically within Kafka
Only consumers using auto-commit
questions.explanation: Kafka transactions atomically commit produced records and consumed offsets together, so pipelines from Kafka to Kafka are exactly-once. Effects outside Kafka, such as DB writes or emails, still need their own idempotency or dedup.

questions.prompt: Which operations are naturally idempotent if executed twice with the same input? Select all that apply.
options: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING
DELETE FROM sessions WHERE id = 'abc'
Appending a line to an audit log
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 5
UPDATE accounts SET status = 'closed' WHERE id = 5
questions.explanation: Setting an absolute value, deleting by key, and an insert deduplicated on a request id all reach the same final state when repeated. Relative increments and appends add another effect each time.

questions.prompt: Which are sound design choices for an idempotency-key store behind a payments API? Select all that apply.
options: Scope keys per client or API key so tenants can't collide
Generate a fresh key on the server for each attempt
Expire keys after a bounded window, such as 24 hours
Store the response status and body so retries can be replayed
questions.explanation: TTLs bound storage, stored responses make retries return identical results, and scoping prevents cross-tenant collisions. Keys must come from the client and stay the same across retries; a server-generated key per attempt makes every retry look new.

questions.prompt: After a timeout, retrying a non-idempotent operation can cause duplicate side effects, because a timeout doesn't tell you whether the server executed it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The request may have been lost, executed with the response lost, or still be in progress. Without idempotency the client can't safely retry, which is the main reason idempotency keys exist.

questions.prompt: Enabling Kafka's idempotent producer ensures that a downstream consumer's writes to an external PostgreSQL database happen exactly once.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The idempotent producer only stops producer retries from creating duplicate records in a partition. The consumer can still be redelivered a message after a crash and must deduplicate its own Postgres writes.

questions.prompt: A process with Lamport clock 7 receives a message stamped 12. What is its clock after processing the receive event?
questions.explanation: On receive, set clock = max(local, received) + 1 = max(7, 12) + 1 = 13. Answering 12 forgets that the receive is itself an event that must increment the clock.

questions.prompt: Event a has Lamport timestamp 3 and event b has Lamport timestamp 9. What can you conclude?
options: b did not happen before a; a may have happened before b or they may be concurrent
b happened before a
a and b are concurrent
a happened before b
questions.explanation: Lamport clocks guarantee: if a → b then L(a) < L(b). The reverse doesn't hold, so L(a) < L(b) only rules out b → a. Detecting concurrency needs vector clocks.

questions.prompt: Two versions of a key carry vector clocks V1 = [A:2, B:1, C:0] and V2 = [A:1, B:2, C:0]. How do they relate?
options: V1 happened before V2
V2 happened before V1
They are identical versions
They are concurrent, so both are siblings to reconcile
questions.explanation: V1 is ahead on A and V2 is ahead on B, so neither dominates the other: they are concurrent and the store must keep both or merge. One version supersedes another only if every entry is ≤ and at least one is <.

questions.prompt: All Lamport clocks start at 0. P1 does a local event, then sends message m. P2 does three local events, then receives m. What is the timestamp of P2's receive event?
questions.explanation: P1: local = 1, send m = 2 (m carries 2). P2: locals 1, 2, 3; receive = max(3, 2) + 1 = 4. Answering 5 adds the sender's timestamp instead of taking the max.

questions.prompt: A Dynamo-style store adds a vector-clock entry for every client that writes a key. What problem does this cause at scale?
options: Vector clocks can no longer detect concurrency
Every read requires a global lock
Clock skew corrupts the vector entries
Clocks grow without bound as clients come and go, so systems truncate them or use server-side dotted version vectors
questions.explanation: Vector size grows with the number of actors. Client-as-actor clocks grow without bound; Dynamo truncated old entries (risking false conflicts), and Riak moved to server-side dotted version vectors. Vector clocks use counters, not wall time, so skew isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: A multi-leader system resolves conflicts with last-write-wins using each server's wall-clock timestamp. Two users update the same field within 50 ms on different nodes. What's the main risk?
options: The write is rejected with a conflict error
The system falls back to vector clocks automatically
Both updates are kept as siblings forever
One update is silently discarded, and with clock skew the 'later' write can lose
questions.explanation: LWW keeps one value and drops the other with no notice. If clocks are skewed, the write that really happened later may carry an earlier timestamp and be the one lost. Keeping siblings is what vector-clock systems do, not LWW.

questions.prompt: What do Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC), used by CockroachDB, provide?
options: Timestamps that stay close to physical time while still respecting causality via a logical counter
A replacement for consensus in replicated writes
Exact global time with no uncertainty, like atomic clocks
Vector clocks with one entry per client
questions.explanation: HLC timestamps pair a physical component with a logical counter, so they track wall time closely and still preserve happens-before. Exact global time with bounded uncertainty is what Spanner's TrueTime hardware provides; HLC still tolerates skew.

questions.prompt: Which statements about vector clocks are correct? Select all that apply.
options: VC(a) < VC(b) if and only if a happened before b
They can detect that two events are concurrent
Their size is fixed no matter how many nodes participate
They keep one counter per participating process
questions.explanation: Vector clocks characterize causality exactly (the 'if and only if'), which lets them detect concurrency, unlike Lamport clocks. The price is one counter per process, so size grows with the number of participants.

questions.prompt: Given vector clocks A = [3,0,1], B = [2,0,1], C = [3,1,0], which are true? Select all that apply.
options: A and C are concurrent
C happened before A
B happened before A
B happened before C
questions.explanation: B ≤ A on every entry and is smaller on one, so B → A. A has 1 > 0 in the third slot and C has 1 > 0 in the second, so they are concurrent. B vs C is also concurrent (B's third slot is 1 > 0), so 'B before C' is false.

questions.prompt: Lamport timestamps can produce a total order of all events by breaking ties with the process id.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Ordering by (timestamp, processId) gives a total order consistent with causality. This is the basis of Lamport's mutual exclusion algorithm. The order is arbitrary for concurrent events, but it is consistent everywhere.

questions.prompt: If two events have the same Lamport timestamp, they must be the same event.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Events on different processes can easily have equal Lamport timestamps; such events are concurrent. Equal timestamps imply the same event only within a single process, since each process's clock strictly increases.
