questions.prompt: In a Mercator-style URL frontier, what roles do the 'front' queues and 'back' queues play?
options: Front queues store fetched HTML, and back queues store parsed links
Front queues order URLs by priority, and each back queue holds URLs for a single host so politeness delays can be enforced per host
Front queues are in memory, and back queues are an on-disk copy of the same data
Front queues handle DNS, and back queues handle robots.txt
questions.explanation: Front queues decide what to crawl next (importance, freshness). A selector moves URLs into per-host back queues, and a heap keyed by each host's next allowed fetch time decides which host a worker may hit. That separates prioritization from politeness.

questions.prompt: Which behavior best defines crawler politeness?
options: Sending a custom User-Agent and nothing else
Fetching as many pages per second from each site as bandwidth allows
Only crawling sites that have a sitemap
Limiting concurrency and request rate per host (e.g. one connection, with a delay between fetches) and honoring robots.txt
questions.explanation: A crawler can easily overload a small site, so it caps per-host load and respects robots.txt rules (and a Crawl-delay where supported). A User-Agent identifies you but doesn't limit load, and sitemaps are optional hints.

questions.prompt: A crawler uses a Bloom filter of seen URLs to skip duplicates across billions of URLs. What is the consequence of a false positive?
options: The filter crashes and must be rebuilt
Two different URLs get merged into one page
A never-seen URL is wrongly treated as seen and skipped
An already-crawled URL is fetched again
questions.explanation: Bloom filters never give false negatives but can give false positives. So the risk is missing some new pages, not re-crawling old ones. You size the filter (bits per element, hash count) to keep that rate acceptably low, e.g. about 1%.

questions.prompt: Many URLs serve nearly identical pages that differ only in an ad block or timestamp. Which technique detects such near-duplicates?
options: Comparing HTTP status codes
Locality-sensitive fingerprints such as SimHash, where similar documents have fingerprints differing in only a few bits
Comparing full SHA-256 hashes of the HTML
Comparing URL lengths
questions.explanation: A cryptographic hash changes completely if one byte differs, so it only catches exact duplicates. SimHash or MinHash map similar content to nearby fingerprints, allowing a Hamming-distance check. Google has described using SimHash for near-duplicate detection in web crawling.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a sensible URL normalization step before deduplication?
options: Lowercase the scheme and host, drop default ports and #fragments, and sort query parameters where safe
Convert https URLs to http
Remove every query parameter from every URL
Lowercase the entire URL, including the path
questions.explanation: Scheme and host are case-insensitive, default ports and fragments don't change the resource, and parameter order usually doesn't either. Paths can be case-sensitive, and stripping all query parameters would merge genuinely different pages (e.g. ?id=1 vs ?id=2).

questions.prompt: A crawler gets stuck on a site whose calendar page links to 'next month' forever, generating endless unique URLs. What is the standard defense against such spider traps?
options: Only crawl pages with fewer than 10 links
Cap crawl depth, URL length and pages per host, and flag hosts with abnormal URL growth
Retry the site later with more workers
Increase the Bloom filter size
questions.explanation: Each trap URL is genuinely new, so dedup doesn't help. Per-host budgets, depth and length limits and pattern detection stop the crawler wasting resources. A bigger filter only remembers more trap URLs, and more workers make it worse.

questions.prompt: A crawler must fetch 1 billion pages per month. Roughly what average fetch rate is that?
options: About 4,000 pages/s
About 40 pages/s
About 40,000 pages/s
About 390 pages/s
questions.explanation: A 30-day month is 30 × 86,400 ≈ 2.6 million seconds, and 1,000,000,000 / 2,592,000 ≈ 386 pages/s. Plan for about 2x that at peak. At ~100 KB per page this is roughly 40 MB/s of download, and about 100 TB of raw HTML per month.

questions.prompt: Which practices are correct for handling robots.txt? Select all that apply.
options: Fetch robots.txt once ever per host and never refresh it
Cache each host's robots.txt and refresh it periodically (e.g. daily)
Treat robots.txt as access control that stops anyone else from fetching those pages
Apply the rules for the group matching your crawler's user-agent, falling back to the `*` group
questions.explanation: RFC 9309 has crawlers pick the most specific user-agent group and allows caching (generally no longer than 24 hours). Sites change their rules, so never refreshing is wrong. robots.txt is a voluntary convention, not security, and real access control needs authentication.

questions.prompt: Which properties of a standard Bloom filter are true? Select all that apply.
options: It answers membership exactly with no errors
It never returns false negatives for inserted items
Standard Bloom filters can't delete items
Its false-positive rate rises as more items are added beyond its design capacity
Its memory grows with the length of each inserted URL
questions.explanation: Inserted items always test positive, filling the bit array raises false positives, and clearing bits could erase other items (counting Bloom filters work around that). Memory is a fixed bit array regardless of key length, and membership is probabilistic.

questions.prompt: Partitioning the frontier by a hash of the hostname makes politeness easier, because one worker owns all URLs for a given host.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Host-based partitioning means one place controls each host's request rate with no cross-worker coordination, and per-host state (robots.txt, DNS) stays local. Partitioning by full-URL hash would spread one host across many workers.

questions.prompt: A crawler should recrawl every page at the same frequency so that all sites are treated fairly.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Pages change at very different rates: news front pages change every few minutes, archived pages almost never. Recrawl schedules should adapt to observed change frequency and importance, often using conditional GETs (If-Modified-Since, ETag) to save bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Why does a Dropbox-like sync client split files into blocks (Dropbox has described 4 MB blocks) instead of uploading whole files?
options: Blocks are encrypted, while whole files can't be
Blocks make files load faster in the web preview
Object storage can't store files over 4 MB
Only changed blocks need uploading, uploads can resume per block, and identical blocks can be deduplicated
questions.explanation: Editing part of a 2 GB file re-uploads only the blocks that changed, a failed upload resumes at the block level, and content-hashed blocks are stored once. Storage limits and encryption aren't the reason; whole files can be encrypted too.

questions.prompt: With fixed-size chunking, a user inserts one byte at the start of a large file and almost every block changes. What fixes this?
options: Content-defined chunking (e.g. a Rabin rolling hash) that picks boundaries from the content, so boundaries after the edit realign
Making blocks smaller
Compressing each block before hashing
Hashing the file name instead of the content
questions.explanation: Fixed offsets shift after an insertion, so every later block's hash changes. Content-defined chunking sets a boundary wherever a rolling hash matches a pattern, so after the edited region boundaries fall on the same content and later blocks dedupe again (as in rsync, restic and LBFS). Smaller fixed blocks still shift.

questions.prompt: How does block-level deduplication work in a file sync service?
options: Files with the same name are stored once
Duplicate files are zipped together nightly
Each block is stored under its cryptographic content hash, so a block already stored is never stored again
Users are asked to delete duplicates manually
questions.explanation: Content addressing (e.g. SHA-256 per block) means identical bytes give an identical key, so a second copy only adds a reference. Names say nothing about content: two files can share a name and differ, or differ in name and be identical.

questions.prompt: In a Dropbox-style design, how are metadata and file contents stored?
options: Both on the user's device only
A metadata service maps each file path and version to an ordered list of block hashes, while a separate block store holds the immutable blocks
Both in one relational table, with file bytes in a BLOB column
Metadata in object storage and blocks in the SQL database
questions.explanation: Metadata is small, relational and updated transactionally, while blocks are large, immutable and content-addressed. Splitting them lets each scale independently. Dropbox built Magic Pocket for blocks and keeps metadata in its own database systems. BLOBs in SQL scale poorly at exabyte size.

questions.prompt: How should a desktop client learn promptly that files changed on another device, without hammering the server?
options: Have the server email the client
Re-download every file hourly
Hold a long-poll (or push) connection that signals 'something changed', then fetch only the delta since the client's cursor
Poll the full file listing every 5 seconds
questions.explanation: A cheap notification channel plus cursor-based delta fetching keeps traffic proportional to changes. Dropbox's public API exposes this pattern as list_folder/longpoll plus list_folder/continue with a cursor. Full listings every few seconds waste huge amounts of work for idle accounts.

questions.prompt: Two offline laptops both edit report.docx and then reconnect. Dropbox's documented behavior is to:
options: Merge the two Word documents automatically line by line
Reject the second upload and lose its changes
Keep one version and save the other as a separate 'conflicted copy' file
Keep whichever save has the later device clock timestamp and discard the other
questions.explanation: For opaque binary files there's no safe automatic merge, so Dropbox preserves both: one keeps the name and the other becomes '... (conflicted copy)'. Last-writer-wins by device clock would silently lose work, and clocks can be skewed.

questions.prompt: Before uploading a modified file, the client sends the server the list of its block hashes. Why?
options: Because HTTP requires a manifest before a body
To reserve storage quota for the whole file
To let the server verify the user's password
So the server can reply with only the hashes it doesn't already have, and the client uploads just those blocks
questions.explanation: This 'have/need' exchange skips blocks that already exist from earlier versions or (with cross-user dedup) other users, saving bandwidth. The metadata commit then references the full block list. Authentication and quota are handled separately.

questions.prompt: Which are real risks or costs of deduplicating blocks across different users? Select all that apply.
options: A side channel: an attacker can infer whether a file exists elsewhere by seeing if an upload is skipped
Deleting data safely requires reference counting or garbage collection across users
It increases total storage used
It complicates per-user encryption, since identical plaintext must map to an identical stored block
It makes uploads of popular files slower
questions.explanation: Instant 'upload complete' responses can leak existence, which is why many services dedupe only within a user or on the server side. Shared blocks need refcounts before deletion, and per-user keys conflict with global dedup. Dedup saves storage and speeds up uploads.

questions.prompt: Which fields belong in a file's metadata record in a block-based sync system? Select all that apply.
options: The file's raw bytes
The file path within the user's namespace
The ordered list of block hashes making up the content
A copy of every other user's file list
A version or revision identifier
questions.explanation: Path, revision and block list let any client reconstruct the file by fetching blocks from the block store. Raw bytes belong in the block store, and other users' listings have no place in one user's metadata.

questions.prompt: When one user deletes a file, its blocks can be removed from the block store as soon as the file disappears from that user's namespace.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Deduplicated blocks may be referenced by other files, older versions kept for history or restore, or other users. Blocks must be reference-counted or garbage-collected after a retention window, never deleted eagerly.

questions.prompt: Magic Pocket is Dropbox's in-house block storage system, which it built to move most user file data off Amazon S3.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Dropbox announced in 2016 that it had migrated the vast majority of user data from S3 to Magic Pocket, its own exabyte-scale, erasure-coded block store, to cut costs and gain control over performance.

questions.prompt: In a news feed, what does fan-out on write (push model) mean?
options: Each follower's client polls the author's profile
When a user posts, the post id is pushed into each follower's precomputed timeline, so reading a feed is a cheap lookup
Posts are written to every data center synchronously
When a user opens the app, the system queries all followees' posts and merges them
questions.explanation: Push does the work at write time by inserting into followers' timelines (often Redis lists), making reads fast. Merging followees' posts at read time is fan-out on read (pull).

questions.prompt: Why does pure fan-out on write break down for celebrity accounts with 50 million followers?
options: Redis cannot store 50 million keys
A single post triggers 50 million timeline writes, creating a huge write spike and delivery lag, much of it for inactive followers
Celebrities post less often, so their timelines go stale
Followers cannot read posts from verified accounts
questions.explanation: Write amplification equals follower count: one celebrity post means tens of millions of inserts, delaying delivery and wasting work on users who never log in. Redis can hold that many keys; the problem is the burst of writes per post.

questions.prompt: What is the standard hybrid solution to the celebrity problem?
options: Pull every post at read time for all users
Limit celebrities to 1,000 followers
Push posts from normal users into followers' timelines; for celebrities, skip fan-out and merge their recent posts into the feed at read time
Push celebrity posts only to their most active followers and drop the rest
questions.explanation: The hybrid model keeps reads cheap for the common case (push) while avoiding massive write amplification for high-follower accounts (pull + merge at read). Dropping posts for less active followers would break correctness.

questions.prompt: An average user has 300 followers and the system sees 6,000 new posts/second with pure fan-out on write. Roughly how many timeline inserts per second is that?
options: 18 million
1.8 million
questions.explanation: 6,000 posts/s × 300 followers = 1,800,000 timeline inserts per second. This kind of estimate shows why fan-out workers must be horizontally scaled and why celebrity accounts (far above average) are handled separately.

questions.prompt: Fan-out on read (pull) is chosen for a system. What is its main downside?
options: Posts take longer to be written
Feed reads become expensive: each request must fetch and merge recent posts from every followee, which is slow for users who follow thousands of accounts
It stores many more copies of each post
Users can't see posts from people they follow
questions.explanation: Pull shifts work to read time; with feeds read far more often than posts are written, that means many queries per page load. Pull actually stores fewer copies than push.

questions.prompt: With fan-out on write, a user unfollows an account. What must happen to keep the feed correct?
options: Nothing; the timeline will naturally expire in 30 days
Delete the user's entire timeline and rebuild it from scratch every time
Block the author globally
Remove (or filter at read time) that author's post ids from the user's precomputed timeline, and stop future fan-out to them
questions.explanation: Precomputed timelines contain stale entries after an unfollow, so either clean them up asynchronously or filter by the current follow graph when reading. Full rebuilds on every unfollow are wasteful.

questions.prompt: Many users have accounts but haven't logged in for months. How should a push-based feed system treat them?
options: Fan out only celebrity posts to them
Fan out to them like everyone else so their feed is instantly ready
Delete their accounts
Skip fan-out to inactive users and build their timeline on demand (pull) when they next log in
questions.explanation: Writing into timelines nobody reads wastes most of the fan-out budget; lazily building on login trades a slower first load for a large saving. Fanning out to all inactive users spends writes and cache memory for nothing.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the hybrid push/pull feed model are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Celebrities' recent posts can be cached heavily because many users read the same ones
Reads for a user who follows celebrities must merge their precomputed timeline with celebrities' recent posts
The hybrid model needs no ranking or merge logic
The celebrity threshold (e.g. followers > some N) is a tunable trade-off between write and read cost
Celebrity posts become invisible to followers
questions.explanation: The threshold tunes the trade-off, reads merge pushed and pulled posts, and celebrity posts are hot so they cache well. Celebrity posts remain visible via the pull path, and merging at read time obviously needs merge/ranking logic.

questions.prompt: A celebrity posts and a fan-out queue backlog forms, delaying normal users' posts by minutes. Which mitigations make sense? Select all that apply.
options: Process fan-out synchronously inside the post request
Route celebrity accounts to the pull path so they never enter the fan-out queue
Shard fan-out work into batches of followers processed in parallel
Fan out to active followers first and inactive ones later (or never)
Use separate queues/worker pools so huge fan-outs don't block ordinary ones
questions.explanation: Pulling celebrities, isolating queues, prioritising active users and batching parallel work all reduce lag. Fanning out synchronously in the post request would make posting slow and fragile.

questions.prompt: Pure fan-out on write gives the lowest feed-read latency, because the timeline is already precomputed when the user opens the app.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Reads become a single lookup of precomputed post ids (plus hydration). The price is write amplification and storage, which is why it's combined with pull for high-follower accounts.

questions.prompt: With fan-out on write, timelines typically store full post content (text, media) for each follower to avoid any further lookups.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Timelines usually store only post ids (maybe with a score), and posts are hydrated from a post cache/store at read time. Copying full content per follower would multiply storage and make edits and deletes very costly.

questions.prompt: Which Redis data structure fits a per-user timeline of post ids ordered by time or score, trimmed to the latest 800 entries?
options: A Redis string holding a JSON array
A Redis HyperLogLog
A Redis set
A Redis sorted set (ZADD with score, ZREVRANGE to read, ZREMRANGEBYRANK to trim)
questions.explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score with O(log N) inserts and range reads, and trimming by rank caps memory. A JSON string needs read-modify-write races; sets are unordered; HLL only counts.

questions.prompt: Why do feed systems cap cached timelines (e.g. only the latest few hundred post ids per user)?
options: Users are not allowed to see older posts
Ranking algorithms only work on 800 items
Most users only scroll recent items; capping bounds memory, and older pages can fall back to slower storage or pull
Redis cannot hold more than 1,000 items per key
questions.explanation: Memory cost scales with users × entries, while deep scrolling is rare, so caching only the head of each timeline is efficient. Redis sorted sets can hold far more; the cap is an economic choice.

questions.prompt: Timeline entries store post ids. What is 'hydration' in this context?
options: Compressing the timeline
Fetching full post objects, author info and counts for the ids (usually via batched cache lookups) before returning the feed
Replicating the timeline to another region
Re-ranking the feed every second
questions.explanation: The timeline gives ids; hydration batch-fetches post content, author profiles and engagement counts from caches (e.g. MGET) and the store. Doing it per id sequentially would cause many round trips.

questions.prompt: A feed API uses OFFSET-based pagination over a timeline that receives new posts constantly. Users see duplicate posts when loading page 2. Why, and what's the fix?
options: OFFSET is too large; use smaller pages
The cache is corrupt; flush it
Ranking is non-deterministic; disable ranking
New items shift positions between requests; use cursor pagination keyed on the last seen score/id
questions.explanation: With offsets, inserts at the top push items down, so page 2 repeats items from page 1. A cursor ('items with score below X, tiebreak by id') is stable under inserts. Smaller pages don't change the shifting problem.

questions.prompt: Moving from a chronological feed to a ranked feed, what is a common two-stage architecture?
options: Let the client rank posts locally with all data
Candidate generation (gather a few hundred to thousands of recent candidates from followees, interests) followed by a ranking model that scores and orders them
Sort only by like count
Rank every post in the system for every request
questions.explanation: Scoring everything is infeasible, so systems retrieve a manageable candidate set cheaply and then apply a heavier ranking model (engagement predictions, freshness, diversity). Pure like-count sorting ignores freshness and personalisation.

questions.prompt: The Redis cluster holding timelines loses a node and some users' cached timelines vanish. What should the read path do?
options: Return HTTP 500 for those users
Read every user's timeline from a nightly backup
Return an empty feed until the next post arrives
Rebuild the timeline on a cache miss by pulling recent posts from followees (with rate limiting to avoid a stampede), then repopulate the cache
questions.explanation: Timelines are a derived cache, so a miss should trigger a rebuild from the source of truth (follow graph + posts), throttled or coalesced to avoid overwhelming the post store. Empty feeds or errors are bad user experience for a recoverable situation.

questions.prompt: A ranked feed scores posts with engagement predictions. Why might it also apply rules like 'no more than 2 consecutive posts from the same author'?
options: It reduces storage
Redis sorted sets reject duplicate authors
Pure score ordering can produce repetitive, low-diversity feeds; diversity and freshness re-ranking improves user experience and long-term engagement
Ranking models can't score posts from the same author
questions.explanation: Score-only ranking can cluster one prolific author or topic. Post-ranking adjustments (diversity, freshness, dedup) balance short-term predicted engagement with feed quality. It's a product rule, not a storage constraint.

questions.prompt: Which signals are commonly used when ranking feed candidates? Select all that apply.
options: Post age (freshness decay)
The author's database shard number
Affinity between viewer and author (past interactions)
Predicted engagement (like, comment, share probability)
Content type preferences of the viewer (video vs text)
questions.explanation: Freshness, affinity, predicted engagement and content preferences are classic ranking features. A shard number is an infrastructure detail with no relevance to what the viewer wants.

questions.prompt: A viral post's like count is displayed in millions of feeds, and the counter row becomes a write hotspot. Which techniques help? Select all that apply.
options: Buffer increments in memory or Redis and flush aggregated deltas periodically
Shard the counter into N sub-counters and sum them on read
Show approximate counts (e.g. '1.2M') served from cache with a short TTL
Store each like as an event and count asynchronously
Increment the same SQL row synchronously on every like with a row lock
questions.explanation: Sharded counters, batched deltas, cached approximate display values and async event counting spread or defer writes. A synchronous locked update per like serialises all writers on one row, which is exactly the hotspot.

questions.prompt: In a ranked feed, using the ranking score alone as a pagination cursor can cause skipped or repeated posts if scores change between page loads.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Scores shift as engagement changes, so 'score < X' can skip or repeat items. Systems often snapshot the ranked list per session (cache the ordered ids) and paginate over that snapshot.

questions.prompt: Because the timeline cache is a derived view, losing it means losing users' posts.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Posts live in a durable store; the timeline cache only holds ids derived from the follow graph and posts, so it can be rebuilt. Losing it costs latency and rebuild load, not data.

questions.prompt: Why do chat apps like WhatsApp use persistent connections (e.g. WebSockets) rather than clients polling over HTTP?
options: A persistent connection lets the server push messages instantly with low overhead, while polling adds latency and wastes requests when nothing is new
WebSockets encrypt messages end-to-end automatically
WebSockets don't need TCP
HTTP cannot carry text messages
questions.explanation: Server push over a long-lived connection delivers messages in milliseconds without constant empty polls. WebSockets run over TCP and are not end-to-end encrypted by themselves (TLS only secures the hop; E2E needs something like the Signal protocol).

questions.prompt: Users' WebSocket connections are spread across 500 gateway servers. User A (on gateway 12) messages user B. How does the system know where to deliver?
options: Always place A and B on the same gateway
A connection registry (e.g. Redis: userId → gatewayId) records which gateway holds each user's connection, and the message is routed there
Broadcast the message to all 500 gateways
User B polls every gateway
questions.explanation: A registry maps user (or device) to gateway so a message is routed only to the right server, often via a per-gateway queue or pub/sub channel. Broadcasting to every gateway wastes work and doesn't scale.

questions.prompt: A gateway server crashes, dropping 100,000 connections. What happens to its entries in the connection registry if they were written without expiry?
options: Clients update the registry before disconnecting
Nothing; registries don't need cleanup
Redis deletes them automatically when the gateway's TCP connection closes
Stale entries keep pointing users to a dead gateway, so messages are routed nowhere until cleaned up
questions.explanation: A crashed server can't clean up, so entries need TTLs refreshed by heartbeats, plus delivery logic that treats a missing/dead target as 'offline, store for later'. Clients that lose connection can't write anything either.

questions.prompt: Each gateway holds ~500k idle WebSocket connections. What resource limits the number of connections per server most directly?
options: The number of CPU cores, since each connection needs its own thread
Memory per connection and OS limits like file descriptors (ulimit), plus kernel socket buffers
Disk space for each message
Database connection pool size
questions.explanation: Each socket uses a file descriptor and buffer memory, so fd limits and RAM dominate for mostly idle connections. Event-driven servers (Node.js, Netty, Erlang) don't need a thread per connection.

questions.prompt: A WebSocket gateway fleet sits behind a load balancer. You deploy a new gateway version. What is the key concern?
options: Messages are re-encrypted with a new key
Load balancers don't support WebSockets
Users must reinstall the app
Restarting a gateway drops all its connections; drain gradually and have clients reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a reconnect storm
questions.explanation: Long-lived connections make deploys disruptive: a mass disconnect leads to everyone reconnecting at once. Rolling drains (close connections gradually with a reconnect hint) and client jitter spread the load. Modern L7 load balancers do support WebSockets.

questions.prompt: In a Node.js WebSocket gateway, what should the gateway do and NOT do?
options: Run ranking models for each message
Hold connections, authenticate, forward messages to backend services and push outbound messages; keep heavy business logic and storage in separate services
Run all chat business logic, including message storage, inside each gateway process
Store all message history in gateway memory
questions.explanation: Keeping gateways thin means they can be scaled and restarted independently of chat logic; durable storage and processing live behind them. Gateway memory is lost on restart and doesn't scale as a store.

questions.prompt: A user has the app open on a phone and on a laptop. How should the connection registry model this?
options: Reject the second login
Map userId → set of (deviceId, gatewayId) entries, each with its own TTL, and deliver to every active device
Store one entry and let the phone forward messages to the laptop
Store only the most recent connection and drop the other
questions.explanation: Multi-device support needs one registry entry per device connection; delivery fans out to all of them, and per-device TTLs handle individual disconnects. Keeping only the latest connection silently stops delivery to the other device.

questions.prompt: Which practices help keep WebSocket connections healthy at scale? Select all that apply.
options: Client reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter
Open a new WebSocket for every message sent
Authenticate on connect (e.g. a token in the handshake) and re-check on expiry
Keep load-balancer idle timeouts longer than the heartbeat interval
Application-level heartbeats (ping/pong) to detect dead connections that TCP hasn't noticed
questions.explanation: Heartbeats detect half-open connections, jittered reconnects avoid storms, handshake auth secures sessions, and idle timeouts above the heartbeat interval stop the LB from cutting healthy idle connections. Opening a socket per message defeats the purpose.

questions.prompt: Gateway A must hand a message to the gateway that holds the recipient's connection. Which inter-gateway routing approaches are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Write the message to a shared file that all gateways tail
Send every message to every gateway and let each filter
Gateways connect directly to each other over an internal RPC mesh using the registry
Route via a message broker (e.g. Kafka partitioned by recipient, consumed by the owning gateway)
Each gateway subscribes to its own Redis pub/sub channel or queue; senders publish to the target gateway's channel
questions.explanation: Per-gateway pub/sub channels, a partitioned broker or direct RPC are all used in practice. Shared files don't scale or survive failures, and broadcasting to every gateway multiplies traffic by the fleet size.

questions.prompt: Pure Redis pub/sub is durable: if the target gateway is briefly disconnected, it receives the missed messages when it resubscribes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget; messages published while a subscriber is disconnected are lost. Durability must come from persisting messages first (message store, Redis Streams or Kafka) and syncing on reconnect.

questions.prompt: Server-Sent Events (SSE) can be a simpler alternative to WebSockets when the server only needs to push data to the client, such as live notifications.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. SSE is one-way server-to-client over plain HTTP with built-in reconnect and event ids. Chat needs frequent client-to-server messages too, which is why WebSockets are the usual choice there.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a chat system order messages within a conversation by each client's device timestamp?
options: Device timestamps use the wrong time zone
Device clocks are skewed or wrong, so messages could appear out of order; the server should assign a per-conversation sequence number
Clients don't have clocks
Timestamps can't be stored in databases
questions.explanation: Client clocks drift or are set manually, so ordering by them is unreliable. A server-assigned, monotonically increasing sequence per conversation gives one agreed order.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a client-generated message id (e.g. a UUID) on each sent chat message?
options: It encrypts the message
It lets the server deduplicate retries, so a resend after a network glitch doesn't create a second copy
It replaces the server sequence number for ordering
It identifies the recipient's device
questions.explanation: If the client times out waiting for an ack and resends, the server recognises the same client message id and returns the original ack instead of storing a duplicate. Ordering still comes from the server sequence.

questions.prompt: WhatsApp-style ticks show sent, delivered and read. What do these receipts correspond to?
options: Sent = server stored the message; delivered = recipient's device acknowledged receiving it; read = recipient opened the conversation
Sent = typed; delivered = server stored; read = recipient replied
All three are set together when the server stores the message
Sent = encrypted; delivered = decrypted; read = deleted
questions.explanation: The server ack gives 'sent', the recipient device's ack gives 'delivered', and a read event when the chat is viewed gives 'read'. Each is a separate event flowing back to the sender.

questions.prompt: A user comes back online after 3 days offline. How should the client catch up efficiently?
options: Wait for each sender to resend
Download the user's entire message history again
Poll each conversation every second until nothing new arrives
Send the last sequence number it has per conversation (or a global sync cursor); the server returns only newer messages, paginated
questions.explanation: Cursor-based sync transfers only the delta and is resumable if interrupted. Re-downloading everything wastes bandwidth, and senders shouldn't be responsible for re-delivery.

questions.prompt: A group chat with heavy traffic stores messages in Cassandra with partition key conversation_id and clustering key message sequence (descending). What does this design optimise?
options: Counting unique senders across all conversations
Fetching the latest N messages of one conversation with a single-partition, already-sorted read
Global full-text search across all chats
Joins between messages and users
questions.explanation: All of a conversation's messages live in one partition sorted by sequence, so 'latest 50' is a cheap slice. Very active conversations may also need time-bucketing in the partition key to keep partitions bounded. Cassandra doesn't do joins.

questions.prompt: How can a server assign increasing sequence numbers per conversation without one global counter becoming a bottleneck?
options: Use the current Unix time in seconds
Use one global auto-increment across all conversations
Keep a counter per conversation (e.g. Redis INCR on conv:{id}:seq, or route each conversation to one owner that increments locally)
Let each client pick its own sequence
questions.explanation: Ordering only matters within a conversation, so per-conversation counters spread load across keys/shards. A global counter serialises everything; client-chosen sequences conflict; second-resolution timestamps collide.

questions.prompt: A sender's message is stored and pushed to the recipient's gateway, but the recipient's phone loses network before acknowledging. What should the system do?
options: Ask the sender to resend manually
Keep it as undelivered (in the recipient's pending/offline queue) and deliver it on reconnect sync; the client dedupes by message id
Delete the message
Mark it delivered anyway since it reached the gateway
questions.explanation: Delivery is only confirmed by the device ack; until then the message stays pending and will be re-sent during sync, with dedup by id preventing duplicates. Treating the gateway push as delivered would lose messages.

questions.prompt: Which statements about message delivery guarantees in chat are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Exactly-once network delivery is easy to guarantee with TCP alone
At-least-once delivery plus client-side dedup by message id gives effectively-once display
Per-conversation ordering is usually enough; global ordering across all chats is unnecessary
Read receipts must be delivered before the message itself
The server should persist a message before acknowledging 'sent' to the sender
questions.explanation: Persist-then-ack, at-least-once with dedup and per-conversation ordering are the standard design. TCP only guarantees delivery within one connection and can't prevent app-level resends across reconnects, and receipts naturally come after messages.

questions.prompt: In a 1,000-member group chat, per-member read receipts become expensive. Which designs reduce cost? Select all that apply.
options: Batch and debounce receipt updates from clients
Store a per-member 'last read sequence' instead of a receipt row per message per member
Disable or limit detailed receipts above a group size threshold
Aggregate receipts and show counts or 'read by all' rather than pushing every individual receipt to every member
Send each read receipt to all 1,000 members immediately as it happens
questions.explanation: A last-read pointer per member replaces N×M receipt rows; aggregation, batching and size thresholds cut fan-out. Broadcasting every receipt to every member is O(members²) traffic per message read wave.

questions.prompt: If a server assigns sequence numbers per conversation, two messages sent at nearly the same moment by different members will still be shown in the same order on every member's device.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The server sequence is the single source of order, so all clients sort by it and agree, even if the senders' perceived order differed. That consistency is the reason to use server-assigned sequences.

questions.prompt: Once a message is delivered to the recipient's device, the server must keep it forever in all chat designs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Some designs (classic WhatsApp) treat the server as a relay and delete messages after delivery, with history living on devices and backups; others (Slack, Telegram cloud chats) keep server-side history. It is a product and privacy trade-off.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest scalable way to track whether a user is online?
options: Run a SQL query over all open WebSocket connections
Write every keystroke to the database
Ask the user's contacts whether they can see the user
Clients send periodic heartbeats; the server sets a presence key with a short TTL (e.g. 30-60 s) that expires if heartbeats stop
questions.explanation: A TTL key refreshed by heartbeats naturally flips to offline when the client disappears, without needing a clean disconnect. Querying connections or writing per keystroke doesn't scale.

questions.prompt: Why rely on heartbeat expiry rather than only on WebSocket close events to mark users offline?
options: Close events always arrive twice
Heartbeats use less bandwidth than close events
Close events are not part of the WebSocket protocol
When a phone loses network or the app is killed, no close frame is sent, so the server may not notice the disconnect for a long time
questions.explanation: Abrupt disconnects (tunnels, airplane mode, crashes) leave half-open TCP connections with no close event, so a TTL/heartbeat timeout is needed. Clean close events can still be used to mark offline faster when they arrive.

questions.prompt: A user with 2,000 contacts flickers online/offline every few seconds on a weak mobile network. What problem does this cause, and what's a common fix?
options: It increases the user's battery usage only; no server fix needed
Each transition fans out to all contacts, generating a flood of presence events; debounce transitions (e.g. only mark offline after a grace period)
It corrupts the message store; fix by disabling presence
Contacts receive duplicate messages; fix with idempotency keys
questions.explanation: Presence changes fan out to every interested contact, so flapping multiplies traffic. A grace period before announcing 'offline' (and coalescing rapid changes) suppresses flicker. Message duplication is unrelated.

questions.prompt: For a user with 5,000 contacts, pushing every presence change to all contacts is expensive. Which approach reduces fan-out most effectively?
options: Store presence in the database and let clients query it every second
Push presence only to contacts who are currently online and actually viewing something that shows it (e.g. subscribed to that user's status while a chat or list is open)
Push presence changes to all contacts via SMS
Send presence once per day
questions.explanation: Subscription-based presence sends updates only to viewers who care right now, cutting most fan-out. Per-second polling by every client creates even more load, and daily updates make presence useless.

questions.prompt: How is 'last seen at 10:42' typically implemented alongside online presence?
options: Derived from the load balancer's access logs
Stored only on the user's device
When the presence key expires or the user disconnects, record a durable last-seen timestamp (e.g. updated on heartbeat at a coarse interval)
Computed from the latest message the user sent
questions.explanation: Online status lives in a short-TTL cache, while last-seen is persisted on disconnect (or periodically from heartbeats) so it survives the key expiring. Last message sent misses users who read without writing.

questions.prompt: Presence data lives in Redis with TTL keys. A Redis node fails and its presence keys are lost. How bad is this?
options: All messages to those users will be dropped permanently
Very bad: message history is lost
Users can no longer log in
Mostly cosmetic and self-healing: affected users briefly show offline until their next heartbeat recreates the key
questions.explanation: Presence is soft state continuously refreshed by heartbeats, so loss recovers within one heartbeat interval. That's why presence usually doesn't need durable, strongly consistent storage. Message delivery uses the connection registry and offline queue, not presence.

questions.prompt: What heartbeat interval trade-off do mobile chat apps face?
options: Shorter intervals make presence more accurate but drain battery and increase server load; longer intervals save resources but make presence stale
Interval has no effect on presence accuracy
Shorter intervals always save battery
Longer intervals require more server memory
questions.explanation: Frequent heartbeats keep the radio awake and multiply requests across millions of clients; infrequent ones delay offline detection. Apps pick a middle ground (tens of seconds) and use OS push when backgrounded.

questions.prompt: Which statements about presence systems are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Presence state is usually kept in memory/cache rather than a primary relational database
Presence must be strongly consistent across all regions before a message can be sent
Presence is typically eventually consistent: a few seconds of staleness is acceptable
Typing indicators are ephemeral events that generally don't need to be persisted
A user with multiple devices is online if any device is connected
questions.explanation: Presence is soft, ephemeral, cache-backed state aggregated across devices, and typing indicators are fire-and-forget. Sending messages never waits on presence; offline recipients simply get messages on sync.

questions.prompt: Presence updates for 100 million online users are overwhelming the system. Which optimisations are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Hide exact presence in large groups (show only for 1:1 chats or small groups)
Use a grace period to suppress short offline/online flaps
Shard presence keys across a Redis cluster by user id
Batch presence updates and push them to clients in periodic digests instead of one event per change
Write every heartbeat to a durable, replicated SQL table with fsync
questions.explanation: Batching, limiting presence where it adds little value, sharding and flap suppression cut load. Persisting every heartbeat durably turns a cheap soft-state signal into a massive write workload.

questions.prompt: A presence key with a 30-second TTL refreshed by 10-second heartbeats tolerates a couple of missed heartbeats before the user shows as offline.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With heartbeats at a third of the TTL, one or two lost heartbeats (brief network blips) don't flip the user offline; only about 30 s without any heartbeat does. Setting the TTL equal to the heartbeat interval would cause constant flapping.

questions.prompt: Presence should be fanned out to all of a user's contacts in real time, even those who are offline, so it's ready when they open the app.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Offline contacts can't receive pushes, and queueing presence for them is wasted work since it would be stale anyway. When they come online, they fetch the current presence of the contacts they're viewing.

questions.prompt: In a 'design a food-delivery app' interview, which of these is a non-functional requirement?
options: Order placement responds within 300 ms at p99
Restaurants can update their menu
Customers can rate a delivery
Customers can track their courier on a map
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities (latency, availability, durability, scale), not features. Tracking, menu updates and ratings are functional: things the system does.

questions.prompt: The interviewer says 'Design a chat app.' What's the best first move?
options: Ask clarifying questions to agree on core features, scale and constraints
Draw the high-level architecture with WebSockets
Start estimating storage for messages
Pick a database and justify it
questions.explanation: The problem is intentionally vague; scoping first (1:1 vs group, history, media, users, latency) prevents designing the wrong system. Diagrams, estimates and DB choices depend on those answers.

questions.prompt: For 'Design Twitter' in 45 minutes, how should you handle the long list of possible features?
options: Cover every feature briefly so nothing is missed
Design only the database and skip features
Pick a few core features (post, follow, home timeline) and state what's out of scope
Let the interviewer pick features as you go
questions.explanation: Explicitly narrowing scope to the core flows and naming what you're deferring shows prioritization and leaves time for depth. Covering everything shallowly leaves no time for the hard parts.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly needs strong consistency rather than eventual consistency?
options: Showing the like count on a post
Updating a follower count
Displaying 'last seen' timestamps
Debiting a wallet balance so it can't go negative
questions.explanation: Money movement must not double-spend, so reads and writes on the balance need strong consistency. Like counts, follower counts and last-seen can be slightly stale without real harm.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks for 99.99% availability. Roughly how much downtime per year does that allow?
options: About 8.8 hours
About 3.7 days
About 5.3 minutes
About 52.6 minutes
questions.explanation: 525,600 minutes/year × 0.0001 ≈ 52.6 minutes. 8.8 hours is 99.9%, 5.3 minutes is 99.999%, and 3.7 days is 99%. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

questions.prompt: Why does asking about the read/write ratio early matter so much?
options: It shapes key decisions like caching, read replicas and how data is stored
It sets the number of microservices
It only matters for estimating cost
It determines which programming language to use
questions.explanation: A 100:1 read-heavy system pushes you toward caches, replicas and precomputed views; a write-heavy one toward partitioning, append-friendly storage and queues. It drives architecture, not language choice.

questions.prompt: You're designing a URL shortener. The interviewer says links must never break once created. Which non-functional requirement does this mostly express?
options: Low latency
High durability of stored mappings
Horizontal scalability of writes
Strong read-your-writes for analytics
questions.explanation: 'Never break' means the short-to-long mapping must not be lost: durability (replication, backups). Latency and scalability matter too but aren't what this statement asks for.

questions.prompt: Which of these are non-functional requirements? Select all that apply.
options: Users can search posts by keyword
p95 read latency under 200 ms
99.9% monthly availability
No acknowledged write is ever lost
Users can follow other users
questions.explanation: Availability, latency and durability targets are qualities of the system. Following and searching are features, so they're functional requirements.

questions.prompt: For 'Design a URL shortener', which are useful clarifying questions? Select all that apply.
options: Which programming language should I use?
Do users need custom aliases?
How many new links per day, and what's the read/write ratio?
Should links expire, and do we need click analytics?
questions.explanation: Volume, custom aliases, expiry and analytics change the design (key generation, storage, extra pipelines). Language choice rarely affects a system design discussion.

questions.prompt: Jumping straight into a diagram before agreeing on requirements is a common red flag in system design interviews.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Interviewers look for scoping first; designing without requirements often solves the wrong problem and suggests poor judgement in real projects.

questions.prompt: Non-functional requirements are minor details that rarely change the architecture.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Latency, availability, consistency and scale targets often decide the architecture: e.g. 99.99% forces multi-zone redundancy, and strong consistency rules out some data stores.

questions.prompt: For quick QPS estimates, roughly how many seconds are in a day?
options: About 3,600
About 10,000
questions.explanation: A day has 86,400 seconds, which rounds to ~10^5 for mental math. 3,600 is one hour; 1,000,000 is about 11.6 days.

questions.prompt: Average write QPS is 2,000 and peak traffic is about 3× average. What peak QPS should you design for?
options: About 2,000
About 20,000
About 6,000
About 666
questions.explanation: Peak = 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 QPS. Systems must handle peaks, not averages; designing for 2,000 would fall over at daily highs.

questions.prompt: Users upload 1 million photos per day, average 2 MB each. Roughly how much new storage per year (before replication)?
options: About 7.3 PB
About 73 TB
About 2 TB
About 730 TB
questions.explanation: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB/day; × 365 ≈ 730 TB/year. With 3× replication that's ~2.2 PB. 2 TB is just one day, and 73 TB drops a factor of 10.

questions.prompt: A service serves 5,000 image reads per second at 200 KB each. Roughly what egress bandwidth is needed?
options: About 100 Mbps
About 8 Gbps
About 1 Gbps
About 80 Gbps
questions.explanation: 5,000 × 200 KB = 1,000,000 KB/s ≈ 1 GB/s; × 8 bits ≈ 8 Gbps. Answering 1 Gbps is the common mistake of forgetting to convert bytes to bits.

questions.prompt: 100M DAU each post 2 tweets/day with ~300 bytes of text and metadata. Roughly how much text storage over 5 years?
options: About 1.1 PB
About 110 TB
About 60 GB
About 11 TB
questions.explanation: 100M × 2 × 300 B = 60 GB/day; × 365 ≈ 22 TB/year; × 5 ≈ 110 TB. 60 GB is a single day. Media would dominate if included, so state that you're counting text only.

questions.prompt: There are 100M read requests per day, each returning ~500 bytes. Following the 80/20 rule, you cache the hottest 20% of a day's data. Roughly how much cache memory?
options: About 100 GB
About 10 GB
About 1 GB
About 50 GB
questions.explanation: 100M × 500 B = 50 GB per day of responses; 20% ≈ 10 GB, which fits on one or a few cache nodes. 50 GB would be caching everything.

questions.prompt: What's the main purpose of back-of-the-envelope estimation in a design interview?
options: To prove the interviewer's numbers are wrong
To size the problem and drive decisions like caching, sharding or replication
To produce exact capacity numbers for procurement
To fill time while thinking about the design
questions.explanation: Order-of-magnitude numbers tell you whether one DB suffices, whether data fits in memory, or whether you need sharding. Precision isn't the goal; decisions are.

questions.prompt: Which are good habits during estimation? Select all that apply.
options: Write units on every number
Compute exact figures to the byte
Round to convenient numbers (e.g. 86,400 ≈ 100,000)
Say what each result implies for the design
State your assumptions out loud
questions.explanation: Rounding, stated assumptions, labelled units and tying numbers to design choices make estimates fast and useful. Exact arithmetic wastes time and adds no insight.

questions.prompt: Which latency figures are roughly correct in order of magnitude? Select all that apply.
options: SSD random read: ~100 µs
Round trip across continents: ~1 ms
Disk (HDD) seek: ~1 ns
Main memory reference: ~100 ns
Round trip within one data center: ~0.5 ms
questions.explanation: Memory ~100 ns, SSD random read tens to ~150 µs, same-DC RTT ~0.5 ms match the classic latency numbers. Cross-continent RTT is ~100–150 ms, and an HDD seek is ~10 ms.

questions.prompt: A 1 Gbps link can move roughly 125 MB per second, ignoring protocol overhead.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: 1 Gbps = 1,000 Mb/s ÷ 8 bits per byte = 125 MB/s. Real throughput is a bit lower due to protocol overhead.

questions.prompt: 1 million requests per day is roughly 1,000 requests per second on average.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 12 requests per second. A million a day is small; you need ~86M a day to average 1,000 QPS.

questions.prompt: After agreeing on requirements and rough estimates, what's a good next step in the classic interview flow?
options: Choose a cloud provider
Discuss the CI/CD pipeline
Deep dive into database index tuning
Define the core API endpoints for the main use cases
questions.explanation: The API pins down the system's contract, which then drives the data model and diagram. Deep dives come later; CI/CD and cloud vendor choice are rarely the point.

questions.prompt: For GET /feed on a fast-moving timeline, why prefer cursor-based pagination over OFFSET/LIMIT?
options: Cursors make responses smaller
Cursors avoid duplicates or gaps as new items arrive and avoid scanning skipped rows
Cursors let clients jump to any page number
OFFSET is not supported by SQL databases
questions.explanation: A cursor (e.g. last seen created_at + id) continues from a stable point, so inserts don't shift pages, and the index seek avoids reading and discarding OFFSET rows. Random page jumps are actually easier with OFFSET.

questions.prompt: The main query is 'latest 20 posts by user X, newest first'. In PostgreSQL, which index best supports it?
options: An index on post_id only
An index on created_at only
A composite B-tree index on (user_id, created_at DESC)
A hash index on user_id
questions.explanation: A (user_id, created_at) index finds the user's rows already ordered by time, so the DB reads just 20 entries. created_at alone scans all users; a hash index can't provide ordering.

questions.prompt: You have 15 minutes left for deep dives in 'Design Instagram'. What should you pick?
options: The login form's validation rules
The hardest part driven by the requirements, e.g. feed fan-out for celebrity accounts
Choice of logging library
CRUD for user profile edits
questions.explanation: Deep dives should target the bottleneck the NFRs make hard (fan-out, hot keys, media storage). Simple CRUD or library choices don't show senior-level reasoning.

questions.prompt: Your POST /payments may be retried by mobile clients on timeouts. Which API design avoids double charges?
options: Return 202 Accepted for every request
Require an Idempotency-Key header and return the stored result for repeats
Tell clients never to retry
Use PUT instead of POST without other changes
questions.explanation: The server stores the result keyed by the client-supplied idempotency key; a retry with the same key gets the original response instead of a second charge. Switching verbs alone doesn't dedupe, and clients will retry anyway.

questions.prompt: What should the first high-level diagram mainly show?
options: Every class and method in each service
Kubernetes pod resource limits
End-to-end request flow through clients, load balancer, services, data stores, caches and queues
Only the database schema
questions.explanation: The high-level diagram should show how a request flows through the major components so the interviewer sees a working whole before you zoom in. Class diagrams and pod limits are far too detailed.

questions.prompt: How should you justify SQL vs NoSQL in the data-model step?
options: Tie it to access patterns, relationships, consistency needs and scale
SQL is always safer, so never use NoSQL
NoSQL always scales better, so choose it for any large system
Pick whatever the interviewer's company uses
questions.explanation: A good answer maps the choice to requirements: relational integrity and transactions vs simple key access at massive scale. Blanket claims either way signal shallow reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which are signs of good API design in an interview? Select all that apply.
options: List endpoints that return the entire table
Pagination on list endpoints
Resource-oriented endpoints with clear request and response fields
Idempotency for writes clients may retry
questions.explanation: Clear contracts, pagination and idempotent retries show production thinking. Returning whole tables doesn't scale and wastes bandwidth.

questions.prompt: What should a strong deep dive cover? Select all that apply.
options: Alternatives considered and why you chose one
The scaling bottleneck and how to remove it
A re-read of the full requirements list
Failure modes and how the system recovers
questions.explanation: Failure handling, bottlenecks and trade-offs between alternatives are what interviewers probe. Re-reading requirements burns time without adding depth.

questions.prompt: It's fine to revise your high-level design when a deep dive reveals a bottleneck.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Iterating on the design in response to new insight is exactly what real engineering looks like; interviewers value it far more than defending a flawed first sketch.

questions.prompt: A good data model can be designed before knowing the main read and write queries.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Keys, indexes, partitioning and denormalization all follow from access patterns, which is why the API (and main queries) usually comes before the data model.

questions.prompt: Per the CAP theorem, what must a distributed data store choose between during a network partition?
options: Durability and partition tolerance
Latency and throughput
Scalability and cost
Consistency and availability
questions.explanation: When nodes can't communicate, the system either rejects some requests to stay consistent (CP) or answers with possibly stale data to stay available (AP). Partition tolerance isn't optional in real networks.

questions.prompt: Which statement best demonstrates trade-off reasoning to an interviewer?
options: 'Fan-out on write gives fast reads for our 100:1 ratio; the cost is heavy writes for big accounts, so we'd handle those differently.'
'Cassandra is the best database, so we'll use it.'
'We'll use a cache; it has no real downside.'
'I'd use microservices because that's industry standard.'
questions.explanation: Strong answers name the choice, tie it to a requirement, state the cost and say when you'd change course. The others assert a choice without context or deny any downside.

questions.prompt: In a news feed, what's the main downside of fan-out on write (push to followers' timelines at post time)?
options: Reads become slow because timelines are built at read time
Timelines can't be cached
Posts by accounts with millions of followers cause huge, slow write bursts
Users can't see their own posts
questions.explanation: Pushing a post into millions of timelines is expensive and delays delivery for celebrities. Slow read-time assembly is the downside of fan-out on read (pull), the opposite approach.

questions.prompt: How do large feed systems usually handle the celebrity problem?
options: Ban accounts above a follower limit
Push all posts synchronously before returning 200
Hybrid: push posts from normal users, pull celebrity posts at read time and merge
Pull every timeline at read time for all users
questions.explanation: A hybrid keeps cheap precomputed timelines for most authors and merges in the few celebrity posts at read time, avoiding giant write fan-outs. Pure pull makes every read expensive.

questions.prompt: PACELC extends CAP. What does the 'ELC' part say?
options: Even with partitions, choose latency over cost
Else, when there's no partition, systems trade latency against consistency
Eventually, every system becomes consistent
Elections need a leader and consensus
questions.explanation: PACELC: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Even in normal operation, stronger consistency (waiting for replicas) costs latency.

questions.prompt: What's the main trade-off of denormalizing data (duplicating author names into each post row)?
options: Faster reads, but writes must update many copies and risk inconsistency
Slower reads, but simpler writes
It removes the need for indexes
Less storage and faster writes
questions.explanation: Denormalization avoids joins on reads, but when the author renames, every copy must be updated, and copies can drift. It also uses more storage, not less.

questions.prompt: You're designing a double-entry ledger for payments. Which choice and justification fit best?
options: An in-memory cache, because ledgers are read-heavy
A wide-column store, because writes are high volume
A relational database, for ACID transactions and constraints that keep entries balanced
A document store, because ledger entries are JSON
questions.explanation: Ledgers need atomic multi-row writes (debit and credit together), constraints and auditability: classic relational strengths. Write volume or JSON shape doesn't outweigh correctness for money.

questions.prompt: Which statements show good trade-off reasoning? Select all that apply.
options: Claiming the chosen option has no downside
Tying the choice to a stated requirement
Naming the downside you're accepting
Saying what would make you revisit the decision
questions.explanation: Requirement link, acknowledged cost and a revisit condition are the hallmarks of mature trade-off discussion. Every real option has a downside; claiming otherwise is a red flag.

questions.prompt: Which are real costs of adding a cache in front of a database? Select all that apply.
options: Another component to operate and monitor
Possible stale reads
Higher database load on cache hits
Invalidation logic that's easy to get wrong
questions.explanation: Caches bring staleness, invalidation complexity and operational overhead. Cache hits reduce database load; that's the whole point.

questions.prompt: Strong consistency across geographically distant regions usually costs higher write latency.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Strongly consistent cross-region writes must coordinate with remote replicas, paying cross-region round trips (often 50–150+ ms). That's the latency-vs-consistency trade-off PACELC describes.

questions.prompt: Presenting one design as universally best, without discussing alternatives, signals seniority in a design interview.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Senior engineers compare alternatives and explain why one fits these requirements. Presenting a single 'best' answer suggests you haven't considered the trade-offs.

questions.prompt: A candidate starts sharding the database in the first five minutes, before discussing features or scale. What's the core mistake?
options: Diving into details before clarifying requirements and scale
Sharding is never needed in interviews
Using too many diagrams
Not choosing a cloud provider first
questions.explanation: Without requirements and estimates you don't know whether sharding is even needed. Clarify scope first, then let numbers justify complexity.

questions.prompt: Requirements say 100 QPS and 10K users. The candidate proposes Kafka, 12 microservices and multi-region active-active. What's the main critique?
options: Over-engineering: the complexity isn't justified by the stated scale
Microservices can't talk to Kafka
Multi-region requires a NoSQL database
Kafka can't handle 100 QPS
questions.explanation: Matching the design to requirements is the skill being tested. At 100 QPS a monolith with a replicated DB is likely enough; heavy infrastructure adds cost and risk without need.

questions.prompt: A candidate thinks silently for several minutes at a time, then presents finished conclusions. Why is this a problem?
options: Interviewers penalize any pause
It makes the interview end early
Silence means the candidate doesn't know the answer
The interviewer can't see the reasoning or steer, and design rounds score the thought process
questions.explanation: Thinking aloud lets the interviewer follow your reasoning, give hints and evaluate how you handle ambiguity. Short pauses are fine; long silent stretches hide the signal.

questions.prompt: Mid-design, the interviewer asks, 'What happens if this cache node dies?' What does this usually signal?
options: They're making small talk
They want you to address a failure mode or single point of failure you've glossed over
They want you to switch to a different cache product
They want you to remove the cache
questions.explanation: Interviewer questions are often hints toward a weakness. Explain the impact (DB stampede), then mitigations (replication, warm-up, request coalescing), instead of brushing it off.

questions.prompt: Asked how the system handles 10× traffic, a candidate says 'just add more servers.' What makes this answer weak?
options: It should be 'add more RAM' instead
Adding servers is never valid
It ignores which component is stateful or bottlenecked, such as the database or a hot key
Servers can't be added without downtime
questions.explanation: Stateless tiers scale by adding servers, but the hard part is usually the database, shared state or hot partitions. A strong answer identifies the bottleneck and how to scale it specifically.

questions.prompt: In a 45-minute round, a candidate spends 25 minutes on estimates. What's the main problem?
options: Estimates should never be done
Estimates must be done at the end
Too little time left for the design and deep dives that carry most of the signal
The interviewer wanted exact numbers
questions.explanation: Estimates should take a few minutes and feed decisions. Over-investing leaves no time for architecture, trade-offs and deep dives, which are what's mainly evaluated.

questions.prompt: A candidate says 'we'll use Cassandra because it scales' without further detail. What's the better approach?
options: Always choose PostgreSQL instead
Avoid naming specific technologies
Name more databases to show breadth
Explain which requirement it meets (e.g. write-heavy, partition-key access) and what you give up
questions.explanation: Naming a technology is fine; justifying it with the access pattern and accepting its costs (limited queries, eventual consistency) is what shows understanding. Buzzwords alone are a common red flag.

questions.prompt: Which are common mistakes in system design interviews? Select all that apply.
options: Not clarifying requirements
Leaving an obvious single point of failure unaddressed
Ignoring non-functional requirements such as latency and availability
Summarizing the design and its trade-offs at the end
questions.explanation: Skipping requirements, ignoring NFRs and leaving SPOFs are classic failures. A closing summary of the design and trade-offs is a good habit, not a mistake.

questions.prompt: Which habits help you drive a design round well? Select all that apply.
options: Managing time across requirements, design and deep dives
Checking in with the interviewer at transitions
Stating assumptions explicitly
Refusing to change the design when challenged
questions.explanation: Check-ins, explicit assumptions and time management keep the round on track and collaborative. Digging in when challenged signals poor collaboration; consider the point and adapt or defend with reasons.

questions.prompt: Asking clarifying questions wastes interview time and signals weakness.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Design prompts are intentionally vague; good clarifying questions are expected and show you'd scope real projects properly. Just keep them focused and brief.

questions.prompt: Designing for 100× the stated scale without being asked can be seen as over-engineering.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Designing well beyond the stated requirements adds cost and complexity without justification. Better: design for the target, then explain how you'd evolve it if scale grew.

questions.prompt: Amazon's original Dynamo was built so the shopping cart is 'always writable'. Which design choice most directly reflects this?
options: Two-phase commit across all replicas for each write
Leaderless replication with sloppy quorums, accepting writes during failures and reconciling later
Single-leader replication with synchronous followers
Rejecting writes whenever any replica is unreachable
questions.explanation: Dynamo chose availability: any reachable nodes can accept a write (sloppy quorum + hinted handoff), and conflicting versions are reconciled on read. 2PC and strict replica requirements give up availability during failures.

questions.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store, a client sends a PUT to any node. What role does that node play?
options: It acts as coordinator, forwarding the write to the key's N replicas and waiting for W acks
It rejects the request unless it owns the key
It becomes the permanent leader for that key
It stores the value locally and gossips it eventually
questions.explanation: Any node can coordinate: it finds the key's preference list on the ring, sends the write to the N replicas and replies once W acknowledge. There's no per-key leader, and it doesn't rely on gossip to spread data.

questions.prompt: Dynamo uses vector clocks. A read returns two versions whose clocks are [A:2, B:1] and [A:1, B:2]. What does this mean?
options: The versions are concurrent; both are returned as siblings for the client to reconcile
[A:2, B:1] is newer because A has a higher counter
[A:1, B:2] is newer because B was written last
The data is corrupt and must be restored from backup
questions.explanation: Neither clock dominates the other (each is higher in one entry), so the writes were concurrent. Dynamo returns both and the application merges them, e.g. a union of cart items. Comparing a single node's counter is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: Cassandra resolves conflicting writes to the same cell with last-write-wins by timestamp. What's the main risk compared with Dynamo's vector clocks?
options: Concurrent updates are silently lost, and clock skew can drop the truly later write
It requires a central timestamp oracle
Writes are rejected when timestamps are equal
Reads become slower because siblings must be merged
questions.explanation: LWW keeps one value and throws away the rest without telling anyone, and with skewed clocks it can keep the older one. Vector clocks detect concurrency and keep siblings instead, at the cost of pushing merges to the client.

questions.prompt: Which storage engine design do Cassandra and many Dynamo-inspired stores use for write-heavy workloads?
options: B-tree pages updated in place
A single append-only file scanned on every read
An in-memory hash table with no persistence
An LSM tree: commit log + in-memory memtable, flushed to immutable SSTables and compacted
questions.explanation: LSM trees turn random writes into sequential appends (commit log, then memtable flushes) and merge SSTables in the background. Reads may check several SSTables, helped by Bloom filters. B-trees update pages in place, which costs more random I/O on writes.

questions.prompt: In Cassandra, a key is deleted, but a replica that was down during the delete comes back after gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) without repair having run. What can happen?
options: The cluster refuses to start the replica
The delete is automatically re-sent to the replica
Nothing; tombstones live forever
The deleted data reappears ('zombie' resurrection) because the tombstones were already purged elsewhere
questions.explanation: After gc_grace_seconds, compaction can purge tombstones. A replica that missed the delete still has the old value, and with no tombstone left to override it, repair spreads it back. That's why repair must run more often than gc_grace_seconds.

questions.prompt: Designing a distributed key-value store for an interview, you're asked to support values up to 1 MB, about 10 billion keys, and 99.9th percentile reads under 10 ms. Which architecture is most appropriate?
options: A shared NFS volume mounted by all application servers
A single large PostgreSQL instance with a key-value table
Consistent-hashing ring with replication and an LSM-based storage engine on each node
A blockchain ledger for strong auditability
questions.explanation: Partitioning on a ring with replicas spreads 10B keys and load over many machines, and LSM storage handles heavy writes with fast key reads. One Postgres instance won't hold or serve that scale, and NFS or a blockchain can't meet the latency target.

questions.prompt: Which techniques were part of Amazon's original Dynamo design? Select all that apply.
options: Vector clocks for versioning
Merkle trees for anti-entropy
Raft consensus for every write
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes
Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
questions.explanation: The 2007 Dynamo paper combines consistent hashing (with vnodes), vector clocks, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy and gossip-based membership. It avoids consensus on the write path, so no Raft.

questions.prompt: Which consequences come with a Dynamo-style AP design? Select all that apply.
options: Applications may need to merge conflicting versions
Multi-key ACID transactions are provided by default
The system keeps accepting writes during some network partitions
Clients may read stale data
Background repair is needed to converge replicas
questions.explanation: Choosing availability means stale reads, possible conflicts, repair processes, and writes accepted during partitions. Dynamo-style stores don't give multi-key ACID transactions by default; those need coordination.

questions.prompt: In Dynamo, vector clocks can grow large when many different nodes coordinate writes to the same key, so the paper truncates them by dropping the oldest entries past a threshold.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Each coordinating node adds an entry, so the paper keeps a timestamp per entry and drops the oldest once the clock exceeds a size limit (e.g. 10). That can lose causality information, but the paper reports it wasn't a problem in practice.

questions.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store, a GET for a key must always be sent to the node that originally handled the PUT for that key.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Any node can coordinate a GET: it looks up the key's replicas on the ring and queries R of them. There's no fixed owner per write, which is part of what removes single points of failure.

questions.prompt: How does a gossip protocol spread cluster membership information?
options: A central master broadcasts the member list to all nodes
Clients report node status to a registry
Every node sends heartbeats to every other node each second
Each node periodically exchanges state with a few randomly chosen peers
questions.explanation: In gossip, every node regularly picks random peers and swaps what it knows, so information spreads epidemically in roughly O(log N) rounds. All-to-all heartbeats cost O(N^2) messages, and a central master is a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: Why do gossip protocols scale better than all-to-all heartbeating for large clusters?
options: They use UDP instead of TCP
They only detect failures of seed nodes
Each node sends a constant number of messages per round, while information still reaches everyone in about log N rounds
They need no network at all for healthy nodes
questions.explanation: Per-node cost stays fixed (a few peers per round) instead of growing with cluster size, and epidemic spreading still reaches the whole cluster quickly. The transport protocol isn't the reason.

questions.prompt: Cassandra uses a phi accrual failure detector instead of a fixed 'no heartbeat for 5 seconds = dead' rule. What's the advantage?
options: It requires no heartbeats at all
It outputs a suspicion level based on the observed heartbeat interval distribution, adapting to network conditions
It detects failures instantly with zero delay
It guarantees no false positives
questions.explanation: Phi accrual looks at the history of arrival intervals and outputs a continuous suspicion value, which is compared to a threshold (phi_convict_threshold, default 8). It adapts to jittery networks. No failure detector can be perfect in an asynchronous network.

questions.prompt: SWIM-style failure detection: node A pings B and gets no reply. Before declaring B suspect, what does A do?
options: Asks k other nodes to ping B indirectly, in case only the A-B path is broken
Immediately removes B from the ring
Waits for B's next gossip message for up to an hour
Restarts B over SSH
