questions.explanation: Indirect probes through other members separate 'B is down' from 'the link between A and B is flaky', cutting false positives. SWIM then marks B suspect for a while before confirming it dead.

questions.prompt: Why does Dynamo treat a node that's unreachable as temporarily failed rather than removing it from the ring?
options: Removing nodes is impossible with consistent hashing
The ring can only be changed during startup
Most outages are transient, and removing a node triggers expensive data movement
Unreachable nodes still serve reads
questions.explanation: Removing a node reassigns its ranges and streams data around, which is wasteful for a reboot or brief network blip. Dynamo uses hinted handoff for temporary failures and explicit admin commands for permanent membership changes.

questions.prompt: Gossip-based clusters configure a few seed nodes. What are seeds mainly used for?
options: Storing all the data in the cluster
Giving new or restarting nodes an initial contact so they join the same gossip cluster
Acting as the leader for writes
Holding the only copy of the schema
questions.explanation: Seeds are well-known contact points for bootstrapping and help keep the cluster from splitting into separate gossip islands. They aren't leaders and don't hold special data.

questions.prompt: A gossip heartbeat state includes a generation number (set at node startup) plus a heartbeat counter. Why the generation?
options: So peers can tell a restarted node's fresh state from stale state of its previous run
To pick which node becomes leader
To encrypt gossip messages
To count how many keys the node owns
questions.explanation: After a restart, the heartbeat counter resets. A higher generation tells peers this is a new incarnation, so they accept its lower counter instead of treating it as stale. Gossip has no leader and doesn't count keys.

questions.prompt: Which are properties of gossip-based membership? Select all that apply.
options: Robust to message loss because information is re-sent in later rounds
Every node always has an identical, instantly updated view
No single point of failure for membership information
Eventually consistent: nodes may briefly disagree on membership
Bandwidth per node stays roughly constant as the cluster grows
questions.explanation: Gossip is decentralised, redundant and cheap per node, but views converge over time rather than instantly. Instant identical views would need a consensus system like ZooKeeper or etcd.

questions.prompt: A node in a gossip cluster suffers a 20-second GC pause. Which consequences are plausible? Select all that apply.
options: Its data is permanently deleted from the cluster
Coordinators route requests to other replicas, and hints may be stored for it
The whole cluster stops accepting writes
When it resumes, gossip spreads that it's back up
Peers raise its suspicion level and may mark it down
questions.explanation: Missed heartbeats raise suspicion, traffic shifts to other replicas with hints stored, and once it resumes gossip marks it up again. Being marked down doesn't delete data, and other replicas keep serving writes.

questions.prompt: In an asynchronous network, a failure detector can't perfectly tell a crashed node from a very slow one, so timeouts always trade detection speed against false positives.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Without bounded message delays, silence can mean crashed, slow or partitioned. Shorter timeouts catch failures faster but wrongly suspect slow nodes more often, which is why adaptive detectors exist.

questions.prompt: Gossip protocols require every message to be delivered reliably; a single lost message can leave a node permanently unaware of a membership change.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Gossip is redundant by design: the same information is re-sent in later rounds through many paths, so occasional message loss only delays convergence.

questions.prompt: Replica C is down when a write for key K arrives. With hinted handoff, what happens?
options: Another node stores the write with a hint saying it belongs to C, and forwards it when C recovers
The write is stored only in the client's local cache
The write fails until C returns
C's data is permanently reassigned to a new node
questions.explanation: Hinted handoff keeps writes available: a stand-in node holds the data plus a note of its real owner and delivers it when C is back. Ownership isn't permanently reassigned.

questions.prompt: What does read repair do?
options: Rewrites the whole SSTable file on every read
During a read, detects replicas with stale versions and updates them with the newest value
Rebuilds a crashed node from backup
Rejects reads until all replicas agree
questions.explanation: When a read compares replica responses and finds an outdated one, the coordinator writes the newer value back to it. It only fixes keys that are actually read, which is why background anti-entropy is also needed.

questions.prompt: Two replicas each hold 100 million keys in a range and want to find which keys differ. How does a Merkle tree help?
options: It encrypts the data so differences are visible
It sorts the keys so a binary search finds differences
Compare root hashes; if they differ, recurse only into child subtrees whose hashes differ, ending at the differing key ranges
It compresses all keys so both replicas can be sent in full cheaply
questions.explanation: A Merkle tree hashes key ranges hierarchically. Matching hashes mean identical subtrees, so replicas only walk and transfer the parts that differ, keeping repair traffic proportional to the differences, not the data size.

questions.prompt: In Cassandra, a node is down for 5 hours, longer than max_hint_window (default 3 hours). After it returns, what's needed to make it consistent?
options: Nothing; hints are kept indefinitely
Restart the whole cluster
Increase the replication factor
Run anti-entropy repair (e.g. nodetool repair), since hints stopped being stored after the window
questions.explanation: Coordinators stop writing hints for a node once it's been down past the window, so later writes it missed are only fixed by read repair or full repair. Hints aren't kept forever, precisely to bound their storage.

questions.prompt: Why are hinted handoff and read repair alone not enough to guarantee replicas converge?
options: They only work when every replica is up
They both require strong consistency
They only work with range partitioning
Hints can be lost or expire, and read repair only fixes keys that are read
questions.explanation: A stand-in node can die with its hints, hint windows expire, and rarely read keys never trigger read repair. Merkle-tree anti-entropy repair periodically compares full ranges to catch everything else.

questions.prompt: A Merkle tree covers a replica's whole token range, and the data changes constantly. What's a practical challenge?
options: Hash collisions make every comparison fail
Merkle trees can't handle more than 1,000 keys
Building trees requires reading and hashing the data, and ranges change when nodes join or leave, forcing rebuilds
Merkle trees only work in single-leader systems
questions.explanation: Building a Merkle tree means scanning and hashing the data (heavy I/O), and changes to token ownership invalidate the trees. Dynamo noted this cost on node changes. Repairs are scheduled and throttled for this reason.

questions.prompt: Key K's home replicas are A, B and C (N = 3, W = 2, sloppy quorum). B and C are down, so the write is acknowledged by A plus stand-in node D, which holds a hint for B. D then dies permanently before handing off. What's the state of the write?
options: It was never acknowledged, because W counts only home replicas
It exists only on A until repair copies it to B and C, so losing A now would lose it
It's safely on three replicas because the write was acknowledged
It's recovered automatically because gossip spreads D's hints to other nodes
questions.explanation: Sloppy quorum counted D toward W = 2, but D was only a stand-in. With D gone, A holds the sole copy until anti-entropy repair reaches B and C. Hints aren't spread by gossip, so they die with D.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms help a Dynamo-style store converge replicas after failures? Select all that apply.
options: Vector clocks or timestamps to decide which version wins
Two-phase commit on every write
Read repair on keys that are read
Hinted handoff for writes missed during short outages
Merkle-tree-based anti-entropy repair in the background
questions.explanation: Hints, read repair and anti-entropy bring data back to replicas, and versioning decides which value is newest or detects conflicts. 2PC is a different (CP) approach that Dynamo-style stores avoid on the write path.

questions.prompt: A Cassandra cluster shows deleted rows reappearing after a node outage. Which practices prevent this? Select all that apply.
options: Disable hinted handoff entirely
Don't bring back nodes that were down longer than gc_grace_seconds without wiping and rebuilding them
Prefer TTLs over explicit deletes where they fit the data model
Lower gc_grace_seconds to 0 on all tables
Run full repair on every node more often than gc_grace_seconds
questions.explanation: Repair within gc_grace spreads tombstones before they're purged, and long-dead nodes should be rebuilt rather than rejoined. TTL data expires the same on every replica, so fewer explicit deletes means fewer resurrection risks. gc_grace 0 and disabling hints make resurrection more likely.

questions.prompt: If two replicas' Merkle tree root hashes match, the replicas hold identical data for that range (barring hash collisions), so no further comparison is needed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The root hash summarises every key in the range, so matching roots mean the ranges match, and repair can skip it entirely. That's what makes Merkle trees cheap for in-sync replicas.

questions.prompt: Read repair runs on every write so that all replicas stay in sync without any background process.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Read repair runs during reads, when the coordinator notices replicas disagree. Writes rely on replication, hints and background anti-entropy; keys that are never read need anti-entropy repair.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference in what happens to a message after it is consumed in a RabbitMQ classic queue versus a Kafka topic?
options: RabbitMQ removes it once acked; Kafka keeps it until retention or compaction removes it, whoever has read it
Both keep messages forever unless an admin purges them
Both delete the message once any consumer reads it
Kafka deletes it once acked; RabbitMQ keeps it for replay
questions.explanation: A queue is a work list: once a message is acked it's gone. A log is an append-only record; consumers just move an offset, and data expires by time, size or compaction. That is what makes replay and multiple independent readers cheap in Kafka.

questions.prompt: A bug corrupted a read model built from order events over the last 3 days. You want to fix the code and rebuild from the original events. Which messaging model makes this straightforward?
options: Pub/sub over Redis channels
A log/stream with sufficient retention, where you reset the consumer offset
A work queue with competing consumers
A queue with a dead-letter exchange
questions.explanation: Logs keep events after consumption, so a consumer group can rewind its offsets and reprocess. Queues have already deleted acked messages, and Redis Pub/Sub doesn't persist messages at all.

questions.prompt: Billing, analytics and search each need every 'OrderPlaced' event, and each processes at its own pace. How does a log like Kafka handle this compared with a plain queue?
options: All three services must join the same consumer group
Kafka must copy the topic three times, one per service
Each service uses its own consumer group with its own offsets, reading the same data once stored
Logs cannot support more than one reader per topic
questions.explanation: In a log, consumer groups are independent cursors over shared data. With queues you'd need a fan-out (e.g. a RabbitMQ fanout exchange) that copies each message into one queue per service. Joining one group would split events between the services instead.

questions.prompt: A task system needs per-message priorities, per-message delays and routing by header patterns. Which fits more naturally?
options: A log with compaction enabled
An S3 bucket polled every minute
Kafka, since partitions can be prioritized
A traditional broker such as RabbitMQ, with priority queues, TTL/delayed delivery and topic/header exchanges
questions.explanation: RabbitMQ has priority queues, per-message TTL and routing exchanges built in. Kafka partitions have no priority or per-message delay; you'd emulate them with extra topics. Compaction is about keeping the latest value per key, not scheduling.

questions.prompt: Video transcoding jobs take from 5 seconds to 20 minutes. They run on a Kafka topic with 12 partitions, and short jobs often wait behind long ones. What's the underlying issue?
options: The producer is using acks=all
Kafka's retention is too short
Consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count, and each partition is processed in order, so slow jobs block the ones behind them
Kafka cannot store messages larger than 1 KB
questions.explanation: Kafka assigns each partition to one consumer and processes offsets in order, so a long job causes head-of-line blocking. Queues with competing consumers and per-message acks let any idle worker take the next job, which suits uneven task durations.

questions.prompt: A RabbitMQ queue has 5 competing consumers with prefetch 10. Events for the same account must be processed in order. What goes wrong?
options: RabbitMQ rejects messages with the same routing key
Messages for one account can be processed in parallel or out of order across consumers, especially after redelivery
Nothing, since RabbitMQ delivers in FIFO order so processing stays ordered
Prefetch causes messages to be dropped
questions.explanation: Delivery order out of the queue doesn't mean processing order: different consumers finish at different times, and a nacked message is requeued after later ones. Per-key ordering needs partitioning by key, e.g. Kafka keyed partitions or consistent-hash exchanges with one consumer per queue.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Amazon SQS queue types is correct?
options: FIFO queues order messages within a message group and deduplicate within a 5-minute window; standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering
Both types keep messages for up to one year
FIFO queues offer unlimited throughput with no ordering
Standard queues guarantee strict ordering and exactly-once delivery
questions.explanation: SQS Standard offers very high throughput but may deliver duplicates or out of order. FIFO orders per MessageGroupId and deduplicates by deduplication id within 5 minutes. SQS retention is at most 14 days.

questions.prompt: Which are characteristics of a log-based system like Kafka? Select all that apply.
options: The broker tracks an ack state for every individual message
Data is removed by time/size retention or key-based compaction
Consumers track their own position (offset) in the log
Ordering is guaranteed within a partition
questions.explanation: Kafka stores one committed offset per consumer group per partition, not per-message acks. Per-message ack tracking is how queues like RabbitMQ and SQS work. Order is per partition, and retention or compaction controls how long data stays.

questions.prompt: You're adopting event sourcing and want to rebuild new read models from the full history at any time. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Compaction keeps at least the latest record per key, which suits 'current state' topics
A log with long or infinite retention (or compaction for state topics) supports this
A classic work queue suits this, since consumed messages remain available
SQS alone is unsuitable as the event store because retention maxes out at 14 days
questions.explanation: Rebuilding projections requires stored history, so you need logs with long retention or a durable event store. Compaction keeps the latest value per key for state snapshots. Classic queues delete acked messages, so they can't replay history.

questions.prompt: In Kafka, a slow consumer group holds back other consumer groups reading the same topic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each group has its own offsets, and data stays until retention expires, so a slow group only builds its own lag. The real risk is that a very slow group falls behind retention and loses data that expired before it was read.

questions.prompt: RabbitMQ Streams (introduced in RabbitMQ 3.9) provide an append-only, replayable log in which consumers can start from any offset.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Streams are a persistent, replicated log type in RabbitMQ. Reading doesn't remove messages, and consumers can attach at first, last, next, an offset or a timestamp. This blurs the old split between queues and logs.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions. A consumer group scales up to 8 consumers. What happens?
options: Every consumer reads all 6 partitions
Each consumer gets 0.75 partitions on average, so messages are split per record
Kafka automatically adds 2 partitions to the topic
6 consumers get one partition each and 2 sit idle
questions.explanation: Within a group each partition is assigned to at most one consumer, so the partition count caps parallelism. Extra consumers sit idle as hot standbys. Kafka never adds partitions automatically.

questions.prompt: Payment events for each account must be processed in order. How do you achieve this with Kafka?
options: Use the account id as the message key, so the default partitioner sends each account to one partition
Use a topic with a single partition for the whole system
Set acks=all on the producer
Enable log compaction
questions.explanation: Kafka orders records only within a partition. Keying by account id hashes all of an account's events to the same partition, which keeps per-account order and still allows parallelism across accounts. A single partition works but discards all parallelism.

questions.prompt: A keyed topic grows from 12 to 24 partitions. Shortly after, a consumer sees events for one customer out of order. Why?
options: Kafka disables ordering while partitions are being added
The key-to-partition mapping changes for new records, so a customer's new events can land on a different partition from their older, unprocessed ones
Consumer offsets reset to earliest when partitions are added
Adding partitions rewrites existing records into new partitions
questions.explanation: The default partitioner uses hash(key) % numPartitions, so changing the count remaps keys. Old records stay where they were, which allows cross-partition reordering during the transition. That's why keyed topics are sized up front, or migrated to a new topic.

questions.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, and producers use acks=all. Two of the three replicas go down. What happens to writes?
options: They are buffered by the broker until replicas return
Producers get NotEnoughReplicas errors, since the ISR falls below 2
They succeed, acknowledged by the remaining leader
They are written but marked uncommitted
questions.explanation: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 requires at least 2 in-sync replicas to accept a write. With only the leader left, Kafka refuses writes instead of risking data loss. This setup tolerates one replica down for writes.

questions.prompt: A Node consumer uses enable.auto.commit=true and hands messages to async workers without waiting. After a crash, some messages were never processed. Why?
options: The broker's retention expired during the crash
Kafka deletes messages once offsets are committed
Auto-commit may commit offsets for messages that were fetched but not yet processed, so they are skipped on restart
Auto-commit always commits offsets in reverse order
questions.explanation: Auto-commit periodically commits the latest polled position, regardless of whether async processing finished. A crash then skips those messages, giving at-most-once behaviour. Commit manually after processing for at-least-once. Committing offsets doesn't delete data.

questions.prompt: A consumer's batch processing sometimes takes 8 minutes. The group keeps rebalancing and messages are reprocessed. Default max.poll.interval.ms is 300000. What's the most direct fix?
options: Lower max.poll.records (or raise max.poll.interval.ms) so each poll loop finishes in time
Switch to acks=1
Increase session.timeout.ms to 10 minutes
Add more partitions
questions.explanation: If poll() isn't called within max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is considered stuck and evicted, which triggers a rebalance and redelivery. session.timeout.ms covers heartbeats, which run on a background thread, so it doesn't fix slow processing. Smaller batches or a longer interval do.

questions.prompt: What is the trade-off of setting unclean.leader.election.enable=true?
options: Faster rebalances but more duplicates on the consumer side
A partition can stay available by electing an out-of-sync replica, at the cost of losing committed messages
It allows two leaders per partition for higher throughput
Stronger durability at the cost of higher producer latency
questions.explanation: If every in-sync replica is gone, unclean election lets a lagging replica become leader. Writes resume, but messages it never received are lost. The default (false) keeps the partition offline instead, choosing consistency over availability.

questions.prompt: Ops reports 'consumer lag = 2,000,000' for the analytics group on partition 3. What does this number mean?
options: The partition's log-end offset is 2 million ahead of the group's committed offset
The consumer is 2 million milliseconds behind wall clock
2 million messages failed processing
The partition holds 2 million messages in total
questions.explanation: Lag is log-end offset minus committed offset: how many records the group hasn't yet confirmed processing. Lag measured as time is a separate metric that some tools derive. Lag says nothing about failures by itself.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kafka replication are correct? Select all that apply.
options: By default, a new leader is elected only from the ISR
Consumers read only up to the high watermark, the offset replicated to all in-sync replicas
With acks=1 the producer waits for every ISR member to acknowledge
A follower drops out of the ISR if it doesn't catch up within replica.lag.time.max.ms
questions.explanation: With acks=1 only the leader acknowledges, so data can be lost if the leader fails before followers copy it. acks=all waits for the full ISR. The high watermark stops consumers seeing records that could disappear on failover.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kafka log compaction are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It guarantees consumers never see an older value for any key
A record with a null value (tombstone) eventually removes the key, after delete.retention.ms
It retains at least the latest record for each key
Offsets of surviving records are unchanged; compaction does not renumber them
questions.explanation: Compaction runs in the background on closed segments, so the uncompacted head can still hold several values per key, and a consumer may see old ones. It keeps the latest value per key, keeps original offsets (leaving gaps), and tombstones delete keys.

questions.prompt: By default, Kafka consumer groups store committed offsets in the internal __consumer_offsets topic, not in ZooKeeper.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Since Kafka 0.9, offsets have been committed to the compacted __consumer_offsets topic, managed by the group coordinator. ZooKeeper-based offsets are legacy, and Kafka 4.x drops ZooKeeper entirely in favour of KRaft.

questions.prompt: A consumer acks each message as soon as it's received, then processes it. If it crashes mid-processing, which delivery semantics results?
options: Exactly-once
At-least-once
At-most-once
Effectively-once
questions.explanation: Acking first means the broker won't redeliver, so a crash loses the message: at most once. Acking after processing gives at-least-once, since a crash before the ack causes redelivery and possible duplicates.

questions.prompt: A worker sends a welcome email and then acks the message. Sometimes users get two emails. What is the most likely cause?
options: The worker crashed or the ack was lost after sending, so the message was redelivered under at-least-once semantics
The email provider is replaying old requests
The broker is configured for at-most-once delivery
Two different queues hold the same message by design
questions.explanation: Process-then-ack is at-least-once: if the ack never reaches the broker, the message comes back. The fix is idempotency, e.g. record 'welcome sent for user X' or pass an idempotency key to the email provider.

questions.prompt: An SQS consumer takes about 90 seconds per message. The queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What happens?
options: SQS rejects messages that take longer than the timeout
The message is moved straight to the DLQ
SQS waits for the consumer to finish before redelivering
The message becomes visible again after 30 seconds and another consumer processes it concurrently
questions.explanation: After the visibility timeout, SQS assumes the consumer failed and makes the message visible again, which causes duplicate processing. Set the timeout above the processing time or extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility as a heartbeat.

questions.prompt: You dedupe at-least-once deliveries by message id. What is the most robust way to store 'already processed' markers when the side effect is a Postgres write?
options: A processed_messages row with a unique message_id, inserted in the same Postgres transaction as the side effect
A Redis key written after the Postgres transaction commits
A log line that you grep on redelivery
An in-memory Set inside each consumer process
questions.explanation: Writing the marker atomically with the effect means both happen or neither does; a unique constraint also catches concurrent duplicates. Writing Redis after commit leaves a gap where a crash leaves the effect done but unmarked. In-memory sets vanish on restart.

questions.prompt: A Kafka Streams-style app uses transactions to consume, transform and produce. Which downstream consumer setting is required so it doesn't see records from aborted transactions?
options: enable.auto.commit=false
isolation.level=read_committed
acks=all
auto.offset.reset=earliest
questions.explanation: The default isolation.level=read_uncommitted returns records from aborted transactions too. read_committed reads only up to the last stable offset and filters aborted data. acks is a producer setting.

questions.prompt: A Node service publishes to RabbitMQ without publisher confirms, on persistent messages to a durable queue. The broker restarts. What can happen?
options: Messages the publisher thinks it sent can be lost if they weren't yet written to disk; confirms let you retry them
All messages are delivered twice after restart
The broker converts the queue to transient
Nothing is lost, because durable queues and persistent messages are enough
questions.explanation: Without confirms the publisher never learns whether the broker safely stored a message. Confirms (plus retrying unconfirmed messages) give at-least-once publishing, at the cost of possible duplicates, which consumers then deduplicate.

questions.prompt: What does Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true, the default since Kafka 3.0) prevent?
options: Consumers processing the same record twice
Messages being lost when a broker disk fails
Two applications sending identical payloads
Duplicate records in a partition caused by producer retries, detected using a producer id and sequence numbers
questions.explanation: The broker tracks (producer id, partition, sequence) and drops retried batches it has already written. It protects only that producer session's writes; it doesn't stop consumer-side redelivery or deduplicate across different producers.

questions.prompt: In an at-least-once system, which situations lead to duplicate processing? Select all that apply.
options: The consumer acks before starting to process
The ack is lost on the network, so the broker redelivers
The consumer crashes after the side effect but before acking
The producer retries after a timeout although the broker had already stored the message
questions.explanation: Duplicates come from uncertainty: a lost ack or a lost produce response leads to a retry. Acking before processing causes message loss rather than duplicates; that's at-most-once.

questions.prompt: A consumer charges customer cards from Kafka events. Which measures give effectively-once charging? Select all that apply.
options: Increase producer retries so delivery becomes exactly-once
Record processed event ids in a table with a unique constraint
Send a deterministic idempotency key (e.g. the event id) with each payment provider call
Rely on Kafka transactions alone, since they cover external API calls
questions.explanation: External side effects need their own deduplication: idempotency keys stop the provider charging twice, and a unique-keyed record lets you skip redeliveries. Kafka transactions only cover Kafka reads and writes, and more retries add duplicates rather than removing them.

questions.prompt: Kafka Streams can provide exactly-once processing for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: exactly_once_v2 uses transactions to atomically commit output records, state-store changelogs and input offsets. It covers effects within Kafka, while calls to external systems from inside the topology still need idempotency.

questions.prompt: At-most-once delivery is never an acceptable choice for a production system.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For high-volume, low-value data such as metrics samples, telemetry or presence pings, losing an occasional message is fine and avoids the cost of retries and deduplication. The right choice depends on what a lost message costs.

questions.prompt: A message with malformed JSON fails every time it's consumed and is retried forever, blocking the queue. What's the standard remedy?
options: After a bounded number of attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
Delete the whole queue and recreate it
Lower the prefetch count to 1
Increase the consumer's memory
questions.explanation: A poison message will never succeed, so endless retries waste capacity and can block messages behind it. A DLQ isolates it while keeping it for debugging and possible redrive. Prefetch changes throughput but not this failure.

questions.prompt: A downstream API has a 30-second outage. 10,000 clients all retry with pure exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s...) and no jitter. What problem appears when the API recovers?
options: Exponential backoff stops retrying after 30 seconds
Clients retry in synchronized waves that hit the recovering service at the same moments
Retries are spread evenly over time
Clients give up immediately
questions.explanation: Clients that failed together keep retrying together, causing thundering-herd spikes that can knock the service over again. Jitter randomizes each delay to spread the load. Plain backoff stretches out the gaps, but clients stay in lockstep.

questions.prompt: Retries use exponential backoff: retry n waits 1s × 2^(n−1), with no jitter. What is the total waiting time across 5 retries?
options: 16 seconds
32 seconds
31 seconds
63 seconds
questions.explanation: Delays are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 seconds. 16 is only the last delay, and 63 would be the total for 6 retries. Estimates like this help size visibility timeouts and alert thresholds.

questions.prompt: A consumer calls a partner API. Which failure should go straight to the DLQ without retries?
options: 400 Bad Request caused by an invalid field in the message
A connection timeout
429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable
questions.explanation: A 400 caused by the message's content will fail the same way every time, so retrying only adds load and delay. 503, timeouts and 429 are usually transient and worth retrying with backoff (respecting Retry-After for 429).

questions.prompt: A Kafka consumer retries failed messages in place with sleeps of up to 10 minutes. Lag explodes on that partition. What's a common pattern to avoid this, and its main cost?
options: Increase partitions; the cost is higher broker CPU
Use acks=0; the cost is message loss
Republish failures to delayed retry topics (e.g. retry-1m, retry-10m) and then a DLT; the cost is losing strict per-key ordering
Disable retries entirely; the cost is nothing
questions.explanation: Blocking retries stall everything behind the failing record in that partition. Non-blocking retry topics keep the main partition moving, but a failed record is then processed after later records with the same key, so ordering-sensitive flows need extra care.

questions.prompt: A bug sent 50,000 messages to the DLQ. You've deployed a fix and want to redrive them. Which concern is most important?
options: DLQ messages must be re-encrypted before redrive
Redriven messages always lose their payload
Redrive in reverse order to restore causality
Make sure consumers are idempotent and throttle the redrive, since some messages may have been partly processed and a burst can overload dependencies
questions.explanation: Some messages may have had partial side effects before failing, so replay must be safe to repeat; dumping 50k at once can also swamp downstream services. Also watch for stale messages that newer events have superseded. Reversing order doesn't restore causality.

questions.prompt: In Amazon SQS, what decides when a failing message moves to the dead-letter queue?
options: The consumer must explicitly call a SendToDLQ API
The message's retention period
The visibility timeout reaching zero once
The redrive policy's maxReceiveCount: after that many receives without deletion, SQS moves it
questions.explanation: SQS counts receives. When ApproximateReceiveCount exceeds maxReceiveCount, the message goes to the configured DLQ. Each failed attempt is one receive whose visibility timeout expires without a delete.

questions.prompt: When dead-lettering a message, what context is worth attaching so on-call engineers can debug and redrive it? Select all that apply.
options: The last error message or stack trace
The attempt count and first/last failure timestamps
The original payload, unchanged
The source topic/queue (and partition/offset if relevant)
Only the message id, to save space
questions.explanation: Debugging and redriving require the exact payload, why it failed, how often, and where it came from. Storing only an id forces you to reconstruct the message, which may be impossible once the source has expired it.

questions.prompt: Which retry practices help protect a struggling downstream service? Select all that apply.
options: Cap the maximum delay and the number of attempts
Full jitter: sleep a random time between 0 and min(cap, base × 2^attempt)
Retry immediately in a tight loop to minimize latency
Use a retry budget or circuit breaker to stop retries from amplifying an outage
questions.explanation: Jitter spreads load, caps bound the worst case, and budgets or circuit breakers stop retry storms multiplying traffic during an incident. Tight-loop retries are the classic way to turn a partial outage into a full one.

questions.prompt: DLQ depth should be monitored and alerted on, because a growing DLQ usually means a bug or a downstream outage.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A DLQ nobody watches is where data quietly disappears. Alerting on depth or arrival rate surfaces deploy regressions, schema changes and partner outages quickly, before retention deletes the messages.

questions.prompt: Retrying a non-idempotent operation is safe as long as you wait long enough between attempts.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Backoff controls load, not correctness. If the first attempt actually succeeded but its response was lost, any retry repeats the side effect. Non-idempotent operations need idempotency keys or deduplication before retrying them.

questions.prompt: A service commits an order to Postgres and then publishes 'OrderCreated' to Kafka. What happens if the process crashes between the two steps?
options: The event is published twice
Postgres rolls back the order automatically
The order exists but the event is never published, so downstream services never learn about it
Kafka publishes the event from its write-ahead log
questions.explanation: This is the dual-write problem: two systems with no shared transaction. Committing then crashing loses the event; publishing first then failing the commit creates a phantom event. The transactional outbox solves this by writing the event in the same DB transaction.

questions.prompt: How does the transactional outbox pattern ensure an event is published if and only if the business change commits?
options: It retries the Kafka publish inside the DB transaction until it succeeds
It publishes to Kafka first and has consumers write to the DB
It wraps the DB write and the Kafka publish in a 2PC transaction
It inserts the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the change; a separate relay publishes it later
questions.explanation: The outbox row commits or rolls back atomically with the business data. A relay (poller or CDC) then publishes committed rows at least once. No distributed transaction is needed, and nothing slow runs inside the DB transaction.

questions.prompt: Compared with a relay that polls the outbox table every second, what does log-based CDC (e.g. Debezium reading the PostgreSQL WAL) mainly offer?
options: Strict global ordering across all tables
Lower latency and no polling queries on the DB, at the cost of running CDC infrastructure and needing logical replication
Exactly-once delivery to consumers
No need for the outbox table at all in any design
questions.explanation: CDC streams committed changes from the transaction log in near real time, without SELECT polling load. It needs wal_level=logical, a replication slot and a connector to operate. Delivery is still at-least-once, so consumers must deduplicate.

questions.prompt: An outbox relay publishes a row, crashes before marking it as sent, restarts and publishes it again. How should the system cope?
options: Consumers deduplicate using a unique event id carried in each outbox message
Delete outbox rows before publishing them
Use 2PC between the relay and Kafka
Run only one consumer instance
questions.explanation: Outbox relays are inherently at-least-once, since 'publish' and 'mark sent' can't be atomic. Each event has a stable id so consumers can detect repeats. Deleting before publishing turns this into possible event loss.

questions.prompt: Debezium was down for two days over a weekend. On Monday the PostgreSQL primary's disk is nearly full. What is the most likely cause?
options: Debezium writes snapshots to the primary's disk
Autovacuum is disabled on the outbox table
The logical replication slot kept WAL that the absent consumer hadn't confirmed, so WAL piled up
The outbox table has no index
questions.explanation: A replication slot makes PostgreSQL keep WAL until the consumer confirms it, so a stalled consumer causes unbounded WAL growth. Monitor slot lag and set max_slot_wal_keep_size (PostgreSQL 13+) to cap it. An outbox table without vacuum bloats too, but far more slowly than retained WAL.

questions.prompt: To scale a polling outbox relay you run 3 instances, each running SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100. What problem can this introduce?
options: Deadlocks on every poll
SKIP LOCKED makes rows invisible permanently
Postgres rejects concurrent FOR UPDATE queries
Events for the same aggregate can be published out of order, since different instances take different rows
questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED spreads rows across workers without blocking, but two events for the same order may be published by different instances in either order. Partition work by aggregate id or use a single active relay (leader election) when per-aggregate order matters.

questions.prompt: Why not publish the event to Kafka inside the DB transaction, before COMMIT, to avoid the dual-write problem?
options: Postgres forbids network calls inside transactions
It reduces Kafka throughput by half
If the transaction later rolls back, the event is already out: a phantom event for a change that never happened
Kafka rejects messages sent during an open DB transaction
questions.explanation: Publishing before commit just reverses the failure: consumers may act on an order that rolled back. It also holds DB locks during a network call. Postgres doesn't forbid the call, but nothing ties its result to the commit.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, an outbox relay polls with the query below and remembers the highest id it has published. Occasionally an event is never published. Why?
questions.code:
SELECT * FROM outbox
WHERE id > $1   -- last published id
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 100;
options: LIMIT skips rows when there are more than 100
Sequence values are assigned before commit, so a transaction holding a lower id can commit after the relay has moved past it
ORDER BY id is non-deterministic for bigserial columns
PostgreSQL reuses deleted ids
questions.explanation: Transaction A gets id 10, B gets 11; B commits first, the relay publishes 11 and moves its cursor past 10. When A commits, id 10 is never seen. Use a 'published' flag, or CDC, which reads in commit order. LIMIT just pages; the next poll continues.

questions.prompt: Which columns are useful in an outbox table? Select all that apply.
options: A unique event id
The downstream consumer group's committed offset
The serialized event payload
Aggregate type and aggregate id (useful for routing and partition keys)
Created-at timestamp
questions.explanation: The event id enables deduplication, aggregate fields drive topic routing and keys (which keep per-aggregate order), and the payload and timestamp describe the event. Consumer offsets belong to the broker or consumer, not the producer's outbox.

questions.prompt: Comparing CDC directly on business tables with CDC on a dedicated outbox table, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Both avoid the dual-write problem, since events come from committed DB changes
Direct table CDC turns your internal schema into a public contract for consumers
Direct table CDC naturally captures business intent such as 'OrderShipped' vs 'AddressCorrected'
An outbox lets you publish explicit, versioned domain events shaped for consumers
questions.explanation: Row-level CDC emits 'row changed' facts tied to your schema, so renaming a column breaks consumers, and intent is lost: an update to status looks the same whatever the reason. Outbox events are designed contracts. Both read committed data, so both avoid dual writes.

questions.prompt: Debezium's Outbox Event Router transformation can route outbox rows to Kafka topics based on an aggregate type column.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The Outbox Event Router SMT reads outbox inserts, routes by the aggregatetype field (configurable) to topics like outbox.event.<type>, uses the aggregate id as the message key, and passes the payload through as the message value.

questions.prompt: What does 'back-pressure' mean in a data pipeline?
options: A slower downstream stage signalling upstream to slow down or stop sending, so buffers stay bounded
Compressing messages to reduce network usage
Retrying failed messages with increasing delays
Sending acknowledgements back to producers
questions.explanation: Back-pressure is flow control: demand flows upstream so producers never outrun consumers without limit. Retries with backoff are a different mechanism, although both involve slowing down.

questions.prompt: In Node.js, writable.write(chunk) returns false. What should well-behaved code do?
options: Call writable.end() and open a new stream
Stop writing and resume after the stream emits 'drain'
Retry the same chunk immediately
Throw an error because the write failed
questions.explanation: false means the internal buffer has reached highWaterMark; the chunk was still accepted. Keep writing anyway and memory grows without limit. Wait for 'drain', or use pipeline(), which handles this for you.

questions.prompt: An ingestion service pushes incoming webhooks into an in-memory array that workers drain. During a traffic spike, the pod gets OOM-killed. What's the best structural fix?
options: Give the pod more memory
Use a Map instead of an array
Use a bounded queue: when full, slow intake (e.g. respond 429/503) or persist to a durable broker
Process items in LIFO order
questions.explanation: An unbounded buffer only delays failure. A bounded buffer forces a decision when full: push back, shed load, or move to durable storage such as a broker. More memory buys time but doesn't change the failure mode.

questions.prompt: Why do pull-based consumers, as in Kafka, provide natural back-pressure compared with brokers that push without limits?
options: Pull is always faster than push
Pull consumers fetch only when ready, so a slow consumer builds lag in the durable log instead of piling up messages in its memory
Pull consumers never need to commit offsets
Brokers that push cannot persist messages
questions.explanation: With pull, the consumer sets the pace and the excess stays in the broker's storage as lag. Push systems need explicit limits (e.g. RabbitMQ prefetch) or they can flood consumers. Pull isn't inherently faster.

questions.prompt: An API's p99 latency climbs to 30 s under overload, and most requests time out on the client anyway. What's the better server-side strategy?
options: Accept every request and add more worker threads
Queue requests on disk and answer them hours later
Increase client timeouts to 60 seconds
Reject excess requests early with 503/429 when queue depth or queueing time exceeds a threshold, prioritizing critical traffic
questions.explanation: Work for requests whose clients have already given up is wasted and delays everyone else. Load shedding keeps latency bounded for accepted requests. Longer timeouts only lengthen the queue, and unbounded workers add contention.

questions.prompt: This script copies a 20 GB file and its memory use climbs to several GB. Why?
options: createReadStream loads the whole file before emitting 'data'
The 'end' handler runs before any data is written
fs streams default to a 1 GB highWaterMark
Disk writes are slower than reads and write()'s false return value is ignored, so chunks pile up in dst's buffer
questions.explanation: The reader keeps emitting while the writer's buffer grows, since nobody pauses src when write() returns false. Use pipeline(src, dst) or src.pipe(dst), which pause and resume on 'drain'. The default highWaterMark is 64 KiB for fs read streams.

questions.prompt: A job calls await Promise.all(userIds.map(id => fetchProfile(id))) with 1,000,000 ids against a partner API. What's the main problem?
options: Promise.all cannot handle more than 65,536 promises
All requests start at once: unbounded concurrency exhausts sockets and memory and floods the partner
Promise.all runs the requests one after another, which is slow
fetchProfile results come back in random order
questions.explanation: map() starts every call immediately; Promise.all only waits for them. Use bounded concurrency (a worker pool, p-limit, or batching) so in-flight requests stay capped. Promise.all preserves result order and has no 65,536 limit.

questions.prompt: Which are legitimate strategies when a producer outpaces a consumer? Select all that apply.
options: Block or pause the producer until there's capacity
Grow the in-memory buffer without limit
Rate-limit the producer
Buffer in a bounded queue
Drop or sample excess data where loss is acceptable
questions.explanation: The classic options are buffer (bounded), drop, block, or control the producer's rate. An unbounded buffer just postpones the problem until the process runs out of memory, so it isn't a strategy.

questions.prompt: A Node.js Kafka consumer calls a slow downstream API for each message. Which techniques apply back-pressure correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Fetch as fast as possible into an in-memory array and process it later
Cap the number of concurrent in-flight messages per partition or per consumer
Scale consumers up to the partition count to add throughput
Pause partitions when in-flight work exceeds a limit, and resume as it drains
questions.explanation: Pausing fetches and bounding concurrency keep memory flat and let lag build in Kafka, where it's durable. Adding consumers up to the partition count increases throughput. Draining the broker into RAM removes the back-pressure that pull-based consumption provides.

questions.prompt: Node's stream.pipeline() handles back-pressure between stages and also forwards errors and cleans up every stream in the chain.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: pipeline() (or its promise form in stream/promises) wires up back-pressure like pipe(), and also destroys every stream and reports the error if any stage fails. Plain .pipe() doesn't forward errors, so streams can leak.

questions.prompt: TCP has no built-in back-pressure, so applications must implement all flow control themselves.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: TCP's receive window is flow control: a slow receiver shrinks the window and the sender's writes eventually block or buffer. Node surfaces this as socket.write() returning false. Applications still need back-pressure at higher levels, such as queues and worker pools.

questions.prompt: A 6-engineer startup with one product and unclear domain boundaries asks whether to start with microservices. What is the most defensible recommendation?
options: Start with microservices so each feature can scale independently from day one
Start with serverless functions per endpoint to avoid any shared deployment
Start with a monolith with no internal structure, since boundaries can be added during extraction
Start with a modular monolith with clear internal module boundaries, and extract services later when a real need appears
questions.explanation: With a small team and unstable boundaries, a modular monolith keeps one deploy and in-process calls while enforcing module boundaries, making later extraction cheap. Starting with microservices pays the distributed-systems tax (network failures, distributed data, ops) before boundaries are known, and wrong boundaries are expensive to move.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a modular monolith from a plain ("big ball of mud") monolith?
options: It is deployed as several processes that share one database
Modules expose explicit interfaces and own their data; other modules cannot reach into their internals or tables
It uses a message broker for every call between modules
It runs each module in its own container but in the same pod
questions.explanation: A modular monolith is still one deployable unit, but code is split into modules with enforced public APIs and private internals (often private schemas/tables). Multiple processes or containers would make it a distributed system; a broker for every in-process call is unnecessary overhead.

questions.prompt: A team split its monolith into 12 services, but every feature still requires coordinated releases of 4-5 services, and they all read the same database tables. What anti-pattern is this?
options: A distributed monolith
A modular monolith
Event sourcing
A service mesh
questions.explanation: Lockstep deploys plus a shared database means the services are tightly coupled: you have the operational cost of microservices without independent deployability, i.e. a distributed monolith. A modular monolith is a single deployable, which is the opposite situation.

questions.prompt: Which signal is the strongest reason to extract a module from a monolith into its own service?
options: The module has the most lines of code in the repository
The module could be rewritten in a more fashionable language
The module has very different scaling or release needs, and a separate team owns it end to end
A new engineer finds the module hard to read
questions.explanation: Extraction pays off when it buys independent scaling, independent deploys or team autonomy. Code size or readability are solved by refactoring inside the monolith; extracting a hard-to-read module just makes it a hard-to-read service behind a network call.

questions.prompt: Conway's Law is often cited in microservice discussions. What does it predict?
options: System structure tends to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds it
Service count should grow logarithmically with request volume
Each service should be small enough to be rewritten in two weeks
Latency grows linearly with the number of network hops
questions.explanation: Conway's Law says systems mirror the organisation's communication structure, so service boundaries tend to follow team boundaries (the 'inverse Conway manoeuvre' shapes teams to get the architecture you want). The two-week rewrite idea is a sizing heuristic, not Conway's Law.

questions.prompt: You are migrating a legacy monolith incrementally. Which approach is the strangler fig pattern?
options: Freeze the monolith, rewrite everything as services, then cut over in one release
Put a routing layer in front, move one capability at a time to a new service, and route its traffic there until the monolith is empty
Run the monolith and the new system in parallel on all traffic and compare results forever
Copy the monolith's database into each new service and keep them in sync with triggers
questions.explanation: The strangler fig routes traffic through a facade and moves capabilities piece by piece, so each step is small and reversible. A big-bang rewrite is the high-risk alternative it avoids; shadow comparison is a useful verification tool but not the migration pattern itself.

questions.prompt: In a modular monolith (Node.js, one PostgreSQL database), the Orders module directly runs SQL joins against the Billing module's tables. What is the main long-term risk?
options: Billing cannot change its schema without breaking Orders, and later extracting Billing into a service requires untangling hidden data coupling
The Node.js event loop will block on cross-module joins
PostgreSQL does not allow joins across tables owned by different code modules
Joins across modules are slower than calling a REST API
questions.explanation: Reaching into another module's tables creates implicit coupling: schema changes ripple, and extraction becomes a data-migration project. The join itself is fast and legal in PostgreSQL; the problem is ownership, not performance.

questions.prompt: Which costs do you take on when moving from a monolith to microservices? Select all that apply.
options: Inability to use different languages per component
More operational surface: deploy pipelines, monitoring and tracing per service
Loss of the ability to scale any component horizontally
Cross-service consistency without local ACID transactions
Partial failures and network latency between components
questions.explanation: Microservices add network failure modes, distributed consistency problems (sagas, outbox) and operational overhead. They do not remove horizontal scaling (they make it more granular) and they enable, not prevent, polyglot stacks.

questions.prompt: Which practices help keep module boundaries honest inside a modular monolith? Select all that apply.
options: One database schema (or table prefix) per module, accessed only by that module
Lint or build rules that forbid importing another module's internal files
Communicating between modules through public interfaces or in-process domain events
Letting any module read any table to avoid duplicating queries
A single shared 'utils' module that every module may put domain logic into
questions.explanation: Enforced import rules, per-module data ownership and public interfaces/events keep coupling explicit. A shared domain 'utils' dumping ground and unrestricted table access are exactly how modular monoliths decay into a big ball of mud.

questions.prompt: Microservices generally reduce end-to-end request latency compared with an equivalent monolith, because each service is smaller.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. In-process calls become network calls with serialization, so a request that fans across services usually gets slower, not faster. The benefits of microservices are independent deployment, scaling and ownership, not lower per-request latency.

questions.prompt: A modular monolith can still be scaled horizontally by running many identical instances behind a load balancer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A stateless monolith scales out like any service; the limitation is that you scale all modules together rather than only the hot one. That coarse-grained scaling, not an inability to scale, is the usual trade-off.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility belongs in an API gateway rather than inside each microservice?
options: Persisting user profiles to the profile service's database
Business validation of an order's line items
Calculating tax for an invoice
Edge concerns such as TLS termination, authentication of the token, rate limiting and routing
questions.explanation: Gateways handle cross-cutting edge concerns once, so every service does not re-implement them. Domain logic like validation or tax rules belongs in the owning service; putting it in the gateway turns the gateway into a coupled, hard-to-change bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Your mobile app needs a compact payload aggregated from 4 services, while the web dashboard needs richer data in a different shape. Which pattern fits best?
options: Add mobile-specific fields to every downstream service's API
One generic gateway endpoint returning every field so each client filters locally
Let each client call the 4 services directly from the device
Backend for Frontend (BFF): a thin backend per client type that aggregates and shapes responses
questions.explanation: A BFF per client lets each frontend team shape and aggregate data for its needs, cutting round trips on mobile. A generic over-fetching endpoint wastes mobile bandwidth, and pushing client-specific fields into every service couples domain services to UI concerns.

questions.prompt: After adding an API gateway, the team keeps adding request transformations, business rules and orchestration logic to it. What is the main risk?
options: Rate limiting will stop working
Clients will need to use gRPC
The gateway will stop supporting HTTP/2
The gateway becomes a shared bottleneck owned by one team, coupling all services and slowing every release
questions.explanation: A 'smart' gateway accumulates domain logic that every team must change through one owner, recreating a monolith at the edge. Keep the gateway thin (routing, auth, limits) and put aggregation in BFFs or services.

questions.prompt: A BFF aggregates calls to Profile, Orders and Recommendations for a home screen. Recommendations is slow and sometimes fails. What should the BFF do?
options: Call the three services sequentially and fail the whole response if any fails
Cache the entire home screen for all users for 24 hours
Retry Recommendations indefinitely until it succeeds
Call them in parallel with per-call timeouts and return a partial response (e.g. empty recommendations) if the non-critical call fails
questions.explanation: Parallel calls bound latency to the slowest call, timeouts cap that, and graceful degradation keeps the screen usable when a non-critical dependency fails. Failing everything amplifies one outage; infinite retries pile up load and latency.

questions.prompt: Where should JWT signature verification typically happen in a gateway-fronted architecture, and what should services still do?
options: Only in the gateway; services should trust any request on the internal network
At the gateway to reject bad tokens early, while services still enforce authorization on the identity/claims they receive
In the client; the server only checks the token exists
Only in each service; the gateway should forward tokens untouched
questions.explanation: Verifying at the edge rejects junk cheaply, but services must still authorize actions (does this user own this order?) and should not blindly trust the network (zero-trust, mTLS or re-verification). Trusting everything internal means one compromised pod can impersonate anyone.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between an API gateway and a load balancer?
options: A gateway works only at layer 4, while a load balancer works only at layer 7
A load balancer authenticates users, while a gateway only distributes traffic
A load balancer distributes traffic across instances of a service; a gateway adds API-aware routing across many services plus auth, quotas and transformations
They are identical; 'gateway' is the cloud vendor marketing term
questions.explanation: Load balancers spread traffic across replicas (L4 or L7). Gateways are API-aware: path-to-service routing, auth, rate limits, request shaping. Gateways often sit behind or include a load balancer, but they are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: An API gateway is the single entry point for all traffic. What design choice best avoids it becoming a single point of failure?
options: Run exactly one large gateway instance with lots of memory
Store sessions in gateway memory so failover is faster
Let clients bypass the gateway when it is slow
Run multiple stateless gateway instances across zones behind a load balancer, keeping shared state like rate-limit counters in an external store
questions.explanation: Stateless replicas across availability zones remove the single point of failure; shared state (rate-limit counters) lives in something like Redis. In-memory sessions make instances non-interchangeable, and a single big instance is still a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: Which are good reasons to introduce a BFF layer? Select all that apply.
options: Reducing chatty round trips from mobile devices over slow networks
Letting the frontend team own the API contract their UI consumes
Centralising all business rules for every client in one place
Replacing the domain services' databases
Different clients need differently shaped or aggregated data
questions.explanation: BFFs exist to tailor APIs per client, reduce round trips and give frontend teams ownership. They should not own domain data or become the home of all business rules; that logic stays in domain services so BFFs remain thin.

questions.prompt: Your gateway adds 40 ms p99 latency after a new plugin rollout. Which are reasonable things to investigate? Select all that apply.
options: The browser's DNS cache on end-user devices
Large request/response body transformations buffering whole payloads
Gateway instances CPU-saturated during peaks
Connection reuse to upstreams being disabled, causing a new TCP/TLS handshake per request
A plugin making a synchronous network call (e.g. token introspection) per request without caching
questions.explanation: Uncached introspection calls, buffering transforms, lost keep-alive to upstreams and CPU saturation all add latency inside the gateway. End-user DNS caching affects connection setup to your edge, not latency that appeared inside the gateway after a plugin change.

questions.prompt: Using a BFF means each client type gets its own backend, so it is acceptable for BFFs to duplicate some aggregation code across clients.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Some duplication across BFFs is an accepted trade-off for independent evolution per client. If shared logic grows, move it into a domain service or library rather than merging BFFs back into one general-purpose API.

questions.prompt: Rate limiting at the API gateway removes the need for any overload protection inside downstream services.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Internal callers, batch jobs and other services bypass edge limits, and a gateway quota cannot know a service's real capacity at a given moment. Services still need their own load shedding, timeouts and concurrency limits.

questions.prompt: Why do microservices need service discovery instead of hard-coding IP addresses?
options: Hard-coded IPs are slower to connect to than hostnames
Service discovery encrypts traffic between services
Instances are created, rescheduled and scaled dynamically, so their addresses change constantly
IP addresses cannot be used over HTTP/2
questions.explanation: In autoscaled or containerised environments, instances come and go and get new addresses, so callers need a registry or DNS name that tracks healthy instances. Discovery is about location, not encryption or protocol support.

questions.prompt: In client-side discovery, what does the calling service do?
options: Asks the DNS server for a single static IP that never changes
Queries a service registry for healthy instances and picks one itself using a load-balancing strategy
Sends all requests to a central load balancer that picks an instance
Broadcasts the request to every instance and takes the first reply
questions.explanation: Client-side discovery puts the registry lookup and load-balancing choice in the caller (often via a library). Sending everything to a central load balancer that picks an instance is server-side discovery.

questions.prompt: In Kubernetes, how does a pod typically reach another service named `orders` in the same namespace?
options: By calling the DNS name `orders` (or `orders.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`), which resolves to the Service's stable virtual IP
By reading the target pod IPs from a ConfigMap updated by hand
By using the node's public IP and a NodePort for every internal call
By querying etcd directly from application code
questions.explanation: A Kubernetes Service gets a stable cluster IP and DNS name; kube-proxy (or the CNI) routes to ready pod endpoints. Applications should not query etcd directly, and NodePorts are for external exposure, not routine internal calls.

questions.prompt: After a deployment, some requests still go to terminated instances for ~30 seconds. Discovery is DNS-based. What is the most likely cause?
options: TLS certificates were rotated during the deploy
Clients or resolvers are caching DNS answers longer than the instances live (TTL/client caching)
The new instances failed their readiness probe
The load balancer is using round robin instead of least connections
questions.explanation: DNS answers are cached by resolvers and often by client runtimes or connection pools, so stale addresses linger after instances disappear. Failing readiness would remove new instances, not keep old ones; the balancing algorithm does not resurrect dead endpoints.

questions.prompt: A service registry uses heartbeats with a 30 s timeout to mark instances dead. An instance freezes in a long GC pause. What happens in the meantime?
options: Callers automatically skip it because TCP detects the pause
It stays listed as healthy for up to 30 s, so callers may send requests that time out unless they have their own timeouts and retries
The registry removes it immediately because the process is unresponsive
The registry restarts the process
questions.explanation: Heartbeat-based health is only as fresh as its timeout; during that window callers keep routing to the frozen instance. That is why callers need timeouts, retries to other instances and outlier detection rather than trusting the registry alone. Registries generally do not restart processes.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a Kubernetes liveness probe and a readiness probe, in terms of discovery?
options: Both restart the container; they differ only in timing
Liveness is for HTTP services and readiness is for TCP services
Readiness failure restarts the container; liveness failure removes it from Service endpoints
Readiness failure removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it; liveness failure restarts the container
questions.explanation: Readiness controls whether the pod receives traffic (it is removed from endpoints while not ready). Liveness decides if the container is broken and must be restarted. Confusing them causes restart loops or traffic to pods that are still warming up.

questions.prompt: A readiness probe checks the pod's database AND three downstream services. One downstream has an outage. What happens, and why is it a problem?
options: Only one pod is removed, so capacity drops slightly
Kubernetes automatically routes traffic to the downstream service's pods instead
Every pod becomes not-ready at once, all are removed from endpoints, and a partial dependency outage becomes a total outage of this service
Nothing; readiness probes ignore downstream failures
questions.explanation: Because all replicas share the same dependency, a deep readiness check fails everywhere at once and the Service has zero endpoints, turning a degraded state into a hard outage. Keep probes about the pod's own ability to serve and handle dependency failures with circuit breakers and degradation.

questions.prompt: Which are server-side (or platform-side) discovery mechanisms, where the caller does not choose the instance itself? Select all that apply.
options: An application library that reads instances from Consul and does round robin in-process
A service mesh sidecar proxy that resolves and balances on the app's behalf
A Kubernetes ClusterIP Service routed by kube-proxy
A cloud load balancer in front of an autoscaling group
questions.explanation: Load balancers, kube-proxy Services and sidecar proxies all choose the instance outside the application code. An in-process library that reads from Consul and balances is classic client-side discovery.

questions.prompt: You run a self-hosted service registry. Which properties matter most for it? Select all that apply.
options: High availability, since every service depends on it to find others
Storing large business payloads alongside instance records
Health checking so dead instances are removed
Callers caching the last known instance list so a short registry outage does not stop traffic
Strong ACID transactions across all registered services
questions.explanation: The registry is critical infrastructure, so it must be highly available, health-check instances, and callers should keep a cached view to survive brief outages. Multi-record ACID transactions and business payloads are not what a registry is for.

questions.prompt: In a Kubernetes cluster, a headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns the individual pod IPs from DNS instead of a single virtual IP.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Headless Services publish A records for each ready pod, which is useful for client-side balancing or stateful sets that need stable per-pod identities. A normal Service returns one cluster IP and lets kube-proxy balance.

questions.prompt: Once a service registry marks an instance healthy, callers can safely skip timeouts on requests to it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Health status is periodic and can be stale; an instance can hang, pause or overload between checks. Every remote call still needs a timeout, and ideally retries to a different instance.

questions.prompt: What problem does a circuit breaker primarily solve?
options: It encrypts traffic between two services
It stops sending calls to a dependency that is failing, failing fast instead of piling up waiting requests, and probes for recovery later
It balances requests across healthy instances
It guarantees every request is eventually delivered
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker opens after a failure threshold, fails calls immediately (or uses a fallback), then lets trial requests through in half-open state. It protects the caller's resources and gives the dependency room to recover; it is not about delivery guarantees or balancing.

questions.prompt: A circuit breaker is in the half-open state. What happens next?
options: Requests are queued until the dependency recovers
All traffic flows normally until the next failure
A limited number of trial requests are allowed; success closes the circuit, failure re-opens it
All calls are rejected until an operator resets it
questions.explanation: Half-open lets a few probe requests through to test recovery. If they succeed the breaker closes; if they fail it re-opens for another cool-down. Sending all traffic at once could knock a recovering service back over.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service calls a payment API with no timeout. The payment API starts hanging. What is the most likely effect on the Node.js service?
options: The OS kills the process for having too many sockets
Nothing; Node.js drops hung requests automatically after 5 seconds
Incoming requests pile up waiting on open sockets, memory and connection pools are exhausted, and the service itself becomes unresponsive
The event loop blocks completely on the first hung call
questions.explanation: Without a timeout, each request holds a socket, memory and often a pooled connection while waiting, so the backlog grows until the service fails too (cascading failure). The event loop is not blocked by awaiting I/O, and Node's fetch/http have no short default deadline that saves you.

questions.prompt: Service A calls B, which calls C. Each layer retries failed calls 3 times (4 attempts total). C goes down. How many attempts can hit C for one user request to A?
questions.explanation: Retries multiply across layers: A makes 4 attempts to B, and each of those makes 4 attempts to C, so 4 × 4 = 16 calls to C. This retry amplification is why you retry at one layer only, use retry budgets, and back off.

questions.prompt: Why should retries use exponential backoff with jitter rather than a fixed delay?
options: Exponential backoff is required by the HTTP specification
Jitter guarantees idempotency of the retried request
Fixed delays cause clients that failed together to retry together, creating synchronized load spikes; jitter spreads them out
Jitter makes each individual retry succeed faster
questions.explanation: When many clients fail at the same moment, fixed or pure exponential delays keep them in lockstep, hammering the recovering service in waves (thundering herd). Randomized jitter de-synchronizes them. Jitter does nothing for idempotency.

questions.prompt: What does the bulkhead pattern do?
options: Isolates resources (thread pools, connection pools, concurrency limits) per dependency so one slow dependency cannot exhaust resources needed by others
Splits a database into shards by tenant
Caches responses at the edge to absorb traffic spikes
Retries a call against a different region when the primary fails
questions.explanation: Like watertight compartments in a ship, bulkheads give each dependency its own bounded pool so a hang in one only exhausts its own compartment. Regional failover and sharding are different resilience/scaling techniques.

questions.prompt: A user-facing request has an 800 ms budget. The gateway calls service A, which calls B. How should timeouts be set?
options: Give every hop a generous 30 s timeout so nothing fails spuriously
Propagate a deadline: each hop uses the remaining budget minus its own work, so inner timeouts are shorter than outer ones
Give B a longer timeout than A so the deepest call has the most time
Use no timeouts and rely on circuit breakers
questions.explanation: Deadline propagation ensures inner calls give up before the outer caller has already abandoned the request; otherwise B keeps doing work nobody will use. Inner timeouts longer than outer ones waste capacity, and circuit breakers need timeouts to detect slow failures at all.

questions.prompt: You add automatic retries to a `POST /payments` call on timeout. Customers report double charges. What is the correct fix?
options: Increase the timeout so retries are rarer
Send an idempotency key with each logical payment so the server deduplicates retried attempts
Retry only on HTTP 500 instead of timeouts
Stop retrying any POST request ever
questions.explanation: A timeout does not mean the payment failed; it may have succeeded with the response lost. An idempotency key lets the server return the original result for a retried attempt. Longer timeouts only reduce frequency, and a 500 can also occur after the side effect happened.

questions.prompt: Which errors are generally safe and sensible to retry (assuming the operation is idempotent)? Select all that apply.
options: HTTP 401 Unauthorized due to an invalid token
HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
HTTP 400 Bad Request from a validation failure
Connection refused / connection reset
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, honouring Retry-After
questions.explanation: Transient network errors, 503 and 429 (with backoff/Retry-After) may succeed later. 400 and 401 are deterministic client errors: retrying the same request will fail the same way and just adds load.

questions.prompt: A dependency's latency spikes and the caller's circuit breaker never opens. Which could explain it? Select all that apply.
options: The failure-rate threshold uses a minimum request volume that low traffic never reaches
The dependency returns 200 with an error payload that the breaker treats as success
The breaker only counts errors, and the slow calls eventually succeed, so no failures are recorded
The breaker is configured with a half-open state
The caller has no timeout, so slow calls never become failures
questions.explanation: Breakers only react to what they count: slow-but-successful calls, missing timeouts, unmet minimum-volume thresholds and errors hidden inside 200 responses all keep it closed. Having a half-open state is normal and does not stop it from opening.

questions.prompt: Retries are a safe default for any failed call as long as you use exponential backoff.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Backoff controls timing, but retries are only safe for idempotent operations (or with idempotency keys), and they must be bounded and done at one layer to avoid amplification. Non-idempotent retries can double-charge or double-send.

questions.prompt: What does 'database per service' mean in microservices?
options: Each service runs its own physical database server
Each service must use a different database engine
Each service owns its data, and other services access it only through that service's API or events, never by querying its tables
Every service keeps a full copy of every other service's data
questions.explanation: The principle is ownership and encapsulation: only the owner reads and writes its tables. Services may share a physical server or engine (separate schemas), and full copies of everything would defeat ownership.

questions.prompt: An order needs to reserve stock (Inventory service) and charge a card (Payments service). Distributed 2PC is not an option. Which pattern coordinates this?
