Keep a balance column updated in the same DB transaction that inserts the entries, and periodically verify it against the sum of entries
questions.explanation: Updating the materialized balance atomically with the entries keeps reads O(1) and consistent, and periodic checks against the entries catch drift. Deleting entries loses auditability, and nightly-only updates show stale balances that allow overspending.

questions.prompt: Which are properties of a well-designed payments ledger? Select all that apply.
options: Each entry links to the transaction it belongs to
Entries older than a month are deleted once balances are cached
Amounts are integer minor units with an explicit currency
Amounts use floating point for extra precision
Entries are append-only and never updated in place
questions.explanation: Immutability, traceability and exact amounts are core. Floats introduce rounding errors, and deleting entries breaks audits, reconciliation and point-in-time balance queries.

questions.prompt: Which operations need explicit idempotency protection (keys or dedup IDs)? Select all that apply.
options: GET /charges/:id to read a charge
A consumer handling 'payment.succeeded' events from a queue
POST /charges to create a charge
POST /refunds to create a refund
questions.explanation: Anything that creates side effects and may be retried (client retries, at-least-once queues) must deduplicate. GET is safe by HTTP semantics: repeating it changes nothing, so it needs no key.

questions.prompt: Under HTTP semantics, PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent, while POST is not.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True (RFC 9110). Repeating a PUT or DELETE has the same intended effect as doing it once. POST may create a new resource each time, which is why payment APIs add idempotency keys to POST.

questions.prompt: It is safe to record the idempotency key only after the call to the payment processor returns.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. If two requests race, or the server crashes after charging but before saving, a retry finds no key and charges again. Claim the key, with an in-progress status, before calling the processor, then store the final response.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of payment reconciliation?
options: Retrying failed webhook deliveries
Converting all amounts into a single currency
Comparing the internal ledger against PSP/bank settlement reports to find and resolve mismatches
Generating invoices for customers
questions.explanation: Reconciliation is the safety net. It matches each internal record to the external record (processor reports, bank statements) and flags missing, duplicated or mismatched transactions. Webhooks are real-time and can be lost; reconciliation catches what they miss.

questions.prompt: Which webhook receiver design is most robust?
options: Return 500 for events you don't recognize so the provider stops sending them
Return 200 immediately without verifying, then verify later
Process everything synchronously, then return 200 when all side effects finish
Verify the signature, persist the event, return 2xx quickly, and process it asynchronously
questions.explanation: Fast acknowledgment avoids provider timeouts and retries, and persisting first means nothing is lost if processing fails. Skipping verification lets anyone forge events, and returning 500 for unknown types causes endless retries.

questions.prompt: Your handler receives 'charge.refunded' before 'charge.succeeded' for the same charge. How should it cope?
options: Discard the refund event because it arrived out of order
Sleep for 30 seconds and hope the earlier event arrives
Don't assume ordering: use the event's object state or version, or fetch the latest object from the provider's API, before acting
Ask the provider to resend all events in order
questions.explanation: Providers don't guarantee delivery order. Treat events as hints, reconcile against the current object (or compare versions/timestamps), and make transitions monotonic. Dropping the refund risks never recording it.

questions.prompt: The provider delivers the same webhook event twice. What is the standard guard?
options: Process both; the second will usually fail anyway
Rate-limit the provider's IP addresses
Compare the payload byte-for-byte with the previous event
Record processed event IDs under a unique constraint and skip IDs already seen
questions.explanation: Webhooks are at-least-once. Dedupe on the provider's event ID, ideally in the same transaction as the side effect. Byte comparison breaks if the provider adds a delivery-attempt field.

questions.prompt: Why do webhook signature schemes (e.g. Stripe's) include a timestamp in the signed payload, with receivers rejecting old timestamps?
options: To prevent replay attacks where a captured valid request is resent later
To let receivers sort events by time
To make the HMAC computation faster
Because HTTP requires a Date header to be signed
questions.explanation: A signature alone proves authenticity but not freshness, so an attacker who captured one valid request could replay it forever. Signing the timestamp and enforcing a tolerance window (Stripe's libraries default to 5 minutes) blocks that. It isn't meant for ordering.

questions.prompt: An Express app verifies webhook HMACs, but valid events keep failing verification. What is the most likely bug?
options: express.json() rejects webhook content types
Header names are case-sensitive in Express
The HMAC is computed over re-serialized JSON instead of the exact raw request bytes
The secret must be base64-decoded before every request
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body)) can change whitespace, key order or number formatting, so the bytes differ from what the sender signed. Capture the raw body (e.g. express.raw() on that route) and use a timing-safe comparison. req.get() is case-insensitive.

questions.prompt: Reconciliation finds a charge in the processor's settlement report with no matching entry in your ledger. What failure most likely caused it?
options: The customer's bank reversed the charge
The processor double-counted the charge
Settlement reports always include test-mode charges
Your service crashed after the processor charged the card but before the ledger write, and the webhook was missed
questions.explanation: This is the dual-write gap between an external call and a local commit. The fix is to record a PENDING ledger intent before calling the processor, then resolve it from the response, a webhook or reconciliation. A reversal would appear as an extra debit, not a missing charge.

questions.prompt: You are building a platform that SENDS webhooks to merchants. Which practices should you adopt? Select all that apply.
options: Guarantee strict global ordering of events to every endpoint
Retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff
Include a unique event ID for receiver-side deduplication
Promise exactly-once delivery
Sign each payload so receivers can verify it
questions.explanation: Backoff retries, signatures and event IDs are standard (Stripe, GitHub). Global ordering and exactly-once delivery over HTTP to arbitrary receivers aren't achievable. Document at-least-once, unordered delivery instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine reconciliation breaks that need investigation? Select all that apply.
options: A webhook that was delivered twice and correctly deduplicated
Same charge ID with different amounts or currencies in each
Charge exists in the ledger but not in the processor report
Charge exists in the processor report but not in the ledger
questions.explanation: Missing-on-either-side and amount mismatches mean money is unaccounted for. A duplicate webhook that was deduplicated produced one ledger record that matches the report, so there's nothing to reconcile.

questions.prompt: If a webhook endpoint returns 200 only after a slow 30-second downstream call, the provider may time out and retry, causing duplicate processing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Providers enforce short delivery timeouts and treat a timeout as failure, so the same event comes back while the first is still processing. Acknowledge fast and queue the work.

questions.prompt: Comparing an expected HMAC signature with `===` is fine; constant-time comparison only matters for password hashes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A short-circuiting compare leaks how many leading bytes matched through timing, which can help forge signatures. In Node, use crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length Buffers.

questions.prompt: In a ticket-booking system, a user selects a seat and is sent to payment. What should happen to the seat?
options: Mark it SOLD immediately and refund if payment fails
Place a hold with an expiry (e.g. 10 minutes) and release it automatically if payment doesn't complete
Remove it from the database until payment completes
Nothing until payment succeeds; first to pay wins
questions.explanation: A TTL hold gives the user a fair window to pay without blocking the seat forever. Without a hold, users finish payment only to find the seat gone, and marking SOLD up front creates refund churn and inflates 'sold out'.

questions.prompt: Which SQL statement safely places a hold on a specific seat under concurrency (in PostgreSQL, default READ COMMITTED)?
options: INSERT INTO holds (seat_id) VALUES ($1) with no constraints
SELECT status FROM seats WHERE id=$1; then UPDATE seats SET status='HELD' WHERE id=$1 if it was AVAILABLE
UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', held_by=$2, held_until=now()+interval '10 min' WHERE id=$1 AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR held_until < now()), then check the row count
UPDATE seats SET status='HELD' WHERE id=$1
questions.explanation: The conditional UPDATE is atomic: concurrent attempts re-check the WHERE clause after the row lock, so only one gets row count 1. SELECT-then-UPDATE is a race, and an unconditional UPDATE overwrites someone else's hold.

questions.prompt: Which Redis command atomically places a 10-minute hold on seat 123 only if nobody else holds it?
options: SETEX seat:123 600 user42
INCR seat:123
SET seat:123 user42 NX EX 600
EXPIRE seat:123 600
questions.explanation: NX sets the key only if it doesn't already exist, and EX gives it a TTL, in one atomic command. SETEX overwrites an existing holder, INCR doesn't record the holder, and EXPIRE only changes a TTL.

questions.prompt: Seat holds are stored in the database with a held_until column. How should expired holds be handled?
options: An admin releases them manually
A cron job releases them once a day
Queries treat a hold with held_until < now() as available, and a background sweeper tidies expired rows
They are released only when the holder logs out
questions.explanation: Lazy expiry in the availability check makes release effectively instant without depending on job timing, and the sweeper just cleans up. A daily job would leave seats unsellable for hours.

questions.prompt: What is the primary job of a virtual waiting room in front of a flash sale?
options: To randomly reject most users so the site stays fast
To admit users to the purchase flow at a rate the backend can sustain, using signed admission tokens
To cache the checkout page at the CDN
To show ads while users wait
questions.explanation: The waiting room absorbs a spike (millions arriving at 10:00:00) and meters admission to match backend capacity, often in FIFO or randomized order. A signed token proves admission, so users can't skip the queue by hitting checkout directly.

questions.prompt: A general-admission event sells 100,000 identical tickets from a single `remaining` counter row, which becomes a hot spot. What is a good fix?
options: Let every request decrement without checks and fix oversells later
Cache `remaining` in the CDN for 60 seconds
Split inventory across N bucket rows (or Redis keys) and decrement a random bucket, falling back to others when it's empty
Use SERIALIZABLE isolation on every decrement
questions.explanation: Sharding the counter spreads lock contention across N rows, and each bucket still enforces >= 0 atomically. An atomic Redis DECR with a check is another option. SERIALIZABLE increases conflicts, and a cached count doesn't prevent overselling.

questions.prompt: A user's payment succeeds 30 seconds after their seat hold expired, and the seat has already been sold to someone else. What should the system do?
options: Overwrite the other buyer's booking, since this user started first
Confirm both bookings and let the venue sort it out
Silently keep the payment and email the user later
Confirm only via a conditional update that checks this user still holds the seat; if not, void or refund the payment and tell the user
questions.explanation: Confirmation must re-check ownership atomically. When it fails, compensate by voiding the authorization (better: authorize first and capture only after confirming) or refunding. Double-selling or overwriting a valid sale is never acceptable.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a sound flash-sale waiting room design? Select all that apply.
options: An admission rate tied to measured backend capacity
A queue position recorded when the user arrives
Each web server keeping its own in-memory queue with no shared state
Letting everyone in and relying on autoscaling to react within seconds
A signed, short-lived admission token checked at checkout
questions.explanation: Fair ordering, unforgeable admission and capacity-based metering are the core. Autoscaling is too slow for a step spike (and databases don't autoscale instantly), and per-server queues are unfair and lost on restarts.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1` give you when allocating seats? Select all that apply.
options: Concurrent transactions each grab a different available row instead of queueing on the same one
Row locks that persist after the transaction ends
A good fit for 'any seat in this section' allocation
A guarantee that the specific seat the user clicked is the one returned
questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED skips rows other transactions have locked, so parallel buyers get different seats without blocking, which is ideal for interchangeable inventory or job queues. It may return a different row than the one you wanted, and locks are released at commit or rollback.

questions.prompt: Optimistic concurrency with a version column works well at low contention but causes many failed retries on a single hot item during a flash sale.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With thousands of buyers updating the same row, almost every commit fails the version check and retries, wasting work. Hot items call for atomic conditional decrements, sharded counters or queue-based serialization.

questions.prompt: A Redis key with an EX TTL is guaranteed to vanish at exactly the expiry instant, so the database never needs to check whether a hold has expired.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The Redis TTL is enforced (an expired key is never returned), but Redis and the DB are separate systems: failover can lose recent writes, and clock or ordering gaps exist. The final booking write should still verify the hold conditionally in the system of record.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea of Operational Transformation (OT) for collaborative editing?
options: Transform each concurrent operation against the others so all replicas converge whatever order ops arrive in
Give every character a globally unique ID and merge by ID
Lock the paragraph a user is editing so nobody else can change it
Keep only the most recent full copy of the document
questions.explanation: OT rewrites operations, e.g. shifting an insert's index past another user's concurrent insert, so applying them in different orders gives the same document. Unique per-character IDs describe sequence CRDTs, and locking isn't real-time co-editing.

questions.prompt: The document is "abc". User A inserts "X" at index 0 while user B concurrently deletes the character at index 2 ("c"). After A's insert is applied, how must B's delete be transformed?
options: Delete at index 2 (unchanged)
Delete at index 3
Delete at index 1
Discard B's delete as a conflict
questions.explanation: A's insert at 0 shifts every later character right by one, so "c" is now at index 3 in "Xabc". Applying B's delete unchanged would remove "b". Transforming it to index 3 gives "Xab" on both replicas.

questions.prompt: Why do classic OT systems (like the Jupiter-style approach behind Google Docs) usually rely on a central server?
options: OT ops are too large to send peer-to-peer
Browsers can't run the transform functions
The server stores each user's document separately
The server gives operations a single order (revision numbers), which keeps the transformation logic tractable
questions.explanation: With a central sequencer, each client only transforms against the server's history from its last known revision. Fully decentralized OT needs much harder transformation properties that many published algorithms got wrong. Transforms run fine in browsers.

questions.prompt: How does a sequence CRDT (e.g. RGA, or the algorithm in Yjs) make concurrent inserts converge without a central server?
options: Each inserted element gets a unique ID and its position is defined relative to other IDs, so merges are commutative
It uses last-writer-wins on the entire text
It sends the whole document on every keystroke
It locks a region of the document while it's being edited
questions.explanation: Positions are expressed by stable identifiers rather than integer indexes, with deterministic tie-breaking for concurrent inserts at the same spot. Merges therefore commute and every replica converges regardless of delivery order. Whole-document LWW would lose edits.

questions.prompt: What is a well-known cost of text CRDTs compared with OT?
options: Per-element metadata and tombstones for deleted characters add memory and storage overhead
They only support plain ASCII text
They can't converge if messages arrive out of order
They need a central server to assign revision numbers
questions.explanation: Each character carries an ID, and deletions often leave tombstones so concurrent ops can still find their anchors. That overhead is why libraries such as Yjs and Automerge invest heavily in compression and GC. Convergence under reordering is a CRDT strength.

questions.prompt: A note-taking app must support long offline editing on several devices and peer-to-peer sync with no always-on server. Which approach fits best?
options: Pessimistic locking per document
CRDTs
Server-centric OT
Last-write-wins on the whole file
questions.explanation: CRDTs merge any replicas' states in any order with no coordinator, which suits offline-first and P2P use. Server-centric OT assumes a central sequencer is reachable, and locking or whole-file LWW lose concurrent work.

questions.prompt: Where should live cursor positions and 'who's viewing' presence go in a collaborative editor?
options: On an ephemeral broadcast channel that isn't persisted, with stale entries expiring
In the relational database, updated on each keystroke
In the persistent operation log alongside text edits
In the CRDT document so they are versioned forever
questions.explanation: Presence changes constantly and is meaningless later. Putting it in the op log bloats history and replay. Editors send it over a separate ephemeral channel (e.g. Yjs's awareness protocol) with heartbeats and timeouts.

questions.prompt: For a state-based CRDT, the merge function must be which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Associative: merge(merge(a, b), c) = merge(a, merge(b, c))
Idempotent: merge(a, a) = a
Commutative: merge(a, b) = merge(b, a)
Dependent on a total order assigned by a server
Guaranteed to preserve every user's intent in all cases
questions.explanation: These three properties (a join-semilattice) make replicas converge regardless of delivery order, grouping or duplication. CRDTs specifically avoid needing a server-assigned order, and convergence doesn't guarantee the merged result matches what every user intended.

questions.prompt: Which are part of a typical client/server OT protocol? Select all that apply.
options: Each op carries the revision it was based on
The client buffers unacknowledged local ops and transforms incoming server ops against them
The server assigns increasing revision numbers to accepted operations
Clients overwrite the whole document with their copy on conflict
The server relays each op to other clients untransformed, even if it was based on an older revision
questions.explanation: Revisions establish order, the base revision tells the server how far to transform, and client-side buffering keeps the UI responsive while staying consistent. Whole-document overwrite loses edits, and relaying a stale op untransformed applies it at the wrong position.

questions.prompt: Last-write-wins on the whole document is an acceptable conflict strategy for real-time collaborative text editing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Two people typing in different paragraphs would constantly overwrite each other. Real-time co-editing needs character-level merging via OT or CRDTs.

questions.prompt: Yjs and Automerge are CRDT libraries for building collaborative applications.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Both implement CRDTs for shared text, lists and maps, with sync protocols that support offline and peer-to-peer use. They are common choices when you don't want to build OT around a central server.

questions.prompt: Why do typeahead tries often store a precomputed top-K suggestion list at every node?
options: So the trie needs less memory
To make inserting new terms cheaper
So a prefix query costs O(prefix length) instead of traversing and sorting the whole subtree
Because tries can't otherwise store frequencies
questions.explanation: Walking to the prefix node and returning its cached list is fast and predictable. Without it, a short prefix like 'a' would require visiting millions of descendants and sorting them. The trade-off is more memory and more expensive updates.

questions.prompt: Storing top-K lists at every trie node blows past the memory budget. Which change is most sensible?
options: Remove the trie and scan a sorted list of all queries
Store full query strings in every ancestor's list
Increase K so fewer nodes need lists
Keep small K (e.g. 5–10), store lists only up to a maximum prefix depth, and keep references rather than full strings
questions.explanation: Users rarely type more than ~10–20 characters before picking, so caching beyond a depth gives little benefit. Small K and pointers or IDs cut memory a lot. A larger K increases memory, and a linear scan is far too slow.

questions.prompt: How are suggestion frequencies in a large-scale typeahead usually kept up to date?
options: Increment counts in the live trie synchronously on every search
Let the client compute frequencies from local history
Rebuild or refresh the trie periodically (e.g. hourly) from aggregated query logs, and serve an immutable snapshot
Never update; frequencies are fixed at launch
questions.explanation: Serving reads from immutable snapshots avoids locking on the hot path, and batch aggregation over logs is cheap and robust. Synchronous increments on every search would contend on top-level nodes, and each one could reshuffle top-K lists up the tree.

questions.prompt: A user types 'iphone' quickly and the client sends 6 requests in 300 ms. What is the simplest client-side fix?
options: Send requests over UDP
Disable autocomplete on mobile
Debounce input (e.g. 100–200 ms) and cancel stale in-flight requests
Increase the server's thread pool
questions.explanation: Debouncing collapses keystroke bursts into one request, and aborting stale requests (AbortController) avoids out-of-order responses overwriting newer ones. A bigger thread pool only absorbs the waste instead of removing it.

questions.prompt: Short prefixes like 'a' or 'th' make up a huge share of typeahead traffic. What is the most effective way to serve them?
options: Route them to a dedicated database replica
Reject queries shorter than 3 characters
Compute them on the fly with a full-text search query
Cache responses for short prefixes at the CDN or browser with a short TTL
questions.explanation: The set of short prefixes is small and their results are the same for everyone (absent personalization), so edge caching absorbs much of the load. Rejecting them hurts UX, and on-the-fly computation is the expensive path you're trying to avoid.

questions.prompt: A team shards the typeahead trie by first letter (26 shards), and the 's' shard melts while the 'x' shard idles. What is a better partitioning?
options: Split by prefix ranges sized from historical traffic (e.g. 'sa–sh', 'si–sz') so each shard gets similar load
Put every shard on the same machine
Use 52 shards for upper and lower case
Shard by the last letter of the query instead
questions.explanation: Letter frequencies are highly skewed, so ranges should come from measured traffic and be split further when hot (as range-partitioned stores do). Last-letter sharding breaks prefix locality, so one lookup would hit every shard.

questions.prompt: What is the query time complexity for prefix length p if each trie node stores its top-K list, compared with the naive trie approach over a subtree of n terms?
options: O(p · K) vs O(n²)
O(p + K) vs O(p + n log n)
O(K log n) vs O(1)
O(n) vs O(p)
questions.explanation: With caching you walk p nodes and read K items. Naively you walk p nodes, then visit all n descendant terms and sort or heap-select them (O(n log n), or O(n log K) with a heap). The cached version is independent of subtree size.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a production typeahead design? Select all that apply.
options: Filtering offensive or blocked terms before serving
Client-side debouncing
A `LIKE '%prefix%'` query against the main database on each keystroke
Synchronously recomputing counts before replying to each request
Precomputed top-K suggestions per prefix
questions.explanation: Debounce, precomputation and safety filtering are standard. A leading-wildcard LIKE can't use a B-tree index and scans the table, and doing aggregation on the request path adds latency and contention.

questions.prompt: A news event makes a new query explode in popularity. Which techniques help it appear in suggestions quickly? Select all that apply.
options: Increasing K at every node
Rebuilding the trie weekly instead of daily
A small real-time trending layer merged with the offline top-K at serve time
Time-decayed scoring that weights recent queries more heavily
questions.explanation: Decay lets fresh demand outrank stale all-time counts, and a streaming trending layer adds new items within minutes without rebuilding the whole trie. Less frequent rebuilds make freshness worse, and a bigger K doesn't help a term that isn't in the snapshot.

questions.prompt: Locating a prefix's node in a trie costs time proportional to the prefix length, not to the total number of stored terms.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. You follow one edge per character, which is O(p) for prefix length p, whether the trie holds a thousand terms or a billion. That's the main reason tries suit prefix lookups.

questions.prompt: With top-K lists cached at each node, changing one query's count only requires updating that query's leaf node.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Every ancestor along the query's path may include it in its top-K, so a count change can require updating up to p ancestor lists. That's a key reason updates are batched into periodic rebuilds.

questions.prompt: A rate limiter does GET count, checks it in Node, then calls INCR. Under load, clients exceed the limit. Why does moving the logic into a Redis Lua script fix it?
options: Lua scripts are cached on the client, avoiding network calls
Lua scripts automatically replicate the key to every shard
Lua makes INCR return the count before incrementing
Lua scripts run atomically, so no other command interleaves between the read and the write
questions.explanation: Redis runs a script without interleaving other commands, so read-check-write becomes one atomic step. With separate GET and INCR, many app servers can read the same count and all pass the check. Scripts are cached on the server (EVALSHA), not the client.

questions.prompt: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute, windows aligned to the minute. What is the worst-case number of requests a client can send in a 2-second span?
questions.explanation: The client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00, since each falls in a different window. This boundary burst is the main weakness of fixed windows and why sliding windows or token buckets are used.

questions.prompt: A sliding-window-log limiter uses a Redis sorted set per user: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE (drop old), ZCARD (count), ZADD (record). What is its main cost?
options: It allows double the limit at window edges
It cannot be made atomic in Redis
Memory grows with the number of requests per window, since every timestamp is stored
It requires clocks synchronized to the microsecond
questions.explanation: The log is exact but stores one entry per request per key, so a 10,000/hour limit can mean 10,000 members per user. It doesn't have the boundary burst problem, and the three commands can be wrapped in a Lua script.

questions.prompt: Product wants: sustained 10 requests/second per API key, with short bursts up to 50 allowed. How do you configure a token bucket?
options: Capacity 50, refill 10 tokens/second
Capacity 10, refill 10 tokens/second
Capacity 10, refill 50 tokens/second
Capacity 50, refill 50 tokens/second
questions.explanation: Bucket capacity sets the maximum burst (50) and refill rate sets the long-run average (10/s). A full bucket allows 50 back-to-back requests, after which the client is limited to the refill rate.

questions.prompt: On Redis Cluster, a Lua limiter touches keys rl:user:42:tokens and rl:user:42:ts and fails with a CROSSSLOT error. What's the fix?
options: Switch from EVAL to MULTI/EXEC
Use hash tags, such as rl:{user:42}:tokens and rl:{user:42}:ts, so both keys map to one slot
Run the script with EVAL on every node
Increase cluster-node-timeout
questions.explanation: In Redis Cluster, all keys a script touches must be in the same hash slot. With a hash tag only the part in {} is hashed, which co-locates related keys. MULTI/EXEC has the same single-slot requirement, so it doesn't help.

questions.prompt: A token-bucket Lua script takes 'now' as an argument from each Node server's Date.now(). Servers' clocks differ by up to 2 seconds. What's the issue and fix?
options: Refill math depends on whose clock called last, so tokens appear or vanish; read time inside the script with redis.call('TIME')
Date.now() is too coarse; use process.hrtime instead
No issue, since Lua scripts are atomic
Lua can't do floating-point maths, so use integers
questions.explanation: Atomicity doesn't fix inconsistent inputs: a server with a fast clock grants extra refill and one with a slow clock makes elapsed time negative. Using the Redis server's TIME gives every caller one clock. hrtime is per-process and not comparable across hosts.

questions.prompt: Redis for a general API fairness rate limiter becomes unreachable. What is usually the most defensible default behaviour?
options: Fail closed: reject every request with 429 until Redis is back
Fail open with a coarse per-instance in-memory limit, and alert
Disable the API gateway
Queue all requests in memory until Redis recovers
questions.explanation: For a fairness limiter, turning a cache outage into a full API outage is usually worse than briefly being less precise. A local fallback still caps abuse. Security-critical limiters such as login brute-force protection may justify failing closed.

questions.prompt: This fixed-window limiter script runs on every request (ARGV[1] = window seconds, ARGV[2] = limit). What is the bug?
questions.code:
local current = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
if current > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then
  return 0
end
return 1
options: tonumber cannot parse ARGV values
The script isn't atomic, so two requests can both pass
EXPIRE resets the TTL on every call, so a steadily active client's window never resets
INCR on a missing key raises an error
questions.explanation: Each request pushes expiry forward, so a client sending at least one request per window keeps the counter alive forever and stays blocked. Set the TTL only when INCR returns 1. INCR on a missing key starts at 0 and returns 1, and the script is atomic.

questions.prompt: When a request is rate limited, which response behaviours are good practice for an HTTP API? Select all that apply.
options: Expose remaining quota (e.g. X-RateLimit-Remaining or the IETF RateLimit headers)
Return 503 Service Unavailable to signal the limit
Include a Retry-After header
Return status 429 Too Many Requests
Silently drop the request without responding
questions.explanation: 429 is the specific status for rate limiting, and Retry-After plus quota headers let clients back off intelligently. 503 means the server is overloaded or down, which misleads clients and monitoring; silently dropping wastes client resources on timeouts.

questions.prompt: A sliding-window-counter limiter estimates usage as current_count + previous_count × (1 − elapsed_fraction_of_current_window). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: It is exactly as precise as a sliding-window log
It must store every request timestamp
It needs only two counters per key, so memory is O(1)
It assumes requests in the previous window were spread evenly
questions.explanation: The counter approach weights the previous window's count by how much of it still overlaps, which assumes an even distribution. It's cheap (two integers) but approximate; exact precision with stored timestamps is what the log approach provides.

questions.prompt: With a token bucket, a client that stays idle for hours builds up an unlimited number of tokens.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Tokens are capped at the bucket's capacity, so after a long idle period the client can burst at most 'capacity' requests and then falls back to the refill rate. That cap is what bounds burst size.

questions.prompt: What is the classic Twitter Snowflake 64-bit ID layout?
options: 32-bit seconds timestamp, 16-bit machine id, 16-bit sequence
1 sign bit, 41-bit ms timestamp, 10-bit machine id, 12-bit sequence
1 sign bit, 31-bit timestamp, 32-bit random
48-bit ms timestamp, 16-bit random
questions.explanation: Snowflake uses an unused sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits for the worker (datacenter + machine) and a 12-bit per-millisecond sequence. A 48-bit timestamp plus randomness describes ULID or UUIDv7 instead.

questions.prompt: With a 12-bit sequence per millisecond, what's the maximum number of IDs one Snowflake worker can generate per second?
options: About 4,096
About 409,600
About 4.1 million
About 1 million
questions.explanation: 2^12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond, × 1,000 ms = 4,096,000 per second per worker. Answering 4,096 forgets that the sequence resets every millisecond, not every second.

questions.prompt: Why do Snowflake-style generators use a custom epoch (e.g. the service's launch date) instead of the Unix epoch?
options: Unix epoch timestamps are not monotonic
The 41-bit millisecond field lasts about 69 years, so starting near launch maximizes the usable lifespan
Custom epochs make IDs unguessable
Databases can't index timestamps before 2000
questions.explanation: 2^41 ms ≈ 2.2 × 10^12 ms ≈ 69.7 years. Counting from 1970 would already use up over half that range. A custom epoch hides the absolute time a little, but it isn't a security feature.

questions.prompt: An NTP correction moves a Snowflake worker's clock back by 200 ms. What should a correct generator do?
options: Add 200 to the sequence number
Refuse or wait until the clock passes the last timestamp used, since reusing timestamps risks duplicates
Keep generating with the earlier timestamp and reset the sequence
Switch to a random machine id temporarily
questions.explanation: Reusing old milliseconds with a reset sequence can produce IDs identical to ones already issued. Generators track the last timestamp and either block until the clock catches up or throw for large jumps. Running NTP in slew mode reduces backward steps.

questions.prompt: A worker has already issued all 4,096 sequence values within the current millisecond. What does a typical Snowflake implementation do with the next request?
options: Borrow a sequence range from another worker
Spin or wait until the next millisecond, then reset the sequence to 0
Wrap the sequence to 0 within the same millisecond
Return a UUID instead
questions.explanation: Wrapping within the same millisecond would duplicate IDs, so the generator waits briefly for the clock to tick. This caps per-worker throughput at about 4.1M/s; more throughput needs more workers.

questions.prompt: Snowflake worker ids come from an env var on Kubernetes Deployment pods. During a rolling deploy, duplicate IDs appear. What's the most likely cause and fix?
options: Old and new pods briefly share a worker id; lease ids from etcd/ZooKeeper or use StatefulSet ordinals
The sequence is too short; widen it to 16 bits
Clock skew between pods; fix with more NTP servers
BigInt overflow in Node; use Number instead
questions.explanation: Uniqueness depends entirely on no two live generators sharing a worker id. Static config breaks when old and new pods overlap. Leasing ids with TTLs (etcd/ZooKeeper) or using stable StatefulSet ordinals ensures exclusivity. Clock skew alone doesn't cause duplicates across different worker ids.

questions.prompt: This builds and decodes a Snowflake-style ID with BigInt. What does it print?
questions.explanation: 1000 << 22 = 4,194,304,000; 5 << 12 = 20,480; plus 7 gives 4,194,324,487. Decoding shifts right 22 for the timestamp offset (1000), masks 10 bits after shifting 12 for the worker (5), and masks 12 bits for the sequence (7).

questions.prompt: A Node API returns Snowflake IDs as JSON numbers, and a browser client parses them with JSON.parse. Some IDs no longer match database rows. Why?
options: IDs above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1) lose precision as doubles; serialize them as strings
Snowflake IDs are negative due to the sign bit
JSON.parse converts large integers to strings
Browsers truncate numbers to 32 bits
questions.explanation: Snowflake IDs are about 2^60 or more today, far above 2^53, so JSON.parse rounds them to the nearest representable double. That is why Twitter's API added id_str. The sign bit is always 0, so IDs are positive.

questions.prompt: Compared to UUIDv4 primary keys, which are real advantages of Snowflake IDs? Select all that apply.
options: They reveal nothing about when a record was created
Roughly time-ordered, so B-tree inserts are mostly appends
No coordination needed at all between generators
64 bits instead of 128, so indexes are smaller
questions.explanation: Half the size and near-monotonic order make Snowflake IDs index-friendly. They still need worker-id coordination, and the timestamp prefix exposes creation time, so the last two options are wrong.

questions.prompt: You expose Snowflake IDs from a Node.js API. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: JSON.stringify serializes BigInt values natively as numbers
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 2^53 − 1
Sending IDs as JSON strings avoids client-side precision loss
Use BigInt (or strings) to handle IDs in Node
questions.explanation: JSON.stringify throws a TypeError on BigInt unless you add a toJSON or replacer, so the third statement is false. Handling IDs as BigInt on the server and strings on the wire keeps all 64 bits intact.

questions.prompt: Two Snowflake IDs from different machines in the same millisecond are ordered by worker id, so their numeric order always reflects true creation order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Within a millisecond, order across machines depends on worker id, which has nothing to do with which event came first, and clock skew can reorder across milliseconds too. Snowflake IDs are only roughly time-sortable (k-sorted).

questions.prompt: How many bits of a UUIDv4 are actually random?
questions.explanation: Of 128 bits, 4 encode the version and 2 encode the variant, leaving 122 random bits. That is still about 5.3 × 10^36 possibilities, so collisions are negligible with a proper CSPRNG.

questions.prompt: What is the structure of a UUIDv7 as defined in RFC 9562?
options: A SHA-1 hash of a namespace and name
48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp prefix followed by random (or counter) bits
60-bit Gregorian timestamp plus the MAC address
122 fully random bits
questions.explanation: UUIDv7 puts Unix epoch milliseconds in the top 48 bits, then version/variant bits and random or counter data, so values sort by creation time. A Gregorian timestamp plus MAC is v1, and SHA-1 namespace hashing is v5.

questions.prompt: A MySQL InnoDB table uses UUIDv4 as its clustered primary key. Insert throughput drops sharply as the table grows past RAM. Why?
options: UUIDs force every insert to take a table lock
InnoDB cannot index 16-byte values
Random keys insert all over the B-tree, causing page splits and cache misses instead of appends
UUIDv4 values collide more often as tables grow
questions.explanation: Random keys touch random leaf pages; once the index doesn't fit in the buffer pool, each insert may need a disk read and page splits fragment the tree. Time-ordered IDs (v7, ULID, Snowflake) insert near the right edge. Collisions are not the problem.

questions.prompt: Which description of a ULID is correct?
options: 128 bits fully random, encoded as 36 hex characters with dashes
64 bits: 41-bit timestamp + 23 random bits, as a decimal string
128 bits: 48-bit ms timestamp + 80 random bits, encoded as 26 Crockford Base32 characters
96 bits: seconds timestamp + machine id + counter, as 24 hex characters
questions.explanation: ULIDs are 128-bit, sort lexicographically by time, and use Crockford Base32 (26 chars, no ambiguous letters). The 96-bit timestamp + machine + counter layout describes a MongoDB ObjectId, not a ULID.

questions.prompt: You need password-reset tokens placed in emailed URLs. Which ID choice is most appropriate?
options: UUIDv7, since it's newer and sortable
A Snowflake ID, so tokens are compact
A purely random token (UUIDv4 or 32 CSPRNG bytes); time-prefixed IDs leak creation time and carry fewer random bits
A ULID, since its 80 random bits hide the timestamp
questions.explanation: Secrets should be unguessable. v7 and ULID expose the issue time and have fewer random bits (v7: about 74; ULID: 80, and fewer still if a monotonic counter is used), while Snowflake IDs are guessable. A ULID's timestamp is in plain view in its first 10 characters.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16 a team stores ULIDs in a text column with a B-tree index. What would most improve storage and index size?
options: Convert to varchar(26) instead of text
Add a hash index alongside the B-tree
Store as bigint, keeping the top 64 bits
Store the 128-bit value in the native uuid type (16 bytes) and format it as ULID in the app
questions.explanation: A 26-character text value takes about 27 bytes plus overhead, against a fixed 16 bytes for uuid, and comparisons on uuid are cheaper. varchar(26) and text are stored the same way. Keeping only 64 bits throws away randomness and risks collisions.

questions.prompt: In Node.js 22, which UUID version does the built-in crypto.randomUUID() generate?
options: Version 5
Version 7
Version 1
Version 4
questions.explanation: crypto.randomUUID() returns an RFC-compliant random v4 UUID from a CSPRNG. For time-ordered v7 IDs in Node you need a library such as the uuid package (v7()).

questions.prompt: A service creates several UUIDv7 rows within the same millisecond and is surprised they don't sort in insertion order. What explains this, and what's the fix?
options: UUIDv7 timestamps are in seconds, so collisions are common
UUIDv7 must be generated by the database to sort correctly
The random bits after the timestamp order IDs arbitrarily within a millisecond; use a generator that adds a monotonic counter
PostgreSQL sorts uuid columns by the random part first
questions.explanation: Only the 48-bit millisecond prefix is ordered; the rest is random by default. RFC 9562 allows a counter or sub-millisecond fraction in rand_a (and ULID has a monotonic mode) for ordering within one generator. PostgreSQL compares uuids byte by byte from the left.

questions.prompt: Which properties does UUIDv7 have? Select all that apply.
options: Embeds the host's MAC address
Strictly monotonic across all nodes in a cluster
Roughly time-ordered by creation
Fits existing 128-bit uuid columns and parsers
questions.explanation: v7 is time-ordered and uses the standard 128-bit UUID format. There's no cross-node ordering guarantee, since clocks differ and random bits break ties, and embedding the MAC is a v1 trait that v7 deliberately avoids.

questions.prompt: A multi-region service needs primary keys generated without a central coordinator, sortable by time, stored in a PostgreSQL uuid column. Which options fit? Select all that apply.
options: ULID stored as its 128-bit value in a uuid column
UUIDv4
UUIDv7
A PostgreSQL bigserial sequence
questions.explanation: Both v7 and ULID are 128-bit, coordination-free and time-sortable. v4 is coordination-free but random, so it isn't sortable. A sequence needs a single authority, which conflicts with generating keys independently in several regions.

questions.prompt: Generated with a proper CSPRNG, UUIDv4 collisions are negligible for practical workloads, even at billions of IDs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With 122 random bits, the birthday bound gives about a 50% chance of one collision only after roughly 2.7 × 10^18 IDs. Real-world collisions come from broken RNGs (e.g. cloned VM seeds), not from the format.

questions.prompt: In a single-server setup, a user types app.example.com into a browser. What turns that name into the server's IP address?
options: The browser's built-in load balancer
A CDN edge node that proxies to the server
DNS, usually a third-party managed service
The web server, which answers on port 80 for any name
questions.explanation: The browser asks DNS (typically a managed service, not the app server) for the IP, then sends HTTP to that IP. The web server only sees the request after resolution has already happened; a CDN is not part of a minimal single-server setup.

questions.prompt: One server runs the Node app, the PostgreSQL database and Redis. During a traffic spike, page latency jumps even for simple endpoints. What is the most likely cause?
options: DNS resolution slows down under high traffic
Node.js cannot accept more than a few hundred connections
The app, database and cache compete for the same CPU, RAM and disk
Redis forces the database into single-threaded mode
questions.explanation: With everything on one box, a heavy query or cache memory growth steals CPU, memory and disk I/O from the web process, so unrelated endpoints slow down too. Node can handle many concurrent connections; DNS is resolved and cached client-side.

questions.prompt: What is the main reliability weakness of a single-server architecture?
options: It requires a CDN to serve images
It cannot serve HTTPS traffic
Any hardware or process failure takes the whole product offline
It cannot run a relational database
questions.explanation: A single server is a single point of failure: a crash, disk failure or reboot means total downtime. It can absolutely serve HTTPS, run a database and serve images itself; those are scaling or performance concerns, not the core reliability issue.

questions.prompt: A Node.js API on an 8-core single server is CPU-bound and top shows one core at 100% while the rest idle. What's the cheapest improvement before buying more servers?
options: Increase the server's RAM
Run one Node process per core (cluster module or a process manager)
Raise the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 64
Move static files to a CDN
questions.explanation: A Node process runs JavaScript on one thread, so a CPU-bound app uses one core. Running several processes (node:cluster, PM2) uses all cores on the same box. A bigger libuv thread pool only helps fs/crypto/dns work, not your JS; more RAM doesn't add CPU.

questions.prompt: You move the single server to a new IP and update the DNS A record (TTL 86400). Hours later some users still hit the old IP. Why?
options: DNS changes only take effect after the old server is shut down
The registrar must approve every A-record change
Browsers never re-resolve DNS during a session
Resolvers cache the old record until its TTL expires
questions.explanation: Recursive resolvers and OS caches keep the record for up to its TTL (here 24h). Lowering the TTL well before a migration shortens the window. Shutting down the old server just makes those cached users fail; it doesn't speed propagation.

questions.prompt: Why is a single-server deployment still a reasonable choice for a brand-new product with a few hundred users?
options: It removes the need for backups because data is in one place
It scales horizontally automatically as users grow
It provides higher availability than a replicated setup
It is the simplest and cheapest option, and premature distribution adds complexity
questions.explanation: Early on, simplicity and low cost matter more than fault tolerance; distributing too early adds ops burden without users to justify it. It does not give better availability (it's a SPOF), doesn't scale horizontally on its own, and still needs backups.

questions.prompt: On a single server you deploy a new version by restarting the Node process. Without any extra infrastructure, what user-visible effect is hard to avoid?
options: The database schema is reset on restart
Users must clear their cookies after each deploy
DNS records must be updated for each deploy
A short window of refused or dropped requests while the process restarts
questions.explanation: With only one instance there is nothing else to route traffic to while it restarts, so in-flight and new requests fail briefly. Zero-downtime deploys need at least a second instance (or socket handoff). DNS, cookies and the schema are unaffected by a process restart.

questions.prompt: In a single-server setup, which of these are single points of failure? Select all that apply.
options: The server's hardware (power supply, motherboard)
The visitor's browser cache
The one application process serving requests
The local disk holding the database files
questions.explanation: Hardware, the only disk with data, and the only app process can each take the product down. The browser cache is on the client and its failure only affects that user's performance, not the service.

questions.prompt: A user loads a page from a single-server app. Which steps normally happen? Select all that apply.
options: The browser resolves the domain via DNS
A load balancer picks one of several replicas
The server responds with HTML or JSON
The browser sends an HTTP(S) request to the returned IP
questions.explanation: The flow is DNS lookup, HTTP request to that IP, then an HTML (browser) or JSON (API/mobile) response. There is no load balancer or replica pool in a single-server setup.

questions.prompt: In a typical single-server setup, the DNS service is also hosted on that same application server.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: DNS is almost always a paid or free third-party service (registrar DNS, Route 53, Cloudflare). Hosting it on the app server would add another failure mode with no benefit.

questions.prompt: Vertical scaling (moving to a bigger machine) only postpones the single-point-of-failure problem of a single server; it doesn't remove it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A bigger machine adds capacity but it's still one machine; if it fails the product is down. Removing the SPOF needs redundancy (multiple servers, replicas).

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of moving the database off the web server onto its own host?
options: The web and data tiers can be scaled and tuned independently
Web servers can now share session memory
The database can no longer become a bottleneck
Database queries no longer need a network hop
questions.explanation: Separating tiers lets you size each one for its workload (CPU for web, RAM/disk for the DB) and scale them separately. It actually adds a network hop, and the DB can still bottleneck; sessions are a separate concern.

questions.prompt: After moving PostgreSQL to a separate host in the same data center, one endpoint's latency rose from 20 ms to 120 ms. It runs about 50 sequential queries per request. What's the best fix?
options: Increase PostgreSQL shared_buffers
Add more web servers
Reduce round trips by batching or joining the queries
Move the database back onto the web server
questions.explanation: Each query now pays a network round trip (~0.5–2 ms), so 50 sequential queries add up. Batching, using a JOIN or IN-list (fixing N+1) cuts round trips. More web servers don't shorten one request; shared_buffers helps disk reads, not network RTT.

questions.prompt: Which requirement most strongly suggests a non-relational store over a relational one?
options: Very low-latency access to massive amounts of schemaless key-value data
Strong referential integrity enforced with foreign keys
Ad-hoc SQL reporting across many related tables
Multi-row transactions that join orders, payments and inventory
questions.explanation: NoSQL stores shine for huge volumes of simple, loosely structured data accessed by key with low latency. Multi-table transactions, foreign keys and ad-hoc joins are exactly where relational databases are the better default.

questions.prompt: After separating tiers, what is the recommended network posture for the database host?
options: Public IP but on a non-default port
Private subnet, reachable only from app servers on the DB port
Same public subnet as the load balancer for lower latency
Public IP with a strong password
questions.explanation: The DB should never be internet-facing: put it in a private subnet and allow only the app tier's security group on its port. A non-default port or strong password still exposes it to scanning and brute force.

questions.prompt: Each web request opens a brand-new TCP + TLS connection to the separate database host and closes it afterwards. What's the standard fix?
options: Open one connection per user at login
Use a connection pool that reuses open connections
Disable TLS between web and database
Use UDP instead of TCP for queries
questions.explanation: Connection setup (TCP handshake, TLS, DB auth) is expensive; a pool keeps a bounded set of warm connections for reuse. Disabling TLS weakens security and still pays handshakes; per-user connections don't scale.

questions.prompt: You scale to 20 Node instances, each with a pg pool of size 20, against PostgreSQL with max_connections = 100. What happens under load?
options: Nothing; idle pool connections don't count
Pools automatically shrink to share the 100 slots
New connections are rejected with 'too many clients' errors
PostgreSQL queues extra connections until slots free up
questions.explanation: 20 × 20 = 400 potential connections against a 100 limit; once exceeded PostgreSQL refuses new ones. Pools don't coordinate across processes, and idle connections still occupy slots. Fix with smaller pools or a pooler like PgBouncer.

questions.prompt: Why might you give the separated database server a lot of RAM but the web servers more CPU?
options: CPU is only used by the database during writes
Databases benefit from caching hot pages in memory; web servers spend time on request handling
RAM is cheaper on database instances
Web servers store the database's indexes
questions.explanation: A DB serves reads fastest from its buffer cache, so RAM reduces disk I/O; app servers mostly burn CPU on JSON, templating and business logic. Separation is what makes this per-tier sizing possible.

questions.prompt: Which benefits come from separating the web tier and the database tier? Select all that apply.
options: The database stops being a single point of failure
Each tier can be scaled independently
The database can be tuned for its own workload
A crashed web process no longer competes with the DB for resources
questions.explanation: Independent scaling, per-tier tuning and resource isolation are the gains. With one DB host it is still a single point of failure; that needs replication.

questions.prompt: Which new concerns appear once the database lives on its own server? Select all that apply.
options: Securing network access and credentials to the DB
Losing the ability to use SQL
Managing connection counts from all app instances
Network latency on every query
questions.explanation: You now pay a network round trip per query, must lock down network access and secrets, and must budget connections across instances. SQL works the same over the network.

questions.prompt: Moving the database onto its own dedicated server removes the database as a single point of failure.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It's still one database host; if it dies, the app can't read or write. Removing that SPOF requires replication with failover.

questions.prompt: After separating tiers, an N+1 query pattern usually hurts more than it did when the database ran on the same machine.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: On the same host, each query used a local socket with tiny latency. Across the network every extra query adds a round trip, so N+1 patterns multiply latency.

questions.prompt: What does horizontal scaling mean?
options: Splitting one table's columns into two tables
Moving a server to a larger data center
Adding more servers to a pool that shares the load
Upgrading a server to more CPU and RAM
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds machines behind a load balancer or partitioning scheme. Upgrading one machine is vertical scaling (scale up).

questions.prompt: Which component is usually the hardest to scale horizontally?
options: A single-primary relational database with heavy writes and transactions
Stateless HTTP API servers
A read-through cache of immutable product images
Static file serving
questions.explanation: Writes and cross-row transactions on one primary can't simply be spread across copies; scaling them needs sharding with its own complexity. Stateless servers, static files and immutable caches scale out by just adding nodes.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't vertical scaling improve availability?
options: Bigger machines fail more often
It still leaves one machine; if it fails, the service is down
It requires a load balancer that can fail
Bigger machines can't run databases
questions.explanation: Scaling up adds capacity, not redundancy. Availability needs multiple instances so one can fail without an outage.

questions.prompt: You double web servers from 4 to 8, but throughput rises only 30%. CPU on the web servers is now low. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The load balancer only supports 4 targets
A shared downstream resource, such as the database, is the bottleneck
Node.js limits throughput per machine
DNS is still pointing at the original 4 servers
questions.explanation: When added web capacity sits idle, the limit is something every server depends on, usually the DB, a lock or an external API. Scaling one tier just moves the bottleneck. A real LB handles many targets and DNS points at the LB, not the servers.

questions.prompt: What is a genuine advantage of vertical scaling?
options: Simplicity: usually no code or architecture changes are needed
Built-in failover between machines
Linear cost growth at every size
Unlimited capacity as long as you pay
questions.explanation: Scaling up is attractive because the app doesn't change: no distributed state, no LB. But it has a hardware ceiling, no redundancy, and the largest instances cost disproportionately more.

questions.prompt: A Node service keeps per-user rate-limit counters in process memory (limit 100 req/min). You scale from 1 to 4 instances behind round-robin. What happens?
options: The load balancer enforces the limit instead
Limits stay at 100/min because round-robin is deterministic
Requests start failing because counters conflict
Users can effectively make up to about 400 requests per minute
questions.explanation: Each instance counts independently, so a user spread across 4 instances gets ~4× the intended limit. Shared state like rate limits must live in a shared store (e.g. Redis INCR with expiry) once you scale out.

questions.prompt: At the high end of instance sizes, how does price usually relate to performance?
options: Price scales down per core on bigger machines
Price grows faster than performance, so top-tier machines are poor value
Bigger machines are free on most clouds
Price is identical per core at every size
questions.explanation: The largest machines carry a premium and eventually hit hardware limits, so many smaller nodes usually give better price-performance and redundancy at scale.

questions.prompt: Which are prerequisites for horizontally scaling a web tier? Select all that apply.
options: Identical code and config across instances
A load balancer or similar mechanism to spread requests
Every server keeps its own writable copy of the database
Servers don't keep per-user state in local memory or disk
questions.explanation: Stateless servers, a traffic distributor and identical deployments let any instance serve any request. Per-server writable DB copies would create divergent data, not scale.

questions.prompt: Which are drawbacks of horizontal scaling compared with vertical scaling? Select all that apply.
options: State and consistency must be coordinated across nodes
Network partitions between nodes become possible
A hard upper limit set by the largest available machine
More operational complexity (deploys, monitoring many nodes)
questions.explanation: Scale-out brings ops overhead, partial failures and coordination problems. The hard hardware ceiling is the classic drawback of vertical scaling, not horizontal.

questions.prompt: Horizontal scaling usually requires the application to be designed for it (e.g. no local state), while vertical scaling usually doesn't.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A stateful app runs fine on a bigger box, but behind multiple instances its local state breaks. Scaling out demands externalized state; scaling up doesn't.

questions.prompt: Vertically scaling a single physical database server can always be done with zero downtime.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Resizing typically means a restart or a migration to new hardware. Avoiding downtime usually needs a replica to fail over to, which is no longer purely vertical scaling.

questions.prompt: Web server 2 of 3 crashes behind a load balancer. What normally happens?
options: All traffic fails until server 2 is restarted
DNS automatically removes server 2's record
Health checks mark it unhealthy and traffic goes to servers 1 and 3
The load balancer restarts server 2 itself
questions.explanation: The LB's health checks detect the failure and stop routing to that target; the others absorb its traffic. Restarting it is the job of an orchestrator or autoscaling group, not the LB, and clients resolve the LB, not individual servers.

questions.prompt: Why are web servers often placed in a private network with only the load balancer having a public IP?
options: Load balancers can't route to public IPs
Private networks remove the need for TLS
Private IPs make requests faster
So servers can't be reached directly from the internet, reducing attack surface
questions.explanation: Clients only talk to the LB; backends accept traffic only from it, so they're not directly exposed to scanning or attacks. TLS inside the network is still often used; private IPs aren't inherently faster.

questions.prompt: Request durations vary wildly (some 5 ms, some 30 s long-polls). Which balancing algorithm usually spreads load better than round-robin?
options: IP hash
Weighted DNS
Least connections
Random with replacement
questions.explanation: Least connections sends new requests to the server with the fewest active ones, so a server stuck with slow requests gets fewer new ones. Round-robin and random ignore current load; IP hash pins clients regardless of load.

questions.prompt: You need /api/* to go to one server pool and /static/* to another, based on the URL path. What kind of load balancer do you need?
options: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP)
DNS round-robin
Layer 3 (IP routing)
Layer 7 (HTTP-aware)
questions.explanation: Path-based routing requires reading the HTTP request, which only an L7 balancer does. L4 balancers route by IP/port without inspecting the HTTP path; DNS can't see paths at all.

questions.prompt: Every instance's readiness check queries the shared database. During a 20-second DB blip, what is the main risk?
options: All instances fail the check at once, leaving no healthy targets and causing a full outage
Only write requests fail; reads continue
The database gets more connections and recovers faster
The load balancer starts sticky sessions
questions.explanation: Deep health checks on a shared dependency fail everywhere simultaneously, so the LB removes every instance, even ones that could serve cached or DB-free requests. Keep liveness/readiness checks shallow or tolerant, and handle dependency failures in the request path.

questions.prompt: How do you stop the load balancer itself from becoming a single point of failure?
options: Put the load balancer behind the database
Use sticky sessions
Increase the health-check interval
Run redundant load balancers (e.g. managed LB or active-passive pair with a floating IP)
questions.explanation: Managed cloud LBs are internally redundant across zones; self-hosted ones use pairs with failover (keepalived/VRRP). Sticky sessions and health-check tuning don't add LB redundancy.

questions.prompt: What is the main downside of sticky sessions compared with a stateless web tier?
options: They break TLS termination
Uneven load, and users lose their session if their server dies
They require HTTP/2
They make DNS lookups slower
questions.explanation: Pinning users to a server creates hotspots and ties session state to one machine, so a crash or scale-in logs users out. A stateless tier with shared session storage avoids both.

questions.prompt: Besides spreading requests, which features does a typical load balancer provide? Select all that apply.
options: Automatic database sharding
Health checking of targets
Connection draining when removing a target
Exactly-once request delivery
TLS termination
questions.explanation: LBs commonly terminate TLS, check health and drain connections during deploys or scale-in. They don't shard databases, and they can't guarantee exactly-once delivery (clients may retry).

questions.prompt: During a rolling deploy behind a load balancer, which practices help avoid dropped requests? Select all that apply.
options: Handle SIGTERM by stopping new accepts and finishing in-flight work
Fail readiness before shutdown so the LB stops sending traffic
Kill all old instances at once, then start the new ones
Deregister the instance and wait for in-flight requests to drain
questions.explanation: Draining, graceful SIGTERM handling and failing readiness first let in-flight requests finish while new ones go elsewhere. Killing everything at once guarantees an outage.

questions.prompt: Round-robin load balancing guarantees equal CPU usage across all servers.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Round-robin equalizes request counts, not cost. Requests differ in CPU and duration, and servers may differ in size, so CPU can be very uneven.

questions.prompt: If web servers are stateless, the load balancer can send consecutive requests from the same user to different servers without breaking anything.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With session and user state stored externally, any server can handle any request, which is what makes scaling out and failover simple.

questions.prompt: In a classic single-primary replication setup, where do writes go?
options: Only to the primary
To the replica with the lowest lag
To any replica, which forwards them
To all replicas in parallel by the client
questions.explanation: Only the primary accepts writes; it streams changes to replicas, which serve reads. Clients writing to replicas would create conflicting histories.

questions.prompt: A user updates their display name, the page reloads, and the old name appears; a second later it's correct. Reads go to replicas. What's the best targeted fix?
options: Route that user's reads to the primary for a short time after their write
Add more replicas
Increase the replica's cache size
Disable replication
questions.explanation: This is replication lag breaking read-your-writes. Reading from the primary (or a replica known to be caught up) right after a user's own write fixes it without sending all reads to the primary. More replicas don't reduce lag.

questions.prompt: With asynchronous replication, the primary crashes and a replica is promoted. What data risk exists?
options: The promoted replica refuses reads until resynced
Writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated may be lost
Indexes must be rebuilt from scratch
All data on the replica is lost
questions.explanation: Async replication acknowledges commits before replicas have them, so the newest writes can vanish on failover. Synchronous replication avoids this at the cost of write latency.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you configure a synchronous standby. What's the main trade-off?
options: Reads on the primary become slower than on the standby
Replication becomes eventually consistent
Commits wait for the standby, raising write latency and stalling writes if it's unavailable
The standby can accept writes too
questions.explanation: With synchronous_standby_names set and synchronous_commit on, each commit waits for standby confirmation: better durability, slower writes, and writes block if no synchronous standby responds. It doesn't make standbys writable.

questions.prompt: After a failover, the old primary comes back online still believing it's the primary, and both accept writes. What is this called and how is it prevented?
options: Cache stampede; prevented by jittered TTLs
Write skew; prevented by SERIALIZABLE isolation
Split brain; prevented by fencing the old primary and consensus-based leader election
Replication lag; prevented by more replicas
questions.explanation: Two primaries accepting writes is split brain, producing divergent data. Fencing (STONITH, revoking access) and a consensus-based failover manager (e.g. Patroni with etcd) ensure only one primary. Isolation levels act within one node.

questions.prompt: With one primary and one replica, the replica goes offline. What typically happens?
options: Writes stop until it's back
Reads are temporarily served by the primary while a new replica is provisioned
The primary is demoted
The application must switch to a different database engine
questions.explanation: Losing the only replica means the primary takes read traffic too (possibly with reduced capacity) until a replacement syncs. Writes are unaffected because they always went to the primary.

questions.prompt: A user refreshes a comments page twice; the first load shows a new comment and the second doesn't. Reads are load-balanced across replicas with different lag. Which guarantee is violated?
options: Monotonic reads
Atomicity
Strong isolation
Durability
questions.explanation: Monotonic reads means a user never sees data go backwards in time. Hitting a fresher replica then a laggier one breaks it; pinning a user's session to one replica is a common fix.

questions.prompt: Which are benefits of a primary/replica database setup? Select all that apply.
options: Write throughput scales linearly with the number of replicas
Replicas in other regions can serve local reads
Read throughput scales by adding replicas
A replica can be promoted if the primary fails
questions.explanation: Replicas spread reads, enable failover and give regional read locality. Every write still goes through the single primary (and is replayed on each replica), so writes don't scale with replicas.

questions.prompt: Reads normally go to replicas. Which reads should still go to the primary? Select all that apply.
options: An internal analytics dashboard refreshed hourly
Checking stock inside the same transaction that decrements it
Showing a user the record they just created
A public list of blog posts
questions.explanation: Read-your-writes and reads that drive a write decision need the latest data, so they belong on the primary. Hourly dashboards and public lists tolerate a little lag and are ideal replica traffic.

questions.prompt: Adding read replicas increases the write capacity of a single-primary database.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: All writes still land on one primary, and each replica must apply them too. Scaling writes requires sharding or a different architecture.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL streaming replication, a hot standby can serve read-only queries but cannot accept writes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A hot standby replays WAL from the primary and allows read-only queries; writes are rejected until it is promoted.

questions.prompt: Which data is the best candidate for a cache?
options: A bank account balance updated on every transaction
Audit logs written once and rarely read
A one-time password valid for a single use
Product catalog details read thousands of times per update
questions.explanation: Caching pays off for data read far more often than it changes. Constantly updated balances risk staleness, OTPs are single-use, and rarely read logs gain nothing from caching.

questions.prompt: What's the main trade-off when choosing a cache TTL?
options: Short TTLs use more memory than long TTLs
TTL only matters for write-through caches
Too short causes frequent misses and DB load; too long serves stale data
Long TTLs make cache reads slower
questions.explanation: TTL balances freshness against hit ratio. Short TTLs reload often (more DB load); long ones keep stale data around. Memory depends on the working set, and read latency doesn't depend on TTL.

questions.prompt: A hot key (homepage feed) expires and thousands of concurrent requests all miss and query the database at once, which slows down sharply. What's the best mitigation?
options: Switch the cache from Redis to Memcached
Let only one request rebuild the key (lock or single-flight) while others wait or get stale data
Add another read replica
Lower the TTL so the key refreshes more often
questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede. Coalescing rebuilds to one request per key (or serving stale while refreshing) protects the DB. A shorter TTL makes stampedes more frequent; a replica only partly absorbs the burst.

questions.prompt: Redis 7 hits maxmemory with maxmemory-policy set to noeviction. What happens when a client issues a SET that needs more memory?
options: Redis returns an out-of-memory error for that command
Redis writes the key to disk instead
Redis silently drops the oldest keys with a TTL
Redis evicts the least recently used key
questions.explanation: With noeviction, commands that would grow memory fail with an OOM error, while reads still work. Evicting keys happens only under policies like allkeys-lru or volatile-lru.

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, which write path best limits stale cache entries?
options: Update the database, then delete the cache key
Update the database, then set the cache to the new value from the request
Only update the cache and sync the DB nightly
Update the cache first, then the database
questions.explanation: Deleting after the DB commit forces the next read to load fresh data. Setting the cache from each writer can race (an older writer's SET lands last), and cache-first leaves stale cache if the DB write fails.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't important data be stored only in the cache?
options: Cache reads are slower than database reads
Caches can't store JSON
Caches only support integer keys
Cache memory can be lost on restart or evicted under pressure
questions.explanation: Caches are typically memory-first and evict keys under memory pressure; even with Redis persistence they aren't the system of record. Keep the source of truth in a durable database.

questions.prompt: The whole app relies on one cache server. What's the main risk and mitigation?
options: Higher latency; use bigger keys
Slower writes; switch to write-behind
Data corruption; disable TTLs
If it fails, the DB is flooded; run multiple cache nodes and size the DB for cold starts
questions.explanation: A single cache node is a SPOF: when it dies, every request falls through to the DB. Replicated or clustered cache nodes and DB headroom (or gradual warm-up) reduce the impact.

questions.prompt: Which techniques help prevent a cache stampede on hot keys? Select all that apply.
options: A per-key lock so only one request rebuilds the value
Random jitter added to TTLs
Giving every key exactly the same TTL
Serving the stale value while refreshing in the background
questions.explanation: Locks/single-flight, jittered TTLs and stale-while-revalidate all spread or coalesce rebuilds. Identical TTLs make many keys expire together, which causes the stampede problem.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine risks introduced by adding a cache? Select all that apply.
options: Serving stale data after the source changes
Guaranteed slower reads for hot keys
Invalidation bugs that are hard to reproduce
A cold cache after restart flooding the database
questions.explanation: Staleness, cold starts and invalidation bugs are the classic caching risks. Hot keys are where a cache is fastest, not slowest.

questions.prompt: With write-through caching, each write updates both the cache and the database as part of the write, so reads right after a write find fresh data in the cache.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Write-through keeps the cache in sync on every write at the cost of write latency and caching data that may never be read.

questions.prompt: A high cache hit ratio proves the cache is serving correct, up-to-date data.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Hit ratio only measures how often reads are served from cache. A cache with a long TTL and broken invalidation can have a great hit ratio while serving stale data.

questions.prompt: What does a CDN mainly do for a web app?
options: Caches content on edge servers close to users
Balances writes across database shards
Runs the application's business logic
Replicates the primary database to every region
questions.explanation: A CDN serves cached (mostly static) content from edge locations near users, cutting latency and origin load. It doesn't replicate your DB or run your core app logic.

questions.prompt: You deploy new CSS, but many users keep getting the old file from the CDN for hours. What's the most robust long-term practice?
options: Set max-age=0 on all assets
