Purge the entire CDN after every deploy
Serve CSS directly from the origin
Use content-hashed file names (app.3f9c1a.css) with long cache lifetimes
questions.explanation: Fingerprinted names make each version a new URL, so you can cache aggressively and never serve stale assets. Purging works but is slow and blunt; max-age=0 or bypassing the CDN throws away its benefit.

questions.prompt: Which Cache-Control directive sets a cache lifetime for shared caches like CDNs, separately from browsers?
options: must-understand
max-stale
s-maxage
no-transform
questions.explanation: s-maxage applies only to shared caches and overrides max-age there, so you can cache longer at the CDN than in browsers. max-stale is a request directive; no-transform blocks content changes.

questions.prompt: The origin server goes down for 10 minutes. Which setup lets the CDN keep serving users?
options: Disabling compression at the edge
Setting Cache-Control: no-store
Using stale-if-error (or the CDN's serve-stale setting) on cacheable responses
Shortening TTLs to 1 second
questions.explanation: stale-if-error lets caches serve expired content when the origin errors, so cached pages stay up during an origin outage. no-store and tiny TTLs mean the edge has nothing usable to serve.

questions.prompt: After putting the whole site behind a CDN, users report seeing someone else's account page. What's the most likely cause?
options: Personalized responses were cacheable, so the edge served one user's page to others
The CDN's TLS certificate expired
The origin is too slow
DNS TTL is too long
questions.explanation: If user-specific responses lack Cache-Control: private/no-store (or vary correctly), a shared cache stores them and serves them to everyone. This is a serious data leak, not a performance issue.

questions.prompt: Why might you avoid putting rarely requested assets on a CDN?
options: Rare files corrupt the CDN cache
You pay for transfer while they rarely get cache hits, so the benefit is small
CDNs can't serve rarely requested files
Rare files make DNS slower
questions.explanation: CDNs bill by data transfer, and rarely requested files mostly miss the edge cache anyway, so cost outweighs benefit. Serve them from origin or object storage.

questions.prompt: Why is URL versioning usually preferred over CDN purge APIs for invalidating static assets?
options: Purge APIs only work for images
Versioning reduces the file size
Purge is instant and free, but versioning is more secure
Purges take time to propagate across edges and can be rate-limited; a new URL is fetched fresh immediately
questions.explanation: A new URL is a cache miss everywhere at once, and old pages keep consistent old assets. Purges propagate across many edges with delay and often have limits.

questions.prompt: Which are good candidates to serve through a CDN? Select all that apply.
options: Video segments for streaming
POST requests that create orders
Public API responses that are fine to cache for 30 seconds
A user's current account balance
Images, JS and CSS bundles
questions.explanation: Static assets, media segments and short-lived public responses cache well at the edge. Personal balances and order-creating POSTs must reach the origin every time.

questions.prompt: Which are benefits of a CDN? Select all that apply.
options: Less bandwidth and load on the origin
Absorbing traffic spikes and some DDoS traffic at the edge
Strong consistency for frequently changing data
Lower latency for geographically distant users
questions.explanation: CDNs cut latency, offload origin and absorb spikes. Edge caches are by nature eventually consistent, so they're a poor fit for frequently changing data needing strong consistency.

questions.prompt: On a cache miss, a CDN edge typically fetches the object from the origin, returns it, and caches it according to its cache headers.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That's the standard pull-CDN flow: miss, fetch from origin, store with the TTL from Cache-Control (or CDN rules), serve later requests from the edge.

questions.prompt: Setting Cache-Control: max-age=31536000 on index.html is a safe way to speed up a single-page app.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: index.html references the hashed bundles; caching it for a year means users won't see new deploys. Cache hashed assets long and keep index.html short-lived or revalidated.

questions.prompt: What does a stateless web tier mean?
options: Servers don't keep per-user state locally; it lives in a shared store or the client
Servers never read from a database
Servers don't use HTTP cookies
Servers restart after every request
questions.explanation: Stateless servers keep no user-specific data in memory or local disk between requests; session data goes to a shared store (or a signed token). They still use databases and cookies.

questions.prompt: After scaling from 1 to 3 servers, users are randomly logged out. The app uses express-session with the default in-memory store. What's the cause?
options: The session secret differs on each request
The load balancer strips cookies
Cookies are too large for three servers
Sessions live in one process's memory, so other servers don't recognize the session
questions.explanation: MemoryStore keeps sessions per process. When the LB sends a request to a different server, that session doesn't exist there. Use a shared store like Redis. (The default MemoryStore isn't meant for production anyway.)

questions.prompt: Which is the most common choice for a shared session store in a horizontally scaled web tier?
options: Environment variables
The load balancer's memory
Redis with key expiry
Each server's local SQLite file
questions.explanation: Redis gives fast lookups from any server, and TTLs naturally expire old sessions. Local files and LB memory aren't shared state; env vars aren't per-user storage.

questions.prompt: You switch to stateless JWT sessions with 7-day expiry. A user's laptop is stolen and they want all sessions revoked now. What's the core problem?
options: Valid JWTs keep working until expiry unless you add a denylist or short expiry with refresh tokens
JWTs can't contain a user id
JWTs require sticky sessions
Revocation is automatic because JWTs are signed
questions.explanation: Signature checks don't consult server state, so a stolen token stays valid until exp. Common fixes: short-lived access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens, or a denylist/token version check, which reintroduces some state.

questions.prompt: What's the biggest operational benefit of a stateless web tier?
options: Responses can never be cached
No need for a database
Instances can be added or removed freely, enabling autoscaling
Requests never need authentication
questions.explanation: Because no instance holds unique state, autoscaling can add or terminate servers without losing user data. Statelessness doesn't remove databases or auth.

questions.prompt: Sessions are in a single Redis instance. It crashes. What happens and what's the right mitigation?
options: Every user is logged out or requests fail; use replicated Redis with automatic failover
The load balancer recreates sessions from its logs
Nothing; sessions fall back to cookies automatically
Only writes fail; logins continue
questions.explanation: A single session store becomes a new SPOF for the stateless tier. Redis Sentinel or a managed replicated Redis gives failover; apps should also degrade gracefully (e.g. clear error, re-login) rather than crash.

questions.prompt: Users upload avatars that are saved to the web server's local disk, then later requests can't find them. What's the stateless fix?
options: Store uploads in shared object storage (e.g. S3) and keep only the key
Copy files to every server with a cron job
Enable sticky sessions for upload routes
Store images in the session cookie
questions.explanation: Local disk is per-instance state. Object storage is shared, durable and serves any instance (and pairs well with a CDN). Sticky sessions or rsync jobs are fragile workarounds.

questions.prompt: Which of these make a Node.js web server stateful? Select all that apply.
options: Per-process in-memory rate-limit counters
A module-level Map of logged-in sessions
Reading configuration from env vars at startup
Saving uploaded files to local disk for later download
questions.explanation: Sessions, local files and in-memory counters are per-instance state that breaks behind a load balancer. Startup config read identically on every instance isn't per-user state.

questions.prompt: Which are valid places to keep session state for a horizontally scaled web tier? Select all that apply.
options: A database sessions table
A shared Redis cluster
A signed cookie or token holding the claims
A global variable in the Node process
questions.explanation: Shared stores (Redis, DB) or client-held signed tokens work with any server. A process global is lost on restart and invisible to other instances.

questions.prompt: Sticky sessions are a full substitute for a stateless web tier because sessions survive server crashes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: With sticky sessions, the session still lives on one server; if it crashes or is scaled in, those users lose their session. Stickiness also skews load.

questions.prompt: Moving session data to a shared store lets any web server handle any request from the same user.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Every server looks up the session in the same store, so routing no longer matters, which is the point of a stateless tier.

questions.prompt: With two data centers (US-East and EU-West), how are users usually routed to the nearest one?
options: GeoDNS or anycast routes them by location
Clients pick a region from a dropdown
The database decides on each query
Each web server forwards to the other region randomly
questions.explanation: GeoDNS returns region-specific IPs based on the resolver's location, and anycast advertises the same IP from multiple sites. Manual selection or app-level forwarding is not the standard approach.

questions.prompt: EU-West goes completely offline. In a well-designed active-active setup, what should happen?
options: EU users see errors until EU-West recovers
DNS is updated manually by the on-call engineer the next day
All traffic is routed to US-East, which needs enough headroom to absorb it
EU users are switched to read-only mode permanently
questions.explanation: Healthy regions take over failed-region traffic via health-checked routing, which only works if they have spare capacity or can autoscale quickly. Planning for N+1 regional capacity is part of the design.

questions.prompt: Each region has its own database and changes replicate asynchronously across regions. A region fails suddenly. What's the main data risk?
options: All data in the surviving region is corrupted
Cross-region replication speeds up and causes duplicates
Recent writes not yet replicated may be lost or arrive late
Indexes in the surviving region become invalid
questions.explanation: Async cross-region replication trades durability for latency: the last few seconds of writes in the failed region may not have reached the survivor. Synchronous cross-region replication avoids it but adds large write latency.

questions.prompt: You fail over by changing DNS, but traffic to the dead region trickles on for a long time. What's the most likely reason?
options: Resolvers and clients cache the old records until TTL expires (some ignore TTL)
Anycast always prefers the dead region
Load balancers ignore DNS changes
TLS certificates are region-specific
questions.explanation: DNS failover is limited by caching: long TTLs and resolvers that hold records longer delay the switch. Short TTLs on failover records, or anycast/global load balancers, react faster.

questions.prompt: In an active-active multi-region database, the same user profile is edited in both regions within a second. Which approach avoids silent data loss?
options: Retry the write until it succeeds in both regions
Give each user a home region that owns their writes (or use CRDT-style merges)
Ignore conflicts because they are rare
Last-write-wins by timestamp
questions.explanation: Last-write-wins silently discards one edit (and depends on clock accuracy). Routing a user's writes to a single home region avoids conflicts; CRDTs merge concurrent edits deterministically for suitable data types.

questions.prompt: Why is synchronous database replication between continents usually avoided on the write path?
options: Continents use different SQL dialects
Synchronous replication doesn't work over TLS
Each write waits a cross-continent round trip, often 100 ms or more
It breaks primary keys
questions.explanation: Light in fiber across an ocean plus routing gives ~70–150+ ms RTT, which every synchronous commit pays. Most designs use async cross-region replication and accept a small data-loss window, or keep synchronous replicas within a region.

questions.prompt: What helps keep multiple data centers running the same, correct version of the service?
options: Automated, identical deployment pipelines for every region
Deploying only to the primary region
Manual SSH deploys region by region
Letting each region choose its own release schedule
questions.explanation: Automated pipelines (ideally staged region by region with health checks) keep regions consistent and testable. Manual or ad-hoc regional deploys drift and cause region-specific bugs.

questions.prompt: Which are key technical challenges of running in multiple data centers? Select all that apply.
options: Synchronizing data across regions
Redirecting traffic to a healthy region
Keeping tests and deploys consistent across regions
Eliminating the need for backups
questions.explanation: Traffic redirection, data sync and deployment consistency are the classic multi-DC challenges. Replicas across regions don't replace backups; a bad write or delete replicates everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which practices reduce the blast radius of a regional failure? Select all that apply.
options: Avoiding synchronous cross-region calls in the request path
A single global primary database for all writes
Regular failover drills
Regions that can serve requests without calling other regions
questions.explanation: Independent regions, drills and no cross-region synchronous dependencies keep one region's failure contained. A single global write primary means its region's outage stops writes everywhere.

questions.prompt: In an active-passive multi-region setup, the passive region needs enough capacity, or the ability to scale up fast, to take full traffic on failover.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A passive region sized too small just fails under the redirected load. It needs provisioned capacity or fast autoscaling, plus warm data.

questions.prompt: Running in two data centers automatically gives strong consistency between them.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Most multi-DC setups replicate asynchronously and are eventually consistent. Strong consistency across regions requires synchronous replication or consensus, at a latency cost.

questions.prompt: What is the core reason to put a message queue between a web server and a worker?
options: To decouple them so the producer doesn't wait and each side scales independently
To make every request return the worker's result faster
To replace the database
To guarantee requests are processed in strict global order
questions.explanation: A queue lets the web tier enqueue work and respond immediately, while workers consume at their own pace and scale separately. It doesn't return results synchronously, replace storage, or guarantee global ordering.

questions.prompt: A photo app enqueues resize jobs. At peak, queue depth climbs steadily for an hour. What's the most appropriate response?
options: Drop the oldest jobs to keep the queue short
Make the web servers process resizes synchronously
Increase the queue's maximum message size
Scale out workers, ideally autoscaling on queue depth or message age
questions.explanation: A growing backlog means consumers are slower than producers; adding workers (driven by depth/oldest-message age) catches up. Dropping jobs loses work; synchronous processing brings back the latency the queue was meant to hide.

questions.prompt: Your queue offers at-least-once delivery. A worker sends a welcome email, then crashes before acking. What must the design handle?
options: The producer is notified and resends it
The message is redelivered, so processing must be idempotent
The message is lost forever
The queue switches to exactly-once mode
questions.explanation: Unacked messages are redelivered, so the same job may run twice (duplicate email). Idempotency keys or dedupe records make repeats harmless. At-least-once avoids loss, not duplicates.

questions.prompt: One malformed message makes the consumer throw every time, and it keeps being redelivered, blocking progress. What's the standard fix?
options: Delete the whole queue and re-enqueue jobs
Restart the consumer every minute
Increase the visibility timeout to one day
After N failed attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
questions.explanation: A dead-letter queue isolates poison messages after a retry limit so other messages flow, and lets you inspect and replay them. Longer timeouts only slow the retry loop.

questions.prompt: Events for each user must be processed in order, but you need many consumers in parallel. Which design fits in Kafka?
options: Partition by userId so a user's events land in one partition
One partition for the whole topic
Random partitioning with a timestamp sort in consumers
One topic per user
questions.explanation: Kafka orders messages within a partition. Keying by userId keeps each user's events ordered while different partitions are consumed in parallel. One partition kills parallelism; per-user topics don't scale.

questions.prompt: Which metric best signals that consumers are falling behind?
options: Number of queues defined
Age of the oldest unprocessed message (or consumer lag)
Producer CPU usage
Average message size
questions.explanation: Oldest-message age or consumer lag directly shows how far behind processing is. Producer CPU and message size don't tell you whether consumers are keeping up.

questions.prompt: All workers are down for 10 minutes for a deploy. What happens to new jobs with a durable queue?
options: They're rejected by the queue
They wait in the queue and are processed when workers return
They're processed by the web servers instead
They're lost unless the producer retries
questions.explanation: A durable queue buffers messages while consumers are unavailable, which is a key benefit of decoupling. Producers keep enqueuing and workers catch up afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which are benefits of introducing a message queue? Select all that apply.
options: Automatic exactly-once processing
Absorbing traffic spikes
Isolating failures so slow workers don't break the web tier
Scaling producers and consumers independently
Returning the worker's result synchronously to the user
questions.explanation: Queues buffer spikes, decouple scaling and isolate failures. They make processing asynchronous (no synchronous result), and most give at-least-once, not exactly-once, semantics.

questions.prompt: Which practices make at-least-once message processing safe? Select all that apply.
options: Record processed message or idempotency IDs and skip repeats
Use upserts or conditional writes instead of blind inserts
Ack the message before doing the work
Ack only after the work has committed
questions.explanation: Dedupe records, ack-after-commit and idempotent writes make redeliveries harmless without losing work. Acking first means a crash mid-work loses the job.

questions.prompt: Acking a message before the work is done risks losing that work if the consumer crashes mid-processing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Once acked, the broker deletes or advances past the message, so a crash means it's never retried. That's at-most-once behaviour.

questions.prompt: Publishing to a message queue tells the producer whether the consumer's processing succeeded.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The producer only learns that the broker accepted the message. Processing outcomes need a separate channel (status table, callback, reply queue).

questions.prompt: With 30 web servers, why centralize logs (e.g. into ELK, Loki or a hosted service)?
options: Because local logs can't be rotated
So servers can skip writing logs
So you can search and correlate logs across all servers in one place
Because centralized logs are free
questions.explanation: SSHing into 30 machines to grep doesn't work, and instances get replaced. Central aggregation gives search, correlation and retention across the fleet.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a business metric rather than a host or service metric?
options: Database replication lag
Daily active users
CPU utilization on web servers
p99 request latency
questions.explanation: Business metrics (DAU, sign-ups, revenue, retention) show product health. CPU is a host metric; replication lag and p99 latency are service/tier metrics.

questions.prompt: A request touches the API, an auth service and a worker. How do you find all log lines for one failing request?
options: Sort all logs by timestamp
Increase log verbosity to debug everywhere
Log the client IP only
Propagate a request/correlation ID and include it in every structured log line
questions.explanation: A correlation (trace) ID passed through headers and messages and written into every log line lets you filter one request across services. Timestamps interleave thousands of requests; IPs aren't unique per request.

questions.prompt: On-call gets paged dozens of times a night for brief CPU spikes that don't affect users. What's the better alerting approach?
options: Page on every warning log line instead
Raise the CPU threshold to 99%
Alert on user-facing symptoms like error rate or latency SLO burn, and keep CPU on dashboards
Disable alerting at night
questions.explanation: Paging on symptoms that hurt users (errors, latency, SLO burn rate) cuts noise and alert fatigue. Cause metrics like CPU belong on dashboards or low-urgency tickets. Tweaking one threshold just moves the noise.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a userId label to a Prometheus request counter. Soon the monitoring system slows and memory explodes. Why?
options: userId values are too long for the exposition format
Each unique label value creates a new time series, so cardinality explodes
Prometheus only supports numeric labels
Counters can't have labels
questions.explanation: Every label combination is its own series; millions of users means millions of series. Keep labels low-cardinality (route, status, method) and put per-user detail in logs or traces.

questions.prompt: Average API latency is 80 ms, but some users complain of very slow responses. Which metric should you check?
options: Average response size
Total request count
Median CPU usage
p99 (or p95) latency
questions.explanation: Averages hide the tail: a few multi-second requests barely move the mean. High percentiles show what the slowest users experience.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a CI/CD pipeline that runs tests and deploys automatically?
options: It removes the need for code review
It removes the need for monitoring
It makes production immune to bugs
Consistent, repeatable releases with fewer manual mistakes
questions.explanation: Automation makes builds, tests and deploys repeatable and fast, catching regressions early. It doesn't replace review or monitoring, and bugs still reach production.

questions.prompt: Which are the four 'golden signals' for monitoring a service? Select all that apply.
options: Number of git commits
Traffic
Saturation
Lines of code deployed
Errors
Latency
questions.explanation: Google's SRE golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Code volume and commit counts say nothing about user-facing health.

questions.prompt: Which practices make logs useful at scale? Select all that apply.
options: Structured (JSON) log lines
A correlation ID on every line
Logging full request bodies, including passwords
Consistent log levels so noise can be filtered
questions.explanation: Structured fields, correlation IDs and consistent levels make logs searchable and filterable. Logging secrets is a security incident waiting to happen; redact sensitive fields.

questions.prompt: Average latency alone is enough to detect a regression that makes 2% of requests ten times slower.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A 2% slow tail shifts the mean only modestly and can be lost in normal variance, but it shows clearly in p99. Track percentiles, not just averages.

questions.prompt: A canary deployment routes a small share of traffic to the new version and watches metrics before rolling out fully.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Canaries limit the blast radius of a bad release: if error rate or latency worsens on the canary, you roll back before most users are affected.

questions.prompt: What does database sharding mean?
options: Splitting a table's columns into separate tables
Splitting data across multiple databases by a shard key, each holding a subset
Compressing a database into smaller files
Copying the full dataset to several read replicas
questions.explanation: Sharding is horizontal partitioning across database instances: each shard has the same schema but different rows. Replicas hold full copies; splitting columns is vertical partitioning.

questions.prompt: A social app shards by user_id. One celebrity's shard is overwhelmed with reads and writes while others idle. What's this problem and a reasonable fix?
options: Split brain; add fencing
A hotspot; give the celebrity a dedicated shard or further split their data
Replication lag; add synchronous replicas
Write skew; use SERIALIZABLE isolation
questions.explanation: A single very hot key overloads one shard (the celebrity problem). Fixes include dedicated shards, sub-partitioning that key's data, or caching its reads heavily. Replication lag and split brain are unrelated.

questions.prompt: After sharding users and orders by user_id, a report needs to join orders across all users by product. What's the typical approach?
options: Disable sharding for reporting queries
Run the join as a normal SQL JOIN; the database handles shards transparently
Scatter-gather across shards, or feed an analytics store or denormalized table for reporting
Use foreign keys across shards
questions.explanation: Joins across shards aren't native; you query every shard and merge, or replicate data into a warehouse or denormalized view built for that query. Cross-shard foreign keys aren't enforceable.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant B2B SaaS shards by tenant_id. Most queries are within one tenant. What's the main risk of this choice?
options: Tenants can see each other's data by default
IDs can no longer be generated
Queries for one tenant must touch every shard
A few very large tenants can overload their shard
questions.explanation: tenant_id keeps each tenant's queries on one shard (great locality), but tenant sizes are skewed, so a giant tenant becomes a hotspot. Mitigate by isolating large tenants on dedicated shards.

questions.prompt: Keys are placed on shards with consistent hashing across N nodes. You add one node. Roughly how many keys move?
options: None; only new keys go to the new node
Almost all of them
About half
About 1/(N+1) of them
questions.explanation: With consistent hashing the new node takes over only its portion of the ring, about 1/(N+1) of keys. Modulo hashing (key % N) remaps most keys when N changes.

questions.prompt: When is sharding usually the right next step?
options: As soon as the product launches
When write volume or data size exceeds what one primary can handle, after simpler options
When you want to avoid creating indexes
Whenever read traffic grows
questions.explanation: Sharding adds major complexity, so teams first try vertical scaling, indexing, caching and read replicas. It's warranted when writes or data volume outgrow a single primary.

questions.prompt: Each shard uses its own auto-increment primary key. What problem appears, and what's a common fix?
options: IDs leak tenant names; hash them
Shards can't use indexes; use hash keys
IDs collide across shards; use globally unique IDs like Snowflake-style IDs or UUIDv7
Auto-increment stops working past 1M rows; use strings
questions.explanation: Independent sequences produce the same IDs on different shards. Snowflake-style IDs (time + machine + sequence) or UUIDv7 are unique globally and roughly time-ordered, which keeps B-tree inserts efficient.

questions.prompt: Which challenges does sharding introduce? Select all that apply.
options: Hotspots when keys are unevenly accessed
Resharding data when shards fill up
Indexes can no longer be used
Cross-shard joins and transactions become hard
questions.explanation: Resharding, hotspots and cross-shard queries/transactions are the core sharding costs. Each shard is a normal database and uses indexes normally.

questions.prompt: Which are properties of a good shard key? Select all that apply.
options: A monotonically increasing timestamp used with range sharding
Matches the most common query pattern
High cardinality
Spreads load evenly across shards
questions.explanation: Good keys have many distinct values, distribute evenly and keep common queries on one shard. A rising timestamp with range sharding sends every new write to the newest shard.

questions.prompt: Range sharding on created_at sends nearly all new writes to the shard holding the latest range.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: New rows always have the newest timestamps, so they land on one shard, creating a write hotspot while older shards sit idle.

questions.prompt: After sharding, a transaction spanning two shards is as simple and cheap as a single-node ACID transaction.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Cross-shard atomicity needs two-phase commit, sagas or similar coordination, which add latency and failure modes. That's why shard keys are chosen to keep transactions on one shard.

questions.prompt: Users upload 200 MB videos. Why is a presigned S3 PUT URL usually better than streaming the upload through your Node.js API server?
options: The client uploads directly to object storage, so large bytes never tie up your API servers' bandwidth, memory and connections
Presigned URLs make the object publicly readable forever
Presigned URLs compress the file automatically
S3 rejects uploads that pass through an application server
questions.explanation: Direct-to-storage uploads offload the heavy transfer to S3, which scales for it, while your API only issues a short-lived signed URL. They do not compress anything, and a presigned PUT grants upload permission, not public read access.

questions.prompt: What does a presigned URL actually contain that authorises the request?
options: A one-time password emailed to the user
Your AWS secret access key in plain text
A session cookie for the user
A signature computed with the issuer's credentials over the method, bucket/key, expiry and other parameters, which S3 verifies
questions.explanation: The URL carries the access key id, expiry and an HMAC-based signature (SigV4) over the request details; S3 recomputes and checks it. The secret key itself is never included, and changing the method or key invalidates the signature.

questions.prompt: A presigned download URL for a private invoice leaks in a support chat. What property limits the damage most?
options: Cross-region replication
Bucket versioning
Server-side encryption with S3-managed keys
A short expiry on the presigned URL (e.g. minutes), after which it no longer works
questions.explanation: Anyone with a valid presigned URL can use it until it expires, so short expiries bound exposure. Server-side encryption protects data at rest but S3 decrypts it transparently for any authorised request, including a leaked presigned URL.

questions.prompt: After a client uploads to a presigned URL, how should your backend learn the upload finished and is valid?
options: Trust the client's 'upload done' call without checking anything
Poll the bucket listing every second
Assume success once the presigned URL was issued
Use a storage event notification (or have the client confirm and the server HEAD the object) and then validate size/type before marking it usable
questions.explanation: Issuing a URL does not mean an upload happened. Event notifications (e.g. S3 to SQS/Lambda) or a confirm-then-HEAD check, followed by validation (and malware scanning if needed), are reliable. Bucket listing polls are slow and costly.

questions.prompt: Uploads of multi-GB files over mobile networks often fail near the end and restart from zero. What should you use?
options: Base64-encode the file before uploading
A longer expiry on a single presigned PUT
Upload through a WebSocket to your API
Multipart upload: split into parts uploaded (and retried) independently, then complete the upload to assemble them
questions.explanation: S3 multipart upload lets parts upload in parallel and retry individually, then a CompleteMultipartUpload call stitches them together (each part can get its own presigned URL). A longer expiry does not fix restarting from zero, and base64 inflates size by about 33%.

questions.prompt: Why is object storage like S3 a poor fit as the primary store for a frequently updated user-profile record?
options: Objects cannot exceed 1 MB
Objects are replaced whole on every write (no partial updates or queries on fields), and per-request latency is higher than a database
S3 does not support HTTPS
Object storage has no notion of keys
questions.explanation: Object stores are optimised for large immutable blobs: you PUT the whole object, cannot query by field, and pay tens of ms per request. Small mutable, queryable records belong in a database. S3 objects can be up to 5 TB.

questions.prompt: A presigned PUT URL is issued for key `avatars/123.png` with no constraints. What abuse is possible?
options: The client can delete the whole bucket
The client can read every object in the bucket
The client can upload any content of any size (e.g. a 5 GB file or HTML instead of an image) to that key until the URL expires
The client can change the bucket policy
questions.explanation: A presigned PUT allows exactly one operation on one key, but without constraints the content is unchecked. Use a presigned POST policy with content-length-range and content-type conditions, short expiries, and server-side validation after upload.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices for serving user-uploaded files from object storage? Select all that apply.
options: Serve files from a separate domain to avoid uploaded HTML/JS running on your main app origin
Keep the bucket private and issue short-lived presigned GET URLs (or use a CDN with signed URLs/cookies)
Make the bucket public-read so the CDN can cache everything
Set lifecycle rules to delete abandoned incomplete multipart uploads
Use random or unguessable object keys rather than sequential ids
questions.explanation: Private buckets with signed access, unguessable keys, a separate serving domain and lifecycle cleanup are standard. Public-read buckets expose all private uploads; a CDN can use origin access control to read a private bucket instead.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Amazon S3 are correct today? Select all that apply.
options: S3 supports appending bytes to the middle of an existing standard object in place
Storage classes (e.g. Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier) trade retrieval cost/latency for cheaper storage
S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs of objects
A single object can be up to 5 TB
questions.explanation: Since December 2020, S3 is strongly consistent for object reads after writes; objects can be 5 TB; storage classes trade access cost for storage cost. Standard objects are immutable, so you cannot edit bytes in place; you rewrite the object.

questions.prompt: A presigned URL can grant more permission than the IAM identity that signed it has.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A presigned URL acts with the signer's permissions; if the signer lacks access (or its temporary credentials expire), the URL fails even before its own expiry. Sign with a narrowly scoped role.

questions.prompt: Putting a CDN in front of object storage reduces latency for globally distributed users and cuts egress requests to the bucket for popular files.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Edge caches serve repeat requests close to users, so the origin bucket sees only cache misses. Private content can still be protected with signed URLs or cookies at the CDN.

questions.prompt: What is an inverted index in Elasticsearch?
options: A cache of the most recent queries
A B-tree on the document id sorted in descending order
A map from each term to the list of documents (and positions) that contain it
A copy of the index stored in reverse byte order
questions.explanation: Lucene, under Elasticsearch, maps terms to posting lists of document ids, so finding documents containing 'timeout' is a lookup rather than a scan. That is why full-text search is fast where a SQL LIKE '%timeout%' scans every row.

questions.prompt: A product search for 'Running Shoes' must match a document containing 'running shoe'. Which Elasticsearch feature makes this work?
options: Doc values
Index replicas
Analyzers: tokenising and normalising text (lowercasing, stemming) at index time and query time
Shard routing
questions.explanation: An analyzer splits text into tokens and applies filters like lowercase and stemming, so both sides normalise to 'run' and 'shoe'. Replicas and routing are about distribution; doc values are a column store for sorting and aggregations.

questions.prompt: In Elasticsearch, what is the difference between `text` and `keyword` field types?
options: They are the same type with different names
`keyword` is analysed; `text` is stored exactly
`text` is analysed into tokens for full-text search; `keyword` stores the exact value for filtering, sorting and aggregations
`text` fields are limited to 256 characters
questions.explanation: Use `text` for search over prose and `keyword` for exact matches like status codes, ids or tags, and for terms aggregations. A term query on an analysed `text` field often surprises people because the stored tokens are lowercased/split.

questions.prompt: Why can't you change the number of primary shards of an existing Elasticsearch index in place?
options: Primary shard count is limited to 1 for indexes over 1 GB
Shards are stored on separate clusters
Documents are routed to a primary shard by hash(routing) mod number_of_primary_shards, so changing the count would invalidate every document's location
Replica count also cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Routing depends on the shard count, so changing it needs a reindex (or the split/shrink APIs, which create a new index). Replica count, by contrast, can be changed at any time.

questions.prompt: A document is indexed successfully, but an immediate search does not return it. A second later it appears. Why?
options: The document was routed to the wrong shard at first
The replica shard rejected the write
The analyzer runs asynchronously once per minute
Elasticsearch search is near real-time: new documents become searchable after a refresh (default every 1 s) creates a new segment
questions.explanation: Indexed documents are written to a buffer and become visible to search at the next refresh (default 1 second for indexes that are being searched). A GET by id can still read it immediately. You can force refresh=wait_for on writes, at a throughput cost.

questions.prompt: A team creates a new index per day with 5 primaries and 1 replica, keeping 2 years of small log indexes. The cluster becomes slow and unstable. What is the most likely cause?
options: Daily indexes are not supported
The inverted index is too large
Oversharding: thousands of tiny shards, each with fixed memory and cluster-state overhead
Too few replicas
questions.explanation: 730 indexes × 10 shards = 7,300 shards, mostly tiny. Each shard has overhead on the master and data nodes. Use fewer primaries, rollover by size (e.g. tens of GB per shard via ILM) and delete or shrink old data.

questions.prompt: Why is Elasticsearch usually NOT used as the primary system of record for orders, with the database as the source of truth instead?
options: Elasticsearch has no replication
Elasticsearch cannot handle more than 1 million documents
Elasticsearch cannot store JSON documents
It lacks multi-document ACID transactions and is near real-time, so it is better as a derived index rebuilt from the source of truth
questions.explanation: Search indexes are optimised for querying, not transactional integrity: no multi-document transactions, refresh delays and mapping changes that need reindexing. Keep the database authoritative and sync to Elasticsearch via CDC or events so you can rebuild it.

questions.prompt: How do replica shards help an Elasticsearch cluster? Select all that apply.
options: They let you increase the primary shard count later
They can serve search requests, increasing read throughput
They increase write throughput because writes go only to replicas
They provide failover if a node holding the primary is lost
questions.explanation: Replicas give redundancy and spread search load. Writes go to the primary and are then replicated, so replicas add write work rather than reducing it, and they have nothing to do with changing the primary count.

questions.prompt: You keep a PostgreSQL products table in sync with an Elasticsearch index. Which approaches are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Periodic full reindex into a new index plus alias swap to repair drift
Change data capture (e.g. Debezium reading the WAL) streaming changes to an indexer
Dual writes from the API: write PostgreSQL, then Elasticsearch, with no retry or reconciliation
Transactional outbox events consumed by an indexer that upserts by product id
Use external versioning (e.g. the row's updated version) so out-of-order updates don't overwrite newer data
questions.explanation: CDC or outbox give reliable change streams; versioned upserts handle reordering; alias-swapped reindexes repair drift with zero downtime. Unprotected dual writes leave the two stores inconsistent whenever the second write fails.

questions.prompt: Deep pagination with `from` + `size` (e.g. page 10,000) is cheap in Elasticsearch because each shard returns only the requested page.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Each shard must collect from + size top hits and the coordinator merges them all, so cost grows with depth; index.max_result_window defaults to 10,000. Use search_after (with a point-in-time) for deep paging.

questions.prompt: Elasticsearch ranks full-text matches by default using BM25 relevance scoring.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Since Elasticsearch 5, the default similarity is BM25, which considers term frequency (with saturation), inverse document frequency and field length. Plain TF-IDF was the older default.

questions.prompt: Which workload is a typical OLTP workload?
options: A dashboard of average session length per country
Training a churn model on all customer history
A checkout flow inserting an order and updating stock for one customer in milliseconds
Monthly revenue by region over 3 years of data
questions.explanation: OLTP is many small, short transactions touching few rows with low latency. The other options scan and aggregate large data volumes, which is OLAP territory.

questions.prompt: Why are columnar stores (e.g. BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse) faster for analytical queries like SUM(amount) GROUP BY country over billions of rows?
options: They store each column contiguously, so a query reads only the columns it needs and compresses them very well
They use B-tree indexes on every column
They keep all data in RAM
They enforce foreign keys more efficiently
questions.explanation: Reading 2 of 50 columns means scanning a fraction of the bytes, and same-typed column data compresses and vectorises well. Row stores must read whole rows. Columnar warehouses usually avoid per-row B-tree indexes rather than adding them everywhere.

questions.prompt: Analysts run heavy reporting queries directly on the production PostgreSQL primary, and checkout latency spikes every morning. What is the best long-term fix?
options: Move analytics to a separate store (a read replica short-term, a data warehouse fed by CDC/ETL long-term)
Add more indexes to every table
Increase max_connections
Run reports at noon instead
questions.explanation: Isolating analytical load protects OLTP latency; a warehouse also suits large scans with columnar storage. More indexes slow writes and don't fix big scans, and more connections increase contention.

questions.prompt: In a star schema, what are fact and dimension tables?
options: Facts hold only aggregates; dimensions hold raw logs
Facts are lookup tables; dimensions are event tables
Facts hold measurable events (e.g. order lines with amount, quantity) with keys to dimensions; dimensions hold descriptive attributes (customer, product, date)
Both are fully normalised to 3NF to save space
questions.explanation: A central fact table of events references denormalised dimension tables used to filter and group. Star schemas deliberately denormalise dimensions for simpler, faster analytical joins, unlike 3NF OLTP design.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL loads directly into OLTP databases only
ETL is for streaming; ELT is only batch
ETL transforms data before loading into the warehouse; ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse (e.g. with SQL/dbt)
ELT cannot handle JSON
questions.explanation: Modern cloud warehouses are powerful enough to transform in place, so ELT keeps raw data and makes transformations reproducible SQL. ETL transforms in a separate engine before loading. Both can be batch or near-real-time.

questions.prompt: Why do OLTP schemas tend to be normalised while warehouse schemas are often denormalised?
options: Normalisation avoids update anomalies for frequent small writes; warehouses are mostly append/read-heavy, so denormalising cuts expensive joins over huge scans
Denormalised schemas are required for ACID
Warehouses don't support joins
Normalised schemas use more disk
questions.explanation: OLTP writes constantly, so storing each fact once keeps updates consistent. Analytical data is loaded in batches and read massively; duplicating attributes trades storage for faster queries. Warehouses do support joins, just at a higher cost at scale.

questions.prompt: A product dimension changes a product's category. Analysts need last year's revenue to stay attributed to the old category. Which technique handles this?
options: Overwrite the category in place (SCD Type 1)
Store the category only in the fact table's JSON
Delete the old product row
A Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2: add a new row with a new surrogate key and validity dates, keeping the old row for historical facts
questions.explanation: SCD Type 2 versions dimension rows, so old facts keep pointing to the old version while new facts use the new one. Type 1 overwrites history, so last year's revenue would move to the new category.

questions.prompt: Which are characteristics of OLAP workloads? Select all that apply.
options: Mostly read-heavy with bulk or streaming loads
Data often lags the source by minutes or hours
Queries scan and aggregate many rows
Each query touches only a few columns of wide tables
High volume of single-row updates with strict millisecond latency
questions.explanation: OLAP scans and aggregates, reads more than it writes, accepts some freshness lag and typically touches few columns. Frequent single-row low-latency updates describe OLTP.

questions.prompt: A product team wants a real-time dashboard (seconds-fresh) of orders per minute at high scale. Which options are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Use a materialised/rollup table in the analytical store refreshed incrementally
Use a nightly batch ETL into the warehouse
Stream order events (e.g. Kafka) into a real-time OLAP store like ClickHouse or Apache Druid
Maintain pre-aggregated per-minute counters updated by a stream processor
Run COUNT(*) on the OLTP orders table every second from every dashboard viewer
questions.explanation: Streaming into a real-time OLAP store, stream-processor counters and incremental rollups all give seconds-fresh results without loading OLTP. Polling COUNT(*) per viewer hammers production, and nightly ETL is far too stale.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL read replica is a full replacement for a data warehouse for large-scale analytics.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A replica isolates load from the primary but is still a row store with the OLTP schema, so huge scans and joins stay slow, and long queries can conflict with replication (query cancellation or bloat). It's a stopgap, not a warehouse.

questions.prompt: Columnar storage makes updating a single row expensive compared with a row store, which is one reason warehouses favour batch appends.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A row's values are spread across many compressed column files, so a point update touches many of them; columnar engines handle updates via deletes plus appends and background merges. Hence batch or append-heavy ingestion.

questions.prompt: A Bloom filter says an element is 'possibly present' or 'definitely not present'. What kind of error can it make?
options: Both false positives and false negatives
False negatives only
No errors, it is exact
False positives only: it may say present when the item was never added
questions.explanation: Bits are only ever set, never cleared, so an added item always finds its bits set (no false negatives). Other items can set the same bits, giving false positives at a rate that depends on size, hash count and fill.

questions.prompt: A URL shortener wants to check whether a randomly generated short code is already taken without querying the database for most new codes. What is a good use of a Bloom filter here?
options: Use the Bloom filter to delete expired codes
Use the Bloom filter to count how many times each code is clicked
If the filter says 'definitely not present', accept the code without a DB lookup; if 'possibly present', check the database
Store all codes in the Bloom filter and skip the database entirely for every check
questions.explanation: 'Not present' answers are reliable, so most new codes avoid a DB round-trip; 'maybe' answers fall back to the source of truth. Trusting the filter alone would reject free codes on false positives, and plain Bloom filters can't delete or count.

questions.prompt: Why can't you remove an item from a standard Bloom filter?
options: Removal would require rehashing all items
The hash functions are not reversible
Clearing its bits could clear bits shared with other items, creating false negatives
Bloom filters are stored on disk only
questions.explanation: Multiple items share bits, so clearing one item's bits can make other items appear absent. Counting Bloom filters (counters instead of bits) or Cuckoo filters support deletion at extra space cost.

questions.prompt: Which problem is HyperLogLog designed to solve?
options: Estimating the frequency of each item
Estimating the number of distinct elements (cardinality) using a small, fixed amount of memory
Sorting a stream of numbers
Testing set membership
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality, e.g. unique visitors, with about 0.81% standard error in Redis using at most 12 KB per key. Membership is Bloom filter territory and per-item frequency is Count-Min Sketch territory.

questions.prompt: You keep a Redis HyperLogLog of unique visitors per day. How do you get unique visitors for the whole week?
options: PFMERGE (or PFCOUNT over all seven keys) to union the sketches, then count
Average the seven daily counts
Sum the seven daily PFCOUNT results
It is impossible to combine HyperLogLogs
questions.explanation: HyperLogLogs merge losslessly into the sketch of the union, so PFCOUNT key1..key7 or PFMERGE gives weekly uniques. Summing daily counts double-counts users who visited on several days.

questions.prompt: What does a Count-Min Sketch estimate, and in which direction is its error?
options: Distinct count; it can under- or over-estimate equally
Item frequencies; it never underestimates, but may overestimate due to hash collisions
Exact top-k items with no error
Set membership; it gives false negatives
questions.explanation: Each item increments one counter per row; collisions only add counts, and taking the minimum across rows reduces but cannot remove the overestimate. So estimates are always at least the true count.

questions.prompt: You need the top 100 most-searched terms in the last hour from a stream of 1 billion searches, with limited memory. Which approach fits best?
options: Store an exact hash map of every term in one process
A Bloom filter of seen terms
A HyperLogLog of all terms
A Count-Min Sketch for frequency estimates combined with a min-heap of the current top 100 candidates (per time window)
questions.explanation: CMS gives approximate counts in fixed memory and the heap tracks the current leaders; window by hour (e.g. a sketch per minute bucket). HLL only counts distinct terms and Bloom filters only test membership, and an exact map may not fit for a long-tailed stream.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Bloom filter sizing are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Inserting far more items than the filter was sized for raises the false-positive rate
There is an optimal number of hash functions for a given bits-per-item ratio; too many or too few raises false positives
For a fixed number of items, more bits lowers the false-positive rate
Adding more hash functions always lowers the false-positive rate
A filter sized for 1% false positives needs roughly 10 bits per item
questions.explanation: False-positive rate depends on bits per item and hash count; the optimum is k ≈ (m/n)·ln 2, and 1% needs about 9.6 bits per item. Beyond the optimum, extra hashes fill the bit array faster and raise false positives.

questions.prompt: Which are well-known real uses of these probabilistic structures? Select all that apply.
options: LSM-tree databases (e.g. Cassandra, RocksDB) use Bloom filters to skip SSTables that cannot contain a key
HyperLogLog for checking whether a password was in a breach list
Redis offers PFADD/PFCOUNT for HyperLogLog cardinality estimates
Count-Min Sketch to find heavy hitters (e.g. abusive IPs) in network traffic
Bloom filters for exact billing totals
questions.explanation: Bloom filters avoid useless disk reads in LSM stores, Redis ships HLL, and CMS finds heavy hitters. HLL cannot answer membership questions (that is a Bloom filter job), and nothing probabilistic should compute exact billing.

questions.prompt: A Bloom filter can give a false negative if two items hash to the same bits.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Shared bits cause false positives, not false negatives: once an item is added, its bits stay set, so querying it always returns 'possibly present' (unless you use an unsafe deletion scheme).

questions.prompt: The memory used by a HyperLogLog stays roughly constant whether it has counted ten thousand or ten billion distinct items.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. HLL keeps a fixed number of registers (Redis uses up to 12 KB per key, with a sparse encoding for small sets), so memory does not grow with cardinality; accuracy stays around the same relative error.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes logs, metrics and traces?
options: Logs are for production and metrics are for development
Traces are aggregated logs; metrics are sampled traces
All three are just different names for structured logs
Metrics are numeric time series aggregated over time; logs are discrete event records; traces follow one request across services as a tree of spans
questions.explanation: Metrics answer 'how much/how often' cheaply, logs give detailed context for single events, and traces show where time went across service hops. They complement each other, and you often link them via trace ids.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between SLI, SLO and SLA?
options: SLA is the internal target, SLO is the measured value, SLI is the contract
SLI is a measured indicator (e.g. % of successful requests under 300 ms); SLO is the internal target for it (99.9%); SLA is the external contract with consequences if missed
They are synonyms used by different companies
SLO is the penalty, SLA is the indicator, SLI is the target
questions.explanation: SLIs are measurements, SLOs are targets for them, and SLAs are customer agreements (usually looser than the SLO) with credits or penalties. Setting SLO tighter than SLA gives a buffer before contractual breaches.

questions.prompt: A service has a 99.9% monthly availability SLO. Roughly how much downtime (error budget) does that allow in a 30-day month?
options: About 3.6 days
About 43 minutes
About 7.2 hours
About 4.3 minutes
questions.explanation: 30 days × 24 h × 60 min = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. 4.3 minutes would be 99.99%, and 7.2 hours would be 99%.

questions.prompt: In OpenTelemetry, how does a trace stay connected when service A calls service B over HTTP?
options: A injects trace context (W3C `traceparent` header with trace id and parent span id) into the request, and B extracts it to create child spans
The collector matches spans by timestamp
B queries A's database for the parent span
Both services write to the same log file
questions.explanation: Context propagation carries the trace id and parent span id across process boundaries; instrumentation injects and extracts it. Timestamp matching is unreliable and is not how OTel links spans.

questions.prompt: A team adds a `user_id` label to its request-latency Prometheus metric. Memory usage on the metrics backend explodes. Why?
options: High cardinality: each unique label value creates a separate time series, so millions of users means millions of series
Histograms cannot have labels
user_id values are too long to store
Prometheus does not support string labels
questions.explanation: Every label combination is a separate series, so unbounded labels like user id or request id multiply series count and memory. Put such ids in logs or trace attributes, and keep metric labels low-cardinality (route, status, region).

questions.prompt: Why should latency SLOs usually use percentiles (p95/p99) rather than the average?
options: Averages are harder to compute
Averages hide the tail: a few very slow requests affect many users' experience but barely move the mean
Percentiles are always lower than averages
Prometheus cannot compute averages
questions.explanation: A mean of 100 ms can coexist with 1% of requests taking 5 s; p99 exposes that tail. Percentiles are not necessarily lower than averages; for skewed latency, p99 is typically far higher.

questions.prompt: You run 20 instances and each reports its own p99 latency. A dashboard averages the 20 p99 values to get the service p99. What is wrong?
options: You should use the median of the p99s
You should take the minimum of the p99s instead
Percentiles can't be averaged meaningfully; aggregate the underlying histogram buckets across instances and compute the percentile from the combined distribution
Nothing; averaging percentiles is correct
questions.explanation: The average of per-instance p99s isn't the p99 of all requests, especially with uneven traffic or one slow instance. Sum histogram buckets (e.g. histogram_quantile over sum by (le) in Prometheus) and compute the quantile from that.

questions.prompt: Which make logs more useful in a microservices system? Select all that apply.
options: Structured (JSON) logs with consistent field names
Including trace id and span id in each log line to correlate with traces
Centralised log aggregation with retention policies
Appropriate levels so noisy debug logs can be turned off in production
Logging full request bodies including passwords and card numbers for debugging
questions.explanation: Structured, correlated, levelled and centralised logs are searchable and joinable with traces. Logging secrets or card data is a security and compliance violation (PCI DSS); redact sensitive fields.

questions.prompt: Which practices align with good SLO-based alerting? Select all that apply.
options: Alert on slow burn with a ticket rather than a page
Alert on fast error-budget burn rate (e.g. budget would be exhausted in hours), paging a human
Page whenever any single host's CPU exceeds 70%
Freeze risky launches when the error budget is spent
Base alerts on user-facing symptoms (errors, latency) rather than every internal cause
questions.explanation: Burn-rate alerts with page/ticket tiers, symptom-based alerting and budget-driven release policy are core SRE practice. Paging on per-host CPU thresholds is noisy cause-based alerting that often doesn't reflect user impact.

questions.prompt: Head-based trace sampling (deciding at the start of a request) can miss rare slow or failed requests, which tail-based sampling at the collector can keep.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Head sampling decides before knowing the outcome, so a 1% sample drops 99% of errors too. Tail sampling buffers complete traces and keeps interesting ones (errors, high latency), at the cost of collector memory and complexity.

questions.prompt: An SLO of 100% availability is a good goal for most user-facing services.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. 100% is unachievable (networks, dependencies and user devices fail) and leaves zero error budget, which freezes all change. Pick a target users actually notice, like 99.9%, and spend the remaining budget on shipping.

questions.prompt: What is a blue-green deployment?
options: Rolling pods one by one in place
Gradually shifting a small percentage of traffic to the new version
Running two full environments (blue = current, green = new) and switching all traffic to green at once, keeping blue for instant rollback
Deploying only on weekdays (green) and never on weekends (blue)
questions.explanation: Blue-green swaps traffic between two complete environments, so rollback is just switching back. Gradual percentage shifting is canary; replacing pods one by one is a rolling update.

questions.prompt: A canary release sends 5% of traffic to v2. What should decide whether to proceed to 25%?
options: A fixed timer, regardless of metrics
Whether the build passed unit tests
Developer confidence in the change
Comparing the canary's error rate, latency and key business metrics against the baseline, ideally automatically
questions.explanation: A canary is only useful if real production signals decide promotion; automated analysis against the stable version catches regressions tests miss. Timers and test results alone ignore what the canary actually does in production.

questions.prompt: Blue-green switch to a new version that renames a database column fails, and rolling back to blue breaks because blue expects the old column. What practice prevents this?
options: Always deploy schema changes and code together in one step
Expand/contract migrations: add the new column, deploy code that works with both, migrate data, then remove the old column in a later release
Never change the schema
Run the migration after rolling back
questions.explanation: Backward-compatible (expand/contract) migrations keep the old and new versions both working against the schema, so either can run and rollback is safe. Coupling schema and code in one step is exactly what breaks rollback.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of feature flags in deployment strategy?
options: They replace database migrations
They decouple deploying code from releasing a feature: code ships dark and is turned on (or off) for users without a redeploy
They make the code run faster
They remove the need for testing
questions.explanation: Flags let you merge and deploy incomplete or risky features hidden, release to a cohort, and kill-switch instantly. They add complexity and need cleanup; they don't replace testing or migrations.

questions.prompt: In Docker, what is the difference between an image and a container?
options: Images run on Linux and containers run on Windows
An image is a read-only, layered template (filesystem + metadata); a container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer
They are the same thing
An image is a running process; a container is the file on disk
questions.explanation: Images are immutable templates built from a Dockerfile in layers; containers are instances of an image with a thin writable layer and process isolation. Many containers can run from one image.

questions.prompt: A Node.js Dockerfile copies the whole repo, then runs `npm ci`. Every code change re-installs all dependencies, making builds slow. What is the fix?
options: Install dependencies at container start-up instead of build time
Copy `package.json` and `package-lock.json` first, run `npm ci`, then copy the rest of the source, so the dependency layer is cached until the lockfile changes
Use `npm install` instead of `npm ci`
Add more RAM to the build machine
questions.explanation: Docker caches layers until an input changes; copying everything first invalidates the install layer on every code edit. Ordering lockfile-then-install-then-source keeps that layer cached. Installing at start-up makes containers slow and non-reproducible.

questions.prompt: During a Kubernetes rolling update, users see errors because pods receive traffic before the Node.js app has connected to its database. What is missing?
options: A larger container image
A higher replica count
A readiness probe that only passes once the app can serve requests
A liveness probe with a very short timeout
questions.explanation: Without readiness, Kubernetes treats the pod as ready once the container starts and sends traffic immediately. A readiness probe holds traffic until the app is ready. An aggressive liveness probe would just restart slow-starting pods.

questions.prompt: Which Kubernetes objects are correctly described? Select all that apply.
options: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage
A ConfigMap stores encrypted secrets by default
A HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjusts replica counts based on metrics such as CPU
A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to keep a desired number of identical pods and performs rolling updates
A Service gives a stable network endpoint that load-balances across matching pods
questions.explanation: Deployments, Services, Pods and HPAs are described correctly. ConfigMaps hold non-secret configuration; Secrets are a separate object, and even they are only base64-encoded unless encryption at rest is configured.

questions.prompt: A Node.js app in Kubernetes drops in-flight requests on every deploy. Which changes help achieve graceful shutdown? Select all that apply.
options: Fail the readiness probe on SIGTERM so the pod is removed from endpoints
Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close DB pools, then exit
Use a short preStop sleep so endpoint removal propagates before the server stops listening
Run Node under a shell form CMD (`sh -c node server.js`) so the shell handles signals
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than the longest expected request
questions.explanation: Handling SIGTERM, leaving the load-balancer pool first, a preStop delay and a sufficient grace period let in-flight requests finish. A shell-form CMD makes sh PID 1, which typically does not forward SIGTERM to Node, so the app never sees it and gets killed.

questions.prompt: Long-lived feature flags that are never removed are harmless because disabled code paths do not run.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Stale flags pile up untested combinations, dead code and confusing behaviour; a mistakenly toggled stale flag has caused real outages. Treat release flags as temporary and remove them after full rollout.

questions.prompt: Compared with blue-green, a canary release limits the blast radius of a bad version to a small fraction of users, at the cost of running two versions side by side for longer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Canary exposes a few users first and needs both versions (and the schema/APIs) to coexist during the rollout. Blue-green flips everyone at once, which is simpler but means a bad version hits all users until rollback.

questions.prompt: You generate short codes by taking the first 7 characters of base62(MD5(longUrl)). What's the main problem at scale?
options: Truncated hashes collide, so you need collision detection and retry
Hash-based codes can't be stored in a database index
MD5 is too slow to compute per request
Base62 can't represent MD5 output
questions.explanation: Truncating a hash to about 42 bits makes collisions likely as the table grows (birthday paradox), so you must check for an existing code and retry with a salt. MD5 is cheap to compute, and any bytes can be base62-encoded.

questions.prompt: Short codes come from a single auto-increment counter encoded in base62. Which concern is most significant?
options: Base62 encoding of integers is not reversible
Codes are sequential and guessable, and one counter is a bottleneck and single point of failure
Codes will be much longer than with hashing
Codes will collide frequently
questions.explanation: A counter never collides and gives the shortest codes, but sequential IDs let people enumerate links, and a single counter must be made highly available and fast. Common fixes are counter ranges per server and shuffling/obfuscating IDs.

questions.prompt: How does a Key Generation Service (KGS) typically avoid handing the same key to two app servers?
options: KGS pre-generates unique keys and atomically moves batches from 'unused' to 'used' before handing them out
Each app server hashes the URL and asks KGS to check it
KGS generates keys on demand using the current timestamp
App servers pick random keys and KGS rejects duplicates later
questions.explanation: A KGS pre-generates keys offline and hands out batches, marking them used atomically, so no two servers get the same key and no check is needed at write time. Random keys with later rejection is just collision handling moved elsewhere.

questions.prompt: With a KGS, each app server caches a batch of 1,000 keys in memory. An app server crashes. What happens?
options: The KGS must roll back every URL created by that server
The same keys get issued to another server, causing duplicates
All servers must stop until the batch is recovered
Its unused keys are lost; that's acceptable given the huge keyspace
questions.explanation: Keys were marked used when handed out, so a crash just wastes the unused ones. With 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion keys that's negligible, and it's safer than risking reuse. They are never re-issued, which is the whole point of marking them used first.

questions.prompt: Product wants the same long URL to always return the same short code. Which approach supports this most directly?
options: Deterministic hashing of the long URL, or a lookup index on longUrl before creating
Snowflake IDs per request
A global counter per request
A random KGS key per request
questions.explanation: Deduplication needs either a deterministic function of the URL (hash) or an index from longUrl to code that you check before creating a new one. Counters, KGS keys and Snowflake IDs all produce a new value per request.

questions.prompt: To avoid one central counter, each app server is assigned a range (server A gets 1–1M, B gets 1M–2M) from a coordinator like ZooKeeper. What's the main trade-off?
options: Codes are no longer roughly time-ordered globally, and unused range parts are wasted on crashes
The coordinator is called on every URL creation
Codes can collide across servers
Codes become much longer than a single counter's
questions.explanation: Ranges remove the per-request bottleneck: the coordinator is only contacted when a range runs out. IDs from different servers interleave, so global ordering is lost, and a crashed server's unused range is skipped. Ranges never overlap, so there are no collisions.

questions.prompt: You use hash-based codes with collision retry: on collision you append a salt and rehash. Two requests for different URLs collide at the same moment. What's needed for correctness?
options: An atomic insert-if-absent, such as a unique constraint on the short code
A larger hash function like SHA-512
A cache in front of the database
Retrying with exponential backoff only
questions.explanation: 'Check then insert' races: both requests can see the code as free. A unique index (or conditional put) makes the insert atomic, so one wins and the other gets an error and retries with a new salt. A bigger hash lowers the odds but doesn't remove the race.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of a pre-generated KGS over hashing the long URL? Select all that apply.
options: Keys can be non-sequential, so they're hard to guess
No collision checks at write time
The same long URL automatically gets the same code
No extra service to run and keep available
Key generation work happens offline, off the request path
questions.explanation: A KGS guarantees uniqueness up front, can hand out shuffled keys and moves work off the hot path. It doesn't dedupe identical URLs (each request gets a new key), and it's an extra component that must be highly available.

questions.prompt: Users can choose custom aliases (e.g. /my-sale) alongside generated codes. Which problems must you handle? Select all that apply.
options: Custom aliases can't be cached
Racing requests for the same alias need an atomic uniqueness check
Reserved words such as /api or /admin must be blocked
A custom alias can clash with a code the generator will produce later
Custom aliases make base62 encoding impossible
questions.explanation: Aliases share the namespace with generated codes, so either reserve them in the KGS or keep separate namespaces, block route names, and enforce uniqueness atomically. Aliases are just keys, so they cache normally, and base62 still works for generated codes.

questions.prompt: A Snowflake-style 64-bit ID (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) encoded in base62 produces codes of about 11 characters, longer than a typical 7-character short code.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. 62^10 ≈ 8.4×10^17 is below 2^63 ≈ 9.2×10^18, while 62^11 is far above it, so large 64-bit IDs need about 11 base62 characters. That's why shorteners prefer compact counters or KGS keys.

questions.prompt: Using a cryptographic hash like SHA-256 and truncating it to 7 base62 characters eliminates collisions because SHA-256 is collision-resistant.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Collision resistance applies to the full 256-bit output. Truncating to 7 base62 characters leaves about 42 bits, and by the birthday bound collisions become likely after a few million URLs.

questions.prompt: Why do URL shorteners commonly use base62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z) instead of base64?
options: Base62 is faster to decode
Base64 can't encode integers
Base64's + and / characters aren't URL-safe without escaping
Base62 produces shorter strings than base64
questions.explanation: Standard base64 uses + and /, which have special meaning in URLs. Base62 only uses alphanumerics. Base64 is actually slightly denser (6 vs about 5.95 bits per char); base64url (- and _) is the other common choice.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many unique codes does a 7-character base62 code space provide?
options: About 78 billion
About 56 billion
About 218 trillion
About 3.5 trillion
questions.explanation: 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 ≈ 3.5 trillion. 56.8 billion is 62^6 and about 218 trillion is 62^8. At 100M new URLs/day, 3.5T lasts nearly 100 years.

questions.prompt: What does this base62 encoder print?
options: z 10 zz
Z 10 ZZ
Z 11 Z0
Z 01 ZZ
questions.explanation: 61 is the last digit, 'Z'. 62 = 1×62 + 0, so it's '10' (most significant digit first). 3843 = 61×62 + 61, so it's 'ZZ', the largest 2-char value. '01' would come from forgetting to prepend.

questions.prompt: You expect 1 billion URLs in total over the service's life. What's the minimum base62 code length that can hold them all?
options: 8 characters
5 characters
7 characters
6 characters
questions.explanation: 62^5 ≈ 916 million, just under 1 billion, while 62^6 ≈ 56.8 billion is enough. Many designs still pick 7 for headroom and so codes can be random rather than dense.

questions.prompt: A base62 short code is stored in MySQL with the default case-insensitive collation (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci). What bug will appear?
options: Digits sort after letters, breaking range scans
'abc' and 'ABC' are treated as equal, so lookups and uniqueness checks break
Codes longer than 6 characters get truncated
Inserts fail because base62 contains non-ASCII characters
questions.explanation: Base62 is case-sensitive: 'a' and 'A' are different digits. A case-insensitive collation makes 'abc' equal 'ABC', so a unique index rejects valid codes and lookups can return the wrong row. Use a binary or case-sensitive collation.

questions.prompt: Encoding counter value 125 in base62 gives '21'. What does the leftmost '2' represent?
options: The number of digits in the code
questions.explanation: Positional base62: '21' = 2×62^1 + 1×62^0 = 124 + 1 = 125. Using base 10 place values would give 21, a common slip.

questions.prompt: Some shorteners drop look-alike characters (0/O, 1/l/I) from the alphabet, giving about base56. What's the trade-off?
options: The code space becomes unlimited
Codes become easier to read and type but slightly longer for the same keyspace
Codes become shorter because the alphabet is smaller
Codes can no longer be decoded back to integers
questions.explanation: A smaller alphabet means fewer bits per character, so you need slightly longer codes for the same capacity, but humans make fewer transcription mistakes. Any alphabet with a fixed order still decodes back to an integer.

questions.prompt: You base62-encode an auto-increment ID directly. Which issues does this create? Select all that apply.
options: Consecutive links have predictable codes that can be enumerated
Codes reveal roughly how many links exist
The encoding can't be reversed to recover the ID
Different IDs can map to the same code
Early codes are shorter than later ones unless padded
questions.explanation: Direct encoding is a bijection: no collisions and it's reversible. But it leaks volume, allows enumeration and gives variable length. Fixes include a reversible shuffle (e.g. a Feistel cipher over the ID) and padding.

questions.prompt: Which properties hold for base62 encoding of non-negative integers with a fixed alphabet order? Select all that apply.
options: It compresses arbitrary data to fewer bits than the input
It hides the original integer from anyone who knows the alphabet
