Each character carries about 5.95 bits (log2 62)
Decoding is the reverse of the repeated divide-by-62 process
Each integer has exactly one unpadded encoding
questions.explanation: Base62 is just positional notation: unique, reversible, about 5.95 bits per char. It isn't compression (no entropy is removed) and it isn't encryption: anyone with the alphabet can decode it.

questions.prompt: Base62-encoding a sequential ID makes short codes unpredictable, as long as the alphabet order is kept secret.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A shuffled alphabet is a simple substitution: sequential IDs still give visibly related codes, and a handful of samples reveal the mapping. Use a proper keyed permutation or random keys if unpredictability matters.

questions.prompt: Going from 6 to 7 base62 characters multiplies the number of available codes by 62.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Each extra position multiplies capacity by the base: 62^7 / 62^6 = 62, taking you from about 56.8 billion to about 3.5 trillion codes.

questions.prompt: Marketing needs accurate click counts for every visit to a short link. Which redirect status should the shortener return?
options: 308 Permanent Redirect
302 Found
304 Not Modified
301 Moved Permanently
questions.explanation: Browsers can cache 301 (and 308) redirects and go straight to the destination on repeat visits, so your server never sees those clicks. 302 is temporary, so every visit comes back to you. 304 isn't a redirect at all.

questions.prompt: What's the main benefit of returning 301 for short links?
options: Browsers and caches can remember it, cutting load and latency on repeat visits
It prevents search engines from indexing the target
It guarantees every click is logged
It lets you change the destination later without anyone noticing
questions.explanation: A permanent redirect is cacheable by default, so repeat visits skip your servers entirely. The flip side is exactly why it's bad for changing destinations or counting every click.

questions.prompt: Users can edit where a short link points. A few months after launch they complain that edits 'don't work' for some visitors. You've been returning 301. What's going on?
options: Visitors' browsers cached the old 301 and never ask your server again
Your database replica is lagging behind the primary
301 responses can't include a Location header
The CDN rejects 301 responses with long URLs
questions.explanation: Browsers can cache 301s for a long time, so returning visitors follow the old target without contacting you. For editable links, use 302/307 or 301 with a short Cache-Control max-age. Replica lag would resolve in seconds, not months.

questions.prompt: A short link is used as the target of an HTML form POST, and the method must be preserved after the redirect. Which status code is correct for a temporary redirect?
options: 302 Found
303 See Other
301 Moved Permanently
307 Temporary Redirect
questions.explanation: 307 requires the client to repeat the same method and body. Browsers historically turn POST into GET on 301/302, and 303 explicitly asks for a GET. 308 is the permanent version of 307.

questions.prompt: You want 302 semantics (every click reaches you) but also want a CDN to absorb most redirect traffic. What's a sensible approach?
options: Return 301 so the CDN caches it forever
Cache the redirect at the CDN briefly and log clicks from CDN edge logs or an edge function
Disable the CDN for redirect paths
Return 200 with a meta-refresh tag instead
questions.explanation: A CDN can cache a 302 with s-maxage while edge logs or edge workers capture every click, so you keep analytics and offload origin. 301 loses browser-side clicks for good, and meta refresh is slower and worse for SEO and clients.

questions.prompt: How do search engines like Google generally treat a 301 compared with a 302?
options: They penalise any site that uses 301
A 301 signals the target is the canonical URL; a 302 suggests the original may come back
They treat both identically in all cases
They ignore 301s and only follow 302s
questions.explanation: A 301 tells search engines the move is permanent, so they consolidate ranking signals on the destination. A 302 is a temporary move, so the original URL may stay indexed. Google says it handles both, but the signals differ.

questions.prompt: A shortener returns 301 with Cache-Control: max-age=300. What does a browser do on the next click 10 minutes later?
options: Uses the cached redirect forever, since 301 overrides Cache-Control
Follows the redirect but sends a POST
Shows an error because 301 can't carry Cache-Control
Contacts the shortener again, because the cached redirect expired
questions.explanation: Explicit Cache-Control limits how long a 301 is cached; after 300 s the browser revalidates by requesting the short URL again. That's a way to keep some cacheability while still allowing edits and counting most clicks.

questions.prompt: Which statements about 301 vs 302 for a URL shortener are correct? Select all that apply.
options: 302 makes changing the destination later safe
302 always preserves POST bodies in all browsers
301 guarantees the redirect is never cached anywhere
302 sends more traffic to your servers because browsers don't cache it by default
301 can cause click analytics to undercount returning visitors
questions.explanation: 302 isn't cached by default, so every click reaches you: more load, accurate analytics, editable targets. 301 is the opposite and is cached. Browsers commonly turn POST into GET on 302, which is why 307 exists.

questions.prompt: Which redirect codes tell the client to repeat the same HTTP method and body? Select all that apply.
options: 308 Permanent Redirect
301 Moved Permanently
307 Temporary Redirect
302 Found
303 See Other
questions.explanation: 307 and 308 were added specifically to guarantee method and body are preserved. 301/302 allow clients to change POST to GET (and browsers do), and 303 explicitly requires a GET.

questions.prompt: Returning 302 for short links means browsers never cache the redirect, no matter what headers you send.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A 302 isn't cached by default, but it becomes cacheable if you send explicit freshness headers like Cache-Control: max-age or Expires. The default behaviour is what matters for most shorteners.

questions.prompt: A 302 redirect adds one extra round trip to the shortener for every click compared with a cached 301.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With a cached 301, repeat visits go straight to the destination. With a 302, the browser asks the shortener each time, which adds a round trip of latency and load in exchange for control and analytics.

questions.prompt: A shortener has about 100:1 read:write traffic. What should sit in front of the database for redirect lookups?
options: A cache keyed by short code (e.g. Redis), filled via cache-aside
A full-text search index
A write-back cache for new URLs
A message queue for redirect requests
questions.explanation: Redirects are simple key lookups with a heavily skewed popularity distribution, a textbook fit for a cache-aside key-value cache. Queuing redirects would add latency, and full-text search is irrelevant to exact-key lookups.

questions.prompt: You estimate 20,000 redirects/s at peak, and the top 20% of links get 80% of traffic. Total mappings are 5 TB. What's a sensible cache sizing approach?
options: Skip caching since the dataset is too big
Cache all 5 TB so every lookup hits
Cache only links created in the last hour
Cache only the hot fraction (a small slice of the dataset) with LRU/LFU
questions.explanation: With skewed traffic, caching a small hot fraction gives a high hit rate at a fraction of the cost. Caching all 5 TB in RAM is expensive for little extra benefit, and creation time is a poor proxy for popularity.

questions.prompt: Bots request millions of random short codes that don't exist. Your cache hit rate drops and DB load rises. What helps most?
options: Cache 'not found' with a short TTL and/or check a Bloom filter of existing codes
Increase cache TTL for existing links
Use 301 instead of 302
Add more DB read replicas only
questions.explanation: This is cache penetration: unknown keys always miss. Negative caching or a Bloom filter answers 'doesn't exist' without the DB. Replicas absorb load but don't fix the waste, and the status code doesn't affect lookups for missing codes.

questions.prompt: A link is deleted for abuse, but users still get redirected to the malicious site for an hour. What's the most likely cause?
options: Base62 decoding returns the wrong ID
The DB delete wasn't committed
LRU evicted the deletion record
The cached mapping (Redis/CDN) wasn't invalidated when the link was deleted
questions.explanation: Delete must also invalidate the cache and CDN (and ideally return 410). Otherwise the old mapping lives until its TTL expires. A one-hour delay matching a TTL points to caching, not the DB.

questions.prompt: A tweet with a short link goes viral: 500k requests/s for one code. Even Redis is struggling on the node that holds that key. What's the best next layer?
options: Switch to write-through caching
Add an in-process cache on app servers and/or cache the redirect at the CDN edge
Lower the TTL of that key to 1 second
Shard the database by short code
questions.explanation: One key lives on one Redis node, so more shards don't help. An in-memory LRU on each app server and edge caching spread the load horizontally. A shorter TTL would just add misses.

questions.prompt: Which store characteristic best suits short code → long URL mappings at a scale of billions of rows?
options: A graph database for link relationships
Strong multi-row ACID transactions across tables
A time-series database
A horizontally scalable key-value or wide-column store with lookups by primary key
questions.explanation: The access pattern is 'get by key', and writes are independent inserts, so a partitioned KV store (e.g. DynamoDB, Cassandra) scales simply. Cross-table transactions aren't needed for this workload. Sharded Postgres also works but needs more manual effort.

questions.prompt: Redirect latency p99 jumps every time a cache node restarts, as all its keys miss at once and the DB spikes. Which fix targets this directly?
options: Warm the cache from a hot-key list before taking traffic, and coalesce concurrent misses
Increase the base62 code length
Use 302 instead of 301
Remove the TTL from all keys
questions.explanation: A cold cache node sends a burst of misses to the DB. Pre-warming with popular codes and request coalescing (single-flight per key) smooth the restart. Removing TTLs doesn't help because the keys are gone, not expired.

questions.prompt: Which make sense for the read path of a high-traffic URL shortener? Select all that apply.
options: Reading from DB replicas on cache miss
Locking the URL row for each redirect
Cache-aside lookup in Redis keyed by short code
CDN or edge caching of redirects for popular links
Synchronously writing an analytics row to the main DB before redirecting
questions.explanation: Edge caching, a KV cache and replica reads all offload the primary. Synchronous analytics writes and row locks put write cost on every read and destroy redirect latency; analytics should be async.

questions.prompt: You read from DB replicas on cache miss. A user creates a link and clicks it immediately, getting a 404. Which fixes are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: On a replica miss for a fresh code, fall back to the primary
Write the new mapping into the cache at creation time
Switch the redirect code from 302 to 301
Increase the cache TTL to 30 days
Route reads from the creating user to the primary for a short window
questions.explanation: The 404 comes from replica lag. Populating the cache on write, falling back to the primary on miss, or read-your-writes routing all fix it. TTL length and redirect status don't help a code that isn't on the replica yet.

questions.prompt: Because short-link mappings rarely change once created, they can usually be cached with long TTLs as long as deletes and edits explicitly invalidate the cache.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Mappings are effectively immutable, so long TTLs are safe and give high hit rates, provided edits, deletes and abuse takedowns invalidate the cache and CDN explicitly.

questions.prompt: With a 99% cache hit rate, the database still sees about half of redirect traffic, since misses are expensive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A 99% hit rate means only 1% of lookups reach the DB, e.g. 200/s out of 20,000/s. Each miss costs more than a hit, but the request count to the DB is still just 1% of total.

questions.prompt: Where should click analytics be recorded so they don't slow down redirects?
options: By re-running the redirect query with an extra UPDATE
In the browser using localStorage
Emitted asynchronously (e.g. to Kafka) and processed off the request path
Inside a DB transaction before sending the redirect
questions.explanation: Redirects should be as fast as possible. Fire-and-forget events to a log or queue let consumers aggregate later. A synchronous DB write adds latency and couples redirects to analytics DB health.

questions.prompt: You count clicks with UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1 WHERE code = $1 on every redirect. A viral link makes the DB slow for everyone. Why?
options: UPDATE statements can't use indexes
PostgreSQL disallows UPDATE during reads
Every redirect contends for the same row lock, serialising writes on that link
The clicks column overflows past 2^31
questions.explanation: All increments hit one row, so they queue behind a single row lock and generate heavy write/WAL traffic. Buffer counts (in memory or Redis) or stream events and aggregate in batches. The UPDATE does use the index on code.

questions.prompt: Analytics must show unique visitors per link per day across billions of clicks, with about 1% error acceptable. Which data structure fits best?
options: A Bloom filter per link
A set of all visitor IDs per link
HyperLogLog per link per day
A sorted set of timestamps
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts with about 0.8% standard error in roughly 12 KB (as in Redis), regardless of cardinality. Exact sets grow with visitors. Bloom filters answer membership, not counts.

questions.prompt: Kafka gives at-least-once delivery to your click consumer. After a consumer restart, click counts are inflated. What's the best fix?
options: Retry failed messages more aggressively
Add more partitions to the topic
Give each click an event ID and make aggregation idempotent (dedupe or commit offsets with results atomically)
Switch Kafka to at-most-once and accept losses
questions.explanation: At-least-once means replays after restarts. Dedupe by event ID, or store consumer offsets in the same transaction as the aggregates, so reprocessing doesn't double-count. At-most-once trades duplicates for silent loss.

questions.prompt: Dashboards query 'clicks per hour by country for link X over 90 days'. Which storage fits that query pattern best?
options: Redis strings keyed by link
The same row-store table that holds URL mappings
A columnar OLAP store (e.g. ClickHouse) with pre-aggregated rollups
An object store with one file per click, scanned at query time
questions.explanation: Analytical group-by queries over time ranges suit columnar stores and rollup tables. Running them on the OLTP mapping table competes with redirects, and scanning one file per click is far too slow.

questions.prompt: Your click stream aggregates by event time into hourly windows. Mobile clients send events up to 10 minutes late. What should the stream processor do?
options: Drop any event that arrives after its window closes
Use watermarks with allowed lateness, updating windows as late events arrive
Wait 24 hours before emitting any result
Use processing time instead so lateness doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Watermarks with allowed lateness keep windows open long enough for typical delays and then finalise. Processing time puts late events in the wrong hour, dropping them loses data, and waiting a day makes dashboards useless.

questions.prompt: A redirect service publishes click events to Kafka, but the Kafka cluster is down. What's the best behaviour for the redirect path?
options: Return 503 until Kafka recovers
Block the redirect until the publish succeeds
Still redirect; buffer events locally or drop them, and alert
Write each event synchronously to the main URL database instead
questions.explanation: Redirects are the core product; analytics is secondary. Degrade gracefully with a bounded local buffer (or drop and count the losses). Failing or blocking redirects turns an analytics outage into a full outage.

questions.prompt: Which steps belong in a URL shortener's click analytics pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: Block the redirect until the event is stored in the warehouse
Emit an event with code, timestamp, referrer and user agent
Enrich events (e.g. IP to country, UA to device) in a consumer
Roll up raw events into time-bucketed aggregates
Filter or flag bot traffic before reporting
questions.explanation: Emit, enrich, filter bots and roll up is the standard flow. Waiting for warehouse storage puts analytics latency on every redirect.

questions.prompt: Raw click events for 3 years would be about 500 TB. Which strategies keep cost under control? Select all that apply.
options: Duplicate events into the OLTP database for backup
Keep raw events briefly, then keep only hourly/daily rollups
Move old raw data to cheap object storage in a compressed columnar format
Sample very high-volume links for non-billing metrics
Store every event in Redis for fast queries
questions.explanation: Tiered retention, compressed cold storage and sampling all reduce cost while keeping useful metrics. Keeping 500 TB in Redis memory or duplicating it into OLTP is extremely expensive.

questions.prompt: Counting clicks at the CDN edge from access logs can work even when redirects are cached at the edge and never reach your origin.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Edge logs record every request the CDN serves, including cache hits, so you can ship them into your pipeline. That lets you cache redirects at the edge without losing click data, though logs arrive with some delay.

questions.prompt: Real-time per-second click counters on a dashboard require every event to be written to the warehouse before it's displayed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A common split is a fast path (stream processing or Redis counters) for near-real-time numbers and a batch path into the warehouse for accurate historical reports. The dashboard reads the fast path.

questions.prompt: A creator uploads a 3 GB video from a phone on a flaky mobile network. Why should the upload API accept the file as resumable chunks instead of one HTTP request?
options: Chunks let the CDN start caching the video before upload finishes
Object storage cannot store any single object larger than 1 GB
Chunking compresses the video so less data crosses the network
A dropped connection only loses the in-flight chunk, so the client resumes from the last acknowledged one
questions.explanation: Resumable chunked uploads (e.g. S3 multipart, tus) track which parts arrived, so a network drop costs one chunk rather than restarting 3 GB. Object stores do support multi-GB objects, and chunking itself does no compression.

questions.prompt: Why do upload services typically hand the client a pre-signed object-storage URL rather than streaming the video bytes through the API servers?
options: Pre-signed URLs make the uploaded file publicly readable by default
It keeps gigabytes of traffic off the stateless API tier while still authorizing the upload
API servers cannot terminate TLS for large request bodies
It is the only way to attach metadata such as the title to a video
questions.explanation: The API authenticates the user and signs a short-lived URL scoped to one key; the bytes then go straight to object storage, so API servers aren't tied up proxying huge bodies. Pre-signed upload URLs don't make objects public, and metadata goes through the normal API.

questions.prompt: In HLS or MPEG-DASH adaptive bitrate streaming, which component decides which bitrate rendition to fetch next?
options: The CDN edge, based on the cache hit ratio
The client player, based on measured throughput and buffer level
The transcoder, which embeds one fixed choice in the manifest
The origin server, based on its current CPU load
questions.explanation: ABR is client-driven: the manifest lists all renditions and the player picks the next segment's rendition from its own throughput estimate and buffer state. Servers and CDNs just serve plain HTTP GETs for whatever segment is requested.

questions.prompt: A 2-hour movie takes 4 hours to transcode on one machine. What is the standard way to cut this to minutes?
options: Transcode only the 1080p rendition and let clients downscale it themselves
Delay transcoding until the first viewer presses play, then encode on demand
Split the source into short segments, transcode them in parallel on many workers, then stitch the outputs
Use a faster disk so the encoder reads the source file more quickly
questions.explanation: Transcoding is CPU-bound and parallelizes well when the source is split at keyframe boundaries into independent chunks fed to a worker pool (a DAG of split, encode, merge). Disk speed isn't the bottleneck, and encoding on first play would make the first viewer wait.

questions.prompt: Transcoding workers pull jobs from a queue and sometimes crash mid-job. What makes the pipeline reliable without producing corrupt or duplicate output?
options: Have a single coordinator machine run all jobs serially so crashes are rare
Delete each job from the queue as soon as a worker receives it
Use at-least-once delivery (visibility timeout) with idempotent outputs keyed by video, rendition and segment
Run every job on two workers simultaneously and keep whichever finishes first
questions.explanation: If the worker dies, the message becomes visible again and another worker retries it; writing output to a deterministic key means a retry overwrites rather than duplicates. Deleting on receipt loses jobs on crash, and running every job twice doubles cost without fixing partial writes.

questions.prompt: Why must keyframes (IDR frames) be aligned at the same timestamps across all renditions of a video in an ABR ladder?
options: Aligned keyframes reduce the file size of the highest-bitrate rendition
Aligned keyframes are required for the CDN to compute cache keys
So each segment starts with a keyframe at the same time in every rendition, letting the player switch at segment boundaries
Without alignment the audio track would drift out of sync
questions.explanation: A segment can only be decoded independently if it begins with a keyframe. When segment N starts at the same instant in every rendition, the player can switch from 720p segment N-1 to 1080p segment N seamlessly. Audio sync and cache keys don't depend on this.

questions.prompt: A team proposes cutting HLS segment duration from 6 s to 1 s. What is the main trade-off?
options: No real trade-off: shorter segments are strictly better
Better compression efficiency, but the player can no longer switch bitrates mid-stream
Lower CDN request rate, but much higher latency for live streams
Faster startup and bitrate adaptation, but more HTTP requests, manifest churn and slightly worse compression
questions.explanation: Short segments let the player react sooner and reduce live latency, but each segment needs its own request and starts with a keyframe, which costs bits. 6x more requests also raises per-request overhead at the CDN. Request rate goes up, not down.

questions.prompt: Which of these are typical outputs of a VOD transcoding pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: Several renditions at different resolutions and bitrates
A manifest or playlist (e.g. .m3u8 or .mpd) listing the renditions and segments
Thumbnail or preview images
One single high-bitrate MP4 served identically to every device
Each viewer's bandwidth estimate for future playback
questions.explanation: The pipeline produces a bitrate ladder, manifests that describe it, and artwork such as thumbnails. Bandwidth estimates are measured live by each player, and serving one file to everyone is exactly what ABR exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: Which signals do client-side ABR algorithms commonly use to choose the next segment's bitrate? Select all that apply.
options: How many other people are watching the same video
Throughput measured while downloading recent segments
The size of the original file the creator uploaded
How many seconds of video are currently buffered
questions.explanation: Throughput-based and buffer-based algorithms (and hybrids) use exactly these two signals. The original upload's size and global viewer counts tell the player nothing about its own network conditions.

questions.prompt: In HLS, the server pushes each next segment to the player at the bitrate it has chosen for that viewer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. HLS is pull-based: the player downloads the playlist and issues plain HTTP GETs for segments it picks. That is why HLS works through ordinary CDNs and caches without server-side session state.

questions.prompt: For a very popular video, spending much more CPU on a slower, higher-compression encode can pay off, because encoding is paid once while bandwidth savings repeat on every view.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Encode cost is fixed per video, while egress cost scales with views. That's why large platforms use per-title encoding or newer codecs (VP9, AV1) for popular content, and cheaper encodes for the long tail that few people watch.

questions.prompt: Video segments are immutable once transcoded. What caching policy fits them best at the CDN?
options: Long TTL with versioned or content-addressed URLs, since a segment's bytes never change
Short TTL (a few seconds) so edits propagate quickly
No caching, so view counts stay accurate
Cache only at the origin, never at the edge
questions.explanation: Immutable content can be cached for a very long time (e.g. Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable). If content does change, it gets a new URL. Short TTLs just cause needless revalidation, and view counts shouldn't rely on CDN misses.

questions.prompt: A platform has a few thousand hugely popular videos and millions of rarely watched ones. Which CDN strategy is most cost-effective?
options: Push every video to every edge location at upload time
Pick a random subset of videos to cache at each edge
Serve everything from origin and use the CDN only for thumbnails
Pre-position popular content at edges and let long-tail videos be fetched from regional caches or origin on demand
questions.explanation: Popularity follows a power law. Edge storage is limited, so you proactively place the head of the distribution near users and pull tail content on demand through a cache hierarchy. Pushing everything everywhere wastes storage on videos nobody watches.

questions.prompt: Each view runs `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ?`. A viral video gets 50k views/s and the database falls over. What is the standard fix?
options: Switch the column type to BIGINT
Run the UPDATE inside SERIALIZABLE transactions
Emit view events to a stream, aggregate counts in short windows, and write batched increments
Put a unique index on the views column
questions.explanation: A single hot row turns into a lock-contention bottleneck. Buffering events and flushing periodic aggregates (e.g. +48,213 every few seconds) cuts writes by orders of magnitude. SERIALIZABLE would make contention worse, and the column type isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: Product wants an approximate count of unique viewers per video per day using little memory. Which structure fits?
options: HyperLogLog
Count-min sketch
Bloom filter
A sorted set of viewer IDs
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality (distinct count) in a few KB with ~1% error. Redis has it built in as PFADD/PFCOUNT. A Bloom filter answers membership rather than counts, count-min estimates per-item frequency, and a set of IDs uses memory that grows with viewers.

questions.prompt: A highly anticipated video goes live and thousands of edge servers miss on the same segments at the same moment, flooding the origin. Which mitigation targets this directly?
options: Lower the segment TTL so edges refresh more often
Add more replicas of the metadata database
Disable HTTP/2 between edges and origin
Use an origin-shield tier and request coalescing so one miss per segment reaches the origin
questions.explanation: Request collapsing makes concurrent misses for the same object wait on a single upstream fetch, and an origin shield funnels all edges through one mid-tier cache. A lower TTL would cause more misses, and the metadata DB isn't on the segment path.

questions.prompt: Why do large video platforms often show a view count that lags behind or freezes for a while on new videos?
options: Counting happens in an asynchronous pipeline that also filters bots and invalid views before publishing totals
The CDN hides view requests from the application servers
SQL databases can't store numbers above a few million
Counts are only recomputed when the creator logs in
questions.explanation: Views pass through an async pipeline (stream, dedup and fraud checks, then aggregation) so that only valid views count. The displayed number is eventually consistent. Freshness is traded for accuracy and lower write load. It has nothing to do with database limits.

questions.prompt: Paid videos must not be playable by anyone who copies a segment URL. What is the usual CDN-friendly approach?
options: Issue short-lived signed URLs or signed cookies that the edge can verify without contacting origin
Rename segment files every hour
Serve paid content from origin only, bypassing the CDN
Have the CDN call the auth service on every segment request
questions.explanation: The edge checks an HMAC or signature and an expiry locally, so access control scales with the CDN. Calling auth on every segment adds latency and load, and bypassing the CDN gives up its whole benefit.

questions.prompt: Which changes improve the CDN cache hit ratio for video segments? Select all that apply.
options: Using long TTLs for immutable segments
Normalizing the cache key to ignore irrelevant query parameters
Adding an origin-shield tier between edges and origin
Sending Cache-Control: no-store on segments
Embedding a per-user session ID in every segment URL
questions.explanation: Fewer distinct keys, a shared mid-tier, and long lifetimes all raise hits. A per-user token inside the cache key makes every user's segment a different object (use signed cookies or ignore the token in the key instead), and no-store disables caching entirely.

questions.prompt: View events go through a Kafka-style partitioned log before aggregation. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The log can be replayed to recompute counts after a bug in the aggregator
The log alone guarantees exactly-once increments in the database, with no idempotence needed
Ingestion and aggregation are decoupled, so a slow aggregator doesn't drop events
Partitioning by videoId lets one consumer own each video's running count
questions.explanation: A durable log gives you replay, key-based ownership and backpressure isolation. End-to-end exactly-once still needs idempotent or transactional sinks (e.g. storing consumer offsets with the counts). The log by itself only provides at-least-once delivery to the DB.

questions.prompt: Partitioning view events by videoId avoids cross-partition coordination for a video's count, but a viral video can turn its partition into a hotspot.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Key-based partitioning sends all of one key's events to one partition. For extreme keys you can salt the key (videoId#0..N), pre-aggregate on producers, and then merge the sub-counts.

questions.prompt: In a YouTube-style design, exact real-time view counts are a hard requirement, so eventual consistency for the counter is unacceptable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. View counts are the classic example of data that can be approximate and lag by seconds or minutes. Accepting eventual consistency is what allows batching, fraud filtering and cheap writes.

questions.prompt: A rider sits near the edge of a geohash cell. Why does a 'find nearby drivers' query look at the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbors?
options: Geohash cells overlap, so drivers are stored in several cells
Redis requires at least nine keys per geospatial query
Points that are physically close can fall in adjacent cells with different prefixes
Neighbor lookups are needed to decode the geohash back into latitude/longitude
questions.explanation: A shared prefix implies proximity, but the reverse isn't true: two points a few meters apart across a cell boundary can have very different geohashes. Querying the 3x3 block covers the search radius. Cells don't overlap, and decoding needs no neighbors.

questions.prompt: Geohash uses a base-32 alphabet. Adding one more character to a geohash multiplies the number of cells covering the world by:
questions.explanation: Each base-32 character encodes 5 bits, so one more character splits each cell into 2^5 = 32 sub-cells (alternating 4x8 or 8x4 arrangements). The 4 comes from quadtrees, which split each node into 4.

questions.prompt: Why does a quadtree handle uneven density (dense downtown, sparse suburbs) better than a fixed grid?
options: It replicates dense cells across more servers automatically
It splits a node into four children only when it holds too many points, so dense areas get small cells and sparse areas stay coarse
It uses hexagonal cells, which have equal-distance neighbors
It stores every point in a balanced binary tree sorted by latitude
questions.explanation: A point-region quadtree recursively subdivides until each leaf is under a capacity threshold, so cells adapt to density. A fixed grid either has huge downtown cells or millions of empty rural ones. Hexagons are H3, not quadtrees.

questions.prompt: Why are hexagonal cells (as in H3) attractive for things like surge pricing or demand heatmaps compared with square grids?
options: Hexagons nest perfectly inside their parent cell at every resolution
Hexagons can be encoded as shorter strings than squares
Square grids cannot be indexed hierarchically
Every neighbor of a hexagon shares an edge and its center is the same distance away, which makes smoothing and ring queries uniform
questions.explanation: A square has 4 edge-neighbors and 4 corner-neighbors at different distances. A hexagon's 6 neighbors are all equidistant, so k-ring aggregation and gradients behave consistently. H3 children only approximately fit their parent, and square grids can be hierarchical (quadtrees, S2).

questions.prompt: A team stores drivers in PostgreSQL with a B-tree index on (lat, lng) and runs `WHERE lat BETWEEN ? AND ? AND lng BETWEEN ? AND ?`. Why is this slow at scale?
options: The query needs a full table scan because BETWEEN is never indexable
B-trees cannot index floating-point columns
PostgreSQL ignores composite indexes in range queries
The index narrows efficiently on lat only, so it scans a thin band around the whole globe and filters lng row by row
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree can range-scan its leading column. The second column's range only filters within that band. Spatial indexes (geohash, GiST/R-tree via PostGIS, S2, H3) map 2-D proximity onto structures that prune in both dimensions.

questions.prompt: Driver positions change every few seconds. Why do many designs prefer a fixed grid or geohash buckets over a classic quadtree for this data?
options: Quadtrees only work for points inside a single city
Geohashes are more accurate than quadtree coordinates
Constant moves force frequent node splits/merges and locking in a shared tree, while a grid update is just moving an ID between two buckets
Quadtrees cannot answer nearest-neighbor queries
questions.explanation: A quadtree is great for mostly static points (restaurants), but high write churn causes restructuring and contention. With fixed cells, an update is remove-from-old-cell plus add-to-new-cell, which is cheap and easy to shard. Quadtrees do support nearest-neighbor queries.

questions.prompt: In Redis 6.2+, which command returns members of a geo set within a radius or box of a point?
options: GEOSEARCH
GEOHASH
GEOADD
ZRANGEBYLEX
questions.explanation: GEOSEARCH (and GEOSEARCHSTORE) replaced the now-deprecated GEORADIUS family in 6.2. GEOADD inserts points, and GEOHASH returns a point's geohash string. Under the hood a geo set is a sorted set scored by a 52-bit geohash.

questions.prompt: You need drivers within 2 km of a rider using geohash buckets. Which steps belong in a correct approach? Select all that apply.
options: Post-filter candidates by exact distance to the rider
Treat the length of the shared prefix as the distance in meters
Query only the rider's own cell
Query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbors
Pick a precision whose cell size is at least the search radius
questions.explanation: Cell size bounds how many neighbors you need, the 3x3 block covers boundary cases, and exact distance filtering removes corner candidates beyond 2 km. Prefix length is only a coarse proximity hint, and querying a single cell misses nearby drivers across the border.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine limitations of geohash? Select all that apply.
options: It requires a dedicated spatial database to compute
Nearby points across a cell boundary may share little or no prefix
Cell width in meters shrinks toward the poles, so cell size isn't uniform
Geohashes can't be stored in an ordinary string index
questions.explanation: Boundary effects and latitude distortion are the real caveats. A geohash is just a string or integer, so it works in any B-tree, sorted set or key-value store, and it's computed with simple bit interleaving.

questions.prompt: A quadtree always splits every node into four children, so all of its leaves cover equal areas.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. An adaptive quadtree splits only nodes over capacity. Leaves in dense areas are deep and small, while leaves in sparse areas are shallow and large. That adaptivity is the main reason to use one.

questions.prompt: Two points with a long common geohash prefix are guaranteed to be close, but two points only 10 m apart may share no prefix at all.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Sharing a prefix means both lie in the same cell, which bounds their distance. Across a major boundary (e.g. the equator or prime meridian), even very close points differ from the first character.

questions.prompt: 1 million drivers are online and each sends a GPS update every 4 seconds. Roughly what write rate must the location service absorb?
options: 4 million writes/s
25,000 writes/s
2.5 million writes/s
250,000 writes/s
questions.explanation: 1,000,000 / 4 s = 250,000 updates per second. This rate is why the live-location store is usually in memory (Redis or sharded in-process maps) rather than a disk-bound primary database.

questions.prompt: Where should the latest position of each active driver live for matching?
options: The CDN, so riders can fetch it directly
Object storage, written as one JSON file per update
The trips table in the primary relational database
An in-memory, geo-indexed store keyed by driver with a short TTL
questions.explanation: Matching needs only the latest location, read and written at very high rates. An in-memory geo index with TTL serves that. Historical pings can be streamed asynchronously to cold storage. The trips table would be crushed by 250k writes/s.

questions.prompt: The nearest driver by straight-line distance is across a river with the closest bridge 5 km away. What should matching rank candidates by?
options: Estimated time of arrival over the road network
Haversine distance, because it is cheapest to compute
Geohash prefix length shared with the rider
Driver rating only
questions.explanation: Geo cells give a cheap candidate set, then ranking uses road-network ETA (traffic, one-ways, bridges). Straight-line distance is just a filter. Using it for ranking produces exactly the river problem.

questions.prompt: Two matcher instances pick the same idle driver for two different riders at the same moment. What prevents double-assignment?
options: Have riders refresh the app before confirming
Run the matchers on the same server
Atomically transition the driver from AVAILABLE to OFFERED with a conditional write (compare-and-set) and a TTL
Rely on the driver to reject the second request
questions.explanation: A conditional update (e.g. `SET driver:42:lock rider NX EX 15` or `UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE'`) lets exactly one matcher win. The loser moves to the next candidate. The TTL frees the driver if the offer is never answered. Running on one server doesn't remove the race.

questions.prompt: The backend must instantly notify a specific driver of a new ride offer. Which transport fits?
options: A persistent connection (WebSocket/gRPC stream) or mobile push, so the server can push to the driver
Email notification
The driver re-sends its location and checks the response for offers
The driver app polls the trips API every 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Offers expire in seconds, so the server needs a push channel. Long polling intervals add up to a minute of latency. Piggybacking on location pings ties offer latency to ping frequency and fails when pings pause.

questions.prompt: A driver drives into a tunnel and stops sending updates. How should the system avoid matching riders to them?
options: Keep them matchable until the next trip completes
Run a nightly job that removes inactive drivers
Give each driver's live-location entry a TTL slightly above the ping interval so stale drivers drop out automatically
Wait until the driver manually goes offline
questions.explanation: Expiring entries (e.g. TTL ~3x the ping interval) means silence equals unavailability, with no cleanup job. A nightly sweep or manual logout leaves ghost drivers that riders get matched to.

questions.prompt: You shard the live-location store. Why shard by geography (city or cell) rather than by hash of driverId?
options: Hashing driverId would put each driver in multiple shards
Hash sharding doesn't support TTLs
Nearby-driver queries are spatial, so geo sharding keeps a query on one or few shards (with dense cities split further)
Geographic shards never become hot
questions.explanation: With hash-by-driver, every 'who's near me' query fans out to all shards. Geo sharding localizes reads, but a big city can become hot, so you subdivide busy regions into finer cells. That's why geo shards are not hotspot-free.

questions.prompt: Why is writing every GPS ping synchronously to the main trips database a poor design? Select all that apply.
options: Relational databases can't store floating-point coordinates
Location data must never be persisted anywhere
It creates massive write load for data where matching only needs the latest value
Historical pings can be streamed asynchronously to cheaper storage instead
It couples ping latency to the primary database's health
questions.explanation: The hot path needs only the current position. History (for fare disputes, analytics, ETA models) can flow through a stream to a warehouse or time-series store. Relational DBs store floats fine, and trip routes are typically persisted for billing and safety.

questions.prompt: A driver doesn't respond to a ride offer within 15 seconds. Which behaviors are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: The driver's offer lock is released automatically by its TTL
The offer expires and the next-best candidate is offered the ride
The driver stays locked until they respond, however long it takes
The system keeps re-offering the same driver until they accept
questions.explanation: Offers are time-boxed: on timeout the lock expires and matching continues with other candidates, possibly marking the driver as less likely to accept. Indefinite locks or repeated retries to one driver strand the rider.

questions.prompt: Batching ride requests over a short window and solving the assignment jointly can give better overall outcomes than greedily giving each rider the nearest free driver.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Greedy assignment can strand a later rider whose only nearby driver was taken by someone who had other options. Solving a small bipartite matching every few seconds lowers total pickup time, at the cost of a slight delay.

questions.prompt: Straight-line (haversine) distance is generally a good-enough proxy for ETA when ranking candidate drivers in a city.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Rivers, highways, one-way streets and traffic make road ETA diverge sharply from straight-line distance. Haversine is useful to build the candidate set cheaply, not to rank it.

questions.prompt: Why model a trip as an explicit state machine (REQUESTED → ACCEPTED → ARRIVED → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED, plus CANCELLED)?
options: It makes trips render faster in the mobile app
It lets the database skip indexes on the trips table
Invalid transitions (e.g. COMPLETED → ARRIVED) can be rejected centrally, keeping trip data and billing consistent
It removes the need for any concurrency control
questions.explanation: A transition table makes every allowed move explicit and rejects the rest, so late or duplicate events can't corrupt a trip. You still need concurrency control for simultaneous events; the state machine only defines which transitions are legal.

questions.prompt: A rider taps Cancel at the same instant the driver taps Accept. How do you make exactly one of these win?
options: Apply both and let the app show whichever arrives last
Process whichever HTTP request reached the load balancer first
Use conditional updates such as `UPDATE trips SET state='ACCEPTED' WHERE id=? AND state='REQUESTED'` and check the affected row count
Lock the whole trips table during every transition
questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency on the current state turns the race into a compare-and-set: one update matches and the other affects 0 rows and is told the trip moved on. Arrival order at the load balancer isn't the commit order, and table locks kill throughput.

questions.prompt: At what granularity is surge pricing typically computed?
options: Per rider, from their trip history only
Per small geographic cell over a short time window, from demand vs. available supply
Once per city per day
Globally, one multiplier for all markets
questions.explanation: Imbalance is local and fast-changing: a stadium emptying affects a few cells for minutes. Cell-level (e.g. hexagon) multipliers recomputed every minute or so match that. City-wide daily pricing can't react.

questions.prompt: Surge changes between the moment the rider sees a fare and taps Confirm. How do you guarantee they are charged what they saw?
options: Disable surge recalculation while any rider has the app open
Issue a fare quote with an ID and expiry, and have the confirm request reference that quote ID
Recompute the fare at confirm time and charge the new value
Store the multiplier in the client and trust what it sends back
questions.explanation: The server stores the quote (price, multiplier, expiry) and binds the trip to it, so the price is locked and can't be tampered with. Trusting a client-supplied multiplier invites manipulation, and freezing surge globally is unworkable.

questions.prompt: Adjacent cells show surge multipliers of 1.0x and 2.5x, and drivers cluster right on the boundary. What is a common mitigation?
options: Hide multipliers from drivers entirely
Recompute surge only once per hour
Smooth multipliers across neighboring cells (e.g. averaging over a k-ring) and limit how fast they change
Make cells much larger so a city is one cell
questions.explanation: Spatial smoothing and rate limiting soften sharp edges that cause gaming and oscillation, while keeping local responsiveness. Huge cells or hourly updates throw away the locality and freshness surge needs.

questions.prompt: Billing, receipts and driver payouts all react to trip state changes. How do you reliably publish those changes without dual-write bugs?
options: Have each downstream service poll the trips table every second
Publish to the broker first, then update the DB when consumers acknowledge
Write the new state to the DB, then publish to the broker in a separate call
Write the state change and an outbox event in the same DB transaction, then relay the outbox to the broker
questions.explanation: The transactional outbox makes the state change and its event atomic; a relay (or CDC) publishes at-least-once and consumers dedupe by event ID. Write-then-publish loses events if the process crashes between the two steps.

questions.prompt: The driver app times out and resends 'start trip' for a trip that is already IN_PROGRESS. What should the API do?
options: Move the trip back to ARRIVED and start it again
Return success without changing anything, treating the repeated transition as idempotent
Create a second trip record in IN_PROGRESS
Return a 500 error so the app knows something went wrong
questions.explanation: Mobile networks retry. If the requested target state equals the current state (same trip, same driver), returning success makes retries safe. Erroring confuses the driver, and re-running the transition could reset timers or fare meters.

questions.prompt: Which trip state transitions should a ride-hailing state machine allow? Select all that apply.
options: COMPLETED → IN_PROGRESS
REQUESTED → ACCEPTED
IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED
ACCEPTED → CANCELLED
REQUESTED → COMPLETED
questions.explanation: Accepting, cancelling before pickup, and finishing are the normal flow. A completed trip is terminal (corrections go through adjustments or refunds), and a trip can't complete without being accepted and started.

questions.prompt: Which inputs are sensible for computing a cell's surge multiplier? Select all that apply.
options: Available (online, idle) drivers in or near the cell
Total drivers registered in the city, including offline ones
Open ride requests in the cell over the last few minutes
Recent rate at which riders accept quoted fares
questions.explanation: Surge reflects live supply versus demand and how price-sensitive demand is right now. Registered-but-offline drivers aren't supply. Counting them would understate the shortage.

questions.prompt: Storing the full history of trip state transitions with timestamps, not just the current state, makes fare disputes and debugging easier.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. An append-only transition log shows who did what and when (e.g. when the driver arrived and when the trip started). That supports waiting-time fees, cancellation fees, support cases and replaying bugs.

questions.prompt: Surge multipliers should be recomputed synchronously from the whole city's data on every individual ride request.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Surge is computed periodically (e.g. every minute per cell) by a background aggregation job and cached. Requests just read the current value. Per-request recomputation adds latency and load and makes prices jitter.

questions.prompt: A nearby-business search using geohash queries the user's cell plus its 8 neighbouring cells. Why the neighbours?
options: A point just across a cell boundary can be very close yet have a completely different geohash prefix
Neighbouring cells hold older versions of the same businesses
Geohash ignores longitude, so neighbours are needed to cover east-west distance
Geohash cells are circles, so neighbours fill the gaps between them
questions.explanation: Shared prefixes imply closeness, but closeness doesn't imply a shared prefix: two points a metre apart on opposite sides of a boundary can differ from the first character. Checking the 8 neighbours covers that edge case.

questions.prompt: For a 'businesses within ~500 m' search, which geohash precision is a typical choice for the search cells?
options: Length 4 (about 39 km x 20 km)
Length 6 (about 1.2 km x 0.6 km)
Length 5 (about 4.9 km x 4.9 km)
Length 8 (about 38 m x 19 m)
questions.explanation: A length-6 cell plus its neighbours comfortably covers a 500 m radius without scanning a huge area. Length 8 cells are so small that you would need to query hundreds of cells to cover 500 m.

questions.prompt: Why might you choose a quadtree over a fixed grid to index millions of businesses?
options: It adapts to density: dense areas are subdivided further so each leaf holds a bounded number of places
It handles constantly moving points with no rebalancing cost
It offers O(1) lookup for any radius query
It is natively supported as a Redis data type
questions.explanation: A fixed grid gives Manhattan and a desert the same cell size, so some cells are overloaded and others empty. A quadtree splits only where density is high. Updates for moving points are actually a weakness of quadtrees.

questions.prompt: A nearby-friends feature has 10 million concurrent users, each sending a location update every 30 seconds. Roughly how many location updates per second must the system ingest?
options: About 3.3 million
About 10 million
About 334,000
About 33,000
questions.explanation: 10,000,000 / 30 is about 333,000 updates per second. Each update may fan out to several online friends, so outbound messages are a multiple of this.

questions.prompt: Which architecture fits a nearby-friends feature where friends within 5 miles see each other's location update in near real time?
options: Broadcast every update to every connection on the same WebSocket server
On every update, run a geospatial radius query over all users and push to everyone found
Persistent WebSocket connections plus a pub/sub channel per user; friends subscribe to each other's channels and the server forwards an update only if the distance is within range
Store locations in PostgreSQL and have each client poll for friends' locations every second
questions.explanation: Pub/sub per user limits fan-out to actual friends, and the distance check on receipt filters out far-away friends. A global radius query on every update finds strangers rather than friends and is far more expensive.

questions.prompt: How does Redis store points added with GEOADD?
options: In a sorted set whose score is a 52-bit interleaved geohash value
In a quadtree that is rebuilt on every insert
In a hash of member to latitude/longitude string
In an R-tree maintained by a built-in geospatial module
questions.explanation: Redis GEO commands are built on sorted sets: coordinates are encoded as a 52-bit geohash used as the score, and radius searches become score-range scans over neighbouring cells. There is no R-tree.

questions.prompt: Why is an in-memory quadtree built at startup a good fit for business locations but a poor fit for user locations that change every few seconds?
options: Frequent moves mean constant removals, reinsertions and node splits/merges, while businesses barely change
Quadtrees can hold at most four points per node, which users exceed
Quadtrees store data on disk, which is too slow for users
Quadtrees cannot answer radius queries, only exact matches
questions.explanation: Businesses change rarely, so building the tree once and refreshing it occasionally is cheap. Moving users would force constant restructuring; a geohash key in a cache with TTL is cheaper for them. Quadtrees do support range and radius queries.

questions.prompt: Which statements about geohash are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A longer shared prefix means both points fall within a smaller common cell
It is a base32 string where each character adds 5 bits of precision
All cells of the same length cover the same ground area anywhere on Earth
Any two nearby points always share a long common prefix
questions.explanation: Each base32 character encodes 5 bits, and longer prefixes mean smaller cells. Cells are equal in degrees, not in ground area, which varies with latitude. Nearby points across a boundary may share no prefix at all.

questions.prompt: You use Redis pub/sub as the message bus for nearby friends. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Channels can be spread across a fleet of pub/sub servers by consistently hashing the user id
Messages are not persisted; a subscriber that is offline misses them, which is acceptable for ephemeral locations
Every message is written to a durable log so late-joining subscribers can replay it
In Redis Cluster, classic PUBLISH is broadcast to all nodes, while sharded pub/sub (SPUBLISH, Redis 7) routes by channel hash slot
questions.explanation: Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget, which suits locations that are stale in seconds anyway. Sharded pub/sub in Redis 7 avoids cluster-wide broadcast. Durable replay is what Redis Streams or Kafka provide, not pub/sub.

questions.prompt: A geohash of length 8 represents a smaller area than a geohash of length 5.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each extra character adds 5 bits, splitting the cell into 32 sub-cells. Length 8 is about 38 m x 19 m; length 5 is about 4.9 km x 4.9 km.

questions.prompt: Searching only the single geohash cell that contains the user is enough to guarantee finding the nearest business.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The nearest business may sit just across a cell boundary, closer than anything inside the user's own cell. You must also search neighbours and expand when results are too few.

questions.prompt: Why do map services serve the map as tiles at discrete zoom levels?
options: Tiles make shortest-path routing faster
The client downloads only tiles for the current viewport and zoom, and static tiles cache well on a CDN
Mobile devices cannot render vector graphics, so tiles are required
Tiles are needed for the device's GPS to work
questions.explanation: Tiling splits the world into small, cacheable, URL-addressable pieces, so panning and zooming only fetch what is visible, mostly from a CDN. Routing and GPS are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: In the standard web-map tiling scheme, zoom level z has 2^z x 2^z tiles. About how many tiles exist at zoom level 10?
options: About 1.05 million
About 1,000
About 20,000
About 1.07 billion
questions.explanation: 2^10 x 2^10 = 4^10 = 1,048,576 tiles. Tile counts grow 4x per zoom level, which is why the deepest levels dominate storage and are often rendered on demand.

questions.prompt: What is a main advantage of vector tiles over raster (PNG) tiles?
options: They don't need the client's GPU or any rendering on the device
They usually have smaller payloads and allow client-side styling, rotation and smooth zoom
They cannot be cached by CDNs, which keeps data fresh
They are better for satellite imagery
questions.explanation: Vector tiles carry geometry, which the client renders, so one tile set supports many styles, languages and smooth zooming. Satellite imagery is inherently raster, and vector tiles cache on CDNs just as well.

questions.prompt: Plain Dijkstra on a continent-sized road graph is too slow per query. What do production routing engines typically do?
options: Use breadth-first search, which is faster on road networks
Use Bellman-Ford, which handles more road types
Use preprocessing-based speedups such as contraction hierarchies or hierarchical partitioning so each query explores few nodes
Precompute all-pairs shortest paths nightly with Floyd-Warshall
questions.explanation: Contraction hierarchies and partition-based methods preprocess the graph so queries take milliseconds. Floyd-Warshall is O(n^3) time and O(n^2) storage, which is infeasible for hundreds of millions of nodes; BFS ignores edge weights.

questions.prompt: A* for travel-time routing uses 'straight-line distance divided by the maximum speed limit' as its heuristic. Why must the heuristic never overestimate the remaining cost?
options: Overestimating causes A* to visit every node in the graph
Overestimating makes the heuristic slower to compute
An admissible heuristic guarantees A* still returns an optimal path
A* only works with heuristics measured in meters
questions.explanation: If the heuristic never overestimates, A* cannot finalize a suboptimal path before the optimal one. An overestimating heuristic may find routes faster but can return a non-optimal route.

questions.prompt: ETAs must reflect current traffic, but the routing engine relies on heavy preprocessing. How is live traffic usually incorporated?
options: Rebuild the full contraction hierarchy from scratch for every request
Ask users to report traffic and only reroute when reports arrive
Use a technique whose edge weights can be updated separately from preprocessing (e.g. customizable route planning) and refresh travel times from live probe data
Use static road distances and add a fixed traffic buffer to every ETA
questions.explanation: Customizable approaches split the expensive metric-independent preprocessing from a fast customization step, so edge travel times from GPS probes can be refreshed every few minutes. Rebuilding per request is far too slow.

questions.prompt: GPS points from phones are noisy and drift off roads. What is the process of snapping a trace to the most likely sequence of road segments called?
options: Tile rendering
Geocoding
Map matching
Reverse geocoding
questions.explanation: Map matching (often done with a Hidden Markov Model) aligns noisy GPS traces to the road network, which is needed for both navigation and building traffic speeds. Geocoding converts addresses to coordinates.

questions.prompt: Which design choices are reasonable for a navigation service? Select all that apply.
options: Serve map tiles from a CDN
Batch location updates on the client to save battery and bandwidth
Run Floyd-Warshall nightly to precompute every possible route
Partition the road graph into routing tiles that servers load on demand
questions.explanation: CDN tiles, partitioned routing graphs and batched client updates are standard. All-pairs precomputation is infeasible at road-network scale in both time and storage.

questions.prompt: Which statements about rerouting and ETA during active navigation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Detect off-route driving by comparing the map-matched position with the planned route
Combine live and historical speeds because live probe data is sparse on minor roads
Recompute every active user's route every second regardless of conditions
Suggest a new route when traffic makes an alternative faster by more than a threshold
questions.explanation: Rerouting is event-driven (off-route, significant traffic change), and ETAs blend historical patterns with live data. Recomputing every route every second wastes huge compute for almost no benefit.

questions.prompt: Geocoding converts a street address into latitude and longitude coordinates.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Geocoding is address to coordinates; reverse geocoding is coordinates to a human-readable address.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm returns correct shortest paths even when some edge weights are negative.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Dijkstra assumes a finalized node can't later get a shorter path, which breaks with negative weights. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges. Road travel times are non-negative, so Dijkstra-based methods work for routing.

questions.prompt: What ordering guarantee does Apache Kafka provide?
options: No ordering guarantee at all
Order only within a single partition
Total order across all partitions of a topic
Order across all topics of the cluster
questions.explanation: Kafka orders records within a partition by offset. Across partitions there is no global order, which is why related events must share a key to land on the same partition.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 10 consumers. How many consumers actively receive messages?
options: 5, Kafka uses half of the consumers as standbys
6, and the other 4 sit idle
10, each partition is split across consumers
1, a single leader consumer reads everything
questions.explanation: Within a group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the partition count. The 4 extra consumers are idle until a rebalance gives them a partition.

questions.prompt: Events for each order must be processed in sequence. How should the producer publish them?
options: Put the event timestamp in the key so consumers can sort events
Create one partition per consumer and choose partitions randomly
Use order_id as the message key so all events for an order go to the same partition
Use round-robin partitioning to balance load evenly
questions.explanation: The default partitioner hashes the key, so the same order_id always lands on the same partition, which is consumed in order. Round-robin spreads one order's events across partitions and loses ordering.

questions.prompt: A consumer commits its offset right after polling, before processing, and then crashes mid-processing. Which delivery semantics does this give?
options: At-most-once: the uncommitted work is lost because the offset already moved past it
At-least-once: the message is redelivered after restart
It depends only on the producer's acks setting
Exactly-once: the commit and processing are atomic
questions.explanation: Committing before processing means a crash skips the message on restart, so it is processed at most once. Committing after processing flips this to at-least-once with possible duplicates.

questions.prompt: What does Kafka's idempotent producer combined with transactions actually provide?
options: Global ordering across all partitions of a topic
Atomic read-process-write across Kafka topics and consumer offsets; side effects outside Kafka still need their own idempotency
No duplicates even when consumers auto-commit and write to an external DB
End-to-end exactly-once for any external database without extra work
questions.explanation: Kafka transactions make output records and offset commits atomic within Kafka. Calling an API or writing to Postgres is outside that transaction, so those sinks need idempotency keys or a transactional outbox/inbox.

questions.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, and the producer uses acks=all. Two of the three replicas go down. What happens to writes?
options: They are buffered by the broker until replicas return
They are rejected with a not-enough-replicas error, trading availability for durability
They are written to the leader only and replicated later
The producer automatically falls back to acks=1
questions.explanation: With only one in-sync replica, acks=all cannot be satisfied under min.insync.replicas=2, so the broker rejects writes. This configuration deliberately refuses writes rather than risk losing acknowledged data.

questions.prompt: Kafka keeps messages after they are consumed until retention expires. What does this enable compared with a classic queue that deletes on acknowledgement?
options: Automatic exactly-once delivery to every consumer
Lower latency than any in-memory queue
Multiple independent consumer groups and replay by resetting offsets
Strict global ordering of all messages
questions.explanation: Because the log is retained, each consumer group tracks its own offset, and you can rewind to reprocess. Retention has nothing to do with global ordering or exactly-once delivery.

questions.prompt: Which events trigger a consumer group rebalance in Kafka? Select all that apply.
options: A new consumer joins the group
A consumer exceeds max.poll.interval.ms between polls
Partitions are added to a subscribed topic
A producer sends a message with a key never seen before
questions.explanation: Membership changes (join, leave, being considered dead after a slow poll) and partition count changes trigger reassignment. New keys just hash to existing partitions and don't affect the group.

questions.prompt: One message always fails processing and blocks its partition. Which handling strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Add partitions to the topic so the blocked message moves elsewhere
Route it through retry topics with increasing delays before the DLQ
Silently commit past it without recording it anywhere
Retry a bounded number of times, then publish it to a dead-letter topic and move on
questions.explanation: Bounded retries plus delayed retry topics and a DLQ keep the partition moving while preserving the message for investigation. Silently skipping loses data; adding partitions doesn't move existing messages.

questions.prompt: Adding partitions to an existing Kafka topic can change which partition a given key maps to, so new and old messages for that key may be on different partitions.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The default partitioner uses hash(key) mod partitionCount, so changing the count remaps keys. Existing data stays where it was, which can break per-key ordering around the change.

questions.prompt: Within one consumer group, two consumers can read the same partition at the same time to double throughput.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A partition is assigned to only one consumer per group. To get more parallelism you need more partitions, or a separate consumer group, which receives every message independently.

questions.prompt: Which observability signal best answers 'why was this particular request slow as it passed through five services'?
options: Aggregated metrics such as request rate and p99 latency
Uptime checks from external probes
A distributed trace showing spans for each service hop
Host-level CPU and memory dashboards
questions.explanation: A trace follows one request across services with timing per span, pinpointing where the time went. Metrics are aggregated, so they show that latency rose but not which hop caused it for a given request.

questions.prompt: Why put Kafka between metric collectors and the time-series storage writers?
options: Kafka compresses metrics better than any TSDB
It makes alert evaluation exactly-once
It removes the need for a time-series database
It buffers bursts and decouples the two sides, so writers can fall behind and catch up without dropping data
questions.explanation: A durable buffer absorbs ingest spikes and storage outages, and lets other consumers (anomaly detection, archiving) read the same stream. You still need a TSDB for efficient queries.

questions.prompt: An alert fires whenever CPU exceeds 90%, including 20-second spikes, and pages on-call several times a night. What is the best first fix?
options: Send the alert by email instead of paging
Require the condition to hold for a duration (e.g. 'for: 5m') before firing
Lower the threshold to 80% so issues are caught earlier
Raise the scrape interval so short spikes are not recorded
questions.explanation: A pending duration filters transient spikes while still catching sustained problems. Coarser scraping only hides data, and switching channels leaves a noisy, non-actionable alert in place.

questions.prompt: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. A simple 'error rate above 0.1% for 5 minutes' alert is noisy for blips yet slow for a full outage. What is the recommended improvement?
options: Increase the threshold to 1% errors over 1 hour
Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts, e.g. page when both the 1-hour and 5-minute windows burn the budget at 14.4x
A single 30-day error-budget alert that fires when the budget hits zero
Alert on CPU instead of errors, since it leads errors
questions.explanation: Burn-rate alerts measure how fast the error budget is being spent; 14.4x over an hour consumes 2% of a 30-day budget, and the short window confirms it is still happening. A budget-exhausted alert fires far too late.

questions.prompt: A network partition causes 500 hosts to fire the same alert simultaneously. Which Alertmanager feature turns this into one notification?
options: A longer rule evaluation interval
Deduplicating alerts by host name
Grouping alerts by labels such as alertname and cluster
Silences created after the page arrives
questions.explanation: Grouping batches alerts sharing chosen labels into a single notification (inhibition can additionally suppress dependent alerts). Deduplicating by host keeps 500 distinct alerts because each host is different.

questions.prompt: Head-based sampling at 1% means rare error traces are usually dropped. What is the main alternative and its cost?
options: Convert traces into logs, which are always cheaper to store
Tail-based sampling in the collector, keeping all error or slow traces, at the cost of buffering every span until each trace completes
Sample by service name so each service keeps 1%
Sample 100% of traces at the client, which costs nothing extra
questions.explanation: Tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so it can keep interesting ones, but collectors must hold spans in memory and route all spans of a trace to the same instance. Per-service 1% sampling still drops most errors.

questions.prompt: Why does a TSDB such as Prometheus append incoming samples to a write-ahead log before adding them to its in-memory head block?
options: Because compression only works on WAL files
So remote clients can tail the WAL for alerts
So in-memory data that hasn't been flushed to disk blocks can be recovered after a crash
So queries read from the WAL instead of memory
questions.explanation: Recent samples live in memory for hours before being compacted into blocks; the WAL lets the server replay them after a restart. Queries are served from the head block and persisted blocks, not the WAL.

questions.prompt: Which are good alerting practices? Select all that apply.
options: Make every page actionable and link it to a runbook
Alert on user-facing symptoms such as error rate and latency rather than every possible cause
Page on-call for every warning-level threshold on every metric
Route by severity: urgent issues page, lower-severity ones create tickets
questions.explanation: Symptom-based, actionable, severity-routed alerts keep pages meaningful. Paging on every warning causes alert fatigue, and people start ignoring pages.

questions.prompt: How do horizontally scaled metrics backends (Thanos, Cortex, Mimir style) handle storage at scale? Select all that apply.
options: Upload compacted blocks to object storage for long-term retention
Shard ingesters by a hash of the series labels, with replication
Keep all data forever on a single large node's local SSD
Queriers fan out to stores, merge results and deduplicate HA replicas
questions.explanation: These systems use hash-sharded, replicated ingesters, cheap object storage for history, and fan-out queriers that merge and deduplicate. A single node caps both capacity and availability.

questions.prompt: Logs and traces can be correlated by writing the trace ID into each log line.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Putting the trace ID (and span ID) into structured logs lets you jump from a slow trace to its logs and back. OpenTelemetry log correlation is built on this.

questions.prompt: In Prometheus, if a metric stops being reported and its series disappears, an alert like 'errors > 0' automatically fires because the missing value is treated as zero.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A missing series yields no result, so a threshold rule simply stops matching; it is not treated as zero and it does not fire. Use absent() or up == 0 alerts to detect disappeared targets.

questions.prompt: Which protocol do mail servers use to transfer email to each other?
options: POP3
JMAP
SMTP
IMAP
questions.explanation: SMTP handles server-to-server relay (and client submission). IMAP, POP3 and JMAP are protocols for clients to read mail from their own mailbox.

questions.prompt: How does a sending mail server find where to deliver mail addressed to someone@example.com?
options: It asks the recipient's IMAP server for a delivery address
It looks up the MX records for example.com and tries the lowest preference value first
It looks up the TXT record containing the SPF policy
It looks up the A record for mail.example.com by convention
questions.explanation: MX records list the domain's mail exchangers with preference values; lower is tried first. SPF in TXT records authorizes senders and says nothing about where to deliver.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism adds a cryptographic signature over selected headers and the body so the receiver can verify the message came from the signing domain and wasn't altered?
options: DKIM
DMARC
STARTTLS
SPF
questions.explanation: DKIM signs the message with the domain's private key; receivers verify with the public key in DNS. SPF only checks whether the sending IP is authorized, and DMARC is a policy built on top of SPF and DKIM.

questions.prompt: A user reads mail on a phone and a laptop and wants folders and read/unread status to stay in sync. Which client access protocol fits?
options: FTP, because mailboxes are stored as files
IMAP, because state such as folders and flags lives on the server
POP3, because it downloads messages to each device
SMTP, because it pushes changes to every device
questions.explanation: IMAP keeps the mailbox and its flags on the server, so every client sees the same state. POP3 is designed to download (often delete) messages, so state diverges between devices.

questions.prompt: You must store email for a billion users. Typical queries list a folder sorted by date and show unread counts; bodies and attachments are large. Which storage design fits best?
options: One file per user on local disk on the server that received the mail
Elasticsearch as the single primary store for metadata and bodies
Metadata in a store partitioned by user_id and clustered by folder and time, with bodies and attachments in object storage
One relational database holding all messages, with bodies and attachments as BLOBs
questions.explanation: Partitioning by user keeps each mailbox's queries on one shard, and clustering by folder/time makes listings range scans. Large immutable blobs belong in object storage. A single relational DB can't scale to that volume, and local files lack durability.

questions.prompt: Why is mailbox full-text search usually built as per-user partitioned indexes rather than one global index sorted for relevance?
options: Every query is scoped to one user, so partitioning by user keeps searches on one shard and isolates users from each other
A global index ranks results better, but per-user indexes are cheaper to license
Search libraries cannot hold more than a million documents in one index
A global index is cheaper to update when each new email arrives
questions.explanation: Users only search their own mail, so a per-user partition means a query touches one small shard and a heavy user can't slow others. A global index would make every write and query hit a huge shared structure.

questions.prompt: How should an inbound spam-filtering pipeline be ordered?
