options: Rely only on users clicking 'report spam'
Run cheap checks first (IP reputation, blocklists, SPF/DKIM/DMARC results), then content-based ML classification on what remains
Run the expensive ML classifier on every message before any other check
Deliver every message first and scan the inbox later in a batch job
questions.explanation: Cheap connection-level checks reject a large share of spam before costly content analysis, saving compute. Delivering first exposes users to phishing and makes cleanup harder.

questions.prompt: Which practices improve outbound deliverability for a new email-sending service? Select all that apply.
options: Warm up new sending IPs by gradually increasing volume
Publish SPF, DKIM and a DMARC policy for the sending domain
Rotate through many random sending domains to stay ahead of filters
Process bounces and complaints and suppress those addresses
questions.explanation: Authentication, IP warm-up and list hygiene build sender reputation. Rotating random domains looks like spammer behaviour (snowshoeing) and damages deliverability.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SMTP delivery are correct? Select all that apply.
options: On a 4xx temporary failure, the sender retries with backoff, often for days
On a 5xx permanent failure, the sender stops and returns a bounce (DSN) to the original sender
SMTP guarantees end-to-end encryption from the sender's device to the recipient's device
A receiving server should reply 250 only after the message is durably stored, since that transfers responsibility
questions.explanation: SMTP is store-and-forward: a 250 means the receiver has taken responsibility, 4xx means try again later, 5xx means give up and bounce. STARTTLS encrypts individual hops only, not end to end.

questions.prompt: DMARC lets a domain owner tell receivers what to do (none, quarantine or reject) with mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment, and where to send reports.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: DMARC publishes a policy (p=none/quarantine/reject) and reporting addresses in DNS, based on whether SPF or DKIM pass and align with the From domain.

questions.prompt: Deduplicating attachments by content hash is never useful in email storage, because every message is unique.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Messages are unique, but attachments often aren't: the same file sent to 200 recipients or forwarded repeatedly can be stored once and referenced by its hash, saving a lot of storage.

questions.prompt: Why do S3-style object stores separate the metadata service from the data storage nodes?
options: Metadata is small and needs fast consistent lookups and listings, while data is large immutable blobs, so each side scales independently
Separation removes the need for any replication
Metadata must be stored on tape for durability
Data nodes cannot store keys longer than 64 bytes
questions.explanation: Name lookups and listings have very different access patterns from streaming gigabytes of bytes. Splitting them lets the metadata tier optimize for consistency and the data tier for throughput and cheap capacity.

questions.prompt: An object store uses Reed-Solomon erasure coding with 8 data fragments and 4 parity fragments. What are the storage overhead and failure tolerance?
options: 1.33x overhead; any 4 fragments can be lost
1.5x overhead; any 4 fragments can be lost
1.5x overhead; any 2 fragments can be lost
3x overhead; any 4 fragments can be lost
questions.explanation: 12 fragments store 8 fragments' worth of data: 12 / 8 = 1.5x. Any 8 of the 12 can rebuild the object, so up to 4 can be lost. 3x replication tolerates only 2 losses at double the cost.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of erasure coding compared with 3x replication?
options: No trade-off; erasure coding is strictly better
Higher durability with higher storage cost
Faster small reads because fragments are read in parallel from one disk
Much lower storage cost, but more CPU and network for encoding, degraded reads and repairs
questions.explanation: Erasure coding cuts overhead (e.g. 1.5x versus 3x), but reconstruction must read from many nodes and compute parity. That is why hot or small data is often replicated and cold data erasure-coded.

questions.prompt: All 12 fragments of an RS(8,4) object were placed on servers in the same rack. What is the main risk?
options: No risk, since erasure coding already tolerates 4 failures
Parity fragments cannot be computed within a single rack
One rack-level failure (power, top-of-rack switch) removes more than 4 fragments at once, making the object unavailable or lost
Reads are slower because fragments share one network switch
questions.explanation: The 4-failure tolerance assumes independent failures. Correlated failures within a rack or AZ break that assumption, so fragments must be spread across failure domains.

questions.prompt: Why do object stores often pack many small objects into large data files instead of storing one file per object?
options: Large files encrypt faster than small ones
Small files cannot be erasure-coded at all
Packing makes each object mutable in place
Per-file filesystem overhead (inodes, metadata, seeks) is huge for billions of tiny objects; appending to large files and recording (file, offset, size) is far cheaper
questions.explanation: Billions of tiny files exhaust inodes and make metadata operations dominate. Appending to large files turns writes into sequential I/O; the metadata service maps each object to its location.

questions.prompt: An object is deleted: its metadata is marked deleted, but its bytes remain inside a large packed data file. How is the space usually reclaimed?
options: They are never reclaimed; storage just grows
The bytes are zeroed in place immediately
Background compaction copies live objects into new files, updates metadata, then deletes the old files
The filesystem's TRIM command frees them automatically
questions.explanation: Compaction (garbage collection) rewrites files that contain mostly dead data, preserving immutability of written files. Zeroing bytes in place wouldn't free space in the file anyway.

questions.prompt: A client must upload a 5 GB file over an unreliable connection. Which object-storage feature is designed for this?
options: Splitting the file into separate objects that the client must reassemble on every read
Uploading through a byte-range PATCH on the existing object
Multipart upload: parts are uploaded in parallel, retried individually, then combined with a completion call
Increasing the HTTP timeout for one big PUT
questions.explanation: Multipart upload lets a failed part be retried without restarting, and the parts become one object on completion. Incomplete uploads still use storage, so lifecycle rules should clean them up.

questions.prompt: Which techniques do object stores use to reach very high durability? Select all that apply.
options: Relying only on local RAID inside each storage node
Checksums on write and periodic background scrubbing to detect silent corruption
Repairing corrupted or lost fragments from replicas or parity
Replicating or erasure-coding data across multiple availability zones
questions.explanation: Durability comes from detecting corruption, spreading redundancy across independent failure domains, and repairing quickly. Node-level RAID doesn't survive losing the whole node, rack or AZ.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the metadata service for prefix-based LIST operations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Hot key prefixes may require splitting range partitions to spread load
Storing keys sorted in range partitions makes a prefix LIST a range scan
Hash-partitioning by full key forces prefix listings to query every shard
Metadata should be stored inside the data blobs so no separate index is needed
questions.explanation: Range partitioning preserves key order for listing but can create hot ranges that must be split; hash partitioning spreads load but scatters prefixes. Without a separate index, listing would require scanning all data.

questions.prompt: Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for new objects, overwrites and LIST operations.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Since December 2020, S3 is strongly consistent for GET, PUT and LIST, so a successful write is immediately visible. Earlier it was eventually consistent for overwrites and listings.

questions.prompt: With erasure coding, reading an object when one data fragment is missing costs no more than reading a healthy object.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A degraded read must fetch parity fragments from other nodes and decode the missing data, which adds network, CPU and latency. That is part of erasure coding's trade-off.

questions.prompt: In a double-entry ledger, what invariant does every transaction satisfy?
options: The receiving account's balance is always updated first
Each entry stores the account's running balance instead of an amount
Each transaction touches exactly one account
Total debits equal total credits, so the entries sum to zero
questions.explanation: Money moves between accounts, so every transaction has balancing debit and credit entries. That makes errors detectable: if the ledger doesn't sum to zero, something is wrong.

questions.prompt: In a Node.js wallet backed by PostgreSQL, how should monetary amounts be represented?
options: Strings converted with parseFloat when doing arithmetic
JavaScript numbers, rounded with toFixed(2) before saving
Integer minor units (e.g. cents as bigint/BigInt) or NUMERIC, always with a currency code
A float8 column, since it has 15 digits of precision
questions.explanation: Binary floating point can't represent values like 0.1 exactly, so sums drift (0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3). Integer minor units or decimal types are exact. parseFloat brings back the same float problem.

questions.prompt: A client's POST /transfers times out and the client retries. How do you prevent the transfer from happening twice?
options: Reject any transfer with the same amount within 10 seconds
Rate-limit the client to one request per second
Have the client send an idempotency key stored under a unique constraint; on a repeat, return the stored result
Rely on TCP retransmission to avoid duplicates
questions.explanation: The server records the key with the outcome in the same transaction as the transfer, so a retry returns the original result. Amount-based heuristics block legitimate identical transfers and miss real duplicates.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, two concurrent withdrawals each read balance = 100, check it is at least 100, then write balance - 100. The balance ends up at -100. Which fix is correct?
options: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 100, and treat 0 updated rows as insufficient funds
Read the balance from a replica so the check is cheaper
Keep READ COMMITTED with SELECT then UPDATE, but add a retry loop
Wrap the check in an in-process mutex in the Node service
questions.explanation: The conditional update makes the check and debit one atomic statement (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE also works). An in-process mutex doesn't help when several Node instances run, and a retry loop doesn't fix the race.

questions.prompt: Accounts A and B live on different database shards, and you want to avoid two-phase commit. What is a common way to transfer money between them?
options: Two independent writes with no tracking, since failures are rare
A saga: debit A into a pending state, credit B, compensate A on failure, with every step idempotent and tracked
A nightly batch job that fixes any mismatched balances
A global lock over all shards during every transfer
questions.explanation: A saga breaks the transfer into idempotent local steps with compensations and a recorded state machine, so it can resume or undo after failures. Untracked writes can lose or create money when one side fails.

questions.prompt: An event-sourced wallet derives balances by replaying all events. Reads are getting slow for old, busy accounts. What is the standard fix?
options: Switch reads to a cache with a 24-hour TTL
Merge old events into one event and rewrite history
Delete old events once they are older than a year
Store periodic snapshots and/or maintain a read-model projection, replaying only events after the snapshot
questions.explanation: Snapshots and projections keep the event log as the source of truth while making reads cheap. Deleting or rewriting events destroys the audit trail, which is the main reason to use event sourcing.

questions.prompt: A credit of $50 was posted to the wrong account. How should it be corrected in a ledger?
options: Update the original entry's account id in place
Post a reversing entry, then post the correct entry
Adjust the account's cached balance without touching the ledger
Delete the original entry and insert the correct one
questions.explanation: Ledgers are append-only: corrections are new entries, so the history shows what happened and when. Editing or deleting entries breaks auditability and reconciliation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about event sourcing for a wallet are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It provides a complete audit trail of every change
Evolving the schema of old events needs versioning or upcasting
Querying current state needs no extra components
Current state can be rebuilt by replaying events
questions.explanation: Event sourcing gives auditability and replay, but stored events live forever, so schema changes need versioning. Queries on current state usually need projections or snapshots, which are extra components.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ledger reconciliation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The sum of all ledger entries per currency should be zero
Mismatches go to an investigation queue and are fixed with adjusting entries
Compare the internal ledger daily with bank or payment-provider settlement reports
Reconciliation is unnecessary when double-entry bookkeeping is used
questions.explanation: Double-entry keeps the ledger internally consistent but can't detect disagreement with external systems (missed webhooks, fees, chargebacks). Reconciliation catches those, and fixes are new entries.

questions.prompt: Storing money as IEEE-754 floating point is fine as long as you round to two decimals when displaying it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Rounding only hides the error in display; stored sums still accumulate representation error, and comparisons such as balance >= amount can be wrong. Use integer minor units or decimals.

questions.prompt: An idempotency key should be stored with a hash of the request, so a reused key with a different payload can be rejected.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: If a client mistakenly reuses a key for a different transfer, returning the old result would silently drop the new request. Comparing request hashes lets the server return a clear error instead.

questions.prompt: In an exchange order book, what does price-time priority mean?
options: The best price matches first, and among orders at the same price the earliest one matches first
Orders are matched randomly among the best prices
Market makers always match before other participants
Larger orders match first, then earlier ones
questions.explanation: Price-time (FIFO) priority rewards the best price first and then whoever arrived first at that price. Size-based (pro-rata) matching exists in some markets but isn't price-time priority.

questions.prompt: The ask side has 300 shares at 100.10 and 500 shares at 100.20. A market buy order for 600 shares arrives. What is the average fill price?
questions.explanation: It fills 300 at 100.10 (30,030) and 300 at 100.20 (30,060): 60,090 / 600 = 100.15. 100.16 is what you get by wrongly weighting by the full 500 shares at 100.20.

questions.prompt: Bids: 400 @ 99.95, 300 @ 99.90, 500 @ 99.85. A limit sell for 1,000 @ 99.90 arrives. What happens?
options: Fills 400 @ 99.95 and 300 @ 99.90; the remaining 300 rests on the book as an ask at 99.90
Rests entirely as an ask at 99.90 because it is a limit order
Fills 1,000 at 99.90
questions.explanation: A sell limit at 99.90 matches any bid at or above 99.90, best price first. The 99.85 bid is below the limit, so the remaining 300 shares rest on the book at 99.90.

questions.prompt: Why do exchanges typically run a single-threaded matching engine per instrument behind a sequencer?
options: Processing a totally ordered input stream deterministically means replaying the same log yields identical state, enabling recovery and hot standbys
Multithreading is impossible in the languages exchanges use
Regulators forbid multiple threads in trading systems
It minimizes memory usage per instrument
questions.explanation: Determinism plus a sequenced input log means any replica fed the same sequence produces the same book and fills, which gives fast failover and auditability. A single thread on in-memory data is also extremely fast because it avoids locks.

questions.prompt: The primary matching engine fails. How does a backup take over without losing or duplicating fills?
options: Participants resubmit all their open orders after the failover
The backup reloads the order book from a database snapshot taken nightly
The backup re-matches all of today's orders from scratch and re-sends every fill
The backup consumes the same sequenced input and processes it deterministically; it resumes from the last sequence number, and outputs are deduplicated by sequence number
questions.explanation: Feeding the hot standby the same sequenced log keeps it in lockstep, and sequence numbers let downstream systems drop duplicates. A nightly snapshot would lose the whole day's state.

questions.prompt: Which data structure supports an order book with fast best-price access and O(1) add/cancel at a known price level?
options: One sorted array of all orders
Price levels each holding a doubly linked FIFO list, an order_id to node map, and a sorted structure (or array) of price levels
A binary heap of orders only
A hash map from order_id to order, with nothing else
questions.explanation: The linked list keeps time priority within a level, the hash map finds an order for O(1) cancel, and the sorted levels give the best price. A heap makes cancellations O(n); a sorted array makes insertion O(n).

questions.prompt: Why do exchanges often publish market data using UDP multicast?
options: It fans out to many participants with low, uniform latency; receivers detect gaps by sequence number and request retransmission
It lets each participant receive a personalized feed
UDP guarantees delivery, unlike TCP
Multicast encrypts data automatically
questions.explanation: Multicast sends one packet to all subscribers at once, which is fast and fair. UDP doesn't guarantee delivery, so feeds carry sequence numbers and offer recovery or retransmission channels.

questions.prompt: Which are appropriate pre-trade risk checks? Select all that apply.
options: Price collars and fat-finger checks against a reference price
Run risk checks asynchronously after matching to keep latency low
Check buying power and position limits before the order enters the book
Reject orders above a maximum quantity or notional value
questions.explanation: Pre-trade checks must run before matching, or a bad order can execute before anyone notices. Checking after matching is post-trade surveillance, which can't undo the fill.

questions.prompt: Which techniques do low-latency matching engines commonly use? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the entire order book in memory
Use a ring buffer and an append-only event log, as in the LMAX Disruptor
Write every order synchronously to a relational database before matching
Avoid allocations and GC pauses in the hot path, e.g. with object pools
questions.explanation: In-memory books, allocation-free hot paths and ring buffers with sequential journaling keep latency in microseconds. A synchronous relational write per order adds milliseconds; durability comes from the sequenced log instead.

questions.prompt: A market order guarantees the execution price but not that the order will execute.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It is the reverse: a market order executes immediately against available liquidity at whatever prices are there, so the price isn't guaranteed. A limit order guarantees the price (or better) but not execution.

questions.prompt: Under price-time priority, many exchanges let an order keep its time priority when its quantity is reduced, but it loses priority when the quantity is increased.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reducing quantity doesn't disadvantage others queued behind, so priority is kept; increasing it would let a trader jump the queue with new size, so it is treated as a new order at the back of the level.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
0
cleanup

0
1
cleanup

cleanup
0
questions.explanation: for...of logs 0, then gets 1 and hits break. Leaving the loop early calls the iterator's optional return() method, so 'cleanup' prints. return() is not called when the loop finishes normally, only on early exit (break, return, throw).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 3 undefined
questions.explanation: An iterator is single-pass. The first spread drains it; the second spread calls next() on an exhausted iterator, which returns done: true at once, giving an empty array. The array itself is re-iterable because each for...of or spread asks it for a fresh iterator.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
start
1

start
mid
end
1

start
mid
1
questions.explanation: Array destructuring pulls only as many values as it needs: one next() call runs the body up to the first yield ('start'). Because the iterator isn't done, destructuring then calls return(), which finishes the generator without running 'mid' or 'end'.

questions.prompt: What makes a plain object usable in a for...of loop?
options: Defining a [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an object with a next() method
Defining a next() method directly on the object that returns { value, done }
Giving the object a numeric length property and integer keys starting at 0
Defining a [Symbol.asyncIterator]() method that returns an object with next()
questions.explanation: for...of calls obj[Symbol.iterator]() to get an iterator, then calls next() until done is true. An object that only has next() is an iterator but not an iterable. Array-likes with length are not iterable, and Symbol.asyncIterator is only used by for await...of.

questions.prompt: Why is for...of preferred over for...in for walking the elements of an array?
options: for...in visits enumerable string keys (including inherited ones), not the element values
for...in skips index 0 of an array, because the key 0 is falsy and the loop treats it as a stop signal
for...in can't be used on arrays at all; it throws a TypeError because arrays aren't plain objects
for...of is the only loop that works on arrays created with new Array(), which have no own keys yet
questions.explanation: for...in enumerates property keys as strings, including enumerable inherited properties (e.g. something added to Array.prototype). for...of uses the array's iterator and yields values in order. for...in does work on arrays; it just iterates the wrong thing.

questions.prompt: A paginated REST client should let callers process items one at a time and stop early without fetching the remaining pages. Which design fits best?
options: A method that fetches every page up front in parallel and resolves a Promise with one combined array
An EventEmitter that emits an 'item' event for every result as fast as the pages arrive from the API
A synchronous iterator whose next() starts every page request and returns a Promise for each page
An async generator (Symbol.asyncIterator) that fetches the next page only when the consumer asks for more
questions.explanation: An async iterator is pull-based: the next page is only requested when the for await...of loop asks for more, and break triggers return() so no further fetches happen. Fetching everything up front wastes requests and memory; an emitter pushes data with no back-pressure.

questions.prompt: Why does map.keys()[0] evaluate to undefined for a non-empty Map?
options: map.keys() returns an iterator object, not an array, so it has no index properties
Map keys can only be read back with map.get() or map.has(), never enumerated
Map keys are stored in hash order, so there's no stable index 0 to return
map.keys() returns a Promise of the key list that has to be awaited first
questions.explanation: keys(), values() and entries() return Map iterator objects. They are iterable but are not arrays, so there's no [0] property. Use [...map.keys()][0] or map.keys().next().value. Maps actually keep keys in insertion order, so ordering isn't the problem.

questions.prompt: Which of these are iterable by default (usable with for...of)? Select all that apply.
options: A Set
A string
The arguments object inside a regular function
A WeakMap
A plain object literal { a: 1 }
questions.explanation: Strings (by code point), Set, Map, arrays, typed arrays and arguments implement Symbol.iterator. Plain objects don't (use Object.entries). WeakMap isn't iterable because its keys can be garbage-collected at any time.

questions.prompt: Which of these consume their argument through the iterable protocol (Symbol.iterator)? Select all that apply.
options: Spread into an array literal: [...x]
Object.keys(x)
Array destructuring: const [a] = x
JSON.stringify(x)
Promise.all(x)
questions.explanation: Spread, array destructuring, Promise.all/allSettled/race/any, Array.from, new Map/Set and for...of all use Symbol.iterator. Object.keys reads own enumerable properties and JSON.stringify serialises properties; neither calls the iterator, which is why a Map stringifies to {}.

questions.prompt: If a hand-written iterator never returns done: true, spreading it with [...it] will never finish (it loops until memory runs out).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Spread keeps calling next() until done is true, collecting values into an array. An infinite iterator is fine with for...of plus break, or with destructuring that takes a fixed number of items, but spread and Array.from try to drain it completely.

questions.prompt: Every iterator is also an iterable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Built-in iterators (and generator objects) are iterable because their [Symbol.iterator]() returns this. A hand-written object that only has next() is an iterator but not an iterable, so for...of over it throws 'is not iterable' unless you also add [Symbol.iterator]() { return this; }.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
got 5
1
10

1
got 5
10

1
got ignored
NaN
questions.explanation: The value passed to next() becomes the result of the yield the generator is paused at. The first next() starts the body, so there's no paused yield and 'ignored' is discarded. The second next(5) resumes yield 1 with 5, logs 'got 5', then yields 10.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
1,2
{"done":true}

1,2
{"value":2,"done":false}

1,2
{"value":3,"done":true}

1,2,3
{"value":3,"done":true}
questions.explanation: A generator's return value is delivered with done: true. Spread and for...of stop as soon as done is true and ignore that value, so the array is [1, 2]. Calling next() manually a third time shows { value: 3, done: true }.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
1
{"value":9,"done":true}
questions.explanation: return(9) resumes the paused generator as if a return statement ran at the yield. The finally block runs first (logging 'finally'), then the generator completes with { value: 9, done: true }. This is how for...of with break lets generators release resources.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: a r r
a undefined
a r
a
questions.explanation: yield* re-yields every value from inner ('a'), and the expression evaluates to inner's return value ('r'), which outer then yields itself. The return value of the delegate isn't yielded automatically, which is why the output isn't 'a r r'.

questions.prompt: What happens when you call a generator function g()?
options: It returns a Promise that resolves with the return value once the generator body finishes
It runs the whole body immediately and returns an array of every value that was yielded
It runs the body up to the first yield, pauses there, and returns the first yielded value
It returns a suspended generator object; the body starts running on the first next() call
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function runs none of its body. It creates a generator object in the suspended-start state; each next() runs until the following yield. Running to the first yield on call is a common misconception.

questions.prompt: An async generator streams rows from a database cursor and a for await...of loop processes each row slowly. What happens to the producer while the consumer is busy?
options: It throws a back-pressure error once more than 16 unread rows are waiting in its internal queue
It keeps fetching rows in the background and buffers all of them in memory until they're read
It stays paused at its yield and does not fetch more rows until the loop asks for the next one
It drops any rows the consumer hasn't processed yet and resumes from the newest one later
questions.explanation: Async generators are pull-based. After yielding, the generator is suspended until the consumer calls next() again (which for await does only after the loop body finishes). That gives natural back-pressure, unlike push-based emitters that keep producing.

questions.prompt: Inside async function main(), a for await...of loop iterates an async generator that throws on its third item. What happens?
options: The loop finishes normally and the error is stored on the generator's .error property
The loop silently skips the failed item and continues with the next one
The error is thrown from the for await statement and can be caught by a try/catch around the loop in main()
The error becomes an uncaught exception that crashes the process even if the loop is wrapped in try/catch
questions.explanation: A rejected next() promise is surfaced at the for await statement, just like a rejected await. A surrounding try/catch in the async function handles it; if nothing catches it, main()'s promise rejects. Nothing is skipped or stored.

questions.prompt: Which statements about async generators (async function*) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: They can be consumed with for await...of
Their next() returns a Promise of { value, done }
Their body may use both await and yield
Array.from(asyncGen()) returns an array of the resolved values
They can be consumed with a plain for...of loop
questions.explanation: Async generators implement Symbol.asyncIterator, not Symbol.iterator, so a plain for...of throws 'is not iterable' and Array.from doesn't see them as iterable (Array.fromAsync is the async counterpart). Inside, you can await and yield freely.

questions.prompt: Which are good uses for generators in a Node.js backend? Select all that apply.
options: Running CPU-heavy work in parallel on multiple cores
Implementing [Symbol.iterator] for a custom collection in a few lines
Streaming paginated API or DB results one item at a time with an async generator
Producing a lazy, potentially infinite sequence such as ID or backoff-delay values
questions.explanation: Generators give you lazy evaluation and a compact way to write iterators. They still run on the same thread: yielding doesn't create parallelism, so CPU-heavy work needs worker_threads or a separate process.

questions.prompt: Calling next() on a generator that has already completed returns { value: undefined, done: true } instead of throwing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Once a generator has finished (returned or thrown), any further next() calls return { value: undefined, done: true }. That's why iterating an exhausted generator a second time just produces nothing.

questions.prompt: Rewriting a long CPU-bound loop as a generator moves the work to another thread, so the event loop stays responsive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Generators only pause and resume on the same thread. Each next() call runs synchronously until the next yield. You could yield and schedule chunks with setImmediate to give the event loop room, but real parallelism needs worker_threads.

questions.prompt: An ES module running on Node 22 uses __dirname and crashes with a ReferenceError. What's the idiomatic fix?
options: Use import.meta.dirname (or derive the path from import.meta.url with fileURLToPath)
Import __dirname from the node:path module
Rename the file to .mts so Node injects the CommonJS wrapper variables
Add 'use strict' at the top of the file so the CommonJS globals are defined
questions.explanation: __dirname, __filename, require and module come from the CommonJS module wrapper, which ES modules don't have. Node 20.11+ provides import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename; on older versions use path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)). node:path doesn't export __dirname.

questions.prompt: counter.mjs exports a live counter. What does main.mjs print?
options: TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
undefined
questions.explanation: ES module imports are live bindings to the exporter's variable, not copies. After inc() updates count inside counter.mjs, main sees 1. With CommonJS, destructuring module.exports would copy the value 0 at require time, which is the usual trap.

questions.prompt: On a recent Node version where require() can load ES modules (Node 22.12+ / 24), a CommonJS file calls require('./setup.mjs'), and setup.mjs uses top-level await. What happens?
options: require() returns the namespace immediately, with exports still undefined until the await finishes
require() returns a Promise of the module namespace
require() blocks the thread until the top-level await settles, then returns the namespace
require() throws (ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE); use dynamic import() instead
questions.explanation: require() is synchronous, so it can only load an ES module whose graph evaluates synchronously. If the module (or one of its dependencies) uses top-level await, Node throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. await import() handles async module graphs.

questions.prompt: config.mjs uses top-level await to fetch secrets before exporting them. app.mjs imports config.mjs. How does this affect app.mjs?
options: app.mjs must switch to await import('./config.mjs'), because a static import won't wait for it
app.mjs runs right away and sees undefined exports from config.mjs until the secrets arrive
app.mjs's body doesn't run until config.mjs's awaited promise settles; if it rejects, app.mjs fails to load
Top-level await is only allowed in the entry module, so config.mjs fails to parse at startup
questions.explanation: Top-level await makes a module's evaluation asynchronous, and modules that import it wait for it to finish before their own bodies run. A rejection propagates and the importing graph fails. It's handy for one-off initialisation but delays startup and should not be used for slow, optional work.

questions.prompt: Why can bundlers tree-shake ES modules much more reliably than CommonJS?
options: import/export are static, so the used exports are known without running any code
ES modules are loaded lazily, so exports nobody imports are never downloaded at all
ES modules are compiled to bytecode ahead of time, so unused code is already stripped
CommonJS modules can't export functions, only plain objects, which can't be split
questions.explanation: ESM imports and exports must appear at the top level with literal specifiers, so tools can analyse them statically. require() is an ordinary function call that can be conditional, computed, or mutate module.exports at runtime, which blocks safe dead-code removal.

questions.prompt: Your package.json has "type": "module", but a tool needs one config file written in CommonJS (module.exports = ...). What's the simplest fix?
options: Remove "type": "module" and rename every other file to .mjs
Add 'use commonjs' at the top of the file
Wrap the file's contents in an async IIFE
Give that file the .cjs extension
questions.explanation: The .cjs extension always means CommonJS and .mjs always means ESM, whatever the nearest package.json "type" says. There's no 'use commonjs' directive, and flipping the whole package for one file is unnecessary churn.

questions.prompt: In CommonJS, a.js requires b.js and b.js requires a.js. b.js reads a.helper at load time and gets undefined, although a.js defines module.exports.helper. Why?
options: helper is hoisted to the top of a.js only when it's declared with var
b.js receives a's exports object while a.js is still running, before helper has been assigned
CommonJS doesn't support circular requires and always returns undefined for the second one
require caches modules by file size, so the cached copy of a.js is stale
questions.explanation: When a cycle is hit, Node returns the partially built module.exports of the module that's still executing. Anything a.js assigns after its require('./b') line isn't there yet. Fixes: move the shared code into a third module, or read a.helper lazily inside a function.

questions.prompt: In a Node ES module, import { db } from './db' fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND even though db.js exists next to it. What's wrong?
options: Relative ESM imports in Node need the full file extension: './db.js'
The import must be written as require('./db') inside an ES module
Named imports require the exporting file to be renamed to .mjs
ES modules can only import from node_modules, not relative paths
questions.explanation: Node's ESM resolver doesn't guess extensions or index files the way require() does. Relative specifiers must be exact ('./db.js', './lib/index.js'). TypeScript with module/moduleResolution set to nodenext enforces the same rule.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ES modules vs CommonJS in Node are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Top-level `this` is undefined in an ES module
require() can be called conditionally, e.g. inside an if block
require() returns a Promise of the module
Named imports from any CommonJS module work for every property it sets at runtime
Static imports are resolved and evaluated before the importing module's body runs
questions.explanation: Static imports are hoisted and the dependency graph is evaluated first. require() is a normal synchronous function call. In ESM top-level this is undefined (in CJS it's module.exports). Named imports from CJS only work for exports Node can detect statically; the default import (module.exports) always works.

questions.prompt: Which statements about dynamic import() are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It's only allowed at the top level of a module
It's synchronous, like require()
It can be used inside CommonJS files
It returns a Promise that resolves to the module namespace object
The specifier can be computed at runtime
questions.explanation: import() is an expression that works in both module systems, accepts a runtime-computed string and returns a Promise, which makes it the standard way to load ESM-only packages from CJS or to lazy-load code. It can appear anywhere an expression can, inside functions and conditionals.

questions.prompt: In an ES module, after import x from './a.js', the importer can reassign x = 5 because it holds its own copy of a's default export.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Imported bindings are read-only views of the exporter's binding. Assigning to x throws a TypeError (Assignment to constant variable). Only the exporting module can change the value, and importers see the change because the binding is live.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: config load failed | Error
Unexpected token | SyntaxError
config load failed | undefined
config load failed | SyntaxError
questions.explanation: The inner catch wraps the JSON SyntaxError in a new Error with the options bag { cause }. The outer handler sees the wrapper's message, and e.cause still points at the original SyntaxError with its own name and stack.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: true true Error: bad email email
false true ValidationError: bad email email
true true ValidationError: bad email email
true false ValidationError: bad email email
questions.explanation: class extends Error sets up the prototype chain correctly, so both instanceof checks are true. Error.prototype.toString uses this.name, which the constructor overrode, giving 'ValidationError: bad email'. Without that assignment it would print 'Error: bad email'.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: object boom
object undefined
string Error: boom
string undefined
questions.explanation: throw accepts any value. Throwing a string gives you the string itself, with no stack trace or name. That's why code should always throw Error objects, and why TypeScript types catch variables as unknown.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: Error a,b
AggregateError b
AggregateError a,b
Error a
questions.explanation: Promise.any resolves with the first fulfilment. If every input rejects it rejects with an AggregateError whose errors array holds all the rejection reasons in input order. It doesn't reject with just the first or last error.

questions.prompt: An HTTP API needs to turn domain failures (not found, conflict, validation) into the right status codes. Which approach is most robust?
options: Throw custom error classes carrying a status or code, and map them in one central handler
Check err.message for phrases like 'not found' or 'already exists' in the error handler
Catch every error inside each route handler and always respond with a 500 and the message
Return null from services on any failure and let each controller decide which status fits
questions.explanation: Typed errors (instanceof checks, or a stable code field) give one place that maps failures to responses, and messages can change freely. Matching on message text breaks on rewording or translation, and returning null throws away the reason.

questions.prompt: Production logs show 'ReferenceError: user is not defined'. What's the most likely cause?
options: Code reads an identifier that isn't declared in scope, or a let/const before its declaration
Code reads a property such as user.id on a variable whose value is currently undefined
JSON.parse was given an invalid string while deserialising the user from the session store
A recursive function that loads the user exceeded the maximum call stack size
questions.explanation: ReferenceError means name resolution failed: an undeclared identifier, a typo, or a let/const accessed in its temporal dead zone. Reading a property of undefined is a TypeError, invalid JSON gives a SyntaxError, and stack overflow is a RangeError.

questions.prompt: Why wrap a low-level error with new Error('Failed to charge card', { cause: err }) instead of building a new message by concatenating err.message?
options: cause keeps the original error object (type, stack, code) available for logs and checks
cause makes the outer error catchable by try/catch blocks that would otherwise miss it
V8 truncates error messages to 100 characters, so concatenated messages lose the original
cause makes Node retry the failed operation once automatically before the error is thrown
questions.explanation: With cause you add context while keeping the full original error: its stack shows where the failure really began, and its code (e.g. ECONNRESET) can still be inspected. cause doesn't change how the error is caught; any thrown value can be caught.

questions.prompt: Many Node APIs and libraries expose err.code (e.g. 'ECONNREFUSED', 'ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE') and recommend checking it rather than err.message or instanceof. Why?
options: err.code is the only Error property that survives JSON serialisation between services
Node only fills in err.message when NODE_ENV is set to 'development', not in production
Codes are a stable contract; messages get reworded and instanceof can fail across realms
instanceof doesn't work on Error subclasses when the code runs in strict mode
questions.explanation: Messages are for humans and get reworded. instanceof compares prototype identity, which breaks when an error comes from another vm context or worker, or when two copies of a library are installed. A documented string code is the stable thing to branch on.

questions.prompt: Which statements about JavaScript errors are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Passing { cause } as the second Error constructor argument sets err.cause
Subclassing Error with class extends loses the stack trace
catch {} without a binding is valid syntax
A Promise can only be rejected with an Error instance
throw accepts any value, not only Error instances
questions.explanation: ES2022 added the { cause } option, and optional catch binding (catch {}) has been valid since ES2019. Subclassing with class extends keeps a proper stack. Promises can be rejected with any value, which is why rejection reasons should be treated as unknown.

questions.prompt: Which of these are operational errors (expected failures to handle gracefully) rather than programmer errors (bugs to fix)? Select all that apply.
options: A request body that fails validation
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined in your own handler
A timeout calling a downstream service
ECONNRESET from the database connection
Calling an internal function with arguments in the wrong order
questions.explanation: Operational errors come from the environment or inputs (network, timeouts, bad user data) and should be retried, reported or turned into 4xx/5xx responses. TypeErrors from your own code and wrong internal calls are bugs: log them, fix them, and don't try to recover in place.

questions.prompt: An error thrown inside a setTimeout callback is caught by a try/catch that wraps the setTimeout() call.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: setTimeout returns immediately; the callback runs later on a fresh call stack after the try block has already exited. The error becomes an uncaught exception. Put the try/catch inside the callback, or use promises with await.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: missing:a missing:b
1 undefined
undefined missing:b
1 missing:b
questions.explanation: There's no set trap, so p.a = 1 is forwarded to the target. The get trap then finds 'a' on the target and returns 1, and returns a fallback string for the missing key 'b'. Any operation without a trap is forwarded to the target unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
TypeError
x,y
x,y
x

TypeError
x
questions.explanation: When a set trap returns false, assignment in strict mode throws a TypeError (in sloppy mode it fails silently). y is never written. Object.keys has no ownKeys trap to intercept it, so it reads the target's keys, which only include 'x'.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: true false false
false false false
true false true
true true false
questions.explanation: The has trap intercepts the in operator. The key arrives as the string '5', and Number('5') is in range. Number('a') is NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false, so 'a' in range is false.

questions.prompt: Why do get traps usually call Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) rather than return target[key]?
options: Passing receiver keeps `this` correct for getters, including when the proxy is a prototype
Reflect.get is the only way to read symbol-keyed properties from inside a proxy handler
target[key] returns a shallow copy of object values instead of the original reference
target[key] would recursively trigger the same get trap again and overflow the call stack
questions.explanation: If the property is a getter, target[key] runs it with this === target, which skips the proxy (and any traps on the properties the getter reads) and breaks inheritance through the proxy. Reflect.get with receiver forwards the right this. Reading target directly doesn't recurse, because target isn't the proxy.

questions.prompt: A proxy wraps a frozen object, and its get trap returns a different value for one of the frozen properties. What happens when that property is read?
options: The original value is returned and the trap's result is silently ignored
The proxy unfreezes the target so that the two values become consistent again
The trap's value is returned, because traps always take precedence over the target
A TypeError is thrown, because the trap breaks an invariant of frozen properties
questions.explanation: Proxies enforce invariants: for a non-configurable, non-writable data property, get must report the real value. Breaking that throws a TypeError. Invariants stop proxies from lying about guarantees like Object.freeze.

questions.prompt: Vue 3 switched from Object.defineProperty getters/setters to Proxy for reactivity. What's the main capability this added?
options: It deep-clones the state automatically on every write, preventing mutation bugs
It detects properties added or deleted after creation, and array index changes
It makes reactive property reads faster than reads on plain objects
It lets reactive state be shared safely across worker threads
questions.explanation: defineProperty can only intercept properties that already exist, so new keys, delete and some array mutations needed special APIs. A Proxy intercepts get/set/deleteProperty/has for any key. It's actually slower than plain property access, not faster.

questions.prompt: A team wraps every database row object in a Proxy to log property reads, and p99 latency on a hot endpoint rises noticeably. What's the most likely reason?
options: Proxies force each wrapped object onto the old-generation heap, so GC runs more often
console.log inside a trap always performs synchronous disk I/O on every single call
Every property read now calls a trap function, bypassing V8's inline-cache fast paths
Proxies copy the whole target object on every property read to keep the target safe
questions.explanation: A property read on a plain object can be a single optimised load once inline caches warm up. On a proxy, every read calls a JavaScript function through the handler, which is far slower. Keep proxies off hot paths, or log at a coarser level.

questions.prompt: What does Proxy.revocable() give you that new Proxy() doesn't?
options: A proxy that only allows reads, with no extra handler code
A revoke() function; after calling it, every operation on the proxy throws a TypeError
A proxy whose traps can be swapped at runtime
A proxy that automatically reverts the target's changes when it's garbage-collected
questions.explanation: Proxy.revocable returns { proxy, revoke }. Once revoked, the proxy drops its target and handler and any trap-able operation throws. That's useful for handing out temporary access to an object, for example to plugin code.

questions.prompt: Which operations can a Proxy handler intercept? Select all that apply.
options: The in operator (has)
Calling the proxy as a function, if its target is a function (apply)
The result of typeof proxy
Strict equality proxy === other
delete obj.prop (deleteProperty)
Reading a property (get)
questions.explanation: There are 13 traps, including get, set, has, deleteProperty, ownKeys, apply and construct. typeof just reflects the target (function or object), and === compares identity, so neither can be trapped.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Reflect are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Reflect.ownKeys(obj) returns both string and symbol own keys, including non-enumerable ones
Reflect.defineProperty returns false on failure instead of throwing like Object.defineProperty
Reflect methods only work when the target is a Proxy
Reflect.has(obj, key) behaves like key in obj
new Reflect() creates a reflection wrapper around an object
questions.explanation: Reflect is a plain namespace object (not a constructor) whose methods mirror the proxy traps and work on any object. They give the default behaviour as a function, with boolean results where Object.* would throw, which makes them the natural way to forward from a trap.

questions.prompt: A proxy and its target are the same object, so proxy === target is true.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: new Proxy(target, handler) creates a separate exotic object. proxy === target is false, which matters when objects are used as Map/WeakMap keys or compared by identity. Code holding the raw target also bypasses every trap.

questions.prompt: A Node service's memory climbs for hours until it's restarted. What's the most effective first step to find what's retaining memory?
options: Raise --max-old-space-size step by step until the restarts stop happening in production
Take two heap snapshots some time apart and compare which objects grew and what retains them
Start node with --expose-gc and call global.gc() at the end of every request handler
Rewrite the hot paths to use var instead of let so fewer block scopes are allocated
questions.explanation: Comparing heap snapshots (Chrome DevTools or --heapsnapshot-signal) shows which constructors keep growing, and the retainers view shows the reference chain keeping them alive, often a module-level Map, a listener array or a closure. A bigger heap only delays the crash.

questions.prompt: Two objects reference each other, and nothing else references either of them. What does V8's garbage collector do?
options: Collects both, because neither is reachable from a root
Collects one of them and keeps the other
Keeps both forever, because their reference counts never reach zero
Throws a RangeError for a circular structure
questions.explanation: V8 uses tracing (mark-and-sweep style) collection: anything not reachable from roots (stack, globals, handles) is garbage, cycles included. Leaking cycles is a problem of pure reference counting, which V8 doesn't use for JS objects.

questions.prompt: You want to attach computed metadata to request objects you don't own, without stopping them from being garbage-collected after the request ends. What should you use?
options: A WeakMap keyed by the request object
A plain object keyed by a request ID string
An array of [request, metadata] pairs
A Map keyed by the request object
questions.explanation: A WeakMap holds its keys weakly: once the request object is otherwise unreachable, the entry and its metadata can be collected. A Map, plain object or array keeps strong references and grows forever unless you remove entries yourself.

questions.prompt: This function runs once per incoming request. Why does memory keep growing?
options: Arrays filled with strings can never be garbage-collected
Each setInterval is never cleared, so its closure keeps `big` alive forever
The if check inside the interval makes a copy of `big` every second
new Array(1e6) is always allocated outside the V8 heap
questions.explanation: Active timers are GC roots. The interval callback closes over big, so every call adds another live interval holding a million-element array. Store the handle and clearInterval it when the work is done, or don't use an interval at all.

questions.prompt: Why are lots of short-lived objects (temporary arrays and objects inside a request handler) relatively cheap for V8?
options: V8 allocates them on the C++ stack, so they're freed as soon as the function returns
They die in the young generation, where a scavenger only copies the few survivors
V8 reference-counts them and frees each one the moment it becomes unreachable
The garbage collector skips objects younger than one event-loop tick entirely
questions.explanation: V8's heap is generational. New objects go into a small young space, collected by a scavenger whose cost scales with the surviving objects, not the dead ones. Objects that survive a couple of scavenges are promoted to old space, which uses the more expensive mark-sweep-compact.

questions.prompt: Node prints 'MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 close listeners added'. What's the most likely cause?
options: A close listener threw an error 11 times, so Node assumes its state is leaking
One emitter fired the close event more than 10 times without anyone listening
Code adds a listener to a long-lived emitter on every request and never removes it
More than 10 different EventEmitter instances exist in the process at the same time
questions.explanation: The warning fires when one emitter has more than 10 listeners for the same event. The usual cause is calling .on() per request or per retry on a shared object (a socket, DB pool or process). Use once(), remove the listener when finished, or attach it a single time.

questions.prompt: A batch job reads a 2 GB CSV with fs.readFileSync, splits it into lines and crashes with 'JavaScript heap out of memory'. What's the most robust fix?
options: Increase --max-old-space-size to 8192 and rerun
Convert the whole file buffer to a string with toString('utf8') first
Call global.gc() after splitting the file
Stream the file and process it line by line (e.g. a read stream with readline)
questions.explanation: Reading the whole file, then building a giant string and an array of lines, needs several times the file size in memory. Streaming keeps memory flat regardless of file size. Raising the heap limit only moves the ceiling and fails again on the next bigger file.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a FinalizationRegistry callback be used to close database connections or file handles?
options: FinalizationRegistry callbacks run synchronously inside the allocation that triggered GC
Using it disables garbage collection for the registered objects
FinalizationRegistry only works with primitive values
The callback may run much later or never, since GC timing isn't guaranteed
questions.explanation: The spec makes no promise about when or whether cleanup callbacks run. They're for optional, best-effort cleanup. Resources need deterministic release: try/finally, an explicit close(), or `using` with Symbol.dispose.

questions.prompt: Which of these commonly cause memory leaks in long-running Node servers? Select all that apply.
options: An unbounded in-memory cache (a Map that only ever grows)
Local variables inside a function that has already returned and isn't referenced by any closure
setInterval timers that are never cleared
Two unreachable objects that reference each other
Adding a listener per request to a global emitter without removing it
questions.explanation: Leaks are unwanted reachability: caches, timers and listener arrays all keep data reachable from roots. Locals of a finished function with no surviving closure are collectable, and unreachable cycles are collected by V8's tracing GC.

questions.prompt: Which statements about WeakMap are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A value stays alive as long as its key is reachable
It can't be iterated and has no size property
Using an object as a key prevents that object from being garbage-collected
Primitive strings and numbers can't be used as keys
questions.explanation: WeakMap keys are held weakly, so they don't keep objects alive. Once a key becomes unreachable, its entry and value can go. Because entries can disappear at any GC, iteration and size aren't offered. Keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols), never strings or numbers.

questions.prompt: A closure keeps the outer-scope variables it uses alive for as long as the closure itself is reachable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That's how closures work, and it's the root of many leaks: a callback stored in a long-lived structure (timer, listener, cache) keeps everything it captured alive. Releasing the closure (clearing the timer, removing the listener) releases what it captured.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
after emit
L1 e
L2 e

L1 e
L2 e
after emit

L1 e
after emit
L2 e

L1 e
after emit
questions.explanation: emit calls each listener synchronously. L1 logs right away; L2 only schedules a microtask. 'after emit' runs next on the same synchronous path, and the microtask runs once the current script finishes. Node's EventEmitter behaves the same way: synchronous dispatch.

questions.prompt: In Node.js, when does a listener registered with emitter.on('data', fn) run after emitter.emit('data', x)?
options: In the next iteration of the event loop, during the poll phase
Synchronously, inside the emit() call, in the order they were registered
In parallel on a libuv thread-pool worker, so emit() returns at once
On the next tick (process.nextTick), after the current function returns
questions.explanation: EventEmitter.emit calls every listener synchronously, in registration order, before returning. A listener that needs to defer work must schedule it itself (setImmediate, queueMicrotask). That's why a slow listener blocks the code that called emit().

questions.prompt: A job runner does emitter.on('job', async (job) => { await process(job); }) and process() sometimes rejects. What happens to that rejection by default?
options: The rejection is swallowed silently, because listeners' return values are discarded
EventEmitter always catches it and re-emits it as an 'error' event on the same emitter
emit() awaits each async listener in turn and rethrows the error to whoever called emit()
It becomes an unhandled rejection, because emit() ignores the listener's returned promise
questions.explanation: emit() calls listeners but ignores their return values, so the async listener's promise is dropped. In Node 15+ an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default. Catch inside the listener, or enable captureRejections so rejections are routed to the 'error' event.

questions.prompt: What does await once(emitter, 'ready') (from node:events) resolve with?
options: The emitter itself, for chaining
Only the first argument passed to emit('ready', ...)
undefined, since it only signals that the event happened
An array of the arguments passed to emit('ready', ...)
questions.explanation: events.once returns a Promise that resolves with an array of all the event's arguments (const [conn] = await once(server, 'connection')). It also rejects if the emitter emits 'error' while waiting, which makes it handy for startup code.

questions.prompt: Code calls emitter.on('tick', () => update()) and later emitter.off('tick', () => update()), but the listener keeps firing. Why?
options: off() is asynchronous and the removal only takes effect on the next event-loop tick
The two arrow functions are different objects, so off() finds no matching listener
off() only removes listeners that were originally registered with once()
A listener can only be removed from inside its own callback, while it's running
questions.explanation: Listeners are matched by reference. Each arrow-function expression creates a new function, so off() is given one that was never registered. Store the handler in a variable and pass that same reference to both on() and off().

questions.prompt: A logging listener must run before listeners that other modules have already registered on the same emitter. Which Node EventEmitter method fits?
options: emitter.once('event', fn), since once-listeners always run first
emitter.setMaxListeners(0) before calling on()
emitter.on('event', fn) with a priority argument of 0
emitter.prependListener('event', fn)
questions.explanation: prependListener (and prependOnceListener) inserts the listener at the front of the array, so it runs first. on() has no priority parameter, once() listeners run in registration order like any other, and setMaxListeners only changes the leak-warning threshold.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Node's EventEmitter are correct? Select all that apply.
options: off(event, fn) removes every listener registered for that event
A once() listener is removed after its first call
emit() returns true if the event had listeners and false otherwise
By default it warns when more than 10 listeners are added for a single event
Listeners are invoked asynchronously on the next tick
questions.explanation: The default maxListeners is 10 per event (a warning, not a hard limit). emit() returns a boolean and runs listeners synchronously. off/removeListener removes a single registration of that exact function; removeAllListeners(event) clears all of them.

questions.prompt: You're writing your own minimal event emitter. Which are good implementation choices? Select all that apply.
options: Store listeners in an object or Map of arrays keyed by event name
Call each listener through setTimeout so one slow listener can't block the others
Make off(event, fn) also work for handlers registered with once(), e.g. by storing the original fn on the wrapper
Iterate over a copy of the listener array in emit()
Store listeners in a Set so registering the same function twice is ignored
questions.explanation: Copying protects iteration against listeners that add or remove listeners. Mapping wrappers back to the original makes off() symmetric with once(). Wrapping in setTimeout changes the synchronous contract callers depend on, and a Set silently dedupes, which Node's emitter doesn't do.

questions.prompt: Node's EventEmitter lets you add the same listener function more than once, and it is then called once per registration.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: on() doesn't check for duplicates; each call appends another entry, so the function runs once per registration on each emit. removeListener removes only one entry at a time (the most recently added matching one).

options:

questions.prompt: In modern V8, what is Ignition's role?

questions.prompt: A hot function that has always received integers suddenly gets a string from a rare code path, and it briefly runs slower. What most likely happened?

questions.prompt: A utility reads obj.id from objects built in six different ways (different property orders and optional fields). What state does the inline cache at that property access most likely end up in?

Polymorphic with unlimited entries, so it stays just as fast

questions.prompt: Which statement about V8 array 'elements kinds' is correct?

questions.prompt: Which coding habits help V8 generate fast code? Select all that apply.
