It becomes minFreq + 1, because the evicted bucket may now be empty
It becomes 1, because the newly inserted key has frequency 1
questions.explanation: A new key always enters with frequency 1, which is the lowest possible, so minFreq resets to 1 without any scan. minFreq + 1 is the rule for a get/put hit when the node's old bucket was the min bucket and is now empty, not for inserts.

questions.prompt: Which statements about building an LRU cache on a JavaScript Map are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A plain object is equally safe here, since object keys always iterate in insertion order
set() on an existing key does not change that key's position in iteration order
Map.prototype.delete is O(n) because the remaining entries have to be shifted
m.keys().next().value returns the oldest key in O(1), making it the eviction candidate
Map iterates keys in insertion order, so the first key is the least recently inserted
questions.explanation: Map preserves insertion order, set() on an existing key keeps its slot, and the first key from keys() is the LRU entry. Map deletes are O(1) on average (engines use hash tables with tombstones). Plain objects list integer-like keys first in ascending numeric order, so they break recency ordering.

questions.prompt: If an LRU cache uses a plain JS object as its store, numeric-looking keys such as '42' and '7' iterate in ascending numeric order rather than insertion order, which breaks recency tracking.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Ordinary objects enumerate integer-like keys first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order. So a cache keyed by user IDs would see '7' before '42' regardless of access time. Map has no such rule and always uses insertion order.

questions.prompt: In an LRU cache, get() is a pure read and does not need to modify any internal state on a hit.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A hit must mark the key as most recently used (move it to the MRU end), otherwise frequently read keys would be evicted as if they were cold. That is why even 'reads' on an LRU need care under concurrency.

questions.prompt: A nightly batch job reads each of 1M product keys exactly once through a shared LRU cache, and afterwards the hit rate for the usual hot keys collapses. What explains this?
options: The batch job's keys hash into the same buckets as hot keys, causing collisions that evict them
Every one-time read becomes most recent, so a large scan pushes the hot keys out by recency
The hot keys' TTLs expire during the job because LRU timestamps are reset on scans
LRU caches lower their capacity automatically when the request rate spikes
questions.explanation: This is scan pollution: LRU only looks at recency, so a burst of one-off accesses evicts genuinely hot data. Frequency-aware or admission-controlled policies (LFU, segmented LRU, TinyLFU) resist it. Hash collisions don't evict entries in a correctly sized map.

questions.prompt: An LFU cache serves a news site. Yesterday's viral article built up a huge hit count and now sits in cache unread, while today's stories keep getting evicted. What is the standard remedy?
options: Break frequency ties by key name so new articles win more often
Switch to a larger cache so both old and new articles fit
Reset an item's frequency to zero every time it is read
Age the counts, e.g. periodically halving all frequencies, so old popularity decays
questions.explanation: Plain LFU never forgets: a once-hot item keeps its big count and becomes unevictable. Aging/decay (as TinyLFU does by halving counters) lets recent popularity win. Resetting on read inverts the policy, and a bigger cache only postpones the problem.

questions.prompt: An LRU cache of capacity N is full. Which describe correct put(key, value) behaviour? Select all that apply.
options: If key already exists, update its value and mark it most recently used, with no eviction
If key is new, evict the most recently used entry, because it was just served
If key is new, evict the least recently used entry and then insert key as most recent
If key already exists, evict the LRU entry anyway, since put always adds an entry
questions.explanation: Updating an existing key doesn't grow the cache, so nothing is evicted; it is just refreshed to MRU. Only inserting a new key past capacity triggers eviction of the LRU entry. Evicting on every put loses data needlessly, and evicting the MRU entry is the opposite of the policy.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 10 and refills at 5 tokens/second; each request costs 1 token. After a long idle period, what traffic does it allow?
options: Exactly 5 requests in any one-second window, never more
A burst of 10 immediately, then about 5 requests/second sustained
10 requests/second sustained, since capacity sets the rate
A burst of 15 (capacity plus one second of refill), then nothing for 2 seconds
questions.explanation: Capacity bounds the burst (the bucket is full after idling), and the refill rate bounds the long-run average. Capacity is not a rate, and refill is continuous, so it doesn't add a second's worth on top of a full bucket.

questions.prompt: Your service calls a fragile downstream API that must receive requests at a steady pace with no bursts at all; excess requests can wait briefly. Which algorithm fits best?
options: Token bucket with a large capacity
Leaky bucket used as a queue, draining at a constant rate
Sliding window log with a one-minute window
Fixed window counter, resetting the count every second
questions.explanation: A leaky bucket queue releases requests at a fixed output rate, smoothing bursts into a steady stream (and drops when the queue is full). A token bucket deliberately permits bursts up to capacity, and window counters only limit totals per window, not spacing.

questions.prompt: A fixed window counter allows 100 requests per minute, with windows starting on the minute. What is the most a client can get through in roughly a 2-second span?
questions.explanation: The client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00, because the counter resets at the boundary. That boundary burst is the main weakness of fixed windows and the reason sliding window variants exist.

questions.prompt: A sliding window counter limits 100 requests/minute. The previous minute had 80 requests, the current minute has 30 so far, and we are 25% into the current minute. What estimated count does the algorithm compare to the limit?
questions.explanation: Estimate = current + previous × (fraction of previous window still inside the sliding window) = 30 + 80 × 0.75 = 90, so the request is allowed. Using 0.25 as the weight (giving 50) is the common slip: the overlap with the previous window is 75%, not 25%.

questions.prompt: Why is a sliding window log often rejected for a high-traffic public API, despite being exact?
options: It allows boundary bursts of up to twice the limit
It stores a timestamp per request, so memory per client grows with the allowed rate
It requires a background timer per client to expire timestamps
It can't enforce limits shorter than one minute
questions.explanation: The log keeps every request timestamp inside the window, so a limit of 10k/min means up to 10k entries per key. Expired timestamps are trimmed lazily on each check, so no timer is needed, and being exact it has no boundary burst.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: YYYNYYN
YYYNNYN
YYYNNYY
YYYYNYN
questions.explanation: Three tokens serve the first three calls at t=0; the fourth is rejected. At 500 ms only 0.5 token has refilled (rejected), and at 1000 ms it reaches 1.0, so one call passes and the next fails. Lazy refill on each call means no timer is needed.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 0 and 100 fill the log; 200 is rejected (and not logged). At 1000 the entry 0 expires, so it passes; at 1100 the entry 100 expires, so it passes; at 1150 the log holds 1000 and 1100, so it's rejected. Rejected requests aren't recorded, which is why 200 never counts.

questions.prompt: Which statements about rate-limiting algorithm trade-offs are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Token bucket requires a background timer that adds tokens to every bucket on a schedule
Sliding window counter uses O(1) memory per key but assumes the previous window's requests were evenly spread
Fixed window counter is immune to bursts at window boundaries
Sliding window log is exact but its memory grows with the number of requests in the window
questions.explanation: The log stores timestamps (exact, memory-heavy); the counter interpolates from two counts (cheap, approximate). Fixed windows are the algorithm with the boundary-burst flaw, and token buckets are normally refilled lazily from elapsed time when a request arrives.

questions.prompt: An HTTP API rejects a request because the client exceeded its rate limit. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Return 500 Internal Server Error so clients back off
Silently drop the TCP connection without a response
Include a Retry-After header telling the client when to try again
Return status 429 Too Many Requests
Optionally include remaining-quota headers so clients can self-throttle
questions.explanation: 429 is the defined status for rate limiting, and Retry-After plus quota headers let well-behaved clients back off precisely. A 500 misreports a client-side condition as a server fault, and dropping connections makes clients retry blindly.

questions.prompt: A token bucket with capacity 1 effectively allows no bursting: requests can't come faster than the refill rate even after a long idle period.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Capacity is the maximum stored tokens, so with capacity 1 at most one request can be served immediately after idling, and each further one must wait for refill. Larger capacities are what permit bursts.

questions.prompt: The sliding window counter algorithm gives exact counts as long as the client stays below the limit.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It is always an approximation: it weights the previous window's total by the overlap fraction, assuming those requests were uniformly spread. Being under the limit doesn't make that assumption true; exactness requires a log.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in this Redis-backed limiter when many requests for the same key arrive concurrently across instances?
options: GET returns a string, so the comparison with LIMIT always fails
Redis SET with EX is not supported alongside GET on the same key
The 60-second TTL is reset on each request, so the window never ends
Concurrent calls can read the same count and each write count + 1, losing increments
questions.explanation: Read-then-write across an await is a classic lost update: two callers both read 4, both pass, and both write 5. Use atomic INCR (with expiry set atomically via Lua or MULTI). The TTL reset is a real side issue, but the concurrency bug is the lost update; Number() handles the string.

questions.prompt: A limiter runs INCR key, and if the result is 1 it then runs EXPIRE key 60 as a separate command. What failure mode does this create?
options: INCR on a key with no TTL raises an error, so the first request always fails
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero, so the limit is never reached
Two INCRs can return the same value, letting both requests in
If the process dies between the two commands, the key has no TTL and the client stays blocked forever
questions.explanation: INCR is atomic, so duplicate values can't happen, but the pair isn't: a crash or network failure after INCR leaves a counter that never expires. Run both in a Lua script or MULTI/EXEC (or use SET key 0 EX 60 NX before INCR) so the TTL is always attached.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service caches user profiles behind an async loader. When a popular key expires, 500 concurrent requests miss at once and all hit the database. What is the standard in-process fix?
options: Use a Map for the cache instead of a plain object
Wrap the loader call in try/catch so failures don't propagate
Lower the TTL so keys expire more evenly across time
Store the in-flight Promise for the key so concurrent misses await the same load
questions.explanation: Request coalescing (single-flight) caches the pending promise, so only the first miss calls the database and the rest await its result; remove it on settle so errors aren't cached forever. A shorter TTL makes stampedes more frequent, not less.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: A,A,B 2 0
A,A,B 3 0
A,B 2 0
A,A,B 2 2
questions.explanation: The second load('a') returns the stored in-flight promise, so the loader runs only twice (a and b). Each stored promise is the .finally() result, which settles only after the delete runs, so by the time Promise.all resolves the map is empty. Promise.all keeps one result per input, giving A,A,B.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: a:ok b:no 0
a:ok b:ok -1
a:no b:ok 0
a:ok b:ok 0
questions.explanation: Both calls read tokens = 1 before either reaches the await, so both pass and both write 0: one token served two requests. Node is single-threaded, but an await between read and write lets other calls interleave, the same lost-update bug as GET/SET against Redis.

questions.prompt: Four API instances share a Redis-based rate limiter. Which approaches make the check-and-increment atomic across instances? Select all that apply.
options: An async mutex inside each Node process around the GET/SET pair
A Lua script run with EVAL that reads, checks and updates in one step
A MULTI/EXEC transaction that issues INCR and EXPIRE together
GET the count, compare in Node, then SET the new value
questions.explanation: Redis runs a Lua script and a MULTI/EXEC block without interleaving other clients' commands, so the update is atomic cluster-wide for that key. A per-process mutex only serializes calls inside one instance; the other three can still interleave, and plain GET/SET is the lost-update pattern.

questions.prompt: You serialize async updates per key with a promise chain: `locks.set(k, (locks.get(k) ?? Promise.resolve()).then(fn))`. Which pitfalls must you handle? Select all that apply.
options: The map grows without bound unless the entry is removed when the tail of the chain settles
If fn rejects, later callers chained with .then(fn) are skipped unless the chain swallows or handles the error
It makes fn run on a separate thread, so fn must avoid touching shared objects
It only serializes within one process; other replicas can still interleave on shared state
questions.explanation: A rejected link makes every subsequent .then(fn) skip, so chain with .catch or .then(fn, fn)-style handling; delete the key when the latest promise settles to avoid leaks; and in-process locks do nothing across replicas. Promises don't create threads; fn still runs on the event loop.

questions.prompt: Several API instances add request timestamps to a shared Redis sorted set (sliding window log), each using its own Date.now(). Limits behave inconsistently between instances. What is the likely cause and the usual fix?
options: Sorted sets lose precision past 2^32, so use a list of timestamps instead
ZADD is not atomic, so wrap every call in a JS mutex
Clock skew between hosts distorts the window; take the time from Redis (TIME) inside a Lua script
The window is too long; switch to a fixed window counter to fix ordering
questions.explanation: If hosts disagree by a few hundred ms, trimming by now - window removes or keeps the wrong entries depending on which instance handled the call. Using one clock (Redis TIME inside a script) makes the window consistent. ZADD is atomic, and scores are doubles that hold ms timestamps exactly.

questions.prompt: A rate limiter keeps counts in a Map inside each Node process. The service runs 4 instances behind a round-robin load balancer with a limit of 100/min per user. What effective limit does a user see?
options: Exactly 100/min, because the load balancer routes each user to one instance
Up to about 400/min, since each instance counts only its share of the requests
25/min, since the limit is divided among instances
Unlimited, because Maps are cleared on every request
questions.explanation: Each instance enforces 100 on its own subset of traffic, so a user spread across 4 instances can reach ~4× the limit. Round-robin doesn't pin users (that would need sticky sessions); a shared store like Redis fixes it.

questions.prompt: In Node.js, two concurrent calls to the same async function can interleave only at await points (or other yields to the event loop), never in the middle of synchronous code.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: JavaScript runs each task to completion on one thread. A fully synchronous check-and-decrement on an in-memory bucket is therefore race-free within a process; races appear when an await sits between the read and the write.

questions.prompt: Two clients calling Redis INCR on the same key at the same moment can lose an increment.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Redis executes commands one at a time per instance, and INCR is a single atomic read-modify-write, so two concurrent INCRs always yield n+1 and n+2. That atomicity is why INCR-based counters are the standard building block.

questions.prompt: In a turn-based game with a players array, which update correctly advances to the next player and wraps around?
options: turn = turn + 1
turn = Math.min(turn + 1, players.length - 1)
turn = (turn + 1) % players.length
turn = players.length % (turn + 1)
questions.explanation: Modulo by the number of players wraps the index back to 0 after the last player. Plain increment runs off the end, and Math.min gets stuck on the last player forever.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: A6 B3 C2 A6 B6 C1
A6 A3 B2 C6 C6 A1
A6 A3 B2 C6 A6 B1
A6 A3 B2 C6 C6 C1
questions.explanation: A six grants another roll, so the turn only advances on non-six rolls: A rolls 6 and 3, B rolls 2, C rolls 6, 6 and 1. The log records who rolled before the turn moves, so the last entry is C1, not A1.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 0+3 = 3 hits the ladder to 22; 22+5 = 27 hits the snake to 1; then 1+4 = 5 and 5+4 = 9. Modelling snakes and ladders as one jumps map keeps move() generic; overshooting SIZE leaves the token in place.

questions.prompt: Why should a Game class expose something like `makeMove(playerId, move): MoveResult` instead of reading input and printing output inside its loop?
options: JavaScript classes can't call console.log from their methods
The same rules can then serve a CLI, web or multiplayer front end and be unit-tested without I/O
It ensures moves are always valid, so no validation is needed
It makes the game run faster because console I/O is slow
questions.explanation: Separating rules from the driver (UI, network, tests) is the key LLD point: the loop that collects input lives outside, and the domain model just applies moves and reports results. It doesn't remove the need for validation.

questions.prompt: In an online two-player game, two move requests for the same game arrive at the server at once (a double-click and a retry). How do you keep the turn order consistent?
options: Trust the client's turn counter, since it was the one that made the move
Process moves in order of the timestamps the clients send
Require the expected move number with each move and apply it only if it matches the stored one (optimistic concurrency)
Process both moves and let the board end up in whichever state is last written
questions.explanation: A version/move-number check makes the server the authority: the first matching request wins and the duplicate is rejected as stale. Client timestamps and counters are untrusted and can be skewed, and last-write-wins can corrupt the board.

questions.prompt: For an n×n tic-tac-toe, how can you detect a win after each move in O(1) instead of scanning the board?
options: Keep a counter per row, column and both diagonals: +1 for X, −1 for O; a win is when one reaches ±n
Sort the moves of each player and look for n consecutive cell indices
Check only the cell that was played, since a win requires that cell to be a corner
Hash the board after each move and look it up in a precomputed table of winning boards
questions.explanation: Only the move's row, column and (if applicable) diagonals change, so updating those counters is O(1), and reaching ±n means one player filled the line. A table of winning boards explodes for large n, and wins don't need corners.

questions.prompt: Players are [A, B, C, D] and it is currently C's turn (turn = 2). B leaves, and the code does `players.splice(1, 1)` without touching turn. What goes wrong, and what's the fix?
options: turn now points at D, so C's turn is skipped; decrement turn when the removed index is below it
A gets an extra turn; reset turn to 0 whenever anyone leaves
Nothing; splice keeps the indices of later elements unchanged
turn now points past the end of the array, so the game crashes
questions.explanation: After splice the array is [A, C, D], and index 2 is D, so C loses their turn. Removing an element before the current index must shift turn down by one. Resetting to 0 changes the order unfairly.

questions.prompt: Why model each move as an object (Command pattern) in a game engine? Select all that apply.
options: It provides a move history for replays
It makes moves easy to serialize and send over the network
It removes the need to validate moves against the rules
It enables undo/redo by keeping executed moves on a stack
questions.explanation: A move object can be stored, replayed, reversed and serialized. It changes how moves are represented, not whether they follow the rules, so validation is still required.

questions.prompt: Which state should a turn-based Game object own? Select all that apply.
options: The HTML used to render the board in the browser
The players and whose turn it is
The game status (in progress, won, draw)
The board
questions.explanation: The game model owns rules-related state: players, turn, status and board. Rendering is a view concern; putting HTML in the model ties the rules to one UI and makes them harder to test.

questions.prompt: Using a queue (take the current player from the front, put them at the back after their turn) is a valid alternative to a modulo index for round-robin turns.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Both give the same rotation. A queue also handles players leaving naturally (just don't re-enqueue them), while an index needs adjustment on removal. Extra turns are handled by putting the player back at the front.

questions.prompt: In a server-authoritative online game, a client's message 'I won' should be accepted as long as the request is authenticated.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Authentication proves who sent it, not that it's true. The server must apply moves itself and decide the outcome from its own state; otherwise any modified client can claim victory.

questions.prompt: A Snake & Ladder game must support a normal die, a 'crooked' die that only rolls even numbers, and two-dice mode. What is the cleanest design?
options: Store all dice types in a global variable that the game reads on each turn
Inject a Dice strategy with a roll() method; the game just calls dice.roll()
Create subclasses CrookedGame and DoubleDiceGame that override the whole play loop
Add boolean flags isCrooked and isDouble to the Game class and branch on them
questions.explanation: Dice behaviour varies independently of the rest of the game, so a Dice strategy keeps Game unchanged when variants are added. Flags grow into branching messes, and subclassing the entire game for one varying piece explodes combinations (crooked + double = another subclass).

questions.prompt: Tic-tac-toe must support 3×3 three-in-a-row, and also 10×10 five-in-a-row. Where should the win logic live?
options: Hard-coded in Board as a list of the 8 winning lines
In the UI layer, which highlights winning lines anyway
In an injected WinningStrategy configured with board size and line length
In the Player class, since players are the ones who win
questions.explanation: A WinningStrategy (or rule object) parameterized by n and k lets one Game class serve both variants. A hard-coded list of 8 lines only works for 3×3, and win detection isn't a player or UI responsibility.

questions.prompt: A Game has methods start(), makeMove() and resign(), each beginning with checks like `if (this.finished) ...; if (!this.started) ...`. What does refactoring to the State pattern buy you?
options: It makes the game run in a separate thread per state
Each state class (NotStarted, InProgress, Finished) defines what each action does there, removing scattered flag checks
It removes the need for a Game class, since states can talk to each other directly
It guarantees that no new states will ever be needed
questions.explanation: With State, Game delegates each call to its current state object, so 'what does resign do when finished?' lives in one place, and flag combinations like started && finished can't exist. The context (Game) still exists and owns the shared data.

questions.prompt: State and Strategy have nearly identical class diagrams. Which difference is the most accurate?
options: State is used only in games, Strategy only in business applications
State objects must be singletons, while strategies must be created per call
Strategy can only be used for algorithms that return numbers
States usually trigger transitions to other states themselves, while a strategy is chosen by the client and doesn't swap itself
questions.explanation: The difference is intent: a State models a lifecycle and decides what comes next (InProgress → Finished), while a Strategy is a pluggable algorithm the client selects. Neither requires singletons, and both appear in every domain.

questions.prompt: In Snake & Ladder, a candidate models snakes and ladders as one `Jump { start, end }` entity on the board instead of separate Snake and Ladder classes. What is the best justification?
options: Both have identical behaviour (move from start to end); only the direction differs, so one entity avoids duplicate code
A single class makes it impossible to place a snake and a ladder on the same cell
Inheritance is not supported for small classes in TypeScript
Separate classes cannot be stored in the same Map
questions.explanation: When two types have no behavioural difference, polymorphism adds classes without value; a jump map captures both. Separate types do fit in a Map, and preventing two jumps on one cell is a validation rule, not a consequence of the class design.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 19 10 NaN
questions.explanation: doubleSix: 12 + 2 + 5 = 19. capped: 4 + 2 + 4 = 10. 'turbo' isn't registered, so ?? falls back to the normal strategy: 6 + 2 + 5 = 13. A map of functions is the lightweight JS form of Strategy, and the fallback avoids calling undefined.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: start,move1,ignored,ignored,ignored
start,move1,move2,ignored,ignored
move1,move2,ignored,ignored,ignored
start,move1,move2,move3,ignored
questions.explanation: The first call is handled by Idle (start) and swaps in Playing. Playing returns move1, then move2 while switching to Over, which ignores later calls. The state object changes how the same g.state.move() call behaves, without any if/else in the context.

questions.prompt: Game, Dice, WinningStrategy and TurnPolicy are separate injected objects. Which rule changes can you add without modifying the Game class? Select all that apply.
options: A four-in-a-row win condition on a 6×6 board
A crooked die that only rolls even numbers
An extra turn whenever a player rolls a six
Switching from turn-based play to real-time simultaneous moves
questions.explanation: Each of the first three maps to an existing extension point (Dice, WinningStrategy, TurnPolicy). Real-time simultaneous play changes the game loop itself, which no turn-based extension point covers, so Game must change.

questions.prompt: Which are real drawbacks or pitfalls of the State pattern? Select all that apply.
options: It makes it impossible to add new states later
Transitions spread across state classes make the overall machine harder to see
Sharing state objects as singletons while they hold per-game data leaks data between games
Many states mean many small classes
questions.explanation: State trades conditionals for classes, scatters transition logic (a transition table is a common remedy), and shared state instances must stay stateless. Adding a state is actually easy: write a class and wire its transitions.

questions.prompt: A rule like 'a player must roll the exact number to land on the final square' is a good candidate for an injected policy object rather than a hard-coded if/else inside Game.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: End-of-board rules vary between variants (exact roll, bounce back, any overshoot wins). A policy object lets you swap them without editing Game, which is the Open/Closed principle in practice.

questions.prompt: In the State pattern, the context object typically checks `if (state === 'X')` before delegating each operation to the state.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The point is that the context simply calls this.state.operation() and the current state object decides. Checking the state name in the context brings back the conditionals the pattern removes.

questions.prompt: In an OO chess design, where does the knowledge 'a knight moves in an L-shape' usually live?
options: In the Player class, since players decide moves
In a single giant validateMove() switch inside Game
In a Knight subclass of Piece (or its move-generation strategy)
In the Board, which stores a lookup table per square
questions.explanation: Polymorphism puts each piece's movement pattern in its own class, so adding or changing a piece doesn't touch others. A giant switch in Game grows with every rule, and players choose moves but don't define how pieces move.

questions.prompt: Rook, bishop and queen share most of their move logic. What is the shared abstraction?
options: Sliding along a set of direction vectors until hitting the board edge or a piece
They all jump over pieces, so no path checking is required
They all move exactly one square, differing only in direction
They share an inheritance chain Queen extends Rook extends Bishop
questions.explanation: A sliding piece is defined by its directions: rook = orthogonal, bishop = diagonal, queen = both. One helper walks each direction, stopping at a blocker (capturing if it's an enemy). Knights are the ones that jump, and Queen-extends-Rook-extends-Bishop is a misleading is-a relationship.

questions.prompt: Your engine generates moves from each piece's movement rules. How do you make sure it never allows a move that leaves the player's own king in check (including pinned pieces)?
options: Only check for check after the opponent's next move
Generate pseudo-legal moves, apply each one, and discard it if the own king is attacked afterwards
Ask each piece whether it is pinned before generating its moves
Hard-code a list of pin patterns and check each one
questions.explanation: Filtering pseudo-legal moves by 'is my king attacked after this move?' handles pins, discovered checks and moving into check uniformly. Hand-written pin detection is easy to get wrong, and delaying the check lets illegal positions occur.

questions.prompt: When testing each candidate move for king safety, engines often use make/unmake (apply the move, test, revert) instead of deep-cloning the board per move. Why?
options: Deep-cloning can't copy class instances in JavaScript
Cloned boards would share the same king object, giving wrong results
Make/unmake avoids the need to store captured pieces
Cloning a board per candidate allocates heavily; make/unmake mutates in place and reverts cheaply
questions.explanation: With dozens of candidates per position (and many positions in search), allocation dominates. Make/unmake must record extra info such as the captured piece, castling rights and en passant square to revert correctly; structuredClone or custom copy methods can clone classes but are slow.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a requirement for castling to be legal?
options: Neither the king nor that rook has moved earlier in the game
All squares between the king and the rook are empty
The king is not in check and does not pass through or land on an attacked square
The rook is not under attack
questions.explanation: The rook may be attacked, and on the queenside it may even pass over an attacked square (b1/b8). The restrictions on attacked squares apply only to the king's start, path and destination. This is a classic edge case to test in a move validator.

questions.prompt: Which information is needed to validate moves but CANNOT be derived from the current piece placement alone?
options: Whether the king is currently in check
Which squares are attacked by the opponent
Whether a pawn can capture en passant this turn
Whether the path between a rook and its target square is clear
questions.explanation: En passant depends on the previous move (a two-square pawn advance), so the game must store it, alongside castling rights, side to move and move clocks (the extra fields in FEN). Attacks, check and clear paths can all be computed from the board.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: From a corner only (1,2) and (2,1) stay on the board: 2. From (0,1): (1,3), (2,2) and (2,0): 3. From a central square all 8 targets are on the board. Delta tables plus a bounds check is the standard way to generate jump moves.

questions.prompt: Which statements about detecting the end of a chess game are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Checkmate: the side to move is in check and has no legal moves
Stalemate counts as a win for the side that delivered it
Stalemate: the side to move is not in check and has no legal moves
Detecting threefold repetition requires storing previous positions (e.g. as hashes)
questions.explanation: Both checkmate and stalemate come from 'no legal moves', distinguished by whether the king is in check, so legal-move generation does double duty. Stalemate is a draw, not a win. Repetition needs a position history, commonly Zobrist hashes.

questions.prompt: How should responsibilities for move validation be split in a chess LLD? Select all that apply.
options: The Player class validates moves before sending them
Game or Board checks king safety, since it needs the whole position
Castling, en passant and promotion use game state such as castling rights and the last move
Each Piece knows its own movement pattern
questions.explanation: Pieces handle local geometry, while whole-position rules (check, special moves) need the board and game history. Validation in Player would be bypassable and duplicated across human and AI players; the game must be authoritative.

questions.prompt: A move that fits a piece's movement pattern can still be illegal if it exposes the player's own king to check.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A pinned piece can be blocked from moving off the pin line even though its pattern allows it. That is why validators separate pseudo-legal generation from the king-safety filter.

questions.prompt: When a pawn reaches the last rank, it must be promoted to a queen.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The player may choose a queen, rook, bishop or knight (underpromotion, e.g. to a knight to give check, is sometimes the best move). A move model needs a promotion field rather than assuming a queen.

questions.prompt: A logger's minimum level is set to WARN, with levels DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < FATAL. Which messages are emitted?
options: Only WARN
WARN, ERROR and FATAL
Everything, with WARN and above highlighted
DEBUG and INFO
questions.explanation: The minimum level is a threshold: messages at that severity or higher pass, lower ones are dropped. It is not an exact-match filter, which is why setting WARN still surfaces errors.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: error:b
info:a error:b warn:c
warn:c error:b
error:b warn:c
questions.explanation: Only levels with a numeric value ≥ 30 pass, so error:b and warn:c are kept in call order. Numeric levels make the threshold a single comparison, the approach pino and winston use.

questions.prompt: You need to add an HTTP sink that ships logs to a collector, alongside the console and file sinks, without modifying the Logger class. Which design allows that?
options: Each call site decides where to write and calls fs or fetch directly
Logger holds a list of objects implementing a Sink interface (write(record)) and calls each one
Logger extends FileLogger, which extends ConsoleLogger, adding one level per sink
Logger has a switch on a sinkType string with one case per destination
questions.explanation: Depending on a Sink abstraction lets you register new destinations (console, file, HTTP, test spy) without touching Logger. A switch must be edited for each new sink, and an inheritance chain can't mix sinks freely.

questions.prompt: Profiling shows `logger.debug('state: ' + JSON.stringify(hugeState))` is costly even though production runs at INFO. Why, and what is the fix?
options: debug() still writes to disk at INFO level; disable the file sink
The argument is built before debug() is called; check isLevelEnabled('debug') first or pass a function evaluated lazily
JSON.stringify is cached between calls; clear the cache
The logger is synchronous; switching to console.debug avoids the cost
questions.explanation: JavaScript evaluates arguments eagerly, so the expensive string is built and then discarded by the level check. Guarding with a level check, passing a thunk, or passing the object for the logger to serialize only if enabled avoids the work.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service writes every log line with fs.appendFileSync. Under load, p99 latency rises sharply. What is the cause and the usual remedy?
options: appendFileSync opens a new thread per call; use a thread pool
Synchronous writes block the event loop; buffer and write asynchronously (e.g. a worker-thread transport), flushing on shutdown
The file grows too big; rotate it every hour
Log lines are too long; truncate them to 80 characters
questions.explanation: Every sync write stalls all requests on the event loop. Async/buffered writers or worker transports (as pino does) move that cost off the hot path; the trade-off is that a hard crash may lose the last buffered lines, so flush on exit signals. Rotation doesn't change per-write blocking.

questions.prompt: Why do production services emit structured (JSON) logs with fields like level, msg, requestId and durationMs instead of free-form strings?
options: JSON is smaller on disk than plain text
Aggregators can filter and aggregate by field (e.g. all errors for one requestId) without fragile regex parsing
Free-form strings can't contain timestamps
Structured logs don't need a log level
questions.explanation: Fields make logs queryable: count errors by route, trace a requestId, chart durations. JSON is usually larger than plain text, and levels and timestamps remain essential fields.

questions.prompt: You want every log line written while handling a request to include that request's ID, even deep inside async helpers that never receive the ID as a parameter. Which Node.js feature fits?
options: AsyncLocalStorage, which carries a store through the async calls started from a request
A WeakMap keyed by the current function
A module-level variable set at the start of each request
process.env.REQUEST_ID, set per request
questions.explanation: AsyncLocalStorage propagates context across awaits, timers and callbacks started within run(). A module-level variable or env var is shared by all concurrent requests, so interleaved requests overwrite each other's ID.

questions.prompt: Which of these should never appear in application logs? Select all that apply.
options: Session tokens and API keys
Request IDs
HTTP status codes
User passwords, even when a login fails
Full card numbers
questions.explanation: Secrets and card data in logs turn the log store into a breach target and violate PCI-DSS. Request IDs and status codes are exactly what logs are for. Redaction at the logger (e.g. configured redact paths) is safer than relying on every call site.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a shared logger instance in a Node.js app are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Exporting one instance from a module makes it effectively a singleton, because modules are cached
A singleton logger is unsafe because worker threads share the same module instance and can corrupt it
Child loggers with bound context, e.g. logger.child({ requestId }), avoid repeating fields at every call
A hard-wired global logger makes tests harder unless sinks or the instance can be injected
questions.explanation: Module caching gives one instance per process (per realm), which is convenient but needs an injection seam for tests; child loggers add context cheaply. Worker threads each load their own module instances, so they don't share the singleton.

questions.prompt: If one sink, such as a remote HTTP collector, is slow or down, a well-designed logger should keep it from blocking or crashing the request path.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Logging is a side concern: a failing sink should be isolated with async buffering, bounded queues, timeouts and error handling, dropping or spilling logs rather than taking down the service.

questions.prompt: Setting the logger level to ERROR means ERROR messages and all lower-severity messages such as INFO are emitted.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The level is a minimum severity: ERROR emits ERROR and above (e.g. FATAL) and suppresses INFO, DEBUG and WARN. Setting a lower level like DEBUG is what makes everything visible.

questions.prompt: What is the core data structure of a simple in-memory pub-sub broker?
options: A single array of all messages that every subscriber scans
A priority queue ordered by message size
A linked list of topics where each topic points to the next publisher
A map from topic name to a collection of subscriber callbacks or queues
questions.explanation: publish(topic, msg) looks up the topic's subscribers and delivers to each; subscribe and unsubscribe add to or remove from that collection. Scanning one global array makes every publish O(all messages).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: A1 B2
A1 B1 B2 B3
A1 B1 A2 B2
A1 B1 B2
questions.explanation: A unsubscribes itself during the first publish; deleting the current element from a Set during iteration is safe and B still runs. The second publish only reaches B, and topic 'y' has no subscribers (?? [] avoids a crash).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: first,late
first,late,late
late,first
first
questions.explanation: Set iteration is live: an element added during a for...of is visited later in the same loop, so the subscriber added mid-publish receives the current message. Brokers often iterate over a snapshot ([...subs]) to avoid this.

questions.prompt: In a synchronous in-memory broker, one subscriber does a slow 200 ms computation per message, and publishers start timing out. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the publishers' timeout to 500 ms
Give each subscriber its own queue and deliver asynchronously, so publish only enqueues
Call the slow subscriber last so the others aren't delayed
Convert the slow subscriber to an async function without changing the broker
questions.explanation: Decoupling via per-subscriber queues makes publish O(subscribers) enqueues and isolates slow consumers (with bounded queues and backpressure or drop policies). Reordering still blocks the publisher, and making a CPU-bound handler async doesn't free the event loop.

questions.prompt: In a naive broker, publish loops over subscribers and calls each one. A subscriber throws. What happens, and what should the broker do?
options: The exception is ignored automatically by for...of
The message is re-delivered to every subscriber until none throws
The throwing subscriber is unsubscribed automatically by JavaScript
Later subscribers don't get the message; wrap each call in try/catch and report the error
questions.explanation: An exception aborts the loop and propagates to the publisher, so one buggy consumer breaks delivery for everyone after it. Isolate each delivery, log or route failures (e.g. to a dead-letter list) and keep going.

questions.prompt: Topic 'orders' has consumer group 'billing' with 3 instances and consumer group 'email' with 2 instances. How many deliveries does one published message produce under standard group semantics?
options: 2, one per group
3, one per billing instance
1, to a random instance
5, one per instance
questions.explanation: Each group receives every message, but within a group only one instance processes it (competing consumers), so one delivery per group. Broadcasting to all 5 instances would make billing charge three times.

questions.prompt: You want a consumer that was offline for an hour to catch up on missed messages, while other consumers keep their own pace. Which design supports this?
options: Delete each message as soon as the first consumer acknowledges it
Store each topic as an append-only log and keep a committed offset per consumer group
Push messages only to currently connected consumers
Keep only the latest message per topic
questions.explanation: With a retained log, each group reads from its own offset, so a returning consumer resumes where it stopped (subject to retention). Deleting on first ack or push-only delivery loses the messages the offline consumer needed. This is the Kafka-style model.

questions.prompt: Which statements about delivery semantics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Acknowledging before processing gives at-most-once delivery, so messages can be lost on a crash
At-least-once delivery requires idempotent consumers to be safe
A purely in-memory broker keeps undelivered messages across a process restart
Acknowledging after processing gives at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible
questions.explanation: When you ack decides what a crash costs: ack-late risks redelivery, ack-early risks loss, and idempotency makes redelivery harmless. Anything held only in memory is gone after a restart unless persisted.

questions.prompt: Which practices prevent memory leaks in an in-memory pub-sub? Select all that apply.
options: Remove a topic's entry when its last subscriber leaves
Store subscribers in a WeakMap keyed by topic string
Bound per-subscriber queues and apply a drop or backpressure policy for slow consumers
Return an unsubscribe function from subscribe() and call it when the consumer is done
questions.explanation: Leaks come from forgotten subscriptions, unbounded queues and empty topic entries. WeakMap keys must be objects, not strings, and weak references wouldn't help anyway, since the broker itself holds the callbacks.

questions.prompt: Node.js EventEmitter calls listeners synchronously, in the order they were registered, when emit() is called.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: emit() runs each listener inline before returning, so a slow or throwing listener affects the emitter. Listeners that need async work must schedule it themselves (e.g. setImmediate or queueMicrotask).

questions.prompt: With 3 consumers in a single competing-consumers group, every message is delivered to all 3 consumers.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Competing consumers share the work: each message goes to exactly one member of the group, which is how you scale processing. Fan-out to everyone is what separate groups (or plain broadcast subscribers) provide.

questions.prompt: Which data structure is the standard core of an in-memory delayed task scheduler?
options: An unsorted array scanned on every tick
A FIFO queue in insertion order
A hash map keyed by task ID
A min-heap ordered by run time: O(log n) insert, O(1) peek at the next task
questions.explanation: The scheduler always needs the earliest task next, which a min-heap provides cheaply. A FIFO only works if tasks are inserted in run-time order, and a hash map has no ordering (though it's often added for lookup by ID).

questions.prompt: In Node.js, what happens with `setTimeout(fn, 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000)` (30 days)?
options: fn runs after 30 days, as requested
The delay exceeds the 32-bit timer limit (~24.8 days), so Node warns and runs fn after about 1 ms
It throws a RangeError immediately
The timer is silently ignored and fn never runs
questions.explanation: Delays above 2^31 − 1 ms trigger a TimeoutOverflowWarning and are set to 1 ms. Long-delay schedulers therefore keep tasks in a heap or database and only arm a timer for the nearest one, capped below the limit.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: report,ping,email,cleanup 0
email,report,cleanup,ping 0
report,ping,cleanup,email 0
report,ping 2
questions.explanation: Tasks are ordered by time, and Array.prototype.sort is stable (guaranteed since ES2019), so email stays ahead of cleanup at the same time. All four are due at 300. Sorting on each insert is O(n log n), which is why real schedulers use a heap.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: bac
bca
abc
acb
questions.explanation: Timers fire in order of due time, and timers with the same delay fire in the order they were created, so a (10 ms) runs first, then b and c (20 ms) in creation order. The 30 ms timer logs after all three.

questions.prompt: A scheduler keeps tasks in a min-heap and arms a single setTimeout for the earliest task. A new task is scheduled to run before the current earliest. What must happen?
options: Clear the current timer and re-arm it for the new task's run time
Arm a second timer just for the new task and keep both
Nothing; the new task will be found when the existing timer fires
Rebuild the heap from scratch so the timer picks up the change
questions.explanation: The single timer must always target the heap's head. If you don't re-arm, the new task runs late (when the old timer fires). Arming a timer per task defeats the purpose of the single-timer design.

questions.prompt: A report job is scheduled every 60 s but sometimes takes 70 s. With fixed-rate scheduling (next run based on the previous start time), what happens, compared with fixed-delay (next run 60 s after the previous finishes)?
options: Fixed-rate runs can overlap or pile up; fixed-delay never overlaps but drifts later over time
Fixed-rate skips the job permanently after one overrun
Both behave identically when the job takes longer than the interval
Fixed-delay runs overlap; fixed-rate always waits for completion
questions.explanation: Fixed-rate keeps the cadence, so a slow run means the next one is already due (overlap, or a backlog if runs are serialized). Fixed-delay waits for completion, avoiding overlap but shifting the schedule. Pick based on whether cadence or exclusivity matters.

questions.prompt: Your in-memory scheduler loses all pending tasks on every deploy. Which PostgreSQL-backed design lets several workers run due tasks durably without running a task twice at the same time?
options: Use one worker only and keep a setTimeout per task loaded at boot
Workers claim tasks with SELECT ... WHERE run_at <= now() ORDER BY run_at LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then mark them taken
Store tasks in a JSON file on each worker's local disk
Each worker runs SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE run_at <= now() and executes everything it gets
questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED lets concurrent workers claim disjoint batches without blocking each other, and persisting tasks survives restarts. A plain SELECT lets every worker run the same tasks, and a single worker with timers is a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: How can a heap-based scheduler support cancel(taskId)? Select all that apply.
options: Keep a map from task ID to heap index so the task can be removed in O(log n)
Cancellation is impossible once a task is in a binary heap
With lazy deletion, cancelled entries still occupy memory until popped, so many cancellations may call for periodic compaction
Mark the task as cancelled (lazy deletion) and skip it when it reaches the top of the heap
questions.explanation: Lazy deletion is simple and O(1) to cancel, at the cost of tombstones in the heap; an index map allows true O(log n) removal by sifting. Both are standard, so cancellation is very much possible.

questions.prompt: Which concerns apply when a Node.js scheduler executes its tasks? Select all that apply.
options: Catch task errors and rejections so one failing task doesn't crash the process
A CPU-heavy task on the main thread delays every other timer
Timers guarantee a task runs at exactly its scheduled millisecond
Limit how many async tasks run at once, e.g. with a concurrency pool
questions.explanation: Timers are 'not before' guarantees: a busy event loop makes them late. Long CPU work belongs in worker threads, concurrency limits protect downstream systems, and an unhandled rejection crashes Node by default.

questions.prompt: In Node.js, setTimeout(fn, 100) means fn will not run earlier than about 100 ms later, but it can run later if the event loop is busy.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The delay is a minimum: the callback runs in the timers phase once the time has elapsed and the loop gets there. Long synchronous work or a backlog of callbacks pushes it later.

questions.prompt: Keeping tasks in a sorted array gives O(log n) insertion, because binary search finds the right position.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Binary search finds the position in O(log n), but inserting into an array shifts later elements, which is O(n). A heap gives O(log n) insertion and removal of the minimum.

questions.prompt: The interviewer says 'Design a parking lot.' What should you do first?
options: Start writing the ParkingLot class so there is code on the board early
Clarify requirements and scope: users, use cases, constraints and what's out of scope
Draw the full class diagram with every pattern you might use
Pick a database and design its tables
questions.explanation: LLD prompts are deliberately vague; clarifying scope (vehicle types, payments, multiple floors, concurrency) decides which entities matter. Jumping to code or patterns risks solving the wrong problem.

questions.prompt: During entity identification, what is the usual heuristic for reading the requirements?
options: Every sentence becomes one class
Nouns suggest candidate classes or attributes; verbs suggest methods and responsibilities
Adjectives become interfaces and adverbs become enums
Only words the interviewer repeats become classes
questions.explanation: Noun/verb analysis gives a first list ('a vehicle parks in a spot, gets a ticket'), which you then prune: some nouns are just attributes (color) and some are out of scope.

questions.prompt: A candidate spends 25 of 45 minutes writing polished code for a vending machine before asking any questions. What is the main risk?
options: The code may be too fast and confuse the interviewer
Interviewers never look at code in LLD rounds
They may build the wrong thing and miss the requirements and trade-offs the interviewer wanted to discuss
The candidate will run out of whiteboard space
questions.explanation: LLD rounds assess requirement gathering, modeling and reasoning as well as code. Late discoveries (e.g. 'it must support refunds') force rewrites and leave no time for extensibility or concurrency discussion.

questions.prompt: In an e-commerce design, an OrderLine only exists as part of one Order and is deleted with it. Which relationship models this best?
options: Plain association
Inheritance
Aggregation
Composition
questions.explanation: Composition means the part's lifecycle is owned by the whole. Aggregation is a weaker 'has-a' where parts can exist independently (a Team and its Players). OrderLine is not a kind of Order, so inheritance is wrong.

questions.prompt: Midway through, the interviewer asks: 'Later we'll add EV charging spots with per-kWh billing.' What is the strongest response?
options: Say it's out of scope and continue with the original design
Show the extension point, e.g. a new spot type and a pricing strategy, so existing allocation code doesn't change
Rewrite the allocation code now with an if-branch for EV spots everywhere
Add a boolean isEV to every class in the system
questions.explanation: Interviewers probe extensibility. Pointing to where a new SpotType and FeeStrategy plug in (Open/Closed) shows the design absorbs change. Scattered if-branches or flags show it doesn't.

questions.prompt: Car, Bike and Truck differ only in which spot sizes they can use. Which model is most appropriate?
options: A deep hierarchy Vehicle -> MotorVehicle -> FourWheeler -> Car, each overriding fits()
Separate unrelated classes for each vehicle with duplicated fields
One Vehicle class with a size/type enum that the allocation logic uses
A switch on the vehicle's class name inside every service
questions.explanation: When variants differ only by data, an attribute is simpler than subclasses; introduce subclasses only when behavior genuinely differs. Deep hierarchies and class-name switches are common LLD anti-patterns.

questions.prompt: Why define the public API (e.g. `parkVehicle(v): Ticket`, `exit(ticketId): Receipt`) before writing the classes' internals?
options: Interviewers grade only on method names
It pins down the contract clients rely on, which drives what classes and data you need
It lets you skip writing any implementation
TypeScript needs method signatures before class fields can be declared
questions.explanation: The API turns use cases into concrete operations and reveals which objects must collaborate. It's a design step, not a substitute for implementation.

questions.prompt: Which questions are worth clarifying at the start of an LLD round? Select all that apply.
options: Which features are in scope (payments, reservations, notifications)
Scale and concurrency, e.g. one machine or many entry gates at once
The interviewer's favourite editor
Pricing rules and edge cases such as lost tickets or overstays
Which logo the product will use
questions.explanation: Concurrency, scope and business rules change the model. Tooling preferences and branding don't affect the design.

questions.prompt: What do interviewers typically evaluate in an LLD round? Select all that apply.
options: Extensibility for the likely changes they mention
Using as many named design patterns as possible
Handling concurrency where it actually matters
Clear, cohesive responsibilities for each class
questions.explanation: Good LLD shows sound responsibilities, sensible extension points and awareness of races. Forcing patterns in without a reason is a red flag, not a plus.

questions.prompt: In an LLD interview, it's better to name a design pattern only when it solves a concrete problem in your design than to force patterns in.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Saying 'pricing varies by vehicle and time, so I'll use a Strategy' shows judgement. Listing patterns without a need suggests memorization.

questions.prompt: You should design classes for every conceivable future requirement before writing any code.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Over-engineering wastes interview time and adds complexity (YAGNI). Design for the stated requirements plus the likely changes the interviewer hints at.

questions.prompt: In a UML class diagram, a line from Order to OrderLine has a filled (black) diamond at the Order end. What does it mean?
options: Composition: OrderLines are owned by the Order and die with it
Inheritance: OrderLine is a subclass of Order
Aggregation: OrderLines can exist without the Order
Dependency: Order uses OrderLine temporarily as a parameter
questions.explanation: A filled diamond is composition, with the diamond on the whole's side. A hollow diamond is aggregation; a hollow triangle is generalization; a dashed arrow is dependency.

questions.prompt: In a UML class diagram, CardPayment has a dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing to «interface» PaymentMethod. What does this show?
options: CardPayment realizes (implements) the PaymentMethod interface
CardPayment extends a PaymentMethod base class
CardPayment depends on PaymentMethod at runtime
CardPayment is composed of PaymentMethod objects
questions.explanation: A dashed line with a hollow triangle is realization (implements). A solid line with a hollow triangle is generalization (extends). A plain dashed arrow is a dependency.

questions.prompt: In a UML class box, an attribute is written as `- balance: number`. What does the `-` mean?
options: Private visibility
A derived (computed) attribute
Protected visibility
A static member
questions.explanation: UML visibility markers: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package. Static members are underlined and derived attributes are prefixed with '/'.

questions.prompt: An association is drawn as Customer `1` ---- `0..*` Order. How should it be read?
options: An order may exist without any customer
Customers and orders have a many-to-many relationship
Each customer has exactly one order, and each order has many customers
Each customer has zero or more orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer
questions.explanation: Each multiplicity sits next to the class it constrains: '0..*' next to Order means a customer has any number of orders; '1' next to Customer means each order has exactly one customer.

questions.prompt: In a UML sequence diagram, what does a solid line with a filled arrowhead from Gate to TicketService show?
options: A return message carrying a result back to the caller
An asynchronous message that doesn't wait for a reply
The creation of a new TicketService object
A synchronous call where Gate waits for TicketService to respond
questions.explanation: Solid line + filled arrowhead = synchronous message. Asynchronous messages use an open arrowhead; returns are dashed lines; creation is a dashed message to the new object's head, often labelled «create».

questions.prompt: You want a sequence diagram to show: 'if payment succeeds, issue a ticket; otherwise release the spot.' Which combined fragment fits?
options: alt
opt
par
loop
questions.explanation: alt shows mutually exclusive alternatives with guards ([success] / [else]). opt is a single optional block with one guard, loop repeats, and par shows parallel regions.

questions.prompt: A Department has Professors, but professors exist independently and can move between departments. Which UML relationship fits best?
options: Aggregation (hollow diamond at Department)
Realization (dashed line with hollow triangle)
Generalization (Professor extends Department)
Composition (filled diamond at Department)
questions.explanation: Aggregation is a whole-part 'has-a' where parts outlive the whole. Composition would mean deleting the department deletes its professors, which contradicts the requirement.

questions.prompt: TicketService.issue(clock: Clock) uses a Clock passed as a parameter but never stores it. How is this best shown in a class diagram?
options: A dependency: a dashed arrow from TicketService to Clock
An association with multiplicity 1 stored as a field
A composition: a filled diamond at TicketService
A generalization: TicketService extends Clock
questions.explanation: A dependency (dashed open arrow) means 'uses temporarily', e.g. as a parameter or local. An association implies a lasting structural link such as a field.

questions.prompt: What are sequence diagrams good for in an LLD discussion? Select all that apply.
options: Showing which object owns each responsibility in a flow
Distinguishing synchronous from asynchronous interactions
Listing every attribute of every class
Showing inheritance hierarchies
Showing the order of calls between objects in one scenario
questions.explanation: Sequence diagrams capture dynamic behavior over time for a use case. Attributes and inheritance are static structure, which belongs in class diagrams.

questions.prompt: Which UML class-diagram notations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The «interface» stereotype marks an interface
An italic class name or {abstract} marks an abstract class
A dashed line with a filled diamond means composition
Static members are underlined
questions.explanation: Italics or {abstract}, «interface» and underlining for statics are standard. Composition uses a solid line with a filled diamond; there's no dashed-diamond notation.

questions.prompt: In UML, composition implies that when the whole is destroyed, its parts are destroyed too.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Composition means exclusive ownership and a shared lifecycle; a part belongs to at most one whole at a time.

questions.prompt: In a UML sequence diagram, time flows from left to right across the lifelines.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Lifelines are arranged left to right, and time flows from top to bottom. Messages lower on the diagram happen later.

questions.prompt: Which set of core entities best fits a multi-floor Parking Lot design?
options: Driver, Car, Engine, Tyre and SteeringWheel
ParkingLot, Level, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, and a fee calculator
Ticket only, with every other concept stored as fields
Server, Database, Cache and LoadBalancer
questions.explanation: These map directly to the use cases: find a spot on a level, issue a ticket, compute the fee on exit. Car internals are out of scope, and infrastructure components belong in HLD.

questions.prompt: Parking fees vary: hourly on weekdays, a flat weekend rate, and an EV surcharge, with more rules likely. Which design fits best?
options: A FeeStrategy interface with one implementation per rule, chosen when the vehicle exits
A subclass of ParkingLot for each pricing rule
Hard-coding the rates as constants in the exit gate
A long if/else in Ticket.computeFee()
questions.explanation: Pricing is a family of interchangeable algorithms, so Strategy lets new rules be added without editing existing code. Subclassing the lot per rule mixes unrelated concerns.

questions.prompt: You must always assign the free spot nearest to the entrance for a given size. Which structure gives O(log n) allocation and release?
options: A singly linked list of free spots in insertion order
A min-heap of free spots per size, keyed by distance
A hash set of free spot ids per size
An unsorted array of all spots scanned on every request
questions.explanation: A min-heap pops the nearest free spot and re-inserts released ones in O(log n). A hash set is O(1) but can't give 'nearest'; an array scan is O(n); a linked list loses distance ordering.

questions.prompt: Gates run as several Node processes sharing a PostgreSQL database. Two cars at different gates get the same spot. What is the right fix?
options: Retry the allocation after a random delay whenever it looks busy
Rely on Node being single-threaded to serialize allocations
Cache free spots in each process's memory to reduce DB load
Allocate atomically in the DB, e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional UPDATE that checks the spot is still free
questions.explanation: Separate processes don't share an event loop, so the DB must serialize: row locks or compare-and-set updates let only one transaction claim a spot. Per-process caches make the race worse.

questions.prompt: In a single Node process, two park() calls run concurrently. What is the bug?
options: issueTicket() runs before occupy() because of hoisting
Another park() can run during the await and find the same free spot; occupy it before awaiting or reserve it atomically
There is no bug, since Node is single-threaded and code never interleaves
findFree() throws because it isn't async
questions.explanation: Single-threaded doesn't mean atomic across an await: the check (findFree) and the act (occupy) are separated by a suspension point. Do the check-and-occupy synchronously, then await the side effects.

questions.prompt: Motorcycles fit any spot, cars fit compact or large, and trucks fit only large. Where should this rule live?
options: Inside each Ticket so it can be checked on exit
In the UI, which filters spots before calling the API
In one place, e.g. a compatibility map or spot.canFit(vehicle), used by the allocator
Duplicated in the entry gate, exit gate and display board
questions.explanation: Centralizing the fit rule means a new size or vehicle type changes one place. Duplicating it causes drift, and UI-only checks can be bypassed.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Partial hours round up, with a one-hour minimum: 30 min is 1 hour (10), 61 min is 2 hours (20), 120 min is 2 hours (40), and 0 min still bills the 1-hour minimum (20).

questions.prompt: Which edge cases should a strong Parking Lot answer mention? Select all that apply.
options: The brand of tyres on each vehicle
The lot being full when a car arrives
A payment failure at the exit gate
A lost ticket and how the fee is then charged
questions.explanation: Lost tickets, full capacity and failed payments are realistic flows interviewers probe. Tyre brand has no effect on parking logic.

questions.prompt: Which design choices for a Parking Lot follow SOLID principles? Select all that apply.
options: Pricing behind a FeeStrategy interface so new rules don't modify Ticket (OCP)
The allocator depends on a SpotRepository interface rather than a concrete database client (DIP)
Separate EntryGate and ExitGate classes, each with one job (SRP)
One ParkingLot class that handles allocation, payments, printing and DB access
Spot subclasses whose park() throws for vehicle types the base class says are supported
questions.explanation: Strategy for pricing, depending on abstractions and focused gate classes are SOLID. A do-everything ParkingLot breaks SRP, and subclasses that reject what the base type promises break LSP.

questions.prompt: Modeling each spot size as its own subclass is mandatory; a size enum on a single ParkingSpot class is considered wrong.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: If spot sizes differ only in data, an enum is simpler and perfectly acceptable. Subclasses make sense when spots differ in behavior (e.g. EV spots that track charging).

questions.prompt: Making ParkingLot a hard-wired Singleton makes unit tests harder unless the instance can be injected or reset.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A global instance carries state between tests and can't easily be replaced with a fake. Creating one instance at the composition root and injecting it keeps 'one lot' without the testing pain.

questions.prompt: Which set of classes best captures the core of an Elevator System design?
options: Passenger, Ticket, Payment and Receipt
Elevator, Floor and a single global function that moves all cars
Building, Wall, Window and Staircase
Elevator (car), Controller/Dispatcher, Request (hall and car calls), Door, and Direction/State
questions.explanation: Cars with state, a dispatcher assigning requests, request types, doors and direction cover the behavior interviewers expect. Building structure and payments are out of scope.

questions.prompt: Which behavior describes the LOOK scheduling algorithm for one elevator?
options: Travel to the top floor and bottom floor on every cycle
Keep moving in the current direction, serving requests on the way, and reverse once none remain ahead
Always go to the closest requested floor, whichever direction it is
Serve requests strictly in the order they arrived
questions.explanation: LOOK sweeps in one direction and turns around at the last pending request. FCFS serves in arrival order, nearest-first can starve far floors, and always touching both ends is SCAN.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with first-come-first-served scheduling for an elevator?
options: It always starves the top floor
It causes lots of back-and-forth travel and passes floors with waiting requests without stopping
It can't handle more than one request at a time
It requires knowing every request in advance
questions.explanation: Serving 9, then 2, then 8 makes the car zig-zag and ignore requests it passes, increasing wait and travel time. Direction-aware algorithms like LOOK fix that.

questions.prompt: Why should a design model hall calls and car calls as different kinds of request?
options: There's no real difference; it only affects the button colors
Hall calls are always higher priority than car calls
A hall call (floor + direction) can be served by any car and needs dispatching; a car call (destination) belongs to one car
Car calls must be stored in the database, while hall calls stay in memory
questions.explanation: Hall calls go to the dispatcher, which picks the best car; car calls are pressed inside a car and only that car can serve them. Mixing them makes dispatch logic tangled.

questions.prompt: Car A is at floor 3 moving up; car B is idle at floor 8. A hall call comes from floor 5, going up. Using a simple cost of distance plus a penalty for moving away, which car should be assigned?
options: Car A, because floor 5 is on its way in the same direction and only 2 floors away
Neither; the request must wait until a car is idle at floor 5
Car B, because idle cars should always be preferred
Car B, because it is on a higher floor
questions.explanation: A is heading up and will pass floor 5 after 2 floors with no penalty, while B is 3 floors away. Preferring cars already moving toward the call in the same direction is the core dispatch heuristic.

questions.prompt: A car's state is DoorsOpen and a new car call arrives for floor 7. What should the state machine do?
options: Queue the call; the car may move only after the doors close
Start moving immediately with the doors open
Ignore the call because the car is busy
Throw an error and reset the car to Idle
questions.explanation: Safety rules belong in the state machine: from DoorsOpen the only move transition goes through DoorsClosed. Requests are recorded and served afterwards, never dropped.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Moving up from 5, the car serves floors above in ascending order (6, 7, 9), then reverses and serves floors below in descending order (2, 1).

questions.prompt: Buttons on many floors send requests at any moment while each car's control loop is running. Which design avoids race conditions on a car's request list?
options: Copy the request list into each button object
Poll every button once a minute and rebuild the list from scratch
Send requests as events into a queue that a single controller loop per car processes, or synchronize access
Let every button handler modify the car's request array directly
questions.explanation: Funnelling inputs through a queue to one owner (actor-style) or locking access means only one writer at a time. Direct concurrent mutation from many sources is the classic race; minute-long polling hurts responsiveness.

questions.prompt: Which requirements are worth clarifying before designing an elevator system? Select all that apply.
options: The colour of the buttons
Number of elevators and floors
Emergency and maintenance modes
Capacity or weight limits per car
The dispatch goal, e.g. shortest wait vs lowest energy use
questions.explanation: Scale, capacity, special modes and the optimization goal all change the design. Button colour doesn't.

questions.prompt: Which design patterns fit naturally into an elevator system? Select all that apply.
options: Strategy for pluggable dispatch algorithms (nearest car, zoning, LOOK)
Decorator to make each floor a Singleton
Observer to update floor displays when a car's position changes
State for car states (idle, moving up, moving down, doors open, maintenance)
questions.explanation: Car behavior depends on state, dispatch policies are interchangeable, and displays react to position changes. 'Decorator to make floors singletons' mixes up two unrelated patterns and solves no problem here.

questions.prompt: In an elevator design, a hall call must be bound to one specific car the moment the button is pressed and can never be reassigned.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Many dispatchers re-evaluate assignments as conditions change (a car fills up or goes into maintenance). Allowing reassignment improves wait times and handles failures.

questions.prompt: LOOK differs from SCAN in that the car reverses at the last pending request instead of travelling all the way to the end floor.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: SCAN sweeps to the physical end before reversing; LOOK only goes as far as the furthest request in that direction, saving travel.

questions.prompt: A vending machine's behaviour for insertCoin(), selectItem() and dispense() depends entirely on whether it is idle, has money, is dispensing or is sold out. Which design pattern targets exactly this?
options: State
Factory Method
Composite
Observer
questions.explanation: State lets an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating each call to a state object. Observer is for notifying listeners, Factory Method for creating objects, and Composite for tree structures.

questions.prompt: A VendingMachine class has insertCoin(), selectItem(), dispense() and refund(), and each method starts with the same four-way switch on this.state. What does refactoring to the State pattern change?
options: Each state becomes a class implementing all four operations, and the machine delegates to its current state
The switches move into a single dispatch() method, which is otherwise unchanged
States are stored in the database, so the switches are no longer needed
The machine stops tracking its current state
questions.explanation: The behaviour for one state is gathered in one class (e.g. SoldOutState.insertCoin refunds), so adding a state doesn't mean editing every method's switch. The machine (context) still holds the current state and shared data like balance and inventory.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: need 15 | bal 10 | need 5 | bal 20 | item, change 5 | refund 5
insert money | bal 10 | need 5 | bal 20 | item, change 5 | bal 5
insert money | bal 10 | need 5 | bal 20 | item, change 5 | refund 5
insert money | bal 10 | need 5 | bal 10 | item, change 0 | refund 5
questions.explanation: Selecting while IDLE is rejected; 10 isn't enough, so it reports need 5; a second coin makes 20, so the item dispenses with 5 change. Stock hits 0, the machine moves to SOLD_OUT, and the last coin is refunded instead of added to the balance.

questions.prompt: In an ATM state machine (Idle → CardInserted → Authenticated → TransactionSelected → Dispensing), the user enters a wrong PIN for the third time. What is the appropriate transition?
options: Retain or block the card per bank policy, log the event, and return to Idle
Stay in CardInserted and allow unlimited further attempts
Move to Dispensing with a zero amount to end the session
Move to Authenticated, since the card itself is valid
questions.explanation: Security policy caps PIN attempts; after the limit the session ends with the card retained or blocked, and the machine resets to Idle for the next customer. Unlimited retries enable brute force, and authenticating anyway is obviously wrong.
