questions.prompt: Your state classes each create the next state directly (`ctx.setState(new HasMoneyState(ctx))`). An interviewer says the full machine is hard to see and states are coupled to each other. What is a common alternative?
options: Use a central transition table mapping (state, event) to the next state, with guards, while states handle their actions
Let the client code decide the next state after each call
Merge all states into one class with boolean flags
Make every state a global singleton that any code can switch to
questions.explanation: A transition table puts the whole machine in one readable place and decouples states from each other; it is easy to validate and even to draw. Flags reintroduce scattered conditionals, and letting callers choose states breaks encapsulation.

questions.prompt: A vending machine has taken ₹50 and moved to Dispensing, but the drop sensor reports the item never fell (motor jam). How should the state machine handle it?
options: Retry the motor forever until the sensor reports success
Treat it as an explicit failure transition: refund or credit the customer, mark the slot faulty, then return to a safe state
Show 'thank you' and rely on the customer to call support
Return to Idle and keep the money, since the sale was started
questions.explanation: Real machines fail mid-transaction, so a robust design models failure states and compensations (refund or credit, disable the slot, alert maintenance). Infinite retries can hang the machine, and keeping the money without delivering is the worst outcome.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of the State pattern for machine-like objects? Select all that apply.
options: Each state's behaviour can be tested in isolation
It removes the same conditional being repeated across many methods
It makes what each operation does in each state explicit, including rejections
It makes the object thread-safe automatically
questions.explanation: State organizes behaviour by state, which clarifies and isolates it. It says nothing about concurrency: two threads (or interleaved async calls) can still race on transitions, so locking or serialization is a separate concern.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing the State pattern with an enum plus switch are correct? Select all that apply.
options: For two or three states with trivial behaviour, an enum plus switch can be the simpler choice
An enum plus switch makes it impossible to reject invalid operations
The State pattern adds a class per state
State objects are often stateless and shareable when data like balance lives in the context
questions.explanation: Patterns cost classes, so small machines may not need them; keeping data in the context lets states be shared singletons. An enum switch can reject invalid operations perfectly well; it just scatters that logic across methods as the machine grows.

questions.prompt: In the State pattern, the client calls methods on the context (the machine), which delegates them to the current state object.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Clients don't know which state is active; they call machine.insertCoin() and the machine forwards to this.state. That keeps the client API stable while behaviour changes underneath.

questions.prompt: A vending machine should check stock only at dispense time, after the customer has inserted money for the item.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Checking at selection (and showing sold-out slots up front) avoids taking money for something you can't deliver. A final check at dispense is still wise for races or sensor errors, but it shouldn't be the only one.

questions.prompt: A vending machine runs firmware in Node.js and receives events from both a coin acceptor and a touchscreen. Two events arrive back to back while a state transition awaits a hardware call. What is the risk?
options: The second event is handled by the old state while the transition is mid-flight, e.g. selecting an item twice; queue events and process them one at a time
No risk, because JavaScript is single-threaded
The coin acceptor's event always wins, since hardware has priority
Node.js drops the second event automatically
questions.explanation: Single-threaded doesn't mean no interleaving: across an await, another handler can run against half-updated state. Serializing events through a queue (one transition at a time) keeps the machine consistent.

questions.prompt: In a library system, why separate Book from BookItem?
options: Book holds title metadata (ISBN, author); BookItem is a physical copy with its own barcode, status and location
Book is for fiction and BookItem is for non-fiction
BookItem is just a cache of Book for faster reads
Book represents borrowed books and BookItem represents available ones
questions.explanation: A library owns many copies of one title, and loans, holds and damage apply to a specific copy. Mixing them forces duplicate metadata per copy or makes per-copy status impossible to track.

questions.prompt: Two members try to borrow the last available copy at the same moment. Which approach prevents both succeeding?
options: Retry the borrow request three times if it fails
A conditional update such as SET status = 'LOANED' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'AVAILABLE', checking the affected row count
Check availability in the UI and disable the button for others
Read the copy's status, then insert a loan if it was AVAILABLE, in two separate statements
questions.explanation: Combining the check and the write in one statement means only one transaction can flip the status; the other matches 0 rows and gets 'not available'. Read-then-write leaves a race window, and the UI can't see concurrent requests.

questions.prompt: A copy is returned while three members have holds on that title. What should the system do?
options: Assign the copy to the oldest hold, mark it ON_HOLD for that member with a pickup deadline, and notify them
Notify all three members and give it to whoever replies first
Mark the copy AVAILABLE so whoever arrives first can take it
Cancel all holds, since a copy is now available
questions.explanation: Holds are a FIFO queue per title: the next member gets the copy reserved for a limited time, and if they don't collect it, it moves to the next hold. 'First to reply' or a free-for-all ignores the queue that holds exist to provide.

questions.prompt: Fines differ by member type: students pay ₹2/day capped at ₹100, staff pay nothing, and the rules may change each year. Which design handles this best?
options: An if/else chain in Book.returnItem() checking member type
A nightly job that adds ₹2 to every overdue loan's fine field
Storing the fine amount on the BookItem when it is borrowed
A FinePolicy strategy selected by member type, computing the fine from due date and return date
questions.explanation: A strategy isolates the variable rule (rate, cap, exemptions) and can be swapped yearly without touching return logic. A nightly increment job is fragile: a missed run under-charges, and caps and member-type changes must be patched in many places.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: An early return clamps to 0 late days. Two days and one hour late rounds up to 3 days, giving 15. One month late is 31 days × 5 = 155, capped at 50. Note that months are 0-based in Date.UTC, so 1 is February.

questions.prompt: Members may hold at most 5 loans. The borrow code counts the member's active loans and inserts a new loan if the count is under 5. A member with 4 loans borrows two books at the same moment from two kiosks. What happens and how do you fix it?
options: Both succeed, leaving 6 loans; serialize per member, e.g. lock the member row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before counting, in the same transaction
One request fails automatically, because COUNT(*) locks the loans table
Both fail, because the database detects the conflict
Both succeed, which is fine because the limit is only advisory
questions.explanation: Count-then-insert is a check-then-act race: both see 4. Locking a per-member row (or keeping an active_loans counter updated with a conditional UPDATE) forces the second request to see the first one's loan. A plain COUNT takes no locks.

questions.prompt: On return, the code marks the copy AVAILABLE and a separate job later assigns it to the next hold. Between the two, a walk-in member borrows the copy. What is the design fix?
options: In the same transaction as the return, move the copy directly to ON_HOLD for the next reserver if a hold exists
Block walk-in borrowing entirely
Let the walk-in keep it and email the hold member an apology
Run the hold-assignment job more often
questions.explanation: The state after return depends on the hold queue, so deciding it in the same atomic step removes the window. Running the job more often only narrows the race, and blocking walk-ins punishes everyone for a design bug.

questions.prompt: Which concepts are best modelled as their own entities in a library system? Select all that apply.
options: Book (title-level metadata)
A borrowedBy array of member names stored on each Book
Loan (who borrowed which copy, with borrow, due and return dates)
BookItem (a physical copy)
questions.explanation: A Loan entity holds the relationship and its history (due dates, returns, fines), which a borrowedBy array can't represent per copy or over time. Book and BookItem separate title data from copies.

questions.prompt: Which practices are sound for library notifications (hold ready, due tomorrow, overdue)? Select all that apply.
options: Publish a 'hold ready' event when a copy is assigned, with a notifier subscribed to it
Run a scheduled job that finds loans due tomorrow and queues reminders
Make sends idempotent, e.g. record which reminders went out, so retries don't spam members
Send the email inside the database transaction, before it commits
questions.explanation: Events decouple the lending logic from notification channels, and scheduled queries cover time-based reminders. Sending before commit can notify about a change that then rolls back; send after commit or via an outbox.

questions.prompt: Fines should be computed from the stored due date and return date when needed, rather than incremented daily by a job that might miss days.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A derived fine is always consistent with the facts (dates and policy) and survives job outages. A running counter drifts if the job skips or runs twice, and is hard to correct when the policy changes.

questions.prompt: Because each Book has an ISBN, the ISBN alone is enough to identify which physical copy a member borrowed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: All copies of a title share the ISBN. To know which copy is out, damaged or overdue, a loan must reference the BookItem's unique ID (its barcode).

questions.prompt: A vending machine uses greedy change-making (largest coin first). For which coin system does greedy fail to give the fewest coins for some amount?
questions.explanation: For {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, greedy gives 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 uses 2. The other systems are canonical, so greedy is optimal for them; non-canonical systems need dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
{"10":3}
cannot
questions.explanation: With only one 10 in stock, greedy uses 10 + 3×5 + 5×1. Integer-like object keys serialize in ascending numeric order, hence {"1":5,...}. For 8 with {5:1, 4:2}, greedy takes the 5, is left with 3 and fails, even though 4+4 works: limited inventory breaks greedy too.

questions.prompt: A customer inserts ₹100 for a ₹35 item, but the machine can't make ₹65 change from its coin inventory. What should happen?
options: Check change availability before committing the sale; if it can't be made, refuse the sale and return the ₹100
Dispense the item and owe the customer the change
Dispense the item and give as much change as possible
Keep the ₹100 and dispense two items instead
questions.explanation: A sale should commit only when every part of it (stock and change) can complete; otherwise roll back by returning the money. That is why machines show 'exact change only' when coin stock is low.

questions.prompt: An ATM dispenses ₹2000, ₹500 and ₹100 notes. Each dispenser handles as many notes as it can, then passes the remaining amount to the next smaller dispenser. Which pattern is this?
options: Mediator
Visitor
Decorator
Chain of Responsibility
questions.explanation: Each handler processes what it can and forwards the rest along a chain, so dispensers can be added or reordered without changing others. Decorator wraps one object to add behaviour, and Mediator centralizes communication among peers.

questions.prompt: Two ATMs process withdrawals of ₹8,000 from a joint account holding ₹10,000 at the same moment. In PostgreSQL, which update prevents an overdraft?
options: Add a CHECK (balance >= -10000) constraint so small overdrafts are allowed
SELECT balance; if balance >= 8000 then UPDATE accounts SET balance = <balance read> - 8000
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 8000 WHERE id = $1
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 8000 WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 8000, then check the affected row count
questions.explanation: The guarded update re-evaluates balance >= 8000 on the latest row version after waiting for the other transaction's lock, so the second withdrawal matches 0 rows. Read-then-write with the stale value loses an update, and an unguarded decrement simply goes negative.

questions.prompt: An ATM withdrawal was recorded twice in the ledger due to a bug. In a double-entry ledger, how should it be corrected?
options: Append a reversing entry that cancels the duplicate, keeping the full history
Delete the duplicate ledger rows
Overwrite the account's balance column with the correct value
Update the duplicate entry's amount to zero
questions.explanation: Ledgers are append-only: corrections are new entries, so the audit trail shows the error and its fix and balances stay derivable. Deleting or editing rows destroys evidence auditors and reconciliation depend on.

questions.prompt: A vending machine has 40 slots, and the same cola can be loaded in several slots. How should inventory be modelled?
options: A single array of 40 product names, with duplicates for repeated products
A Slot entity (code, productId, quantity, capacity) referencing a separate Product (name, price)
One class per product, each with a static stock counter
A Product table only, with a quantity column per product
questions.explanation: Stock lives in physical slots, while price and name belong to the product; separating them lets one product sit in many slots and lets a price change apply everywhere. A per-product quantity can't tell you which slot to dispense from.

questions.prompt: Which are sound ways to represent money in a Node.js and PostgreSQL system? Select all that apply.
options: Plain JS numbers holding rupee amounts like 0.1 and 0.2
PostgreSQL NUMERIC columns rather than REAL or DOUBLE PRECISION
Integers in minor units, such as paise or cents
BigInt or a decimal library when amounts may exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
questions.explanation: Binary floats can't represent 0.1 exactly (0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 in JS), so totals drift. Integer minor units, BigInt or decimal libraries, and NUMERIC columns keep arithmetic exact.

questions.prompt: An ATM's withdrawal request to the bank times out and the terminal retries. Which practices keep this safe? Select all that apply.
options: The server deduplicates by that ID and returns the original result for a repeat
Each retry generates a new transaction ID so it isn't mistaken for a duplicate
Retries reuse the same transaction ID
The terminal attaches a unique transaction ID to the request
questions.explanation: Idempotency hinges on a stable ID across retries: the server recognizes the repeat and returns the first outcome instead of debiting twice. A new ID per retry turns every timeout into a potential double debit.

questions.prompt: Greedy change-making (always take the largest coin that fits) gives the fewest coins for every coin system.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It works only for canonical systems like most real currencies. For {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, greedy gives 3 coins versus the optimal 2 (3+3); dynamic programming handles arbitrary systems.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100` is safe against two concurrent withdrawals overdrawing the account, even at READ COMMITTED.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The second UPDATE waits for the first's row lock, then re-checks the WHERE clause against the newly committed row version. If the balance is now too low, it updates 0 rows. That's why guarded updates are a standard way to avoid lost updates.

questions.prompt: You start a 45-minute timed DSA mock and have just read the problem. What is the most effective first step?
options: Restate the problem and ask about input size, value ranges and edge cases before choosing an approach
Prove the lower bound on time complexity for the problem
Write a full set of unit tests before discussing any approach
Start coding the most optimal solution you can think of so you don't waste time
questions.explanation: Clarifying first (constraints, duplicates, empty input, size of n) decides which approach is even acceptable and is a scored signal. Jumping straight to code is the tempting mistake: it often solves the wrong problem or misses a constraint that changes the algorithm.

questions.prompt: In a JS DSA mock you sort numbers like this. What does it print?
questions.code: console.log([10, 9, 1, 2].sort().join(','));
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.sort without a comparator converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so '10' sorts before '2' and '9'. Always pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers; expecting 1,2,9,10 is the classic interview bug.

questions.prompt: You initialise a 2-row adjacency list this way, then push to row 0. What does it print?
questions.explanation: fill([]) evaluates [] once and puts the SAME array reference in every slot, so pushing to grid[0] is visible through grid[1]. Use Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) to get independent rows.

questions.prompt: Your BFS on a graph with 10^5 nodes uses `queue.shift()` to dequeue and times out. What is the most likely cause?
options: shift() is O(n) because it re-indexes the array, making BFS roughly O(n^2)
Map lookups for the visited set are O(log n) in V8
push() reallocates the array on every call, which is O(n)
Recursion depth is exceeded inside the BFS loop
questions.explanation: shift() moves every remaining element down one index, so each dequeue is linear. Keep a head index (queue[head++]) or a proper deque. push() is amortised O(1), so blaming it is wrong.

questions.prompt: 30 minutes into a mock you have a working O(n^2) brute force; 15 minutes remain and the interviewer hints that a hash map might help. What should you do?
options: Acknowledge the hint, explain how a map gives O(n), confirm, then implement it
Explain that time is short and stop coding to discuss only the theory
Keep polishing the brute force so at least one solution is clean
Ask the interviewer to explain the hash-map solution fully before you touch the code
questions.explanation: Taking a hint, explaining the improvement and its complexity, and implementing it shows coachability and problem solving. Polishing the brute force ignores the interviewer's direction and leaves the optimal solution unattempted.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine JavaScript-specific pitfalls in DSA rounds? Select all that apply.
options: Using a plain object as a hash map can misbehave for keys like "__proto__"
Integers above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1) lose precision unless you use BigInt
Array.prototype.includes is O(1) because arrays are hash tables
Default sort() compares elements as strings
Deep recursion is safe because V8 performs tail-call optimisation
questions.explanation: Precision loss past 2^53 - 1, the __proto__ key on plain objects, and string-based default sort are all real traps. V8 does not implement tail-call optimisation, so deep recursion can overflow the stack, and includes() is a linear scan.

questions.prompt: In a DSA interview, interviewers generally prefer that you code silently and only explain once the solution is complete.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Thinking aloud lets the interviewer follow your reasoning, give hints and score communication. Long silent stretches hide your process and make it hard to give partial credit if you don't finish.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log^2 n)
questions.explanation: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop doubles j, so it runs about log2(n) times per outer iteration: O(n log n). Calling it O(n^2) misses that j grows geometrically, not linearly.

questions.prompt: You have finished coding with 5 minutes left in a timed mock. Which actions are a good use of that time? Select all that apply.
options: Rename every variable to be more descriptive
Look for off-by-one errors at loop boundaries
Declare it correct and move on, since tracing wastes time
Check edge cases such as empty input or a single element
Trace the code by hand on a small example
questions.explanation: Dry-running a small input, edge cases and boundary checks catch most bugs and show testing discipline. Claiming correctness without testing is a red flag, and mass renaming burns time without improving correctness.

questions.prompt: In V8, `Math.max(...arr)` can throw a RangeError for a very large array (millions of elements) because spreading passes every element as a separate argument.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Spread into a call pushes each element as an argument on the stack, and very large arrays exceed the engine's limit, throwing RangeError. A simple loop or reduce avoids this. It is not a TypeError and it does not silently return Infinity.

questions.prompt: With 5 minutes left in a mock you realise your solution fails when the input contains duplicates. What is the best response?
options: Rewrite the whole solution from scratch with a new approach
Point out the bug, explain the fix, and patch it if time allows
Stay quiet and hope the interviewer doesn't test duplicates
Tell the interviewer duplicates are out of scope
questions.explanation: Spotting and explaining your own bug is a positive signal; a clear fix plan earns credit even if you can't finish typing. Starting a full rewrite with 5 minutes left usually ends with nothing working.

questions.prompt: What should you do in the first 5–10 minutes of a 45-minute HLD (system design) mock?
options: Draw the full architecture with every component you know
Start with the deep dive on the hardest component
Clarify functional and non-functional requirements and rough scale
Pick the database technology first, since everything depends on it
questions.explanation: Requirements and scale (users, QPS, read/write ratio, latency, consistency) drive every later choice. Picking a database or drawing boxes first means you design without knowing what matters.

questions.prompt: A system has 100M daily active users, each making about 10 reads per day. Roughly what is the average read QPS?
questions.explanation: 100M × 10 = 1B reads/day. 1B / 86,400 s ≈ 11,600 ≈ 12K QPS on average (peak is often 2–3× that). ~120K comes from dividing by ~8,640 instead of 86,400.

questions.prompt: In an HLD mock, the interviewer asks: "What happens if your cache cluster goes down?" Which answer shows the strongest judgement?
options: Requests fall through to the database, which simply handles the extra load
The DB faces a load spike; mitigate with request coalescing, load shedding and gradual cache warm-up
The cache is replicated, so it cannot go down
Return errors to all clients until the cache recovers
questions.explanation: A cold or missing cache sends a thundering herd to the DB. Naming that failure mode and the mitigations (coalescing, rate limiting, warm-up, replicas) shows senior thinking. Assuming the DB 'just handles it' ignores that the cache exists because it can't.

questions.prompt: Which behaviours do interviewers typically reward in an HLD round? Select all that apply.
options: Explaining trade-offs behind each major choice
Identifying bottlenecks and single points of failure
Reproducing a memorised reference architecture unchanged
Naming as many technologies as possible
Driving the conversation and managing time across phases
questions.explanation: Trade-off reasoning, ownership of the discussion and finding bottlenecks are the core senior signals. Buzzword lists and unadapted memorised diagrams suggest you can't reason about the actual requirements.

questions.prompt: In an HLD round you should go equally deep on every component rather than choosing a few areas for deep dives.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Time doesn't allow depth everywhere. Strong candidates sketch the whole system, then go deep on the riskiest or most interesting parts (often agreed with the interviewer).

questions.prompt: In an LLD mock for a parking lot, adding a new vehicle type forces you to edit `switch (vehicle.type)` statements in five classes. Which principle does this design violate most directly?
options: Dependency Inversion Principle
Interface Segregation Principle
Open/Closed Principle
Liskov Substitution Principle
questions.explanation: Open/Closed says code should be extendable without modifying existing code; scattered type switches must all change for each new type. Polymorphism (each vehicle type knows its spot size/fee) fixes it. LSP is about subtypes honouring the base contract, which isn't the problem here.

questions.prompt: In an LLD round, each user picks ONE delivery channel (email, SMS or push), which can be changed at runtime, and the sending code should not know channel details. Which pattern fits best?
options: Strategy
Template Method
Decorator
Singleton
questions.explanation: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and lets you swap them at runtime. Decorator layers extra behaviour around an object, which isn't needed when exactly one channel is chosen.

questions.prompt: In a parking-lot LLD mock, the interviewer asks how you prevent two entry gates assigning the same spot at the same moment. What is the best answer?
options: Make the check-and-assign atomic, e.g. a lock or a conditional update/unique constraint in the DB
Use a Singleton ParkingLot class so there is only one instance
Assign spots randomly so collisions are unlikely
Check availability twice before assigning
questions.explanation: This is a check-then-act race; it needs atomicity (mutex, compare-and-set, or UPDATE ... WHERE free = true with a row count check). A Singleton gives one object, not mutual exclusion, so two threads can still race inside it.

questions.prompt: Which practices make an LLD (object-oriented design) mock go well? Select all that apply.
options: Start from use cases and identify core entities and their relationships
Model every noun in the prompt as its own class up front
Make most classes Singletons so they are easy to access
Prefer composition over deep inheritance hierarchies
Keep interfaces small and focused
questions.explanation: Use-case-driven entities, composition and small interfaces keep designs extensible and testable. Singletons everywhere create hidden global state, and turning every noun into a class produces bloated designs.

questions.prompt: For the 'like' counter on social-media posts, strong consistency on every read is usually a requirement worth paying for.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A like count that is briefly stale harms no one, so eventual consistency (with batched/sharded counters) is the usual choice. Strong consistency would add latency and contention on hot posts for no user benefit.

questions.prompt: Designing a news feed, some accounts have 50M followers. Which fan-out approach is usually recommended?
options: Hybrid: push posts of normal users, pull celebrity posts at read time and merge
Store every feed only in the client and sync periodically
Fan-out on read for everyone, computing every feed at request time
Fan-out on write for everyone, including celebrities
questions.explanation: Pushing one celebrity post into 50M feeds is a massive write burst, while pulling for everyone makes reads slow. The hybrid model bounds write amplification and keeps reads fast for the common case.

questions.prompt: A Node deep-dive interviewer shows this CommonJS snippet. What does it print?
options:
sync
tick
promise
timeout

sync
timeout
tick
promise

tick
sync
promise
timeout

sync
promise
tick
timeout
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first. Then Node drains the nextTick queue before the promise microtask queue, and timers run in a later event-loop phase. Putting 'promise' before 'tick' is the common mix-up.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
start
end
a1
a2

start
a1
a2
end

a1
start
end
a2

start
a1
end
a2
questions.explanation: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, so 'a1' prints immediately. The rest is resumed as a microtask after the current synchronous code, so 'end' prints before 'a2'.

questions.prompt: A Node API resizes images in the request handler and every other request stalls while a resize runs. You want to keep one process. What is the best fix?
options: Wrap the resize in an async function
Run the resize in a worker_threads pool
Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
Split the resize with setImmediate between pixel rows
questions.explanation: CPU-bound JavaScript blocks the single event-loop thread; worker_threads move it to separate threads. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE only affects libuv-backed work (fs, crypto, zlib, dns.lookup), not your own JS, and async doesn't make CPU work parallel.

questions.prompt: A service runs many concurrent `crypto.pbkdf2` and `fs.readFile` calls. Latency jumps sharply once more than four run at once. What is the most likely reason?
options: TCP connections are capped at four per process by default
Both use the libuv threadpool, which has 4 threads by default
V8 limits each process to four concurrent promises
The event loop only processes four callbacks per tick
questions.explanation: pbkdf2, fs operations, zlib and dns.lookup run on libuv's threadpool, default size 4, so a fifth job queues. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (set before the pool starts) or reducing that work helps. Network sockets don't use the pool.

questions.prompt: Heap usage of a long-running Node service grows steadily until it crashes. Which are common causes of such leaks? Select all that apply.
options: A module-level Map used as a cache with no size limit or TTL
Adding an event listener on a shared emitter per request and never removing it
Using const instead of let for request-scoped variables
Awaiting promises sequentially inside a for loop
A setInterval callback whose closure keeps large objects alive and is never cleared
questions.explanation: Unbounded caches, accumulating listeners and live timers holding closures all keep objects reachable so GC can't free them. const vs let has no effect on retention, and sequential awaits are slower but don't leak.

questions.prompt: A Node script reads a large file with a read stream and writes chunks to a slow network stream with `dest.write(chunk)` in a 'data' handler, ignoring the return value. Memory balloons. Why?
options: The 'data' event fires only once with the whole file
Read streams always load the entire file into memory first
Ignoring write()'s false return value ignores backpressure, so chunks pile up in the write buffer
Network streams cannot be written to from a 'data' handler
questions.explanation: write() returns false when the internal buffer passes highWaterMark; you should pause until 'drain'. stream.pipeline() (or pipe) handles this automatically and propagates errors. Read streams do read in chunks; the reader is just outpacing the writer.

questions.prompt: Using `await` inside an async function blocks the entire Node.js event loop until the awaited promise settles.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: await only suspends that async function; the event loop keeps serving other callbacks and requests. What does block the loop is long synchronous work such as heavy loops or sync fs calls.

questions.prompt: In Node.js 15 and later, an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process by default.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Since Node 15 the default --unhandled-rejections mode is 'throw', so an unhandled rejection surfaces as an uncaught exception and exits the process. Earlier versions only printed a warning.

questions.prompt: How do `process.nextTick` callbacks and `setImmediate` callbacks differ?
options: setImmediate runs before nextTick because 'immediate' has higher priority
They are aliases; Node schedules them identically
nextTick runs in the timers phase; setImmediate runs in the poll phase
nextTick runs right after the current operation, before promise callbacks; setImmediate runs in the check phase
questions.explanation: nextTick callbacks drain as soon as the current JS stack finishes, even before promise microtasks; setImmediate is a macrotask in the check phase after poll. The names are misleading, which is why 'setImmediate first' is a common wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Node's cluster module and worker_threads are correct? Select all that apply.
options: cluster forks separate processes, each with its own memory and event loop
worker_threads share one JS heap, so objects are passed by reference without copying
Workers in cluster can share the same listening server port
worker_threads can share memory explicitly using SharedArrayBuffer
worker_threads are the right tool to speed up I/O-bound database calls
questions.explanation: cluster gives separate processes sharing a port; worker threads run in the same process with separate heaps, and data is copied via structured clone unless you transfer buffers or use SharedArrayBuffer. I/O-bound work is already async, so threads don't help it.

questions.prompt: Inside an `fs.readFile` callback, you schedule `setTimeout(cb1, 0)` and `setImmediate(cb2)`. In what order do they run?
options: cb2 always runs first, because the check phase follows the I/O poll phase
Both run in the same phase in insertion order
The order is random and cannot be predicted
cb1 always runs first because its delay is 0
questions.explanation: From an I/O callback the loop is in the poll phase; next comes the check phase (setImmediate) before looping back to timers. The order only looks random when both are scheduled from the main module, where timer granularity decides.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of recording yourself during mock interviews?
options: It lets you see habits you can't notice live, like long silences or skipping complexity analysis
It replaces the need for feedback from other people
It lets you memorise your answers word for word
It proves to the interviewer that you practised
questions.explanation: While solving, your attention is on the problem, so communication habits go unnoticed; playback reveals them. It complements peer feedback rather than replacing it, and memorising scripts makes answers sound rehearsed.

questions.prompt: Reviewing a DSA mock recording, you see six minutes of silent typing. What is the best habit to build?
options: Narrate what you're about to do and why before each chunk of code
Type faster so the silence is shorter
Skip explaining and summarise at the end instead
Ask the interviewer to look away while you code
questions.explanation: Brief narration ('now I'll expand the window until the constraint breaks') keeps the interviewer aligned and earns credit for reasoning. Summarising only at the end leaves no chance for hints or partial credit if you get stuck.

questions.prompt: Which items belong in a self-review rubric for a recorded coding mock? Select all that apply.
options: Did I state time and space complexity?
Did I clarify constraints and edge cases?
How many lines of code did I write?
Did I test with an example before saying I was done?
Did I use the newest language syntax?
questions.explanation: Clarification, complexity analysis and testing are signals interviewers actually score. Line count and fancy syntax don't measure problem solving; concise readable code matters, not volume or novelty.

questions.prompt: Reviewing a recording is only useful when the mock went badly.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Good mocks also hide habits (rambling clarifications, untested code) and show what to keep doing. Reviewing only failures gives you a skewed picture of your performance.

questions.prompt: Your recordings show you often start coding before the interviewer agrees with your approach. What should you change?
options: Write pseudocode silently before speaking
State the approach and its complexity, then check in before coding
Code faster so there's time to change approach later
Present two approaches in code and let the interviewer pick
questions.explanation: A short check-in ('O(n) with a hash map; does that sound good before I code it?') catches misunderstandings early and often prompts useful hints. Coding two solutions wastes time you need for testing.

questions.prompt: In a recorded HLD mock, the interviewer hinted that your single primary DB would be a bottleneck, and you kept defending it. What does this signal, and what should you do instead?
options: It is neutral; interviewers don't score reactions to hints
It signals poor coachability; acknowledge the concern and adapt the design, explaining the trade-off
It shows confidence; keep defending your choices
It signals strong knowledge; add more detail to the original design
questions.explanation: Interviewers use hints to test collaboration and adaptability. Acknowledging the bottleneck and adjusting (read replicas, sharding, caching) with clear trade-offs scores well. It's fine to defend a choice with reasoning, but ignoring a valid concern reads as uncoachable.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to track improvement across many recorded mocks?
options: Score each session on a consistent rubric and note 1–2 concrete action items
Rely on your overall feeling about each session
Count total hours of mocks completed
Rewatch only the most recent recording each week
questions.explanation: A consistent rubric makes progress comparable over time, and a few specific action items make the next mock purposeful. Feelings and hour counts don't show which skills actually improved.

questions.prompt: Playing back a recorded behavioural answer, which signs indicate a weak STAR story? Select all that apply.
options: You explain the specific decision you made and why
The situation setup takes most of the answer's time
The result has no measurable outcome or impact
You mostly say "we" and rarely describe your own actions
The result cites a concrete metric, such as p99 latency cut from 800 ms to 200 ms
questions.explanation: Interviewers assess YOUR contribution and impact, so 'we'-heavy, metric-free stories with long setup score poorly. Concrete metrics and explicit personal decisions are what a strong answer looks like.

questions.prompt: Filler words are the most important thing to fix from recordings, because interviewers mainly grade delivery polish.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Problem solving, correctness, communication of reasoning and trade-offs dominate scoring. Reducing filler helps clarity, but a polished delivery of a wrong or untested solution still fails.

questions.prompt: A recording shows: 20 min clarifying and discussing brute force, 25 min coding, 0 min testing, and the code had a bug. What is the most impactful change?
options: Stop discussing brute force and only present the optimal solution
Tighten clarification and always reserve the last ~5 minutes for tracing and edge cases
Skip clarification entirely to save time
Spend more time coding so the code is perfect first time
questions.explanation: The fix is time budgeting: shorter, focused clarification and a protected testing window catch bugs like this one. Skipping clarification removes a scored signal, and briefly mentioning brute force is still useful as a baseline.

questions.prompt: Reviewing an HLD recording, you notice you never estimated scale (users, QPS, storage). Why does this matter?
options: Scale estimates only matter for storage, not for compute
Without numbers you can't justify choices like sharding, caching or replication
Estimation is optional and never affects the design
Interviewers only care that the arithmetic is exactly right
questions.explanation: Back-of-envelope numbers tell you whether one DB suffices or you need sharding, caches or queues, and they anchor your trade-offs. Interviewers care about order-of-magnitude reasoning, not exact arithmetic.

questions.prompt: At which OSI layer does a router make forwarding decisions based on destination IP addresses?
options: Layer 4, Transport
Layer 3, Network
Layer 2, Data Link
Layer 7, Application
questions.explanation: Routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses, which is the Network layer. Switches forward frames by MAC address at layer 2.

questions.prompt: Which header field does an Ethernet switch use to forward a frame within a LAN?
options: Destination IP address
HTTP Host header
Destination TCP port
Destination MAC address
questions.explanation: A switch learns which port each MAC address is on and forwards frames by destination MAC, a layer-2 operation. It doesn't inspect IP addresses or ports.

questions.prompt: You need to send /api/* and /static/* to different backend pools based on the URL path and Host header. Which kind of load balancer do you need?
options: A layer-7 load balancer that parses HTTP requests
A layer-3 router using equal-cost multipath routing
A layer-4 load balancer that balances TCP connections
A DNS round-robin setup with multiple A records
questions.explanation: Paths and Host headers only exist inside the HTTP request, so the balancer must parse layer 7. A layer-4 balancer only sees IPs and ports and can't tell /api from /static.

questions.prompt: ping 203.0.113.10 succeeds, but curl https://203.0.113.10 times out. Where is the problem most likely?
options: ARP resolution for the server's address failed
At the transport layer or above, e.g. a firewall dropping TCP 443
IP routing to the server is broken
The physical link to the server is down
questions.explanation: A successful ping proves the physical link, ARP and IP routing work. A timeout on port 443 points to packets being dropped by a firewall or security group. Using the IP directly rules out DNS.

questions.prompt: Over a VPN, small API responses arrive fine, but large responses hang. What is the most likely cause?
options: TCP's receive window is too small for large responses
The server's TLS certificate is too large for the VPN
An MTU problem: full-size packets with Don't Fragment set are dropped, and the ICMP 'fragmentation needed' replies are blocked
The VPN only supports UDP traffic
questions.explanation: VPN encapsulation lowers the effective MTU. If ICMP is filtered, path MTU discovery fails, so large packets vanish while small ones pass. A small receive window slows transfers but doesn't make them hang.

questions.prompt: The TCP/IP model's Link (Network Access) layer corresponds to which OSI layers?
options: Data Link and Network (layers 2 and 3)
Network only (layer 3)
Physical and Data Link (layers 1 and 2)
Session and Presentation (layers 5 and 6)
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP model groups physical transmission and framing into its lowest layer. OSI's Network layer maps to the TCP/IP Internet layer, and OSI session/presentation fold into the application layer.

questions.prompt: A Node client gets ECONNREFUSED from one host and ETIMEDOUT from another. What does the difference usually mean?
options: Refused means the server is overloaded; timed out means the server rejected the client's certificate
Refused means DNS failed; timed out means TLS failed
Refused means the host replied with a TCP RST because nothing listens on that port; timed out means packets got no reply, e.g. firewall or host down
Both mean the same thing; Node picks one at random
questions.explanation: A refusal is an active response (RST), so the host is reachable but the port is closed. A timeout means silence, typical of firewalls that drop packets or unreachable hosts.

questions.prompt: Which of these are transport-layer responsibilities? Select all that apply.
options: Flow control between sender and receiver
Port numbers that identify processes
Congestion control
MAC addressing on the local link
Routing packets between networks
questions.explanation: Ports, flow control and congestion control belong to the transport layer (TCP). Routing is the Network layer, and MAC addressing is the Data Link layer.

questions.prompt: A home router performs NAT for outgoing TCP connections. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It only changes the destination MAC address and leaves IP and TCP headers alone
It often rewrites the source port too (port address translation)
It must recompute the TCP checksum, because that checksum covers a pseudo-header that includes the IP addresses
It rewrites the source IP address to its public address
questions.explanation: NAT rewrites layer-3 and often layer-4 fields, and since the TCP checksum includes IP addresses, it must be updated. This is a classic example of real devices crossing clean layer boundaries. Changing only MACs is what ordinary routing does.

questions.prompt: TCP and UDP both operate at the transport layer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Both are transport protocols on top of IP; TCP offers a reliable byte stream, while UDP offers best-effort datagrams.

questions.prompt: The TCP/IP model defines TLS as its own dedicated layer between the transport and application layers.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP model has four layers (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) and no separate security layer. TLS is usually described as part of the application layer or as sitting on top of TCP.

questions.prompt: What is the correct sequence of the TCP three-way handshake?
options: SYN, SYN, ACK
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number, the server replies SYN-ACK with its own and acknowledges the client's, and the client ACKs. Both sides then know each other's sequence numbers.

questions.prompt: A client opens a new HTTPS connection using TLS 1.3 over TCP, with no session resumption. How many round trips occur before it can send the HTTP request?
questions.explanation: The TCP handshake costs 1 RTT, and the TLS 1.3 full handshake costs 1 more, so the request goes out after 2 RTTs. TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTTs for TLS alone, making 3 in total.

questions.prompt: A Node service opens a new TCP connection to the database for every query and starts failing with EADDRNOTAVAIL. netstat shows thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the server's listen backlog
Switch the database protocol to UDP
Disable TCP checksums on the host
Reuse connections through a connection pool or keep-alive
questions.explanation: The side that closes first keeps the socket in TIME_WAIT for a while, so short-lived connections exhaust ephemeral ports. Pooling reuses a few long-lived connections. The listen backlog affects incoming connections, not outbound ports.

questions.prompt: An attacker floods a server with SYN packets from spoofed addresses, filling its half-open connection queue. Which defense encodes connection state into the server's initial sequence number so no state is stored until the final ACK?
options: Selective acknowledgements
TCP Fast Open
SYN cookies
Nagle's algorithm
questions.explanation: With SYN cookies, the server answers with a SYN-ACK whose sequence number encodes the connection details and keeps no state; a legitimate final ACK lets it rebuild them. TCP Fast Open is about sending data in the SYN.

questions.prompt: Why can one lost TCP segment stall every HTTP/2 stream on that connection?
options: TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so data after the gap waits in the kernel until the retransmission arrives
HTTP/2 resets all streams when any packet is lost
The server must re-send all streams from the beginning after a loss
HTTP/2 uses UDP, which has no retransmission
questions.explanation: TCP has no notion of streams; it presents one ordered byte stream, so a missing segment blocks delivery of everything after it, including unrelated streams. QUIC fixes this with per-stream ordering.

questions.prompt: A protocol sends many small writes on a TCP socket and sees ~40 ms delays caused by Nagle's algorithm interacting with delayed ACKs. Which socket option addresses this?
options: TCP_NODELAY (socket.setNoDelay(true) in Node)
SO_LINGER with a zero timeout
SO_REUSEADDR
SO_KEEPALIVE
questions.explanation: Nagle holds small segments until earlier data is acknowledged, and delayed ACKs make the receiver wait, which adds latency. TCP_NODELAY disables Nagle. SO_KEEPALIVE only probes idle connections.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what UDP provides?
options: Ordered delivery, but lost datagrams are not retransmitted
A connection handshake, but no ordering
Reliable delivery, but without congestion control
Datagram boundaries are preserved, but there is no guarantee of delivery or ordering
questions.explanation: UDP delivers each datagram whole or not at all, with an optional checksum, and provides no ordering, retransmission, handshake or congestion control. Anything more must be built on top, as QUIC does.

questions.prompt: Which statements about closing a TCP connection are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The side that sends the first FIN (active close) ends up in TIME_WAIT
TIME_WAIT always happens on the side that receives the first FIN
An RST aborts the connection immediately, discarding unsent data
Each direction is closed with its own FIN, so a connection can be half-closed
questions.explanation: A graceful close uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and the active closer holds TIME_WAIT so delayed segments die out. The passive side goes through CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK instead.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms are part of TCP? Select all that apply.
options: A congestion window with slow start
Sequence numbers and acknowledgements that drive retransmission
A receive window advertised by the receiver for flow control
Forward error correction added to every segment
questions.explanation: TCP's reliability comes from sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission, while windows provide flow and congestion control. It doesn't use forward error correction; lost data is simply retransmitted.

questions.prompt: UDP has no built-in congestion control, so protocols built on it, such as QUIC, implement their own.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: UDP sends whatever the application gives it. QUIC implements loss recovery and congestion control (e.g. CUBIC or BBR) in user space on top of UDP.

questions.prompt: Because TCP preserves message boundaries, two 100-byte writes from the sender always arrive as two separate 100-byte reads at the receiver.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries: writes can be merged or split, so the receiver may read 200 bytes at once or 37 then 163. Applications need framing such as length prefixes or delimiters.

questions.prompt: With an empty cache everywhere, what is the order of servers involved in resolving www.example.com?
options: Stub resolver, authoritative server, TLD server, root server
Recursive resolver, stub resolver, authoritative server, root server
Root server, recursive resolver, TLD server, stub resolver
Stub resolver, recursive resolver, root server, .com TLD server, example.com authoritative server
questions.explanation: The OS stub asks a recursive resolver, which walks the hierarchy: root gives the .com servers, .com gives example.com's nameservers, and those give the answer. Only then does the resolver reply to the stub.

questions.prompt: You will move a service to a new IP address. Its A record currently has a TTL of 86400 seconds. What is the safest plan?
options: Ask users to restart their browsers after the change
Keep the TTL at 86400 so resolvers can find the new IP faster
Change the record and its TTL at the same moment as the cutover
Lower the TTL (e.g. to 300) at least 24 hours before the move, then change the record
questions.explanation: Resolvers may cache the old answer for the old TTL, so the TTL must be lowered at least one old-TTL period before the switch. Changing both at once leaves some clients on the old IP for up to a day.

questions.prompt: Who performs the iterative queries to the root, TLD and authoritative servers?
options: The browser's JavaScript engine
The recursive resolver, such as an ISP resolver or 8.8.8.8
The authoritative nameserver of the queried domain
The root servers, which forward the query down the tree
questions.explanation: The stub sends a single recursive query, and the recursive resolver does the iterative work, following referrals down the hierarchy. Root servers only return referrals; they don't forward queries.

questions.prompt: You queried new.example.com before creating its record. After creating it, some clients still get NXDOMAIN for a while. Why?
options: NXDOMAIN responses are permanent until the resolver restarts
New records always take exactly 48 hours to propagate
Resolvers cache negative answers, for a duration derived from the zone's SOA record
Authoritative servers need a reboot to publish new records
questions.explanation: Negative caching (RFC 2308) lets resolvers remember 'this name doesn't exist' for a period based on the SOA minimum and SOA TTL. There is no fixed propagation delay; it all comes down to cached TTLs.

questions.prompt: A Node service makes many outbound HTTP calls to hosts with slow DNS. File reads and crypto calls in the same process also slow down. What explains this?
options: The http module disables the threadpool while resolving names
dns.lookup(), used by http by default, calls getaddrinfo on the libuv threadpool (default 4 threads), which is shared with fs and crypto work
Slow DNS blocks the event loop thread directly
c-ares resolution runs on the main thread and pauses timers
questions.explanation: dns.lookup is a blocking OS call run on libuv's small threadpool, so slow lookups occupy threads that fs and crypto also need. dns.resolve*() uses c-ares over the network without the threadpool, and caching or a larger UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE also helps.

questions.prompt: A CDN uses GeoDNS to return the nearest edge IP. A user in Mumbai using a public resolver whose egress is in Singapore gets a Singapore edge. What helps with this?
options: Lowering the TTL of the CDN's records
Using DNSSEC so the answer is signed
Switching the record from A to CNAME
EDNS Client Subnet, which passes part of the client's IP to the authoritative server
questions.explanation: GeoDNS sees the resolver's address, not the user's. EDNS Client Subnet includes a truncated client subnet so the authoritative server can choose by the user's location. DNSSEC proves authenticity but doesn't change which IP is chosen.

questions.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
options: PTR
AAAA
SRV
A
questions.explanation: AAAA records hold IPv6 addresses, while A records hold IPv4. PTR records are used for reverse lookups from an IP back to a name.

questions.prompt: Which statements about how DNS messages are transported are correct? Select all that apply.
options: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) carries queries inside encrypted HTTPS
DNS always uses TCP port 443
Resolvers retry over TCP when a UDP response is truncated (TC bit set)
Classic DNS queries use UDP port 53
questions.explanation: DNS defaults to UDP/53 and falls back to TCP/53 for large responses and zone transfers. DoH uses HTTPS on 443, but classic DNS does not.

questions.prompt: Which statements about delegation and glue records are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Glue A/AAAA records are needed when a nameserver's name lies inside the zone it serves, e.g. ns1.example.com for example.com
Glue records live only in the client's hosts file
Without glue in that case, resolving the nameserver's address would depend on itself
NS records in the .com zone delegate example.com to its authoritative nameservers
questions.explanation: Delegation uses NS records in the parent zone; when nameservers are inside the delegated zone, the parent also publishes their addresses (glue) to break the circular dependency. Hosts files are unrelated.

questions.prompt: A DNS record's TTL tells resolvers how long they may cache the answer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The TTL, in seconds, is the maximum time a resolver may serve the cached answer before asking again. Some resolvers clamp very low or very high values.

questions.prompt: Lowering a record's TTL instantly forces resolvers to drop copies they cached under the old, longer TTL.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Resolvers keep cached answers for the TTL that came with them. The new TTL only applies once they fetch the record again, which is why TTLs must be lowered well before a change.

questions.prompt: What is the main improvement HTTP/2 brings over HTTP/1.1 for a page making many requests?
options: It encrypts headers without needing TLS
It multiplexes many concurrent requests as streams over one TCP connection
It replaces TCP with UDP
It makes every request stateless for the first time
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 interleaves frames from many streams on one connection, removing HTTP/1.1's one-request-at-a-time-per-connection limit. It still runs over TCP; HTTP/3 is the version that uses QUIC over UDP.

questions.prompt: Why did browsers open about 6 parallel connections per host under HTTP/1.1?
options: Servers refused to send more than one file per connection
Each HTTP/1.1 connection can carry only one request/response at a time, since pipelining was rarely usable
HTTP/1.1 limits each connection to 6 requests before it must close
TLS required a separate connection for each resource type
questions.explanation: Without multiplexing, a connection is busy until its response finishes, so browsers opened several to download in parallel. Pipelining existed but suffered head-of-line blocking and proxy bugs, so it was effectively disabled.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP/2 feature reduces the overhead of sending large, repetitive headers like cookies on every request?
options: Gzip compression of the header block
Server push
HPACK header compression
QPACK header compression
questions.explanation: HPACK uses static and dynamic tables plus Huffman coding to avoid resending repeated headers. QPACK is the HTTP/3 equivalent. Generic compression of headers was avoided because of attacks like CRIME.

questions.prompt: A mobile user switches from Wi-Fi to cellular in the middle of a large download. Which HTTP/3 property helps the transfer continue without a new handshake?
options: Larger TCP initial congestion windows
QUIC connection IDs, which aren't tied to the client's IP and port
HPACK header compression
TLS session tickets in HTTP/2
questions.explanation: A TCP connection is identified by its address/port 4-tuple, so a new IP kills it. QUIC identifies connections by connection IDs, so it can migrate to the new path.

questions.prompt: On a link with 2% packet loss, a site performs worse over HTTP/2 than over HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections. Why?
options: Header compression fails when packets are lost
HTTP/2's binary framing is slower to parse
Everything shares one TCP connection, so each loss stalls all streams and shrinks the single congestion window
HTTP/2 disables TCP retransmission
questions.explanation: With one connection, a loss blocks every stream (TCP head-of-line blocking) and cuts the only congestion window. Six connections spread the impact. This is a main motivation for HTTP/3.

questions.prompt: How do a browser and server agree to use HTTP/2 on an HTTPS connection?
options: Through an 'Upgrade: h2c' header on the first request
Through ALPN during the TLS handshake
Through an Alt-Svc header in the first response
Through the version number in the request line
questions.explanation: ALPN negotiates 'h2' inside the TLS handshake, costing no extra round trip. 'Upgrade: h2c' is for cleartext HTTP/2, which browsers don't support, and Alt-Svc is used to advertise HTTP/3.

questions.prompt: How does a browser typically learn that a server supports HTTP/3?
options: The URL uses an h3:// scheme
The server advertises it with an Alt-Svc response header (or a DNS HTTPS record)
It always tries UDP first for every new site
It is negotiated using the TCP options in the SYN packet
questions.explanation: Browsers usually connect over TCP first, see 'Alt-Svc: h3=":443"' or an HTTPS DNS record, and then use QUIC. There is no h3:// URL scheme; HTTPS URLs stay the same.

questions.prompt: Which statements about HTTP/2 are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Flow control applies per stream as well as per connection
It uses a binary framing layer instead of plain-text messages
Requests are still sent as plain-text lines on the wire, as in HTTP/1.1
Browsers typically use a single connection per origin
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 encodes messages in binary frames with per-stream flow control and normally uses one connection per origin. The semantics (methods, headers) are unchanged, but the wire format is no longer text.

questions.prompt: Which statements are correct about using HTTP/2 in practice? Select all that apply.
options: HTTP/2 requires a different URL scheme such as h2://
Chrome has removed support for HTTP/2 server push
Node.js ships a built-in node:http2 module
Browsers only use HTTP/2 over TLS
questions.explanation: Node has had node:http2 for years, browsers only negotiate h2 via TLS, and Chrome removed server push in 2022 in favour of preload hints and 103 Early Hints. URLs stay https://.

questions.prompt: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which runs over UDP.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: QUIC implements reliability, streams, congestion control and TLS 1.3 on top of UDP, and HTTP/3 maps HTTP onto QUIC streams.

questions.prompt: HTTP/2 eliminates head-of-line blocking completely, including at the TCP layer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 removes application-level head-of-line blocking, but TCP still delivers bytes in order, so one lost segment blocks every stream. Only QUIC/HTTP/3 removes it at the transport layer.

questions.prompt: What does a valid server certificate actually prove to a client?
options: That the public key belongs to the named domain, as vouched for by a chain of signatures to a trusted CA
That the server has no vulnerabilities
That the server operator's company is legally registered
That the connection uses the strongest available cipher
questions.explanation: A certificate binds a public key to names (SANs), signed by a CA the client trusts. It says nothing about the server's security or cipher choice; legal identity is only checked for some certificate types.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data?
options: Early data can be replayed by an attacker, so it should only carry idempotent requests
It forces a downgrade to TLS 1.2
It disables certificate validation
Early data is sent unencrypted
questions.explanation: 0-RTT data is encrypted with keys from a previous session, but it can be captured and resent, so servers should accept it only for safe, idempotent requests. It is not plaintext.

questions.prompt: Browsers load https://api.internal.example fine, but a Node client fails with 'unable to verify the first certificate'. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server's private key is too short for Node
Node doesn't support TLS 1.3
The certificate has expired, but browsers ignore expiry
The server doesn't send its intermediate certificate, which browsers can work around but Node can't
questions.explanation: Browsers often fill in missing intermediates from caches or by fetching them (AIA), but Node only trusts what the server sends plus its CA store. Fix it by serving the full chain. Browsers do reject expired certificates.

questions.prompt: Why does TLS 1.3 require an ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange?
options: It provides forward secrecy: stealing the server's long-term private key later can't decrypt previously recorded sessions
It allows the same session key to be reused across all clients
It lets servers skip certificate validation
Ephemeral keys make the handshake use fewer bytes
questions.explanation: Session keys come from per-connection ephemeral secrets that are discarded, so a later key compromise doesn't expose past traffic. With TLS 1.2 static RSA key exchange, recorded traffic could be decrypted later.

questions.prompt: One IP address hosts many HTTPS domains, each with its own certificate. How does the server know which certificate to present?
options: From the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension in the ClientHello
From the Host header of the first HTTP request
From a reverse DNS lookup on the client's IP
From the destination TCP port
questions.explanation: The certificate is sent before any HTTP data, so the Host header is too late. SNI carries the hostname in the ClientHello so the server can choose the right certificate.

questions.prompt: A developer sets rejectUnauthorized: false in Node to call an internal service with a certificate signed by a private company CA. What is the better fix?
options: Trust the private CA explicitly via the 'ca' option or NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, keeping verification on
Switch the internal call to plain HTTP
Set NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 globally instead
Pin the server's IP address instead of checking the certificate
questions.explanation: Adding the private CA keeps full chain and hostname verification. Disabling verification, locally or globally, lets anyone on the path impersonate the service (man-in-the-middle).

questions.prompt: After the TLS handshake completes, how is the bulk application data encrypted?
options: With symmetric AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, using keys derived during the handshake
With a hash of each record and no encryption
With the server's RSA public key, one record at a time
With the certificate's signature algorithm
questions.explanation: Asymmetric cryptography is used for authentication and key agreement, then fast symmetric ciphers protect the data. Encrypting every record with RSA would be far too slow.

questions.prompt: Which checks does a client perform when validating a server certificate? Select all that apply.
options: The current time is within the certificate's validity period
The requested hostname matches a Subject Alternative Name
The chain leads to a trusted root CA
The certificate file is under a size limit set by the browser
questions.explanation: Clients verify the signature chain to a trusted root, hostname match and validity dates (and may check revocation). There is no size-based check.

questions.prompt: Your services use mutual TLS (mTLS) to talk to each other. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Certificate issuance and rotation should be automated, especially with short-lived certificates
mTLS removes the need for authorization checks in each service
Both sides authenticate each other with certificates
The server requests a certificate from the client during the handshake
questions.explanation: mTLS authenticates both peers and works best with automated, short-lived certificates. It establishes who the caller is, but services still need to decide what that caller may do.

questions.prompt: A TLS 1.3 full handshake takes one round trip before the client can send application data.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The client sends key shares in its ClientHello, so after the server's reply the client can send encrypted data, which takes 1 RTT. TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTTs.

questions.prompt: Certificate pinning has no operational downsides, which is why it is recommended for public websites.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Pinning can lock users out if keys rotate or a CA changes unexpectedly; browsers dropped HTTP Public Key Pinning for that reason. It's mostly used in controlled clients like mobile apps, with backup pins.

questions.prompt: A user enters https://example.com in a fresh browser with nothing cached. What is the order of the main network steps?
options: TLS handshake, DNS lookup, TCP handshake, HTTP request
HTTP request, DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake
DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP request, response
TCP handshake, DNS lookup, TLS handshake, HTTP request
questions.explanation: You need an IP (DNS) before connecting (TCP), and TLS runs over that connection before any HTTP can be sent. With HTTP/3, the TCP and TLS steps merge into the QUIC handshake.

questions.prompt: A user types example.com (no scheme), and example.com is on the browser's HSTS preload list. What does the browser do?
options: Shows a warning and asks the user to choose a scheme
Goes straight to https://example.com without ever sending a plain HTTP request
Tries HTTP and HTTPS in parallel and uses whichever responds first
Sends a plain HTTP request and follows the server's redirect to HTTPS
questions.explanation: HSTS, especially preloaded, makes the browser upgrade internally to HTTPS before any request, closing the window for SSL-stripping attacks on the first HTTP hop.

questions.prompt: A request goes from browser to CDN to load balancer to Node app. Where is TLS most commonly terminated first?
options: In the Node app only, because proxies can't handle TLS
At the edge, on the CDN or load balancer, optionally re-encrypting toward the origin
At the user's ISP
At the database, since the data is stored there
questions.explanation: Edges terminate TLS to cache, inspect and route HTTP; many setups re-encrypt to the origin for end-to-end protection. Proxies handle TLS routinely.

questions.prompt: The first request from a browser to your API takes 400 ms, but later ones take 60 ms. The server's processing time is constant. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The browser throttles the first request to save bandwidth
The first request pays for DNS, TCP and TLS setup; later requests reuse the connection and cached DNS
Later responses are served from the browser's disk cache
The server's JIT compiler warms up on the first request
questions.explanation: Connection setup adds several round trips for the first request; keep-alive or HTTP/2 connection reuse avoids them later. API responses are often not cacheable, and server time is stated as constant.

questions.prompt: JavaScript on app.example.com calls https://api.example.com with an Authorization header. DevTools shows an OPTIONS request before the real one. Why?
options: The TLS handshake uses OPTIONS to exchange certificates
It is a CORS preflight, triggered because the Authorization header makes the request non-simple
The server redirected the request to OPTIONS
Browsers send OPTIONS to measure latency before every HTTPS request
questions.explanation: Cross-origin requests with non-safelisted headers (like Authorization) or methods require a preflight so the server can approve them via Access-Control-Allow-* headers. TLS has nothing to do with HTTP methods.

questions.prompt: http://example.com redirects to https://example.com, which then redirects to https://www.example.com. What is the main cost and fix?
options: Each redirect adds round trips (and possibly a new connection); redirect straight to the final URL and use HSTS
Redirect responses can't be compressed; enable gzip
No cost, since redirects are handled locally by the browser
Redirects disable HTTP/2; switch to HTTP/1.1
questions.explanation: Every hop is a new request, and a different host can mean new DNS, TCP and TLS setup. Redirecting directly to the canonical URL, plus HSTS for the scheme, removes the extra hops.

questions.prompt: Your laptop resolves a server to an IP outside its local subnet. Which destination MAC address goes into the Ethernet frame?
options: The MAC address of the default gateway, learned via ARP
The DNS server's MAC address
The remote server's MAC address, learned via ARP across the internet
The broadcast MAC address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
questions.explanation: MAC addresses only matter on the local link. For off-subnet destinations, the host sends the frame to its gateway's MAC (resolved via ARP), while the IP header still carries the remote server's IP. ARP doesn't cross routers.

questions.prompt: Which caches can satisfy part of a request before it reaches your origin server? Select all that apply.
options: The OS or browser DNS cache
Your database's query cache
The browser's HTTP cache
A CDN edge cache
questions.explanation: Browser HTTP caches, DNS caches and CDN caches all sit in front of the origin. A database query cache lives behind the application, so the request has already reached your servers.

questions.prompt: An Express app behind a load balancer sees req.ip as the load balancer's address and req.protocol as 'http'. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The load balancer terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP, adding X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto
Disabling HTTP keep-alive makes req.ip show the real client
Trusting X-Forwarded-For from any source lets clients spoof their IP address
Configuring app.set('trust proxy', ...) makes Express use those forwarded headers
questions.explanation: Express ignores forwarded headers unless trust proxy is set, and it should only trust the known proxy hops, because clients can send their own fake X-Forwarded-For. Keep-alive has no effect on which IP is seen.

questions.prompt: If the browser has a cached copy that is still fresh (within max-age), it can use it without contacting the server.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Fresh responses are served directly from cache. Once stale, the browser revalidates with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since and may get a 304 Not Modified.

questions.prompt: The Host header is optional in HTTP/1.1 requests, because the destination IP address already identifies the website.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 requires Host, because one IP often serves many sites (virtual hosting); servers answer 400 if it is missing. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same information in the :authority pseudo-header.

questions.prompt: A dashboard needs one-way, server-to-client text updates over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnection built into the browser API. Which technology fits best?
options: Long polling
Server-Sent Events via EventSource
WebSockets
WebRTC data channels
questions.explanation: SSE streams text events over a normal HTTP response, and EventSource reconnects automatically. WebSockets are bidirectional but you have to implement reconnection yourself.

questions.prompt: How is a WebSocket connection established?
options: An HTTP/1.1 GET with 'Upgrade: websocket' headers, answered by '101 Switching Protocols'
A DNS SRV lookup followed by a UDP exchange
A separate TCP handshake on port 8080 with a custom protocol
A POST request whose response body stays open forever
questions.explanation: WebSockets start as an HTTP upgrade request on the same port (80/443), so they pass through HTTP infrastructure. After the 101 response, the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames.

questions.prompt: A chat app runs on 4 Node instances behind a load balancer, with WebSocket connections spread among them. User A (instance 1) messages user B (instance 3). What is needed?
options: Increasing the WebSocket frame size limit
Having B poll instance 1 every second
Sticky sessions alone, so A and B land on the same instance
A pub/sub backplane such as Redis that every instance subscribes to, so messages reach the instance holding B's socket
questions.explanation: Each instance only knows its own sockets, so cross-instance delivery needs a shared bus. Sticky sessions keep one user on one instance but can't put every pair of chatting users on the same instance.

questions.prompt: WebSocket connections behind a load balancer drop after exactly 60 seconds whenever no messages are sent. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: TCP itself closes idle connections after 60 seconds; switch to UDP
The proxy's idle timeout is closing them; send periodic ping/heartbeat frames or raise the timeout
The browser limits WebSocket lifetime to 60 seconds; reconnect each minute
The server runs out of file descriptors after 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Load balancers and proxies (such as nginx or cloud LBs) close connections that are idle past a timeout, often 60 seconds. Heartbeats keep the connection active. TCP has no default 60-second idle close.

questions.prompt: An SSE client reconnects after a brief network drop. How can it avoid missing events sent during the gap?
options: The client must open a WebSocket to fetch missed events
SSE guarantees delivery, so nothing is ever missed
The server includes an 'id:' field in each event; the browser sends Last-Event-ID on reconnect, and the server replays from there
Set the 'retry:' field to 0 so reconnection is instant
questions.explanation: EventSource remembers the last event id and sends it as the Last-Event-ID header when reconnecting, so a server that keeps a short buffer can resume. 'retry:' only controls the reconnect delay.

questions.prompt: How does long polling deliver near-real-time updates?
options: The client polls every 100 ms with short requests
The client opens one persistent bidirectional socket
The server pushes updates over UDP
The server holds each request open until data is available or a timeout passes, and the client immediately sends a new request
questions.explanation: Long polling parks the request until there's something to return, cutting latency compared with short polling while using plain HTTP. Each update still costs a full request/response cycle.

questions.prompt: Users who open your SSE dashboard in 7 tabs find the 7th tab hangs. The site is served over HTTP/1.1. Why?
options: Browsers limit HTTP/1.1 to about 6 connections per host, and each open SSE stream holds one
EventSource only allows one stream per browser
The server rejects more than 6 SSE clients per IP by protocol rule
SSE streams can't be opened in background tabs
questions.explanation: Each SSE stream occupies one HTTP/1.1 connection, and browsers cap connections per host around 6. Serving over HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one connection, or a shared worker can share one stream across tabs.

questions.prompt: When should you choose WebSockets over SSE? Select all that apply.
options: When only the server pushes text updates
When you want reconnection built into the browser API
When the client needs to send frequent low-latency messages on the same connection, as in a multiplayer game
When you need to send binary frames
