questions.explanation: WebSockets offer full-duplex messaging and binary frames. If only the server pushes text, SSE is simpler, and it's SSE (EventSource), not WebSocket, that has automatic reconnection built in.

questions.prompt: You need to support 1 million concurrent WebSocket connections. Which considerations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Raise file descriptor limits and budget memory per connection
Each connection needs its own OS thread in Node.js
Load balancers must support long-lived connections and suitable idle timeouts
Drain connections gracefully on deploys, and have clients reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a thundering herd
questions.explanation: Each socket uses a file descriptor and buffer memory, deploys must avoid mass simultaneous reconnects, and proxies must allow long-lived connections. Node's event loop handles many sockets on one thread, without a thread per connection.

questions.prompt: The browser's EventSource API lets the client send messages to the server over the same SSE connection.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: SSE is one-way, from server to client. The client sends data with separate HTTP requests (e.g. fetch POST); use WebSockets if you need two-way messaging on one connection.

questions.prompt: Under the WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455), frames sent from client to server must be masked.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Clients mask every frame with a random key so attackers can't craft bytes that poison intermediary caches. Server-to-client frames are not masked.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with this plain http server handler?
options: req.body doesn't exist; the body must be read from the req stream
res.end can't accept a string, only a Buffer
listen(3000) must be called before createServer
JSON.parse must be awaited because req.body is a promise
questions.explanation: With the bare http module, req is a Readable stream; there's no parsed body. You collect 'data' chunks (or for await over req), Buffer.concat them on 'end', then parse. req.body is something body-parsing middleware in frameworks adds, and it isn't a promise.

questions.prompt: A raw http server collects all request chunks into an array before parsing. What's the main risk, and the fix?
options: Chunks may arrive out of order; sort them by sequence number first
Chunks are strings, so binary uploads get corrupted; set req.setEncoding('binary')
The array is shared across requests; move it to module scope
A client can send a huge body and exhaust memory; count bytes and reject with 413 past a limit
questions.explanation: Unbounded buffering lets one client allocate gigabytes. Track the running byte count (and check Content-Length up front), and respond 413 and destroy the request once it exceeds your limit. TCP delivers chunks in order, and chunks are Buffers unless you set an encoding.

questions.prompt: A handler writes data with res.write() but never calls res.end(). What does the client see?
options: Node calls res.end() automatically after one second
The response completes as soon as the handler function returns
The request hangs until a client or server timeout closes it
The server crashes with ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END
questions.explanation: The response stays open until res.end() is called; returning from the handler doesn't finish it. The client waits for more data until something times out. WRITE_AFTER_END is the opposite mistake: writing after end().

questions.prompt: Code calls res.write('partial') and then res.setHeader('X-Trace', id). What happens?
options: The header is silently merged into the body
The header is buffered and sent with res.end()
It throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT, because the first write flushed the headers
The header is added to the next response on the same connection
questions.explanation: The first write() sends the status line and headers, so changing headers afterwards throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. Set all headers (or call writeHead) before writing any body. This is the same error Express reports as 'Cannot set headers after they are sent'.

questions.prompt: A Node service behind a load balancer with a 60 s idle timeout returns intermittent 502s on reused connections. Node's server.keepAliveTimeout is the default 5 s. What's the likely cause?
options: The 60 s timeout makes the load balancer drop every request after 5 s
Node closes idle keep-alive sockets before the load balancer does, so it reuses dead ones
The load balancer can't speak HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with Node at all
Node's thread pool is exhausted by idle connections
questions.explanation: Node closes the idle socket at 5 s; the balancer still thinks it's open and sends a request into it, getting a reset and returning 502. Set keepAliveTimeout above the balancer's idle timeout (and headersTimeout above that). Idle sockets don't use the thread pool.

questions.prompt: A raw http router uses `if (req.url === '/users')`, but GET /users?page=2 falls through to 404. What's the proper fix?
options: Read the path from the Host header instead of req.url
Compare with req.path instead, which excludes the query string
Use req.url.startsWith('/users') for every route
Parse with new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost') and compare url.pathname
questions.explanation: req.url is the raw request target, path plus query string. new URL() with a base splits it into pathname and searchParams. req.path only exists in Express, and startsWith would also match '/users-admin'.

questions.prompt: On SIGTERM a service calls server.close(callback). What does server.close() do?
options: Closes the database pool and then exits the process
Pauses the server until a SIGCONT signal resumes it
Stops accepting new connections and calls back once existing connections end
Immediately destroys every open connection, including in-flight requests
questions.explanation: close() stops listening and waits for open connections to finish before its callback fires, which is the basis of graceful shutdown. Idle keep-alive sockets can delay it, so modern Node offers closeIdleConnections()/closeAllConnections(). It knows nothing about your DB pool.

questions.prompt: Which statements about http.IncomingMessage (req) in a plain http server are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Header names in req.headers are lower-cased
It is a Readable stream carrying the request body
req.method is a string such as 'GET' or 'POST'
req.query contains the parsed query string
questions.explanation: Node lower-cases header names, req is a Readable for the body, and req.method is the verb string. req.query is an Express addition; with plain http you parse the query yourself via URL/URLSearchParams.

questions.prompt: Which server settings help defend a raw Node http server against slowloris-style attacks that trickle headers slowly? Select all that apply.
options: Setting server.timeout = 0 to disable socket timeouts
server.headersTimeout
server.requestTimeout
Raising maxHeaderSize to 1 MB
questions.explanation: headersTimeout bounds how long receiving headers may take, and requestTimeout bounds the whole request; both cut off clients that drip bytes. Bigger header limits and disabling timeouts make slow clients more effective at tying up sockets.

questions.prompt: res.end() can be given a final chunk of data, e.g. res.end(JSON.stringify(obj)).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: res.end(data) writes the chunk and finishes the response in one call, equivalent to res.write(data) followed by res.end().

questions.prompt: The http module automatically sets Content-Type: application/json when you res.end() a JSON string.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Node doesn't inspect the body, so it never infers a Content-Type. Without setting it yourself, clients may treat the response as text. Frameworks like Express set it for you in res.json().

questions.prompt: With these Express routes, which handler serves GET /users/me?
questions.code:
app.get('/users/:id', getUser);
app.get('/users/me', getMe);
options: getUser, with req.params.id === 'me'
Neither; Express throws on ambiguous routes
Both, getUser first and then getMe
getMe, because static segments always beat parameters
questions.explanation: Express matches routes in registration order and stops at the first one that sends a response. '/users/:id' matches 'me' first. Register '/users/me' before the parameterized route. Express doesn't rank static segments higher like some routers do.

questions.prompt: In Express 5, an async route handler throws (its promise rejects). What happens?
options: The rejection is passed to next(err) and reaches error-handling middleware
Express retries the handler once before responding 500
The process crashes because Express doesn't catch async errors
The request hangs and an unhandledRejection is logged
questions.explanation: Express 5 handles rejected promises from handlers and middleware by calling next(err). Express 4 didn't, so a rejection there left the request hanging unless you wrapped handlers or used express-async-errors.

questions.prompt: An error-handling middleware is registered with app.use() before all the routes. Route errors aren't reaching it. Why?
options: Error handlers need app.error() instead of app.use()
Express only calls error handlers for 404 responses
Error handlers only catch errors thrown inside other middleware
Error handlers must be registered after the routes whose errors they handle
questions.explanation: next(err) skips forward to the next error-handling middleware in the stack. A handler registered earlier is already behind the route, so Express falls back to its default handler. Put error middleware last.

questions.prompt: A router is mounted with app.use('/api', router). Inside a router handler for GET /api/users, what is req.originalUrl?
options: 'users'
'/api/users'
'/users'
'/api'
questions.explanation: Inside a mounted router, req.url and req.path are relative ('/users') and req.baseUrl is '/api', but req.originalUrl keeps the full original path '/api/users'. Use originalUrl for logging and redirects.

questions.prompt: What's the bug in this auth middleware?
options: Middleware must be declared async before it is allowed to send a response itself
res.status() must be chained after res.json(), so the 401 status is never applied
Header names are case-sensitive, so it must read req.headers.Authorization instead
Missing return: next() still runs after the 401, so a later handler responds again
questions.explanation: Sending a response doesn't stop the function. next() runs anyway, the route executes unauthenticated, and its response attempt throws 'Cannot set headers after they are sent'. Use return res.status(401).json(...). Node lower-cases header names, so 'authorization' is correct.

questions.prompt: A client posting a 2 MB JSON body to an Express app using express.json() gets 413 Payload Too Large. Why?
options: The client must switch to multipart/form-data for any JSON body larger than 1 MB
Node's http module caps all request bodies at 1 MB
express.json() has a default limit of 100kb; raise it with { limit }
Express rejects every JSON body larger than 1 MB by HTTP spec
questions.explanation: body-parser's JSON parser defaults to limit: '100kb'. Raise it per route (express.json({ limit: '5mb' })) only where needed, keeping a small global limit to limit abuse. Node itself imposes no body size cap.

questions.prompt: In a POST handler, req.body is undefined. What's the most likely cause?
options: Express only populates req.body for PUT and PATCH requests, never for POST
express.json() isn't registered before the route, or Content-Type isn't JSON
The handler must call await req.body() first, because the body is read lazily
req.body is only populated inside error-handling middleware with four arguments
questions.explanation: Express doesn't parse bodies by default. express.json() must run before the route and only parses requests whose Content-Type matches application/json. A mismatched header leaves req.body unset (or {} in Express 4).

questions.prompt: Which behaviours belong in a well-designed Express error-handling middleware? Select all that apply.
options: Call next() after sending so later middleware can run
Log the error with the request ID
Delegate to next(err) if res.headersSent is already true
Map known error types to appropriate status codes
Hide stack traces from clients in production
questions.explanation: A central error handler maps errors to statuses, logs with correlation IDs, avoids leaking internals, and hands off to Express's default handler if headers were already sent (e.g. a stream failed midway). Calling next() after responding risks a double response.

questions.prompt: Which middleware should usually be registered before your route handlers? Select all that apply.
options: The error-handling middleware
The 404 catch-all handler
Authentication for protected routers
Body parsing such as express.json()
Request ID and request logging
questions.explanation: Logging, request IDs, parsing and auth must run before handlers that rely on them. The 404 handler goes after all routes (it handles requests nothing matched), and the error handler goes last.

questions.prompt: app.use(fn) without a path runs fn for every request, whatever the HTTP method.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: app.use mounts middleware at '/' for all methods, so it sees every request that reaches that point in the stack. Method-specific handlers use app.get, app.post and so on.

questions.prompt: In Express 4, a rejected promise from an async route handler is automatically forwarded to error middleware.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Express 4 ignores returned promises, so a rejection becomes an unhandledRejection and the request hangs. You needed try/catch with next(err), a wrapper, or express-async-errors. Express 5 added automatic forwarding.

questions.prompt: Injecting UsersService (declared in UsersModule) into OrdersService fails with "Nest can't resolve dependencies". What's the fix?
options: Mark OrdersService with @Injectable({ global: true })
Export UsersService from UsersModule and import UsersModule in OrdersModule
Instantiate UsersService manually with new inside the OrdersService constructor
Add UsersService to OrdersModule's controllers array
questions.explanation: Providers are private to their module unless exported, and a consuming module must import the exporting module. Listing a service under controllers is wrong, and new bypasses DI (and the service's own dependencies).

questions.prompt: What is the default scope of a NestJS provider?
options: Transient: a new instance for every consumer that injects it
Request: a new instance for every incoming request
Module: one instance per importing module
Singleton: one instance shared across the whole application
questions.explanation: By default Nest creates one instance at startup and shares it everywhere, which is efficient and fine for stateless services. Request and transient scopes are opt-in. There's no per-module scope.

questions.prompt: You mark a logging provider as Scope.REQUEST to attach a request ID. What's a significant side effect?
options: It can no longer be injected into controllers, only into other providers
Everything that depends on it also becomes request-scoped, adding per-request cost
Nothing else changes; only that one provider is recreated for each request
Nest caches the instance per authenticated user ID rather than per request
questions.explanation: Request scope bubbles up the injection chain: anything that depends on it must be created per request too, which costs latency and memory under load. Alternatives include AsyncLocalStorage-based context (e.g. nestjs-cls) or passing the ID explicitly.

questions.prompt: In what order does a NestJS request pass through these components?
options: Middleware → guards → interceptors (before) → pipes → handler
Guards → middleware → pipes → interceptors → handler
Interceptors → middleware → guards → handler → pipes
Pipes → guards → middleware → handler → interceptors
questions.explanation: Middleware runs first, then guards decide whether to proceed, interceptors wrap the call, pipes validate and transform arguments, and the handler runs; interceptors see the response on the way out and exception filters handle thrown errors. Guards come after middleware.

questions.prompt: Which NestJS building block is designed for validating and transforming incoming parameters such as a DTO body?
options: Guards
Exception filters
Interceptors
Pipes
questions.explanation: Pipes (e.g. ValidationPipe, ParseIntPipe) operate on handler arguments to validate or transform them. Guards answer 'may this request proceed?' (authn/authz), filters format errors, and interceptors wrap execution for cross-cutting concerns like caching or timing.

questions.prompt: You need to provide a database client that is built asynchronously from values in ConfigService. Which provider definition fits?
options: { provide: 'DB', useClass: ConfigService, inject: [ConfigService] }
{ provide: 'DB', useFactory: async (cfg: ConfigService) => createClient(cfg.get('DB_URL')), inject: [ConfigService] }
{ provide: 'DB', useExisting: ConfigService, scope: Scope.REQUEST }
{ provide: 'DB', useValue: await createClient(ConfigService), inject: [ConfigService] }
questions.explanation: useFactory can be async and declares its dependencies via inject; Nest awaits the factory before the app starts. useValue needs an already-built value (here it would pass the class, not an instance), useClass would instantiate ConfigService, and useExisting just aliases another token.

questions.prompt: A constructor parameter typed as an interface, `constructor(private repo: UserRepo)`, fails to inject. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Nest can only inject classes declared in the same module, never shared interfaces
Interfaces must also be decorated with @Injectable(), exactly like classes
Interfaces are erased at runtime, leaving no token; inject with @Inject(TOKEN)
Constructor parameter properties must be public for Nest to inject them
questions.explanation: Nest reads constructor parameter types from emitted decorator metadata, and interfaces don't exist in JavaScript output. Register the implementation under a token (e.g. { provide: USER_REPO, useClass: PgUserRepo }) and inject with @Inject(USER_REPO), or use an abstract class as the token.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid NestJS custom provider forms? Select all that apply.
options: useExisting
useRequest
useClass
useValue
useFactory
questions.explanation: Nest supports class providers (useClass), value providers (useValue), factory providers (useFactory), and alias providers (useExisting). There's no useRequest; request scoping is set via the scope option.

questions.prompt: OrdersService and PaymentsService inject each other, and Nest reports a circular dependency. Which are reasonable fixes? Select all that apply.
options: Mark both modules with @Global()
Extract the shared logic into a third provider both depend on
Use forwardRef(() => OtherService) on both sides
Make both services request-scoped
questions.explanation: forwardRef lets Nest resolve the cycle lazily, but extracting shared logic usually fixes the design smell. Changing scope or making modules global doesn't remove the cycle in the dependency graph.

questions.prompt: NestJS uses Express as its HTTP platform by default and can switch to Fastify through an adapter.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: @nestjs/platform-express is the default; @nestjs/platform-fastify with FastifyAdapter swaps the underlying HTTP layer while controllers and providers stay the same (platform-specific middleware aside).

questions.prompt: In NestJS, exception filters run before guards, so they can stop unauthorized requests early.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Exception filters handle errors thrown during the request pipeline, after the fact. Guards perform authorization checks before the handler; when a guard denies access it throws ForbiddenException, which a filter then turns into a response.

questions.prompt: What does `schema.safeParse(input)` return in zod when the input is invalid?
options: It throws a ZodError just like parse()
The input unchanged, with an errors array attached
undefined, so you must check the return value for null
{ success: false, error: ZodError } without throwing
questions.explanation: safeParse never throws; it returns a discriminated union: { success: true, data } or { success: false, error }. parse() throws a ZodError on failure. safeParse fits request handlers where you want to turn issues into a 400 response.

questions.prompt: What does this return?
questions.code: z.object({ name: z.string() }).parse({ name: 'Ada', isAdmin: true });
options: { name: 'Ada', isAdmin: true }
It throws because isAdmin isn't in the schema
{ name: 'Ada' }
{ name: 'Ada', isAdmin: undefined }
questions.explanation: zod object schemas strip unknown keys by default, so the parsed result omits isAdmin. Use .strict() to reject unknown keys or .passthrough() to keep them. That's why you should use the parsed result, not the raw req.body.

questions.prompt: A PATCH /users/:id handler validates with a schema but then runs db.users.update(id, req.body). A user sets "role": "admin" on themselves. What's the root cause?
options: Mass assignment: the raw body was saved instead of the parsed, whitelisted data
The database should have rejected unknown columns, so the ORM must be misconfigured
The schema typed role as z.string() rather than a z.enum() of allowed roles
PATCH bodies are partial, so they can't be validated the way PUT bodies are
questions.explanation: Validation only protects you if you use its output. Persisting req.body lets clients set any field the model has. Pass only the parsed data (which strips unknown keys) and keep privileged fields like role out of user-editable schemas.

questions.prompt: A query schema uses page: z.number(), and GET /items?page=2 fails validation. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Query values are strings; use z.coerce.number() (with .int().min(1))
zod can't validate query strings, only JSON bodies
The page value must be sent in a header instead
z.number() only accepts floats, so integer values like 2 need z.int() instead
questions.explanation: URL query parameters always arrive as strings ('2'), so z.number() rejects them. z.coerce.number() converts first, then you can add .int() and bounds. zod validates any value, wherever it came from.

questions.prompt: A handler does `const input = req.body as CreateUserDto;`. What does this protect against at runtime?
options: Nothing: a type assertion is erased and performs no check
Unknown fields, which are stripped by the compiler
Wrong types, which throw a TypeError when accessed
Missing required fields, which TypeScript rejects at runtime
questions.explanation: TypeScript types vanish in the compiled JavaScript, and 'as' just tells the compiler to trust you. Untrusted input needs runtime validation (zod, joi, class-validator) at the boundary.

questions.prompt: Why do teams use `type CreateUser = z.infer<typeof CreateUserSchema>` instead of writing a separate interface?
options: Plain interfaces can't be used to type Express request handlers' bodies
The schema is the single source of truth, so type and validation can't drift
z.infer also generates the matching database migration from the schema
z.infer makes zod run its validation at compile time rather than at runtime
questions.explanation: Deriving the static type from the runtime schema keeps them in sync: change the schema and the type updates. A hand-written interface can silently diverge. Validation still runs at runtime.

questions.prompt: A filter schema uses active: z.coerce.boolean(). What is `active` for GET /users?active=false?
options: undefined
Validation fails with an error
true
false
questions.explanation: z.coerce.boolean() applies JavaScript's Boolean(), and any non-empty string, including 'false', is truthy. Use an explicit transform, e.g. z.enum(['true','false']).transform(v => v === 'true'), or zod 4's z.stringbool().

questions.prompt: Which are good practices for request validation in an API? Select all that apply.
options: Rely on frontend validation so the backend can skip it
Reject unknown fields on write endpoints where strictness matters
Validate params, query and body, not just the body
Return 400 (or 422) with field-level error messages
Include the server stack trace in the validation error response
questions.explanation: Clear 4xx responses with per-field issues, validating every input source, and strict schemas for writes are standard. Stack traces leak internals, and frontend checks are trivially bypassed with curl.

questions.prompt: Which checks need more than schema validation and belong in the service layer? Select all that apply.
options: The coupon code hasn't expired
Quantity is a positive integer
The date string is valid ISO 8601
The email isn't already registered
The user owns the order they are trying to cancel
questions.explanation: Uniqueness, ownership and expiry depend on database state or business rules, so they're checked in services. Shape and format rules like positive integers or ISO dates are what schemas are for.

questions.prompt: Both joi and zod validate data at runtime, but zod also infers static TypeScript types from the schema.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Both run checks at runtime. zod was built TypeScript-first, and z.infer gives you the type for free; with joi you typically maintain types separately or use extra tooling.

questions.prompt: Validating that a field is a valid email with z.string().email() means you no longer need parameterized SQL queries for that field.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Format validation and injection safety are separate layers, and many valid email addresses can contain quotes or other special characters. Always use parameterized queries; validation is defence in depth, not a replacement.

questions.prompt: With refresh-token rotation, an already-used (rotated) refresh token is presented again. What should the server do?
options: Treat it as theft: revoke the whole token family and force a re-login
Issue a new access token but withhold a new refresh token this time
Reject only this request but keep the newest token in the family valid
Accept it, since its signature is valid and it hasn't expired yet
questions.explanation: Rotation issues a new refresh token on every use, so a reused old one means two parties hold it, one possibly an attacker. Revoking the whole family limits the damage. Accepting it defeats the purpose of rotation.

questions.prompt: For a browser app, where is the safest place to keep a refresh token?
options: An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie scoped to the refresh endpoint
localStorage, so it survives page reloads
sessionStorage, because it's cleared automatically whenever the tab is closed
A global JavaScript variable in the SPA bundle
questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies can't be read by JavaScript, so an XSS bug can't exfiltrate the token; Secure and SameSite plus a narrow Path reduce exposure further. localStorage and sessionStorage are fully readable by any injected script.

questions.prompt: You move from bearer tokens in an Authorization header to session cookies. Which attack must you now explicitly address?
options: SQL injection
Timing attacks on password comparison
Brute-forcing the bcrypt hash
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
questions.explanation: Browsers attach cookies automatically to cross-site requests, so another site can trigger authenticated actions. Mitigate with SameSite=Lax/Strict plus CSRF tokens or origin checks. Bearer headers set by your JS aren't sent automatically, which is why CSRF matters less there.

questions.prompt: A service verifies RS256 JWTs with jwt.verify(token, publicKey) and doesn't specify allowed algorithms. What's the risk?
options: Token expiry (exp) is ignored unless an algorithms list is also supplied
Algorithm confusion: a token signed with HS256 using the public key may verify
None; every library infers RS256 from the key type, so nothing can go wrong
Verification falls back to a slow path that is too expensive in production
questions.explanation: If the library trusts the token's alg header, an HS256 token signed with the (public) key may verify, as happened in older libraries, and 'none' is a related attack. Always pin algorithms: ['RS256']. Expiry checks are separate from the alg setting.

questions.prompt: A developer puts a user's address and internal flags into a JWT payload, saying "it's signed, so it's private". What's wrong?
options: The payload is just base64url-encoded; anyone with the token can read it
JWT payloads may only contain string claims, so nested objects get dropped
Signing fails outright when the payload contains personal data like addresses
Nothing; signing a JWT also encrypts its payload, so the data stays private
questions.explanation: A JWS signature proves integrity, not confidentiality; the payload decodes with a single base64 call. Keep tokens to minimal claims (sub, roles, exp), or use JWE if you truly need encrypted contents.

questions.prompt: You raise the bcrypt cost factor from 10 to 12. Roughly how does hashing time change?
options: About 20% slower
About 100x slower
About 4x slower
About 2x slower
questions.explanation: The cost is a log2 work factor: each +1 doubles the rounds, so +2 is ~4x. Pick a cost so a hash takes roughly a few hundred milliseconds on your hardware, and remember async bcrypt runs on the thread pool.

questions.prompt: Why can bcrypt be a problem for very long passphrases?
options: bcrypt rejects any password longer than 32 characters
bcrypt hashing time grows exponentially with each extra character of password length
bcrypt stores long passwords in plaintext alongside the hash
bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of input, silently ignoring the rest
questions.explanation: bcrypt truncates input at 72 bytes, so two passphrases sharing the first 72 bytes produce the same hash. Cap input length explicitly, or use Argon2id (OWASP's current first choice), which has no such limit. bcrypt's time depends on the cost factor, not length.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of server-side sessions over long-lived stateless JWTs? Select all that apply.
options: Sessions can be revoked instantly by deleting them
No session store lookup is needed on each request
The cookie only carries a small opaque ID
Role changes take effect on the next request
They scale horizontally without any shared state
questions.explanation: Because state lives on the server, you can revoke sessions or change permissions immediately, and the cookie stays small. The trade-off is a store lookup per request and shared state (e.g. Redis) across instances, which is what stateless JWTs avoid.

questions.prompt: An app uses short-lived JWT access tokens and refresh tokens. Which steps make a proper logout? Select all that apply.
options: Revoke or delete the refresh token server-side
Rotate the global signing key
Clear the auth cookies on the client
Delete the access token from the server's JWT table
Optionally denylist the access token's jti until it expires
questions.explanation: Revoking the refresh token stops new access tokens, clearing cookies removes local copies, and a short-lived jti denylist covers the remaining access-token lifetime if needed. Stateless JWTs aren't stored server-side, and rotating the signing key would log everyone out.

questions.prompt: A bcrypt hash string embeds its salt and cost factor, so you don't need to store the salt in a separate column.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A hash like $2b$12$<22-char salt><31-char hash> contains the algorithm version, cost and salt. bcrypt.compare reads them from the stored string to recompute and compare.

questions.prompt: Comparing a submitted API key to the stored one with === is safe because string comparison time leaks nothing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: === can return as soon as a byte differs, so response timing can leak how much of a guess is right. Hash both values and compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual (equal-length Buffers), and store API keys hashed.

questions.prompt: A serverless API creates a pg Pool (max 10) per function instance. During a traffic spike Postgres starts refusing connections. Why?
options: Postgres blocks bursts of connections from IP addresses it hasn't seen before
Serverless functions can't hold TCP connections at all
Hundreds of instances × 10 connections exceed Postgres max_connections
pg Pools leak one connection per invocation by design
questions.explanation: Each concurrent instance holds its own pool, so 200 instances × 10 = 2,000 connections against a default max_connections of 100. Use an external pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy, a provider's pooled URL) and a pool max of 1-2 per instance.

questions.prompt: After running for a while, requests hang forever waiting on the database. What's the bug?
options: The client is never released, so the pool runs out of connections
pool.connect() must be called once at startup only
res.json can't serialize rows from pg
LIMIT 50 is too large for pooled connections
questions.explanation: pool.connect() checks out a client that you must return with client.release(), ideally in finally. Each request leaks one, and once max is reached connect() waits forever (or until connectionTimeoutMillis). For single queries, pool.query() handles checkout and release for you.

questions.prompt: Why is this transaction broken with node-postgres?
options: pool.query auto-commits every statement, so the final COMMIT throws an error
Postgres doesn't allow UPDATE statements inside explicit BEGIN/COMMIT blocks
BEGIN, the updates and COMMIT must all be sent together in one query string
Each pool.query may run on a different connection, so it's not one transaction
questions.explanation: Transactions are per connection. pool.query checks out any free client per call, so BEGIN, the updates and COMMIT can land on different connections. Use const c = await pool.connect(), run everything on c, ROLLBACK on error, and release in finally.

questions.prompt: 20 app instances each raise their Postgres pool max from 10 to 200 "for more throughput". What's the likely result?
options: Postgres queues the extra connections in memory at essentially no cost
Throughput scales roughly 20x, since many more queries can run in parallel
Limits are exceeded and extra backends contend for CPU and locks, cutting throughput
Nothing changes, because node-postgres never opens more than 10 connections
questions.explanation: 4,000 connections would far exceed typical max_connections, and each Postgres connection is a process using memory. Past a modest number of active connections (a few per core), contention reduces throughput. Small pools plus a queue usually perform better.

questions.prompt: How should a Node service manage its MongoDB connection with the official driver?
options: Create one MongoClient at startup and reuse it; it maintains its own pool
Create a new MongoClient and connect inside every request handler
Connect once per minute on a timer and close in between
Open one client per collection so queries on different collections don't block each other
questions.explanation: MongoClient manages a connection pool (maxPoolSize, default 100), so a single shared instance handles concurrent requests. Connecting per request adds handshake latency and can exhaust server connections.

questions.prompt: What's the performance problem in this Prisma code, and the usual fix?
options: N+1 queries (101 round-trips); load authors via include or one findMany with id in
The loop fires 100 queries in parallel, overloading the connection pool
findUnique bypasses indexes, so an extra index on users.id is required
findMany is inherently slow, so every query should be rewritten as raw SQL
questions.explanation: The loop issues one query per post sequentially, so latency grows with N. Loading the relation via include, or batching all author IDs in a single where: { id: { in: ids } }, takes one or two queries. The awaits are sequential, not parallel, and the primary key is already indexed.

questions.prompt: Users submit an email to look up their account. Which query is safe from SQL injection?
options: pool.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)
prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ${email}`
prisma.$queryRawUnsafe(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)
pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + JSON.stringify(email))
questions.explanation: $queryRaw used as a tagged template turns interpolated values into bound parameters. Plain template strings, $queryRawUnsafe with interpolation, and JSON.stringify concatenation all splice input into SQL text. With pg, use pool.query('... WHERE email = $1', [email]).

questions.prompt: A team needs complex reporting queries with CTEs and window functions and still wants type safety. Which approach usually fits best?
options: Store report results in MongoDB to avoid writing SQL
Load the whole tables into Node and aggregate them in JavaScript with typed helpers
Force everything through an ORM's high-level model API
A typed query builder like Kysely, or typed raw SQL for the hardest queries
questions.explanation: Query builders stay close to SQL while typing results, and raw SQL escape hatches cover anything else. ORM model APIs are great for CRUD but awkward for advanced SQL. Aggregating in Node moves huge data over the wire.

questions.prompt: Which statements about node-postgres's Pool are correct? Select all that apply.
options: You should attach a pool.on('error') listener for errors on idle clients
pool.query() checks out a client, runs the query and releases it automatically
A pool with max: 10 can run 50 queries at once on the server
Idle clients are reused for later queries instead of reconnecting
questions.explanation: Pools reuse connections, pool.query handles checkout and release, and an idle client error without a listener is emitted as an unhandled 'error' that can crash the process. With max: 10 at most 10 queries run concurrently; the rest wait in the pool's queue.

questions.prompt: Which practices help when running Node serverless functions against Postgres? Select all that apply.
options: Open a new Client per query and never close it
Create the pool outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it
Put an external pooler such as PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the database
Keep the per-instance pool max very low (1-2)
questions.explanation: An external pooler multiplexes many short-lived instances over few server connections, low per-instance limits cap the total, and module-scope pools survive across warm invocations. Unclosed clients leak connections until Postgres refuses new ones.

questions.prompt: PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode transparently supports session state such as SET search_path or session advisory locks across a client's transactions.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: In transaction mode a client may get a different server connection for each transaction, so session-level state (SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN, and traditionally named prepared statements) doesn't carry over. Use transaction-scoped equivalents or session mode.

questions.prompt: A test starts the Express app with supertest and talks to a real Postgres running in Docker. What kind of test is this?
options: An integration test
A contract test
A load test
A unit test
questions.explanation: It exercises several real components together (HTTP layer, handlers, real database), which is integration testing. Unit tests isolate one function with its collaborators replaced; contract tests check API agreements between services; load tests measure performance.

questions.prompt: In Vitest, a test file calls vi.mock('./mailer') below its import statements, yet the code under test still gets the mock. Why?
options: vi.mock calls are hoisted to the top of the file, before imports run
Imports are lazy in Vitest, so they load on first use
vi.mock patches the module cache retroactively at runtime
Vitest silently re-runs the whole file twice, applying the mocks on the second pass
questions.explanation: Vitest (like Jest) hoists vi.mock to the top of the module so the mock is registered before any import executes. That's also why variables used in the factory must be created with vi.hoisted or defined inside the factory.

questions.prompt: Why do many Express codebases put `export const app = express()` in app.ts and call app.listen() in a separate server.ts?
options: TypeScript can't compile listen() and route definitions in the same module
Express requires listen() to be called from a different file than routes
Splitting the files lets the app run across multiple CPU cores automatically
Tests import the app and drive it via supertest without binding a fixed port
questions.explanation: supertest accepts an app (or http.Server) and binds an ephemeral port itself, so importing the app without side effects avoids port conflicts and leftover servers in parallel test runs. It has nothing to do with multi-core or TypeScript limitations.

questions.prompt: Integration tests pass alone but fail randomly when run in parallel. They share one test database. What's the most likely cause and fix?
options: Parallel tests share memory, so fixtures should be stored on globalThis instead
Vitest is unreliable with databases, so parallelism must be disabled forever
Tests interfere via shared rows; isolate each worker's DB/schema or roll back
The database is too slow, so add sleeps before assertions to let writes land
questions.explanation: Concurrent tests insert, delete and count the same rows, so results depend on timing. Give each worker its own database or schema, or wrap each test in a transaction that's rolled back. Sleeps only hide races, and fully serial runs give up speed.

questions.prompt: You need to test that a retry helper waits 1 s, 2 s, then 4 s between attempts, without the test taking 7 seconds. What's the standard approach?
options: Run the test in a worker thread so it finishes faster
Set the test timeout to 10 seconds and wait it out
Use vi.useFakeTimers() and advance time with vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()
Mock Math.random so the delays are zero
questions.explanation: Fake timers replace setTimeout and Date, letting the test advance virtual time instantly and assert attempts at each step. The async variant also flushes promises between timers. Waiting in real time makes tests slow and flaky.

questions.prompt: A test suite mocks every collaborator of every module, and all tests pass, yet production breaks when two modules are wired together. What's the core problem?
options: Each test has too few assertions, so add more expect() calls to every test
Unit tests must always run against a full copy of real production data to be valid
Mocks should never be used at all; every test must hit real dependencies
Over-mocking: the tests check assumptions about collaborators, not real behaviour
questions.explanation: When mocks encode what you think dependencies do, tests can stay green while the real integration breaks. Mock at true boundaries (network, clock, randomness) and add integration tests for wiring. Banning mocks entirely is the opposite extreme.

questions.prompt: What does vi.spyOn(obj, 'method') do by default?
options: Deletes the method so calls throw an error
Copies obj so the original object is untouched
Replaces the method with a function that returns undefined
Wraps the method to record calls while still running the original implementation
questions.explanation: A spy records calls, arguments and results, and calls through to the real method unless you add .mockImplementation() or .mockReturnValue(). vi.fn() is a standalone mock that returns undefined by default.

questions.prompt: In unit tests for an order service, which dependencies are typically worth mocking or faking? Select all that apply.
options: The third-party payment API client
The current time
Built-in Array methods
Random ID generation
The pure price-calculation function being tested
questions.explanation: External services, the clock and randomness make tests slow, flaky or non-deterministic, so they're replaced. The function under test must run for real, and mocking language built-ins tests nothing useful.

questions.prompt: In Vitest, which assertions correctly check that async function fn() rejects with 'boom'? Select all that apply.
options: expect(fn()).rejects.toThrow('boom') with no await or return
return expect(fn()).rejects.toThrow('boom')
expect(() => fn()).toThrow('boom')
await expect(fn()).rejects.toThrow('boom')
questions.explanation: .rejects returns a promise, so the test must await or return it, otherwise the test can finish before the assertion settles. toThrow on () => fn() checks for a synchronous throw, but an async function returns a rejected promise instead of throwing.

questions.prompt: supertest can test an Express app without you calling app.listen() yourself.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: request(app) wraps the app in an http server bound to an ephemeral port and closes it after the request, so tests needn't manage ports or servers.

questions.prompt: 100% line coverage guarantees the code has no bugs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Coverage only shows lines were executed, not that the right things were asserted or that every input combination or edge case was tested. A test with no assertions can still produce full coverage.

questions.prompt: A missing DATABASE_URL in production was only discovered when the first request crashed. What's the better pattern?
options: Catch the error in the handler and return 503 until someone notices the alert
Validate env vars with a schema at boot and exit with a clear error if invalid
Read process.env lazily inside each handler, right at the point where the value is needed
Default DATABASE_URL to localhost so the app can always start successfully
questions.explanation: Fail fast: parse process.env once at boot (e.g. with zod) into a typed config object, so a bad deploy fails health checks immediately instead of in user traffic. Silent localhost defaults can make production talk to the wrong database.

questions.prompt: How should .env files be handled in a Git repository?
options: Commit .env but base64-encode the values so they're not readable
Keep .env in a public gist and link to it from the README file
Commit .env so every developer gets the real working secrets
Ignore .env and commit a .env.example with placeholder values
questions.explanation: Secrets must never enter version control, since history is forever and widely copied. .env.example documents what's required without real values. Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

questions.prompt: process.env values are strings. This simulates it with a plain object. What does it print?
questions.code:
const env = { FEATURE_X: 'false', PORT: '3000' };
console.log(Boolean(env.FEATURE_X), env.PORT + 1, Number(env.PORT) + 1);
questions.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, so 'false' becomes true, a classic feature-flag bug. String + number concatenates ('30001'). Parse explicitly: env.FEATURE_X === 'true' and Number(env.PORT), ideally via a schema at startup.

questions.prompt: At startup a service logs its full config object for debugging. What's the main risk?
options: The logger mutates the config object while it serializes it to JSON
Secrets like DB passwords and API keys land in widely readable log storage
Serializing a large object blocks the event loop for several seconds
Logged config values become frozen and read-only for the rest of runtime
questions.explanation: Logs are shipped to aggregators, retained for a long time and accessed by many people and tools, so secrets in them count as leaked. Log only non-secret keys or use logger redaction. A one-time config log won't meaningfully block the loop.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you bake the production .env into your Docker image?
options: Environment variables are ignored inside containers unless set at build time
Docker images can't contain dotfiles, so the .env is silently dropped
One image should run everywhere with runtime config, and layers leak secrets
It bloats the image so much that most registries will refuse the push
questions.explanation: 12-factor separates build from config: one immutable artifact is promoted from staging to production with different env vars. Secrets in layers persist in history and are exposed to anyone with registry access. Size isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: In Node 22, what's a built-in way to load variables from a .env file without the dotenv package?
options: node --dotenv app.js
process.env.load('.env')
require('node:env').load('.env')
node --env-file=.env app.js
questions.explanation: Node 20.6+ supports --env-file (and process.loadEnvFile() from 21.7/20.12). The other options don't exist. In production, the platform usually injects env vars directly anyway.

questions.prompt: What does the 12-factor methodology say an app should do with its logs?
options: Keep them in memory and expose them on an admin endpoint
Write them unbuffered to stdout as an event stream and let the environment route them
Write rotating log files into a local directory and manage retention and compression itself
Send them directly to a database table from the application
questions.explanation: The app shouldn't care where logs go: it writes to stdout, and the platform (Docker, Kubernetes, a log shipper) collects, routes and stores them. Local files are lost with ephemeral containers and complicate scaling.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in environment-based config rather than in code? Select all that apply.
options: The port to listen on
Database connection string
The list of route handlers
Third-party API keys
The tax calculation algorithm
questions.explanation: Config is whatever varies between deploys: credentials, URLs of backing services, ports. Business logic and routing are the same in every environment, so they belong in code.

questions.prompt: Which practices reduce the risk of leaking secrets in a Node service? Select all that apply.
options: Fetch secrets from a secret manager with IAM-scoped access
Pass secrets as command-line arguments to the process
Configure the logger to redact known secret fields
Print process.env at startup to debug config problems
Rotate secrets regularly and grant least privilege
questions.explanation: Secret managers, log redaction, rotation and least privilege all shrink exposure. CLI arguments are visible to other users via ps or /proc, and printing process.env writes every secret into the logs.

questions.prompt: If you start Node with PORT=3000, then process.env.PORT is the number 3000.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Environment variables are always strings, so process.env.PORT === '3000'. Convert explicitly, e.g. Number(process.env.PORT) or z.coerce.number() in a config schema.

questions.prompt: Under 12-factor, the same build artifact should be deployable to staging and production, differing only in config.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Build, release and run are separate stages: a build is combined with environment config to make a release. Rebuilding per environment risks shipping something different from what was tested.

questions.prompt: Why log JSON objects like { level, msg, userId, durationMs } instead of interpolated strings like `User 42 took 130ms`?
options: JSON logs are encrypted at rest by default in most log platforms
Fields can be indexed, filtered and aggregated reliably by log tools
JSON log lines are always smaller than equivalent plain-text lines
Plain-text logs can't be written to stdout in containerized setups
questions.explanation: Structured fields let you query 'durationMs > 1000 AND route = /checkout' or chart p99 by route without fragile regex parsing. JSON is often larger, not smaller, and has nothing to do with encryption.

questions.prompt: With pino, what's the idiomatic way to make every log line for a request include its request ID?
options: Set a global variable to the current request ID
Configure pino to read the ID back from the outgoing HTTP response headers automatically
Prefix each message string manually with the ID
Create a child logger, logger.child({ reqId }), and use it for that request
questions.explanation: Child loggers bind fields once and add them to every line they write; pino-http does this as req.log. A global variable is wrong under concurrency because many requests are in flight at once.

questions.prompt: Deep inside a repository function you want the current request ID in logs without threading it through every function signature. Which Node API is designed for this?
options: process.env, set per request
AsyncLocalStorage from node:async_hooks
A module-level variable updated by middleware
worker_threads' workerData
questions.explanation: AsyncLocalStorage keeps a store that follows the async execution context, so code awaited from a request's middleware sees that request's store, even with many concurrent requests. process.env and module variables are global and get overwritten by concurrent requests.

questions.prompt: Your API receives an X-Request-Id header from clients. What's the sound way to handle it?
options: Ignore it and never return any request ID to clients, to avoid leaking data
Use it directly as the primary key of the request record in the database
Always trust and log it as-is, so client and server logs line up exactly
Accept it only from trusted proxies, validated for format and length; else generate one
questions.explanation: Client-supplied values can be huge, contain log-injection payloads, or collide on purpose. Accept IDs from your own edge or validate them (e.g. a UUID pattern), otherwise generate one with crypto.randomUUID(), and echo it in the response for support.

questions.prompt: Why is pino-pretty usually avoided in production?
options: Pretty-printing costs CPU and emits text that log pipelines can't parse as JSON
It only works in Windows terminals, so Linux containers lose their logs
It writes logs to a local file instead of stdout, which ephemeral containers then lose
It silently drops every log line below warn level to keep output readable
questions.explanation: In production you want raw NDJSON for collectors; colourized multi-line output is for humans in development and breaks structured ingestion. If you need transforms, pino transports run them in a worker thread.

questions.prompt: Which pino call best records a failed payment for later debugging and querying?
options: logger.info('payment failed for order ' + orderId + ': ' + err)
console.error('payment failed', orderId, userId, err.stack)
logger.debug({ orderId, userId }, JSON.stringify(err))
logger.error({ err, orderId, userId }, 'payment failed')
questions.explanation: Passing err under the err key lets pino's serializer capture type, message and stack as fields, the IDs make it searchable, and the level is error. String concatenation loses the stack, JSON.stringify(err) gives {} because message and stack aren't enumerable, and debug is usually disabled in production.

questions.prompt: Request logs include Authorization headers and passwords from login bodies. What's the cleanest fix with pino?
options: Configure redact paths such as 'req.headers.authorization' and '*.password'
Base64-encode the whole log line before writing it
Delete the sensitive headers and body fields from req before every route handler runs
Lower the log level to warn so request logs aren't written
questions.explanation: pino's redact option censors or removes the given paths efficiently at serialization time, keeping useful context while hiding secrets. Raising the level loses valuable logs, base64 is trivially reversible, and mutating req breaks auth.

questions.prompt: Which fields are useful on every request-completion log line? Select all that apply.
options: Request ID
The user's session cookie value
The full raw request body, including passwords
HTTP method, route and status code
Response time in milliseconds
questions.explanation: Correlation ID, method/route/status and latency let you trace, filter and build dashboards. Raw bodies and session cookies are sensitive: logging them leaks credentials and personal data.

questions.prompt: Which statements about correlating logs across services are correct? Select all that apply.
options: AsyncLocalStorage carries context across awaits within one process
Each service should generate a fresh unrelated ID and never forward it
OpenTelemetry can auto-instrument http and pg to propagate trace context
Forward the request ID or W3C traceparent header on downstream calls
questions.explanation: Propagating an ID or traceparent header links logs and spans across services, AsyncLocalStorage keeps it available inside a process, and OpenTelemetry instrumentation automates both. Unrelated per-service IDs make cross-service debugging impossible.

questions.prompt: By default, pino writes logs as newline-delimited JSON (one JSON object per line) to stdout.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: pino's default destination is stdout and each log is a single JSON line with level, time, pid, hostname and msg. That NDJSON format is what log shippers expect.

questions.prompt: With AsyncLocalStorage, a store set by one request's middleware is visible in that request's later awaits and callbacks, but not in other concurrent requests.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: als.run(store, fn) binds the store to the async context created inside fn, so continuations of that request see it while other requests, running in their own contexts, see their own stores.

questions.prompt: Your code calls fs.readFile(). Which layer actually performs the read so the main JavaScript thread can keep running?
options: A short-lived child process that Node spawns per file read
V8's background compiler threads, which pick up idle I/O work
The kernel's epoll, called directly from JavaScript code
libuv's thread pool, reached through Node's C++ bindings
questions.explanation: Node's fs binding hands the call to libuv, which runs the blocking file syscall on a thread-pool thread and queues the callback for the event loop. V8 only compiles and runs JavaScript; it knows nothing about files, and regular files are not pollable via epoll.

questions.prompt: setTimeout is not part of the ECMAScript spec, yet it is a global in Node. Where does Node's setTimeout come from?
options: V8 ships it as a built-in, alongside Promise, JSON and other ES globals
Node implements timers itself, backed by a libuv timer handle
The operating system exposes it to every JavaScript engine
It is a polyfill that npm installs into every project
questions.explanation: V8 provides the language and its built-ins (Promise, JSON, Map...). Host APIs such as timers, setImmediate and process are implemented by Node in JS plus C++, with libuv driving the timer handle. That's why timer semantics differ slightly between Node and browsers.

questions.prompt: On Linux, how does libuv handle reading from a TCP socket compared with reading a regular file?
options: Both use epoll, and the thread pool is only used for crypto work
Sockets use the kernel's readiness API (epoll); files go to the thread pool
Files use epoll; sockets go to the thread pool because network calls are slower
Both are read on thread-pool threads to keep the design uniform
questions.explanation: Network sockets support non-blocking readiness notification, so libuv watches them with epoll (kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows) on the main loop. Regular file I/O has no portable non-blocking API, so libuv runs it on the thread pool. That's why many idle sockets cost no pool threads.

questions.prompt: Which statement about who runs Promise .then callbacks in Node is most accurate?
options: V8 owns the microtask queue; Node asks V8 to drain it after each callback
Node runs them only once per loop iteration, after the close phase
They run on a thread-pool thread, so slow callbacks never block the main thread
libuv runs them in a dedicated 'promise' phase of the event loop
questions.explanation: Promise jobs live in V8's microtask queue. Node drains it (after its own process.nextTick queue) whenever a JS callback from the loop finishes, including between individual timer and immediate callbacks since Node 11. There is no libuv phase for promises, and they always run on the main thread.

questions.prompt: Why do native addons written against Node-API (N-API) usually keep working after a Node major-version upgrade?
options: Node-API addons are really WebAssembly, so they are version-agnostic
Node recompiles every native addon automatically when it starts up
V8 guarantees its internal C++ API never changes between releases
Node-API is ABI-stable, insulating addons from V8's changing C++ API
questions.explanation: Node-API is a C ABI maintained by Node that hides V8 internals, so a compiled addon keeps working across Node versions. Addons using V8's C++ API directly (via nan or raw headers) must be rebuilt because V8's API changes frequently; V8 makes no such stability promise.

questions.prompt: A colleague says "Node is single-threaded". Which refinement is most accurate?
options: Node is multi-threaded because V8 runs independent JavaScript functions in parallel
JavaScript runs on one main thread, but the process also uses helper threads
Node runs each incoming request on its own OS thread by default
Node has one thread in total, so file I/O blocks JavaScript execution
questions.explanation: Your JS (and its callbacks) execute on a single main thread, but the process also has libuv thread-pool threads plus V8 threads for GC and compilation. Requests are not given a thread each; concurrency comes from the event loop, not parallel JS execution.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of Node's C++ bindings layer (the code behind internalBinding)?
options: Translating TypeScript to JavaScript at runtime for core modules
Bridging JS APIs to C/C++ libraries like libuv, OpenSSL, zlib and llhttp
Scheduling which JavaScript function runs next inside V8's bytecode interpreter
Compiling JavaScript to machine code before V8 sees it
questions.explanation: Core modules like fs, net, crypto and zlib are thin JS wrappers that call C++ bindings, which in turn call libuv, OpenSSL, zlib, llhttp and others. Compilation and scheduling of JS code is V8's job, and Node core does not transpile TypeScript through bindings.

questions.prompt: Which of these are provided by V8 itself rather than by Node or libuv? Select all that apply.
options: Promise and the microtask queue
setImmediate
JSON.parse
fs.readFile
Garbage collection of the JavaScript heap
questions.explanation: V8 implements the ECMAScript language and built-ins (Promise, JSON) and manages the JS heap including GC. fs.readFile and setImmediate are Node host APIs built on libuv; setImmediate is tempting because it looks like a language feature, but it isn't in ECMAScript.

questions.prompt: Which C/C++ libraries does Node bundle and use for core functionality? Select all that apply.
options: libpq, for a built-in PostgreSQL client
libuv, for the event loop and async I/O
zlib, for the zlib compression module
c-ares, for dns.resolve*() network lookups
OpenSSL, for crypto and TLS
questions.explanation: Node vendors OpenSSL (crypto/tls), zlib, c-ares (async DNS for dns.resolve*), and libuv (event loop, thread pool). Node has no built-in PostgreSQL client; drivers such as pg are npm packages.

questions.prompt: You can raise the V8 old-generation heap limit for a Node process with the --max-old-space-size flag.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: --max-old-space-size=<MB> sets V8's old-space heap limit, e.g. node --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js. It's a V8 flag that Node passes through; it does not limit Buffer memory allocated outside the JS heap.

questions.prompt: dns.lookup() and dns.resolve4() both use c-ares on the network and never touch the libuv thread pool.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: dns.lookup() calls the OS getaddrinfo (honours /etc/hosts and nsswitch), which is blocking, so it runs on the thread pool. Only the dns.resolve*() family uses c-ares for asynchronous network queries. http.get uses dns.lookup by default, so heavy DNS use can saturate the pool.

questions.prompt: What does this print when run with Node.js?
options:
sync
tick
promise
timeout

sync
promise
tick
timeout

tick
sync
promise
timeout

sync
timeout
tick
promise
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first. When the current macrotask finishes, Node drains the process.nextTick queue, then V8's promise microtasks, and only then does the event loop reach the timers phase. Promises do not jump ahead of nextTick in CommonJS scripts.

questions.prompt: What does this print when run with Node.js?
options:
tick 1
promise
promise in tick
tick 2
immediate

tick 1
tick 2
promise in tick
promise
immediate

tick 1
promise in tick
tick 2
promise
immediate

tick 1
tick 2
promise
promise in tick
immediate
questions.explanation: Node empties the whole nextTick queue (including ticks added while draining) before running promise microtasks, so tick 2 runs right after tick 1. Promise jobs then run in FIFO order: 'promise' was queued first, 'promise in tick' later. setImmediate waits for the check phase.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
t1
t2
p1

t1
p1
t2

t2
t1
p1

p1
t1
t2
questions.explanation: Since Node 11, microtasks are drained after each individual timer callback (matching browsers), so p1 runs before the second timer. Before Node 11 all expired timers ran first, giving t1, t2, p1, which is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.prompt: What is the order of the main phases in one iteration of Node's event loop?
options: pending callbacks → timers → close callbacks → poll → check
timers → check → poll → pending callbacks → close callbacks
timers → pending callbacks → poll → check → close callbacks
poll → timers → check → pending callbacks → close callbacks
questions.explanation: Each iteration runs timers, pending callbacks (deferred system errors), idle/prepare (internal), poll (I/O), check (setImmediate), then close callbacks. Check comes right after poll, which is why setImmediate inside an I/O callback beats setTimeout(0).

questions.prompt: Why does having a pending setImmediate callback change how long the poll phase waits for I/O?
options: Poll always waits a fixed 1 ms, regardless of what else is queued
Immediates cancel any pending I/O so the loop can exit sooner
With immediates queued, poll won't block for I/O and moves on to check
Immediates run inside the poll phase, so poll must wait for all of them to finish
questions.explanation: When the queue is otherwise empty, poll can block waiting for I/O, bounded by the next timer. If setImmediate callbacks are queued, libuv polls without blocking and proceeds to the check phase. Immediates run in check, not in poll.

questions.prompt: Inside an fs.readFile callback you call setTimeout(a, 0) and setImmediate(b). Which runs first, and why?
options: a, because setTimeout(fn, 0) is executed as a microtask
a, because timers always run before immediates in every iteration of the loop
It is random, depending on how fast the machine is at the time
b, because the check phase follows poll before looping back to timers
questions.explanation: I/O callbacks run in the poll phase. The next phase is check, so the immediate runs before the loop wraps around to timers. The ordering is only nondeterministic when both are scheduled from the main module, where it depends on whether 1 ms has elapsed when the loop starts.

questions.prompt: In the main module (not inside any callback) you schedule setTimeout(a, 0) and setImmediate(b). What order is guaranteed?
options: No order is guaranteed; it depends on whether the 1 ms timer has expired
a always runs first, because the timers phase comes first
Both run in the same callback, in the order they were scheduled
b always runs first, because immediates have a higher priority than any timer
questions.explanation: setTimeout(fn, 0) becomes a 1 ms timer. When the loop starts, if 1 ms has passed the timer runs first, otherwise the loop proceeds to check and the immediate wins. Process startup timing varies, so the order is not deterministic; only within an I/O callback is setImmediate guaranteed first.

questions.prompt: A function reschedules itself with process.nextTick() forever. What happens to incoming HTTP requests?
options: They are never handled: the nextTick queue is drained before the loop continues
Node detects the recursion and throws a RangeError after 1000 ticks
They are served, but only in between nextTick callbacks, so each one adds some latency
They are served normally, because nextTick yields to I/O each time
questions.explanation: Node keeps draining the nextTick queue (and microtasks) until it is empty before returning to the event loop, so a self-rescheduling nextTick starves timers and I/O forever. Recursive setImmediate is the safe alternative because immediates queued during check run next iteration.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Node timers are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Timer callbacks run in the poll phase alongside I/O callbacks
Long synchronous work on the main thread can delay timer callbacks
setTimeout(fn, 0) is treated as a delay of 1 ms
The delay is a minimum; the callback may run later than requested
questions.explanation: Node clamps delays below 1 to 1 ms, and a timer only promises 'not before' the delay: busy JS or a long poll can push it later. Timer callbacks run in the timers phase, not the poll phase.

questions.prompt: Which queues keep running entries that are added while they are being drained, so a callback that keeps re-queueing itself can starve I/O? Select all that apply.
options: The process.nextTick queue
Callbacks scheduled with queueMicrotask
The Promise microtask queue
The setImmediate (check) queue
questions.explanation: nextTick and microtasks (promise reactions and queueMicrotask) are drained until empty, including newly added entries, so infinite re-queueing blocks the loop. Immediates added during the check phase are deferred to the next iteration, which lets I/O run in between.

questions.prompt: 'close' event handlers, such as socket.on('close') after socket.destroy(), run in the close callbacks phase of the event loop.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The close callbacks phase handles handles that were closed abruptly, e.g. socket.destroy() leading to the 'close' event. Otherwise such events are emitted via process.nextTick. It is the last phase of each iteration.

questions.prompt: On an 8-core machine with the default thread pool, a service starts 8 crypto.pbkdf2() calls at once, each taking ~100 ms of CPU. Roughly how long until all 8 finish?
questions.explanation: The default pool has 4 threads, so 4 hashes run in parallel (~100 ms) while the other 4 queue, then run in a second wave (~100 ms), totalling ~200 ms. 8 cores don't help because only 4 pool threads exist; ~800 ms would mean fully serial execution.

questions.prompt: During a burst of large file uploads written with fs, outbound HTTP calls to other services suddenly get slow to start. What's the most likely shared cause?
options: The HTTP agent is single-threaded and waits for fs writes to finish
V8 pauses network activity whenever a large Buffer is allocated
fs writes block the same epoll loop that also handles reading from TCP sockets
fs writes and dns.lookup (used by http) queue on the same libuv thread pool
questions.explanation: http.request resolves hostnames with dns.lookup, which runs getaddrinfo on the thread pool. If fs operations occupy all pool threads, lookups wait in the queue, delaying connections. Socket I/O itself uses epoll and isn't blocked by fs writes.

questions.prompt: When does UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE reliably take effect?
options: Only after calling a dedicated libuv resize API from JavaScript
When set in the environment before the pool is first used, typically at launch
Any time; changing process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE resizes the live pool immediately
Only when set in package.json under an "engines" field
questions.explanation: libuv creates the pool once, lazily, on first use, reading UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE at that moment. Setting it in the launch environment (e.g. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 node app.js) is reliable; changing process.env later has no effect once the pool exists, and there's no resize API.

questions.prompt: An HTTP API holds 10,000 idle keep-alive connections. How many libuv thread-pool threads do those sockets occupy?
options: 4, one per default pool thread
One per CPU core, shared round-robin by all of the idle sockets
10,000, one per socket
Zero; sockets are watched by the OS readiness API
questions.explanation: Sockets are non-blocking and monitored by epoll/kqueue/IOCP on the main event loop, so they consume no pool threads. The pool is for operations without a portable async OS API: file I/O, getaddrinfo, and CPU-heavy crypto/zlib.

questions.prompt: On a 4-core container, someone sets UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=128 to speed up async bcrypt hashing at peak. What's the realistic outcome?
options: Hashing throughput scales roughly 32x, because 128 threads can now hash at once
The main thread gains 128 helpers, so JavaScript runs in parallel
Node rejects the value and falls back to the default of 4 threads
Throughput stays capped by the 4 cores, with more memory and context switching
questions.explanation: CPU-bound work can't exceed the available cores, so extra threads just time-slice the same 4 cores, adding memory and scheduling overhead and inflating per-hash latency. Values up to 1024 are accepted, and pool threads never run your JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Why is crypto.pbkdf2Sync() in a request handler worse than crypto.pbkdf2() with a callback?
options: The Sync version runs on the main thread, stalling every other request
The async version skips the salt, so it is faster but less secure
The Sync version uses all pool threads, starving file I/O
The Sync version produces weaker hashes than the async version
questions.explanation: Sync crypto computes on the main thread, so the event loop can't serve anything else until it finishes. The async version does the same work on a pool thread. Output is identical; the Sync variant doesn't touch the pool at all.

questions.prompt: Operating systems already provide async networking. Why does libuv need a thread pool at all?
options: To emulate async for operations lacking a portable non-blocking OS API
To run user JavaScript in parallel whenever the main thread is busy with other work
To run garbage collection outside the V8 isolate
To hold idle TCP connections so the main loop has fewer handles
questions.explanation: File system calls, getaddrinfo, and CPU-heavy work like crypto and zlib either block or have no cross-platform async interface, so libuv runs them on worker threads and posts results back to the loop. JS never runs on pool threads, and GC is V8's concern.

questions.prompt: Async password hashing is saturating the thread pool and slowing file reads. Which mitigations make sense? Select all that apply.
options: Cap concurrent hashing calls with a semaphore so other pool work isn't starved
Switch to the Sync variant so hashing no longer occupies pool threads
Replace fs.promises with callback fs, which bypasses the thread pool
Move hashing to a dedicated worker_threads pool or a separate service
questions.explanation: Isolating CPU-heavy work in its own pool or service, or bounding its concurrency, keeps pool threads available for fs and DNS. Sync hashing would block the main thread, which is worse. Callback and promise fs both use the same thread pool.

questions.prompt: Which symptoms point to libuv thread-pool starvation rather than a blocked main thread? Select all that apply.
options: Event-loop delay (monitorEventLoopDelay) stays low
Routes doing only in-memory work stay fast
A CPU profile shows one long synchronous JS function
setTimeout callbacks fire hundreds of milliseconds late
fs.readFile and dns.lookup latencies climb together
questions.explanation: With pool starvation the main thread is free, so loop delay is low and pure-JS routes stay fast, while everything queued on the pool (fs, DNS, crypto, zlib) slows together. Late timers and a long synchronous function in a profile indicate main-thread blocking.

questions.prompt: Each worker_threads Worker gets its own separate libuv thread pool of UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE threads.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each Worker has its own V8 isolate and event loop, but the libuv thread pool is process-wide and shared. Heavy fs or crypto in workers competes with the main thread for the same pool threads.

questions.prompt: zlib.gzipSync() compresses on a libuv thread-pool thread, so it doesn't block the event loop.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: All *Sync zlib functions run on the calling (main) thread and block the loop. The async zlib.gzip() and streaming APIs are the ones that use the thread pool.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
timer late: true
loop done

loop done
timer late: true

timer late: false
loop done

loop done
timer late: false
questions.explanation: The busy loop occupies the only JS thread for 50 ms, so the 0 ms timer can't fire until the synchronous code ends. It then runs at least 50 ms after scheduling. A timer never interrupts running JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
after call
resolved
heavy done

after call
heavy done
resolved

heavy done
resolved
after call

heavy done
after call
resolved
questions.explanation: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, so the CPU loop executes before heavy() even returns. Only the .then callback is deferred to a microtask. Marking a function async does not move its work off the main thread.

questions.prompt: An endpoint accepts JSON bodies up to 50 MB and calls JSON.parse on them; other requests stall during parsing. What's the best mitigation?
options: Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE so that JSON parsing gets more threads
Cap body size, and stream-parse or offload truly large payloads to a worker
Make the handler async and await JSON.parse to yield to other work
Wrap JSON.parse in new Promise() so parsing happens asynchronously
questions.explanation: JSON.parse is synchronous CPU work on the main thread; wrapping it in a Promise or awaiting it changes nothing because the executor and the call still run synchronously. Limit sizes, and for genuinely big inputs stream-parse or offload to a worker. The thread pool never runs JSON.parse.

questions.prompt: After deploying a validation regex like /^(a+)+$/, a single crafted input pushes p99 latency to several seconds on every endpoint. Why every endpoint?
options: V8 recompiles every function in the process when a regex is slow
The regex leaks memory, triggering long GC pauses across the process
Catastrophic backtracking runs synchronously on the main thread, blocking the loop
Regex evaluation runs on the libuv thread pool, which every other endpoint shares too
questions.explanation: This is ReDoS: nested quantifiers backtrack exponentially on near-matches, and regex matching is synchronous JS on the single main thread, so all requests wait.
