Fix by rewriting the pattern, bounding input length, or using a linear-time engine. Regexes never run on the thread pool.

questions.prompt: Where is calling fs.readFileSync generally acceptable in a Node web server?
options: Never, because readFileSync always crashes under concurrent load
Inside request handlers, as long as the file is under 1 MB
In any middleware, because sync fs is served from the OS cache
At startup, e.g. loading config or certificates before listening
questions.explanation: Blocking at boot is harmless since no requests are being served yet, and it simplifies initialization. In the request path even small sync reads add up under load because each blocks every concurrent request; the OS cache doesn't change that it's synchronous.

questions.prompt: Which tool best measures how much the event loop is being blocked in production?
options: process.memoryUsage() sampled every second
Counting open sockets with server.getConnections()
os.loadavg() reported to your metrics system every few seconds
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() histogram percentiles
questions.explanation: monitorEventLoopDelay samples how late the loop runs compared with schedule, giving p50/p99 lag that directly reflects blocking. Load average is system-wide and doesn't isolate your process's main thread; memory and socket counts measure different things.

questions.prompt: You must process 1 million array items in a request without worker threads, and other requests must stay responsive. Which approach actually yields to I/O between chunks?
options: Process chunks and await Promise.resolve() between them to give other requests a turn
Process everything inside a single async function with no awaits
Process chunks of ~1,000 items and schedule each next chunk with setImmediate
Process chunks and schedule each next chunk with process.nextTick
questions.explanation: setImmediate puts the next chunk in a later loop iteration, letting the poll phase handle I/O in between. nextTick and resolved-promise awaits are drained before the loop continues, so they never let I/O in, and an async function without awaits is fully synchronous.

questions.prompt: Which of these block the event loop when called inside a request handler? Select all that apply.
options: await fs.promises.readFile()
JSON.stringify() on a 200 MB object
crypto.pbkdf2Sync()
zlib.inflateSync()
await fetch() to another service
questions.explanation: Sync crypto, sync zlib and serializing a huge object all run on the main thread. fs.promises.readFile runs on the thread pool and fetch uses non-blocking sockets, so awaiting them suspends the handler without blocking the loop.

questions.prompt: Which statements about 'non-blocking' code in Node are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Wrapping synchronous code in new Promise() makes it non-blocking
Non-blocking I/O means the main thread doesn't wait while the kernel or pool works
Promise.all runs CPU-bound callbacks in parallel across cores
Code in an async function before its first await runs synchronously
questions.explanation: Async functions run synchronously up to the first await, and non-blocking I/O lets the main thread do other work while the OS or thread pool completes the operation. The Promise executor runs synchronously, and Promise.all only waits on promises; it doesn't create parallel JS threads.

questions.prompt: An async function whose body contains no await still executes its whole body synchronously when called.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Without an await, nothing suspends the function, so its body runs to completion during the call; only the resolution of the returned promise is observed asynchronously by .then or await.

questions.prompt: Moving a CPU-heavy loop into a .then() callback stops it from blocking the event loop.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: .then callbacks are microtasks that run on the same main thread, just slightly later. The loop still blocks everything while it runs. Real offloading needs worker_threads, a child process, or chunking with setImmediate.

questions.prompt: What does this print when run with Node.js?
questions.code:
const s = '€';
console.log(s.length, Buffer.byteLength(s), Buffer.byteLength(s, 'utf16le'));
questions.explanation: '€' (U+20AC) is one UTF-16 code unit, so length is 1. In UTF-8 it takes 3 bytes, and in UTF-16LE 2 bytes. String length counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes, which is why Content-Length must use Buffer.byteLength.

questions.prompt: What does this print when run with Node.js?
options: abc zb ayc
zbc zb zyc
abc zb zyc
zbc zb zbc
questions.explanation: subarray returns a view over the same memory, so writing to b also changes a ('zbc'). Buffer.from(buffer) copies, so changing c leaves a alone and c becomes 'zyc'. Assuming subarray copies (like Array.prototype.slice) gives the wrong 'abc'.

questions.prompt: What does this print when run with Node.js?
options: false 2
true 3
true 2
false 3
questions.explanation: 'é' is two UTF-8 bytes (C3 A9). Decoding each half separately turns each invalid fragment into U+FFFD, giving '\uFFFD\uFFFD!' (length 3), not 'é!'. This is the classic bug of calling chunk.toString() on each stream chunk.

questions.prompt: A handler builds a string with body += chunk.toString() for each 'data' event, and non-ASCII characters are occasionally corrupted. What's the correct fix?
options: Call chunk.toString('latin1'), which supports all Unicode characters
Use readable.setEncoding('utf8') or StringDecoder, or Buffer.concat then decode once
Increase highWaterMark on the stream so chunks are big enough to never split a character
Call chunk.toString('ascii') so every byte maps to one character
questions.explanation: Chunks can split a multi-byte UTF-8 character. setEncoding/StringDecoder buffer incomplete sequences across chunks, and concatenating Buffers before decoding avoids the split. A bigger highWaterMark only makes it rarer; ascii and latin1 can't represent most Unicode.

questions.prompt: What is the key risk of Buffer.allocUnsafe(size) compared with Buffer.alloc(size)?
options: It may contain leftover data from old memory unless you fully overwrite it
It allocates on the V8 heap, so large sizes can trigger an out-of-memory crash quickly
It returns a buffer that is read-only until you call buf.fill()
It can only hold ASCII data, so writing UTF-8 throws an error
questions.explanation: allocUnsafe skips zero-filling for speed, so the bytes are whatever was in memory before, possibly secrets from earlier requests. Only use it when you'll overwrite every byte. Buffer.alloc zero-fills. Both are writable and encoding-agnostic.

questions.prompt: You embed a 3 MB binary file in a JSON response as base64. Roughly how large is the encoded string?
options: About 6 MB
About 4 MB
About 3 MB
About 2.25 MB
questions.explanation: Base64 encodes every 3 bytes as 4 ASCII characters, a ~33% overhead: 3 MB × 4/3 ≈ 4 MB. Hex would double it to ~6 MB. That overhead is why large binaries are better streamed or served from object storage.

questions.prompt: Which call creates a Buffer that shares memory with existing data instead of copying it?
options: Buffer.concat([existingBuffer])
Buffer.from(existingBuffer)
Buffer.from(typedArray.buffer, typedArray.byteOffset, typedArray.byteLength)
Buffer.from(existingBuffer.toString('base64'), 'base64')
questions.explanation: Buffer.from(arrayBuffer, offset, length) creates a view over the same ArrayBuffer memory. Buffer.from(buffer) and Buffer.concat both allocate and copy, and the base64 round-trip obviously copies too.

questions.prompt: You pass buf.buffer from Buffer.from('hi') to an API expecting the raw bytes, and it receives thousands of unrelated bytes. Why?
options: The API was handed the whole V8 heap, because every Buffer is stored directly inside it
Buffer.from always pads strings to the next power of two
Small buffers are slices of a shared pre-allocated pool; use byteOffset and length
buf.buffer returns a UTF-16 encoding of the original string
questions.explanation: For small sizes Node carves Buffers out of a shared 8 KiB pool, so buf.buffer is the entire pool and buf.byteOffset marks where your bytes start. Pass buf itself (a Uint8Array) or slice buf.buffer by byteOffset/byteLength. There's no padding or UTF-16 conversion.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Node's Buffer are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Buffer is a subclass of Uint8Array
buf.length is the number of bytes, not characters
All Buffer memory counts against --max-old-space-size
buf.toString('hex') produces two characters per byte
questions.explanation: Buffer extends Uint8Array, its length is in bytes, and hex uses two characters per byte. Large Buffer contents are allocated outside the V8 JS heap (reported as external/arrayBuffers memory), so they aren't capped by --max-old-space-size.

questions.prompt: You set a Content-Length header for a UTF-8 response body string s. Which expressions give the correct value? Select all that apply.
options: new TextEncoder().encode(s).length
Buffer.from(s).length
Buffer.byteLength(s, 'utf8')
s.length
[...s].length
questions.explanation: Content-Length is in bytes, so you need the UTF-8 byte count: Buffer.byteLength, the length of Buffer.from(s), or a TextEncoder result. s.length counts UTF-16 code units and [...s].length counts code points; both are wrong for any non-ASCII text.

questions.prompt: Buffer.from('ff', 'hex') produces a 1-byte buffer containing the value 255.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Hex decoding maps each pair of hex digits to one byte, so 'ff' becomes a single byte 0xFF = 255. Without the 'hex' argument the default UTF-8 encoding would give two bytes (0x66 0x66).

questions.prompt: An export script reads 10 million rows and calls res.write(row) in a tight loop, ignoring the return value. Memory climbs to several GB. What's going on?
options: V8 can't garbage-collect strings once they have been passed to a socket
Past highWaterMark, write() buffers in memory; ignoring false lets it grow unbounded
res.write is synchronous and blocks until the client has read each row
The rows leak because res.end() was never called on the response stream
questions.explanation: write() returns false when the buffer exceeds highWaterMark, telling you to pause until 'drain'. Ignoring it queues everything in memory because the producer outpaces the client. Fix by awaiting 'drain' or using pipeline() with a Readable. write() is not synchronous.

questions.prompt: What does a stream's highWaterMark control?
options: A hard cap; writes beyond it throw ERR_STREAM_OVERFLOW
The buffer level at which the stream signals back-pressure
How many milliseconds data may sit in the buffer before flushing
The maximum size of a single chunk passed to write()
questions.explanation: highWaterMark is a threshold: past it, write() returns false and readables stop calling _read(). It's advisory, so ignoring the signal lets the buffer keep growing. It is measured in bytes, or object count in objectMode, not in time or chunk size.

questions.prompt: A net.Socket is a Duplex stream, while zlib.createGzip() is a Transform. What distinguishes them?
options: A Duplex can only be written to, while a Transform can only be read
A Transform always runs on the libuv thread pool, while a Duplex runs on the main thread
Duplex streams are faster because they skip internal buffering
A Transform's output is computed from its input; a Duplex's sides are independent
questions.explanation: A Transform is a Duplex whose readable output is derived from what's written (compress in, compressed bytes out). A socket's readable side carries data from the peer, unrelated to what you write. Both can be read and written, and both buffer.

questions.prompt: What happens when you break out of `for await (const chunk of readable)` early?
options: The remaining data is buffered in memory until the process exits
The stream is paused and resumes when you iterate it again
An ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE is thrown from the loop
The stream is destroyed, releasing its underlying resource
questions.explanation: Exiting the loop via break, return or throw calls the async iterator's return(), which destroys the stream (closing file descriptors, etc.). That's convenient for 'read the first N lines', but you can't resume the same stream afterwards. No error is thrown on a deliberate break.

questions.prompt: A Transform turns CSV lines into JS objects and calls this.push(obj), but it throws ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE. What's the fix?
options: Set readableObjectMode: true so the readable side accepts objects
Call JSON.stringify(obj) and push the string to keep using byte mode
Increase highWaterMark so larger objects fit in the buffer
Use stream.Writable instead, because Transforms can't emit objects
questions.explanation: Non-objectMode streams only accept strings, Buffers and Uint8Arrays. readableObjectMode lets the output side carry arbitrary values while the input stays bytes. Stringifying defeats the purpose and highWaterMark is unrelated to type errors.

questions.prompt: With this code, what happens if the destination write stream fails (e.g. the disk is full)?
options: The generator retries the failed write until the disk has space again
Only the write stream is closed; the read stream stays open and its file descriptor leaks
The read stream keeps reading and buffers the whole file in memory
pipeline rejects and destroys every stream in the chain, including the reader
questions.explanation: pipeline wires up error handling across all stages: an error anywhere destroys every stream, ends the generator, and rejects the promise. The leaking file descriptor is the classic .pipe() problem, which pipeline was designed to fix.

questions.prompt: Why stream a 2 GB file to the client instead of using fs.promises.readFile and res.end(data)?
options: Streaming keeps memory roughly constant and starts sending bytes sooner
readFile is synchronous, so it blocks the event loop for the whole read
Streaming lets the OS compress the file automatically
res.end() can't send binary data, only strings
questions.explanation: readFile loads the whole file into one Buffer (2 GB of RAM per concurrent download, near Buffer size limits) before sending anything. Streaming sends chunks as they're read with back-pressure. fs.promises.readFile is async, not blocking, and res.end accepts Buffers.

questions.prompt: Which of these can you read data from, i.e. are Readable or Duplex streams? Select all that apply.
options: process.stdin
net.Socket
fs.createWriteStream('out.log')
http.ServerResponse (res in a server handler)
http.IncomingMessage (req in a server handler)
questions.explanation: req is a Readable carrying the request body, process.stdin is a Readable, and net.Socket is a Duplex. res is a Writable (you write the response into it), and createWriteStream returns a Writable.

questions.prompt: Which ways of copying a source into a destination stream respect back-pressure? Select all that apply.
options: for await (const c of src) { if (!dest.write(c)) await once(dest, 'drain'); }
src.on('data', async (c) => { await dest.write(c); })
Readable.from(asyncGenerator()).pipe(dest)
await pipeline(src, dest)
src.on('data', (c) => dest.write(c))
questions.explanation: pipeline and pipe pause the source when the destination is full, and the manual loop waits for 'drain' when write() returns false. A bare 'data' handler ignores write()'s return, and awaiting write() does nothing because it returns a boolean, not a promise.

questions.prompt: Attaching a 'data' event listener switches a Readable stream into flowing mode.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Readables start paused. Adding a 'data' listener, calling resume(), or piping switches them to flowing mode, where data is pushed as fast as it arrives. That's why a 'data' handler without back-pressure handling can overwhelm a slow consumer.

questions.prompt: Readable.from(['a', 'b', 'c']) creates a stream in objectMode by default.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Readable.from() defaults to objectMode: true, emitting each iterable item as one chunk. It's a handy way to turn arrays or async generators into streams for pipeline().

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: listener, before, after
before, listener, after
before, after (the listener runs on the next tick, after the script)
before, after, listener
questions.explanation: emit() calls listeners synchronously, in registration order, before returning. EventEmitter is not async by itself, so 'listener' prints between 'before' and 'after'. Assuming emit defers listeners like a promise is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: Code calls emitter.emit('error', new Error('boom')) and no 'error' listener is registered. What happens?
options: The error is queued in memory until an 'error' listener is attached to the emitter
emit throws the error, crashing the process if nothing catches it
The event is silently dropped, like any event without listeners
emit returns false and logs a warning to stderr
questions.explanation: 'error' is special: with no listener, emit throws the error (or a generic one), which typically becomes an uncaught exception. Other events without listeners just return false. Always attach 'error' handlers to sockets, streams and custom emitters.

questions.prompt: Production logs show "MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 listeners added". What's the most likely cause?
options: Code adds a listener to a long-lived emitter per request and never removes it
An emitter emitted the same event more than 10 times within a single tick of the loop
The process has more than 10 open sockets at the same time
Node has run out of memory for event objects and is dropping them
questions.explanation: The default limit is 10 listeners per event per emitter. Exceeding it usually means listeners accumulate, e.g. db.on('reconnect', ...) inside a handler, leaking closures. Fix by registering once or removing listeners; raising setMaxListeners only hides a real leak.

questions.prompt: What does path.resolve('/srv', 'uploads', '/etc/passwd') return on Linux?
options: 'srv/uploads/etc/passwd'
'/srv/uploads'
'/etc/passwd'
'/srv/uploads/etc/passwd'
questions.explanation: path.resolve processes segments right to left until an absolute path is formed; an absolute segment discards everything before it. So a user-supplied absolute path escapes your base directory, unlike path.join, which would give '/srv/uploads/etc/passwd'.

questions.prompt: Files are served from root = '/srv/uploads' based on a user-supplied name. Which check correctly prevents path traversal?
options: if (name.includes('../')) reject(); else serve(path.join(root, name));
const p = path.join(root, name); if (!p.startsWith(root)) reject();
const p = path.normalize(name); if (p.startsWith('/')) reject();
const p = path.resolve(root, name); if (!p.startsWith(root + path.sep)) reject();
questions.explanation: Resolve to an absolute normalized path, then require it to lie under root plus a separator. Without the separator, '/srv/uploads-evil' would pass a startsWith(root) check. Blacklisting '../' misses encoded or '..\' variants, and the normalize check still allows '../' escapes.

questions.prompt: Code checks fs.existsSync(file) and, if false, writes the file to create it, but two concurrent requests sometimes both 'create' it. What's the robust fix?
options: Add a short setTimeout between the check and the write
Use fs.promises.access instead of fs.existsSync so the check itself is asynchronous
Open the file with the 'wx' flag, which fails atomically if it already exists
Write the file twice so the second write wins consistently
questions.explanation: Check-then-act is a TOCTOU race: the file can appear between the check and the write. The 'wx' flag (O_CREAT|O_EXCL) makes creation fail with EEXIST in a single atomic syscall. Switching to an async check keeps the same race.

questions.prompt: To size a worker pool to the machine, which API is recommended in modern Node?
options: os.availableParallelism()
os.loadavg()
os.totalmem()
process.memoryUsage()
questions.explanation: os.availableParallelism() (Node 18.14+) returns an estimate of how many parallel tasks the process can run, and is preferred over os.cpus().length. totalmem and memoryUsage are about memory; loadavg is a system load metric.

questions.prompt: What does `await events.once(emitter, 'ready')` give you?
options: A boolean indicating whether 'ready' had already been emitted
An array of the event's arguments; it rejects if 'error' is emitted first
The first listener function that was registered for 'ready'
A promise that resolves again every time 'ready' fires, until you remove the listener
questions.explanation: events.once returns a promise that resolves with an array of the arguments passed to emit, and rejects if the emitter emits 'error' while waiting. Promises settle once; for repeated events use events.on(), which gives an async iterator.

questions.prompt: Which statements about EventEmitter are correct? Select all that apply.
options: prependListener() adds a listener to the front of the list
emit() returns true if the event had listeners, otherwise false
emit() waits for async listeners' promises before returning
Listeners are called synchronously, in the order they were registered
questions.explanation: Listeners run synchronously in order, emit reports whether any listener existed, and prependListener puts a listener first. emit ignores returned promises, so rejections in async listeners aren't awaited and can become unhandled (unless captureRejections is enabled).

questions.prompt: Which fs usages are appropriate inside a busy HTTP server's request path? Select all that apply.
options: fs.createReadStream(file) piped to res for large files
fs.promises.readFile for small files
fs.readdirSync(dir) to list files on each request
fs.writeFileSync to append each audit log line
fs.promises.writeFile to a temp file, then fs.promises.rename for atomic replacement
questions.explanation: Async reads, streaming large files, and write-temp-then-rename (atomic on the same filesystem) are all fine. Sync calls like readdirSync and writeFileSync block every concurrent request while the disk works.

questions.prompt: __dirname and __filename are available in Node ES modules (.mjs or "type": "module").
options: True
False
questions.explanation: They are CommonJS module-wrapper variables. In ESM use import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename (Node 20.11+), or fileURLToPath(import.meta.url).

questions.prompt: You need to hand a 100 MB ArrayBuffer to a worker thread without copying it. How?
options: postMessage(buf); structured clone always shares memory
Assign it to a global variable, which all threads share
JSON.stringify it and post the string, since strings are shared between isolates without copying
postMessage(buf, [buf]); ownership transfers and the sender's copy is detached
questions.explanation: Listing the ArrayBuffer in the transfer list moves it in O(1): the worker owns it and the sender's buffer becomes detached (byteLength 0). Plain postMessage structured-clones (copies). Globals aren't shared across isolates, and JSON is a slower copy.

questions.prompt: You need to transcode videos with the ffmpeg CLI and process its output as it's produced. Which API fits best?
options: cluster.fork, which starts the binary as a worker
child_process.exec, which buffers output into a string
child_process.spawn, which streams stdout/stderr
worker_threads, which can run any executable in-process
questions.explanation: spawn starts the process and exposes stdout/stderr as streams, ideal for long-running or large output. exec buffers everything in memory and fails past maxBuffer. Workers run JavaScript, not external binaries, and cluster forks Node processes running your own script.

questions.prompt: Code runs child_process.exec(`convert ${req.query.file} out.png`). What's the main danger, and the fix?
options: It's slow; switch to worker_threads to avoid process startup cost
Memory leaks; call child.kill() after every conversion
Shell command injection; use execFile/spawn with an argument array and no shell
Zombie processes; wrap the call in cluster.fork() instead
questions.explanation: exec runs through a shell, so input like 'x; rm -rf /' executes arbitrary commands. execFile and spawn (without shell: true) pass arguments directly to the program with no shell parsing. Also validate the filename. Speed and cleanup are secondary concerns here.

questions.prompt: A team runs Node on Kubernetes with autoscaling. Why do many such teams skip the cluster module?
options: cluster doesn't work inside containers at all
Kubernetes forbids processes from forking children
cluster only works with Express, not with other frameworks
The orchestrator already replicates, restarts and load-balances one-process pods
questions.explanation: With one process per container, Kubernetes handles replicas, health checks, restarts and load balancing, and CPU/memory limits map cleanly to one process. cluster works in containers, but duplicating supervision inside the pod adds complexity for little gain.

questions.prompt: With cluster and 4 workers, an in-memory rate limiter (a Map of IP → count) lets clients make about 4x the allowed requests. Why?
options: cluster resets module state after every request
The primary process duplicates each request to all workers
Each worker is a separate process with its own Map; use a shared store like Redis
The Map is shared, but writes from different workers race
questions.explanation: cluster workers are separate processes with separate memory, and connections are spread across them, so each counts only its share. Shared limits need an external store (Redis) or sticky routing. There's no shared Map to race on.

questions.prompt: A service creates `new Worker('./resize.js')` for every incoming image request. Under load, latency and memory spike. What's the better design?
options: Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE so Workers start faster
Keep a fixed-size pool of reusable workers (e.g. Piscina) fed by a queue
Run the resize on the main thread, since workers can't help with CPU work
Use child_process.fork per request, which is lighter than a Worker
questions.explanation: Each Worker boots a new V8 isolate and event loop and loads modules, costing milliseconds and megabytes. A pool amortizes that and bounds concurrency to the cores. fork is even heavier, and the libuv pool size doesn't affect Worker startup.

questions.prompt: An uncaught exception is thrown inside a worker thread. What happens by default?
options: The whole process crashes immediately, like a main-thread exception
The worker stops and the Worker object in the main thread emits 'error'
The worker restarts itself automatically with the same data
The exception is swallowed and the worker keeps running
questions.explanation: A worker's uncaught exception terminates that worker and surfaces as an 'error' event (then 'exit') on the Worker object. If the main thread handles it, the process survives. Nothing restarts automatically; pools such as Piscina replace dead workers for you.

questions.prompt: Which are valid ways to exchange data between the main thread and a worker_threads Worker? Select all that apply.
options: worker.postMessage() with a 'message' listener
Module-level variables, which are shared automatically
A SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics for coordination
process.send(), as with forked child processes
MessageChannel ports passed via postMessage
questions.explanation: Workers communicate via postMessage (structured clone or transfer), MessageChannel ports, and SharedArrayBuffer memory with Atomics. process.send is the child_process IPC channel, and each worker has its own isolate, so module variables are not shared.

questions.prompt: Which workloads clearly benefit from moving to worker_threads? Select all that apply.
options: Resizing images with a pure-JavaScript library
Waiting on many PostgreSQL queries
Compressing with the async zlib API
Generating large PDFs with CPU-heavy JavaScript
Making many concurrent HTTP calls to a slow third-party API
questions.explanation: Workers help with CPU-bound JavaScript that would otherwise block the main thread. Network calls and DB queries are I/O waits the event loop already handles concurrently, and async zlib already runs on the libuv thread pool.

questions.prompt: Each worker thread has its own V8 isolate and event loop, so module-level variables are not shared with the main thread.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A Worker loads its own copy of modules into a separate isolate. Sharing requires explicit messages, transferred buffers, or SharedArrayBuffer. That isolation is what makes workers safe to use without locks for ordinary objects.

questions.prompt: Workers created by the cluster module are threads inside the same process as the primary.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: cluster.fork() starts separate OS processes (via child_process.fork) that share the server port through the primary. For threads in one process you'd use worker_threads.

questions.prompt: A package.json has "type": "module". How does Node treat a file named config.cjs in that package?
options: As JSON, because .cjs stands for configuration JS
It refuses to load it until "type" is changed to "commonjs"
As an ES module, because the package type overrides extensions
As CommonJS, because .cjs always means CommonJS
questions.explanation: "type" only decides how .js files are interpreted. .cjs is always CommonJS and .mjs is always ESM, regardless of "type". That's how one package can mix both formats.

questions.prompt: In an ESM project, `import { slugify } from './utils'` fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND although utils.js exists. Why?
options: ESM resolution doesn't add extensions; the specifier must be './utils.js'
The file must be renamed utils.mjs in every ESM project
Named imports aren't supported for local files in ESM
Relative imports must start with '/' in ESM
questions.explanation: Node's ESM loader follows URL semantics and doesn't try extensions or index files like CommonJS require does, so you must write the full './utils.js'. .js works fine under "type": "module", and named imports from local files are standard.

questions.prompt: From a CommonJS file, how can you load an ESM-only package that uses top-level await?
options: const pkg = await import('pkg'); dynamic import works from CommonJS
const pkg = require('pkg'); require handles all ESM modules synchronously
It's impossible; the whole app must be converted to ESM first
Rename your file to .json so Node switches loaders
questions.explanation: Dynamic import() is available in CommonJS and returns a promise for the module namespace, so it handles async (top-level await) modules. Newer Node versions can require() synchronous ESM graphs, but a module with top-level await can't be loaded synchronously.

questions.prompt: After a library upgrade, `require('lib/dist/internal/helpers.js')` throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED. What changed?
options: The library added an "exports" map that doesn't expose that subpath
The library switched its "main" field to an ESM file
The library removed helpers.js from its published tarball
Node now blocks requiring any file inside a dist folder
questions.explanation: Once "exports" is defined, only the listed entry points can be imported; deep paths are encapsulated even if the file exists. Use a public entry point or ask the maintainer to export it. This error is specific to exports encapsulation, not missing files.

questions.prompt: A library publishes separate ESM and CJS builds via this exports map. Your app imports it with ESM while a dependency require()s it. What's the main risk?
options: The CJS build is ignored and both consumers get the ESM build
Node throws because one package can't be loaded by both systems
Two separate module instances load, so singletons and instanceof checks can break
The "import" condition is only honoured by bundlers, never by Node
questions.explanation: This is the dual-package hazard: ESM and CJS consumers get different files, so module state (caches, registries, classes) exists twice and an object from one copy fails instanceof against the other. Node supports both conditions; it just doesn't dedupe them.

questions.prompt: Two packages depend on different versions of the same library, so node_modules contains two copies. An `err instanceof LibError` check starts failing. Why?
options: The require cache is cleared whenever a second version is loaded
Modules are cached per resolved file path, so each copy has its own LibError class
instanceof never works across packages in Node
Node merges both versions and keeps the older class definition
questions.explanation: The module cache is keyed by resolved filename, so two copies on disk mean two evaluations and two distinct classes. An error built by one copy isn't an instance of the other's class. Deduplicating versions or checking an error code property avoids it.

questions.prompt: How does CommonJS require('lodash') find the package from /app/src/utils/a.js?
options: It looks only in the global npm installation directory
It looks only in the node_modules next to the project's package.json
It downloads lodash from the registry if it isn't cached
It walks up parent directories checking each node_modules folder
questions.explanation: Bare specifiers are searched in /app/src/utils/node_modules, then /app/src/node_modules, /app/node_modules, and so on up to the filesystem root (plus legacy global folders). That walk is why nested node_modules and hoisting work.

questions.prompt: main.js does require('./a'). What does b.js print?
options: in b, a.loaded = true
in b, a.loaded = false
in b, a.loaded = undefined
It throws a circular dependency error
questions.explanation: When b requires a during a's evaluation, CommonJS returns a's partially filled exports object from the cache instead of re-running it. At that moment loaded is still false. Node doesn't throw on cycles; it hands back incomplete exports, which is how cycles cause subtle undefined bugs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ESM versus CommonJS in Node are correct? Select all that apply.
options: CommonJS require() loads modules asynchronously
ESM imported bindings are live views of the exporter's variables
ES modules support top-level await
require, module and __filename are not defined in ES modules
Static import declarations are hoisted and resolved before the module body runs
questions.explanation: ESM imports are static and linked before evaluation, ESM lacks the CommonJS wrapper variables, supports top-level await, and exposes live bindings. require() is synchronous: it reads and evaluates the file before returning.

questions.prompt: A dependency's package.json has "exports": { ".": "./index.js", "./utils": "./src/utils.js" }. Which imports succeed? Select all that apply.
options: import u from 'pkg/src/utils.js'
import p from 'pkg/package.json'
import x from 'pkg'
import u from 'pkg/utils'
questions.explanation: Only the keys of the exports map are public: '.' and './utils'. The real file path 'pkg/src/utils.js' and even 'pkg/package.json' are blocked unless explicitly exported, which is why many packages add "./package.json": "./package.json".

questions.prompt: When a package defines both "main" and "exports", Node uses "exports" to resolve imports of that package.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: In all supported Node versions, "exports" takes precedence over "main". Packages keep "main" only as a fallback for very old Node versions and some tools.

questions.prompt: An API's p99 latency spikes under load. One CPU core is pinned at 100% while the database looks idle. What's the most likely cause?
options: The libuv threadpool has too many threads
The garbage collector is running on other cores
Synchronous CPU work in a request handler (e.g. huge JSON.parse, sync crypto, heavy loops) is blocking the event loop
The database connection pool is too small
questions.explanation: One saturated core plus an idle DB points at the single JS thread doing CPU work, so every other request queues behind it. A small pool would show requests waiting on DB connections, not a pinned core.

questions.prompt: You started a service with `node --prof server.js` and reproduced the slowness. What do you do with the generated isolate-*.log file?
options: Run `node --prof-process isolate-*.log` to get a readable summary of ticks per function
Open it directly in Chrome DevTools
Upload it to npm audit
Pass it to `--inspect` on the next start
questions.explanation: --prof writes V8 tick samples; --prof-process aggregates them into the functions where time was spent. To load a profile in DevTools, use `--cpu-prof`, which writes a .cpuprofile file.

questions.prompt: In a CPU flame graph (e.g. from clinic flame or 0x), what does a wide frame at the top of a stack indicate?
options: A function that was called many times but did little work
A function spending a lot of time on-CPU itself (hot self time)
The oldest function in the program
A function waiting on I/O for a long time
questions.explanation: Width is the share of samples. A frame that's wide at the top of its stack is where the CPU actually was, so it's the hot code to optimise. Flame graphs show on-CPU samples, so time spent waiting on I/O doesn't appear.

questions.prompt: Which built-in API lets you continuously measure event-loop delay in production and export percentiles as metrics?
options: process.hrtime()
process.memoryUsage()
os.loadavg()
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()
questions.explanation: monitorEventLoopDelay returns a histogram (min, max, mean, percentiles) of loop delay, which is ideal for dashboards and alerts. os.loadavg is system-wide CPU load and says nothing about this process's loop.

questions.prompt: A login endpoint validates emails with a complex regex. Certain long, malformed inputs make the whole service unresponsive for seconds. What is this?
options: A memory leak in the regex cache
ReDoS: catastrophic backtracking in the regex blocks the event loop
DNS resolution blocking the threadpool
A slow database index
questions.explanation: Patterns with nested quantifiers can backtrack exponentially on crafted input, and regex matching runs synchronously on the main thread, freezing every request. Fix it with linear-time patterns, input length limits, or a safe-regex check.

questions.prompt: A report-generation endpoint does 2 seconds of pure JavaScript computation per request. What keeps other requests responsive?
options: Run the computation in a worker_threads pool (e.g. Piscina)
Wrap the computation in a Promise
Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
Mark the handler async and await the computation
questions.explanation: Only a separate thread or process takes CPU work off the main event loop. A Promise executor and async functions still run on the main thread, and the libuv threadpool only runs native tasks such as fs, crypto and zlib, not your JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: on time
late

late
on time
(nothing)
questions.explanation: The 10 ms timer can't fire while the synchronous loop holds the thread for 100 ms, so it runs about 90 ms late. Timer delays are minimums, and event-loop blocking shows up exactly like this as latency.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
work
after
then

after
work
then

after
then
work

work
then
after
questions.explanation: The Promise executor runs synchronously, so the heavy loop blocks before 'after' is logged; only the .then callback is deferred. Wrapping CPU work in a Promise doesn't offload it.

questions.prompt: Which observations suggest event-loop blocking in a Node service? Select all that apply.
options: The database's own metrics show slow queries
Event-loop delay p99 jumps from ~5 ms to hundreds of ms
Health checks time out under load even though dependencies are healthy
One core is saturated while other cores are idle
questions.explanation: Loop delay, a single hot core and starved health checks all point at the JS thread being busy. Slow queries in the DB's own metrics point at the database instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these, run inside a request handler, block the event loop? Select all that apply.
options: await pool.query(sql) with the pg driver
fs.readFileSync of a large file
JSON.stringify on a 200 MB object
await bcrypt.hash(pw, 12) with the native bcrypt package
crypto.pbkdf2Sync with a high iteration count
questions.explanation: JSON serialisation and *Sync APIs run on the main thread. A pg query is network I/O, and native bcrypt's async hash runs on the libuv threadpool, so neither blocks the loop while you await.

questions.prompt: Wrapping a CPU-bound loop in an async function moves the computation off the main thread.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: async only changes how results are delivered; the body runs on the same thread until its first await. CPU work needs worker_threads or a separate process.

questions.prompt: What's the purpose of the 'three-snapshot' technique in Chrome DevTools when hunting a Node memory leak?
options: Comparing three different Node versions
Forcing three full GCs to free memory
Measuring CPU usage at three points in time
Taking snapshots before, during and after repeated load, then looking for objects allocated between snapshots 1 and 2 that still survive in 3
questions.explanation: Objects created during the load phase that survive after load stops (and after GC) are the likely leak. A single snapshot can't tell normal caches from growth.

questions.prompt: Heap usage grows steadily with traffic and never drops. The code has a module-level `const sessions = new Map()` that stores an entry per request ID. What's most likely?
options: The leak must be in a native addon
Maps are always slower than objects
V8's GC is broken for Maps
Entries are added but never removed, so the Map keeps every request's data reachable
questions.explanation: Anything reachable from a module-level variable lives forever. An unbounded cache with no eviction or TTL is the most common Node leak. Add deletion, an LRU bound, or a TTL.

questions.prompt: In a heap snapshot, what's the difference between an object's shallow size and its retained size?
options: Shallow size is on-disk; retained size is in-memory
Shallow size is the object's own memory; retained size is the memory that would be freed if the object were collected, including everything only it keeps alive
They're always equal for JavaScript objects
Retained size counts only strings
questions.explanation: A small Map can have a tiny shallow size but a huge retained size because it's the only path to thousands of entries. Sorting by retained size finds leak roots.

questions.prompt: Each request runs `bus.on('config-changed', handler)` on a long-lived EventEmitter. After a while, Node prints MaxListenersExceededWarning and memory climbs. What's going on?
options: The warning is harmless; raise setMaxListeners
A listener is added per request and never removed, so the emitter retains every handler and the closures it captures
EventEmitter leaks memory by design
The handler is too slow
questions.explanation: The emitter holds strong references to its listeners, and each closure retains its request's data. Register once at startup, or remove the listener with off/once when the request ends. Raising the limit just hides the warning.

questions.prompt: Container memory (RSS) keeps rising, but process.memoryUsage().heapUsed stays flat. Where should you look?
options: The JavaScript heap: take more heap snapshots
Memory outside the V8 heap, such as Buffers/ArrayBuffers (external), native addons, or allocator fragmentation
The call stack
The source code cache
questions.explanation: Heap snapshots mostly show the JS heap. Growth in RSS but not heapUsed points at external or arrayBuffers memory (check those fields), native modules, or fragmentation. Flat heapUsed makes a JS-object leak unlikely.

questions.prompt: Why be careful when taking a heap snapshot of a production Node instance?
options: Snapshots permanently disable the GC
Writing a snapshot blocks the process and can need memory comparable to the heap, risking OOM, so take it from an instance out of rotation
It only works on Windows
Snapshots expose environment variables to the network
questions.explanation: Snapshotting is synchronous and memory-hungry, so a busy pod near its limit may freeze or get OOM-killed. Drain one instance first. Snapshots do contain heap data such as secrets in memory, so store them securely too.

questions.prompt: A Node service runs in a container with a 1 GiB memory limit and gets OOM-killed by the kernel without a JavaScript heap error. Which setting helps most?
options: --max-old-space-size set to roughly 70–80% of the container limit, leaving room for non-heap memory
--max-old-space-size set to about 2048
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1
--stack-size=65500
questions.explanation: RSS includes the heap plus buffers, code, stacks and native memory. Capping old space below the limit makes V8 collect harder (or fail with a visible heap error) before the kernel kills the container. Setting it above the limit makes kills more likely.

questions.prompt: Which patterns commonly cause memory leaks in long-running Node services? Select all that apply.
options: A setInterval that's never cleared and captures a large object
Local variables in a function that has returned
A listener on a long-lived emitter whose closure references req/res
A WeakMap keyed by request objects
Pushing every request's log entry into a global array
questions.explanation: Timers, globals and long-lived listeners keep their references reachable forever. WeakMap entries go away with their keys, and locals of a finished call are collectable unless a closure retains them.

questions.prompt: Which are valid ways to capture a heap snapshot from a Node process? Select all that apply.
options: Start with --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2 and send that signal
Start with --prof
Call v8.writeHeapSnapshot() from an admin-only code path
Attach Chrome DevTools via --inspect and use the Memory tab
questions.explanation: The signal flag, the v8 module API and the inspector all produce .heapsnapshot files. --prof records CPU ticks, not heap contents.

questions.prompt: If heapUsed rises during the first minutes after startup, that alone proves a memory leak.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Warm-up fills caches, JIT code and connection pools. A leak is growth that continues under steady load and survives GC, which you confirm by comparing snapshots over time.

questions.prompt: The --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit flag can make Node write heap snapshots automatically as the process approaches its heap limit.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: --heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=N writes up to N snapshots when the heap nears the limit, capturing evidence of an OOM you can't reproduce on demand. Writing a snapshot needs extra memory, so it may not always succeed.

questions.prompt: What does Node's cluster module give you?
options: Multiple threads sharing one heap
Automatic distribution of one request across all cores
Multiple worker processes, each with its own event loop and memory, sharing a listening port
A distributed cache across machines
questions.explanation: cluster forks processes, and the primary distributes incoming connections to them (round-robin by default except on Windows). Each request still runs in one worker. Shared memory between threads is worker_threads territory.

questions.prompt: You deploy a Node API on Kubernetes. What's the usual recommendation for using CPU cores?
options: Run one Node process per container, set CPU requests/limits, and scale replicas (HPA)
Run all services in a single pod
Use cluster inside every pod to fork one worker per host core
Disable the event loop and use threads
questions.explanation: The orchestrator already provides process supervision, restarts and load balancing, so one process per container keeps metrics, health checks and memory limits simple. Forking per host core inside a pod often oversubscribes the CPU limit.

questions.prompt: An app stores sessions in process memory and runs 4 instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Users get randomly logged out. What's the proper fix?
options: Move sessions to a shared store (e.g. Redis) or use stateless signed tokens
Use cluster instead of separate instances
Add more instances
Lower the session TTL
questions.explanation: Each instance sees only its own sessions, so a request routed elsewhere looks logged out. Sticky sessions hide this but break on restarts and uneven load. Externalising state is the real fix, and cluster has the same problem.

questions.prompt: A Socket.IO chat runs on 3 Node instances. Messages sent by a user on instance A don't reach users connected to instance B. What's the standard solution?
options: Switch to HTTP/2
Use a pub/sub adapter (e.g. the Redis adapter) so instances broadcast events to each other
Run a single instance only
Increase the WebSocket timeout
questions.explanation: Each instance only knows its own sockets. A pub/sub backplane relays broadcasts to every instance. Sticky sessions are still needed for long-polling transports, but they don't solve cross-instance fan-out.

questions.prompt: In PM2 cluster mode, how do `pm2 reload app` and `pm2 restart app` differ?
options: reload only re-reads environment variables
They're identical
restart is zero-downtime; reload drops connections
reload replaces workers one by one, keeping some up for zero downtime; restart kills and restarts all of them
questions.explanation: reload rolls through workers, waiting for each new one to be ready before stopping the old one. That works best when the app handles SIGINT gracefully. restart stops everything at once, causing a brief outage.

questions.prompt: Inside a container limited to 2 CPUs on a 64-core host, code forks `os.cpus().length` cluster workers. What happens?
options: The kernel adds more CPUs
It forks 2 workers, because os.cpus respects cgroup limits
It may fork 64 workers that compete for 2 CPUs, adding memory use and context switching; size from configuration or os.availableParallelism() and verify
Node refuses to start
questions.explanation: os.cpus() reports the host's logical CPUs, not the container's CPU quota. Oversubscribing wastes memory and hurts latency. Set the worker count explicitly from config and check what availableParallelism reports in your environment.

questions.prompt: Under load, a service that calls `crypto.pbkdf2` (async) and `fs.readFile` heavily shows rising latency even though CPU is not saturated. What's a likely bottleneck?
options: The number of TCP sockets
The V8 heap size
The libuv threadpool, which has 4 threads by default and is shared by fs, crypto, zlib and dns.lookup
The microtask queue
questions.explanation: Async fs and crypto tasks queue for the threadpool. With 4 threads, slow tasks starve others. Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (set before the pool is first used) or reduce threadpool-bound work. Network sockets don't use the pool.

questions.prompt: You scale a Node service from 1 instance to 5. Which features break or change behaviour unless you redesign them? Select all that apply.
options: Stateless JWT verification with a shared secret
In-memory session storage
In-memory rate-limit counters
A node-cron job scheduled inside the app process
questions.explanation: Counters and sessions split across instances, and in-process cron runs 5 times. JWT verification needs only the shared secret or public key, so every instance can verify on its own.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing cluster and worker_threads are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Cluster workers can all listen on the same port
cluster is the right tool to offload one CPU-heavy request so the same process stays responsive
Cluster workers are separate processes with separate heaps
worker_threads can share memory via SharedArrayBuffer
questions.explanation: cluster scales request handling across processes on one port; worker_threads run CPU work inside a process and can share memory. A CPU-heavy request in a cluster worker still blocks that worker; offloading it needs a worker thread.

questions.prompt: In Kubernetes, a common approach is to run one Node process per container and scale with replicas, rather than using the cluster module inside each pod.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Orchestrators already supervise and load-balance processes, so one process per pod keeps resource limits, health checks and metrics accurate. Cluster is more useful on a VM without an orchestrator.

questions.prompt: With the cluster module, workers share in-memory JavaScript objects, so a Map cache filled in one worker is visible to the others.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each worker is a separate process with its own heap. Shared state needs IPC messages or an external store such as Redis.

questions.prompt: How should readiness and liveness probes differ for a Node API on Kubernetes?
options: Liveness should check every downstream dependency
They should run the same check
Readiness failures restart the pod
Readiness says 'can I take traffic now?' (fails while warming up or draining); liveness says 'is the process wedged?' and should be cheap and local
questions.explanation: A failing readiness probe removes the pod from load balancing without killing it; a failing liveness probe restarts it. Mixing them up causes needless restarts.

questions.prompt: A team's liveness probe pings the database. During a 2-minute DB outage, every API pod restarts repeatedly. What went wrong?
options: The probe timeout was too long
Kubernetes doesn't support HTTP probes
A shared dependency failure made every liveness check fail, so Kubernetes restarted healthy processes, adding cold starts and reconnect storms
The pods lacked enough memory
questions.explanation: Restarting doesn't fix the database and makes recovery worse. Dependency checks belong in readiness (if anywhere); liveness should only detect a stuck process, such as an unresponsive event loop.

questions.prompt: On SIGTERM a Node HTTP server calls server.close(), but the process takes much longer to exit than expected. Clients use HTTP keep-alive. Why?
options: server.close() closes all connections immediately
keep-alive is disabled in Node

close() stops new connections but waits for open ones; long keep-alive connections, and active requests on them, delay the callback, so use closeIdleConnections()/closeAllConnections() with a deadline
SIGTERM is ignored by Node
questions.explanation: Since Node 19, close() also closes idle connections, but connections with in-flight requests stay open until they finish. Older versions waited on idle keep-alive sockets too. A deadline then closeAllConnections() bounds shutdown time.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile ends with `CMD node server.js` (shell form). The SIGTERM handler never runs on `docker stop`, and the container is killed after 10 seconds. Why?
options: docker stop sends SIGKILL first
Node can't handle SIGTERM
Shell form runs `/bin/sh -c`, which becomes PID 1 and doesn't forward SIGTERM to node; use exec form `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` or an init such as tini
The handler must be async
questions.explanation: With shell form, the shell receives the signal and node never sees it, so Docker falls back to SIGKILL after the grace period. Exec form makes node itself receive SIGTERM.

questions.prompt: Why do graceful-shutdown handlers often include `setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref()`?
options: To delay SIGKILL
To force exit if draining hangs (stuck sockets, a pending query), and unref() so the timer itself doesn't keep the process alive
To make shutdown faster in the normal case
To restart the process after 10 seconds
questions.explanation: Without a deadline, one hung connection blocks exit until the orchestrator sends SIGKILL. unref() means a clean drain can exit naturally before the timer fires. Keep the deadline below the platform's grace period.

questions.prompt: By default, how long does Kubernetes wait after sending SIGTERM to a pod before sending SIGKILL?
options: 5 seconds
2 minutes
30 seconds (terminationGracePeriodSeconds)
It never sends SIGKILL
questions.explanation: The default grace period is 30 s, covering any preStop hook plus your shutdown. Your drain deadline must fit inside it, or the process is killed mid-drain.

questions.prompt: Why do many Kubernetes deployments add a short preStop sleep (e.g. 5–10 s) before the app starts shutting down?
options: Kubernetes requires it for SIGTERM to work
Endpoint removal propagates to load balancers and kube-proxy asynchronously, so traffic can still arrive briefly after termination starts
To let the JIT warm up
To flush the npm cache
questions.explanation: Pod deletion and endpoint updates happen in parallel. If the app closes its listener immediately, late-routed requests get connection errors. Sleeping first lets routing converge before draining.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices for health endpoints? Select all that apply.
options: Health endpoints go through the normal auth middleware so only admins can call them
Readiness checks the dependencies needed to serve requests
Liveness is cheap and local, with no deep downstream calls
Readiness returns 503 while the instance is draining
questions.explanation: Probes are unauthenticated calls from the kubelet or load balancer, so put health routes before auth (and expose no sensitive data). Returning 503 during drain takes the instance out of rotation.

questions.prompt: On SIGTERM, which tasks belong in a Node service's graceful shutdown? Select all that apply.
options: Close the BullMQ worker so the current job completes and no new ones are picked up
Run pending database migrations
Let in-flight HTTP requests finish
Flush buffered logs and metrics
questions.explanation: Shutdown should finish in-flight work and release resources (pools, queues, telemetry). Migrations are a deploy step; running them during shutdown risks a partial migration when SIGKILL lands.

questions.prompt: A Node process can register process.on('SIGKILL', ...) to run cleanup before being killed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) can't be caught or ignored; the kernel ends the process immediately. That's why cleanup must happen on SIGTERM within the grace period.

questions.prompt: Calling process.exit() immediately after server.close(), without waiting for its callback, can drop in-flight requests.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: server.close() only stops accepting new connections and returns at once. Exiting immediately kills requests still in progress. Exit in the close callback, or after a deadline.

questions.prompt: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per calendar minute. What burst can a client achieve?
options: At most 50 per 30 seconds
Up to 200 in about two seconds, by sending 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00
At most 100 in any 60-second span
Unlimited, because windows reset
questions.explanation: Counters reset at window boundaries, so two full windows can be spent back to back. Sliding-window or token-bucket limiters smooth this out.

questions.prompt: What's the main trade-off between a sliding-window log limiter and a sliding-window counter limiter?
options: The counter allows unlimited bursts
The log stores a timestamp per request (exact but O(requests) memory); the counter weights the previous window's count (approximate but O(1) memory)
The log is approximate; the counter is exact
Neither works with Redis
questions.explanation: A log in a sorted set per key gives precise limits but grows with traffic. The counter estimates using current + previous × overlap, which is cheap and usually accurate enough.

questions.prompt: A Redis limiter runs `INCR key` and then, as a separate command, `EXPIRE key 60` whenever INCR returns 1. What can go wrong, and what's the fix?
options: INCR doesn't work on missing keys
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero
If the process crashes between the two commands the key never expires and the client is locked out; make it atomic with a Lua script or MULTI/EXEC
Nothing: Redis is single-threaded, so the pair is atomic
questions.explanation: Each command is atomic, but the pair isn't. A crash or network failure between them leaves a counter with no TTL. A Lua script (or MULTI) runs both together. INCR creates missing keys at 0 before incrementing.

questions.prompt: A hot cache key (the homepage feed) expires, and hundreds of concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once. What's this called and how do you mitigate it?
options: Cache poisoning; validate cache input
Cache stampede; coalesce with a per-key lock or single-flight, refresh early, or add TTL jitter
Hot partition; add more shards
Write-behind; switch to write-through
questions.explanation: Simultaneous misses on one key cause a stampede. Single-flight lets one request rebuild while others wait or serve stale data, and jitter avoids synchronised expiries.

questions.prompt: With cache-aside, what's the generally safer way to handle an update?
options: Update the cache first, then the database
Update the database, then delete the cache key so the next read repopulates it
Write the new value to the cache, then the database, in parallel
Update only the cache, and sync the DB nightly
questions.explanation: Deleting after the DB commit avoids caching a value whose DB write failed, and narrows race windows compared with setting the value. Writing the cache first can leave it holding a value that never reached the database.

questions.prompt: What should an HTTP API return when a client exceeds its rate limit?
options: 403 Forbidden
429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header
503 with no headers
500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: 429 tells the client it's being throttled, and Retry-After says when to try again so well-behaved clients back off. 403 implies a permissions problem and won't trigger retry logic.

questions.prompt: When is an in-process LRU cache a better choice than Redis for a Node service?
options: When every instance must see the same value immediately after a write
When the cached data is larger than the instance's RAM
For small, read-heavy, rarely changing data where microsecond lookups matter and brief per-instance staleness is fine
When the cache must survive restarts
questions.explanation: Local memory avoids a network hop, but each instance has its own copy, so invalidation is per instance and memory is duplicated. Shared, consistent or durable caching needs Redis.

questions.prompt: This token bucket has capacity 3 and refills 1 token per second. What does it print?
options: true,true,true,false,false,false
true,true,true,false,true,true
true,true,true,false,true,false
true,true,true,true,true,false
questions.explanation: Three tokens allow a burst of 3 at t = 0; the 4th is denied. By t = 1.5, 1.5 tokens have refilled, enough for one more request but not two. The bucket allows bursts up to capacity and then a steady rate.

questions.prompt: This LRU cache with capacity 2 uses a Map's insertion order. What does it print?
options: c,a
a,b
b,c
a,c
questions.explanation: get('a') moves 'a' to the end, so 'b' becomes least recently used and is evicted when 'c' arrives. The remaining order is a, c. A Map's insertion order gives an O(1) LRU without a linked list.

questions.prompt: Which caching pitfalls should you guard against? Select all that apply.
options: Add jitter to TTLs so many keys don't expire at the same moment
Never store per-user data under a shared key, or users will see each other's data
The cache key must include every input that changes the response (user, locale, query params)
Cache 5xx error responses with the same long TTL as successful ones
questions.explanation: Missing key dimensions serve wrong data, synchronised expiry causes stampedes, and shared keys for personal data are a privacy bug. Errors should be uncached or cached briefly (negative caching), not kept for the normal TTL.

questions.prompt: An Express app behind a load balancer that rate-limits by req.ip may end up throttling all users as one client unless 'trust proxy' is configured correctly.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Without trust proxy, req.ip is the proxy's address, so everyone shares one bucket. Configure it for your proxy hops only; trusting X-Forwarded-For blindly lets clients spoof their IP.

questions.prompt: BullMQ provides at-least-once processing. What does that require from your job processors?
options: Nothing: duplicates can't happen
They must finish in under 1 second
They must run in a separate container
They should be idempotent, because a job can run more than once (e.g. after a crash or stall)
questions.explanation: If a worker dies after doing the work but before acknowledging it, the job is retried. Use idempotency keys or upserts so a second run is harmless, such as not charging a card twice.

questions.prompt: BullMQ logs that a job 'stalled' and processes it again on another worker. What's a common cause?
options: The worker's event loop was blocked by CPU work (or the worker crashed), so it couldn't renew the job lock before it expired
The Redis key was too long
The job had too many attempts
The queue name had uppercase letters
questions.explanation: Workers periodically renew a lock on active jobs. A blocked event loop or a dead process misses renewal, so the job is treated as stalled and moved back to wait. Use sandboxed processors or worker threads for CPU-heavy jobs.

questions.prompt: You want an email job retried up to 5 times with increasing delays when the provider times out. Which BullMQ job options do that?
options: { repeat: { every: 1000 }, limit: 5 }
{ priority: 5 }
{ retry: true }
{ attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 } }
questions.explanation: attempts caps total tries and exponential backoff spaces them out (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...). repeat schedules recurring new runs, which isn't retrying a failure.

questions.prompt: A webhook handler may receive the same event twice and enqueues a job each time. How can you make BullMQ ignore the duplicate?
options: Use a delayed job
Use the event's ID as a custom jobId; adding a job whose jobId already exists in the queue is a no-op
Give the queue a unique name per event
Set attempts: 1
questions.explanation: Custom job IDs dedupe while the original job is still stored. Once it's removed (e.g. removeOnComplete), the same ID can be added again, so the processor should still be idempotent.

questions.prompt: A BullMQ Worker is created with { concurrency: 50 }. When does that help, and when not?
options: It always makes jobs 50× faster
It starts 50 processes
It helps I/O-bound jobs (many awaits in flight on one event loop) but not CPU-bound jobs, which still share one thread
It only affects delayed jobs
questions.explanation: Concurrency lets one worker interleave up to 50 jobs at their await points. CPU-bound processors serialise on the event loop and can stall; use sandboxed processors or more worker processes for those.

questions.prompt: Which Redis maxmemory-policy should the Redis instance backing BullMQ use?
options: allkeys-random
noeviction
allkeys-lru
volatile-ttl
questions.explanation: BullMQ stores queue state in Redis keys. Evicting them under memory pressure silently loses or corrupts jobs. noeviction makes writes fail loudly instead, so give the queue its own instance rather than sharing one with an LRU cache.

questions.prompt: An order service enqueues 'send-confirmation' before its database transaction commits. Sometimes the worker can't find the order. What's the robust fix?
options: Retry with attempts: 100
Read the order from the cache instead
Enqueue only after commit, ideally via a transactional outbox (write an outbox row in the same transaction and have a relay enqueue it)
Add a 2-second delay to every job
questions.explanation: The worker raced the uncommitted transaction. An outbox ties 'order exists' and 'job will be sent' to one commit, which also covers crashes between commit and enqueue. Delays and retries only mask the race.

questions.prompt: A nightly cleanup task runs via node-cron inside a web app scaled to 4 instances, so it runs 4 times. What's a better approach?
options: Increase the cron interval by 4×
Use setInterval instead
Use a BullMQ job scheduler (repeatable job) stored in Redis, so one scheduled job is created and a single worker processes each run
Run it only on the instance with the lowest PID
questions.explanation: Scheduling state in Redis means one job per tick no matter how many instances run. Electing the 'lowest PID' doesn't work across machines. A platform scheduler (e.g. Vercel or Kubernetes CronJob) is another valid option.

questions.prompt: What should go into a BullMQ job's data payload? Select all that apply.
options: Raw third-party API keys the worker needs
An idempotency key for the side effect
Small, JSON-serialisable values
The order ID rather than a full snapshot of the order
questions.explanation: Payloads live in Redis and show up in dashboards, so keep them small and reference data by ID (the worker reads fresh state). Secrets belong in the worker's environment or secret manager, not in job data.

questions.prompt: Which statements about BullMQ failure handling are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Throwing inside the processor fails that attempt and schedules a retry if attempts remain
After all attempts are exhausted, the job moves to the failed set
BullMQ guarantees exactly-once processing, so idempotency is unnecessary
removeOnComplete / removeOnFail limit how many finished jobs Redis keeps
questions.explanation: Failed jobs remain inspectable, retention options keep Redis memory bounded, and a throw is how a processor signals failure. Delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once.

questions.prompt: A BullMQ worker that runs heavy synchronous CPU work inside its processor can cause its own jobs to be marked as stalled.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Lock renewal runs on the same event loop. If the processor blocks it long enough, the lock expires and the job is considered stalled, even though the worker is still running it.

questions.prompt: This naive deep merge receives attacker-controlled JSON. What does it print?
options: false
true
TypeError
undefined
questions.explanation: JSON.parse creates an own key named '__proto__'. The merge then reads t['__proto__'], which is Object.prototype, and writes isAdmin onto it, so every object now has isAdmin === true. Block __proto__, constructor and prototype keys, or validate with a schema.

questions.prompt: Which is the most robust defence against prototype pollution in a JSON API?
options: Call Object.freeze on the request body
Wrap merges in try/catch
Lowercase all keys
Validate request bodies against a strict schema (e.g. zod) that only allows known keys, and avoid recursive merges of untrusted objects
questions.explanation: An allowlist schema drops unexpected keys like __proto__ before they reach merge or assign code. Freezing the body doesn't protect Object.prototype, and nothing throws, so try/catch catches nothing.

questions.prompt: What does adding helmet() to an Express app protect against?
options: Rate limiting of brute-force attacks
Validation of request bodies
It sets security-related HTTP headers (e.g. Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options)
SQL injection
questions.explanation: helmet configures response headers that reduce XSS, clickjacking and MIME-sniffing risks. It doesn't touch your queries or inputs, so injection still needs parameterisation and validation.

questions.prompt: A login route runs `User.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password })` with MongoDB. Why is this dangerous beyond storing plaintext passwords?
options: Mongo can't query two fields
findOne is slow
Email isn't indexed
An attacker can send { "password": { "$ne": null } }, an operator object that matches any password (NoSQL injection)
questions.explanation: JSON bodies can contain objects, and Mongo interprets $-prefixed keys as operators. Validate that fields are strings (zod), consider sanitizeFilter, and compare password hashes in code.

questions.prompt: Why should CI install dependencies with `npm ci` rather than `npm install`?
options: npm ci skips security checks to run faster
npm ci upgrades everything to latest
npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json specifies and fails if it doesn't match package.json, giving reproducible builds
npm ci doesn't need a lockfile
questions.explanation: npm install can rewrite the lockfile and resolve newer versions within your ranges, so CI might build with code you never reviewed. npm ci is strict and deterministic.

questions.prompt: A 'fetch preview for URL' feature lets users submit any URL, which the server fetches. What's the main risk?
options: CSRF on the preview endpoint
Higher bandwidth bills only
XSS in the user's browser
SSRF: the server can be steered to internal addresses such as cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) or admin services
questions.explanation: The server's network position is the attack surface. Mitigate with allowlists, blocking private and link-local ranges after DNS resolution, re-checking redirects, and timeouts.

questions.prompt: Why compare an incoming HMAC signature with crypto.timingSafeEqual instead of ===?
options: === can return early at the first differing byte, leaking through timing how much of the signature matched
timingSafeEqual is faster
timingSafeEqual also decrypts the payload
=== can't compare Buffers
questions.explanation: Early-exit comparisons let attackers guess a secret byte by byte from response times. timingSafeEqual takes time independent of where the inputs differ (it requires equal-length Buffers).

questions.prompt: When verifying JWTs with the jsonwebtoken library, why pass an explicit `algorithms: ['HS256']` option (or whatever you issue)?
options: It makes verification faster
It encrypts the token
It prevents algorithm-confusion attacks where a token's header picks a different algorithm than the server intended
It's required to read the payload
questions.explanation: If the verifier trusts the token's alg header, attackers can try 'none' or RS/HS confusion. Pinning the expected algorithms rejects such tokens. JWTs are signed, not encrypted.

questions.prompt: Which practices reduce npm supply-chain risk? Select all that apply.
options: Set dependency versions to 'latest' so fixes arrive automatically
Review npm audit output and automated update PRs
Use --ignore-scripts where install scripts aren't needed
Commit package-lock.json and install with npm ci
questions.explanation: Lockfiles pin reviewed versions, audits flag known CVEs, and skipping install scripts blocks a common malware vector. 'latest' pulls whatever is published, including a compromised release.

questions.prompt: Which are sound input-handling practices for a Node API? Select all that apply.
options: Use parameterised queries instead of string concatenation
Encode output for its context (HTML, URL, shell) when rendering
Validate inputs against an allowlist schema (types, lengths, formats)
Strip the substring '<script>' from inputs and treat them as safe
questions.explanation: Validation, parameterisation and context-aware encoding are the layered defence. Blacklist filters are trivially bypassed (event handlers, casing, encodings).

questions.prompt: Setting a request body size limit (e.g. express.json({ limit: '100kb' })) helps mitigate denial of service from huge JSON payloads.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: JSON.parse is synchronous and memory-hungry, so a multi-megabyte body can block the loop and spike memory. A limit rejects oversized bodies early with 413.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'Is Node.js single-threaded?' What's the most accurate answer?
options: Yes, everything including I/O runs on exactly one thread
Only when cluster is disabled
No, every request gets its own thread
Your JavaScript runs on one main thread per event loop, but Node also uses the libuv threadpool, OS async I/O and V8 background threads (e.g. GC)
questions.explanation: The single-threaded part is JS execution. Native work runs elsewhere, and worker_threads add more JS threads. Saying 'everything on one thread' misses how async fs and crypto actually work.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations run on the libuv threadpool rather than through OS-level async I/O?
options: Promise resolution
setTimeout callbacks
TCP socket reads for an HTTP server
fs.readFile, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib compression and dns.lookup
questions.explanation: File system calls, some crypto, zlib and getaddrinfo-based dns.lookup use the threadpool. Network sockets use epoll, kqueue or IOCP directly. Timers and promises are event-loop and V8 mechanisms.

questions.prompt: A team proposes Node for a service where each request runs about 2 s of numeric simulation in JavaScript, at hundreds of requests per second. What's the strongest senior response?
options: On the main thread this serialises requests; offload to a worker-thread pool or a separate compute service, or pick a runtime built for CPU parallelism
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 128
Node is fine; async/await makes it parallel
Use more promises
questions.explanation: CPU-bound work blocks the event loop, so throughput is capped at about one simulation per core. Offloading or choosing a better-suited runtime solves that; async syntax and the threadpool size don't run your JS in parallel.

questions.prompt: Why can one Node process hold ~10,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with modest memory, where a naive thread-per-connection server struggles?
options: WebSockets don't use TCP
Node compresses connections
An idle connection in Node is just a socket plus a small object watched by the event loop, while each OS thread reserves its own stack and adds scheduling overhead
Node limits connections to 1,000
questions.explanation: Thread-per-connection pays per-thread stack memory and context switches even when idle. Event-driven I/O costs almost nothing per idle socket: the C10k argument.

questions.prompt: What happens if code keeps scheduling process.nextTick callbacks recursively (each tick schedules another)?
options: Node throws after 1,000 ticks
The nextTick queue never drains, starving I/O and timers, so the server stops responding
They move to the threadpool
Node interleaves them fairly with I/O
questions.explanation: nextTick callbacks run before the loop continues to the next phase. A self-renewing tick chain therefore blocks I/O indefinitely. Use setImmediate to yield between chunks of work.

questions.prompt: What does this print when run with Node.js?
options:
sync-in-then
micro
tick

tick
micro
sync-in-then

sync-in-then
tick
micro

micro
tick
sync-in-then
questions.explanation: The then callback logs synchronously first. While V8 is draining the microtask queue, the newly queued promise job runs before Node gets a chance to process the nextTick queue, so 'micro' comes before 'tick'. nextTick only wins when it's queued from the main script, before the microtask drain begins.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: ab
a
b
ba
