Hard links across file systems are allowed only for root; mv uses rename()
questions.explanation: A directory entry is just (name, inode number) and is meaningful only in its own file system. rename() fails with EXDEV across file systems, so mv falls back to copy + unlink, losing the atomicity that same-file-system renames provide. Symlinks store a path, so they can cross file systems.

questions.prompt: Which items are stored in a Unix inode? Select all that apply.
options: Permission bits (mode)
The path of the parent directory
The file's name
Hard link count
File size
Data block pointers or extents
questions.explanation: The inode holds metadata and the block map: size, mode, owner, timestamps, link count and pointers/extents. Names live in directory entries, and inodes don't record parents, which is why one inode can appear in many directories.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the on-disk structure of a Unix-like file system are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Directory entries contain each file's data inline
The VFS layer lets the same open/read/write calls work across ext4, XFS, NFS and others
Bitmaps or similar structures track which inodes and data blocks are free
A file's data blocks must be physically contiguous
The superblock records file-system-wide metadata such as block size and counts of blocks and inodes
questions.explanation: Superblock, allocation bitmaps and the VFS abstraction are standard. Directory entries hold names and inode numbers, not file data, and inodes can point to scattered blocks (allocators just try to keep them close for speed).

questions.prompt: On Linux, ordinary users can create hard links to directories.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Hard links to directories are forbidden (link() returns EPERM) because they could create cycles and break tools that assume a tree. Symlinks to directories are allowed because they're just paths that tools can choose not to follow.

questions.prompt: Renaming a file within the same file system doesn't change its inode number.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. rename() only changes directory entries; the inode and its data blocks stay where they are. That's why it is cheap and atomic regardless of file size.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of SSTF (shortest seek time first) disk scheduling?
options: It needs to know future requests
It has the highest total head movement of all algorithms
Requests far from the head can starve when nearby requests keep arriving
It only works on SSDs
questions.explanation: SSTF greedily serves the closest request, so a stream of requests near the head can keep postponing a distant one, much like SJF starving long jobs. It usually has far less total movement than FCFS, not more.

questions.prompt: Which disk scheduling algorithm is often called the 'elevator algorithm'?
options: FCFS
SSTF
SCAN
Random
questions.explanation: SCAN moves the head in one direction serving requests until it reaches the end, then reverses, just like an elevator. SSTF jumps to the nearest request regardless of direction.

questions.prompt: Head at cylinder 53; queue in arrival order: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under FCFS?
options: 640 cylinders
236 cylinders
299 cylinders
331 cylinders
questions.explanation: 45 (53 to 98) + 85 + 146 + 85 + 108 + 110 + 59 + 2 = 640. FCFS ignores position, so the head swings back and forth across the disk. 236 is what SSTF achieves on the same queue.

questions.prompt: Head at cylinder 53; pending requests: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under SSTF?
options: 640 cylinders
299 cylinders
236 cylinders
208 cylinders
questions.explanation: Order: 65 (12), 67 (2), 37 (30), 14 (23), 98 (84), 122 (24), 124 (2), 183 (59), total 236. Notice the costly 84-cylinder jump back after reaching 14; SSTF is greedy, not optimal.

questions.prompt: Why does C-SCAN give more uniform waiting times than SCAN?
options: It serves requests in both directions twice
It skips cylinders that have no requests
It always picks the nearest request
After reaching one end it jumps back to the start without serving, so every cylinder is visited at the same interval
questions.explanation: With SCAN, cylinders in the middle are passed twice per cycle, while those at the edges wait a full round trip right after the head has passed. C-SCAN treats the disk as circular and serves in one direction only, evening out wait times. Skipping empty regions is LOOK, not C-SCAN.

questions.prompt: Cylinders 0-199, head at 53 moving toward higher numbers; pending: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under LOOK?
options: 382 cylinders
299 cylinders
236 cylinders
331 cylinders
questions.explanation: LOOK goes up only as far as the last request (183): 183 - 53 = 130, then reverses down to 14: 183 - 14 = 169, total 299. SCAN would continue to 199 before reversing: 146 + 185 = 331.

questions.prompt: Why do Linux systems typically use a very simple I/O scheduler (such as `none` or `mq-deadline`) for NVMe SSDs?
options: NVMe drives perform disk scheduling in the OS kernel by design
SSDs have no moving head, so seek-minimizing reordering brings little benefit and the device's internal parallelism is better fed directly
Elevator algorithms damage flash cells
SSDs only accept one request at a time
questions.explanation: SCAN/SSTF-style reordering exists to reduce mechanical seeks. Flash has roughly uniform access time and many internal queues, so heavy reordering mostly adds CPU overhead and latency. Simple schedulers (or none) keep queues full and let the device parallelize.

questions.prompt: Which statements about disk scheduling algorithms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: SSTF always minimizes total head movement
FCFS minimizes average response time
LOOK reverses at the last pending request in the current direction
C-SCAN returns to the start without serving requests on the return trip
SCAN travels to the end of the disk before reversing
questions.explanation: SCAN goes to the edge, LOOK stops at the last request, and C-SCAN serves in one direction only. SSTF is greedy and can be beaten (it took a long jump back in the classic example), and FCFS is fair but usually slow.

questions.prompt: Besides seek time, which factors contribute to the latency of a request on a spinning hard disk? Select all that apply.
options: Rotational latency while the sector comes under the head
Transfer time for the data itself
Queueing time behind other requests
The length of the file's name
The number of inodes in the file system
questions.explanation: Access time is seek + rotational latency + transfer, plus any time waiting in queues. Inode counts and file name lengths don't affect how long the drive takes to service a block request.

questions.prompt: SSTF is a greedy algorithm similar to shortest-job-first and doesn't always produce the minimum total head movement.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Choosing the nearest request at each step can strand the head on one side and force a long trip back; SCAN gave the same total as SSTF in the textbook example and sometimes does better.

questions.prompt: On NVMe SSDs, minimizing head seek distance is the primary goal of the OS I/O scheduler.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. SSDs have no read/write head; the goals shift to keeping device queues full, fairness and low latency. Seek optimization only matters for rotating media.

questions.prompt: Appending a block to a file requires updating the inode, the data bitmap and the data block. What is the crash consistency problem?
options: The writes can take too long to complete
The disk may reorder reads
Bitmaps can't be written while files are open
A crash can occur after some but not all of these writes reach disk, leaving metadata inconsistent
questions.explanation: The disk persists one block at a time, so a crash between writes can leave, for example, a bitmap marking a block used that no inode points to (a leak) or an inode pointing to garbage. Journaling and copy-on-write designs make such multi-block updates atomic.

questions.prompt: In a journaling file system, what is the essential ordering rule?
options: Write the update to the journal and commit it before writing the blocks to their final locations
Only write the journal; never update final locations
Write blocks to their final locations first, then log them
Write the journal and final locations in parallel, in any order
questions.explanation: Write-ahead logging: once the transaction's commit block is durable, the change can be replayed after a crash, so in-place writes (checkpointing) can happen later. Writing in place first leaves nothing to recover from if the crash comes before logging.

questions.prompt: What does ext4's default `data=ordered` journaling mode guarantee?
options: Nothing is journaled; fsck repairs all damage
Data is journaled and metadata is not
Both file data and metadata are written to the journal
Only metadata is journaled, and data blocks are written to their final location before the related metadata is committed
questions.explanation: Ordered mode journals metadata only but forces data out first, so committed metadata never points at stale garbage. Journaling data too is `data=journal` (safest, slowest); `data=writeback` drops the ordering and can expose stale data after a crash.

questions.prompt: After a crash, the journal has transaction T1 with a valid commit block and transaction T2 without one. What happens during recovery?
options: Neither is replayed; fsck runs instead
T1 is replayed to its final locations; T2 is discarded
Both T1 and T2 are replayed
T2 is replayed and T1 is discarded
questions.explanation: A commit block marks a transaction as complete and durable, so T1 is replayed (redo). T2 may be partial, so it's ignored, as if it never happened. Replaying an incomplete transaction could write half an update.

questions.prompt: A Node.js app calls `fs.writeFile()`, gets a success callback, and the machine loses power a second later. The file system is ext4 with journaling. After reboot, the new data is missing. Why?
options: The file system was mounted read-only after the crash
ext4's journal lost the transaction
writeFile only put the data in the page cache; without an fsync, it may not have reached disk, and journaling protects file system consistency, not unflushed data
Node.js writes files asynchronously only after process exit
questions.explanation: write() returns when data is in kernel memory; writeback happens seconds later. Journaling keeps metadata consistent, but anything not yet flushed is lost. For durability call fsync (e.g., `filehandle.sync()`) before reporting success.

questions.prompt: To replace a file durably and atomically, an app writes `config.tmp`, calls fsync on it, then renames it to `config`. Which extra step is needed so the rename itself survives a power loss?
options: Calling sync() on the temporary file again after renaming
Calling fsync on the parent directory after the rename
Calling fsync on the old `config` before renaming
Nothing; rename() is always durable immediately
questions.explanation: rename() changes the directory, which is itself a file whose update may still be only in memory. fsync on the directory makes the new entry durable. Without it, after a crash you may find the old file (or, on some systems, a missing entry) despite the fsync on the data.

questions.prompt: Copy-on-write file systems such as ZFS and Btrfs achieve crash consistency without a traditional journal. How?
options: They never overwrite live blocks; they write new versions elsewhere and atomically switch a root pointer to the new tree
They write each block twice to the same location
They run fsck on every mount
They keep every write only in RAM
questions.explanation: Because old blocks stay intact until the new tree is committed by a single atomic root-pointer update, a crash leaves either the old consistent tree or the new one. The same mechanism makes cheap snapshots possible.

questions.prompt: Which items make up a journal transaction in a typical journaling file system? Select all that apply.
options: The output of the last fsck run
The blocks being updated (metadata, plus data in full-data mode)
A copy of the entire free-block bitmap of the disk
A transaction-begin record
A commit record written once the logged blocks are durable
questions.explanation: A transaction is begin record + logged blocks + commit record; the commit is written only after the rest are on disk so a torn transaction is detectable. Only the bitmap blocks that changed are logged, not the whole bitmap, and fsck output is unrelated.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL's write-ahead log (WAL) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Every commit must flush all modified data pages to disk
With synchronous_commit on, the commit's WAL is flushed to disk before COMMIT returns
After a crash, recovery replays WAL from the last checkpoint
With synchronous_commit off, a crash can lose the most recent commits but does not corrupt the database
Modified data pages can be written to their final location later, e.g., at checkpoints
questions.explanation: WAL is the database version of journaling: durability comes from flushing the log, and pages are written lazily and redone from WAL after a crash. synchronous_commit = off trades a small window of lost commits for speed without risking corruption. Flushing all pages per commit is exactly what WAL avoids.

questions.prompt: Metadata-only journaling, in any mode, guarantees that a file never contains stale or garbage data after a crash.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. In writeback mode (e.g., ext4 data=writeback) metadata may be committed before the data is written, so after a crash a file can show old block contents. Ordered mode prevents this by writing data before committing metadata.

questions.prompt: Replaying a committed journal transaction twice, for example if the system crashes again during recovery, produces the same result as replaying it once.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Physical journaling logs full block images, so writing them again just rewrites the same contents. Idempotent replay is what makes recovery safe even if it is interrupted.

questions.prompt: On Linux, when does a buffered write() call to a regular file usually return?
options: After the next fsync() by any process
After the data is written to the disk platters or flash
After the data is copied into the kernel's page cache and the pages are marked dirty
After the disk controller acknowledges the write
questions.explanation: Buffered writes complete once the data is in the page cache; background writeback flushes dirty pages later. That's why write() is fast and why durability requires fsync/fdatasync.

questions.prompt: Running the same `grep` over a 2 GB log file takes 20 s the first time and 1 s the second time. Why?
options: grep builds an index on the first run
The disk spins faster after warming up
The second run only reads the end of the file
The second run reads the file from the OS page cache in RAM instead of the disk
questions.explanation: The first read pulled the file's pages into the page cache; the second is served from memory. Benchmarks that ignore this 'warm cache' effect are misleading.

questions.prompt: On a Linux server, `free -h` shows 1 GB 'free', 25 GB 'buff/cache' and 26 GB 'available' out of 32 GB. Is the server short of memory?
options: No; clean cached pages can be reclaimed on demand, and 'available' estimates memory that can be given to applications
Yes, only 1 GB is free so it will soon start swapping
No, because buff/cache is stored on disk
Yes, the cache is a memory leak in the kernel
questions.explanation: Linux uses idle RAM for the page cache, and clean cached pages are dropped instantly when applications need memory. 'available' is the number to watch. Unused RAM is wasted RAM, so low 'free' alone is normal.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL's docs suggest starting shared_buffers at about 25% of RAM rather than 80-90%. What is the main reason?
options: Larger shared_buffers disables WAL
PostgreSQL relies on the OS page cache as well, so a huge shared_buffers mostly duplicates cached data and starves the OS cache
The page cache is faster than shared_buffers
PostgreSQL can't address more than 25% of RAM
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses buffered I/O, so pages often exist both in shared_buffers and in the page cache (double buffering). Leaving RAM to the OS cache gives a second, large cache level. Engines using O_DIRECT, like InnoDB, are typically given most of RAM instead.

questions.prompt: A service writing a large file at high speed suddenly sees write() calls stall for hundreds of milliseconds, even though it never calls fsync. What is the most likely cause on Linux?
options: The page cache is disabled once a file passes 1 GB
The file system ran out of inodes
Dirty pages exceeded vm.dirty_ratio, so the kernel throttles the writing process until writeback catches up
write() always performs synchronous disk I/O after 100 MB
questions.explanation: Background writeback starts at dirty_background_ratio; if dirty pages keep growing to dirty_ratio, writers are throttled and block inside write(). Writes are only 'free' while the disk can keep up on average.

questions.prompt: A process reads a large file sequentially in 4 KB chunks, yet the disk sees much larger read requests. Which kernel feature explains this?
options: Demand zeroing
Write-back caching
Copy-on-write
Readahead: the kernel detects sequential access and prefetches upcoming pages into the page cache
questions.explanation: Readahead turns many small sequential reads into fewer large I/Os and keeps the next pages ready before they're requested. Write-back caching affects writes, not reads.

questions.prompt: A Node.js payment service writes a ledger entry with `await fs.promises.appendFile(...)` and then acknowledges the payment. What durability guarantee does it have?
options: Node.js calls fsync automatically for append operations
The entry may still be only in the page cache; a power loss could lose it unless the file is fsynced first
The entry is on stable storage once the promise resolves
The entry is durable only if the file was opened with O_APPEND
questions.explanation: Node's fs write functions don't fsync. Resolution means the kernel accepted the data, not that it's on disk. Use a FileHandle and call `filehandle.sync()` (or `datasync()`) before acknowledging. O_APPEND affects position, not durability.

questions.prompt: Which accesses go through (or are served from) the Linux page cache? Select all that apply.
options: Ordinary buffered read() calls on a file
Reads on a file opened with O_DIRECT
Fresh anonymous heap memory from malloc
Code pages of running executables and shared libraries
Pages of a file mapped with mmap
questions.explanation: Buffered I/O, mmap'd files and executable images are all backed by cached file pages. O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache, and anonymous memory isn't file-backed (it goes to swap, not the file page cache).

questions.prompt: Which statements about user-space buffering versus the kernel page cache are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Calling fflush() guarantees the data is on disk
A power loss can lose dirty pages that are still in the page cache
User-space buffering (stdio, Node streams) reduces the number of system calls
If a process crashes, data still in its user-space buffer is lost, but data already in the page cache is not
questions.explanation: Two layers of buffering fail differently: user buffers die with the process; the page cache survives process crashes but not power loss. fflush only moves data from the user buffer into the kernel; fsync is what forces it to disk.

questions.prompt: If a process crashes right after write() returns, without calling fsync, the data will typically still reach disk because the kernel flushes its dirty pages later.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The data is in the kernel's page cache, which doesn't belong to the process, so writeback continues after the crash. Only a kernel crash or power loss before writeback loses it.

questions.prompt: Regularly running `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` is a recommended way to keep production servers healthy.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Dropping caches throws away useful cached data, causing a burst of disk reads and slower performance; the kernel already reclaims cache automatically when memory is needed. It's a benchmarking or debugging tool, not maintenance.

questions.prompt: A 4-disk RAID 0 array loses one disk. What happens to the data?
options: Only a quarter of the files are lost
Nothing; the other disks rebuild it
Effectively all data is lost, because every file is striped across all disks with no redundancy
The array keeps running in degraded mode
questions.explanation: RAID 0 stripes blocks across disks for speed and capacity but stores no parity or mirrors. Most files have stripes on every disk, so losing any one destroys the array. Degraded mode exists only for redundant levels.

questions.prompt: What is the usable capacity of a RAID 1 mirror made of two 4 TB disks?
options: 6 TB
4 TB
8 TB
2 TB
questions.explanation: RAID 1 writes identical copies to both disks, so usable space equals one disk: 4 TB. 8 TB would be striping (RAID 0) with no redundancy.

questions.prompt: A RAID 5 array uses five 4 TB disks. What is its usable capacity, and how many disk failures can it survive?
options: 20 TB, survives one failure
16 TB, survives one failure
12 TB, survives two failures
16 TB, survives two failures
questions.explanation: RAID 5 spends one disk's worth of space on distributed parity: (5 - 1) * 4 TB = 16 TB, tolerating one failure. Two failures need RAID 6, which spends two disks' worth.

questions.prompt: A RAID 6 array uses six 2 TB disks. What is its usable capacity?
options: 6 TB
8 TB
12 TB
10 TB
questions.explanation: RAID 6 stores two independent parity blocks per stripe, so capacity is (6 - 2) * 2 TB = 8 TB, and it survives any two disk failures. 10 TB would be RAID 5 on the same disks.

questions.prompt: Why does a small random write on RAID 5 typically cost four disk I/Os?
options: RAID 5 always rewrites the whole stripe
It reads the old data and old parity, then writes the new data and new parity
The controller verifies each write by reading it back twice
Every block is written to four disks
questions.explanation: New parity = old parity XOR old data XOR new data, so the controller reads two blocks and writes two. This 'write penalty' is why RAID 5 is slow for write-heavy random workloads. Full-stripe writes avoid it, but small writes don't fill a stripe.

questions.prompt: Why do many storage engineers avoid RAID 5 for arrays of large (e.g., 16 TB) hard disks?
options: RAID 5 can't use disks larger than 2 TB
RAID 5 has worse read performance than a single disk
Rebuilding after a failure takes a long time and reads every surviving disk; a second failure or an unreadable sector during that window can lose data
RAID 5 doesn't support hot spares
questions.explanation: During the long rebuild the array has no redundancy left, and reading many terabytes makes an unrecoverable read error or another failure (often from the same batch of disks) a real risk. RAID 6 or RAID 10 keeps protection during rebuilds.

questions.prompt: For a write-heavy OLTP database on spinning disks, why is RAID 10 usually preferred over RAID 5 with the same number of disks?
options: RAID 10 has no parity to update, so each write costs 2 I/Os instead of 4, and rebuilds only copy from a mirror
RAID 10 offers more usable capacity
RAID 10 needs fewer disks than RAID 5
RAID 10 can survive the failure of any two disks
questions.explanation: Mirroring avoids the read-modify-write parity penalty and rebuilds are simple copies. The costs: only 50% usable capacity, and it survives two failures only if they're in different mirror pairs.

questions.prompt: Which RAID levels can survive the failure of any single disk? Select all that apply.
options: RAID 6
RAID 1
RAID 5
RAID 0
RAID 10
questions.explanation: Mirroring (RAID 1, RAID 10) and parity (RAID 5, RAID 6) all tolerate any one failure. RAID 0 has no redundancy, so a single failure loses the array.

questions.prompt: Which statements about parity in RAID 5 are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Single parity lets RAID 5 recover from two simultaneous disk failures
Parity is spread across all disks, unlike RAID 4's dedicated parity disk
The parity block of a stripe is the XOR of that stripe's data blocks
A lost block is rebuilt by XOR-ing the remaining blocks of its stripe
questions.explanation: XOR parity can rebuild exactly one missing block per stripe, and distributing it avoids RAID 4's parity-disk bottleneck. Two failures leave two unknowns per stripe, which single parity can't solve; RAID 6 adds a second, independent code.

questions.prompt: RAID 1 protects you if someone accidentally runs `DELETE FROM orders` without a WHERE clause.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. RAID copies every write, including the destructive one, to all mirrors instantly. RAID guards against disk failure, not human error, corruption or ransomware; that's what backups and point-in-time recovery are for.

questions.prompt: RAID 0 across four disks can roughly quadruple sequential throughput, but the array fails if any one disk fails.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Striping lets large reads and writes use all four disks in parallel, but with no redundancy the array's failure probability is roughly four times that of a single disk.

questions.prompt: What happens when a thread calls a blocking read() on a socket that has no data yet?
options: The call returns -1 with EAGAIN
The call returns 0 immediately
The thread is suspended until data arrives (or an error or EOF occurs)
The kernel busy-waits on the CPU on the thread's behalf
questions.explanation: Blocking I/O puts the thread to sleep in the kernel until the operation can complete, freeing the CPU for others. EAGAIN is what a non-blocking socket returns, and 0 means end-of-file (peer closed).

questions.prompt: A socket is set to O_NONBLOCK and read() is called while no data is available. What does it return?
options: -1 with errno EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK
It blocks until data arrives
0, signalling end of file
A partial buffer of zeros
questions.explanation: Non-blocking calls never sleep; they fail with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK so the program can do something else and retry when readiness is signaled (e.g., by epoll). Returning 0 would wrongly suggest the peer closed the connection.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between epoll (Linux) and io_uring or Windows IOCP?
options: epoll is only for files; io_uring is only for sockets
epoll is completion-based; io_uring is readiness-based
epoll reports when a file descriptor is ready so you can then do the I/O; io_uring and IOCP report when a submitted operation has completed
epoll requires one thread per connection
questions.explanation: epoll is a readiness model: it says 'you can read now', and you still call read(). io_uring and IOCP are completion models: you submit the read and are told when the data is already in your buffer. The third option swaps the two.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service hashes passwords with async `crypto.pbkdf2` while also doing lots of async file reads, and DNS lookups via `dns.lookup` become slow. What is the most likely cause?
options: Async crypto, file I/O and dns.lookup all share libuv's thread pool (4 threads by default), so they queue behind each other
pbkdf2 disables network I/O while running
DNS is rate-limited by the OS
The event loop is blocked by the file reads
questions.explanation: libuv uses epoll/kqueue for sockets, but file operations, dns.lookup (getaddrinfo) and some crypto run on a small thread pool. Saturating it delays everything else in it. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or using dns.resolve (which uses the network directly) helps.

questions.prompt: Why can't an event loop use O_NONBLOCK and epoll to make regular disk file reads non-blocking on Linux?
options: epoll on regular files reports readiness only once per minute
Regular files can't be opened with O_NONBLOCK
Disk reads are always served from cache
Regular files are always considered 'ready', so O_NONBLOCK has no effect and epoll refuses to register them; a read may still block on disk I/O
questions.explanation: Readiness is meaningless for regular files, so epoll_ctl returns EPERM for them and reads can still sleep waiting on the disk. That's why libuv uses a thread pool for file I/O (and why io_uring was added for true async file I/O).

questions.prompt: An Express route calls `fs.readFileSync()` on a 50 MB file for each request. Under load, latency for ALL routes spikes, including ones that don't touch files. Why?
options: readFileSync uses up all the libuv thread pool workers
Express queues requests by route
readFileSync blocks the single JavaScript thread, so no other callbacks run until the read finishes
The OS limits each process to one open file at a time
questions.explanation: Sync APIs run on the main thread and block the event loop, so every other request waits. Using fs.promises or streams moves the work off the main thread. Thread pool exhaustion is a real issue for async calls, but readFileSync doesn't use the pool.

questions.prompt: A server uses epoll in edge-triggered mode (EPOLLET). On each readiness event it calls read() once with a 4 KB buffer. Some connections stall with unread data. Why?
options: epoll drops events when more than 1,024 sockets are registered
4 KB buffers are too small for epoll
Edge-triggered epoll notifies only on a change to ready; if more data remains after one read, no new event arrives, so the handler must read until EAGAIN
Edge-triggered mode only works with UDP
questions.explanation: Level-triggered mode keeps reporting while data remains, but edge-triggered reports only on the transition. Leftover data produces no new event, so the connection hangs. Edge-triggered handlers must drain the socket until EAGAIN. The 1,024 limit belongs to select(), not epoll.

questions.prompt: Which of these block the Node.js event loop? Select all that apply.
options: JSON.parse on a 200 MB string
await fs.promises.readFile on a large file
A pending setTimeout of 10 seconds
fs.readFileSync on a large file
crypto.pbkdf2Sync with many iterations
questions.explanation: Synchronous APIs and CPU-heavy JavaScript run on the main thread and block it. fs.promises.readFile does the I/O on the thread pool, and a pending timer is just an entry waiting in the timers queue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about select, poll and epoll are correct? Select all that apply.
options: select() is limited by FD_SETSIZE, typically 1,024 descriptors
epoll's cost scales with the number of ready descriptors rather than all watched ones
On Linux, Node.js reads regular files through epoll
kqueue is the BSD/macOS counterpart to epoll
questions.explanation: select is capped by FD_SETSIZE and, like poll, scans every descriptor on each call; epoll keeps the interest set in the kernel and returns only ready ones; kqueue fills that role on BSD/macOS. Node uses the libuv thread pool for regular files because epoll can't watch them.

questions.prompt: In POSIX terms, non-blocking I/O (O_NONBLOCK plus readiness notification) and asynchronous I/O (completion notification) are the same model.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. With non-blocking I/O you're told when an operation could proceed and you perform it yourself; with async I/O the kernel performs the operation and tells you when it's done. Node offers an async API on top of both mechanisms.

questions.prompt: In Node.js on Linux, TCP socket I/O does not use the libuv thread pool.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Network sockets are handled with non-blocking descriptors and epoll on the event loop thread. The thread pool is used for file system operations, dns.lookup, and some crypto and zlib work.

questions.prompt: What does mmap() do when used on a file?
options: Creates a symbolic link in /proc
Maps the file into the process's virtual address space, so accessing memory loads file pages on demand
Copies the entire file into a new heap buffer immediately
Locks the file so other processes can't read it
questions.explanation: mmap creates a mapping; pages are loaded lazily via page faults as they are touched. Nothing is copied up front, which is why mapping a huge file is instant. mmap doesn't lock the file.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between MAP_SHARED and MAP_PRIVATE file mappings?
options: MAP_SHARED writes go to the file and are visible to other mappers; MAP_PRIVATE writes trigger copy-on-write and never reach the file
MAP_SHARED can only be read; MAP_PRIVATE can be written
MAP_PRIVATE is faster because it bypasses the page cache
There's no difference for regular files
questions.explanation: Shared mappings modify the page cache pages backing the file, so changes are visible to others and eventually written back. Private mappings get a private copy of a page on first write, so the file is untouched; that's how executables' data segments are loaded.

questions.prompt: Why can reading a file through mmap avoid a memory copy that read() requires?
options: read() always goes to disk, while mmap never does
mmap compresses data in transit
With mmap the process accesses the page cache pages directly; read() copies data from the page cache into the user buffer
mmap uses DMA while read() uses the CPU
questions.explanation: read() copies from kernel page cache pages into your buffer. mmap maps those same pages into your address space, so there's no copy. Both use the page cache, and both may need disk I/O on a cache miss.

questions.prompt: A process reads a file through mmap. Another process truncates the file to zero length, and the first process crashes on its next access. Which signal is typical?
options: SIGTERM
SIGSEGV
SIGPIPE
SIGBUS
questions.explanation: Accessing a mapped page beyond the end of the file delivers SIGBUS (as do I/O errors behind a mapping). That's a key downside of mmap: errors arrive as signals at arbitrary memory accesses instead of as return codes from read(). SIGSEGV is for unmapped or forbidden addresses.

questions.prompt: A program reads a 1 GB file once, sequentially, from start to end. How does mmap typically compare with read() using a large (e.g., 1 MB) buffer?
options: They're often similar, and read() can win: mmap adds page-fault and page-table/TLB overhead that offsets the saved copy
mmap is always several times faster
read() is impossible for files above 2 GB
mmap is always slower because it bypasses readahead
questions.explanation: For one-pass sequential streaming, large read() calls amortize syscall cost and benefit from readahead; mmap pays per-page fault and mapping costs (and unmapping can require TLB shootdowns). mmap shines more for random access and data reused or shared across processes. mmap'd files also get readahead.

questions.prompt: Most database engines manage their own buffer pool with pread/pwrite (or O_DIRECT) instead of relying on mmap for their data files. Which reason is most commonly cited?
options: mmap doesn't use the page cache, so it's slow
With mmap the OS decides when to evict pages and when dirty pages are written back, making transactional ordering, stall control and error handling hard
mmap can't map files larger than 4 GB on 64-bit systems
mmap'd memory can't be read by multiple threads
questions.explanation: Databases need to control write ordering (WAL before data), avoid unpredictable page-fault stalls, and handle I/O errors gracefully; mmap hands those decisions to the kernel. MongoDB removed its mmap-based MMAPv1 engine in favor of WiredTiger. 64-bit mmap handles huge files fine.

questions.prompt: A program modifies a MAP_SHARED mapping and must be sure the changes are on disk before continuing. What should it call?
options: msync() with MS_SYNC on the range (or fsync on the file)
mprotect() to make the pages read-only
Nothing; writes to shared mappings are synchronous
munmap(), which always writes changes to disk synchronously
questions.explanation: Writes to a shared mapping just dirty page cache pages; msync(MS_SYNC) flushes them and waits. munmap doesn't guarantee durability, and mprotect only changes permissions.

questions.prompt: Which statements about mmap are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Writes to a MAP_PRIVATE mapping are propagated to the file
Processes mapping the same file with MAP_SHARED see each other's writes
Resident mmap'd pages count toward the process's RSS
On a 64-bit system a file larger than RAM can be mapped
mmap reads the entire file into memory when it is called
questions.explanation: Mapping only reserves address space, so huge files work on 64-bit; shared mappings share page cache pages; resident mapped pages show up in RSS. Pages load lazily rather than at mmap time, and private writes stay in private copy-on-write pages.

questions.prompt: Which workloads are a good fit for mmap? Select all that apply.
options: Reading files on an unreliable network file system where I/O errors must be handled gracefully
Random lookups in a large, read-mostly index file
Streaming a huge file to a network socket once
Sharing a large read-only dataset between several worker processes
Shared-memory communication between cooperating processes
questions.explanation: mmap suits random access, data shared across processes (one copy in the page cache) and shared-memory IPC. One-shot streaming to a socket is better served by sendfile or read/write, and on flaky storage mmap turns I/O errors into SIGBUS at arbitrary loads.

questions.prompt: Writing to a MAP_PRIVATE mapping of a file modifies the underlying file on disk.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The first write to a private page triggers copy-on-write; the process then modifies its own anonymous copy, which never goes back to the file. Use MAP_SHARED if changes should persist.

questions.prompt: The first access to a page of a memory-mapped file can trigger a page fault and even disk I/O, although no read() system call is made.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. mmap moves I/O from explicit system calls to page faults: touching a non-resident page faults, and the kernel reads it from disk (a major fault) or maps a cached page (a minor fault). This hidden I/O is why mmap latency can be unpredictable.

questions.prompt: Which hardware component translates the logical (virtual) addresses generated by the CPU into physical addresses at run time?
options: The memory management unit (MMU)
The linker
The L1 data cache
The disk controller
questions.explanation: The MMU performs translation on every memory access at run time (using relocation registers or page tables). The linker resolves symbols before execution, it does not translate addresses on each access; caches store data, not mappings (the TLB caches translations but is part of the MMU path).

questions.prompt: A process must be movable to a different region of physical memory while it is running (e.g., after being swapped out and back in). At which stage must address binding happen?
options: Execution time
Link time
Compile time
Load time
questions.explanation: Only execution-time binding (with hardware such as an MMU) lets a process move during execution, because every address is translated on each access. Load-time binding fixes physical addresses when the program is loaded, so moving it later would require reloading it.

questions.prompt: A system uses a relocation (base) register set to 14000. A user process generates logical address 346. Which physical address is accessed?
questions.explanation: With dynamic relocation, physical = relocation register + logical = 14000 + 346 = 14346. Subtracting (13654) is a common slip; the process never sees 14346, it only ever works with logical address 346.

questions.prompt: A process has relocation register 30000 and limit register 3000. It generates logical address 3200. What happens?
options: The MMU traps to the OS with an addressing error
The address wraps around to logical address 200
Physical address 33200 is accessed
Physical address 3200 is accessed directly
questions.explanation: The MMU first checks logical < limit. 3200 >= 3000, so it raises a trap (addressing error) before adding the base. Accessing 33200 would let the process read memory belonging to someone else, which is exactly what the limit check prevents.

questions.prompt: After fork(), parent and child both print the address of the same global variable and see the identical value, yet each sets it to a different number without affecting the other. Why?
options: The OS stores two copies at the same physical address and switches them on context switch
The same virtual address maps to different physical frames in each process once a write occurs (copy-on-write)
Pointer values are printed relative to the stack pointer, so they always match
The variable lives in a CPU register, not in memory
questions.explanation: Printed pointers are virtual addresses. Each process has its own page table; after fork the page is shared copy-on-write, and the first write gives the writer its own physical frame at the same virtual address. A physical address cannot hold two values, so the 'switch on context switch' idea is wrong.

questions.prompt: On Linux, `ps` shows a Node.js process with VSZ around 10 GB but RSS around 200 MB on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. What is the best explanation?
options: Most of the virtual address space is reserved or mapped but never touched, so it has no physical frames behind it
VSZ counts the whole machine's memory, RSS counts only this process
Linux compresses the process's memory 50:1 in RAM
The process is leaking 10 GB and will be OOM-killed shortly
questions.explanation: VSZ is the size of the virtual address space (heap reservations, thread stacks, mapped libraries); RSS is what is actually resident in physical frames. Virtual memory can greatly exceed RAM because frames are only allocated on first touch. A large VSZ alone does not indicate a leak; a growing RSS would.

questions.prompt: Why can a shared library such as libc be mapped at a different virtual address in each process (e.g., with ASLR) while its code pages are still shared in physical memory?
options: The MMU ignores the virtual address for code pages and uses the physical one
The kernel patches every absolute address in the code each time a process loads it
Each process gets its own private copy of the library's code pages
It is compiled as position-independent code, using PC-relative addressing and indirection tables instead of absolute addresses
questions.explanation: Position-independent code avoids absolute addresses (using PC-relative addressing plus the GOT/PLT), so the same read-only physical pages work at any virtual base. Patching code per process (load-time relocation) would dirty the pages and destroy sharing, which is why PIC is preferred.

questions.prompt: A program was compiled with compile-time (absolute) address binding for start address 0x4000. The OS now needs to load it at 0x8000. What is required?
options: Nothing; the MMU adds 0x4000 to every address
Restarting the OS so memory is cleared
Recompiling (or relinking) the program for the new start address
Setting the limit register to 0x8000
questions.explanation: With compile-time binding the generated code contains absolute physical addresses, so a different start location means generating new code. Relying on the MMU to add an offset is execution-time binding, which this program was not built for.

questions.prompt: Which are benefits of execution-time address binding with an MMU? Select all that apply.
options: It removes the need for any address translation hardware
Different processes can use the same logical addresses without conflict
A process can be relocated in physical memory, e.g., after swapping
Each memory access can be checked against bounds or protection bits
It guarantees there is never any external fragmentation
questions.explanation: Run-time translation enables relocation, protection checks and independent address spaces. It needs translation hardware rather than removing it, and contiguous allocation with base/limit relocation still suffers external fragmentation (paging is what removes it).

questions.prompt: With execution-time binding, a user program can compute a physical address and dereference it directly to bypass the MMU.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Every address a user program issues is treated as logical and goes through the MMU; user code never deals in physical addresses. That isolation is the whole point of the logical/physical split.

questions.prompt: In compile-time and load-time binding, the logical and physical addresses of a program are the same; they only differ under execution-time binding.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Compile- and load-time binding fix physical addresses before execution, so the CPU emits physical addresses directly. Only execution-time binding introduces a separate logical (virtual) address that the MMU maps at run time.

questions.prompt: A system has 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. How many entries does a single-level page table per process need?
options: 2^20 (about 1 million)
2^32 (about 4 billion)
questions.explanation: 4 KB = 2^12, so 12 bits are the offset and 32 - 12 = 20 bits are the page number, giving 2^20 entries. 2^12 is the number of bytes per page, not the number of pages.

questions.prompt: Which kind of fragmentation does paging eliminate?
options: Both internal and external fragmentation
Internal fragmentation
External fragmentation
Fragmentation inside the page table
questions.explanation: Any free frame can hold any page, so there are no unusable holes between allocations (external fragmentation). Internal fragmentation remains: the last page of a process is usually only partly used.

questions.prompt: With 4,096-byte pages, a process needs 72,766 bytes. How much internal fragmentation does it have?
options: 962 bytes
0 bytes
4,096 bytes
3,134 bytes
questions.explanation: 72,766 / 4,096 = 17.76, so 18 pages (73,728 bytes) are allocated; 73,728 - 72,766 = 962 bytes are wasted. 3,134 is how much of the last page is used, not how much is wasted.

questions.prompt: Page size is 1,024 bytes. Logical address 2,500 is accessed, and the page table maps page 2 to frame 5. What is the physical address?
questions.explanation: Page = 2500 div 1024 = 2, offset = 2500 - 2048 = 452. Physical = frame * page size + offset = 5 * 1024 + 452 = 5,572. Using 1,000 instead of 1,024 gives 5,452, a classic decimal slip.

questions.prompt: When a page is evicted, which page table entry bit lets the OS skip writing it back to disk?
options: The dirty (modified) bit
The referenced (accessed) bit
The valid (present) bit
The execute-disable bit
questions.explanation: The hardware sets the dirty bit on any write to the page. If it is clear, the copy on disk (file or swap) is still current, so the frame can be reused without I/O. The referenced bit tracks recent use for replacement decisions, not modification.

questions.prompt: x86-64 uses 48-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages and 8-byte page table entries. Roughly how large would a flat single-level page table be per process?
options: 4 MB
512 GB
32 MB
256 TB
questions.explanation: 48 - 12 = 36 bits of page number, so 2^36 entries * 8 bytes = 2^39 bytes = 512 GB per process, which is why multi-level tables are used. 256 TB is the size of the whole 48-bit address space, not of the table.

questions.prompt: Redis runs BGSAVE (fork, then the child writes a snapshot). Under a write-heavy load, total memory use rises sharply during the save, and it is worse with transparent huge pages enabled. Why?
options: fork() disables the page cache, so the snapshot file is held in anonymous memory
The child copies the entire dataset into its own memory before writing it out
Copy-on-write duplicates every page the parent writes to during the snapshot, and with 2 MB huge pages each small write copies a whole 2 MB page
Redis switches to a slower allocator while a child process exists
questions.explanation: After fork, parent and child share pages read-only. Each page the parent modifies while the child is running gets copied. With THP the copy granularity is 2 MB instead of 4 KB, which magnifies the spike (Redis recommends disabling THP). The child does not copy the dataset up front; sharing is the whole point of fork.

questions.prompt: Where is a process's page table normally kept on a modern system, and how does the CPU find it?
options: In dedicated CPU registers, reloaded in full on every context switch
In main memory, located through a page-table base register (e.g., CR3 on x86)
Inside the TLB, which holds the complete table
On disk, read in on every memory access
questions.explanation: Page tables are far too large for registers, so they live in RAM and a base register points at the top level; a context switch just changes that register. The TLB caches a small number of recent translations, not the whole table.

questions.prompt: Which statements about paging are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Each process normally has its own page table
The offset bits are translated through the page table along with the page number
A process's pages can be scattered across non-contiguous physical frames
Paging eliminates internal fragmentation
Page sizes are powers of two so the address splits cleanly into page number and offset
questions.explanation: Pages map to any free frames, power-of-two sizes make the split a simple bit slice, and each address space has its own table. Internal fragmentation remains in the last page, and the offset is copied unchanged; only the page number is translated.

questions.prompt: Which fields does a conventional (non-inverted) page table entry typically contain? Select all that apply.
options: Physical frame number
Protection bits such as writable or user-accessible
The name of the file the page came from
Present/valid bit
The virtual page number it describes
questions.explanation: A PTE holds the frame number plus status and permission bits (present, dirty, accessed, R/W, user/supervisor, NX). The virtual page number is the index into the table, so it is not stored; file backing is tracked by kernel structures (e.g., VMAs), not by the PTE.

questions.prompt: Two processes can have page table entries pointing to the same physical frame, for example the read-only code pages of a shared library.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Shared pages are a key benefit of paging: shared libraries, shared memory segments and copy-on-write pages after fork are all several PTEs referring to one frame.

questions.prompt: Doubling the page size halves the number of page table entries and also reduces internal fragmentation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Larger pages mean fewer entries, but the average waste in the last page grows (about half a page per region), so internal fragmentation increases. Page size is a trade-off between table size/TLB reach and fragmentation.

questions.prompt: In a pure segmentation scheme, what does a logical address consist of?
options: A frame number and a limit
A page number and an offset
A segment number and an offset within that segment
A single flat 32-bit number
questions.explanation: Segmentation exposes a two-part address <segment, offset>; the segment table supplies base and limit for each segment. <page, offset> is paging, where pages are fixed size and invisible to the programmer.

questions.prompt: Which kind of fragmentation is the main problem with pure segmentation?
options: Fragmentation of the segment table itself
External fragmentation from variable-sized segments
Fragmentation of the TLB
Internal fragmentation within fixed-size pages
questions.explanation: Segments have variable sizes, so allocating and freeing them leaves holes of assorted sizes in physical memory (external fragmentation), requiring compaction or best-fit strategies. Internal fragmentation is the paging problem.

questions.prompt: Segment 3 has base 3200 and limit 1100. What physical address does logical address <3, 852> map to?
questions.explanation: 852 < 1100, so the access is legal and physical = base + offset = 3200 + 852 = 4052. 4300 is base + limit, the end of the segment, not this byte.

questions.prompt: Segment 0 has base 1400 and limit 1000. A process references <0, 1222>. What happens?
options: Physical address 2622 is accessed
The hardware traps to the OS because the offset exceeds the limit
The access spills over into segment 1
Physical address 1222 is accessed
questions.explanation: The offset must be less than the limit (1000). 1222 fails the check, so the hardware traps (addressing error) before forming 2622. Silently spilling into another segment is exactly what limit checking prevents.

questions.prompt: Why is segmentation said to match the programmer's view of memory better than paging?
options: Segments are always 4 KB, which matches typical function sizes
Segments correspond to logical units such as code, stack and heap, each with its own size and protection
Segmentation needs no hardware support at all
Segments are invisible to the compiler, so programmers never think about them
questions.explanation: A program is naturally a set of variable-sized units (code, globals, heap, stack). Segmentation gives each a segment with its own limit and permissions, e.g., code read/execute and stack read/write. Fixed 4 KB units describe pages, not segments.

questions.prompt: Some architectures combine segmentation with paging (each segment is itself paged). What problem does this mainly solve?
options: It removes external fragmentation, because segments no longer need contiguous physical memory
It lets segments exceed the size of the virtual address space
It eliminates internal fragmentation completely
It removes the need for a TLB
questions.explanation: Paging each segment means a segment is a set of pages in any free frames, so variable-sized contiguous holes no longer matter. Internal fragmentation in the last page of each segment remains, and the TLB is still needed.

questions.prompt: In x86-64 long mode, segmentation is mostly disabled (CS/DS/ES/SS bases are treated as 0). What are the FS and GS segment registers still commonly used for?
options: Enforcing stack limits for each thread
Storing the return address of system calls
Thread-local storage and per-CPU data, via a non-zero base
Holding the page table base address
questions.explanation: FS and GS keep a usable base address, so OSes point them at per-thread data (e.g., TLS on Linux user space uses FS) or per-CPU kernel data (GS). The page table base is in CR3, not a segment register, and segment limits are not enforced in 64-bit mode.

questions.prompt: Two processes run the same editor. With segmentation, how can they share its code while keeping separate data?
options: Each process's segment table has an entry for the code segment pointing to the same base and limit, marked read-only/execute
Sharing is impossible with segmentation; it requires paging
Both processes share one segment table
The code is copied into each process's data segment at load time
questions.explanation: Sharing is natural in segmentation: both segment tables point at the same physical code segment with read/execute protection, while each has private data and stack segments. Sharing a whole segment table would share the data too.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of segmentation? Select all that apply.
options: A whole segment such as library code can be shared between processes
Protection can be set per logical unit, e.g., code read-only
Segments like the stack can grow independently of one another
It avoids external fragmentation
Fixed-size units make physical allocation trivial
questions.explanation: Per-segment protection, sharing and independent growth are the selling points. Variable sizes cause external fragmentation, and fixed-size allocation describes paging, not segmentation.

questions.prompt: In a segmented system, which accesses cause a trap? Select all that apply.
options: Offset greater than or equal to the segment's limit
A write to a segment marked read-only
A read of a code segment shared with another process
Segment number beyond the length of the segment table
Offset 0 in a valid, readable segment
questions.explanation: The hardware checks the segment number against the table length, the offset against the limit, and the access type against the protection bits. Offset 0 is always within a valid segment, and reading a shared segment with read permission is legal.

questions.prompt: On modern Linux x86-64, a 'segmentation fault' almost always means a hardware segment limit was exceeded.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The name is historical. Today SIGSEGV almost always comes from paging: touching an unmapped address (e.g., a null pointer) or violating page permissions such as writing to read-only memory. 64-bit mode does not even enforce segment limits.

questions.prompt: Under demand paging, what does the kernel do when a process touches a valid page that is not currently in memory?
options: Restarts the whole process from the beginning
Returns a zero to the process and continues
Brings the page into a free frame, updates the page table and restarts the faulting instruction
Moves the process to the back of the ready queue without loading anything
questions.explanation: The page fault handler finds a frame (evicting if needed), reads the page from disk (or zero-fills it), marks the PTE present and restarts the instruction so the process never notices. Only the instruction is restarted, not the whole process.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of demand paging compared with loading a whole program into memory at start-up?
options: Page faults become impossible
It removes the need for swap or backing storage
Every memory access becomes faster
Pages that are never used are never loaded, so start-up is faster and more processes fit in RAM
questions.explanation: Large parts of programs (error handlers, rarely used features) are never touched; demand paging skips loading them, saving I/O and memory. It adds page faults rather than removing them, and the pages still need backing storage.

questions.prompt: Memory access time is 200 ns and servicing a page fault takes 8 ms. If 1 in 1,000 accesses faults, what is the effective access time?
options: About 208 ns
About 2 microseconds
About 8 ms
About 8.2 microseconds
questions.explanation: EAT = 0.999 * 200 ns + 0.001 * 8,000,000 ns = 199.8 + 8,000 = about 8,200 ns (8.2 microseconds), roughly 40x slower than RAM. 208 ns comes from forgetting to convert 8 ms to 8,000,000 ns.

questions.prompt: With 200 ns memory access and 8 ms page fault service time, roughly what fault rate keeps the slowdown under 10% (effective access time below 220 ns)?
options: Fewer than 1 fault per 1,000 accesses
Fewer than 1 fault per 400,000 accesses
Fewer than 1 fault per 40 accesses
Fewer than 1 fault per 10 accesses
questions.explanation: 220 > 200 + p * 8,000,000 (approx.) gives p < 20 / 8,000,000 = 2.5e-6, i.e., under 1 fault per 400,000 accesses. Even 1 in 1,000 gives a ~40x slowdown, so demand paging only works because locality keeps fault rates tiny.

questions.prompt: A second instance of the same program starts while the first is running. It incurs many page faults but almost no disk reads. What kind of faults are these?
options: Major faults, each reading from swap
Minor faults: the pages are already in the page cache and only need to be mapped
Segmentation faults that are silently ignored
Protection faults caused by copy-on-write
questions.explanation: The executable and library pages are already cached in RAM from the first instance, so the fault handler only installs a mapping (a minor or soft fault). A major fault requires disk I/O, which is not happening here.

questions.prompt: On Linux with default overcommit settings, malloc(8 GB) succeeds on a 4 GB machine with no swap. Later the process gets killed while filling the buffer. Why?
options: malloc returned a pointer into kernel memory, which caused a protection fault
The kernel zeroes the whole 8 GB at malloc time and ran out of time
malloc only reserved virtual address space; frames are allocated on first touch, and when RAM runs out the OOM killer picks a victim
glibc rejects allocations over 4 GB at the first write
questions.explanation: Linux overcommits: the allocation creates virtual mappings with no frames behind them. Demand paging allocates frames as pages are touched; when memory is exhausted, the OOM killer terminates a process. Nothing is zeroed up front, which is why the malloc call itself was fast.

questions.prompt: A process touches a freshly allocated, never-used page of anonymous memory (e.g., new heap space). What does the page fault handler typically do?
options: Maps a zero-filled frame without any disk read
Reads the page from the executable file on disk
Reads the page from swap
Terminates the process for using uninitialized memory
questions.explanation: Anonymous memory has no file content, so the kernel provides a zeroed frame on first touch (zero-fill-on-demand). This is also a security measure so data from other processes never leaks. Swap is only read for pages that were previously swapped out.

questions.prompt: Which steps are part of handling a page fault on a valid page that is not resident? Select all that apply.
options: Trap into the kernel and check that the address is valid
Send SIGSEGV to the process
Schedule a disk read for the page and let another process run meanwhile
Mark the PTE present and restart the faulting instruction
Find a free frame, evicting a victim page if necessary
questions.explanation: The handler validates the address, gets a frame, does the I/O (the CPU runs something else while waiting), updates the page table and restarts the instruction. SIGSEGV is only for invalid accesses, not valid-but-absent pages.

questions.prompt: For which page faults does the kernel NOT need to read the page from disk? Select all that apply.
options: First touch of anonymous heap memory
The first access to a code page of a binary no process has run since boot
A heap page that was previously written out to swap
A shared library page that another process already loaded into the page cache
questions.explanation: Fresh anonymous memory is zero-filled and already-cached file pages just need mapping; both are minor faults. A swapped-out page must be read back from swap, and a cold binary's code must be read from the file system: both are major faults.

questions.prompt: Under pure demand paging, a process can start executing with none of its pages in memory.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The very first instruction fetch faults, and every page is brought in only when first referenced. In practice OSes also prefetch (e.g., readahead) to reduce the initial burst of faults.

questions.prompt: With demand paging, a process's virtual address space cannot be larger than physical RAM.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Only the pages in use need frames; the rest stay on disk or are never allocated. That is why a 64-bit process can map files or reserve address ranges far larger than RAM.

questions.prompt: Why can't the Optimal (OPT/MIN) page replacement algorithm be used in a real OS?
options: It needs too much memory for counters
It only works with a single frame
It suffers from Belady's anomaly
It requires knowing which page will be referenced farthest in the future
questions.explanation: OPT evicts the page whose next use is farthest away, which requires knowledge of future references. It is a stack algorithm, so it does not suffer Belady's anomaly; it is used offline as a benchmark.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm can exhibit Belady's anomaly, where adding frames increases the number of page faults?
options: FIFO
Least recently used with exact timestamps
Optimal (OPT)
LRU
questions.explanation: FIFO is not a stack algorithm: the set of pages in memory with n frames is not always a subset of the set with n+1 frames, so more frames can mean more faults. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and never get worse with more frames.

questions.prompt: Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. How many page faults does FIFO produce with 3 frames and with 4 frames?
options: 9 with 3 frames, 10 with 4 frames
9 with 3 frames, 8 with 4 frames
12 with 3 frames, 6 with 4 frames
10 with 3 frames, 9 with 4 frames
questions.explanation: This is the classic Belady's anomaly string: FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 frames. Assuming more frames must mean fewer faults (10 then 9) is exactly the intuition the anomaly breaks.

questions.prompt: For the reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1 with 3 frames, LRU causes how many page faults? (FIFO causes 15 and OPT causes 9.)
questions.explanation: Working through LRU (evicting the page unused for longest) gives 12 faults, between OPT's 9 and FIFO's 15. This textbook example shows LRU approximating OPT by using the recent past as a predictor of the near future.

questions.prompt: Clock (second-chance) replacement: frames hold A (ref bit 1), B (ref bit 0), C (ref bit 1), and the hand points at A. A fault occurs. What happens?
options: A's bit is cleared, the hand moves on, and B is evicted
A is evicted because the hand points at it
C is evicted because it was loaded most recently
All bits are cleared and A is evicted
questions.explanation: A page with ref bit 1 gets a second chance: its bit is cleared and the hand advances. B has bit 0, so it is evicted. Evicting whatever the hand points at regardless of the bit is plain FIFO.

questions.prompt: Enhanced second-chance uses (reference bit, dirty bit) pairs. Which class does it prefer to evict first?
options: (1, 0): recently used but clean
(1, 1): recently used and dirty
(0, 1): not recently used but dirty
(0, 0): not recently used and clean
questions.explanation: (0, 0) pages are unlikely to be needed soon and can be dropped without a write-back, so they are the cheapest victims. (0, 1) is next: not recently used, but eviction costs a disk write.

questions.prompt: Why do operating systems approximate LRU (e.g., with Clock or aging) rather than implementing it exactly?
options: Exact LRU needs to update a timestamp or reorder a list on every memory reference, which is far too expensive without special hardware
Exact LRU needs knowledge of future references
Exact LRU only works for read-only pages
Exact LRU suffers from Belady's anomaly
questions.explanation: Memory references happen billions of times per second; maintaining exact recency order on each would cost more than it saves. Hardware only sets a reference bit, which Clock and aging use cheaply. LRU does not need future knowledge (that is OPT) and has no Belady's anomaly.

questions.prompt: A nightly job sequentially reads a 200 GB file through an LRU-managed cache of 32 GB. Afterwards, hit rates for the daytime hot data collapse. What is going on, and what is the usual fix?
options: The file's pages are dirty and block eviction; the fix is to call fsync more often
Each scanned page becomes most-recently-used and pushes out the hot set; scan-resistant policies (2Q, ARC, LRU-K, or ring buffers for scans) fix it
The cache has thrashed its page table; the fix is huge pages
LRU is evicting the scanned pages too early; the fix is a bigger LRU list
questions.explanation: Pure LRU treats a once-only scan as recent use, so a large scan flushes the whole working set. Scan-resistant designs require a second access before promotion or isolate scans (PostgreSQL uses small ring buffers for big sequential scans). A bigger cache cannot hold a scan larger than itself.

questions.prompt: Which page replacement algorithms are immune to Belady's anomaly? Select all that apply.
options: Optimal (OPT)
FIFO
LRU
Any algorithm, as long as frames are only ever added
questions.explanation: LRU and OPT are stack algorithms: the pages held with n frames are always a subset of those held with n+1, so faults never increase. FIFO is not, and adding frames does not save an algorithm that lacks the stack property.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms do real kernels use to approximate LRU recency cheaply? Select all that apply.
options: A hardware-set reference (accessed) bit in each PTE
A clock hand that sweeps frames and clears reference bits
Recording a precise timestamp in software on every memory load
Using only the dirty bit to decide which pages are hot
Aging: periodically shifting reference bits into a per-page counter
questions.explanation: Reference bits, aging counters and clock sweeps give an approximate recency signal at low cost. Per-access software timestamps are impossible at memory speed, and the dirty bit records writes, not recency, so it cannot tell hot read-only pages from cold ones.

questions.prompt: Although OPT cannot be implemented online, it is useful as a yardstick for measuring how close a practical algorithm comes to the best possible fault count.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Given a recorded reference trace, OPT can be computed offline and gives the lower bound on faults, so researchers compare LRU, Clock, ARC and others against it.

questions.prompt: What is thrashing?
options: A process using 100% CPU in a tight loop
A disk failing and remapping sectors
The system spending more time servicing page faults than doing useful work
Two threads repeatedly contending for the same lock
questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when processes do not have enough frames for their working sets: each fault evicts a page that is needed again soon, so the CPU mostly waits on paging I/O. Lock contention is a different problem.

questions.prompt: A naive scheduler sees CPU utilization falling and admits more processes to raise it. Why does this make thrashing worse?
options: The new processes are given lower priority and never run
The scheduler's own code uses too much CPU
New processes take frames from existing ones, raising the fault rate further and lowering CPU utilization even more
More processes increase the TLB size requirement beyond the hardware limit
questions.explanation: Low CPU utilization here comes from processes waiting on paging, not from a lack of work. More processes mean fewer frames each, so faults increase in a feedback loop. The fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, not raise it.

questions.prompt: With a working-set window of 5 references, the most recent references are 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 3, 2, 4 (newest last). What is the working-set size now?
questions.explanation: The last 5 references are 4, 3, 3, 2, 4, whose distinct pages are {2, 3, 4}, so the size is 3. Counting all distinct pages ever referenced (4) ignores the window.

questions.prompt: Using the working-set model, the sum of all processes' working-set sizes exceeds the number of available frames. What should the OS do?
options: Switch from LRU to FIFO replacement
Admit more processes to raise CPU utilization
Suspend (swap out) one or more processes and give their frames to the others
Increase the working-set window so that more pages fit
questions.explanation: If total demand D exceeds available frames, someone will thrash; suspending a process frees frames so the rest can hold their working sets. Increasing the window makes demand larger, not smaller.

questions.prompt: In page-fault-frequency (PFF) control, a process's fault rate rises above the upper threshold. What does the OS do?
options: Takes frames away from the process
Lowers the process's CPU priority
Terminates the process
Allocates more frames to the process, or suspends a process if none are free
questions.explanation: A high fault rate means the process has too few frames, so it gets more; below the lower threshold it has more than it needs and loses some. If no frames are free, a process is suspended. Taking frames away would push it further into thrashing.

questions.prompt: Why is global page replacement more prone to spreading thrashing than local replacement?
options: Local replacement lets a process take frames from the kernel
Global replacement forces all processes to use the same page size
Global replacement cannot use reference bits
A process short of frames can steal frames from other processes, pushing them into thrashing too
questions.explanation: With global replacement, a thrashing process evicts other processes' pages, which raises their fault rates too. Local replacement confines a process to its own frames, so its thrashing hurts mostly itself (though it still slows the shared paging device).

questions.prompt: A Java or Node.js service with a large heap starts swapping on a memory-tight host, and latency becomes terrible during garbage collection. Why are garbage-collected runtimes especially hurt by swap?
options: A collection traverses many live objects across the heap, faulting in swapped-out pages one after another
GC disables the page cache while running
Swapped pages are always compressed, so GC must decompress them
The kernel refuses to swap heap pages, so GC fails
questions.explanation: Marking and compacting touch large parts of the heap, effectively defeating locality: every swapped-out page the collector reaches is a major fault. That turns a pause of milliseconds into seconds, which is why such services usually run with swap avoided and memory limits sized to the working set.

questions.prompt: Which observations on a Linux host point to thrashing? Select all that apply.
options: Low user CPU time with high I/O wait
A very high rate of major page faults
High user CPU time with almost no disk activity
High swap-in and swap-out rates (si/so in vmstat)
A large 'buff/cache' value in free with plenty of 'available' memory
questions.explanation: Thrashing shows as heavy swap traffic, many major faults and CPUs idle waiting on I/O. High user CPU with no disk I/O is compute-bound work, and a large page cache with plenty of available memory is a healthy system.

questions.prompt: Which actions reduce or prevent thrashing? Select all that apply.
options: Improving locality in the program's access patterns
Reducing the degree of multiprogramming
Switching to more aggressive global replacement
Starting more processes to keep the CPU busy
Adding physical memory
questions.explanation: Fewer competing processes, more RAM or smaller working sets (better locality) all let each process keep its working set resident. More processes and more aggressive stealing between them make the shortage worse.

questions.prompt: In the working-set model, a window that is too small fails to capture the whole locality, and one that is too large spans several localities.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Too small a window under-estimates the pages needed (causing faults); too large over-estimates them (wasting frames and reducing multiprogramming). Choosing the window is the model's key tuning problem.

questions.prompt: When thrashing causes low CPU utilization, scheduling more processes will bring utilization back up.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Utilization is low because processes are blocked on paging. Adding processes shrinks everyone's frame allocation and increases faults further; the remedy is fewer processes or more memory.

questions.prompt: What does the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) cache?
options: File blocks recently read from disk
Pages recently written to swap
Recently used virtual-to-physical page translations
Recently used data bytes from main memory
questions.explanation: The TLB is a small, fast cache of page table entries, so most translations avoid walking the page table in memory. Data bytes live in the L1/L2/L3 caches and file blocks in the OS page cache.

questions.prompt: Memory access takes 100 ns and TLB lookup time is negligible. With an 80% TLB hit ratio and a single-level page table, what is the effective memory access time?
options: 100 ns
180 ns
200 ns
120 ns
questions.explanation: Hit: 100 ns (one access). Miss: 200 ns (page table access + data access). EAT = 0.8 * 100 + 0.2 * 200 = 80 + 40 = 120 ns. 180 ns comes from swapping the hit and miss weights.

questions.prompt: x86-64 4-level paging splits a 48-bit virtual address into four 9-bit indexes plus a 12-bit offset. Why 9 bits per level?
options: A 4 KB page-table page holds 512 eight-byte entries, and 512 = 2^9
Each level must cover exactly 9 GB
There are 9 general-purpose registers for page walking
48 divided by 5 rounds to 9
questions.explanation: Each page table level occupies exactly one 4 KB page; 4096 / 8 = 512 entries, which needs 9 index bits. 4 * 9 + 12 = 48, matching the virtual address width.

questions.prompt: A 64-entry data TLB maps 4 KB pages. If the application switches to 2 MB huge pages, how does the TLB reach (memory covered without misses) change?
options: From 256 KB to 128 MB
From 4 MB to 2 GB
From 64 KB to 64 MB
It stays at 256 KB; page size does not affect reach
questions.explanation: Reach = entries * page size: 64 * 4 KB = 256 KB, and 64 * 2 MB = 128 MB, a 512x increase. That is why databases and JVMs with large heaps often benefit from huge pages.

questions.prompt: How do ASIDs (or PCIDs on x86) improve performance on context switches?
options: They let TLB entries be tagged per address space, so the TLB need not be flushed on every switch
They make page faults impossible after a switch
They double the number of TLB entries
They let the kernel skip saving registers
questions.explanation: Without tags, entries from the old process would be wrong for the new one, so the TLB must be flushed and refilled with misses. Tagging entries with an address-space ID lets entries from several processes coexist. The number of entries is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why does a multi-level page table use much less memory than a flat table for a typical process?
options: Inner tables are only allocated for regions of the address space actually in use, which is sparse
It keeps page table entries on disk
It stores entries compressed
It uses larger pages automatically
questions.explanation: A process uses a few regions (code, heap, stacks, mappings) in a huge address space. Unused regions just have an empty entry at an upper level and no lower-level tables at all. The cost is extra memory references per TLB miss.

questions.prompt: A heavily multithreaded process on a 64-core server frequently calls munmap and mprotect, and those calls scale poorly as threads increase. What is the most likely reason?
options: Each mapping change requires a TLB shootdown: interrupting every CPU that may cache the old translation so it invalidates it
The page table becomes read-only while threads are running
munmap must zero every unmapped page synchronously
The kernel serializes all system calls from one process
questions.explanation: TLBs are per CPU and not coherent with page table writes, so after changing or removing a mapping the kernel sends inter-processor interrupts to other CPUs running the process and waits for them to invalidate.
