More cores and threads mean more expensive shootdowns. Zeroing pages happens on allocation, not unmapping.

questions.prompt: Which events require invalidating TLB entries? Select all that apply.
options: Switching address spaces on a CPU without ASID/PCID support
A TLB hit on a valid entry
Unmapping a page
Changing a PTE from writable to read-only, as when marking pages copy-on-write after fork
A read from a page that is already mapped
questions.explanation: Any change that makes a cached translation stale (permission downgrade, unmapping, new address space without tags) needs invalidation. Ordinary reads and TLB hits change nothing in the page tables, so no invalidation is needed.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce TLB misses or their cost? Select all that apply.
options: Improving spatial locality of data accesses
Adding more page table levels
Tagging TLB entries with ASIDs/PCIDs
Using smaller pages
Using huge pages for large, hot memory regions
questions.explanation: Huge pages increase reach, better locality touches fewer pages, and tagged entries survive context switches. Extra levels make each miss more expensive, and smaller pages reduce reach so misses increase.

questions.prompt: Multi-level page tables save memory but make each TLB miss more expensive, because the page walk needs one memory reference per level.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A 4-level walk needs up to four memory references before the data access. Hardware mitigates this with page-walk caches and data caches, but the trade-off is real and is why TLB hit rates matter so much.

questions.prompt: Every TLB miss causes a page fault that the operating system must handle.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. On x86 a TLB miss triggers a hardware page walk; if the PTE is present, the TLB is refilled with no OS involvement. A page fault happens only if the walk finds the page not present or the access not permitted.

questions.prompt: A running process issues a blocking disk read. Which state transition happens?
options: Running → Ready (it gives the CPU back but stays runnable)
Running → Terminated
Ready → Running
Running → Waiting
questions.explanation: A process that must wait for an event (I/O completion) moves to Waiting/Blocked and the CPU goes to another process. Running → Ready happens on preemption, when the process could still run but loses the CPU.

questions.prompt: The disk read that a blocked process was waiting for completes. Where does the process go next?
options: Back to New
To Ready, until the scheduler picks it
To Terminated
Directly to Running, because I/O completion preempts the current task
questions.explanation: I/O completion makes the process runnable, so it joins the ready queue; the scheduler decides when it actually runs. Jumping straight to Running would bypass the scheduler, though some kernels may preempt in favour of the woken task immediately.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT typically stored in a process control block (PCB)?
options: Process id and state
Memory-management info such as page-table pointers
The source code of the program
Saved program counter and CPU registers
questions.explanation: The PCB holds what the kernel needs to manage and resume the process: id, state, saved registers and PC, memory mappings, open files, scheduling info and accounting. Source code isn't part of a running process at all; only the loaded machine code is mapped into memory.

questions.prompt: `ps` shows many processes in state Z (defunct) under your Node parent process. What does this mean?
options: They exited but the parent never called wait()
They are blocked waiting on network I/O
They're spinning at 100% CPU
They have been swapped out to disk because memory is under pressure
questions.explanation: A zombie has finished and freed its memory but keeps its PID and exit status until the parent reaps it. Too many zombies can exhaust PIDs. Fix the parent to handle child exit (Node does this for child_process children it spawned).

questions.prompt: A Node app runs as PID 1 in a Docker container and spawns shell scripts that spawn their own children. Zombies accumulate and `docker stop` takes 10 seconds. What's the standard fix?
options: Run Node with --max-old-space-size so the heap is capped below the limit
Use `kill -9` inside the app
Increase the container's memory limit so zombies have room
Run an init like tini (`docker run --init`)
questions.explanation: PID 1 inherits orphaned processes and must reap them, and it gets no default signal handlers, so SIGTERM is ignored unless handled and Docker waits before sending SIGKILL. A tiny init like tini handles both jobs.

questions.prompt: A parent process exits while its child is still running. What happens to the child on Linux?
options: It is killed immediately along with the parent
It freezes until the parent restarts and re-attaches to it
It becomes a zombie forever
It's re-parented to init (PID 1) or a subreaper
questions.explanation: Orphans keep running and are adopted by init (or a process marked as a child subreaper), which later reaps them. They are only killed if something sends them a signal, e.g. when the terminal session ends.

questions.prompt: `top` shows a process in state D for minutes, and `kill -9` doesn't remove it. What does D mean?
options: Dead: the process has exited and is waiting to be removed
Debugging mode
Daemon process detached from any terminal session
Uninterruptible sleep, usually stuck on I/O
questions.explanation: D is uninterruptible sleep: the task is in a kernel path that can't be interrupted by signals until the I/O completes, so even SIGKILL waits. Long D states point to storage or network-filesystem problems.

questions.prompt: Which state transitions are valid in the classic five-state process model? Select all that apply.
options: Waiting → Running
Terminated → Ready
Running → Ready
Ready → Running
New → Ready
questions.explanation: Admitted processes become Ready, the scheduler dispatches Ready → Running, and preemption sends Running → Ready. Waiting processes go to Ready (not directly to Running) when their event occurs, and terminated processes never come back.

questions.prompt: During a context switch between two processes, which information is saved to or loaded from their PCBs? Select all that apply.
options: Program counter
General-purpose CPU registers
The entire contents of the process heap
Process state
Pointer to the page tables (address-space info)
questions.explanation: The kernel saves the outgoing CPU context, updates state, and loads the incoming process's registers and address-space pointer. Heap memory stays where it is; switching page tables changes which memory is visible without copying anything.

questions.prompt: A zombie process still holds its full memory (heap and stack) until its parent calls wait().
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. On exit the kernel frees the process's memory and most resources; only a small process-table entry with the PID and exit status remains for the parent to collect.

questions.prompt: A process moves from Running to Ready when its time slice expires on a preemptive scheduler.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The timer interrupt preempts it; it's still able to run, so it goes back to the ready queue rather than to Waiting, which is only for processes blocked on an event.

questions.prompt: In the N:1 (many-to-one) threading model, what happens when one user-level thread makes a blocking system call?
options: The kernel creates a new thread automatically to keep the others running
Only that thread blocks; the library switches to another
The whole process blocks
The call is converted to async I/O
questions.explanation: The kernel sees only one schedulable entity, so a blocking call stalls every user thread mapped to it. N:1 also can't use multiple cores. These limits are why early 'green thread' implementations were abandoned.

questions.prompt: Which threading model do Linux (NPTL) pthreads and Windows threads use?
options: M:N
questions.explanation: Each user thread maps to one kernel thread, so the kernel schedules them across cores and a blocking call blocks only that thread. The cost is heavier threads, since each has kernel state and a full stack.

questions.prompt: Go's runtime schedules many goroutines onto a small number of OS threads (bounded by GOMAXPROCS for running Go code). Which model is this?
options: M:N
Process-per-request
questions.explanation: Go multiplexes M goroutines onto N OS threads with its own user-space scheduler (work stealing, handoff on blocking syscalls). That gives cheap concurrency and multicore use. It's not N:1, since many OS threads run in parallel.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of user-level (N:1) threads over kernel threads?
options: They run in parallel on multiple cores
The kernel can preempt each one individually on a timer interrupt
Creating and switching them needs no syscalls
A blocking syscall blocks only the calling thread, not its siblings
questions.explanation: User-space switching is just saving registers in a library, which is fast. The downsides are the opposite of the other options: no parallelism, whole-process blocking, and no kernel preemption between them.

questions.prompt: Why is M:N threading hard to implement well, to the point that systems like Solaris and early NetBSD moved back to 1:1?
options: It can't support more than 64 threads per process
It doesn't allow threads to share memory with each other
It requires a GPU
Two schedulers must cooperate on blocking and signals
questions.explanation: The user-level scheduler doesn't see kernel events directly, so blocking calls, signals and priority handling need careful coordination (e.g. scheduler activations). Language runtimes like Go and Erlang manage it because they control the whole stack.

questions.prompt: Java 21 virtual threads mount on carrier platform threads. A virtual thread does blocking socket I/O. What happens to its carrier thread?
options: The I/O is handed to a dedicated kernel thread per virtual thread
It unmounts, freeing the carrier for others
The JVM crashes
The carrier thread blocks along with it until the I/O completes
questions.explanation: The JDK reimplemented blocking I/O so virtual threads park and release their carrier, giving M:N scalability with simple blocking code. Exceptions exist: in JDK 21, blocking inside synchronized blocks pins the carrier.

questions.prompt: How do Node.js worker_threads map onto the OS?
options: Green threads scheduled by V8 on the main thread between event-loop ticks
Separate processes
Real OS threads, each with its own isolate
Threads that share the main thread's JS heap directly
questions.explanation: Workers are kernel-scheduled threads, so they run JS truly in parallel, but each has its own isolate and heap; data moves by message passing or SharedArrayBuffer. They're not processes (a crash in native code still takes down the whole process).

questions.prompt: Which are true of the 1:1 threading model? Select all that apply.
options: The kernel can't preempt individual threads
A blocking syscall blocks only the calling thread
Threads can run in parallel on multiple cores
Very large thread counts (e.g. 100k) are costly due to kernel structures and stacks
Thread creation is as cheap as a function call
questions.explanation: 1:1 gives real parallelism and independent blocking at the cost of heavier threads. Creation requires a syscall and stack allocation, and the kernel schedules and preempts each thread individually.

questions.prompt: Which runtimes multiplex many lightweight tasks onto fewer OS threads (M:N-style)? Select all that apply.
options: Plain Windows threads created with CreateThread
Java 21 virtual threads
Linux pthreads via NPTL
Go goroutines
Erlang/Elixir BEAM processes
questions.explanation: Go, the BEAM VM and Java virtual threads schedule many lightweight tasks onto a pool of OS threads. NPTL pthreads and CreateThread are 1:1 kernel threads.

questions.prompt: With the N:1 model, a process with 8 user-level threads on an 8-core machine can run all 8 threads in parallel.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. All user threads share one kernel thread, so only one runs at a time regardless of cores. Parallelism needs multiple kernel threads (1:1 or M:N).

questions.prompt: In an M:N model, a user-level scheduler decides which lightweight task runs on each kernel thread, while the kernel decides which kernel thread runs on each CPU.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Two levels of scheduling are the defining trait of M:N: the runtime maps tasks to threads, the OS maps threads to cores. That's both its power and the source of its complexity.

questions.prompt: A job arrives at t=2, first gets the CPU at t=5, and finishes at t=12. Its CPU burst is 4 units. What are its turnaround and response times?
options: Turnaround 10, response 3
Turnaround 7, response 3
Turnaround 10, response 6
Turnaround 12, response 5
questions.explanation: Turnaround = completion − arrival = 12 − 2 = 10. Response = first run − arrival = 5 − 2 = 3. Waiting time would be turnaround − burst = 6, which is the tempting mix-up in the last option.

questions.prompt: Which metric matters most for an interactive desktop or terminal user?
options: Response time to first output
Total CPU utilisation across all cores and processes
Average turnaround of batch jobs
Throughput
questions.explanation: Interactive users feel the delay before the first response, so schedulers favour short, I/O-bound tasks. Throughput and turnaround matter more for batch systems, where nobody watches individual jobs.

questions.prompt: A batch cluster finishes 1,800 jobs in one hour. What is its throughput?
options: 30 jobs per second
0.5 jobs per second
2 seconds per job turnaround
1,800 jobs per second
questions.explanation: Throughput = jobs completed / time = 1800 / 3600 s = 0.5 jobs/s. A 2 s average gap between completions doesn't tell you any individual job's turnaround, which includes its queueing time.

questions.prompt: Why do throughput and response time often conflict in scheduler design?
options: Frequent switching helps latency but costs total work
Throughput only matters on single-core machines
Response time can't be measured
They're the same metric measured over different time windows
questions.explanation: Short time slices improve responsiveness but spend more time on switching and lose cache warmth; long slices improve throughput but increase latency. Real schedulers pick a compromise per workload.

questions.prompt: An API's average latency is 40 ms but p99 is 2 s. Users complain. Which scheduling idea most directly targets the problem?
options: Use FCFS with one queue for all request types
Maximise throughput by batching requests into large groups
Bound queueing so slow work can't block the rest
Increase average CPU utilisation to 100%
questions.explanation: Tail latency comes from some requests waiting behind slow ones (a convoy). Separating or bounding slow work and fair queueing cut p99. Running at 100% utilisation makes queues, and so tail latency, explode.

questions.prompt: Why is running a server CPU at nearly 100% utilisation usually bad for latency?
options: The OS stops scheduling at 100%
CPUs overheat and throttle their clocks once they reach 100%
Waiting time grows sharply as utilisation nears 1
Throughput drops to zero
questions.explanation: In simple queueing models, mean wait scales with ρ/(1 − ρ): at 50% load waits are modest, at 95% they're about 19× the service time. Throughput is near its peak, but latency suffers, hence capacity headroom.

questions.prompt: Which goal means 'no process waits forever to get the CPU'?
options: Minimum context switches, so long jobs keep their caches warm
Freedom from starvation
Maximum throughput
Maximum turnaround
questions.explanation: Fairness and starvation freedom guarantee every runnable task eventually runs. Throughput-maximising policies like SJF can starve long jobs, which is why techniques such as aging exist.

questions.prompt: Which statements about scheduling metrics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Turnaround time is measured from first run to completion
Lower turnaround always means higher CPU utilisation
Response time is measured until the first time the job gets the CPU
Waiting time = turnaround time − CPU burst time (ignoring I/O)
Throughput is the number of jobs completed per unit of time
questions.explanation: Turnaround is from arrival (not first run) to completion; waiting is turnaround minus service time; response is arrival to first run. Utilisation is a separate metric: an idle CPU can still give low turnaround for few jobs.

questions.prompt: A system runs both interactive web requests and nightly batch reports on the same machines. Which choices help both kinds of work? Select all that apply.
options: Run everything in one FCFS queue
Run batch jobs at a lower nice value / lower priority so they use spare CPU
Use cgroups to cap the batch jobs' CPU share
Lengthen the time slice for interactive tasks so they finish without interruption
Give interactive work higher priority or a separate queue
questions.explanation: Separating classes of work and limiting batch CPU keeps response times low while batch still uses idle capacity. One FCFS queue lets long reports block requests, and long slices hurt responsiveness rather than help.

questions.prompt: Minimising average waiting time and guaranteeing that no job starves are always achievable with the same scheduling policy.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. SJF/SRTF minimise average waiting but can starve long jobs if short jobs keep arriving. Adding aging or fairness costs some average performance; the goals trade off.

questions.prompt: For a job that never blocks on I/O, turnaround time equals its waiting time plus its CPU burst time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Its time in the system is spent either waiting in the ready queue or running, so turnaround = waiting + burst. With I/O, time blocked must be added too.

questions.prompt: Three jobs arrive at t=0 in order P1 (burst 24), P2 (3), P3 (3). Under FCFS, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: FCFS runs P1, P2, P3: waits are 0, 24 and 27, average 51/3 = 17. Running the short jobs first (SJF) gives waits 0, 3, 6 and an average of 3, which shows the convoy effect.

questions.prompt: Same jobs, all at t=0: P1 (24), P2 (3), P3 (3). What is the average waiting time under non-preemptive SJF?
questions.explanation: SJF orders P2, P3, P1 (ties broken FCFS): waits 0, 3, 6, average 9/3 = 3. 6 is P1's individual wait, not the average.

questions.prompt: Jobs: P1 arrives 0 (burst 7), P2 arrives 2 (4), P3 arrives 4 (1), P4 arrives 5 (4). Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: P1 runs 0–7 (only job at t=0). At 7: P3 (1) runs 7–8, then P2 8–12 (ties with P4 broken by arrival), then P4 12–16. Waits: 0, 6, 3, 7, giving 16/4 = 4. The preemptive version (SRTF) achieves 3.

questions.prompt: Same jobs: P1 at 0 (7), P2 at 2 (4), P3 at 4 (1), P4 at 5 (4). Under preemptive SJF (shortest remaining time first), what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Timeline: P1 0–2, P2 2–4, P3 4–5, P2 5–7, P4 7–11, P1 11–16. Waits: P1 9, P2 1, P3 0, P4 2, total 12, average 3. Preemption lets short arrivals jump ahead of P1's remaining 5 units.

questions.prompt: What is the 'convoy effect' in FCFS scheduling?
options: Jobs migrate between CPUs in groups to share warm caches
The scheduler batches similar jobs to improve cache use
Short jobs pile up behind one long job
High-priority jobs always run first
questions.explanation: One long job at the head of the queue holds everything up; I/O devices sit idle while short jobs wait for the CPU. It's the main weakness of FCFS. Priority-first describes priority scheduling, not the convoy effect.

questions.prompt: Why is pure SJF hard to implement in a real OS?
options: SJF requires all jobs to have equal priority
Next-burst length is unknown and must be estimated
SJF only works on multi-core machines
Sorting the ready queue on every arrival is too expensive
questions.explanation: SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time, but only with known burst lengths. Real systems predict them, e.g. τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). Sorting a ready queue is cheap.

questions.prompt: A low-priority task holds a lock that a high-priority task needs, while a medium-priority task keeps the CPU busy. The high-priority task is stuck. What is this called and what's the classic fix?
options: Starvation; fix it by switching to FCFS
Deadlock; fix by killing the high-priority task
Convoy effect; fix it by shortening the time slice
Priority inversion; fix with priority inheritance
questions.explanation: The medium task indirectly blocks the high one by starving the lock holder: priority inversion (famously on the Mars Pathfinder). Priority inheritance lets the holder run, release the lock and unblock the high task. No cycle exists, so it isn't deadlock.

questions.prompt: Which techniques address problems of priority scheduling? Select all that apply.
options: Priority inheritance for lock holders
Aging: gradually raise the priority of tasks that have waited long
Always running the lowest-priority task first
Priority ceiling protocol
Disabling preemption permanently
questions.explanation: Aging prevents starvation of low-priority tasks; priority inheritance and priority ceiling prevent priority inversion around locks. Running lowest priority first defeats the policy, and disabling preemption lets one task monopolise the CPU.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing FCFS and SJF are correct? Select all that apply.
options: SJF needs no knowledge or estimate of burst lengths
FCFS is preemptive by definition
SJF minimises average waiting time for a given set of jobs available together
SJF can starve long jobs if short jobs keep arriving
FCFS is simple and never starves a job
questions.explanation: FCFS is fair in arrival order but suffers convoys; SJF is optimal for average wait yet starves long jobs and needs burst estimates. FCFS is non-preemptive: a job runs until it blocks or finishes.

questions.prompt: In a non-preemptive priority scheduler, a newly arrived high-priority job interrupts the currently running lower-priority job immediately.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Non-preemptive means the running job keeps the CPU until it blocks or finishes; the new job is placed at the head of the ready queue. Only a preemptive priority scheduler interrupts immediately.

questions.prompt: If all jobs have the same CPU burst length, FCFS and non-preemptive SJF produce the same average waiting time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With equal bursts, SJF has nothing to reorder by length (ties are broken by arrival), so its schedule matches FCFS. SJF only helps when burst lengths differ.

questions.prompt: Round robin with quantum 2: P1 (burst 5) and P2 (burst 3) both arrive at t=0, P1 first. When does each finish?
options: P1 at 5, P2 at 8
P1 at 8, P2 at 5
P1 at 7, P2 at 8
P1 at 8, P2 at 7
questions.explanation: P1 0–2, P2 2–4, P1 4–6, P2 6–7 (done), P1 7–8 (done). So P2 finishes at 7 and P1 at 8. 'P1 at 5, P2 at 8' is the FCFS answer.

questions.prompt: Round robin, quantum 4: P1 (24), P2 (3), P3 (3), all at t=0 in that order. What is the average waiting time?
options: About 5.67
About 7.33
questions.explanation: P1 0–4, P2 4–7, P3 7–10, then P1 10–30. Waits: P1 30 − 24 = 6, P2 4, P3 7, total 17, average 17/3 ≈ 5.67. 17 is the FCFS average (and the total here), a tempting slip.

questions.prompt: What happens to round robin as the time quantum becomes very large (larger than every burst)?
options: It degenerates into FCFS
It becomes SJF
It becomes priority scheduling
It stops preempting I/O-bound jobs only
questions.explanation: If no job ever exhausts its quantum, each runs to completion in queue order: that's FCFS. A very small quantum goes the other way, approaching processor sharing but with heavy switching overhead.

questions.prompt: Why is round robin usually better than FCFS for interactive systems?
options: It requires knowing burst lengths
It always gives a lower average turnaround time than FCFS
A ready job gets a turn within about (n − 1) × quantum
It never context-switches
questions.explanation: RR's strength is response time: no job waits behind a long one for more than a bounded time. Its average turnaround can actually be worse than FCFS or SJF, especially when bursts are similar.

questions.prompt: In a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ), a job uses its entire time allotment at the top priority level. What usually happens?
options: It is terminated
It is promoted to an even higher level as a reward
It stays at the same level, because MLFQ never moves running jobs
It is demoted to a lower queue
questions.explanation: MLFQ learns from behaviour: jobs that burn their full allotment are treated as CPU-bound and moved down, while jobs that block early (interactive, I/O-bound) stay high. That approximates SJF without knowing burst lengths.

questions.prompt: Why does MLFQ periodically boost all jobs back to the top queue?
options: To force all jobs into FCFS order
To stop starvation and re-rank changed jobs
To reduce memory used by the queues
To make CPU-bound jobs finish before interactive ones arrive
questions.explanation: Without a boost, a steady stream of interactive jobs could starve CPU-bound jobs in low queues forever, and a job that turned interactive would stay stuck low. The boost period is a tuning knob between fairness and responsiveness.

questions.prompt: A program games an MLFQ scheduler by issuing a tiny I/O just before its quantum expires, so it stays at top priority while using most of the CPU. What's the standard fix?
options: Ban I/O for CPU-bound programs
Make the quantum longer so yielding early gains nothing
Track total CPU per level, regardless of yields
Switch to FCFS
questions.explanation: Tracking cumulative CPU time per level (rather than resetting on each yield) removes the incentive to yield early. Longer quanta don't fix gaming; they just change when the trick is needed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about choosing a round-robin quantum are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Too large a quantum hurts response time
A smaller quantum always increases throughput
A quantum slightly longer than a typical interactive burst lets those jobs finish in one slice
It should be large relative to context-switch cost, or overhead dominates
The quantum must equal the average burst length exactly
questions.explanation: Quantum choice balances switching overhead against responsiveness; letting typical short bursts complete in one slice works well. There's no 'exactly the average' rule, and tiny quanta reduce throughput because of overhead.

questions.prompt: Which are core rules of a typical MLFQ scheduler? Select all that apply.
options: New jobs start at the highest priority
Higher-priority queues run before lower ones
Jobs never move between queues
Jobs in the same queue are scheduled round robin
Lower queues often get longer time quanta
questions.explanation: MLFQ runs higher queues first, round-robins within a queue, starts new jobs high and gives lower (CPU-bound) queues longer slices to reduce switching. Movement between queues is the 'feedback' in its name.

questions.prompt: Round robin always gives a lower average turnaround time than FCFS.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. With equal-length jobs, RR interleaves them so they all finish near the end, making average turnaround worse than FCFS. RR's benefit is response time, not turnaround.

questions.prompt: MLFQ tends to favour I/O-bound, interactive jobs without needing to know burst lengths in advance.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Jobs that block before using their allotment stay in high-priority queues, so the scheduler infers 'short burst' from observed behaviour instead of needing predictions like pure SJF.

questions.prompt: On modern hardware, roughly what order of magnitude is the direct cost of a thread context switch on Linux?
options: Microseconds (about 1–10 µs)
Seconds
Milliseconds (about 10–100 ms)
Nanoseconds (about 1–10 ns)
questions.explanation: Saving and restoring state plus scheduler work takes on the order of microseconds. The indirect cost of cold caches and TLB misses afterwards can exceed that. Milliseconds is the scale of time slices, not of the switch itself.

questions.prompt: What is usually the biggest hidden cost of frequent context switches?
options: Network packets being dropped while the CPU is busy switching
The kernel writing each PCB out to disk on every switch
Cache and TLB pollution
Recompiling the program
questions.explanation: After a switch, the CPU caches hold the previous thread's data, so the new thread takes many cache misses. That indirect cost often dwarfs the few microseconds of direct switching. PCBs stay in memory.

questions.prompt: A thread-per-request Java service handles 5,000 concurrent slow requests with 5,000 threads, and CPU shows high system time. What's the most likely explanation?
options: TCP keepalive is disabled
The garbage collector runs too often because of short-lived objects
Thousands of threads: switching and stack overhead
The JIT compiler is disabled
questions.explanation: Thousands of kernel threads mean lots of switching and kernel bookkeeping (system time) and large stack reservations. Event loops (Node, Netty) or virtual threads handle the same concurrency with far fewer OS threads.

questions.prompt: For a purely CPU-bound task pool on an 8-core machine, what thread count is usually best?
options: As many as there are tasks
About 8 (one per core)
About 800
1, to avoid switching
questions.explanation: CPU-bound threads beyond the core count just take turns, adding switches without adding throughput. One thread wastes 7 cores. I/O-bound pools can be larger, since threads spend time blocked.

questions.prompt: How do PCID (x86) or ASID (Arm) tags reduce the cost of switching between processes?
options: They make the CPU clock faster
They let two processes share one stack
TLB entries are tagged, so no full flush
They disable virtual memory for trusted processes to skip translation
questions.explanation: Without tags, changing page tables would flush the TLB and every following access would miss. Tags let entries from several address spaces coexist, which became more important after KPTI (Meltdown mitigation) increased page-table switching.

questions.prompt: Why is an event loop (like Node.js) cheaper than thread-per-connection for 50k mostly idle connections, in terms of switching?
options: Event loops run on faster, dedicated CPU cores
Threads can't handle more than 1,000 connections
No kernel thread per connection to switch between
Event loops don't use the kernel at all, so there are no syscalls
questions.explanation: The event loop switches between connections in user space with a function call, and the kernel reports only ready sockets. The kernel is still involved (epoll, syscalls); there's just no thread per connection to schedule.

questions.prompt: A low-latency trading process busy-polls a network queue on an isolated core instead of blocking. Why accept 100% CPU on that core?
options: It avoids wakeup switches and their jitter
It deliberately increases cache misses on other cores
Busy-polling saves power
Blocking calls are not supported on Linux for network queues
questions.explanation: Blocking means a wakeup, a context switch and cold caches on every message, adding microseconds and variance. Spinning on a dedicated core keeps the thread hot. It wastes CPU, so it only makes sense when latency is worth it.

questions.prompt: Which design choices reduce context-switch overhead in a backend service? Select all that apply.
options: Use very fine-grained locks that threads frequently block on
Batch small work items so each wakeup does more work
Use async I/O or an event loop instead of a thread per blocked connection
Spawn a new OS thread for every incoming request
Size CPU-bound thread pools near the core count
questions.explanation: Fewer runnable threads, non-blocking I/O and batching all reduce how often the scheduler switches. Thread-per-request and lock contention that forces frequent blocking both increase switches.

questions.prompt: `pidstat -w` shows a service with very high voluntary context switches per second. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.
options: Threads sleeping and waking in tight polling loops with short sleeps
Threads frequently blocking on contended locks
The process being CPU-bound and preempted by the timer
Many small blocking I/O calls (e.g. unbuffered tiny writes)
Too few runnable threads to fill the cores
questions.explanation: Voluntary switches mean the thread chose to wait: lock contention, small blocking I/O or short sleeps. Timer preemption of CPU-bound work shows up as involuntary switches, and having few runnable threads doesn't in itself cause switching.

questions.prompt: Switching between two coroutines or async tasks in the same thread usually costs much less than an OS thread context switch, because it doesn't enter the kernel.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A user-space switch is roughly a function call plus saving a little state, with no syscall, scheduler run or address-space change. That's why event loops and green threads scale to huge concurrency.

questions.prompt: Adding more threads to a CPU-bound workload always increases throughput, as long as there's enough RAM for their stacks.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Past the number of cores, extra CPU-bound threads only add context switches and cache contention, so throughput flattens or drops. RAM isn't the limiting factor here; the cores are.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service calls fs.readFile(). How do the file's bytes actually get read from disk?
options: libuv reads the disk controller's registers directly from user space
V8 runs with kernel privileges, so it can access the device itself
The process issues system calls (open/read) that trap into the kernel, which does the I/O and copies data back
The file is always already mapped into the process, so no kernel involvement is needed
questions.explanation: User-mode code cannot touch hardware. libuv (on a threadpool thread) issues open/read syscalls; the CPU switches to kernel mode, the kernel performs the I/O and copies bytes into the user buffer. libuv is ordinary user-space code with no special access to devices.

questions.prompt: Why do CPUs distinguish between user mode and kernel mode at all?
options: So compiled languages can be separated from interpreted languages
So privileged operations like changing page tables or talking to devices can only be done by trusted kernel code
So user programs can run faster by skipping memory protection checks
So the kernel can run several programs on one core without a scheduler
questions.explanation: Hardware privilege levels stop a buggy or malicious program from reconfiguring memory mappings, disabling interrupts or doing raw I/O, which is what isolates processes from each other and from the OS. Memory protection is enforced in user mode, not skipped.

questions.prompt: On Linux x86-64, a user-mode program executes a privileged instruction such as HLT. What normally happens?
options: The CPU switches to kernel mode and executes the instruction on the program's behalf
The instruction is silently ignored and execution continues
The whole machine halts until the next hardware interrupt arrives
The CPU raises a protection fault, the kernel handles it, and the process usually receives SIGSEGV
questions.explanation: Privileged instructions in ring 3 trigger a general-protection exception. The kernel's handler runs and, for a user process, delivers a signal (typically SIGSEGV) that kills it. The CPU never grants the privilege just because user code asked for it.

questions.prompt: Why is a system call noticeably more expensive than an ordinary function call?
options: System calls must be serialised through a single global kernel lock
Every system call creates a short-lived kernel process to handle it
System calls always force the scheduler to switch to a different process
It needs a mode switch: saving state, entering the kernel entry path, validating arguments, and often extra mitigation work
questions.explanation: A syscall switches privilege level, saves/restores registers, runs the kernel entry/exit path and argument checks, and with Spectre/Meltdown mitigations can flush or switch page tables. It does not necessarily switch to another process; that only happens if the call blocks or the scheduler decides to.

questions.prompt: strace on a slow logging service shows millions of write() calls, each writing a handful of bytes. What is the most effective fix?
options: Run the service as root so writes skip permission checks
Switch the log file to a faster filesystem with the same write pattern
Buffer log lines in user space and flush them in larger chunks
Open and close the log file around each write to keep it fresh
questions.explanation: The cost is dominated by per-syscall overhead, not bytes. Batching many lines into one write() cuts the number of mode switches dramatically. Running as root doesn't remove the syscall cost, and a different filesystem keeps the same millions of transitions.

questions.prompt: On Linux, why can clock_gettime() typically return the current time without the cost of a full system call?
options: The kernel pushes the time into a register on every context switch
The kernel maps code and data into the process via the vDSO, so the time is read in user mode
Reading the clock is not privileged, so the CPU skips the mode switch for all time syscalls
The C library caches the time once at process start and adds an offset
questions.explanation: The vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object) is a kernel-provided page mapped into every process; time functions read kernel-maintained data there without trapping into the kernel. libc does not cache a start time, which would drift and break on clock adjustments.

questions.prompt: After enabling Kernel Page-Table Isolation (the Meltdown mitigation), syscall-heavy workloads got slower. Why?
options: KPTI makes the kernel re-validate the binary's signature on every system call
KPTI disables the CPU cache whenever kernel code is running
KPTI forces every system call to be executed on a dedicated CPU core
Most kernel memory is unmapped from user page tables, so each kernel entry/exit switches page tables and can lose TLB entries
questions.explanation: KPTI keeps separate page tables for user and kernel mode so user code can't speculatively read kernel memory. Switching page tables on every transition adds overhead (mitigated partly by PCID). Caches stay enabled; the cost is the page-table switch and TLB effects.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations require entering the kernel through a system call? Select all that apply.
options: Sending bytes on a TCP socket
Requesting new memory pages from the OS with mmap or brk
Sorting an in-memory JavaScript array
Adding two integers already held in registers
Opening a file
questions.explanation: Files, memory mappings and sockets are kernel-managed resources, so they need syscalls. Arithmetic on registers and sorting data already in the process's memory run entirely in user mode.

questions.prompt: Which statements about how a system call works on x86-64 Linux are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The user program can choose any kernel address to jump to when it enters the kernel
Errors come back as negative values, which libc turns into a -1 return plus errno
Arguments are passed in registers, and the kernel must validate any user-space pointers before using them
The syscall instruction switches to ring 0 and jumps to an entry point the kernel configured
questions.explanation: The entry point is fixed by the kernel (via an MSR), so user code can't pick arbitrary kernel addresses; that would defeat protection. User pointers are checked and copied with helpers like copy_from_user, and the raw -errno return is converted by libc.

questions.prompt: A process running as the root user executes its own code in kernel mode.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Root is a user-space identity that passes permission checks; its code still runs in user mode (ring 3) and must use syscalls like any other process. Kernel mode is a CPU state reserved for kernel code.

questions.prompt: When a thread calls a blocking read() on a socket with no data available, the kernel typically puts that thread to sleep and runs other threads until data arrives.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The thread enters the kernel, is placed on a wait queue and descheduled; when data arrives the kernel wakes it. It does not spin in user mode, which is why blocking I/O doesn't burn CPU.

questions.prompt: What is the defining property of Discretionary Access Control (DAC)?
options: Access is granted based on the security clearance level of the user
A central policy set by administrators decides access, and owners cannot change it
The owner of a resource decides who else may access it, e.g. via chmod or ACLs
Access decisions are made by the application rather than the operating system
questions.explanation: In DAC, access is at the owner's discretion: Unix rwx bits and ACLs let the owner grant others access. A central policy owners can't override is Mandatory Access Control.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits Mandatory Access Control (MAC), such as SELinux or AppArmor?
options: A per-file password that users must enter before opening the file
A set of permission bits that the file owner can change at any time
A system-wide policy enforced by the kernel that ordinary users, even file owners, cannot override
A firewall that blocks network access for unknown processes
questions.explanation: MAC rules come from a central policy (types, labels, profiles) enforced by the kernel; an owner running chmod can't relax them. Owner-changeable permission bits are the DAC model.

questions.prompt: A file is listed as `-rw-r----- alice devs report.txt`. Bob is in the devs group but is not alice. What can Bob do?
questions.code: -rw-r----- 1 alice devs 4096 Oct  3 10:00 report.txt
options: Read it but not modify it
Write but not read, because group bits are reversed
Nothing, because only the owner has any permissions
Read and write it, because he belongs to the owning group
questions.explanation: The permission triplets are owner (rw-), group (r--), others (---). Bob matches the group class, which grants read only. Being in the group doesn't give the owner's write bit.

questions.prompt: A web server running as www-data is compromised on a RHEL host with SELinux enforcing the default targeted policy. It tries to read a world-readable file (mode 644) in /home/alice. What is the most likely result?
options: Denied: Linux never lets one user read another user's home directory
Allowed: SELinux only restricts processes running as root
Denied: the web server's SELinux domain isn't allowed to read user home content, even though DAC permits it
Allowed: mode 644 means every process can read the file
questions.explanation: Linux checks DAC and then the LSM; both must allow. The httpd_t domain has no rule to read user_home_t files unless an admin enables a boolean like httpd_enable_homedirs. SELinux applies to all processes, not just root.

questions.prompt: On a Linux system with SELinux in enforcing mode, can a process running as root (UID 0) bypass an SELinux denial?
options: No: root's capabilities bypass DAC checks, but the SELinux policy for its domain still applies
Yes, UID 0 bypasses every access check in the kernel
No, root processes are blocked from all file access under SELinux
Yes, as long as the process holds CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
questions.explanation: Capabilities like CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE skip DAC permission bits, but MAC is a separate check keyed on the process's SELinux domain. Root can only turn SELinux off or change policy if its domain is allowed to. Root isn't blocked from everything; it's confined to its policy.

questions.prompt: /usr/bin/passwd is owned by root and has the setuid bit set. Why?
options: So the program runs inside a sandbox with fewer privileges than the caller
So only root is allowed to run the program
So it runs with root's effective UID and can update /etc/shadow through a controlled interface
So the kernel verifies the binary's checksum before executing it
questions.explanation: setuid makes the process take the file owner's effective UID. Normal users can run passwd, which then has root's rights to edit /etc/shadow but only through its own logic. It doesn't restrict who runs it; it elevates privilege, which is why setuid binaries are high-value targets.

questions.prompt: /tmp has mode drwxrwxrwt (1777). What does the trailing t (sticky bit) achieve?
options: Files in /tmp are kept in memory instead of on disk
Files in the directory are deleted automatically at reboot
Only root can create new files in the directory
Users can delete or rename only their own files, even though everyone can write to the directory
questions.explanation: Without the sticky bit, write permission on a directory lets anyone unlink any entry. With it, only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root can remove or rename entries. Clearing /tmp at boot is a separate distro setting.

questions.prompt: Which of these are Mandatory Access Control mechanisms? Select all that apply.
options: chmod 600 on a private key
AppArmor
SELinux
POSIX ACLs set with setfacl
Windows Mandatory Integrity Control
questions.explanation: SELinux, AppArmor and Windows integrity levels are policy-driven and can't be relaxed by resource owners. chmod and setfacl are owner-controlled, so they are DAC even though ACLs are finer-grained.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Linux file and directory permissions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Read on a directory lets you list names; execute lets you traverse it and access entries by name
Deleting a file needs write and execute permission on its directory, not write permission on the file
With execute but not read on a directory, you can still open a file inside it if you know its exact name
A file with mode 000 cannot be read by root
questions.explanation: Deletion modifies the directory, so the directory's bits matter. x on a directory permits lookup by name even without r (listing). Root bypasses DAC bits via CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, so mode 000 does not stop root reading the file.

questions.prompt: Under discretionary access control, a file's owner can grant read access to another user without involving an administrator.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. That is what 'discretionary' means: the owner can chmod the file or add an ACL entry. Under MAC, a central policy would also have to allow it.

questions.prompt: Under mandatory access control, a file's owner can use chmod to let a process read the file even if the MAC policy forbids that process from reading it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. chmod changes only the DAC bits. The kernel still checks the MAC policy afterwards, and both must allow access, so the denial stands.

questions.prompt: What is a stack buffer overflow?
options: Recursing so deeply that the stack runs out of space
Reading uninitialised memory from a buffer on the stack
Allocating more heap memory than the process limit allows
Writing past the end of a stack-allocated buffer and overwriting adjacent stack data such as the saved return address
questions.explanation: An overflow is an out-of-bounds write into neighbouring memory: other locals, the saved frame pointer and the return address. Running out of stack from deep recursion is a stack overflow (exhaustion), a different bug.

questions.prompt: What is the security bug in this C function?
options: 16 bytes is too small for the stack, so the function always crashes
gets() does no bounds checking, so input longer than 15 characters overflows name
name is not initialised to zero before being read into
printf with %s can execute the name as code
questions.explanation: gets() reads until newline regardless of buffer size; it was removed from C11 for exactly this reason. Use fgets(name, sizeof name, stdin). Here printf uses a fixed format string, so it isn't a format-string bug.

questions.prompt: In a classic stack-smashing attack, what does the attacker usually aim to overwrite, and why?
options: The function's local loop counter, so the loop runs forever
The heap allocator's metadata, so malloc returns NULL
The saved return address, so the function returns to code the attacker chooses
The program's environment variables, so it reads the wrong config
questions.explanation: The return address sits above the locals on the stack. Overwriting it hijacks control flow when the function executes ret. Allocator metadata corruption is a heap-overflow technique, not classic stack smashing.

questions.prompt: Which attack does a non-executable stack (NX / DEP) primarily defeat?
options: Running shellcode that the attacker injected into a stack buffer
Exhausting the stack with unbounded recursion
Overwriting the return address with any value
Leaking addresses through a format-string bug
questions.explanation: NX marks stack (and heap) pages non-executable, so jumping into injected bytes faults. The overflow itself still happens and the return address can still be overwritten, which is why attackers moved to code-reuse techniques like ROP.

questions.prompt: With NX enabled, an attacker still exploits a stack overflow using return-oriented programming (ROP). What is ROP?
options: Repeatedly crashing the process until the OS disables NX
Injecting a new shared library into the process using LD_PRELOAD
Chaining short snippets of existing executable code that end in ret by placing their addresses on the stack
Rewriting the program's code pages so they become writable
questions.explanation: ROP reuses code that is already executable (gadgets in the binary and libc), so no injected code needs to run and NX doesn't stop it. Mitigations include ASLR, CFI and shadow stacks (e.g. Intel CET).

questions.prompt: What does Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) do?
options: Moves the process to a random CPU core to defeat timing attacks
Randomises the order of local variables within each function
Randomises the base addresses of the stack, heap, libraries and PIE binaries so attackers can't reliably predict targets
Encrypts the contents of memory so leaked bytes are unreadable
questions.explanation: ASLR makes addresses of gadgets, libc functions and buffers unpredictable per run, so a hard-coded address in an exploit usually misses. It doesn't encrypt memory; an info leak can still reveal the layout.

questions.prompt: A Node.js service is written entirely in JavaScript. Which statement about its exposure to buffer overflows is most accurate?
options: It has no exposure, because JavaScript has no pointers
It is as exposed as a C program, because V8 compiles JS to machine code
It is only exposed if it uses Buffer.allocUnsafe()
Its JS code is bounds-checked, but native addons and C/C++ parts of the runtime (V8, OpenSSL, libuv) can still have memory-corruption bugs
questions.explanation: JS array and Buffer accesses are bounds-checked, so your JS can't corrupt adjacent memory. But the runtime and any native addons are C/C++, and CVEs in them do happen. Buffer.allocUnsafe returns uninitialised memory (an info-leak risk), not an overflow.

questions.prompt: Which measures make stack-smashing exploits harder? Select all that apply.
options: Raising the stack size limit with ulimit -s
Compiling with -O3
Using bounds-checked APIs like fgets and snprintf with correct sizes
Stack canaries (e.g. -fstack-protector-strong)
A non-executable stack (NX)
ASLR with position-independent executables
questions.explanation: Canaries detect overwrites before return, NX blocks injected code, ASLR hides addresses, and bounded APIs prevent the overflow in the first place. A bigger stack or more optimisation doesn't change whether an unbounded copy can overrun a buffer.

questions.prompt: Which of these can help an attacker defeat ASLR or stack canaries? Select all that apply.
options: An out-of-bounds read that returns memory to the attacker
A forking server whose children inherit the same canary, allowing it to be brute-forced byte by byte
Compiling the program with -fstack-protector-strong
A format-string bug such as printf(user_input) that leaks stack contents
questions.explanation: Info leaks reveal addresses and canary values, and forked children share the parent's canary and layout, so crashes leak one byte at a time. -fstack-protector-strong adds canaries; it doesn't weaken them.

questions.prompt: Buffer overflows can happen on the heap as well as on the stack.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Overrunning a malloc'd buffer can corrupt neighbouring objects or allocator metadata and is often exploitable. Stack canaries don't protect heap data.

questions.prompt: Enabling ASLR on its own makes a buffer overflow impossible to exploit.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. ASLR raises the bar, but info leaks, partial overwrites, non-PIE binaries or brute force on low-entropy systems can still bypass it. Defence in depth and fixing the bug are what matter.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental architectural difference between a Linux container and a virtual machine?
options: Containers can only run one process, while VMs can run many
Containers share the host kernel and are isolated with namespaces and cgroups; VMs run their own kernel on a hypervisor
Containers emulate hardware in software, while VMs run directly on the host CPU
VMs share the host's kernel, while each container has its own kernel
questions.explanation: A container is a set of isolated host processes; a VM boots a full guest OS on virtualised hardware. That shared kernel is the main reason containers are lighter, and the main reason their isolation is weaker.

questions.prompt: Which Linux kernel feature limits how much CPU and memory a container can use?
options: Linux capabilities
Namespaces
cgroups (control groups)
seccomp filters
questions.explanation: cgroups account for and limit resources like CPU, memory, I/O and PIDs. Namespaces control what a process can see (PIDs, mounts, network); they don't cap resource usage.

questions.prompt: Why are VMs generally considered a stronger isolation boundary than containers?
options: VMs cannot make network connections to the host
VMs encrypt all of their memory by default, while containers do not
Containers have no filesystem isolation between them
A kernel exploit inside a container compromises the shared host kernel, while a VM guest also needs a hypervisor escape
questions.explanation: All containers on a host share one kernel with a large syscall surface. A VM's guest kernel is separate, so compromising it only gets the attacker inside the VM; escaping needs a hypervisor bug, a much smaller surface. Containers do have mount-namespace filesystem isolation.

questions.prompt: You are building a platform that runs untrusted code uploaded by many customers. Which isolation choice fits best?
options: Plain Docker containers with default settings, one per customer
One shared Node.js process per host using the vm module for each customer
A separate Linux user account per customer on a shared host
Lightweight VMs like Firecracker, or a user-space kernel sandbox like gVisor, per customer workload
questions.explanation: Multi-tenant untrusted code needs a boundary that doesn't expose the shared host kernel directly; that's why AWS Lambda uses Firecracker microVMs. Node's vm module is explicitly not a security mechanism, and default containers share the kernel.

questions.prompt: A teammate runs a container with `docker run --privileged` to fix a device error. What is the main security impact?
options: The container's network traffic is no longer isolated, but its filesystem still is
The container gets all capabilities and access to host devices, and most confinement is lifted, so escaping to the host is easy
The container runs as root, but its capabilities are unchanged
The container gets a higher CPU scheduling priority
questions.explanation: --privileged grants every capability, exposes /dev, and disables seccomp/AppArmor confinement. From there, mounting the host disk or loading kernel modules is trivial. Grant only the specific device or capability needed.

questions.prompt: A CI job's container mounts the host's /var/run/docker.sock so it can build images. What risk does that create?
options: The container can read build logs from other jobs, but nothing more
Only images can be pushed; containers cannot be started
Anyone in the container can ask the Docker daemon to start a privileged container that mounts the host filesystem, which is effectively root on the host
Builds become slower because the socket serialises requests
questions.explanation: The Docker daemon runs as root and does whatever the socket's client asks. Access to the socket is equivalent to host root. Safer options are rootless builders (BuildKit rootless, Kaniko) or isolated build VMs.

questions.prompt: What does Docker's default seccomp profile do for a container?
options: Blocks a set of rarely needed or dangerous system calls, shrinking the kernel attack surface
Encrypts traffic between containers on the same host
Verifies image signatures before the container starts
Limits the container's memory to a safe default
questions.explanation: seccomp-bpf filters which syscalls a process may make; Docker's default profile blocks calls like kexec_load and others that are rarely needed but often exploited. Memory limits are cgroups, and image signing is a separate feature.

questions.prompt: Which steps reduce the risk of a container escape? Select all that apply.
options: Publish every container port to the host
Enable user namespaces or rootless mode so container root maps to an unprivileged host user
Use a read-only root filesystem
Drop all capabilities and add back only the ones needed
Run the process as a non-root user inside the container
Use a bigger base image with more debugging tools installed
questions.explanation: Each of the first four removes privilege an attacker could use after gaining code execution. Extra tools in the image help an attacker, and exposing ports increases attack surface instead of reducing it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about root inside a Docker container are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Docker drops several capabilities by default, so container root is less powerful than host root
Without user namespaces, UID 0 in the container is UID 0 on the host kernel
With user namespace remapping, container root can map to an unprivileged UID on the host
Container root can never affect the host, no matter how the container is configured
questions.explanation: By default the UIDs are the same; only capabilities, seccomp and LSM profiles limit container root. Misconfigurations (privileged mode, host mounts, the Docker socket) or kernel bugs let it affect the host, so 'never' is wrong.

questions.prompt: If a container exceeds its cgroup memory limit, the kernel's OOM killer can kill a process inside it even when the host still has plenty of free memory.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The limit is enforced per cgroup, so hitting it triggers an OOM kill inside that cgroup (Kubernetes reports OOMKilled) regardless of host-wide free memory.

questions.prompt: Because containers are isolated by namespaces, a kernel vulnerability exploited from inside one container can only affect that container.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Namespaces are views onto one shared kernel. Exploiting a kernel bug gives the attacker kernel-level control of the whole host and every container on it.

questions.prompt: What does the principle of least privilege say?
options: Permissions should be removed only after a security incident
Each user, process or service should get only the permissions it needs for its task, for only as long as it needs them
Administrators should have unrestricted access so they can fix incidents quickly
Every user should get the same baseline permissions to keep things simple
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits the blast radius when something is compromised or buggy. Giving everyone the same broad baseline or standing admin rights is exactly what it argues against.

questions.prompt: A Node.js reporting API only needs to read the orders table in PostgreSQL. Which database credentials should it use?
options: The same owner role the migration tool uses
A role with full access to the orders schema in case reports need fixes
A dedicated role with SELECT granted only on the tables it needs
The postgres superuser, so it never hits permission errors
questions.explanation: A read-only, narrowly scoped role means SQL injection or a leaked password can't modify or drop data. Reusing the superuser or migration owner hands an attacker DDL and write access.

questions.prompt: A Node.js server on Linux must accept HTTPS on port 443. Which approach follows least privilege?
options: Run node as a non-root user behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, or grant only CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
Run node as root and call process.setuid() later only if a vulnerability is found
Disable the low-port restriction and run everything as root in a container
Run node as root, since only root can bind ports below 1024
questions.explanation: Binding a low port is the only privileged need, and it can be met with a single capability or by terminating TLS at a proxy. Running the whole app as root means any RCE becomes root.

questions.prompt: A service only uploads files to one S3 bucket, but its IAM policy grants "Action": "s3:*" on "Resource": "*". What is the best fix?
options: Keep the policy but enable S3 server-side encryption
Move the credentials into environment variables instead of code
Allow only s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::that-bucket/the-prefix/*
Restrict it to s3:* on that one bucket only
questions.explanation: Scope both the action and the resource to exactly what's needed. s3:* on the bucket still allows deletes and policy changes. Encryption and where the keys are stored don't reduce what a leaked credential can do.

questions.prompt: Why are short-lived credentials (e.g. tokens from an IAM role or workload identity) preferred over long-lived access keys?
options: They make the service's API calls cheaper
They give the service broader permissions without extra configuration
A leaked token stops working soon, limiting the window of abuse, and nothing long-lived needs manual rotation
They avoid TLS overhead when calling cloud APIs
questions.explanation: Least privilege applies in time as well as scope. Long-lived keys leak into logs, laptops and repos and stay valid until someone notices. Short-lived tokens don't change permissions or network costs.

questions.prompt: Which Dockerfile change best applies least privilege to a Node.js app image?
options: Install dependencies, then switch to a non-root user (e.g. USER node) before the CMD
Run `npm install` at container start so dependencies are always fresh
Use the latest base image tag so security patches arrive automatically
Add `chmod -R 777 /app` so the app never hits permission errors
questions.explanation: Without a USER instruction the process runs as root inside the container, so any RCE starts with root. chmod 777 lets the compromised process rewrite your code, and installing at startup needs network and write access at runtime.

questions.prompt: Twelve microservices all connect to the same database with one shared admin user. What is the biggest problem?
options: Connection pooling stops working with a shared user
PostgreSQL limits each user to a single connection
Schema migrations will run twelve times
Compromising any one service exposes every service's data, and audit logs can't tell which service did what
questions.explanation: One shared credential makes the blast radius the whole database and removes accountability. Per-service roles scoped to their own tables limit damage and make logs meaningful. Pooling and connection limits aren't the issue.

questions.prompt: Which of these follow the principle of least privilege? Select all that apply.
options: A CI deploy token scoped to one repository and one environment
Setting automountServiceAccountToken: false on pods that never call the Kubernetes API
A reporting service that connects with read-only replica credentials
A feature-flag service with write access to every production database
Giving a developer production admin access 'temporarily' with no expiry
questions.explanation: Scoped tokens, read-only credentials and not mounting unused API tokens all remove unneeded access. Open-ended admin grants and broad write access for an unrelated service are the opposite.

questions.prompt: A dependency of your Node.js service might be compromised in a supply-chain attack. Which measures reduce the blast radius? Select all that apply.
options: Running the process as non-root with a read-only filesystem
Using ^ version ranges so you always get the newest minor releases
Running npm install as root inside the production container at startup
Giving the service only the secrets it actually needs
Restricting outbound network traffic to an allowlist of hosts
questions.explanation: Limiting filesystem rights, egress and available secrets constrains what malicious code can steal or change. Loose version ranges and installing at runtime as root increase exposure to a bad release.

questions.prompt: Least privilege applies to people as well as services; for example, engineers shouldn't keep standing production admin access they rarely use.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Human accounts get phished and their laptops get compromised. Just-in-time, time-boxed elevation with an audit trail is the usual practice.

questions.prompt: If a service runs inside a private network, least privilege for its database account matters less because attackers can't reach the database directly.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Attackers usually arrive through the application itself (SQL injection, RCE, SSRF), and then they act with the app's own credentials. Network placement doesn't limit what those credentials allow.

questions.prompt: What is a TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) bug?
options: A cache entry that is served after its TTL
A decision based on a check whose result can change before the checked resource is actually used
A token that is used after its expiry time
Code that reads the system clock twice and gets different values
questions.explanation: The gap between checking a condition and acting on it lets another actor change the state, so the action runs on stale assumptions. Expired tokens and stale caches are different problems with no check-then-act race.

questions.prompt: A program checks that /tmp/app.lock doesn't exist with stat(), then creates it with open(path, O_CREAT | O_WRONLY). What is the safer approach?
options: Use open(path, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_WRONLY), which atomically fails if the file already exists
Run the program as root so it can always overwrite the file
Sleep briefly between stat() and open() so other processes finish first
Call stat() a second time just before open()
questions.explanation: O_EXCL makes check-and-create one atomic kernel operation, and with O_CREAT it also refuses to follow a symlink at the final path component. Extra checks or sleeps only change the timing of the race; running as root makes a symlink attack worse.

questions.prompt: Two concurrent withdrawals hit this code for the same account with balance 100 and amount 80. What is the best fix?
options: Wrap the two calls in a try/catch so errors are handled
Add an await before getBalance so it finishes first
Cache the balance in memory so both requests see the same value
Use one conditional update: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1, then check the affected row count
questions.explanation: Both requests can read 100, pass the check and write 20, so 160 is withdrawn. Putting the check inside the UPDATE makes it atomic in the database. Awaiting doesn't stop another request interleaving, and a cache makes the stale read worse.

questions.prompt: Node.js code does `if (fs.existsSync(p)) data = fs.readFileSync(p)`. What is the recommended pattern?
options: Call fs.accessSync(p) before reading instead of existsSync
Use fs.statSync(p) to check the size first, then read
Just attempt the read and handle the ENOENT error if the file isn't there
Check existence twice to be sure before reading
questions.explanation: The Node docs recommend opening/reading directly and handling errors, because the file can disappear or be swapped between the check and the read. access/stat are still separate checks with the same race.

questions.prompt: A coupon can be redeemed once per user. The code checks for an existing redemption row and then inserts one. An attacker sends 50 parallel requests and redeems the coupon 7 times. What is the most robust fix?
options: Disable the button on the frontend after the first click
Add rate limiting of 10 requests per second per user
Add a unique constraint on (user_id, coupon_id) and treat a duplicate-key error as 'already redeemed'
Re-check for an existing row after the insert and delete duplicates
questions.explanation: A unique constraint makes the database enforce the invariant atomically, whatever the concurrency. Rate limits shrink but don't close the window, cleanup after the fact can't undo side effects, and frontend checks are bypassed easily.

questions.prompt: Why are setuid-root programs especially dangerous when they have file TOCTOU races?
options: The kernel disables permission checks for setuid programs
setuid programs run in kernel mode, so races corrupt kernel memory
setuid programs can't use file locks, so every file access races
They run with elevated privileges on paths an unprivileged attacker can manipulate, so swapping a path (e.g. via symlink) redirects a privileged action to a sensitive file
questions.explanation: The attacker controls the timing and the path, while the program supplies root's privileges, e.g. writing to /etc/shadow through a swapped symlink. setuid programs still run in user mode and still get permission checks, just as root.

questions.prompt: To stop double-spends you add an in-memory lock (a Map from userId to a pending promise). With 4 pods in production, double-spends still happen. Why?
options: JavaScript Maps aren't safe for concurrent access within one event loop
The garbage collector clears the Map between requests
The lock lives in one process's memory; requests routed to other pods don't see it, so atomicity has to come from the database or a distributed lock
Promises resolve in random order, so the lock is released too early
questions.explanation: Each pod has its own Map, so two pods can both 'acquire' the lock for the same user. Within one Node process the Map works fine thanks to the single-threaded event loop; the problem is having several processes.

questions.prompt: Which of these perform check-and-act atomically, avoiding a check-then-act race? Select all that apply.
options: Redis SET lock:key value NX EX 30
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction, then the update
Checking that a file exists, then writing to it
Redis GET to check a value, then SET in a separate command
MongoDB findOneAndUpdate with the condition in the filter (e.g. { _id, stock: { $gte: 1 } }) and $inc
questions.explanation: Row locks, SET NX and conditional single-document updates combine the check and the write in one atomic step. A separate GET then SET, or exists-then-write, leaves a window for another client.

questions.prompt: Which file-handling practices reduce TOCTOU risk? Select all that apply.
options: Call stat() twice and proceed only if both results match
Use openat() relative to a trusted directory descriptor
Pass O_NOFOLLOW so the final path component can't be a symlink
Open the file once, then use the file descriptor (e.g. fstat) instead of re-resolving the path
Write to a temp file and rename() it over the target to replace it atomically
questions.explanation: Working on descriptors, refusing symlinks, anchoring lookups to a trusted directory and atomic rename all remove the window. Two stat() calls still leave a gap before the use.

questions.prompt: TOCTOU bugs only affect filesystems; they can't occur in web applications.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Any check-then-act on shared state can race: balance checks, inventory, coupon limits, uniqueness checks. Concurrent HTTP requests make these common in backends.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL at the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, two concurrent transactions that each SELECT a balance and then UPDATE it to a value computed in application code can lose one of the updates.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Both read the same old value and the second write overwrites the first. Fix it with an in-place update (balance = balance - x), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a stricter isolation level with retries.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three requirements for a correct critical-section solution?
options: Progress
All processes must run at the same speed
Mutual exclusion
Bounded waiting
questions.explanation: A solution must provide mutual exclusion, progress (no indefinite blocking when the section is free) and bounded waiting, while making no assumptions about relative speeds. Requiring equal speeds is exactly the assumption a correct solution must avoid.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run `counter++` 1,000 times on a shared variable with no locking. The final value is 1,873. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One thread was starved and ran only 873 times
`counter++` is a load, add and store; interleaved updates overwrote each other
Integer overflow wrapped the value
The CPU dropped some instructions under load
questions.explanation: Both threads can load the same old value, add 1 and store it, losing one increment. This race condition can produce any value below 2,000. The threads did run all their iterations; the updates were simply lost.

questions.prompt: In Peterson's solution, process i runs `flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j) {}`. If both processes set their flags at nearly the same time, who enters first?
options: The process with the lower index, always
Both enter, and mutual exclusion is restored on exit
The process whose write to `turn` happened first
The process whose write to `turn` happened last waits; the other enters
questions.explanation: Each process politely sets `turn` to the other. The last writer's value sticks, so it is the one that yields and spins while the other enters. Writing first means your value gets overwritten, which lets you in rather than making you wait.

questions.prompt: A developer reorders Peterson's entry code to `turn = j; flag[i] = true; while (flag[j] && turn == j) {}`. What breaks?
options: Nothing; the order of the two writes doesn't matter
The code deadlocks every time both processes try to enter
Only bounded waiting; mutual exclusion still holds
Mutual exclusion: both processes can end up in the critical section together
questions.explanation: P0 sets turn = 1, P1 sets turn = 0, P1 sets flag[1] and sees flag[0] false, so it enters. P0 then sets flag[0], sees turn == 0 (not 1) and also enters. Announcing interest must come before yielding the turn.

questions.prompt: Why can Peterson's algorithm fail on modern multicore CPUs even when the code looks correct?
options: CPUs and compilers may reorder a store and a later load, so a process can read the other's flag before its own write is visible
Compilers refuse to compile spin loops
It only fails on single-core CPUs
Modern CPUs don't support busy waiting
questions.explanation: Peterson assumes sequential consistency. Store buffers (even on x86, which allows store-load reordering) and compiler optimizations can let both processes read the other's flag as false. Memory fences or atomic operations with sequentially consistent ordering are needed.

questions.prompt: A two-process lock uses only a shared `turn` variable: process i waits while `turn != i`, then sets `turn = j` on exit. Which requirement does it violate?
options: Progress: a process can be blocked even when the critical section is free, if the other doesn't want to enter
Bounded waiting
Mutual exclusion
It satisfies all three requirements
questions.explanation: Strict alternation forces turns: if P1 never wants to enter again, P0 cannot enter a second time because turn stays at 1. Mutual exclusion holds, which is why it looks plausible, but progress fails.

questions.prompt: Disabling interrupts around a critical section is a valid technique in which situation?
options: Inside a kernel on a single-processor system, for very short sections
For long critical sections that do disk I/O
In user-space code on any system
On multiprocessor systems, because it stops all CPUs
questions.explanation: On a uniprocessor, no other code can run if interrupts are off, so short kernel sections are safe. It's a privileged operation (not available to user code), doesn't stop other CPUs on a multiprocessor, and holding it during long operations would lose interrupts and hurt responsiveness.

questions.prompt: Assuming sequentially consistent memory, which properties does Peterson's two-process solution guarantee? Select all that apply.
options: Bounded waiting
No busy waiting
Mutual exclusion
Progress
Correctness for any number of processes as written
questions.explanation: Peterson's solution meets all three critical-section requirements for two processes. It is defined for exactly two (generalizations like the filter algorithm exist), and it spins in a while loop, so it does busy-wait.

questions.prompt: Which approaches make a shared counter increment safe across threads? Select all that apply.
options: An atomic fetch-and-add instruction
Adding a random sleep before each increment
Protecting the increment with a mutex
Declaring the variable `volatile` in C/C++
`Atomics.add` on an Int32Array backed by a SharedArrayBuffer in JavaScript worker threads
questions.explanation: Atomic read-modify-write instructions (including JS `Atomics.add`) and mutexes make the increment indivisible. In C/C++, `volatile` only prevents some compiler optimizations; it does not make `++` atomic. Random sleeps only change how often the race shows up.

questions.prompt: Peterson's solution, written with plain loads and stores, guarantees mutual exclusion on x86 multicore CPUs without any memory fences.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. x86 allows a store to be delayed in the store buffer while a later load to a different address proceeds, which is exactly the store-then-load pattern Peterson depends on. A full fence (e.g., MFENCE) or a locked instruction is required.
