questions.explanation: Every ancestor's total includes the file, so the change must propagate up the parent chain (O(depth)). Updating just the parent leaves higher folders stale; recomputing the whole tree is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Which of these are naturally modeled with Composite? Select all that apply.
options: A retry wrapper around a function
A React component tree
A chain of Express middleware
Nested AND/OR filter expressions in a query builder
A file system with files and folders
questions.explanation: Component trees, boolean expression trees and file systems are part-whole hierarchies with a uniform interface. Middleware is a linear chain, and a retry wrapper is a decorator.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the performance of large Composite trees are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Iterative traversal with an explicit stack avoids recursion depth limits
Very deep trees can overflow the call stack with naive recursion
Composite requires all nodes to be instances of the same class
Aggregate operations like total size visit every node, so they are O(n)
questions.explanation: Aggregates touch every node, recursion depth is limited, and an explicit stack avoids that limit. Nodes only need to share an interface, not a class.

questions.prompt: With Composite, clients normally need to check whether a node is a leaf or a container before calling an operation on it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The point of Composite is that clients don't check: both node kinds implement the same operation, and containers delegate to their children.

questions.prompt: A composite node usually implements an operation by delegating to its children and combining their results.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For example, a folder's size() sums its children's size() and a bundle's price() sums its items. That recursive delegation is the heart of the pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Strategy pattern?
options: Encapsulate a request as an object so it can be queued and undone
Wrap interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so the caller can pick one at runtime
Define the skeleton of an algorithm and let subclasses fill in some steps
Let an object change its behavior automatically as its internal state changes
questions.explanation: Strategy extracts a family of algorithms (pricing, sorting, backoff) behind a common interface and lets the context be configured with one. Self-driven behavior changes are State; fixed skeletons are Template Method.

questions.prompt: A shipping-cost function has a growing if/else on carrier (DHL, FedEx, local courier), each branch with its own formula. Which refactor fits best?
options: Observer: carriers subscribe to order events and react
Composite: carriers arranged in a tree that sums costs
State: one state object per carrier with transitions between them
Strategy: one calculator per carrier behind a common interface
questions.explanation: Each branch is an independent algorithm selected by the caller, which is exactly Strategy. There are no transitions between carriers, so State doesn't fit.

questions.prompt: What is the most idiomatic way to implement Strategy in JavaScript?
options: Store the algorithm source as strings and eval the chosen one
Pass functions, or a map from key to function; a class hierarchy is optional
Use a Proxy whose get trap picks the algorithm
An abstract base class with one subclass per algorithm is required
questions.explanation: Functions are first-class in JS, so a strategy can be a function or an object of functions. Classes are fine when strategies carry state or several methods, but they aren't required. eval is unsafe.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 90 90 NaN
90 90 undefined
questions.explanation: flat gives 90, percent gives 100 * 0.9 = 90, and the unknown key 'bogus' falls back to the 'none' strategy via ??, returning 100.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: apple,fig,kiwi,pear apple
fig,pear,kiwi,apple fig
fig,pear,kiwi,apple apple
fig,kiwi,pear,apple apple
questions.explanation: The comparator is a strategy for sort. Array.prototype.sort is stable (ES2019+), so 'pear' and 'kiwi' (both length 4) keep their original order. Alphabetically, 'apple' comes first.

questions.prompt: Strategy and State have almost the same class structure. What is the key difference?
options: In Strategy the client picks the algorithm; in State the object switches its own state objects as transitions happen
State objects are stateless, while strategies always hold state
Strategy uses inheritance, while State uses composition
Strategy is only for sorting, while State is for any behavior
questions.explanation: Both delegate to an interchangeable object. With Strategy the choice is made from outside and strategies usually don't know each other; with State the states drive transitions themselves (paid -> shipped). Both use composition.

questions.prompt: Each tenant has a different tax calculation configured in the DB. Where should the right strategy be chosen?
options: Inside each strategy, by checking the tenant id and returning early if it isn't theirs
At the composition root or a factory, based on tenant config, then injected into the service
In a mutable global singleton that each request updates with its tenant's strategy
In the service, with a switch on tenant id at the start of every method
questions.explanation: Selecting once and injecting keeps the service unaware of tenants and keeps strategies focused. A shared mutable global races between concurrent requests on the same event loop; switches in every method bring back the conditional mess.

questions.prompt: Which of these are examples of the Strategy pattern? Select all that apply.
options: A pluggable retry backoff policy (fixed, exponential, exponential with jitter)
Passport.js authentication strategies (local, JWT, OAuth)
Node's require cache returning the same module
The comparator function passed to Array.prototype.sort
Express's app.listen() starting the HTTP server
questions.explanation: Each lets the caller plug in one of several interchangeable algorithms. app.listen is just a method call, and the module cache is the basis of module singletons.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Strategy trade-offs are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Clients or a factory must know which strategy to choose, so selection logic moves elsewhere
Strategies that need lots of the context's internal state may signal a poor split
Using Strategy makes it impossible to unit-test each algorithm on its own
With two stable branches that never change, a simple conditional is often clearer
questions.explanation: Strategy adds indirection that only pays off when algorithms vary or grow, and selection still has to happen somewhere. Testing is actually easier, since each strategy can be tested in isolation.

questions.prompt: Strategy relies on composition: the context holds a reference to a strategy object instead of inheriting the algorithm.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The context delegates to whatever strategy it holds, which is why strategies can be swapped at runtime. Inheritance-based variation is Template Method.

questions.prompt: To switch strategies at runtime you must create a new context object each time.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A context can expose a setter or accept a strategy per call; swapping the reference is enough. Recreating the context isn't required.

questions.prompt: What does the Observer pattern provide?
options: A chain of handlers where each one may handle or pass on a request
A stand-in object that controls access to another object
A subject that notifies subscribed observers of changes without knowing their concrete types
A central object that coordinates how a group of objects interact
questions.explanation: Observers register with a subject and get called on changes; the subject only knows the listener interface. A coordinating central object is a Mediator, which contains interaction logic rather than just broadcasting.

questions.prompt: A Node EventEmitter emits an 'error' event and no 'error' listener is registered. What happens?
options: A warning is logged and execution continues
The error is buffered until an 'error' listener is added
The event is silently ignored
The error is thrown, which crashes the process if nothing catches it
questions.explanation: 'error' is special: with no listener, emit('error', err) throws err. Unhandled, that brings down the process. Always attach an 'error' listener to streams, sockets and custom emitters.

questions.prompt: Logs show `MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 listeners added`. What is the most likely cause?
options: One of the listeners threw an uncaught error
A listener is being added repeatedly, e.g. on every request, and never removed
The same emitter is being used from multiple worker threads
More than 10 events are being emitted per second
questions.explanation: The default limit is 10 listeners per event, and the warning usually means code subscribes inside a hot path (per request or per connection) without unsubscribing. It has nothing to do with emit frequency.

questions.prompt: An EventEmitter has `emitter.on('order', async (o) => { await save(o); })` and save() rejects. With default options, what happens?
options: emit() doesn't see the rejection; it becomes an unhandled rejection unless handled inside the listener
emit() returns a rejected promise that the caller can await
The emitter automatically re-emits the failure as an 'error' event
The emitter retries the listener until it succeeds
questions.explanation: emit() is synchronous and ignores listener return values, so a returned promise's rejection is unhandled (crashing on Node 15+ by default). Catch inside the listener, or create the emitter with captureRejections: true to route rejections to 'error'.

questions.prompt: Code does `await once(emitter, 'ready')` (from node:events). What happens if the emitter emits 'error' before 'ready'?
options: The promise resolves with the error as its value
once() throws synchronously at the call site
The returned promise rejects with that error
It keeps waiting for 'ready' and ignores the error
questions.explanation: events.once() listens for 'error' too while waiting (unless you're waiting for 'error' itself) and rejects with it, so startup failures surface instead of hanging forever.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
double 2
log 1
double 4

log 1
double 2

log 1
double 2
log 2
double 4

log 1
double 2
double 4
questions.explanation: Listeners run in registration order. After off() removes `log` by reference, only the doubling listener remains for the second emit.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The two arrow functions look identical but are different objects, so off() removes nothing. Keep a reference to the listener (or use an AbortSignal) to unsubscribe; this is a classic leak source.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly compare classic Observer with publish/subscribe? Select all that apply.
options: In classic Observer, the subject holds direct references to its observers
Systems like Redis Pub/Sub deliver messages across processes and machines
Pub/sub usually goes through a broker or channel, so publishers and subscribers don't know each other
Observer guarantees delivery even if an observer is offline at the time
Pub/sub requires subscribers to run in the same process as publishers
questions.explanation: Observer is in-process with direct references; pub/sub adds a broker that decouples parties and can cross processes. Neither plain Observer nor Redis Pub/Sub is durable: offline listeners miss messages (use streams or queues for that).

questions.prompt: Which practices help avoid EventEmitter listener leaks? Select all that apply.
options: Pass an AbortSignal (to events.once/on or addEventListener) so listeners are removed on abort
Register listeners once at startup instead of inside per-request code where possible
Remove listeners with off()/removeListener() when the subscriber is done, e.g. on socket close
Call setMaxListeners(Infinity) so the warning goes away
questions.explanation: Removing listeners, tying them to an AbortSignal and not subscribing in hot paths fix the leak. Raising the limit to Infinity just hides the warning while memory keeps growing.

questions.prompt: A Node EventEmitter listener can stop later listeners from running by returning false.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: EventEmitter ignores listener return values; every listener runs unless one throws. (Returning false to cancel is a DOM inline-handler quirk, not an EventEmitter feature.)

questions.prompt: emitter.prependListener() registers a listener that runs before the listeners already registered for that event.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: prependListener (and prependOnceListener) add to the front of the listener array, while on() appends to the end.

questions.prompt: What does the Command pattern do?
options: Provides a simple interface over a complex subsystem
Notifies a list of subscribers whenever something changes
Encapsulates a request as an object so it can be queued, logged, retried or undone
Lets an object change behavior when its internal state changes
questions.explanation: Turning 'do X with these arguments' into an object decouples the invoker from the receiver and allows queuing, audit logs and undo. The others describe State, Facade and Observer.

questions.prompt: An editor supports undo and redo using Command objects. Which structure handles this correctly?
options: Storing a full copy of the document after every keystroke and no commands
An undo stack of executed commands and a redo stack of undone ones, with redo cleared when a new command runs
One queue that commands are pulled from in FIFO order for both undo and redo
A single array where undo deletes the first command added
questions.explanation: Undo pops the most recent command (LIFO) and pushes it onto redo; redo does the reverse. A new command invalidates the redo history. A FIFO queue would undo the oldest action first.

questions.prompt: Jobs pushed to a BullMQ queue are commands executed later by workers. Why must the job payload be plain serializable data?
options: Because commands cross process boundaries and are persisted in Redis, so closures and class instances can't travel
Because BullMQ only supports string payloads up to 1 KB
Because workers run in the browser and can't read Node objects
Because serialization makes the command run faster
questions.explanation: A queued command is stored and picked up by another process, possibly after restarts, so it must be data such as { type, orderId }. Functions and live objects can't be serialized and restored.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: 100 + 50 + 20 - 30 = 140. Undo pops the most recent first: undo -30 gives 170, undo +20 gives 150. One command (+50) remains in history.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: abcdX 3 0
abX 2 0
abX 2 1
abXcd 3 0
questions.explanation: 'ab' then 'abcd'; undo gives 'ab' with 'cd' on the redo stack. Executing 'X' gives 'abX' and clears redo, so the final redo does nothing.

questions.prompt: A queue delivers commands at least once, so a ChargeCustomer command may be processed twice. What is the standard fix?
options: Switch the queue to exactly-once delivery, which removes duplicates entirely
Give each command a unique id and have the handler skip ids it has already processed
Add a short sleep before processing so duplicates expire
Process commands one at a time on a single worker
questions.explanation: Idempotent handlers (dedupe on a command or idempotency key, often with a unique DB constraint) make redelivery harmless. Single workers and sleeps don't prevent duplicates, and end-to-end exactly-once isn't something you can rely on.

questions.prompt: In CQRS / event-driven designs, how does a command like PlaceOrder differ from an event like OrderPlaced?
options: They are interchangeable names for the same message
Events can be rejected by consumers; commands never can
A command expresses an intent that can be rejected; an event records a fact that already happened
A command is broadcast to many handlers; an event goes to exactly one handler
questions.explanation: Commands are imperative and target one handler that may validate and refuse. Events are past-tense facts published to any number of subscribers; they can't be 'rejected', only reacted to.

questions.prompt: Which benefits does the Command pattern provide? Select all that apply.
options: Queuing or scheduling requests to run later
Guaranteeing that requests execute faster
Implementing undo and redo
Logging requests for auditing or replay
Removing the need for input validation
questions.explanation: Because a request becomes data, it can be stored, scheduled, logged and reversed. It adds a little overhead rather than speed, and commands still need validation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about undo with Command objects are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Commands must be undone in reverse order of execution
Side effects that can't be reversed (email sent, card charged) need compensating actions instead
Commands should share references to mutable objects to save memory
A command must capture enough previous state to restore it, like a memento
questions.explanation: Undo needs saved prior state, LIFO order, and compensation (refund, apology email) for external effects. Shared mutable references let later changes corrupt the saved state.

questions.prompt: In the Command pattern, the invoker (a button, a scheduler, a queue worker) doesn't need to know what the command actually does.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The invoker just calls execute(); the command knows its receiver and arguments. That decoupling lets one generic worker run many kinds of commands.

questions.prompt: A command object must execute immediately and synchronously when it is created.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Separating creation from execution is the point: commands can be stored, scheduled, sent over a queue and run asynchronously later.

questions.prompt: What does the State pattern do?
options: Lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes, by delegating to state objects
Broadcasts state changes to a list of subscribers
Saves an object's state so it can be restored later
Lets the client choose an algorithm from a family of interchangeable ones
questions.explanation: The context delegates to a current state object (Pending, Paid, Shipped), and state objects decide transitions. Saving and restoring is Memento; broadcasting is Observer.

questions.prompt: An Order class has `switch (this.status)` in pay(), ship(), cancel() and refund(), and each new status means editing all of them. What refactor fits best?
options: Make Order a Singleton so status is consistent
Wrap Order in a decorator for each status
Replace the switches with a chain of if/else statements
Model each status as a state object (or a transition table) that defines allowed actions
questions.explanation: Repeated switches on the same status field are the classic smell State fixes: each state's rules live together and adding a status adds one class or table row. Rewriting as if/else keeps the duplication.

questions.prompt: With the State pattern, a client calls cancel() on an order that has already shipped. What is the cleanest handling?
options: Silently ignore the call so the client doesn't crash
Have the Shipped state reject cancel with a domain error, keeping the rule inside that state
Move the order back to Pending and then cancel it
Let the controller check the status before calling cancel()
questions.explanation: Each state knows which operations are legal; Shipped rejects cancel explicitly (or suggests a return/refund flow). Checking in controllers scatters rules again, and silent ignores hide bugs.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: yellow>red>green>yellow
yellow>red>green>red
yellow>red>green
green>yellow>red>green
questions.explanation: Each iteration moves to the next state before recording it: yellow, red, green, then yellow again. Four transitions, four entries.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: paid
delivered
cancelled
refunded
questions.explanation: pending ignores 'shipped', accepts 'paid'; paid ignores 'cancelled', accepts 'shipped'; shipped accepts 'delivered'; delivered has no outgoing transitions, so 'refunded' is ignored.

questions.prompt: Two API requests try to move the same order from 'paid' to 'shipped' and 'refunded' at the same moment, on different servers. What prevents both from succeeding?
options: A conditional update such as `UPDATE ... SET status='shipped' WHERE id=$1 AND status='paid'`, or an optimistic version check
The State pattern objects in memory make the transition atomic
Wrapping each handler in try/catch
Reading the status first and then writing the new one in a second query
questions.explanation: In-memory state objects live in separate processes, and read-then-write races. A compare-and-set update (check affected rows) or a version column lets exactly one transition win.

questions.prompt: When is a declarative transition table (state -> allowed next states) usually preferable to one class per state?
options: When per-state behavior is small and the main need is validating and auditing transitions
Only when there are fewer than three states
When each state has lots of distinct behavior and its own data
When the app must run without a database
questions.explanation: If states mainly differ in which transitions they allow, a table is compact, easy to review and easy to visualize. State classes earn their keep when each state has substantial behavior.

questions.prompt: Which signs suggest the State pattern (or an explicit state machine) would help? Select all that apply.
options: You need to adapt one interface to another
Many methods contain the same switch on a status field
Transition rules are scattered across controllers and services
The object has a single fixed behavior that never varies
Allowed operations depend on the current lifecycle stage
questions.explanation: Status switches, stage-dependent permissions and scattered transition checks all point to a state machine. Fixed behavior needs nothing, and interface conversion is Adapter.

questions.prompt: An order state machine is persisted in PostgreSQL. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Keep transition rules only in client-side code for speed
Record each transition in a history table for auditing and debugging
Plan for rows holding legacy state values when states are added or removed
Store the state as a constrained enum or text column and rebuild the state object on load
questions.explanation: Persist the state name, rebuild behavior on load, keep an audit trail, and migrate old values carefully. Rules must be enforced on the server; clients can't be trusted.

questions.prompt: In the State pattern, state objects may trigger transitions themselves by setting the context's next state.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For example, PaidState.ship() sets context.state = new ShippedState(). Letting states own transitions keeps the rules next to the behavior.

questions.prompt: State and Strategy have identical intent and differ only in naming.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The structure is similar, but Strategy is chosen by the client and strategies are independent, while states know about each other and drive their own transitions.

questions.prompt: What is the Chain of Responsibility pattern?
options: A request becomes an object so it can be queued and undone
One central object coordinates how several objects talk to each other
A subject notifies every subscriber at the same time
A request passes along a chain of handlers, and each one handles it or passes it on
questions.explanation: Each handler decides whether to process, modify, stop or forward the request, as Express middleware does with next(). Central coordination is Mediator; broadcasting to all is Observer.

questions.prompt: An Express middleware neither sends a response nor calls next(). What does the client experience?
options: Express sends 500 because the middleware returned undefined
Express automatically sends 404 Not Found
Express skips to the next middleware after a short delay
The request hangs until a client or server timeout occurs
questions.explanation: Express only moves on when next() is called; if nothing ends the response, the socket stays open. The default 404 handler only runs if the chain reaches the end via next().

questions.prompt: In Express, `app.use(express.json())` is registered after `app.post('/orders', handler)`. What happens inside the handler?
options: req.body is undefined, because the JSON parser hasn't run for that route
req.body is parsed normally because Express sorts body parsers first
req.body contains the raw request string
Express throws at startup because of the ordering
questions.explanation: Middleware runs in registration order. The route handler runs first and normally ends the response, so the parser never runs for that request (in Express 5, req.body is undefined when unparsed). Register parsers before routes.

questions.prompt: How does Express recognize a middleware function as error-handling middleware?
options: It is registered with app.error() instead of app.use()
It throws an error from inside its body
It is the last app.use() call, whatever its signature
It declares four parameters: (err, req, res, next)
questions.explanation: Express checks the function's arity: four parameters mark error middleware, which only runs after next(err) or a thrown or rejected error. Dropping the unused `next` silently turns it into normal middleware.

questions.prompt: An async Express route handler throws (its promise rejects). What is the difference between Express 4 and Express 5?
options: Express 5 forwards the rejection to error middleware automatically; Express 4 needed try/catch, a wrapper or next(err)
Express 4 forwards rejections automatically, but Express 5 removed that
Neither version handles it; the process always crashes
Both versions forward rejected promises to error middleware automatically
questions.explanation: Express 5 calls next(err) when a handler's returned promise rejects. In Express 4 the rejection escaped the chain, leaving the request hanging and an unhandled rejection, hence express-async-handler style wrappers.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: ok auth,rate,handler ok auth,rate,handler
ok auth,rate,handler denied auth
ok handler denied auth
ok auth,rate,handler denied auth,rate
questions.explanation: With a user, every handler runs and the last returns 'ok'. Without one, auth short-circuits by returning 'denied' without calling next, so only 'auth' is logged for b.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: This is Koa's onion model: code before `await next()` runs on the way in (1, 2), code after it runs on the way out in reverse order (3, 4).

questions.prompt: Which concerns are typically implemented as middleware in a chain? Select all that apply.
options: Running database schema migrations on each request
Attaching a request id and access logging
Rate limiting
Compiling TypeScript on every request
Authentication and authorization checks
questions.explanation: Cross-cutting, per-request concerns fit middleware. Migrations run once at deploy time, and compilation happens at build time, never per request.

questions.prompt: Which are real pitfalls when writing a middleware chain? Select all that apply.
options: Each middleware runs in its own thread, so shared state needs locks
Calling next() twice can run downstream handlers twice
Registering CORS after auth can make browser preflight (OPTIONS) requests fail
Sending a response and also calling next() can cause 'headers already sent' errors downstream
questions.explanation: Double responses, double next() calls and ordering mistakes are common bugs; preflights carry no auth header, so auth placed first rejects them. Middleware runs on the single event-loop thread.

questions.prompt: In Chain of Responsibility, a handler can short-circuit the chain by handling the request and not passing it on.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For example, an auth middleware responds 401 and doesn't call next(), so the route handler never runs.

questions.prompt: Every middleware registered with app.use() in Express runs for every request, whatever its path.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: app.use('/admin', mw) only runs for paths under /admin, and an earlier middleware that ends the response stops the rest of the chain.

questions.prompt: What is the Template Method pattern?
options: A family of interchangeable algorithms selected at runtime
A wrapper that adds steps before and after a method call
An object that builds a complex result step by step
A base class that fixes an algorithm's skeleton and lets subclasses override specific steps
questions.explanation: The base class's template method calls steps in a fixed order; subclasses supply the varying ones. Swapping whole algorithms is Strategy; wrapping calls is Decorator; step-by-step construction is Builder.

questions.prompt: Which pattern does this class implement?
options: Template Method
Builder
Chain of Responsibility
Strategy
questions.explanation: run() fixes the order of steps, and subclasses (CsvImporter, JsonImporter) only implement parse(). That inheritance-based skeleton is Template Method; Strategy would inject a parser object instead.

questions.prompt: In Template Method, what is a 'hook'?
options: A lifecycle event emitted when the template method finishes
A callback that the template method passes to an external library
An optional step with a default (often empty) implementation that subclasses may override
An abstract step that every subclass must implement
questions.explanation: Hooks such as beforeSave() give subclasses optional extension points without forcing them to implement anything. Required steps are abstract methods.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between Template Method and Strategy?
options: Template Method uses inheritance and fixes the skeleton per subclass; Strategy uses composition and swaps whole algorithms at runtime
Template Method can only have one step; Strategy can have many
Template Method uses composition; Strategy uses inheritance
Strategy requires abstract classes, while Template Method works with plain functions
questions.explanation: Template Method varies parts of one algorithm through subclassing, so the choice is made when picking the class. Strategy delegates the whole algorithm to an injected object that can change at runtime.

questions.prompt: A subclass of your TypeScript Importer overrides run() itself and accidentally skips validate(). How do you protect the skeleton?
options: Make run() private so subclasses can still call it but not override it
TypeScript has no `final`; document it, keep steps protected, or use composition (inject the parser) if overriding is a real risk
Mark run() as `final`, which TypeScript enforces at compile time
Declare run() as abstract in the base class
questions.explanation: TypeScript lacks a final modifier, so run() can always be overridden. Composition (base class takes a parser strategy, or a non-inheritable function) removes the risk. Making run() private would stop external callers too.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: H|sales|F H|base|F
H|sales|F2 H|base|F
H|sales|F2 H|sales|F2
H|base|F H|base|F
questions.explanation: generate() is the template method; `this.body()` dispatches to the subclass override. Sales overrides body and footer but inherits header; the base Report uses all its own steps.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: init undefined
init null
ReferenceError
init svc
questions.explanation: The base constructor calls the overridden init() before Child's class fields are initialized (fields are set right after super() returns), so prefix is still undefined. Avoid calling overridable steps from constructors.

questions.prompt: Which of these follow the Template Method idea? Select all that apply.
options: util.promisify wrapping a callback API
A stream.Transform subclass that implements _transform()
A base Repository whose fixed save() flow calls an abstract toRow() step
A Node stream.Readable subclass that implements _read()
A comparator passed to Array.prototype.sort
questions.explanation: In each of the first three, the base class runs the algorithm (buffering, backpressure, saving) and calls a step you supply. A comparator is a Strategy, and promisify is an Adapter.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine drawbacks of Template Method? Select all that apply.
options: Changing the step order in the base class affects every subclass at once
Deep hierarchies make the control flow hard to follow (the yo-yo problem)
Subclasses become coupled to the base class's internals
It provides no way to share common code between variants
questions.explanation: Inheritance creates tight coupling and can make flow hard to trace, and base-class changes ripple everywhere. Sharing common steps is actually its main benefit.

questions.prompt: In Template Method, the base class calls the subclass's step methods, not the other way around (the 'Hollywood Principle').
options: True
False
questions.explanation: 'Don't call us, we'll call you': the base class controls the flow and calls down into overridden steps.

questions.prompt: JavaScript classes can't implement Template Method because the language has no abstract methods.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Any overridable method works, and a base method can throw 'not implemented'. TypeScript also offers `abstract` at compile time.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the Iterator pattern?
options: Encapsulate a request so it can be queued and undone
Combine objects into a tree so they can be treated uniformly
Let an object change behavior as its internal state changes
Give sequential access to a collection's elements without exposing how it is stored
questions.explanation: An iterator hides whether data comes from an array, a tree, a DB cursor or a paginated API behind next(). Trees are Composite; the others are State and Command.

questions.prompt: What makes a JavaScript object iterable with for...of?
options: It has a [Symbol.iterator]() method returning an object whose next() returns { value, done }
It has a length property and numeric keys
It extends Array or implements a forEach method
It is a generator function
questions.explanation: for...of calls obj[Symbol.iterator]() and then next() until done is true. Array-likes with length aren't iterable unless they implement the protocol; a generator function returns an iterable when called.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: The generator yields 0, 3, 6, 9; the next value, 12, fails i < 10, so it stops. Spreading consumes the iterator until done.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
gen 0
gen 1
use 0

gen 0
use 0

gen 0
use 0
gen 1
use 1

gen 0
use 0
gen 1
questions.explanation: Generators are lazy: each value is produced only when the loop asks for it, so production and consumption interleave. On 1 the loop breaks before 'use 1', and the infinite generator never runs again.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options:
1
done

1
2
cleanup
done

1
cleanup
done

1
done
cleanup
questions.explanation: break makes for...of call the iterator's return(), which resumes the generator as if it returned at the yield, so the finally block runs before 'done'. This is how iterators release resources early.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: 3 undefined
questions.explanation: An iterator is a one-shot cursor: the first spread drains it, the second gets nothing. The array is iterable many times because each for...of or spread asks it for a fresh iterator.

questions.prompt: You expose a paginated REST API as `async function* fetchAll()` and consume it with `for await (const item of fetchAll())`. What is the main benefit?
options: The API's rate limits no longer apply
All pages are fetched in parallel, so it finishes faster
Pages are pulled lazily, so memory stays bounded and the consumer can stop early without fetching the rest
Results are cached automatically between runs
questions.explanation: An async generator fetches the next page only when the consumer asks, so you never hold the whole dataset and `break` stops further requests. It's sequential, not parallel, and adds no caching.

questions.prompt: Node readable streams are async iterable. What happens with backpressure when you use `for await (const chunk of stream)` and the loop body awaits a slow DB write?
options: The stream throws because the consumer is too slow
The next chunk isn't pulled until the body finishes, so the stream pauses naturally
Chunks are dropped while the loop body is busy
Chunks pile up in memory without limit while the write runs
questions.explanation: The async iterator only requests the next chunk after the previous iteration completes; the stream fills its internal buffer up to highWaterMark and then stops reading. No data is lost.

questions.prompt: Which of these are iterable with for...of by default? Select all that apply.
options: WeakMap
A plain object literal {}
Map
String
Set
Array
questions.explanation: Arrays, strings (by code point), Maps and Sets implement Symbol.iterator. Plain objects don't (use Object.entries), and WeakMaps can't be iterated because their keys may be garbage collected.

questions.prompt: Which statements about generators are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A finished generator object can be iterated again from the start
gen.return(v) finishes the generator and runs any pending finally blocks
Calling a generator function doesn't run its body until next() is called
yield* delegates to another iterable or generator
questions.explanation: Generators start suspended, can delegate with yield*, and return() triggers cleanup. Once done, a generator object stays done; call the generator function again for a fresh one.

questions.prompt: Using for...in on an array iterates over its values through the iterator protocol.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: for...in enumerates enumerable property keys (as strings, including inherited ones), not values, and ignores Symbol.iterator. Use for...of for values.

questions.prompt: Iterating a Map with for...of yields [key, value] pairs in insertion order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Map's default iterator is entries(), and Maps preserve insertion order, which is one reason to prefer them over objects for ordered key-value data.

questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Mediator pattern?
options: Put the interaction logic between objects into one central object so they don't reference each other directly
Give clients one simpler interface over a complicated subsystem
Let a request pass through a chain until a handler deals with it
Notify subscribers whenever a subject changes
questions.explanation: A mediator turns a many-to-many web of references into many-to-one: colleagues talk only to the mediator, which decides who reacts. A facade simplifies access without coordinating peers.

questions.prompt: In a chat app, users send messages to individual users and to rooms. Which design follows the Mediator pattern?
options: Each User is wrapped in a decorator that adds messaging
Each User object keeps references to every other User and calls them directly
Users form a chain and pass each message along until the recipient is found
A ChatRoom (or server) object receives messages and routes them to recipients
questions.explanation: The room/server is the mediator: users only know it, and it handles routing, offline users and rooms. Direct references create an N-squared web of dependencies.

questions.prompt: In a signup form, ticking 'business account' must show a company field, change the country list and re-validate the VAT input. Where does Mediator put this logic?
options: In a form controller that receives change events and updates the affected fields
Inside the checkbox component, which holds references to the other fields
Inside each field, which polls the others for changes
In a CSS rule that toggles visibility
questions.explanation: A form-level mediator keeps the fields independent and reusable; cross-field rules live in one place. Embedding references in the checkbox couples components to each other.

questions.prompt: Over a year, your OrderMediator has grown to 2,000 lines handling every interaction in checkout. What is the best response?
options: Convert it into a Singleton so there is only one copy
Split it into smaller mediators by use case or bounded context, keeping domain rules in the domain objects
Move all of its logic into the database as stored procedures
Replace it with direct references between all the colleagues
questions.explanation: A mediator that knows everything becomes a god object. Splitting by use case keeps each one cohesive. Going back to direct references just reintroduces the tangle.

questions.prompt: What best distinguishes Mediator from Observer?
options: A mediator contains coordination logic that knows the colleagues; an observed subject just broadcasts and doesn't decide how others react
Mediator broadcasts to every listener; Observer sends to exactly one
Observer requires a message broker, while Mediator never uses events
They are the same; Mediator is the newer name
questions.explanation: A mediator actively decides who does what. A subject merely announces changes. A mediator may use events internally, but its defining trait is centralized coordination.

questions.prompt: In the classic airport analogy for Mediator, which role is the mediator?
options: Each individual aircraft
The passengers
The runway
The control tower
questions.explanation: Planes don't negotiate with each other directly; they talk to the tower, which coordinates takeoffs and landings. The planes are the colleagues.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: delivered delivered a:hi
delivered c offline b:hi
delivered c offline a:hi,c:yo
delivered c offline a:hi
questions.explanation: Users only talk to the room. 'b' is registered, so the message is delivered and recorded as 'a:hi'; 'c' never joined, so the mediator replies 'c offline'.

questions.prompt: Which of these act as mediators? Select all that apply.
options: An array iterator
A memoize wrapper around a function
A chat server routing messages between connected clients
An in-process command dispatcher that routes requests to their handlers
A saga orchestrator telling each service which step to run next
questions.explanation: Each centralizes who talks to whom. A memoizer is a decorator, and an iterator gives sequential access.

questions.prompt: Which statements about saga orchestration vs choreography are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Orchestration makes the overall workflow easier to see in one place
Choreography has services react to each other's events with no central coordinator
Orchestration uses a central coordinator, similar to a mediator, that tells services what to do
Orchestration removes the need for compensating actions on failure
questions.explanation: Orchestration is mediator-like and keeps the flow visible in one place; choreography is event-driven and decentralized. Both still need compensations, because distributed steps can't be rolled back atomically.

questions.prompt: With a Mediator, colleagues typically hold a reference to the mediator rather than to each other.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That's the decoupling: a colleague can be reused or replaced without touching its peers, since it only knows the mediator interface.

questions.prompt: Introducing a Mediator always reduces the total amount of code, because the interaction logic disappears.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The interaction logic moves into the mediator rather than vanishing, and the mediator itself can grow large. The benefit is lower coupling, not less code.

questions.prompt: Which resume bullet is strongest for a senior backend role?
options: Responsible for working on the payments service and fixing bugs
Cut payment API p99 latency from 1.2s to 300ms with Redis caching and batched writes, lifting conversion 3%
Worked with Node.js, Redis, Kafka, PostgreSQL and Docker across many payment and checkout features
Helped the team significantly improve the performance and reliability of various backend services in production
questions.explanation: It names an action, the technical how, and measurable before/after impact tied to business value. A tool list shows exposure, not outcomes, and 'significantly' without numbers is unverifiable.

questions.prompt: What is the widely used structure for an impact bullet (often phrased as the 'XYZ' formula)?
options: Technology used, its version, and your years of experience with it
Accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z
Problem, apology, lesson learned
Job title, company, dates
questions.explanation: 'Accomplished X as measured by Y by doing Z' forces outcome, metric and method into one line. Title/company/dates is header information, not a bullet structure.

questions.prompt: You led a migration but have no exact latency numbers. What's the best way to still quantify impact honestly?
options: Leave every metric out and describe your responsibilities in detail, so nothing can be questioned later
Write 'massively improved everything'
Use numbers you can defend: scale (requests/day, records migrated), scope, or explainable estimates
Invent plausible round numbers, since recruiters rarely check and metrics make bullets stand out
questions.explanation: Scale and scope numbers, or clearly explainable estimates, quantify impact without fabrication. Interviewers probe numbers, so invented metrics collapse under one follow-up question.

questions.prompt: Which verb choice best signals ownership in a bullet?
options: 'Was involved in' the design of the notification service handling 2M pushes/day
'Participated in' the notification service project
'Exposed to' notification service development
'Designed and shipped' the notification service handling 2M pushes/day
questions.explanation: Strong action verbs ('designed', 'led', 'reduced') state what you did. 'Involved in' or 'participated in' hide your contribution and make reviewers assume a minor role.

questions.prompt: A bullet says 'Reduced AWS costs by 40%'. What is the interviewer most likely to probe?
options: How many hours you worked that week
Whether you hold an AWS certification that qualifies you to make cost decisions on production cloud accounts
Your favourite AWS region
Your baseline and absolute figures, what you specifically changed, and how you measured the result
questions.explanation: Metrics invite verification: from what to what, which levers (rightsizing, reserved capacity, caching), your role versus the team's, and how it was measured. Be ready to defend every number.

questions.prompt: Which bullet best balances technical depth with business impact?
options: Used design patterns and SOLID principles to write clean, maintainable code in the webhooks module
Improved customer happiness and reduced support load through better engineering practices across the payments team
Built an idempotent webhook processor (outbox pattern), ending ~150 duplicate charges/month and their tickets
Implemented the outbox pattern
questions.explanation: It names the technique (signals seniority to engineers) and the business result (signals value to managers). The bare 'outbox pattern' line lacks impact; the others lack specifics.

questions.prompt: Your 'Experience' section has 9 bullets for your current role, several describing routine tasks. What's the best edit for a senior role?
options: Keep all 9 to show you're busy
Add more bullets so every technology you used is covered, since recruiters search for keywords
Cut to the 4-6 highest-impact, most role-relevant bullets, ordered by impact
Move everything into one long paragraph
questions.explanation: Recruiters skim quickly; fewer, stronger bullets ranked by impact and relevance make your best work visible. Routine tasks dilute signal, and a dense paragraph is harder to scan.

questions.prompt: Which kinds of metrics make good evidence in backend resume bullets? Select all that apply.
options: Reliability changes (error rate, incidents, uptime)
Cost savings or engineering hours saved
Number of meetings attended
Latency or throughput changes (p95, RPS)
questions.explanation: Performance, reliability and cost/time metrics map directly to backend value. Meetings attended measure activity, not impact.

questions.prompt: Which are common mistakes in resume bullets? Select all that apply.
options: Using metrics you can explain in detail
Listing duties ('responsible for...') instead of results
Claiming team results as solely your own when you can't explain them
Vague adjectives like 'significantly' or 'various' without specifics
questions.explanation: Duties, overclaiming and vagueness all weaken bullets. Metrics you can explain in depth are exactly what you want.

questions.prompt: Adding relevant keywords from the job description (where they truthfully describe your work) can help a resume pass applicant tracking system (ATS) screening and recruiter skims.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Recruiters and ATS filters search for the role's terms (e.g. 'Node.js', 'PostgreSQL', 'microservices'). Use them where accurate, inside impact bullets rather than keyword-stuffed lists.

questions.prompt: For a senior engineer, a longer list of technologies in the skills section is more persuasive than a few quantified achievements.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Senior hiring is about judgement and impact. Demonstrated results with depth outweigh breadth of exposure; huge tool lists also invite questions you may not be able to answer deeply.

questions.prompt: Which resume bullet best presents a personal Next.js + MongoDB interview-prep app with LLM-generated quizzes?
options: Created an app that uses ChatGPT to make quizzes, very useful
Built a modern full-stack application with Next.js, MongoDB, AI, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Vercel and more
Made a study app for myself using lots of modern tech
Built a Next.js + MongoDB prep platform with LLM quizzes validated by zod, falling back to a curated bank
questions.explanation: It shows the stack plus engineering decisions (validation of untrusted output, graceful degradation). 'Next.js app with MongoDB and AI' is accurate but says nothing about design judgement.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'Why validate LLM output with a schema before saving it?' What's the strongest answer?
options: Because the linter requires it
LLM output is untrusted and can be malformed or wrong; validation keeps bad data out of the DB and UI
Because MongoDB rejects JSON that hasn't been validated against a schema before it is inserted into a collection
To make the LLM respond faster
questions.explanation: Treating model output like any untrusted input (validate, then cache only valid results) shows mature engineering. MongoDB will store arbitrary documents happily, which is exactly why app-level validation matters.

questions.prompt: The project uses a scheduled cron job to prepare each day's plan, and also generates the day on dashboard load if cron didn't run. How should you describe this design on the resume or in an interview?
options: An idempotent daily job with a lazy on-demand fallback, so the app stays correct if a scheduled run is missed
As a real-time event streaming pipeline that recomputes the plan whenever any underlying data changes
As a microservices architecture
'Used cron jobs'
questions.explanation: Describing the reliability property (idempotent generation, works without cron) highlights backend thinking. 'Used cron jobs' undersells it, and calling it streaming or microservices misrepresents it.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks why the app computes 'today' in a configured timezone instead of using server-local time. What's the best explanation?
options: Serverless functions usually run in UTC, so day boundaries would be off; an app timezone keeps streaks consistent
It makes the database smaller
Timezones are required by Next.js
Server-local time is slower to compute because every request must first load and parse the host's timezone database
questions.explanation: Day-boundary bugs are a classic issue: a serverless function in UTC would roll over at 5:30am IST. Explaining this shows awareness of real production pitfalls. It isn't about speed or framework requirements.

questions.prompt: Where should this side project go on a resume for someone with 4+ years of backend experience?
options: Only in the cover letter
At the top, above all work experience, because it shows initiative and is the most recent thing you've personally built
Hidden in the skills section as a keyword
In a concise 'Projects' section after experience, with 1-3 bullets on its hardest engineering decisions
questions.explanation: For experienced engineers, professional work leads; a project section adds signal, especially for skills (LLM integration) not shown at work. Putting it above experience suggests the job experience is weak.

questions.prompt: The app runs entirely on free tiers (serverless hosting, a free MongoDB cluster, free LLM tiers). Which framing turns that constraint into a strength?
options: It's free so it isn't a serious project
Leave hosting out entirely, since mentioning free tiers suggests the project isn't production-grade or serious
Claim it's built to handle millions of users
Designed within free-tier limits: connection reuse, provider fallbacks, caching only validated AI output
questions.explanation: Constraints force engineering choices (connection management, caching, fallbacks) that interviewers value. Inflating scale to 'millions of users' for a single-user app is a credibility risk.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks, 'How would this design change if it had 100k users?' What does a strong answer focus on?
options: Rewrite everything as microservices immediately, one per feature, each with its own database and deployment
Concrete limits: multi-user auth, per-user indexes, queued generation instead of cron, LLM quotas and caching
Switching to a different programming language
'It would work the same; Next.js scales automatically'
questions.explanation: This probes whether you understand the limits of your own design. Naming specific bottlenecks (auth, data model, job processing, LLM quotas) shows judgement; claiming automatic scaling or reflexive rewrites doesn't.

questions.prompt: Which details from this project are worth highlighting for a senior Node.js backend role? Select all that apply.
options: Business logic in pure, unit-tested domain functions separate from I/O services
Graceful degradation when no LLM key or cron is available
Treating LLM output as untrusted: schema validation and caching only validated results
The colour palette used in the UI
questions.explanation: Validation, resilience and testable architecture are backend signals. UI colours aren't relevant to a backend role, though they could matter for a frontend one.

questions.prompt: What should you prepare before listing this project on your resume? Select all that apply.
options: A short architecture walkthrough you can sketch in 2-3 minutes
A clean public repo or demo, with secrets removed
A memorised list of every npm dependency version
The trade-offs you made and what you'd change
questions.explanation: Anything on a resume is fair game: be ready to explain architecture and trade-offs and to show code safely. Dependency versions are trivia nobody will ask about.

questions.prompt: Describing a single-user personal tool as a 'scalable platform used by thousands' is acceptable resume polish.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. That's misrepresentation, and a single follow-up ('how many users?') exposes it, damaging trust in the rest of your resume. Accurate framing of real engineering decisions is stronger.

questions.prompt: A side project can be a strong signal for skills your day job doesn't show, such as LLM integration, provided you can discuss its design decisions in depth.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Projects fill gaps in your professional story, but only if you can go deep: why each choice, what failed, what you'd improve. Shallow tutorial-style projects add little.

questions.prompt: Which LinkedIn headline is most effective for someone targeting senior backend roles?
options: Passionate coder | Tech enthusiast | Lifelong learner | Problem solver | Team player | Innovator
Senior Backend Engineer | Node.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL | Distributed systems & payments
Software Engineer at Acme
Looking for opportunities
questions.explanation: Recruiters search by role and keywords; a headline with target title, core stack and domain gets found and is instantly clear. Generic phrases contain no searchable signal.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to ask a former colleague at a target company for a referral?
options: Send just 'Hi' and wait for a reply
Message ten people at the company with the same copy-paste text at once, to maximise the chance of a reply
A short, specific note: role link/id, why you fit in 2-3 lines, and your resume, so it's easy to act on
Ask them to find any job for you
questions.explanation: Specific, low-effort asks get acted on: the referrer needs the job id, a fit summary, and your resume. Vague 'any job' asks push the work onto them and usually stall.

questions.prompt: Why build an explicit target list of ~30 companies instead of applying to every opening you see?
options: It lets you prioritise by fit, track referrals and follow-ups, and tailor applications to each company
Recruiters automatically reject candidates whose applications show up at more than 30 companies in a month
Job portals only allow 30 applications
It guarantees an offer
questions.explanation: A curated list turns a scattershot search into a pipeline you can manage: tiers, contacts, status, dates. No such hard limits exist, and nothing guarantees offers.

questions.prompt: On job portals like Naukri where recruiters search profiles, what typically keeps your profile visible?
options: Using a creative job title nobody searches for
Uploading scanned photos of your certificates instead of a resume, since recruiters trust verified documents more
Leaving it untouched after creation
A complete, keyword-rich profile with current skills, accurate experience and notice period, updated regularly
questions.explanation: Recruiter search relies on keywords, completeness and recency. Stale or creatively titled profiles don't match searches. Specific ranking rules vary, but completeness and freshness consistently help.

questions.prompt: Your LinkedIn 'About' section should mainly do what?
options: Summarise what you build, your strengths and impact, and the roles you're looking for, in a few lines
Contain only a list of 40 skills
List hobbies and favourite movies
Repeat your full resume word for word so recruiters see the same details without having to open the attached PDF
questions.explanation: A concise narrative with impact and a clear target helps recruiters decide quickly to reach out. Copying the resume adds nothing, and skill lists belong in the Skills section.

questions.prompt: You don't know anyone at 12 of your 30 target companies. What's the best next step?
options: Find second-degree connections or alumni there and send brief, specific messages; apply directly otherwise
Only apply through portals and never network
Drop those companies from the list, since cold applications without a referral almost never get a response
Ask strangers for referrals without reading the job post
questions.explanation: Warm intros via mutual connections or alumni convert far better than cold asks, and direct applications remain a valid fallback. Dropping companies or blasting generic asks wastes opportunities.

questions.prompt: Your resume says 'Senior Engineer, 2022-present' but LinkedIn still shows your old title and an extra job. Why does this matter?
options: LinkedIn automatically syncs your profile with uploaded resumes, so any mismatch gets corrected on its own within days
Inconsistencies between profiles and resume raise credibility questions during screening and background checks
It only matters for frontend roles
It doesn't; recruiters never check LinkedIn
questions.explanation: Recruiters cross-check profiles; mismatched titles or dates look careless or deceptive and can surface in background verification. Keep every profile consistent with the resume.

questions.prompt: What should a referral tracking sheet for your 30 companies include? Select all that apply.
options: Status and next follow-up date
Company, role and job link/id
Your guess of each interviewer's salary
Contact person and date you asked for a referral
questions.explanation: Tracking role, contact, ask date, status and follow-ups stops leads from going cold. Guessing interviewers' salaries isn't useful.

questions.prompt: Which LinkedIn practices help recruiters find and trust your profile? Select all that apply.
options: A skills section featuring your core stack
Leaving the profile private and without a photo or headline
Turning on recruiter-visible 'open to work' preferences with target roles and locations
Experience entries with impact bullets matching your resume
questions.explanation: Consistent experience, relevant skills and open-to-work signals improve discoverability. A bare or hidden profile gives recruiters nothing to search or evaluate.

questions.prompt: Referrals typically increase the chance that your application is seen by a human compared with a cold application through a careers page.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Referred candidates are commonly prioritised in screening because someone inside vouches for them. It doesn't skip the interview bar, but it gets your resume read.

questions.prompt: Once someone agrees to refer you, it's best not to follow up even if you hear nothing for several weeks.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A polite follow-up after a week or two (thanking them and asking if the referral went through) is normal and often needed; referrals get lost in busy schedules.

questions.prompt: You're starting to apply to 30 companies. What's the smartest sequencing strategy?
options: Apply only after you've finished all preparation, no matter how long it takes
Apply to everything on the same day
Apply to your dream companies first while you're most excited and motivated, then work your way down the list
Warm up with a few lower-priority companies, then target top choices, timing offers to land close together
questions.explanation: Early interviews are practice; batching later ones lets offers overlap, improving negotiating leverage. Dream companies first risks spending your best shots before you've warmed up.

questions.prompt: You've applied to 25 roles over 3 weeks and received zero callbacks. What should you examine first?
options: Whether interviewers like you
Your system design skills, since senior roles screen out candidates who can't design at scale on the first call
Your resume and targeting: impact-focused bullets, and roles whose level and stack actually match yours
Your LinkedIn profile picture
questions.explanation: No callbacks means the funnel fails at screening, before any interview, so the resume, keywords, and role fit are the levers. Interview skills only matter once you get calls.

questions.prompt: How much should you tailor your resume per application?
options: Write a completely new resume for every application
Keep a strong base resume and tweak a few bullets and the summary to match each role's key requirements
Never change anything
Change your job titles to match the posting's wording, so the ATS sees an exact title match for the role
questions.explanation: Light tailoring (emphasis, keywords, ordering) gives most of the benefit at low cost. Changing actual job titles is misrepresentation, and full rewrites aren't sustainable at volume.

questions.prompt: A recruiter asks for your expected salary on the first call, before you know the role's scope. What's a reasonable response?
options: Ask to understand the role and level first and for their budgeted range; if pressed, give a researched range
Refuse to continue the conversation
State a random high number
Give a number well below your current salary to seem flexible, then negotiate upward once they make an offer
questions.explanation: Deferring until scope is clear, or anchoring with a researched range, protects your leverage. Lowballing can anchor the entire negotiation, and refusing outright can end the process.

questions.prompt: You have a 90-day notice period. How does this affect your application strategy?
options: Apply only to companies that require immediate joiners
Hide it until the offer stage, since companies that like you enough will usually wait out the full period
Ignore it; companies never care
Disclose it upfront, ask about buyout or early release, and favour companies that accept longer notice
questions.explanation: Notice period is a key screening factor for many employers; being upfront avoids wasted rounds and late surprises. Hiding it often causes offers to be withdrawn.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of tracking each application's stage (applied, screen, technical, onsite, offer) in a spreadsheet?
options: Recruiters ask for it
To count rejections over time, which keeps you motivated and shows recruiters how persistent you have been throughout
To share with your current employer
To see where your funnel leaks (e.g. many screens but few onsite passes) and fix the right skill
questions.explanation: Conversion rates per stage tell you what to improve: resume (few screens), coding (fail technicals), or system design/behavioral (fail onsites). It's a diagnostic tool.

questions.prompt: You get an offer from Company A with a 3-day deadline while Company B is mid-process and is your top choice. What's the best move?
options: Tell B about the deadline and ask if they can expedite, and ask A politely for a short extension
Accept A now, then quietly back out later if B comes through, without telling A until you've decided
Accept A immediately and stop B
Reject A to focus on B
questions.explanation: Companies often accelerate for candidates with competing offers, and modest extensions are common requests. Accepting then reneging burns bridges, and rejecting A gives up your leverage.

questions.prompt: Which habits make an application phase effective? Select all that apply.
options: Continuing DSA and system design practice while interviewing
Stopping all preparation once applications are submitted
Applying in focused batches with referrals where possible
Writing a short retro after each interview round
questions.explanation: Batching, ongoing practice and retros compound across interviews. Stopping preparation lets skills decay just as interviews start.

questions.prompt: After an interview loop rejection, which actions are productive? Select all that apply.
options: Note which questions or rounds went poorly and practice them
Ask about the cool-off period to reapply later
Argue with the recruiter that the decision was wrong
Politely ask the recruiter for any feedback
questions.explanation: Feedback, targeted practice and knowing reapply timelines turn rejections into progress. Arguing rarely changes decisions and can damage future chances.

questions.prompt: It's generally better to start applying once you're reasonably prepared rather than waiting until you feel 100% ready.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Real interviews give feedback that practice can't, and hiring processes take weeks. Waiting for perfect readiness delays the loop; a sensible warm-up order manages the risk.

questions.prompt: Using exactly the same generic resume and no referrals for every application is the most efficient approach, because volume matters more than targeting.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Untargeted, high-volume applying usually yields low callback rates. Referrals plus light tailoring typically convert far better per application.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to re-solve a problem you struggled with from a blank editor rather than re-reading its solution?
options: Re-solving lets you memorise the exact code for the interview
Solutions online are usually wrong
Re-reading is slower than re-solving
Retrieving the solution yourself strengthens memory; re-reading creates an illusion of understanding
questions.explanation: Retrieval practice (actively reconstructing an answer) builds durable recall and exposes gaps. Re-reading feels productive because the solution looks familiar, but familiarity isn't the same as being able to produce it under pressure. The goal is the pattern, not memorised code.

questions.prompt: Re-solving 'longest substring without repeating characters', which pattern gives the standard O(n) solution?
options: Binary search on the answer length
Sliding window that tracks each character's last index in a Map or Set
Sort the characters, then scan once
Dynamic programming over all O(n^2) substrings
questions.explanation: Expand the right edge and jump/shrink the left edge past the previous occurrence of a repeated character; each index moves forward at most once, giving O(n). Sorting destroys the order the substring depends on.

questions.prompt: For each element of an array you need the next element to its right that is larger. Which technique gives O(n)?
options: Two nested loops with an early break
A monotonic stack holding indices with decreasing values
Sorting with original indices, then a binary search per element
A min-heap of all elements
questions.explanation: Each index is pushed and popped at most once: when a bigger value arrives, it is the 'next greater' for every smaller index it pops. Nested loops with early break are still O(n^2) in the worst case (e.g. a descending array).

questions.prompt: 'Find the minimum ship capacity to deliver all packages (in order) within D days.' Which approach should you recognise?
options: Sort the packages and use two pointers
Binary search over capacity, with a greedy O(n) check of whether D days suffice
Greedy: always use the largest package as the capacity
Dynamic programming over every split of the array into D parts, O(n^2 · D)
questions.explanation: Feasibility is monotonic in capacity (if C works, C+1 works), so binary search between max(weight) and sum(weights) with a greedy day-count check gives O(n log sum). The largest package is only a lower bound, and sorting breaks the required order.

questions.prompt: What does this two-pointer function print?
options: null
questions.explanation: On a sorted array the first check is a[0] + a[4] = 1 + 9 = 10, so it returns [0,4] immediately. 4 + 6 is also 10, but the pointers never get there because the outer pair already matches.

questions.prompt: Counting ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time, what does this print?
questions.explanation: ways(0) = ways(1) = 1, then 2, 3, 5, 8: it is the Fibonacci sequence shifted by one, so ways(5) = 8. Answering 5 confuses it with fib(5) under the standard indexing.

questions.prompt: Which signs show that you have NOT yet mastered a problem you previously struggled with? Select all that apply.
options: You can't explain why the algorithm is correct
You can't state its time and space complexity
You can say which clue in the prompt points to the pattern
You solve it within time and can explain an alternative and its trade-off
You only remember the approach after peeking at a hint
questions.explanation: Needing a hint, not being able to justify correctness, or not knowing complexity all mean the problem should go back into the 'struggled' pile. Solving in time, explaining alternatives and spotting the pattern trigger are signs of real mastery.

questions.prompt: Spacing re-attempts of a hard problem over several days usually gives better long-term retention than solving it several times in one sitting.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The spacing effect is well established: retrieval after some forgetting strengthens memory more than massed repetition, which mostly reuses short-term memory and feels deceptively easy.

questions.prompt: 'Given course prerequisites as pairs, can you finish all courses?' Which approach should you recognise?
options: Topological sort (e.g. Kahn's algorithm); it fails exactly when the directed graph has a cycle
Union-Find on the prerequisite pairs
Sort the pairs by prerequisite and scan
Dijkstra's shortest path from course 0
questions.explanation: Courses and prerequisites form a directed graph, and all courses can be finished only if it is acyclic. Kahn's BFS (process nodes with in-degree 0) or DFS cycle detection runs in O(V + E). Union-Find detects cycles in undirected graphs, so it gives wrong answers here.

questions.prompt: If your re-solve passes the problem's sample test cases, it's safe to mark the problem as mastered.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Samples rarely cover edge cases (empty input, duplicates, overflow, worst-case size). Mastery means a correct, efficient solution you can explain, ideally re-solved after a gap.

questions.prompt: This 'find first index where ok() is true' binary search hangs on some inputs. What's the bug?
options: The loop condition should be lo <= hi
hi = mid should be hi = mid - 1
mid should be computed with Math.ceil
lo = mid should be lo = mid + 1
questions.explanation: When hi = lo + 1 and ok(lo) is false, mid = lo and lo = mid changes nothing, so the loop never ends. Since mid is known to be false, lo = mid + 1 is correct. Changing hi = mid to mid - 1 could skip the answer, because mid might be the first true.

questions.prompt: Redoing a URL-shortener design: many app servers must generate short codes without collisions. Which approach is most robust?
options: Base62-encode a unique ID from a counter service that hands each server a block of IDs
Generate 7 random characters and hope collisions are rare
Hash the long URL with MD5 and keep the first 7 characters
Use each server's local auto-increment counter
questions.explanation: Pre-allocated ID ranges guarantee uniqueness without a DB round trip per request; base62 keeps codes short. Truncated hashes collide and need collision checks, and per-server counters produce the same IDs on different servers.

questions.prompt: A rate limit of 100 req/min per user must hold across 20 stateless API servers. Which design enforces it correctly?
options: Count requests from access logs every hour
Sticky sessions with no shared state
A shared counter in Redis updated atomically (INCR with expiry or a Lua script)
An in-memory counter on each server with a limit of 100
questions.explanation: A central store with atomic updates gives one consistent count per user. Independent per-server counters allow up to 20 × 100 requests, and hourly log processing can't block requests in real time.

questions.prompt: In a chat-app design, how does a message reach a recipient who is online and connected to a different gateway server?
options: Send it by email, then sync it to the app
Broadcast every message to every gateway server
Look up the recipient's gateway in a connection registry and route the message there to push over its WebSocket
The recipient's client polls the database every second
questions.explanation: A registry (often Redis) maps user to gateway, so the message is routed to exactly the right server, which pushes it over the open connection. Broadcasting to all gateways wastes bandwidth and doesn't scale.

questions.prompt: Why is consistent hashing preferred over `hash(key) % N` for distributing cache keys across nodes?
options: Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of the keys instead of most of them
It removes the need for replication
It distributes keys perfectly evenly without virtual nodes
Lookups become O(1) instead of O(log N)
questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing N changes almost every key's node, causing a mass cache miss. On a hash ring only keys next to the changed node move. Even distribution still needs virtual nodes, and the ring lookup is typically O(log N).

questions.prompt: A URL shortener stores 500M new URLs per month, ~500 bytes each, kept for 5 years. Roughly how much storage is needed?
options: ~15 TB
questions.explanation: 500M × 12 × 5 = 30B records; 30B × 500 B = 15 × 10^12 B ≈ 15 TB (before replication). 150 TB comes from slipping a factor of 10 in the record count.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the cache-aside pattern are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The cache writes updates through to the database automatically
On a miss the application writes the loaded value into the cache
The cache must hold the entire dataset
The application reads the cache first and loads from the DB on a miss
Cached data can be stale after a DB write unless it is invalidated or expires
questions.explanation: In cache-aside the app owns reads, fills and invalidation, so staleness is handled with TTLs or delete-on-write. Writing to the DB through the cache is write-through/write-behind, a different pattern, and cache-aside caches only what is requested.

questions.prompt: A single celebrity key overloads one cache shard. Which mitigations are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Set an infinite TTL on every key in the cache
Add a short-TTL in-process cache on app servers for that key
Move the key to the primary SQL database
Coalesce concurrent misses so only one request rebuilds the value
Replicate the hot key across shards under suffixed keys and read a random copy
questions.explanation: Spreading copies, local caching and request coalescing all reduce load on one shard. Infinite TTLs everywhere cause staleness and memory pressure without fixing the hotspot, and the DB is even less able to absorb the load.

questions.prompt: Redoing designs on a timer helps partly because it forces you to budget time across requirements, high-level design and deep dives.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Running out of time before deep dives is a common HLD failure. Timed practice builds a sense of pacing (e.g. ~5–10 min requirements and estimates, ~15 min high-level design, the rest on deep dives).

questions.prompt: Under the CAP theorem, a multi-region distributed database can simply choose to give up partition tolerance.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Network partitions will happen across regions, so P isn't optional. CAP's real choice is between consistency and availability while a partition is happening.

questions.prompt: A notification service must send millions of push notifications per campaign without overloading providers or losing messages. Which design fits best?
