options: Enqueue jobs on a message queue; rate-limited workers send with retries and a dead-letter queue
Send all notifications synchronously inside the API request
Have a cron job send everything once a day
Have clients poll a /notifications endpoint every second
questions.explanation: A queue absorbs bursts, workers control the sending rate to each provider, and retries plus a DLQ handle failures. Sending synchronously in the request ties API latency and availability to third-party providers.

questions.prompt: A feed uses `OFFSET n LIMIT 20` pagination. Deep pages get slow and users see duplicate posts as new ones arrive. What's the best fix?
options: Return the whole feed in one response
Cache every page for 24 hours
Cursor (keyset) pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < (last_seen) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
Increase the page size to 200
questions.explanation: OFFSET makes the database scan and discard n rows, and inserts shift every page. A keyset cursor uses an index seek and is stable as new posts arrive. Long caching just serves stale feeds.

questions.prompt: You scored 55% on a quiz. What is the most effective way to use the retake?
options: Retake it immediately, several times, until you score 100%
Skip it and only take quizzes on topics you're good at
Memorise the answer letters for each question
Review the concepts behind each miss, then retake after a gap of a day or more
questions.explanation: Understanding why you missed each question and then retesting after a delay checks real recall. Immediate repeats mostly measure short-term memory of the answer key, so a 100% score there is misleading.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16 at the default isolation level, one transaction runs the same SELECT twice and the second run sees a row another transaction committed in between. Why?
options: MVCC is disabled by default
The default is Read Committed, which takes a new snapshot for each statement
The default is Serializable but it allows phantoms
PostgreSQL's default is Read Uncommitted
questions.explanation: Read Committed (PostgreSQL's default) gives each statement its own snapshot, so a re-run can see newly committed rows (non-repeatable reads and phantoms). PostgreSQL never actually provides dirty reads; Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table has a B-tree index on (customer_id, created_at). Which query can use this index LEAST effectively?
options: C
D
A
B
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree is sorted by the leading column first, so filtering only on created_at can't seek into it efficiently (at best a full index scan). A, B and D all use the leading-column prefix, and D also gets its ordering from the index.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 5.x (no `as const`), what type is inferred for `pair`?
questions.code: const pair = [1, 'a'];
options: readonly [1, 'a']
[number, string]
any[]
(string | number)[]
questions.explanation: Array literals are widened to an array of the union of element types. You get a tuple only with an annotation or `as const` (which gives readonly [1, 'a']). Expecting [number, string] is the usual mistake.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: let in a for-loop header creates a new binding per iteration, so each closure captures its own i. With var there would be a single shared binding and every closure would return 3.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code: console.log([typeof null, typeof NaN, Array.isArray([]), typeof []].join(' '));
options: object NaN true object
null number true array
object number true object
object number false object
questions.explanation: typeof null is 'object' (a historical quirk), NaN is of type number, and arrays report 'object' from typeof, which is why Array.isArray exists and returns true here.

questions.prompt: Which are the Coffman conditions that must ALL hold for a deadlock? Select all that apply.
options: Circular wait
Hold and wait
No preemption
Starvation
Priority inversion
Mutual exclusion
questions.explanation: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait; breaking any one (e.g. global lock ordering removes circular wait) prevents it. Starvation and priority inversion are separate scheduling problems.

questions.prompt: Which statements about B-tree indexes in PostgreSQL are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A plain B-tree on name can't serve WHERE name LIKE '%son'
Indexes reduce the table's disk usage
If an index exists, the planner always uses it
They speed up equality and range lookups on the indexed columns
Every extra index adds cost to INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
questions.explanation: B-trees serve equality, ranges and prefix matches but not leading-wildcard patterns, and they must be maintained on every write. The planner picks a sequential scan when it estimates that's cheaper (e.g. low selectivity), and indexes use extra disk space.

questions.prompt: Re-reading your notes until they feel familiar is a reliable sign that you'll answer those questions correctly on a retake.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Familiarity from re-reading is recognition, not recall, and creates an illusion of competence. Self-testing is a much better predictor of how you'll perform.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript, `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` evaluates to false.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: IEEE-754 doubles can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance (Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON for small values) or use integer cents for money.

questions.prompt: A client's payment POST times out and it retries, and occasionally the customer is charged twice. What is the standard server-side fix?
options: Change the endpoint from POST to PUT
Accept a client-generated idempotency key and store it with the result under a unique constraint, returning the saved result on retries
Add a 5-second sleep before processing each payment
Tell clients never to retry payment requests
questions.explanation: An idempotency key lets the server detect a retry and return the original outcome instead of charging again; the unique constraint closes the race between concurrent retries. Renaming the HTTP method doesn't make the handler idempotent.

questions.prompt: You've found a list of questions reportedly asked at a target company. What is the most effective way to use it?
options: Memorise the exact solution to every question on it
Group the questions by pattern and theme, then practise those patterns with similar problems
Ignore it, because company lists are always outdated
Only practise the single most frequent question
questions.explanation: Lists show which patterns and themes a company favours (graphs, intervals, concurrency, payments), so practising the pattern prepares you for variants. Memorising exact solutions breaks as soon as the question is tweaked.

questions.prompt: A payments company's list keeps mentioning 'design a wallet/ledger'. Which property must your design emphasise most?
options: An append-only double-entry ledger with atomic, idempotent transfers
Caching balances in Redis as the source of truth
Storing only the current balance and overwriting it on each transfer
Eventually consistent balances across regions for lower latency
questions.explanation: Money systems need auditability and no lost or duplicated movements: immutable ledger entries, transactions that debit and credit atomically, and idempotency keys for retries. Overwriting a single balance field loses history and invites lost-update bugs.

questions.prompt: 'Implement an LRU cache' appears on many company lists. In JavaScript, what is the simplest way to get O(1) get and put?
options: A Map: on access delete and re-set the key; evict map.keys().next().value when full
A plain array, moving accessed items to the end with splice
A sorted array of timestamps searched with binary search
A WeakMap, so the garbage collector evicts old entries
questions.explanation: Map preserves insertion order, so re-inserting on access moves a key to the newest end and the first key is always the least recently used. Array splice is O(n), and WeakMap keys must be objects and are collected unpredictably, not by recency.

questions.prompt: This Map is used as an LRU cache with capacity 3. What does it print?
options: a,c,d
c,a,d
b,c,d
b,a,d
questions.explanation: Re-inserting 'a' gives order b, c, a; adding 'd' gives b, c, a, d; evicting the first key removes 'b', leaving c,a,d. 'b,c,d' is what you'd get if access didn't refresh 'a'.

questions.prompt: Designing a rate limiter (a common list item), why might you choose a token bucket over a fixed-window counter?
options: Fixed windows can't be implemented in Redis
A fixed window can let through up to 2× the limit around a window boundary; a token bucket smooths this and allows controlled bursts
A token bucket guarantees exactly one request per interval
A token bucket needs no state per user
questions.explanation: With fixed windows, a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next. A token bucket refills at a steady rate with a capped burst size. It still needs per-user state (tokens plus last refill time).

questions.prompt: Which signs suggest a company question list is still a reliable guide? Select all that apply.
options: Most entries are from many years ago for a different role
The list is very long
Reports match your role and level (e.g. senior backend)
The same questions appear across several independent sources
Questions are reported recently (within the last year or so)
questions.explanation: Recency, role/level match and corroboration across sources make a list predictive. Length alone says nothing about accuracy, and old reports for other roles often reflect a hiring process that has changed.

questions.prompt: For a senior backend (Node.js) role, which follow-ups commonly show up in company-style deep dives? Select all that apply.
options: Recite the V8 source code of Array.prototype.sort
How would you rename a heavily used column with zero downtime?
How do you protect the service when a downstream dependency is slow (timeouts, circuit breaker)?
How would you make this endpoint safe to retry (idempotent)?
Which IDE theme do you prefer?
questions.explanation: Retries and idempotency, resilience to slow dependencies, and safe schema migrations (expand/contract) are classic senior backend probes. Reciting engine source code or tooling preferences don't test engineering judgement.

questions.prompt: Memorising verbatim solutions to a company's past questions is a reliable strategy, because the exact same questions are usually asked again unchanged.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Interviewers often modify constraints or add follow-ups, and they probe reasoning. A memorised answer falls apart under 'what if the input doesn't fit in memory?'. Patterns and reasoning transfer.

questions.prompt: When researching a company, you should check its round formats (e.g. practical API-building or debugging rounds), not just its question lists.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Many companies include machine-coding, debugging or take-home rounds alongside algorithm and design rounds, and preparing for the wrong format wastes time. The format tells you what kind of practice to do.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing company asks you to design 'find nearby drivers'. Which data structure choice is most appropriate?
options: A geospatial index such as geohash cells, a quadtree or Redis GEO, queried by cell or radius
Scan all drivers and compute distances on every request
A hash map keyed by exact (lat, lng) pairs
A B-tree index on latitude only
questions.explanation: Geospatial indexes bucket nearby points so a query touches only a few cells, and driver locations can be updated frequently. An index on latitude alone still returns a whole band of the globe, and exact-coordinate keys never match nearby points.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce list asks: 'Prevent overselling the last unit in a flash sale.' Which approach is correct under concurrency?
questions.code:
-- PostgreSQL
UPDATE inventory
SET stock = stock - 1
WHERE product_id = $1 AND stock > 0;
options: Lock the whole inventory table for the duration of the sale
Run the conditional UPDATE above and treat 0 affected rows as sold out
Read stock in the app, check it's > 0, then run an UPDATE that sets the new value
Cache the stock in each app server's memory
questions.explanation: The conditional UPDATE checks and decrements atomically in one statement, so two buyers can't both take the last unit; the row count tells you who won. Read-then-write in the app is a check-then-act race. Locking the whole table works but kills throughput.

questions.prompt: In a timed medium-problem session, how should you handle the brute-force solution?
options: Fully code and test it before thinking about anything better
Never mention it; it makes you look weak
Skip clarifying questions so you have time to code it
State it briefly with its complexity, then look for the optimisation before coding
questions.explanation: A brief brute force shows you understand the problem and gives a complexity baseline to improve on. Fully coding it first often uses the time you needed for the optimal solution, unless you are badly stuck.

questions.prompt: 'Top-k frequent elements' with n = 10^6 and k = 10. Which approach is typical and efficient?
options: A max-heap of all n raw elements, popping k times
Sort the whole array, then count: O(n^2)
For each distinct value, count with a full array scan
Count with a Map, then keep a min-heap of size k: O(n log k)
questions.explanation: Counting is O(n), and a size-k min-heap keeps the top k in O(n log k); bucket sort by frequency even gets O(n). Sorting is O(n log n), not O(n^2), but that option is still the slower, worse choice here.

questions.prompt: What is the standard approach and time complexity for 'merge overlapping intervals'?
options: Sort by end and use binary search: O(log n)
Compare every pair of intervals: O(n^2)
Use a hash map keyed by start: O(n)
Sort by start, then sweep, merging into the last interval: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: After sorting by start, any overlap must be with the last merged interval, so one pass suffices; the sort dominates at O(n log n). A hash map ignores ordering and can't detect overlaps.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Sorted: [1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]. [2,6] overlaps [1,3] and merges to [1,6]; 8 > 6 starts a new interval, and 15 > 10 starts another. [8,10] and [15,18] don't overlap, so they stay separate.

questions.prompt: 'Count subarrays summing to k' using prefix sums. What does this print?
questions.explanation: Prefix sums are 0,1,3,6,3,6. Each prefix P counts earlier prefixes equal to P - 3: 3 matches 0 (1), 6 matches 3 (1), 3 matches 0 (1), 6 matches both 3s (2), total 5. Negative numbers create the extra matches a sliding window would miss.

questions.prompt: Your recursive DFS for 'number of islands' passes small tests but crashes on a 1000×1000 grid of all land. Why, and what's the fix?
options: The visited array must be a Set instead
JavaScript arrays can't hold 10^6 elements
Recursion depth can reach ~10^6 and overflow the call stack; use an explicit stack or BFS queue
Time complexity is O(n^4); switch to binary search
questions.explanation: One big island makes DFS recurse once per cell, far beyond V8's stack limit (RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded). An iterative stack or BFS has the same O(rows × cols) time without the stack depth. The algorithm's complexity is fine.

questions.prompt: Which approaches correctly find the k-th largest element of an unsorted array? Select all that apply.
options: Keep a min-heap of size k; its top is the answer
Quickselect, average O(n)
A single pass that tracks only the maximum
Sort descending and take index k - 1
Binary search directly on the unsorted array
questions.explanation: Sorting (O(n log n)), a size-k min-heap (O(n log k)) and quickselect (average O(n), worst O(n^2)) all work. Binary search needs sorted data, and tracking only the max solves k = 1 only.

questions.prompt: Which problems are good fits for the variable-size sliding-window technique? Select all that apply.
options: Count subarrays with sum exactly k when values can be negative
Minimum window substring containing all characters of t
Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
Longest increasing subsequence
Shortest subarray with sum ≥ target when all numbers are positive
questions.explanation: Sliding windows work when growing or shrinking the window changes the condition monotonically. With negative values, shrinking can increase the sum, so you need prefix sums plus a hash map. LIS is about non-contiguous subsequences and uses DP or patience sorting.

questions.prompt: For n = 10^5, an O(n^2) solution that gives correct output is usually acceptable in a medium interview problem even when the interviewer expects O(n log n).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: 10^5 squared is 10^10 operations, far too slow for typical limits, and missing the expected complexity is usually a fail for that problem. A brute force is a starting point, not the deliverable.

questions.prompt: In 'group anagrams', using each word's sorted characters as a Map key takes O(n · k log k) time, where k is the maximum word length.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Sorting each of the n words costs O(k log k), and the map operations are O(k) per key. A 26-letter count signature reduces this to O(n · k) for lowercase input.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Each call makes two calls on n - 1, so the call tree doubles at each level: about 2^n calls. It looks linear because the argument only drops by 1, but the branching factor of 2 makes it exponential (memoising or computing f(n - 1) once fixes it).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code: console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt).join(','));
options: NaN,NaN,NaN
1,NaN,NaN
1,NaN,3
questions.explanation: map passes (value, index), so this calls parseInt('1', 0), parseInt('2', 1), parseInt('3', 2). Radix 0 is treated as 10 (giving 1), radix 1 is invalid (NaN), and '3' isn't a valid base-2 digit (NaN).

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: undefined
TypeError
ReferenceError
questions.explanation: let declarations are hoisted but stay in the temporal dead zone until their line runs, so reading a first throws a ReferenceError. With var it would print undefined.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code: console.log('5' - 2, '5' + 2, true + 1);
options: 3 52 true1
questions.explanation: Minus only works on numbers, so '5' becomes 5 and the result is 3. Plus with a string concatenates, giving '52'. true + 1 converts true to 1, giving 2.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code prints 1 and 6. The microtask queue then drains completely: 3, then the chained 5. Only after that do timers run in scheduling order: 2, then 4. Printing 2 before 5 forgets that chained microtasks run before any macrotask.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
options: undefined undefined
1 undefined
1 null
questions.explanation: Class bodies are strict mode, so a detached method call has this === undefined, and ?. returns undefined instead of throwing. Expecting '1 1' assumes this stays bound to c, but this depends on how a function is called.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
const o = { b: 1, 2: 1, a: 1, 1: 1 };
console.log(Object.keys(o).join(','));
questions.explanation: Integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order: 1,2,b,a. Assuming plain insertion order is the common mistake.

questions.prompt: This prints 3, 3, 3 instead of 0, 1, 2. Why?
options: The loop runs after the timers fire
setTimeout runs callbacks in reverse order
var is function-scoped, so all callbacks share one i, which is 3 when the timers fire
Arrow functions capture i by value at creation, which is 3
questions.explanation: There is a single i binding. The loop finishes (i = 3) before any timer runs, so every closure reads 3. Using let creates a new binding per iteration. Closures capture variables, not values.

questions.prompt: What does `[] == ![]` evaluate to, and why?
options: false, because an array never equals a boolean
false, because objects are compared by reference
It throws a TypeError
true, because ![] is false, and [] == false coerces both sides to 0
questions.explanation: [] is truthy, so ![] is false. Loose equality converts false to 0 and [] to '' and then to 0, so 0 == 0 is true. The reference-comparison rule only applies when both sides are objects.

questions.prompt: Rapid-fire equality: which of these comparisons evaluate to true? Select all that apply.
options: null == 0
NaN !== NaN
null == undefined
Object.is(0, -0)
Object.is(NaN, NaN)
questions.explanation: NaN is never === itself, but Object.is treats NaN as equal to NaN. null loosely equals only undefined (not 0). Object.is distinguishes 0 from -0, unlike ===.

questions.prompt: Which expressions evaluate to the string "object"? Select all that apply.
options: typeof new Date()
typeof Symbol()
typeof function () {}
typeof []
typeof null
questions.explanation: null (a historical quirk), arrays and Date instances all report 'object'. Functions report 'function' and symbols report 'symbol'.

questions.prompt: `const arr = [1, 2]; arr.push(3);` throws a TypeError because arr is declared with const.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: const stops the variable being reassigned; it doesn't make the array immutable, so push works. Only arr = [...] would throw, and Object.freeze is what prevents mutation.

questions.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: what are the average-case time complexities of `map.get(key)` and `map.set(key, v)` on a JavaScript Map?
options: O(n) each, because Map keeps insertion order
O(1) each on average, because Map is hash-based
O(1) for get and O(log n) for set
O(log n) each, because Map is a balanced tree
questions.explanation: The spec requires Map operations to be sublinear on average, and V8 implements Map as a hash table, so get/set/has/delete are O(1) on average. Keeping insertion order doesn't make lookups linear; the order is tracked alongside the hash table.

questions.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: your API rejects a client for exceeding its request quota. Which HTTP status code should it return?
options: 409 Conflict
429 Too Many Requests
403 Forbidden
503 Service Unavailable
questions.explanation: 429 means the client sent too many requests, ideally with a Retry-After header. 503 means the server itself is overloaded or down, and 403 means the client isn't allowed at all, regardless of rate.

questions.prompt: Under the ANSI SQL isolation levels, which anomaly does Repeatable Read prevent that Read Committed allows?
options: Non-repeatable reads
Dirty reads
Lost updates on unrelated tables
Phantom reads
questions.explanation: Read Committed already prevents dirty reads; Repeatable Read additionally guarantees that re-reading a row gives the same value. In the ANSI definitions phantoms are only ruled out at Serializable (PostgreSQL's snapshot-based Repeatable Read happens to prevent them too).

questions.prompt: Which sequence lists the main Node.js event-loop phases in the order they run?
options: timers → pending callbacks → poll → check → close callbacks
check → timers → poll → close callbacks
poll → timers → check → close callbacks
timers → check → poll → close callbacks
questions.explanation: Each loop iteration runs timers, pending callbacks, (idle/prepare), poll for I/O, check (setImmediate), then close callbacks. That's why setImmediate scheduled from an I/O callback runs before a 0 ms timer.

questions.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: what is the time complexity of inserting into, and removing the top of, a binary heap with n elements?
options: O(1) and O(1)
O(n) and O(log n)
O(1) and O(n)
O(log n) and O(log n)
questions.explanation: Insert sifts up and extract sifts down along the tree height, which is log n. Only peeking at the top is O(1); building a heap from n items at once is O(n).

questions.prompt: Reviewing your TypeScript cheat sheet: which of these utility-type notes are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Pick<T, K> keeps only the properties K from T
Partial<T> makes every property of T optional
Omit<T, K> removes the properties K from T
Record<K, V> validates object keys at runtime
Readonly<T> deep-freezes the object at runtime
questions.explanation: Partial, Pick and Omit are compile-time type transformations. Readonly<T> is shallow and compile-time only (use Object.freeze for runtime), and Record adds no runtime checks; types are erased when compiled.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CAP and PACELC are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A distributed system can be 'CA' and keep both properties during partitions
Eventual consistency means reads are never stale
During a network partition, a system must favour either consistency or availability
Many systems let you tune consistency per operation, e.g. quorum reads and writes
PACELC adds that, even without a partition, there is a latency vs consistency trade-off
questions.explanation: CAP's choice applies during partitions; PACELC adds the normal-operation latency vs consistency trade-off; quorum settings (e.g. in Cassandra) make it tunable. 'CA' isn't achievable once partitions happen, and eventual consistency explicitly allows stale reads for a while.

questions.prompt: The night before an interview, skimming your own condensed notes is usually more useful than starting a brand-new hard topic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Light review reinforces what you already know and keeps it accessible, while a new hard topic is unlikely to stick overnight and can raise anxiety by highlighting gaps.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a plain B-tree index on `email` is enough to speed up `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com'`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The index stores email values, not lower(email), so the planner can't use it for that predicate. Create an expression index ON users (lower(email)), or use the citext type.

questions.prompt: Cheat-sheet check: a POST successfully creates a new order resource. What is the most appropriate response?
options: 202 Accepted
201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource
204 No Content
200 OK with an empty body
questions.explanation: 201 signals that a resource was created, and Location tells the client its URL (often alongside the representation). 202 is for work accepted but not yet completed, such as an async job.

questions.prompt: A Redis instance used as a cache reaches maxmemory and writes start failing with OOM errors instead of old keys being evicted. What is the most likely cause?
options: The keys have TTLs, and keys with TTLs can never be evicted
Redis evicts only when a replica is attached
Redis can't evict keys without persistence enabled
maxmemory-policy is noeviction (the default); a cache should use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
questions.explanation: With noeviction, Redis refuses writes once it's full. For a cache, allkeys-lru/lfu (or the volatile-* policies when keys have TTLs) lets Redis evict old keys. Persistence and replicas are unrelated to eviction.

questions.prompt: Why is a full night's sleep before an interview worth more than a few extra hours of study?
options: Sleep only matters for physical tasks
Studying late is fine as long as you drink coffee in the morning
Sleep helps consolidate memory and restores the attention and working memory problem solving needs
Interviewers can tell visually when you're tired
questions.explanation: Sleep supports memory consolidation, and sleep loss impairs attention and working memory, which are exactly what live coding and design rounds demand. Caffeine can mask sleepiness but doesn't restore the lost cognitive performance.

questions.prompt: It's 11 pm, your interview is at 10 am, and you still feel shaky on graphs. What's the best plan?
options: Stay up and solve as many graph problems as possible
Do a short review of your graph cheat sheet, then sleep
Skip sleep and review graphs in the morning instead
Switch to learning a completely new topic
questions.explanation: A brief skim of key patterns keeps them fresh without costing sleep. Late-night cramming trades a small knowledge gain for a large drop in the reasoning and focus you need tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Which preparation the day before a remote interview prevents the most avoidable problems?
options: Testing camera, mic, internet, and the interview tool or editor, and preparing a quiet space
Buying a new laptop
Rewriting your resume
Reinstalling your operating system
questions.explanation: Technical hiccups waste interview time and add stress; a dry run of the call link and editor (e.g. CoderPad) plus a charger and quiet room removes most risks. Major system changes the day before create new risks.

questions.prompt: Mid-interview, your mind goes blank on a problem. What is the best recovery?
options: Say you need a moment, restate the problem, work a small example out loud and start from a brute force
Ask to skip to a different problem immediately
Stay silent until an idea comes
Start writing code at random to look busy
questions.explanation: Restating and working a concrete example often restarts your thinking and shows a methodical process, and a brute force gives a foothold to optimise. Long silence or aimless coding gives the interviewer nothing to assess or help with.

questions.prompt: Which habits on the day before an interview usually help performance? Select all that apply.
options: Cramming 20 new hard problems
Drinking strong coffee late at night to study longer
Planning the schedule, with buffer time before the interview
Preparing a few thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer
A walk or light exercise
questions.explanation: Light activity, prepared questions and a buffered schedule reduce stress and help you show up focused. Late caffeine disrupts sleep, and cramming new problems adds fatigue and anxiety without much retention.

questions.prompt: Between back-to-back onsite rounds, which actions help you do your best in the next one? Select all that apply.
options: Glance at your one-page notes for the next round's type
Mentally close the previous round instead of replaying it
Ask the next interviewer how you did in the previous round
Replay every mistake from the last round in detail
Take a short reset: water, a few slow breaths
questions.explanation: A quick physical reset, letting go of the last round and a light refresh help you start fresh. Ruminating drains focus, and the next interviewer typically hasn't seen (and shouldn't share) other rounds' feedback.

questions.prompt: Pulling an all-nighter before a problem-solving interview usually improves performance, because the material is fresh.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation impairs attention, working memory and flexible thinking, which outweighs any benefit of last-minute review. Recently crammed material is also poorly consolidated without sleep.

questions.prompt: Some nervousness before an interview is normal, and slow, deliberate breathing is a commonly recommended way to calm it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Moderate arousal is normal and can even sharpen focus; slow breathing (longer exhales) is a widely used, simple way to reduce acute stress before or during a round.

questions.prompt: You have three onsite loops scheduled in one week. How should you arrange them, if you can?
options: All on the same day to get them over with
Schedule them without checking any other commitments
With recovery time between the big loops, ideally a lighter day in between
Back-to-back late at night after work
questions.explanation: Full loops are mentally draining; spacing them lets you rest and briefly review between companies. Stacking them causes fatigue that drags down later loops.

questions.prompt: Which morning-of routine best sets you up for a 10 am interview?
options: Eat a normal meal, skim your one-page notes and STAR stories, and join or arrive 10 minutes early
Skip breakfast and solve two hard new problems
Stay in bed until 9:55 to maximise rest
Start a new system design topic to stay sharp
questions.explanation: A normal meal, a light refresh of familiar material and a buffer for logistics keep you calm and focused. New hard problems in the morning risk shaking your confidence right before the round.

questions.prompt: You feel the first round of an onsite went badly. What's the best mindset for the next round?
options: Tell the next interviewer the first round went badly
Assume the loop is lost and coast
Ask to end the loop early
Reset and give the next round full effort; rounds are often scored independently and your sense of how it went is often wrong
questions.explanation: Interviewers usually write separate feedback, and decisions weigh the whole loop; candidates also often misjudge their own rounds. Coasting or announcing a bad round turns one weak signal into several.

questions.prompt: A user with a valid, unexpired access token calls DELETE on a document owned by another tenant, and your API refuses. Which HTTP status best describes the refusal?
options: 403 Forbidden
500 Internal Server Error
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
questions.explanation: The caller is authenticated but not permitted, which is 403. 401 means credentials are missing or invalid (authentication failed). Some APIs return 404 instead to avoid revealing the resource exists, but among these options 403 is the right one.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication is done by the client; authorization is done by the database
They are synonyms for the same login check
Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do
Authentication protects data at rest; authorization protects data in transit
questions.explanation: AuthN verifies identity (password, token signature, MFA). AuthZ applies policy to that identity for a specific action and resource. Many vulnerabilities come from doing the first and skipping the second.

questions.prompt: A hospital rule says: doctors may view records only of patients in their own department, and only during their shift. Which access-control model expresses this most naturally?
options: RBAC with a single 'doctor' role
DAC, letting each patient choose which doctors may read their record
Access-control lists on each record listing every allowed doctor
ABAC, because the decision depends on attributes of the user, the resource and the environment (time)
questions.explanation: The rule combines user department, record department and current time; ABAC evaluates exactly those attributes. A plain 'doctor' role grants all records at all times, and per-record ACLs would need constant manual updating.

questions.prompt: GET /invoices/:id verifies the JWT and then returns Invoice.findById(id). Users can read other customers' invoices by changing the id. What is this vulnerability, and how do you fix it?
options: CSRF; add an anti-CSRF token to the request
SQL injection; switch to parameterised queries
Broken object-level authorization (IDOR); scope the lookup to the caller, e.g. findOne({ _id: id, customerId: user.customerId })
Session fixation; rotate the session id after login
questions.explanation: Authentication passed, but nothing checked that this caller owns this object. BOLA is #1 on the OWASP API Top 10. Using random UUIDs only makes ids harder to guess; the ownership check is the real fix.

questions.prompt: Your RBAC setup now has roles like editor-team-a-eu, editor-team-a-us, viewer-team-b-eu and hundreds more. What is the most sensible direction?
options: Give everyone the admin role to simplify management
Replace roles with per-user hard-coded checks in each controller
Keep adding roles, since RBAC scales linearly with no downside
Keep a few coarse roles and move team/region conditions into attribute-based policy checks
questions.explanation: This is 'role explosion': encoding attributes into role names. Combining a small set of roles with attribute conditions (team, region, ownership) keeps policy manageable and auditable. Scattered per-controller checks make authorization impossible to review.

questions.prompt: In a Next.js app, where must the check that 'only admins can delete users' be enforced?
options: In the browser's localStorage, by storing an isAdmin flag
Only in proxy.ts / middleware, based on the URL path
Only in the React component, by hiding the delete button from non-admins
On the server in the Server Action or API handler, next to the data access, on every request
questions.explanation: Anyone can call the endpoint directly, so the authoritative check must run server-side where the data is touched. Hiding UI is just UX, and path-based middleware is only an optimistic first filter that can be bypassed or drift.

questions.prompt: In a multi-tenant SaaS backend, what is the strongest default defence against one tenant reading another tenant's data?
options: Encrypt each tenant's rows with the same application key
Derive the tenant id from the authenticated session on the server and scope every query by it (or use PostgreSQL row-level security)
Accept tenantId from the request body and validate it with zod
Use a different URL subdomain per tenant
questions.explanation: The tenant must come from a trusted source (the verified token), never from client input, and be applied consistently, ideally enforced centrally with RLS. zod validates shape, not ownership; a shared key doesn't separate tenants at all.

questions.prompt: Which of these are authorization decisions rather than authentication? Select all that apply.
options: Can this user read a document shared with their team?
Can this user approve refunds over $500?
May service A call service B's /admin endpoint?
Is this password correct for this email?
Is this TOTP code valid for this account?
questions.explanation: Refund limits, service-to-service permissions and document sharing all decide what an identity may do. Checking a password or a TOTP code verifies who the caller is, which is authentication.

questions.prompt: Which statements about RBAC and ABAC are correct? Select all that apply.
options: ABAC removes the need for authentication, since attributes identify the user
RBAC makes it easy to answer 'who can do X?' by listing members of the roles that grant X
ABAC can express context such as time of day, IP range or resource ownership
Many systems combine both: roles grant coarse permissions and attribute checks such as ownership refine them
questions.explanation: RBAC is simple to audit, ABAC is more expressive, and hybrids are common. ABAC still needs a trusted, authenticated identity; its attributes are only meaningful if you know who the subject is.

questions.prompt: A request carrying a valid, unexpired JWT should be allowed to call any endpoint in the API.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A valid token proves authentication (and maybe carries scopes or roles). Each endpoint still has to check that this identity may perform this action on this resource.

questions.prompt: Authorization logic should default to deny, granting access only when a rule explicitly allows it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Deny-by-default means a forgotten rule or a new endpoint fails closed. Allow-by-default fails open, which is how accidental data exposure happens.

questions.prompt: What makes it hard to revoke a stateless JWT access token before it expires?
options: The browser caches JWTs and ignores server instructions
The server accepts any token with a valid signature and unexpired exp without looking anything up, so a stolen token works until expiry
JWTs are encrypted, so the server can't read them to revoke them
Revoking a JWT requires rotating the signing key for every user
questions.explanation: Statelessness is the point of a JWT: no lookup per request. Revoking one requires adding state (a denylist or a per-user token version). Rotating the signing key revokes everyone's tokens, which is a blunt emergency tool, not normal revocation.

questions.prompt: Where should a browser-based app keep a server-side session id?
options: In the URL query string so it survives redirects
In a JavaScript global variable
In localStorage, read by JavaScript and sent in a header
In a cookie marked HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite
questions.explanation: HttpOnly keeps it out of reach of injected scripts, Secure keeps it on HTTPS, and SameSite limits cross-site sending (CSRF). URL tokens leak through logs, history and Referer headers.

questions.prompt: What is the common pattern for getting most of JWT's benefits while keeping revocation manageable?
options: Short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus a refresh token that is stored and revocable on the server
Re-signing each token on every request with a new key
Storing the user's password hash inside the token so the server can recheck it
Long-lived access tokens (30 days) with no refresh token
questions.explanation: A short access-token lifetime caps how long a stolen token is useful, and the server-side refresh token gives a revocation point. Long-lived tokens maximise the abuse window, and a password hash in the token leaks a secret.

questions.prompt: A JWT payload contains the user's email and role. A teammate says this is fine because 'the token is signed'. What is the issue?
options: None; the signature encrypts the payload
The token will be too large to fit in a cookie
Signed tokens can't contain strings, only numeric claims
The payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone holding the token can read it; the signature gives integrity, not confidentiality
questions.explanation: A JWS is readable by anyone; the signature only detects tampering. Keep sensitive data out of it, or use JWE if the payload must be confidential. Email and role are usually acceptable, but they are not secret.

questions.prompt: An API verifies RS256 JWTs, but its library uses whatever alg the token header names. An attacker forges a token signed with HS256, using the server's public key as the HMAC secret, and it's accepted. What fixes this?
options: Check the exp claim more strictly
Make the RSA public key secret
Switch from RS256 to HS256 everywhere
Pin the accepted algorithms when verifying, e.g. jwt.verify(token, key, { algorithms: ['RS256'] })
questions.explanation: This is algorithm confusion: the server treats the public key as an HMAC key. Never let the token choose the algorithm; pin it (and reject alg: none). The public key is public by design, so hiding it isn't a real fix.

questions.prompt: You use refresh-token rotation: each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. An already-used refresh token is presented again. What should the server do?
options: Extend the old token's lifetime to avoid breaking clients
Treat it as likely theft and revoke the whole token family/session, forcing re-login
Ignore the request and keep the current token valid
Issue a new access token, since the user is probably on a slow network
questions.explanation: Reuse means two parties hold the same token, so one is probably an attacker. Revoking the family cuts off both, and the real user logs in again. Accepting it defeats the purpose of rotation.

questions.prompt: Users get 15-minute JWT access tokens. After a password change, all existing tokens must stop working immediately. What does that require?
options: Asking the browser to delete the token from storage
Storing a per-user tokenVersion or passwordChangedAt and rejecting tokens issued before it, which means a lookup per request
Nothing; changing the password invalidates JWTs automatically
Shortening the expiry of new tokens to 1 minute
questions.explanation: A JWT carries no link to the password. Immediate invalidation needs server state to compare against (token version, iat cutoff or denylist). Clearing the client copy doesn't affect stolen copies, and shorter new tokens don't affect existing ones.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine advantages of server-side sessions over self-contained JWTs? Select all that apply.
options: Instant revocation by deleting the session record
Any service can validate them without access to a shared store
Session data never leaves the server, so the client can't read it
Only a small opaque id travels with each request
No storage is needed on the server
questions.explanation: Sessions are revocable, small and opaque. The trade-off is that they need a store (DB or cache) every service can reach. Needing no storage and validating without a shared store are JWT properties, not session properties.

questions.prompt: Which checks should an API perform when validating a JWT access token? Select all that apply.
options: Check that iss is the expected issuer
Trust the role claim even if the signature fails, as long as exp is in the future
Verify the signature with the expected key and pinned algorithm
Check exp (and nbf if present), allowing a little clock skew
Check that aud matches this API
questions.explanation: Signature, time, audience and issuer checks together make sure the token is authentic, current, meant for you and from the right issuer. Claims from a token whose signature fails are attacker-controlled.

questions.prompt: A JWT stored in localStorage can be read by any JavaScript running on the page, so an XSS bug can steal it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. localStorage has no HttpOnly equivalent. An HttpOnly cookie keeps the token away from scripts, though XSS can still make requests as the user while the page is open.

questions.prompt: Logging a user out by deleting the JWT on the client guarantees that a copy stolen earlier can no longer be used.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The server still accepts any copy until exp unless it keeps revocation state. Client-side logout only removes the local copy.

questions.prompt: Which OAuth 2.0 flow is recommended today for a single-page app or mobile app signing users in?
options: Client Credentials
Resource Owner Password Credentials
Authorization Code with PKCE
Implicit grant
questions.explanation: Current best practice (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP, OAuth 2.1) is Authorization Code + PKCE for public clients. The implicit grant returns tokens in the URL and is deprecated; password grant hands the user's password to the client.

questions.prompt: In OAuth 2.0, what is the resource server?
options: The user's browser
The server that shows the login page and issues tokens
The API that accepts access tokens and serves the protected data
The app the user is trying to sign into
questions.explanation: The authorization server authenticates the user and issues tokens; the client is the app; the resource server is the API that validates access tokens and enforces scopes. In small setups one service may play two roles.

questions.prompt: What problem does PKCE solve in the authorization code flow?
options: It binds the authorization code to the client instance that started the flow, so an intercepted code can't be exchanged by someone else
It replaces the need for HTTPS on the redirect
It encrypts the access token so the client can't read it
It lets the API validate tokens without contacting the authorization server
questions.explanation: The client sends a hash (code_challenge) up front and must present the original code_verifier when redeeming the code. A stolen code is useless without the verifier. TLS is still required.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the state parameter in an OAuth authorization request?
options: Protecting the redirect from CSRF by tying the callback to a request this browser started
Telling the authorization server which scopes to grant
Carrying the user's id to the API
Choosing between the code and token response types
questions.explanation: The client stores a random state value and checks it on the callback, so an attacker can't inject their own authorization response into the victim's session. Scopes go in the scope parameter. PKCE also mitigates some of these attacks, but state remains standard.

questions.prompt: A nightly billing job needs to call an internal API. No user is involved. Which OAuth grant fits?
options: Implicit grant
Authorization Code with PKCE
Device Authorization grant
Client Credentials
questions.explanation: Client Credentials lets a confidential client get a token for itself using its own credentials. Authorization Code and Device flows exist to get a user's consent, and the implicit grant is deprecated.

questions.prompt: A SPA sends the OIDC ID token as a Bearer token to your backend API, and the API accepts it. Why is this a design mistake?
options: The ID token is meant for the client to learn who logged in (its aud is the client); APIs should require access tokens issued for their own audience
The API can't read the user's email from an ID token
ID tokens expire too slowly to be safe
ID tokens are not JWTs, so they can't be verified
questions.explanation: ID tokens describe the authentication event to the client. An API accepting them can be fed tokens issued to any client of the same provider. Access tokens with aud set to the API (and scopes) are the right credential.

questions.prompt: An authorization server accepts any redirect_uri that starts with https://app.example.com. Why is this dangerous?
options: Prefix matching makes the login page slower
An attacker can use a URL like https://app.example.com.evil.net or an open redirect on the site to receive authorization codes; redirect URIs should match registered values exactly
It prevents the use of refresh tokens
It forces the client to use the implicit flow
questions.explanation: Loose matching is a classic way to steal codes or tokens. The Security BCP requires exact string matching against pre-registered URIs. It has nothing to do with performance or which grant is used.

questions.prompt: Which of these does OpenID Connect add on top of OAuth 2.0? Select all that apply.
options: The UserInfo endpoint
The openid scope
The client credentials grant
The ID token, a signed JWT describing the authenticated user
Refresh tokens
questions.explanation: OIDC is an identity layer: openid scope, ID token, UserInfo, discovery. Client credentials and refresh tokens are part of core OAuth 2.0.

questions.prompt: Which practices are recommended by the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (and OAuth 2.1)? Select all that apply.
options: Use PKCE for all clients, including confidential ones
Stop using the resource owner password credentials grant
Match redirect URIs exactly against registered values
Send access tokens in the URL query string for simplicity
Stop using the implicit grant
questions.explanation: These are the core hardening steps. Tokens in query strings leak via logs, history and Referer headers; they belong in the Authorization header.

questions.prompt: In the Authorization Code with PKCE flow, the user types their password into the third-party client app.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The user authenticates on the authorization server's own page; the client only receives a code and then tokens. Keeping the password away from clients is the main point of OAuth.

questions.prompt: OAuth scopes limit what an access token is meant to be used for, but the API must still check the scopes on each request.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The authorization server only writes scopes into the token; nothing enforces them unless the resource server checks, for example, that orders:write is present before a write.

questions.prompt: Why is a plain SHA-256 hash a poor choice for storing passwords?
options: SHA-256 has known collisions that reveal passwords
SHA-256 output is too short to store
SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so attackers with GPUs can try billions of guesses per second against a leaked hash
SHA-256 can't hash Unicode passwords
questions.explanation: Speed is good for checksums and bad for passwords. Password hashes like argon2id, bcrypt and scrypt are deliberately slow and tunable. SHA-256 has no practical collisions; the problem is how cheap guessing is.

questions.prompt: What does a per-password salt achieve?
options: It lets you decrypt the password later if needed
It makes identical passwords hash differently and makes precomputed rainbow tables useless
It keeps the hash secret even if the database leaks
It makes each hash computation slower
questions.explanation: A unique random salt forces attackers to crack each hash separately and defeats lookup tables. It isn't secret (it's stored next to the hash) and it doesn't add work per guess; the cost factor does that.

questions.prompt: You raise bcrypt's cost factor from 10 to 12. Roughly how much slower is each hash?
options: 20% slower
12 times slower
2 times slower
4 times slower
questions.explanation: The cost is a base-2 exponent: work = 2^cost rounds. Going from 10 to 12 is 2^2 = 4 times the work, for both your login endpoint and an attacker's guessing.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of argon2id over bcrypt?
options: It can be reversed by the server with a secret key
It doesn't need a salt
It is memory-hard, so the memory each guess needs makes GPU/ASIC cracking much more expensive
It produces shorter hashes that save storage
questions.explanation: argon2id lets you tune memory, iterations and parallelism; requiring lots of memory per guess limits how many guesses specialised hardware can run at once. It still uses a salt and is still one-way.

questions.prompt: Which is a well-known limitation of bcrypt?
options: Its cost factor can't be changed after deployment
It needs a separate salt column in the database
It only uses the first 72 bytes of the password, ignoring the rest
It can only hash ASCII passwords
questions.explanation: bcrypt truncates input at 72 bytes, so long passphrases beyond that add nothing. The salt and cost are encoded in the hash string itself, and the cost can be raised for new hashes at any time.

questions.prompt: A Node.js login route uses bcrypt.hashSync / compareSync at cost 12. Under load, p99 latency spikes for every route, not just login. Why?
options: Synchronous hashing blocks the single event-loop thread for hundreds of milliseconds, stalling all requests
bcrypt opens a new database connection per call
The hash is too long to fit in a TCP packet
bcrypt holds a global mutex that blocks other modules
questions.explanation: The sync variants do CPU-heavy work on the main thread. Use the async APIs (bcrypt.hash/compare, crypto.scrypt with a callback), which run on the libuv threadpool, and consider rate limiting logins.

questions.prompt: What does a pepper add on top of a salt?
options: It's a secret key kept outside the database (e.g. in a secrets manager), so a database dump alone isn't enough to start cracking
It doubles the work factor of every hash
It makes each hash unique per user
It lets users recover forgotten passwords
questions.explanation: A pepper (often applied with HMAC) is secret and shared, unlike the public per-user salt. An attacker who only steals the DB can't test guesses. Uniqueness per user is what the salt provides.

questions.prompt: Which are suitable for storing user passwords? Select all that apply.
options: scrypt
MD5 with a per-user salt
argon2id
PBKDF2 with a high iteration count
bcrypt
AES encryption with an app key
questions.explanation: These four are deliberately slow, salted KDFs (PBKDF2 is acceptable but not memory-hard). Salted MD5 is still extremely fast to brute-force, and encryption is reversible by anyone who gets the key.

questions.prompt: Which practices are correct for verifying and maintaining password hashes? Select all that apply.
options: Return 'user not found' and 'wrong password' as distinct errors for better UX
On successful login, rehash the password if the stored hash uses outdated parameters
Store the algorithm and parameters with the hash (e.g. a $argon2id$v=19$m=... string) so they can evolve
Compare derived hashes in constant time (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual) when doing the comparison yourself
questions.explanation: Constant-time comparison avoids timing leaks, rehash-on-login upgrades old hashes, and self-describing hash strings make upgrades possible. Distinct error messages enable account enumeration; use one generic message.

questions.prompt: Encrypting passwords with AES and a key stored in the app's config is as secure as hashing them with bcrypt.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Anyone who gets the key (often stolen along with the DB or config) can decrypt every password at once. A password hash is one-way, and each guess costs real work.

questions.prompt: Node.js's built-in crypto module includes scrypt, a memory-hard key derivation function suitable for password hashing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. crypto.scrypt (async) and crypto.scryptSync are built in. Use a random salt per password and tune the cost parameters; argon2 needs a third-party package.

questions.prompt: What is the correct fix for this Node.js/PostgreSQL code?
questions.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + req.body.email + "'";
const { rows } = await pool.query(sql);
options: Base64-encode the email before inserting it into the SQL
Use a parameterised query: pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [req.body.email])
Escape single quotes in the email with replaceAll("'", "''")
Reject emails that contain the word SELECT
questions.explanation: Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so input can never change the query's structure. Manual escaping and keyword blocklists are fragile and routinely bypassed.

questions.prompt: User comments are stored and later shown to other users, and an attacker's comment runs <script> in viewers' browsers. What is the primary fix?
options: Validate comments with a SQL injection filter
Serve the page over HTTPS
Store comments base64-encoded in the database
Context-aware output encoding when rendering (React escapes text by default; avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML), backed by a Content Security Policy
questions.explanation: Stored XSS happens when untrusted data is rendered as HTML. Encode on output for the right context and use CSP as defence in depth. HTTPS protects transport, not rendering; base64 at rest changes nothing once it's decoded for display.

questions.prompt: How does setting session cookies to SameSite=Lax mitigate CSRF?
options: It encrypts the cookie so attackers can't read it
It stops JavaScript from reading the cookie
It makes the cookie expire when the tab closes
Browsers don't send the cookie on cross-site subrequests or cross-site POSTs, so a forged form post from evil.com arrives without the session
questions.explanation: CSRF relies on the browser attaching cookies to requests that another site triggers. Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so GET handlers must have no side effects. Stopping script access is what HttpOnly does.

questions.prompt: A link-preview feature fetches any URL a user submits. An attacker submits http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/ and gets cloud credentials back. Which defence addresses this?
options: Require the URL to use HTTPS
Rate-limit the preview endpoint to 10 requests per minute
Escape the URL before calling fetch
Resolve the hostname and refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses (or use an allowlist), and require IMDSv2 on the instance
questions.explanation: This is SSRF: the server is tricked into reaching internal endpoints. Block internal address ranges after resolution (or allowlist domains), and harden the metadata service. Rate limits and HTTPS don't stop a single malicious request.

questions.prompt: Your SSRF filter resolves a hostname, confirms it's a public IP, and then calls fetch(url). Attackers still reach internal services. What is the most likely bypass?
options: fetch ignores the hostname and always uses IPv6
Public IPs can't be validated reliably, so SSRF can't be prevented
The filter should have used a regex on the URL instead of DNS
DNS rebinding: fetch resolves the name again and the attacker's DNS now returns an internal IP; pin the validated IP for the connection or check at connect time
questions.explanation: Checking and then resolving again is a TOCTOU race; a short-TTL record can switch to 127.0.0.1 or 10.x. Validate the address actually being connected to (custom lookup/agent) and also block redirects to internal hosts. Regexes on URLs are easier to bypass.

questions.prompt: A login handler runs User.findOne({ email: req.body.email, password: req.body.password }) against MongoDB. An attacker sends {"email": "admin@x.com", "password": {"$ne": null}} and logs in. What is the fix?
options: Switch to PostgreSQL, which can't be injected
Wrap the query in a try/catch
Use HTTPS so the body can't be modified
Validate input types (e.g. zod: password must be a string), compare a password hash rather than querying on it, and sanitise operator keys
questions.explanation: This is NoSQL operator injection: a JSON object turns the condition into 'password not null'. Strict type validation blocks it, and passwords should be checked with a hash comparison anyway. SQL databases have their own injection risk, and HTTPS doesn't stop a malicious client.

questions.prompt: An API authenticates only via an Authorization: Bearer header that the frontend's JavaScript sets, and uses no cookies. Which statement about CSRF is correct?
options: It is safe from both CSRF and XSS
CSRF tokens are still required on every request
It is highly exposed to CSRF, because headers are sent automatically on cross-site requests
Classic CSRF doesn't apply, because browsers don't attach that header automatically; XSS that steals or uses the token is the bigger risk
questions.explanation: CSRF exploits credentials the browser adds on its own (cookies, HTTP auth). A cross-site page can't set your Authorization header without your CORS permission. The token lives somewhere JS can read it, so XSS becomes the main concern.

questions.prompt: Which measures reduce XSS risk or its impact? Select all that apply.
options: Blocking input containing SQL keywords
HttpOnly on session cookies
Context-aware escaping of untrusted data when rendering
Enabling CORS for all origins
A Content Security Policy restricting script sources (no unsafe-inline)
questions.explanation: Escaping prevents injection, CSP blocks injected scripts from running, and HttpOnly stops scripts stealing session cookies. SQL keyword filters target a different bug, and permissive CORS weakens security.

questions.prompt: Which snippets contain an injection vulnerability? Select all that apply.
options: pool.query('SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id])
child_process.exec(`convert ${req.query.file} out.png`)
eval(req.query.expr)
An LDAP filter built as `(uid=${username})`
res.json(user)
questions.explanation: Shell commands, LDAP filters and eval all interpret attacker-controlled text as code or syntax. Use execFile with an argument array, escape LDAP values, and never eval input. The parameterised query and res.json are safe.

questions.prompt: CORS is a server-side protection that stops attackers from sending requests to your API.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. CORS is a browser rule about which origins may read responses. curl, scripts and servers ignore it, and some cross-site requests are still sent. Authentication and authorization protect the API.

questions.prompt: Prepared-statement parameters can't stand in for identifiers such as table or column names, so a user-chosen ORDER BY column should be checked against an allowlist.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Placeholders like $1 bind values only. For dynamic identifiers, map user input to a fixed set of known column names (or quote with a proper identifier-escaping function).

questions.prompt: You discover a live third-party API key was committed to a public GitHub repo an hour ago. What should you do first?
options: Add the file to .gitignore
Make the repository private
Rewrite git history to remove the commit, then carry on
Revoke or rotate the key immediately, then clean up history and check usage logs
questions.explanation: Assume the key has already been harvested; bots scan GitHub within minutes. Revoking it ends the exposure. Rewriting history, going private or using .gitignore don't invalidate copies that are already out.

questions.prompt: What does TLS provide for traffic between a client and your API?
options: Hiding which IP address the client is connecting to
Protection against SQL injection in request bodies
Confidentiality, integrity, and authentication of the server (and optionally the client)
Encryption of data stored on the server's disk
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts and integrity-protects data in transit and authenticates the server via certificates (mutual TLS also authenticates the client). It doesn't cover data at rest or app-level bugs, and IPs remain visible.

questions.prompt: Your managed database has disk encryption at rest enabled. Which threat does this mainly protect against?
options: An attacker who steals the database credentials
Someone obtaining the physical disks, raw volumes or backup snapshots
An attacker who exploits SQL injection in your app
A malicious insider querying through the admin console
questions.explanation: Storage encryption is transparent to anyone accessing data through the database engine, so injection or stolen credentials still return plaintext. It protects media and snapshots that leave the trust boundary.

questions.prompt: What is envelope encryption, as used with AWS KMS or GCP KMS?
options: Storing the encryption key in the same row as the ciphertext
Encrypting data with a data key, then encrypting that data key with a master key held in KMS that never leaves it
Encrypting data twice with the same key for extra strength
Wrapping each HTTP request in TLS and also in a VPN
questions.explanation: Bulk data is encrypted locally with a DEK; only the small wrapped DEK goes to KMS for decryption. The master key stays in KMS, access is audited, and the master key can be rotated without re-encrypting all the data.

questions.prompt: A service encrypts records with AES-256-GCM using a fixed key, and a bug causes the same 96-bit nonce to be reused for many messages. How serious is this?
options: Severe: nonce reuse leaks the XOR of the plaintexts and lets attackers forge authentication tags
It only matters if the key is shorter than 256 bits
Minor: it just makes ciphertexts slightly larger
Harmless, because AES-256 is strong enough on its own
questions.explanation: GCM is a stream mode, so reusing a nonce reuses the keystream and exposes the authentication subkey, allowing forgeries. Key length doesn't help. Use random nonces from crypto.randomBytes(12) or counters, and rotate keys well before nonce limits.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile has `ENV STRIPE_KEY=sk_live_...` so the app can read the key. What is the problem?
options: The key will be visible only during the build, which is acceptable
Environment variables can't hold strings longer than 32 characters
Docker encrypts ENV values, so the only issue is performance
The secret is baked into the image config and layers, so anyone who can pull the image can read it; inject it at runtime or use BuildKit secret mounts
questions.explanation: ENV and ARG values persist in image metadata and history (docker history/inspect). Provide secrets at runtime from a secret manager or orchestrator, or with --mount=type=secret for build-time needs.

questions.prompt: What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add for service-to-service calls compared with ordinary TLS?
options: Faster handshakes by skipping certificate validation
The client also presents a certificate, so the server can authenticate which service is calling
Encryption of the payload twice
Automatic authorization of every endpoint the caller requests
questions.explanation: Ordinary TLS authenticates only the server. With mTLS the server verifies a client certificate too, giving a strong workload identity (as service meshes do). It authenticates; authorization rules are still needed on top.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices for managing application secrets? Select all that apply.
options: Share the production database password in the team chat channel
Keep secrets in a secret manager (e.g. Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) and inject them at runtime
Use separate secrets for development, staging and production
Rotate secrets regularly and whenever someone with access leaves
Log full request headers, including Authorization, to make debugging easier
questions.explanation: Central storage, rotation and per-environment separation limit exposure and blast radius. Logging Authorization headers and sharing passwords in chat spread secrets to places with weak access control and long retention.

questions.prompt: Which statements about TLS are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An HSTS header tells browsers to use only HTTPS for the domain from then on
TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange, so every handshake has forward secrecy
TLS hides the destination IP address from network observers
Setting rejectUnauthorized: false in Node disables certificate checks and allows man-in-the-middle attacks
questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral (EC)DHE only; turning off verification removes server authentication; HSTS prevents downgrade to HTTP. IP headers are outside TLS, so observers still see the destination IP (and often the SNI).

questions.prompt: The base64-encoded values in a Kubernetes Secret manifest are encrypted.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Base64 is an encoding that anyone can decode. Protect Secrets with RBAC, etcd encryption at rest, and tools like Sealed Secrets or External Secrets instead of committing raw manifests.

questions.prompt: Application-level encryption of a database column protects that data even from a DBA who can read the raw tables, as long as the key is held outside the database.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The database only ever sees ciphertext, so DB-level access isn't enough. The trade-off is that you lose server-side querying on that column (except with techniques like blind indexes).

questions.prompt: An `Employee` class has `calculatePay()` (used by finance), `reportHours()` (used by HR) and `save()` (used by the DBA team). Why does this violate the Single Responsibility Principle?
options: Three different actors can each require changes to the same class for unrelated reasons
It has more than two public methods
Employee should extend a base Person class
`save()` should be static
questions.explanation: SRP is about reasons to change, i.e. the people or groups a module answers to. Here finance, HR and the DBAs all drive edits to one class. Method count alone isn't the test; a class can have many methods serving one actor.

questions.prompt: An Express route handler validates the body, queries PostgreSQL, computes a loyalty discount, sends a confirmation email and formats the JSON response, all inline. What refactor best applies SRP?
options: Split it into five Express middlewares that share state via `res.locals`
Wrap the handler in try/catch so failures are isolated
Keep the handler thin: schema validation, an order service for the discount rule, a repository for queries and a notifier for email
Move the whole handler into a single `OrderManager` class
questions.explanation: Each concern changes for different reasons (API shape, business rules, storage, messaging), so each gets its own unit with the handler just coordinating. Moving everything into one 'Manager' class only relocates the problem, and chaining middlewares through res.locals hides the dependencies.

questions.prompt: Inspired by SRP, a team puts every function into its own class: `PriceRounder`, `PriceTaxAdder`, `PriceDiscountApplier`, each with a single method. What's the likely cost?
options: TypeScript limits the number of classes per module
Related logic gets scattered across many tiny classes, lowering cohesion and making the overall flow hard to follow
Nothing; smaller classes are always better
The code becomes impossible to unit test
questions.explanation: SRP groups things that change for the same reason; it doesn't mean one method per class. Pricing steps that always change together belong together. Tiny classes remain testable, but readers have to chase logic across files.

questions.prompt: Which change request would force edits to this class for a reason unrelated to invoicing rules?
options: Marketing wants a new logo and font in the PDF
Rounding totals to two decimals
Adding a new discount type
Changing how VAT is applied to discounted lines
questions.explanation: PDF branding belongs to presentation, yet it forces a change (and redeploy and retest) in the class that holds tax logic. VAT, discounts and rounding are all invoicing rules, so they're the class's legitimate reason to change.

questions.prompt: Two teams keep getting merge conflicts in `user.service.ts`: one is building password-reset flows, the other is changing profile-photo uploads. What does this most likely indicate?
options: They should use a different branching strategy
The file mixes responsibilities driven by different actors and should be split along those lines
The file is too long and needs more comments
TypeScript's module system is causing the conflicts
questions.explanation: Frequent conflicts between unrelated features in one file are a practical symptom of an SRP violation. Separating auth/reset logic from profile media lets each team change its code independently. Branching tweaks only treat the symptom.

questions.prompt: `calculatePay()` (finance) and `reportHours()` (HR) share a private helper `regularHours()`. Finance changes the helper for a pay rule, and HR's reports silently become wrong. What's the lesson?
options: Code that serves different actors shouldn't share implementation just because it looks the same today; separate it per actor
Private helpers should never be shared
Make the helper public so both teams can see it
Add more unit tests to HR only
questions.explanation: Coincidentally similar logic that belongs to different actors evolves differently. Keeping it in one place couples them, so one actor's change breaks the other. Splitting by actor, even with some duplication, removes the hidden link.

questions.prompt: A `User` domain entity has a `toApiJson()` method that shapes the v1 API response. Now v2 needs a different shape. What's the SRP-friendly move?
options: Pass a version flag into `toApiJson(version)`
Move response mapping into the HTTP layer (a serializer/DTO mapper per API version) and keep the entity focused on domain rules
Add a `toApiJsonV2()` method to the entity
Store both shapes in the database
questions.explanation: API presentation changes for different reasons than domain rules. Mapping in the transport layer keeps the entity stable while API versions evolve. Adding versioned methods or flags keeps tying the entity to every client format.

questions.prompt: Which are common signs that a class violates SRP? Select all that apply.
options: It imports HTTP, database, email and PDF libraries
It has three methods that all deal with price calculation
Its tests need many unrelated mocks to construct it
It is under 50 lines
Its name is vague, like `OrderManager` or `UserHelper`
questions.explanation: Vague names, imports spanning many layers and sprawling test setup suggest several reasons to change. Several cohesive pricing methods serve one purpose, and size alone doesn't decide SRP.

questions.prompt: Which benefits does following SRP usually bring? Select all that apply.
options: Guaranteed better runtime performance
Changes have a smaller blast radius
Units are easier to test in isolation
Fewer merge conflicts between teams working on different features
Fewer files in the codebase
questions.explanation: Separating reasons to change localises edits, simplifies tests and reduces collisions. It usually means more (smaller) files, and it's a maintainability principle with no performance guarantee.

questions.prompt: A class with many methods always violates the Single Responsibility Principle.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. If all the methods serve one actor and change for the same reason (e.g. a rich `Money` value object), the class is cohesive. SRP measures reasons to change, not size.

questions.prompt: The Single Responsibility idea applies to functions and modules as well as to classes.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A function that parses, validates and persists, or a module mixing unrelated features, has the same problem as a multi-purpose class: unrelated changes collide in one place.

questions.prompt: A `discountFor(customer)` function has `if (type === 'gold') ... else if (type === 'silver') ...`. Every new tier means editing and re-testing it. Which change best follows the Open/Closed Principle?
options: Define a `DiscountPolicy` interface with one implementation per tier, looked up from a registry, so new tiers add code without editing existing logic
Add comments listing which tiers exist
Replace the if/else with a switch statement
Move the if/else chain into a class method
questions.explanation: OCP means adding behaviour by adding code rather than modifying tested code. Policies behind an interface make a new tier a new class plus a registration. A switch or a class wrapper still requires editing the same branching logic.

questions.prompt: Shipping cost is computed by a `switch (order.carrier)` with cases for 'ups' and 'fedex'. You must add 'dhl' and expect more carriers. What's the most OCP-friendly refactor?
options: Store rate formulas as JavaScript strings in the database and eval them
Duplicate the function as `shippingCostV2` with dhl added
Add a 'dhl' case and a default that throws
A `CarrierRate` interface implemented per carrier, plus a map from carrier code to implementation built at startup
questions.explanation: A strategy map lets each carrier live in its own module; adding one doesn't touch the others or the calculation flow. Adding another case is fine for one-off changes but keeps the hotspot. Eval'd formulas are a security risk.

questions.prompt: How does Express or Fastify middleware illustrate the Open/Closed Principle?
options: Middleware prevents routes from being modified in future releases
You can add cross-cutting behaviour (auth, rate limiting, logging) by registering new middleware without editing existing route handlers
Each middleware must subclass the framework's Router
Middleware makes route handlers immutable at runtime
questions.explanation: The request pipeline is closed for modification but open for extension: new behaviour plugs in through a registration point. Nothing is frozen, and middleware are plain functions, not subclasses.
