questions.prompt: An engineer adds plugin hooks, strategy interfaces and config switches for ten kinds of variation in a new service 'to be OCP-compliant'. None of them has changed after a year. What's the better practice?
options: Keep adding extension points; they're free
Freeze the service so it can never be modified
Write the code simply first, and introduce an extension point when a real axis of change appears (e.g. the second time it varies)
Remove all interfaces from the codebase
questions.explanation: Extension points cost indirection and maintenance. Guessing them up front often picks the wrong axes. Applying OCP once real change shows up targets the right seam. Removing every interface goes too far the other way.

questions.prompt: You model shapes as classes (`Circle`, `Square`) that each implement `area()`. Adding a `Triangle` class is easy and OCP-friendly. Which change becomes harder?
options: Calling area() through the base interface
Writing unit tests for a single shape
Adding another shape
Adding a new operation (e.g. `perimeter()` or `toSvg()`), which means editing every shape class
questions.explanation: This is the expression problem: class hierarchies make new variants easy and new operations costly, while a discriminated union with switch-based functions is the reverse. OCP is always relative to the axis of change you expect.

questions.prompt: After an order is placed, the business keeps asking for more side effects: loyalty points, analytics, a warehouse webhook. How can checkout stay closed to modification?
options: Publish an `OrderPlaced` domain event and let each side effect subscribe as a separate handler
Run every side effect inside the same database transaction
Add each new call at the end of `placeOrder()`
Add a boolean parameter per side effect to `placeOrder()`
questions.explanation: With events, new reactions are new subscribers; placeOrder doesn't change. Appending calls or adding flags edits checkout every time, and stuffing external calls into the DB transaction couples failures together.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, 'OCP means we can never edit `PaymentService` again, even to fix bugs.' What's the accurate reading?
options: OCP aims to make adding new behaviour not require modifying existing code; fixing bugs or improving the existing code is still fine
Correct: fixes must go into subclasses
OCP means the file must be read-only in the repository
OCP only applies to classes marked `final`
questions.explanation: OCP is about how you accommodate new variations, not a ban on edits. Patching bugs in subclasses would be absurd. 'Closed' means stable against new requirements of the anticipated kind.

questions.prompt: Which techniques help code follow the Open/Closed Principle? Select all that apply.
options: Copying the class and editing the copy
Decorators that wrap an interface to add behaviour
Strategy pattern with a registry of implementations
Injecting dependencies behind interfaces
Adding another `else if` branch for each new case
questions.explanation: Strategies, decorators and injected abstractions all let you add behaviour by adding new code. A new else-if modifies existing logic, and copy-paste-edit creates divergent duplicates.

questions.prompt: Which are signs that a codebase is violating the Open/Closed Principle? Select all that apply.
options: The same `switch (type)` appears in several files
Adding a new variant means many small edits scattered across the code
Each new feature requires editing a core, heavily tested module
A new variant is one new class plus one line registering it
questions.explanation: Repeated type switches, constant edits to the core and scattered changes show the design has no extension points on that axis. One new class plus a registration line is what OCP compliance looks like.

questions.prompt: The Strategy pattern lets you add a new algorithm without changing the context class that uses it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The context depends on the strategy interface; a new implementation plugs in through configuration or injection. That's a textbook OCP mechanism.

questions.prompt: Following the Open/Closed Principle means designing every class so it can be extended through inheritance.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Modern OCP usually relies on composition (interfaces, strategies, decorators, events), and only at the seams that actually change. Making everything subclassable creates fragile base classes.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: For a Rect, setW changes only the width: 5×4 = 20. Square's override also changes the height, giving 5×5 = 25. Code written against Rect expects height to stay 4, so Square is not a safe substitute.

questions.prompt: Does this TypeScript compile under `strict: true`, and what does it say about LSP?
options: It fails because overrides must use identical parameter types
It fails: strictFunctionTypes rejects the narrowed parameter
It compiles, because method parameters are checked bivariantly, yet it narrows the input, so passing a non-Dog Animal crashes at runtime
It compiles, and it's LSP-safe because Dog is a subtype of Animal
questions.explanation: strictFunctionTypes only applies to function-typed properties; methods stay bivariant for compatibility. So TS accepts an override that strengthens the precondition, which is an LSP violation the compiler won't catch.

questions.prompt: Base method `withdraw(amount)` accepts any amount greater than 0 and returns the new balance. Which subclass override is LSP-safe?
options: Requires amounts greater than 100
Returns `undefined` when the account is frozen
Throws for any amount above 1,000
Accepts amounts ≥ 0 (treating 0 as a no-op) and still returns the new balance
questions.explanation: Subtypes may weaken preconditions and must keep (or strengthen) postconditions. Accepting a wider range is fine. Requiring > 100 or rejecting > 1,000 strengthens the precondition, and returning undefined breaks the return guarantee.

questions.prompt: `ReadOnlyList extends List` overrides `add()` and `remove()` to throw. Code using `List` keeps crashing. What's the better design?
options: Split the abstraction: a `ReadableList` interface, and a `MutableList` that extends it; ReadOnlyList implements only ReadableList
Make add() silently do nothing in ReadOnlyList
Document that List methods may throw
Catch errors around every add() call
questions.explanation: A read-only list isn't a substitutable mutable list. Modelling capabilities separately lets each client ask for exactly what it needs. Silently ignoring add() also breaks callers, just more quietly.

questions.prompt: Unit tests use an `InMemoryUserRepo`; production uses `PostgresUserRepo`. Tests pass, but production fails on duplicate emails because the in-memory version never enforced uniqueness. What LSP lesson applies?
options: In-memory fakes should never be used in tests
The Postgres repo should drop its unique constraint for consistency
Every implementation, including fakes, must honour the full contract; run a shared contract test suite against both
Uniqueness is a database concern, not part of the repository contract
questions.explanation: The fake isn't substitutable because it behaves differently on a case callers depend on. Shared contract tests catch this. Dropping the constraint or denying it's part of the contract hides a real requirement.

questions.prompt: `ImmutablePoint` guarantees `x` and `y` never change after construction. A subclass `MovablePoint` adds `moveTo(x, y)`. Code that caches points by coordinates starts returning stale entries. Which LSP rule is broken?
options: The covariant return rule
The history constraint: a subtype must not allow state changes the base type's contract forbids
Nothing; adding methods never affects substitutability
The rule that subclasses can't add methods
questions.explanation: Clients of ImmutablePoint rely on immutability, so a subtype that enables mutation breaks that guarantee. Adding methods is normally fine; the problem is that this method breaks an invariant of the base type.

questions.prompt: A `BlobStore.save()` contract says it may throw `StorageError`. The new `S3BlobStore` lets raw AWS SDK errors escape, and callers' `catch (e) { if (e instanceof StorageError) ... }` logic misses them. What's the fix?
options: Callers should catch every error type
Retry forever inside S3BlobStore
Remove error handling from the contract
Translate SDK errors into `StorageError` (or subclasses) inside S3BlobStore so it honours the contract
questions.explanation: Subtypes shouldn't throw new kinds of exceptions the base contract doesn't allow. Wrapping vendor errors keeps the implementation substitutable. Making every caller handle every vendor's errors leaks implementation details.

questions.prompt: Which overrides are compatible with the Liskov Substitution Principle? Select all that apply.
options: Accepting a broader range of inputs than the base method
Returning a more specific subtype than the base method declares
Adding caching or logging without changing observable results
Requiring callers to call `init()` before using the method
Returning `null` where the base method guaranteed a value
questions.explanation: Covariant returns, weaker preconditions and transparent extras keep callers safe. Returning null breaks a postcondition, and a new required init() call adds a precondition the base never had.

questions.prompt: Which patterns in client code hint at an LSP violation somewhere in a hierarchy? Select all that apply.
options: A subclass override with an empty body that silently does nothing
A subclass that adds an extra helper method
`if (bird instanceof Penguin) { ... } else { bird.fly(); }`
Docs saying 'don't call `export()` on `LegacyReport`'
A subclass that implements the same behaviour more efficiently
questions.explanation: Type checks, no-op overrides and 'don't call this on that subtype' warnings all mean callers can't treat subtypes uniformly. Extra methods and faster implementations that keep the contract are fine.

questions.prompt: If a subclass's method signatures type-check against the base class, the subclass satisfies the Liskov Substitution Principle.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. LSP is about behaviour: preconditions, postconditions, invariants and exceptions. The Square/Rectangle example type-checks perfectly yet breaks callers.

questions.prompt: A subclass can add new methods that its base class doesn't have without violating LSP.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Code using the base type never calls them, so substitutability is unaffected, as long as the new methods don't break the base type's invariants.

questions.prompt: A `Repository<T>` interface has `find`, `save`, `delete`, `bulkImport` and `exportCsv`. A read-only reporting service depends on it and its tests must stub all five. What does ISP suggest?
options: Use `any` for the dependency type in tests
Split into role interfaces such as `Reader<T>` and `Writer<T>`, and have the reporting service depend only on `Reader<T>`
Give the reporting service its own copy of the repository class
Make every method optional with `?`
questions.explanation: Clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. A narrow Reader interface removes irrelevant coupling and test stubbing. Optional methods push runtime checks onto callers, and `any` just hides the problem.

questions.prompt: A function only needs to send messages but its parameter is typed as the full `EmailService` class with 12 methods. What's the ISP-friendly signature?
options: `notify(sender: EmailService)` with a comment explaining which method is used
`notify(sender: { send(to: string, body: string): Promise<void> })`, a narrow type describing just what's used
`notify()` reading a global EmailService instance
`notify(sender: any)`
questions.explanation: Thanks to structural typing, a narrow parameter type accepts the real service and also tiny fakes in tests. A comment doesn't reduce coupling, and a global hides the dependency entirely.

questions.prompt: What is this TypeScript signature achieving?
options: Creating a runtime copy of UserService with one method
Applying ISP at the call site: the function depends only on the one method it uses
Preventing UserService from adding methods
Making `getById` private
questions.explanation: `Pick` derives a narrow type, so greet accepts anything with a compatible getById, including a one-line fake. It's type-level only; no runtime object is created and UserService is unaffected.

questions.prompt: `MultiFunctionDevice` declares `print()`, `scan()` and `fax()`. `BasicPrinter` implements it with `scan()` and `fax()` throwing 'not supported'. What's the ISP fix?
options: Define separate `Printer`, `Scanner` and `Fax` interfaces; devices implement the ones they support
Remove `fax()` from every device
Keep the interface and document which methods throw
Make BasicPrinter extend a scanner class
questions.explanation: Fat interfaces force implementers to stub capabilities they don't have and mislead callers. Small role interfaces let a multifunction device implement all three and a basic printer just one. Documenting throws keeps the trap.

questions.prompt: After applying ISP aggressively, every interface has a single method, and constructors now take nine separate dependencies like `UserGetter`, `UserSaver`, `UserDeleter`. What's the better balance?
options: Go back to one interface for the whole service layer
Use a service locator so constructors take no parameters
Make all dependencies optional
Group methods into interfaces by how clients actually use them together, rather than one method per interface or one giant interface
questions.explanation: ISP aims for interfaces shaped around client needs. Methods that the same clients always use together belong in one interface. A service locator hides dependencies instead of designing them.

questions.prompt: A shared package exports a fat `IUserService`. The admin team adds `impersonate()`, and the mobile backend's test fakes, which implement the interface, stop compiling even though mobile never uses that method. What is this an example of?
options: Normal semantic versioning behaviour
Clients being forced to depend on methods they don't use, which ISP warns against
A TypeScript compiler bug
A Liskov violation in the admin team's code
questions.explanation: Because mobile depends on the whole interface, an unrelated addition breaks it. Client-specific interfaces (or consumers declaring their own narrow types) would isolate it. No subtype is behaving badly, so it isn't LSP.

questions.prompt: How does the Interface Segregation Principle differ from the Single Responsibility Principle?
options: They are the same principle with different names
ISP looks from the client side (interfaces shaped to what each client needs); SRP looks from the implementation side (one reason to change)
ISP is about classes; SRP is about interfaces
ISP applies only to TypeScript
questions.explanation: A class can have one responsibility yet expose an interface too broad for some clients, and ISP addresses that client-facing view. SRP concerns why the implementation changes. Both apply to any language with abstractions.

questions.prompt: Which are signs that an interface is too fat? Select all that apply.
options: Implementations throw 'not implemented' for some methods
Most clients use only a small fraction of its methods
Every implementation meaningfully uses every method
Test doubles stub many methods that the code under test never calls
questions.explanation: Unsupported methods, heavy stubbing and partial use all show clients are coupled to more than they need. If every implementation and client really uses every method, the interface is cohesive.

questions.prompt: Which TypeScript techniques help apply ISP? Select all that apply.
options: Typing dependencies as `any` to avoid coupling
Passing one global `Services` object to every function
Composing larger interfaces from smaller ones with `extends`
Declaring small interfaces in the consuming module
Using `Pick`/`Omit` to derive narrow parameter types
questions.explanation: Narrow derived types, consumer-owned interfaces and composition from small pieces all keep clients' dependencies minimal. `any` throws away type safety, and a global services bag couples everything to everything.

questions.prompt: A TypeScript class can implement several small interfaces at once.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True: `class Mfd implements Printer, Scanner, Fax`. That's what makes segregated role interfaces practical: one class can still offer every capability.

questions.prompt: The Interface Segregation Principle says every interface should have exactly one method.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. ISP says clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. An interface can have many methods if its clients need them together; single-method interfaces everywhere is over-segregation.

questions.prompt: What's the main problem with this Node.js class?
options: `async` methods can't call other async methods
It should use `require` instead of `new`
High-level business logic constructs concrete infrastructure itself, so it can't be tested or reconfigured without changing the class
Private fields can't hold class instances
questions.explanation: The service depends on concrete Postgres and SES classes and on env vars. Injecting `OrderRepo` and `Mailer` abstractions through the constructor inverts that dependency and lets tests pass fakes.

questions.prompt: In a Node app using manual dependency injection, where should concrete implementations be created and wired together?
options: Inside each service's constructor
In a global module that any file can import and mutate
At the composition root, the entry point (e.g. `main.ts`/`server.ts`) that builds the object graph once
In every route handler on each request
questions.explanation: A composition root keeps 'which implementation' decisions in one place, so the rest of the code only sees abstractions. Building dependencies inside constructors or handlers re-couples them, and a mutable global is a service locator in disguise.

questions.prompt: Under the Dependency Inversion Principle, which module should own the `PaymentGateway` interface used by checkout?
options: The checkout (domain) module, which defines what it needs; the Stripe adapter implements it
A shared utils package used by everything
The HTTP controller layer
The Stripe adapter package, which exports it alongside its implementation
questions.explanation: Inversion means the source-code dependency points from infrastructure to the domain: the policy defines the port and adapters conform. If the adapter package owns the interface, the domain still depends on the infrastructure package.

questions.prompt: A module does `export const db = new Pool(...)` and services `import { db } from './db'`. What's the main trade-off compared with constructor injection?
options: Node.js loads the module again on every import, creating many pools
It's simple, but the dependency is hidden and global, so tests need module mocking (e.g. `vi.mock`) and per-test configuration is awkward
Imports are slower than constructor parameters
Module singletons can't be used with async code
questions.explanation: ES modules are cached, so this is effectively a singleton, which is convenient but implicit. Constructor injection makes the dependency visible and swappable. Node does not re-evaluate cached modules per import.

questions.prompt: In a DI container, a singleton `AuditService` is constructed with a request-scoped `CurrentUser`. In production, audit entries show the wrong user. Why?
options: JavaScript closures can't hold request data
The container creates a new AuditService per request
The singleton captured the CurrentUser from the first request it was built for and keeps reusing it (a captive dependency)
Request-scoped objects are garbage-collected too early
questions.explanation: A longer-lived object must not hold a shorter-lived dependency. Make AuditService request-scoped, inject a provider/factory, or read context from AsyncLocalStorage per call. The singleton is created once, which is exactly the problem.

questions.prompt: You want a request ID available to logging deep inside services without adding a parameter to every function. What does Node.js offer for this?
options: `AsyncLocalStorage`, which keeps a per-request store across async calls
Storing it on `module.exports`
A global variable updated at the start of each request
`process.env.REQUEST_ID` set per request
questions.explanation: AsyncLocalStorage propagates context through promises and callbacks for one async execution chain. A global or process.env is shared by all concurrent requests, so interleaved requests overwrite each other's ID.

questions.prompt: Why inject a `clock` (e.g. `{ now(): Date }`) into a subscription service instead of calling `new Date()` inside it?
options: `new Date()` returns UTC only
Tests can control time to check expiry and renewal logic deterministically
Injected clocks automatically apply the server timezone
`new Date()` is slower than a clock object
questions.explanation: Time is a hidden dependency; injecting it lets tests freeze or advance it without flaky sleeps or global fake timers. Performance and timezone handling aren't the reason.

questions.prompt: Which are benefits of dependency injection in a Node service? Select all that apply.
options: No interfaces or types are needed anymore
Guaranteed faster request handling
Dependencies are explicit in constructor or factory signatures
Changing infrastructure (e.g. mail provider) without editing business logic
Swapping in fakes for unit tests
questions.explanation: DI makes dependencies visible and replaceable, which helps testing and changes. It usually works with interfaces rather than replacing them, and it has no performance benefit.

questions.prompt: Which of these violate the Dependency Inversion Principle in a layered Node app? Select all that apply.
options: A service calling `new StripeClient()` inside a method
Domain code reading `process.env.STRIPE_KEY` directly
A service receiving a `PaymentGateway` interface through its constructor
A controller depending on a service interface
A domain entity file importing a Mongoose model
questions.explanation: In the first three, high-level code reaches directly for infrastructure details. Receiving abstractions through the constructor or depending on a service interface is exactly what DIP recommends.

questions.prompt: Dependency injection and the Dependency Inversion Principle are the same thing.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. DIP is a design principle about which way dependencies point (toward abstractions owned by high-level policy). DI is a technique for supplying dependencies; you can inject concrete classes and still violate DIP.

questions.prompt: In Node.js you can do dependency injection without any container library, just by passing dependencies into constructors or factory functions.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Manual (pure) DI with a composition root is common and often enough; containers like tsyringe or Awilix only automate the wiring.

questions.prompt: Usernames and product SKUs both happen to be limited to 50 characters. A developer merges them into one shared `MAX_NAME_LENGTH` rule. What does DRY actually suggest here?
options: Delete both limits and validate in the database
Merge them and add a comment
Keep them separate: they're different pieces of knowledge that just coincide today and will change independently
Merge them: identical code is always duplication
questions.explanation: DRY is about not duplicating knowledge, not about removing every repeated line. When product changes SKU length, usernames shouldn't change too. Merging coincidental duplicates couples unrelated rules.

questions.prompt: A shipping service computes `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()`. What does the Law of Demeter recommend?
options: Cache the customer object globally
Make all the getters return `any`
Use optional chaining: `order.getCustomer()?.getAddress()?.getCity()`
Ask the order for what you need, e.g. `order.shippingCity()`, instead of navigating through its collaborators
questions.explanation: Reaching through a chain couples the shipping service to the structure of Order, Customer and Address. Asking the immediate collaborator hides that structure. Optional chaining handles nulls but keeps the same coupling.

questions.prompt: Which of these chains is generally NOT considered a Law of Demeter violation?
options: `users.filter((u) => u.active).map((u) => u.email)`
`order.getCustomer().getWallet().debit(10)`
`car.getEngine().getPistons()[0].fire()`
`req.app.locals.db.pool.query(sql)`
questions.explanation: Array methods return new arrays (the same kind of data structure), so chaining them doesn't navigate other objects' internals. The others reach through several collaborators and depend on their internal structure.

questions.prompt: A team building an MVP on PostgreSQL adds a storage abstraction that supports MongoDB, DynamoDB and Cassandra 'in case we switch later'. Which principle does this violate most directly?
options: YAGNI: building for speculative needs that may never come
Liskov Substitution
DRY
Law of Demeter
questions.explanation: YAGNI warns against paying now (complexity, tests, maintenance) for features that are only imagined. If a switch ever happens, it'll come with real requirements. Nothing here is duplicated knowledge, so DRY isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: An internal tool needs to send about 100 reminder emails a day at fixed times. Which option best reflects KISS?
options: A custom distributed scheduler with leader election
A Kafka cluster with a consumer group and a dead-letter topic
A microservice per reminder type
A scheduled job (cron) that reads due reminders from a database table and sends them
questions.explanation: At this volume a cron job plus a table is reliable, observable and easy to change. Kafka or a distributed scheduler adds operational burden that's only justified by scale or delivery needs you don't have.

questions.prompt: A shared helper `formatReport(data, isAdmin, isCsv, skipTotals, legacyMode)` has grown flags for every caller, and each change breaks someone. What's often the best move?
options: Inline the helper back into its callers, then re-extract only what's truly common
Make the helper a class with one subclass per flag combination
Add another flag for the next caller
Turn the flags into a single options object and keep going
questions.explanation: This is the 'wrong abstraction': forced sharing that every caller now bends. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, so undo it and find the real commonality. An options object tidies the signature but keeps the tangled logic.

questions.prompt: What does the 'rule of three' suggest about extracting shared code?
options: Each function should be at most three lines
Never have more than three parameters
Every module should have three tests
Tolerate duplication the first and second time; refactor into an abstraction when a third similar case shows the real pattern
questions.explanation: Two examples rarely reveal what actually varies; a third gives enough evidence to extract the right abstraction. It's a guard against premature DRY, not a limit on parameters or lines.

questions.prompt: Which are DRY violations in the sense of duplicated knowledge? Select all that apply.
options: Two unrelated loops that both iterate over arrays
The same GST rate hard-coded in four services
Two tests that each set up their own fixture data explicitly
A hand-maintained TypeScript type that mirrors a DB table and keeps going out of sync
The same password policy written separately in the frontend and backend and drifting apart
questions.explanation: Each of the first three encodes one rule or fact in several places that must change together. Similar loop syntax isn't shared knowledge, and explicit per-test setup is often preferred for readability.

questions.prompt: Which of these are YAGNI violations? Select all that apply.
options: A config flag for a feature nobody has asked for
Adding an index for a query that runs 10,000 times a minute
Writing tests for the feature you're shipping now
A generic `BaseRepository<T, K, Q, O>` used by a single entity
A plugin system that has exactly one plugin and no planned second
questions.explanation: Speculative flags, single-use plugin systems and over-generic bases cost complexity for imagined needs. Tests for current work and an index for a hot query address present, real needs.

questions.prompt: The Law of Demeter says a method should only call methods on itself, its parameters, objects it creates, and its own direct fields.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. That's the 'talk only to your immediate friends' rule; anything reached through those objects' getters is a stranger whose structure you shouldn't depend on.

questions.prompt: YAGNI means you should never design code with extensibility in mind.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. YAGNI targets building speculative features. Keeping code clean, well-factored and easy to change is still essential; it's what makes deferring features safe.

questions.prompt: `createUser(name, email, age, isAdmin, sendWelcome, locale, timezone)` is called in a dozen places, and arguments keep getting swapped. Which refactoring fits best?
options: Add default values to every parameter
Introduce a parameter object (e.g. `createUser({ name, email, ... })`) with a typed interface
Split it into seven setter calls after construction
Rename the function to `createUserWithOptions`
questions.explanation: A parameter object gives named, self-documenting fields and stops positional mix-ups such as swapped booleans. Defaults don't fix ordering, and setter calls allow half-built objects.

questions.prompt: `Invoice.lateFee()` reads `customer.tier`, `customer.joinDate`, `customer.paymentHistory` and `customer.region`, and barely touches Invoice's own data. What smell and refactoring apply?
options: Long method; split it into smaller methods inside Invoice
Dead code; delete the method
Feature envy; move the logic (or most of it) onto Customer
Data clumps; introduce a parameter object
questions.explanation: A method more interested in another object's data than its own wants to live there. Moving it puts behaviour next to the data it uses. Splitting it inside Invoice keeps the misplaced dependency.

questions.prompt: Supporting a new currency requires small edits in 12 different files across the codebase. Which smell is this?
options: Speculative generality
Refused bequest
Divergent change
Shotgun surgery
questions.explanation: Shotgun surgery is one change scattered across many places; consolidate the knowledge (e.g. a Currency module). Divergent change is the opposite: one module changing for many different reasons.

questions.prompt: Amounts are passed around as plain numbers with a separate currency string, and a bug adds USD and EUR values together. What refactoring addresses the root cause?
options: Replace the primitives with a `Money` value object that holds amount (in minor units) and currency and refuses to add mismatched currencies
Add a comment above each addition
Store everything in USD
Use `toFixed(2)` everywhere
questions.explanation: This is primitive obsession: domain rules can't live in a bare number. A value object enforces currency compatibility and avoids float rounding by using minor units. toFixed only affects display.

questions.prompt: You must refactor a tangled 800-line legacy pricing module that has no tests and is critical in production. What's the safest first step?
options: Write characterization tests that pin down current behaviour (including quirks), then refactor in small verified steps
Refactor carefully and rely on code review
Add type annotations and assume the compiler will catch regressions
Rewrite it from scratch in a new file over the weekend
questions.explanation: Characterization tests capture what the code actually does today, so each small refactoring can be checked against them. Big-bang rewrites and review-only changes routinely lose undocumented behaviour, and types don't catch logic changes.

questions.prompt: Callers write `render(report, true)` and `render(report, false)`, and nobody remembers what the boolean means. What's the usual refactoring?
options: Change the boolean to a number
Add a default value of `false`
Split into two clearly named functions such as `renderSummary()` and `renderDetailed()`
Rename the parameter to `flag`
questions.explanation: A flag argument means the function does two things, and call sites become unreadable. Two named functions (or an explicit enum/options field) make intent clear. Renaming the parameter doesn't help at the call site.

questions.prompt: A large legacy billing module must be replaced with minimal production risk while it keeps serving traffic. Which approach fits best?
options: Copy the module and edit the copy in place
Freeze features for six months and rewrite it in one release
Delete the module and rebuild it from the specification
Strangler fig: put a facade in front, move one capability at a time to new code, shift traffic gradually and compare outputs before retiring old paths
questions.explanation: Incremental replacement behind a stable facade keeps each step small, reversible and verifiable (e.g. shadow comparisons). Big-bang rewrites concentrate all risk in one cut-over and often miss undocumented behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which of these are refactorings, meaning they improve structure without changing external behaviour? Select all that apply.
options: Replace a magic number with a named constant
Add caching that can return stale data
Rename a variable to reveal intent
Fix an off-by-one bug in pagination
Extract a function from a long method
questions.explanation: Extracting, renaming and naming constants preserve behaviour. Fixing a bug and adding caching with staleness both change what callers observe, so they're behaviour changes and should be done and reviewed separately.

questions.prompt: Which of these are recognised code smells? Select all that apply.
options: Comments that exist only to explain confusingly written code
Small pure functions with descriptive names
Data clumps: the same few parameters always travel together
Speculative generality: hooks and abstractions nobody uses
questions.explanation: Data clumps want a type, speculative generality wants deleting, and explanatory comments often signal code that should be clarified instead. Small, well-named pure functions are what refactoring aims for.

questions.prompt: Refactoring means changing a program's external behaviour in order to improve its design.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving observable behaviour; that's why a good test suite is its safety net. Behaviour changes are separate work.

questions.prompt: A code smell is a hint that something may be worth investigating, not proof that the code is wrong.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Smells like long methods or duplication point to likely design problems, but context matters; sometimes the 'smelly' version is the simplest acceptable choice.

questions.prompt: What does this query return?
questions.code:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(x.salary)
  FROM employees x
  WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id
);
options: Employees earning more than the company-wide average
Employees earning more than the average of their own department
The highest-paid employee in each department
Departments whose average salary exceeds the company average
questions.explanation: The inner query references e.dept_id from the outer row, so it is correlated: it computes the average for that employee's department. Without the x.dept_id = e.dept_id condition it would be the company-wide average.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, SELECT name, (SELECT city FROM addresses a WHERE a.user_id = u.id) FROM users u fails for some users with "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression". What is the cause?
options: The subquery must use EXISTS when it appears in the SELECT list
Some users have several addresses, and a scalar subquery must return at most one row
users and addresses need a foreign key for the subquery to work
Correlated subqueries are not allowed in the SELECT list
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery must return zero or one row (zero gives NULL). Users with several addresses produce several rows. Add a rule to pick one (ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1, or an aggregate) or use a join. Correlated subqueries are allowed in the SELECT list.

questions.prompt: A colleague changes WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) to EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...). What changes?
options: SELECT 1 returns true even when there are no matching orders
SELECT * may return duplicate customers, while SELECT 1 does not
Nothing: EXISTS only checks whether any row exists and ignores the select list
The SELECT 1 version is much faster because it reads fewer columns
questions.explanation: EXISTS stops at the first matching row and never evaluates its select list, so SELECT *, SELECT 1 or SELECT NULL behave identically. SELECT 1 is just a readability convention. EXISTS never duplicates outer rows either way.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does LATERAL make possible in this query?
questions.code:
SELECT c.id, o.id AS order_id, o.created_at
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, created_at FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
) o;
options: It is required whenever a subquery in FROM uses ORDER BY
It lets the subquery in FROM reference c, so the LIMIT 3 is applied per customer
It turns the CROSS JOIN into a LEFT JOIN automatically
It makes the subquery run once and caches the result for every customer
questions.explanation: Without LATERAL, a FROM subquery cannot see columns of earlier FROM items. LATERAL makes it run per outer row, which gives "top 3 orders per customer". CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops customers with no orders; use LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true to keep them.

questions.prompt: Department 10 has no employees. In PostgreSQL, what does this query return?
options: An error: ALL requires a non-empty subquery
No rows, because there is nothing to compare against
Only employees who earn more than the global maximum
Every employee with a non-NULL salary
questions.explanation: x > ALL (empty set) is vacuously TRUE, so every row with a non-NULL salary passes. Rewriting it as salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) ...) would return no rows instead, because MAX of nothing is NULL. The two forms differ exactly on empty input.

questions.prompt: This query takes minutes on 50k customers and 5M orders, and orders.customer_id has no index. Why is it slow?
options: The subquery result is not cached, so the customers table is rescanned each time
The correlated subquery runs once per customer, and without an index each run scans orders: about 50k x 5M row visits
COUNT(*) always scans the whole table in PostgreSQL
Scalar subqueries disable parallel query, so the plan is single-threaded
questions.explanation: Each customer triggers a new execution of the subquery, and with no index each one is a sequential scan of orders. Index orders(customer_id), or rewrite as a GROUP BY over orders joined to customers so orders is read once.

questions.prompt: What does this query compute?
options: The average number of orders per customer, among customers who have at least one order
The average number of orders across all customers, including those with zero orders
The average order amount per customer
The total number of orders divided by the number of distinct order ids
questions.explanation: The derived table only has rows for customer_ids present in orders, so customers with zero orders are not in the average. To include them, LEFT JOIN customers to the counts and use COALESCE(cnt, 0).

questions.prompt: Which predicates return the same customers as WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)? Select all that apply.
options: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
WHERE c.id = ANY (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
An INNER JOIN to orders without DISTINCT
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
questions.explanation: IN (subquery) is the same as = ANY (subquery), and both are semi-joins equivalent to EXISTS. An inner join repeats customers once per order, and NOT EXISTS returns the opposite set.

questions.prompt: Which statements about correlated subqueries are true? Select all that apply.
options: Logically they are evaluated once per outer row, though PostgreSQL may rewrite them as joins
They can be copied out and run standalone for debugging without changes
They can only be used with EXISTS or IN
They can appear in the SELECT list, WHERE and HAVING
questions.explanation: A correlated subquery references outer columns, so its meaning is per outer row; the planner can still convert EXISTS/IN forms into semi-joins. Because it references outer columns, it does not run on its own until you substitute a value.

questions.prompt: If the subquery in WHERE x IN (SELECT ...) returns the same value several times, the matching outer rows appear several times in the result.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: IN is a membership test (a semi-join), so each outer row is returned at most once no matter how many times its value appears. Duplication happens with a plain JOIN, not with IN or EXISTS.

questions.prompt: A scalar subquery that returns no rows evaluates to NULL instead of raising an error.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Zero rows give NULL; more than one row raises an error. That is why a SELECT-list lookup such as (SELECT name FROM ... WHERE id = ...) shows NULL for missing matches.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a non-recursive CTE (WITH active AS (...) SELECT ...) over the same SQL written as nested subqueries?
options: It always caches the result, so the query runs faster
It is the only way to join a table to itself
It persists the result across statements in the same session
It names an intermediate result so the query reads top-down and the name can be reused within the statement
questions.explanation: A CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement, which improves readability and avoids repetition. It is not stored across statements (use a temp table or view for that), and since PostgreSQL 12 it is not necessarily materialized.

questions.prompt: After upgrading from PostgreSQL 11 to 16, a query of the form WITH recent AS (SELECT * FROM events) SELECT * FROM recent WHERE user_id = 42 becomes much faster. Why?
options: PostgreSQL 16 runs every CTE in parallel automatically
Since PostgreSQL 12, a side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined, so the user_id filter is pushed down and can use an index
PostgreSQL 16 caches CTE results between executions
PostgreSQL 16 creates a temporary index on CTE output
questions.explanation: Before 12, every CTE was an optimization fence: events was fully materialized and then filtered. Since 12 such a CTE is inlined like a subquery, so the predicate reaches the base table. There is no caching between executions.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, which non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE is materialized by default rather than inlined?
options: A CTE referenced once in the main query
A CTE referenced once and filtered by the outer WHERE
A CTE referenced twice in the main query
A CTE referenced once and joined to another table
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL inlines a CTE only when it is non-recursive, has no side effects and is referenced exactly once. Referencing it twice makes it materialize once and reuse the result. You can override either default with MATERIALIZED or NOT MATERIALIZED.

questions.prompt: What makes a WITH RECURSIVE query stop?
options: It stops when an iteration of the recursive term produces no new rows
It stops when the anchor term returns NULL
It stops after a fixed depth configured by max_recursion_depth
It stops after the outer query's LIMIT is reached, every time
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL runs the anchor once, then keeps feeding the latest rows into the recursive term until an iteration returns nothing. There is no built-in depth limit, so a cycle in the data means it never ends unless you guard against it.

questions.prompt: A recursive CTE walks a follows(follower, followee) graph and carries a depth column. The graph has cycles and the query never finishes. A teammate swaps UNION ALL for UNION, and it still never finishes. Why?
options: UNION de-duplicates only after the recursion finishes
UNION only removes duplicates from the anchor term
UNION is not allowed in recursive CTEs, so PostgreSQL ignores it
Each row includes an increasing depth, so revisited nodes are never exact duplicates and UNION removes nothing
questions.explanation: UNION discards rows identical to ones already produced, but (node, depth+1) always differs from (node, depth). Track the visited path (an array plus NOT node = ANY(path)), use the CYCLE clause (PostgreSQL 14+), or cap the depth.

questions.prompt: What does this query return?
questions.code:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE id = 7
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, s.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
options: Employee 7 and its chain of managers up to the CEO
Only employee 7's direct reports
Employee 7 plus all direct and indirect reports, each with its depth below 7
An infinite loop, because sub references itself
questions.explanation: The anchor selects employee 7 (depth 1). Each iteration finds employees whose manager is in the previous level, going down the tree. Walking up to the managers would need the join reversed: e.id = s.manager_id.

questions.prompt: What does this PostgreSQL query return?
options: It never terminates
questions.explanation: The CTE produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: the iteration from x = 5 adds nothing because WHERE x < 5 fails. 1+2+3+4+5 = 15. Answering 21 assumes 6 is also produced.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, consider WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM jobs WHERE done RETURNING *) INSERT INTO jobs_archive SELECT * FROM moved. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The delete and the insert happen atomically as one statement
RETURNING is how the deleted rows reach the main query
A SELECT from jobs in the main query would already see those rows gone
A data-modifying CTE runs to completion even if the main query does not read its output
questions.explanation: All parts share one snapshot and commit together, and RETURNING passes rows along. Because of that shared snapshot, the main query does not see the CTE's changes to jobs. PostgreSQL runs data-modifying CTEs exactly once whether or not they are referenced.

questions.prompt: Which statements about WITH RECURSIVE in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: The recursive term may apply aggregates such as COUNT(*) over the CTE
Each iteration of the recursive term only sees the rows produced by the previous iteration
Each iteration of the recursive term sees every row accumulated so far
The anchor and recursive terms are combined with UNION or UNION ALL
questions.explanation: Recursion works on a working table holding only the previous iteration's rows. Aggregates are not allowed in the recursive term (PostgreSQL raises an error), so aggregate in the outer query instead.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, every non-recursive CTE is materialized and acts as an optimization fence.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That was true up to PostgreSQL 11. Since 12, side-effect-free CTEs referenced once are inlined by default; add AS MATERIALIZED to get the fence back.

questions.prompt: In a recursive CTE, the anchor (non-recursive) term is executed only once.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The anchor seeds the working table once; only the recursive term repeats. Expensive setup therefore belongs in the anchor, not the recursive term.

questions.prompt: Salaries ordered DESC are 100, 90, 90, 80. What do RANK() and DENSE_RANK() assign to the 80?
options: RANK 4, DENSE_RANK 3
RANK 3, DENSE_RANK 3
RANK 3, DENSE_RANK 4
RANK 4, DENSE_RANK 4
questions.explanation: RANK leaves a gap after ties (1, 2, 2, 4), while DENSE_RANK does not (1, 2, 2, 3). ROW_NUMBER would give 1, 2, 3, 4 with an arbitrary order between the two 90s.

questions.prompt: daily_sales(day, amount) has one row per day. Which expression gives the change from the previous day?
options: amount - SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
amount - LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
amount - FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)
questions.explanation: LAG reads the value from the previous row in window order; the first day gets NULL. LEAD reads the next row, so it would give the change to the following day.

questions.prompt: Rows are (day 1, 10), (day 2, 5), (day 2, 5). What does SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) return for the first day-2 row?
options: It varies between runs
questions.explanation: With ORDER BY, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes all peers with the same day. Both day-2 rows get 20. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (with a tiebreaker) for row-by-row totals.

questions.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL reject WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) = 1?
options: ROW_NUMBER returns bigint, which cannot be compared with 1
PARTITION BY cannot be combined with ORDER BY in WHERE
ROW_NUMBER needs an explicit frame clause
Window functions are computed after WHERE, so they cannot be used there; filter in an outer query or CTE
questions.explanation: Window functions run after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so WHERE cannot see their results. Compute rn in a subquery or CTE and filter WHERE rn = 1 outside. The bigint type is not an issue.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) and AVG(salary) ... GROUP BY dept_id?
options: The window version is always faster
PARTITION BY sorts the result by dept_id, while GROUP BY does not
GROUP BY includes NULL salaries in the average, but the window version does not
The window version keeps every employee row and attaches the department average to each
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses each department to one row; a window function computes over the partition but keeps the input rows. That lets you compare each salary with its department average. Both ignore NULLs the same way.

questions.prompt: LAST_VALUE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY sku ORDER BY changed_at) returns each row's own price instead of the latest price for the SKU. Why?
options: LAST_VALUE only works without PARTITION BY
Rows must be sorted DESC for LAST_VALUE to work
The default frame ends at the current row, so the last value in the frame is the current row; add ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
LAST_VALUE ignores the ORDER BY
questions.explanation: With ORDER BY, the frame runs from the partition start to the current row (and its peers), so LAST_VALUE sees only up to the current row. Extend the frame to the end of the partition, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY changed_at DESC.

questions.prompt: daily_metrics(day date, v) has gaps (some days missing). Which frame gives a true 7-calendar-day moving average in PostgreSQL?
options: AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(v) OVER (PARTITION BY day ROWS 6 PRECEDING)
AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(v) OVER (ORDER BY day GROUPS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
questions.explanation: ROWS counts physical rows, so with gaps the 7 rows can span more than 7 days. RANGE with an interval offset (PostgreSQL 11+) is based on the day value itself. PARTITION BY day puts each day in its own partition.

questions.prompt: Which statements about window functions in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER () with no ORDER BY gives a stable numbering across runs
Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING
LEAD(x, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY t) returns 0 for the last row instead of NULL
NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY score) splits the rows into 4 roughly equal buckets
questions.explanation: NTILE buckets rows, and the third LEAD/LAG argument is the default when no row exists at that offset. Window functions run after grouping. Without ORDER BY, row numbering follows whatever order rows arrive in, which is not guaranteed to be stable.

questions.prompt: You need exactly one row per department, even when salaries tie. Which approaches guarantee that? Select all that apply.
options: Filter RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
Filter DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
SELECT DISTINCT ON (dept_id) ... ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC
questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER and DISTINCT ON always keep one row per group (add a tiebreaker to make the choice deterministic). RANK and DENSE_RANK both give tied top earners rank 1, so they can return several rows per department.

questions.prompt: A query can define a named window with a WINDOW clause, e.g. WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary), and reuse it as OVER w in several functions.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The WINDOW clause avoids repeating identical OVER specifications, and PostgreSQL can compute functions that share a window in one pass over the sorted data.

questions.prompt: Window functions can be nested directly, e.g. SUM(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)) OVER ().
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL raises "window function calls cannot be nested". Compute the inner window function in a subquery or CTE, then apply the outer one to its result.

questions.prompt: What does CREATE VIEW active_users AS SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE active store in PostgreSQL?
options: A copy of the matching rows, refreshed nightly
Only the query definition; each query against the view runs it on the current data
A cached result that is invalidated when users changes
An index on users(active)
questions.explanation: A plain view is a saved query that the rewriter expands into each statement that uses it, so it always reflects current data. Storing results is what a materialized view does.

questions.prompt: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY sales_summary fails in PostgreSQL. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: autovacuum must be disabled during the refresh
A unique index on the materialized view covering all rows
The view must be created WITH NO DATA first
A primary key on the base table
questions.explanation: A concurrent refresh diffs old and new contents row by row, which needs a unique index on the materialized view (plain columns, no WHERE clause). Base-table keys are irrelevant, and a view that has never been populated cannot be refreshed concurrently.

questions.prompt: An analytics dashboard runs a 12-second aggregate over 200M rows. Product says data up to 15 minutes old is fine. What is the simplest good fit in PostgreSQL?
options: A plain view over the aggregate
A trigger on the fact table that recomputes the full aggregate on every insert
A materialized view with a unique index, refreshed CONCURRENTLY every 15 minutes by a scheduled job
Increasing work_mem until the query finishes in under a second
questions.explanation: Staleness is acceptable, so precomputing the result and refreshing it on a schedule is cheap and simple. A plain view still runs the 12-second query each time, and a full recompute per insert would cripple writes.

questions.prompt: Every night at 02:00 dashboard queries hang for about 90 seconds and then recover. A job runs REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_summary at 02:00. What is happening?
options: Materialized views cannot be read while autovacuum runs on them
The refresh flushes shared_buffers, so every query reads from disk
The refresh rebuilds the base table's indexes
A non-concurrent refresh takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the view, blocking reads until it finishes
questions.explanation: A plain REFRESH swaps contents under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so SELECTs on the view wait. CONCURRENTLY allows reads during the refresh, at the cost of a slower refresh and the need for a unique index.

questions.prompt: Which of these PostgreSQL views is automatically updatable (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE work without triggers)?
options: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE active
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT u.id, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL auto-updates simple views: a single base table in FROM, no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, set operations or LIMIT. Grouped, DISTINCT and join views need INSTEAD OF triggers or rules.

questions.prompt: Through the view active_users (SELECT * FROM users WHERE active), you run INSERT ... VALUES (..., active = false). The view was created WITH CHECK OPTION. What happens?
options: The row is inserted and immediately disappears from the view
The row is inserted with active forced to true
The insert succeeds but only into the view, not into users
The insert is rejected because the new row would not be visible through the view
questions.explanation: WITH CHECK OPTION makes INSERT/UPDATE through the view fail if the resulting row would not satisfy the view's WHERE. Without it, the insert succeeds and the row silently vanishes from the view. Views store nothing, so writes always go to the base table.

questions.prompt: Role reporting has SELECT on the view customer_public but no privileges on the customers table. Querying the view works. Why, in PostgreSQL 16 defaults?
options: SELECT on a view implicitly grants SELECT on its tables
The reporting role inherits privileges from PUBLIC on every table
Views bypass all permission checks
Base tables are accessed with the view owner's privileges unless the view is created with security_invoker
questions.explanation: By default, a view checks base-table privileges as its owner, which makes views useful for exposing only some columns. PostgreSQL 15 added security_invoker = true to check as the querying user. No grant on the table is implied.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing PostgreSQL views and materialized views are true? Select all that apply.
options: You can create an index directly on a plain view
Querying a plain view always reflects the latest committed data visible to your snapshot
You can create indexes on a materialized view
A materialized view stores its result physically
questions.explanation: Materialized views are real storage, so they can be indexed and can go stale. Plain views store no rows, so there is nothing to index (index the base tables), and they always read current data.

questions.prompt: Which are workable ways to keep a precomputed summary fresh in PostgreSQL 16? Select all that apply.
options: Scheduled REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY from a cron job
A summary table maintained incrementally by triggers or by the application in the same transaction
Relying on PostgreSQL's built-in incremental maintenance of materialized views
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WHERE updated_at > last_run to refresh only changed rows
questions.explanation: Core PostgreSQL has no incremental view maintenance and no partial REFRESH syntax; every refresh recomputes the whole query. For fresher data, maintain a summary table yourself, or refresh on a schedule.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, DROP TABLE on a table that a view depends on fails unless you add CASCADE.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping the table errors with "other objects depend on it". CASCADE drops the dependent views too, which is why it should be used with care in migrations.

questions.prompt: Querying a plain view is inherently slower than writing the same query inline, because the view's full result is computed first and then filtered.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL expands the view definition into the outer query before planning, so outer filters can be pushed down just as with the inline SQL. Materializing first is how materialized views behave, not plain views.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what can a PROCEDURE (invoked with CALL) do that a FUNCTION cannot?
options: Return a result set
Be written in PL/pgSQL
Issue COMMIT or ROLLBACK inside its body to control transactions
Accept parameters
questions.explanation: Since PostgreSQL 11, procedures can commit and roll back mid-body (when called outside an explicit transaction block), which is useful for batched maintenance. Functions always run inside the caller's transaction. Both accept parameters and can be PL/pgSQL.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you want INSERTs into a view that joins customers and addresses to write to both tables. What feature is designed for this?
options: An INSTEAD OF INSERT trigger on the view
WITH CHECK OPTION on the view
A BEFORE INSERT row trigger on the view
An AFTER INSERT statement trigger on customers
questions.explanation: Join views are not automatically updatable; INSTEAD OF row triggers on a view replace the INSERT with your own logic that writes to the base tables. BEFORE/AFTER row triggers apply to tables, and CHECK OPTION only validates rows.

questions.prompt: A BEFORE INSERT FOR EACH ROW trigger function on orders returns NULL for some rows. What happens to those rows?
options: The whole statement fails with an error
Their insert is silently skipped, with no error
They are inserted unchanged, because the return value is ignored
They are inserted with all columns NULL
questions.explanation: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger cancels the operation for that row without raising an error, so rows go missing silently. Return NEW to proceed, or RAISE EXCEPTION to fail loudly. The return value of AFTER row triggers is ignored.

questions.prompt: A team debates putting a discount rule in a PostgreSQL trigger versus the Node service. What is the strongest argument for the service?
options: PostgreSQL triggers cannot be versioned in migrations
The rule changes often and needs unit tests, code review and visibility next to the rest of the domain logic; triggers are hidden side effects
Triggers cannot read other tables
Triggers always make inserts at least 10x slower
questions.explanation: Frequently changing business logic is easier to test, debug and deploy in application code, while a trigger runs invisibly on every write. Triggers can read other tables and can be versioned in migrations; the cost is maintainability, not capability.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the most defensible use of a database trigger?
options: Writing an audit row in the same transaction as every change to a sensitive table
Sending a welcome email when a user row is inserted
Recomputing a recommendation model whenever a product is viewed
Calling a payment provider's HTTP API when an order is inserted
questions.explanation: An audit row written by a trigger is atomic with the change and cannot be skipped by any client, including ad-hoc SQL. External calls and emails do not belong in triggers: they cannot be rolled back and they slow every write.

questions.prompt: An AFTER INSERT trigger calls pg_notify('orders', ...), and a Node listener sends a confirmation email. The inserting transaction later rolls back. Is the email sent?
options: Yes, NOTIFY is delivered as soon as pg_notify runs
It depends on whether synchronous_commit is on
No, notifications are delivered only when the transaction commits
Yes, but only if the listener is on the same connection
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL queues NOTIFY and delivers it at commit; on rollback it is discarded. That is what makes LISTEN/NOTIFY safe to use with transactions, unlike calling an email API directly from the code path that may still roll back.

questions.prompt: A nightly UPDATE touches 1M rows of accounts, and a FOR EACH ROW AFTER UPDATE trigger inserts one audit row per change. The job is slow. Which PostgreSQL feature lets you audit the whole statement in one set-based insert?
options: Using a rule instead of a trigger
Adding a WHEN (pg_trigger_depth() = 0) clause
A FOR EACH STATEMENT trigger using transition tables (REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS o NEW TABLE AS n)
Turning the trigger into a BEFORE trigger
questions.explanation: Statement-level triggers with transition tables (PostgreSQL 10+) fire once and can see all changed rows as tables, so one INSERT ... SELECT replaces 1M separate inserts. Switching to BEFORE still fires once per row.

questions.prompt: Which are good reasons NOT to put a piece of logic in a trigger? Select all that apply.
options: It sets updated_at = now() on every update
It must write an audit record atomically with every change
It changes often and the team tests logic in application code
It needs to call an external service
Developers routinely forget that the trigger exists when debugging writes
questions.explanation: External calls cannot be rolled back with the transaction, fast-changing rules belong where they are tested, and hidden behaviour hurts debugging. Atomic audit rows and updated_at maintenance are standard, low-risk trigger uses.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL triggers are true? Select all that apply.
options: An AFTER ROW trigger can modify NEW to change what is stored
A trigger's own writes can fire other triggers, including cascading ones
Row-level ON DELETE triggers do not fire for TRUNCATE
A trigger's changes are part of the same transaction as the statement that fired it
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE only fires statement-level ON TRUNCATE triggers. Trigger work commits or rolls back with the statement and can cascade into other triggers. Only BEFORE row triggers can modify NEW; by AFTER time the row is already written.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a function called from a SELECT can run COMMIT to persist its work early.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Functions run inside the calling statement's transaction and cannot commit; PostgreSQL raises an error on COMMIT there. Only procedures invoked with CALL (outside an explicit transaction block) can control transactions.

questions.prompt: A BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW trigger in PostgreSQL can change values in NEW, and the modified values are what get stored.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: BEFORE row triggers return the row to store, so assigning NEW.updated_at := now() and returning NEW is the standard updated_at pattern. AFTER triggers see the final row but cannot change it.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which query returns the median salary (interpolated if the count is even)?
options: SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary LIMIT 1 OFFSET (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees) / 2
SELECT MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM employees
SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM employees
questions.explanation: percentile_cont(0.5) is the ordered-set aggregate for the median and interpolates between the two middle values. AVG is the mean, mode() is the most frequent value, and the OFFSET trick returns only one of the two middle rows when the count is even.

questions.prompt: Salaries are 100, 100, 90, 80. Which query returns 80 as the 3rd highest distinct salary?
options: Filter DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 3
Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 3
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2
Filter RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 3
questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK assigns 1, 1, 2, 3, so rank 3 is 80. ROW_NUMBER (1, 2, 3, 4) and RANK (1, 1, 3, 4) both put 90 in position 3, and the OFFSET query without DISTINCT also returns 90.

questions.prompt: Which query lists email addresses that appear more than once in users?
options: SELECT email, COUNT(*) OVER () FROM users WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT DISTINCT email FROM users
SELECT email FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT email FROM users WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY email
questions.explanation: Group by email, then filter the groups with HAVING. Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE, and DISTINCT returns every email, not just duplicates.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which statement deletes duplicate users by email, keeping the row with the smallest id?
options: DELETE FROM users a USING users b WHERE a.email = b.email AND a.id < b.id
DELETE FROM users a USING users b WHERE a.email = b.email AND a.id > b.id
DELETE FROM users a USING users b WHERE a.email = b.email
DELETE FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MAX(id) FROM users GROUP BY email)
questions.explanation: A row is deleted if another row with the same email has a smaller id, so only the minimum id survives. a.id < b.id keeps the largest id, the NOT IN version also keeps the max, and the last option deletes every row whose email matches any row, including itself.

questions.prompt: You need the top earner(s) in each department, showing every employee tied for first. Which approach is correct?
options: Filter RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
Filter ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1
DISTINCT ON (dept_id) ... ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC
GROUP BY dept_id and SELECT MAX(salary), name
questions.explanation: RANK gives every tied top salary rank 1, so ties are kept. DISTINCT ON and ROW_NUMBER pick exactly one row per department, and selecting name next to MAX without grouping by it is an error in PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: For a login streaks report, why does subtracting the row number from each date identify runs of consecutive days?
options: Subtracting integers from dates resets at month boundaries, which separates the runs
grp is the length of the streak so far
ROW_NUMBER skips numbers on missing days, keeping grp constant
Within a consecutive run both day and row number increase by 1 per row, so their difference is constant; a gap shifts it to a new value
questions.explanation: This is the gaps-and-islands trick: consecutive dates and consecutive row numbers move together, so day - rn stays the same within a run and jumps after a gap. GROUP BY user_id, grp then gives each streak's start, end and length. ROW_NUMBER never skips numbers.

questions.prompt: employees(id, name, salary, manager_id). Which query lists employees who earn more than their manager?
options: SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary
SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.id = m.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
SELECT e.name FROM employees e WHERE e.salary > e.manager_id
questions.explanation: Join each employee to their manager row (e.manager_id = m.id) and compare salaries. The reversed join compares managers with their reports, and comparing salary to manager_id compares money with an id.

questions.prompt: Which queries correctly return the 2nd highest distinct salary (returning NULL or no row when it does not exist is acceptable)? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employees) t WHERE r = 2
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
questions.explanation: All three correct forms de-duplicate salaries before picking the second one. The last query skips one row, not one distinct value, so when two people share the top salary it returns the top salary again.

questions.prompt: orders.customer_id is nullable and contains some NULLs. Which queries correctly return customer ids that have no orders? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT c.id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
SELECT id FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM orders
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS, the LEFT JOIN anti-join and EXCEPT all handle NULLs correctly (a NULL from orders cannot remove a real id from EXCEPT). NOT IN returns nothing once the subquery contains a NULL, because every comparison becomes unknown.

questions.prompt: For a "top 3 products per category by revenue" query, filtering RANK() <= 3 can return more than 3 rows for a category.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Ties share a rank: revenues 50, 40, 40, 40 rank 1, 2, 2, 2, so four rows pass RANK() <= 3. Use ROW_NUMBER (with a tiebreaker) if exactly 3 rows are required.

questions.prompt: If every employee earns the same salary, SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) returns zero rows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row; no rows match the WHERE, so MAX is NULL and you get one row containing NULL. The LIMIT/OFFSET variant is the one that returns zero rows.

questions.prompt: A migration file contains CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN and DROP VIEW statements. Which SQL sublanguage do all three belong to?
options: DCL (data control)
DDL (data definition)
DML (data manipulation)
TCL (transaction control)
questions.explanation: All three change schema objects (indexes, tables, views), which is DDL. DML would be statements that read or change rows (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), which none of these do.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL you run the statements below. What is the state of the orders table afterwards?
options: The note column does not exist, because PostgreSQL DDL is transactional
The note column exists, because DDL auto-commits the open transaction
The statement errors, because DDL is not allowed inside a transaction block
The note column exists but is hidden until the next VACUUM runs
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so the ROLLBACK undoes the ALTER TABLE. The auto-commit behaviour is true of MySQL and Oracle, which is why that distractor is tempting, but it does not apply to PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements is DCL (data control language)?
options: COMMIT;
SAVEPOINT before_import;
TRUNCATE audit_log;
GRANT SELECT ON orders TO reporting;
questions.explanation: GRANT and REVOKE manage privileges, which is DCL. COMMIT and SAVEPOINT are transaction control (TCL), and TRUNCATE is classified as DDL even though it removes data.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which rows are in table t after this script completes?
options: Rows 'a', 'b' and 'c'
No rows, because the rollback cancels the whole transaction
Only row 'c'
Rows 'a' and 'c'
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work done after s1 (inserting 'b') and keeps the transaction open, so 'a' and 'c' are committed. A plain ROLLBACK would discard everything, but rolling back to a savepoint does not.

questions.prompt: Your migration tool wraps every migration in a single transaction. Which PostgreSQL statement will fail with "cannot run inside a transaction block"?
options: TRUNCATE sessions;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
CREATE TABLE audit (id bigint PRIMARY KEY);
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY needs several transactions internally so it cannot run inside an explicit transaction block. TRUNCATE, ALTER TABLE and CREATE TABLE are all transactional in PostgreSQL and run fine inside BEGIN/COMMIT.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what is a real difference between DELETE FROM sessions (no WHERE) and TRUNCATE sessions?
options: TRUNCATE ignores foreign keys from other tables that reference sessions
DELETE without a WHERE clause is treated as DDL and auto-commits
TRUNCATE skips per-row ON DELETE triggers and frees the storage immediately
TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back, while DELETE can
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE drops the table's data files instead of deleting row by row, so row-level ON DELETE triggers do not fire and space is reclaimed at once. It is still transactional in PostgreSQL, and it errors on referencing foreign keys unless you add CASCADE.

questions.prompt: Your Node API connects as role app_rw. It must read and write rows in orders but never change the schema. Which setup follows least privilege in PostgreSQL?
options: GRANT USAGE on the schema, then SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on orders; a separate migration role owns the table
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE shop TO app_rw
Make app_rw the owner of orders so it never hits permission errors
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_rw and nothing else
questions.explanation: Table owners can ALTER and DROP the table, so the app role should hold only DML privileges, plus USAGE on the schema so it can find the table. Database-level ALL covers only CONNECT, CREATE and TEMP, not table access, and USAGE alone lets the role see the table but not read it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are TCL (transaction control) statements? Select all that apply.
options: COMMIT
SAVEPOINT
TRUNCATE
ROLLBACK
GRANT
questions.explanation: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT control transaction boundaries. GRANT is DCL (privileges) and TRUNCATE is DDL, even though both change what a session can see.

questions.prompt: You run schema migrations against PostgreSQL 16 inside explicit transactions. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can be part of the same transaction as other DDL
If one statement in the migration fails, none of its earlier schema changes are left behind
Locks taken by ALTER TABLE are held until the transaction ends, so a long migration can block application queries
Each DDL statement implicitly commits whatever came before it in the transaction
questions.explanation: Transactional DDL means a failed migration rolls back cleanly, but ALTER TABLE's ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock lasts until COMMIT, so long transactions are risky. CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block, and implicit commits are MySQL/Oracle behaviour, not PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a TRUNCATE executed inside a transaction can be undone with ROLLBACK.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is transaction-safe in PostgreSQL: the old data files are kept until the transaction commits, so a ROLLBACK restores the rows. Many people assume otherwise because TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back in some other databases.

questions.prompt: REVOKE is a TCL statement because it undoes an earlier change.
options: True
False
