questions.explanation: REVOKE removes privileges previously granted, so it is DCL alongside GRANT. TCL statements (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT) control transaction boundaries, not permissions.

questions.prompt: Why does this PostgreSQL query fail with "column total does not exist"?
options: Aliases need double quotes before they can be referenced
The alias conflicts with a built-in aggregate called total
Arithmetic expressions cannot be compared in WHERE
WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list, so the alias does not exist yet
questions.explanation: Logically FROM and WHERE run before SELECT computes output columns, so WHERE cannot see the alias. Repeat the expression (WHERE price * qty > 100) or wrap it in a subquery; quoting the alias does not change the evaluation order.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, in which clause can you reference a SELECT-list alias such as total?
options: a JOIN's ON condition
WHERE
ORDER BY
HAVING
questions.explanation: ORDER BY runs after the SELECT list is computed, so output aliases are visible there. WHERE, ON and HAVING are evaluated before output columns exist, so in PostgreSQL they must repeat the expression.

questions.prompt: A feed endpoint pages with SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40. Users sometimes see the same post on two pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: There is no ORDER BY, so PostgreSQL may return rows in a different order on each query
LIMIT is not supported together with OFFSET in PostgreSQL
OFFSET is applied before WHERE, so it skips the wrong rows
The posts table needs a VACUUM before OFFSET gives stable results
questions.explanation: Without ORDER BY, SQL guarantees no order, and the plan or physical layout can change between requests, so pages overlap or skip rows. VACUUM may change physical order but is not a fix; only a deterministic ORDER BY is.

questions.prompt: The feed now uses ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20, but many posts share the same created_at and pages still repeat rows. What is the right fix?
options: Add DISTINCT to the SELECT
Add a unique tiebreaker: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
Switch to ORDER BY created_at ASC
Create a non-unique index on created_at
questions.explanation: Rows tied on created_at can come back in any order, so the cut between pages is nondeterministic. A unique tiebreaker such as id makes the order total. An index may speed up the sort but does not make ties deterministic.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY last_login DESC puts users who never logged in (last_login IS NULL) at the top. How do you push them to the bottom?
options: ORDER BY COALESCE(last_login, 0) DESC
WHERE last_login IS NOT NULL ORDER BY last_login DESC
ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS FIRST
ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS LAST
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL sorts NULL as larger than any value, so DESC puts NULLs first by default; NULLS LAST overrides that. Filtering with IS NOT NULL removes those users entirely, and COALESCE with 0 fails on a timestamp column.

questions.prompt: An admin page uses ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET 500000 and is slow even with an index on id. Why, and what is the usual fix?
options: LIMIT is applied before ORDER BY, so the whole table is sorted; move LIMIT into a subquery
OFFSET disables index use; add a hint to force the index
PostgreSQL still produces and discards the 500,000 skipped rows; use keyset pagination such as WHERE id > $lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
Large OFFSET values overflow an int; cast the offset to bigint
questions.explanation: OFFSET n means the executor must walk n rows before returning anything, so cost grows with page depth. Keyset pagination seeks straight to the last seen key using the index. PostgreSQL has no index hints, and LIMIT is applied after ORDER BY.

questions.prompt: Which rows does this PostgreSQL query return?
questions.code:
SELECT * FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'active' OR status = 'trial' AND plan = 'pro';
options: Active or trial accounts, but only on the pro plan
Only accounts that are both active and on the pro plan
All active accounts, plus trial accounts on the pro plan
No rows, because status cannot equal two values at once
questions.explanation: AND binds tighter than OR, so this reads as status = 'active' OR (status = 'trial' AND plan = 'pro'). To restrict both statuses to pro, write (status = 'active' OR status = 'trial') AND plan = 'pro', or use status IN (...).

questions.prompt: orders has a B-tree index on created_at (timestamptz). Which WHERE predicates can use that index directly? Select all that apply.
options: date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-01-15'
created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-02-01'
created_at + interval '1 day' > now()
questions.explanation: A plain index on a column helps when the column appears bare on one side of a comparison. Wrapping it in a function or arithmetic hides it from the index; rewrite as a range on created_at or build an expression index.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which predicates return rows with price from 10 to 20 inclusive? Select all that apply.
options: price BETWEEN 10 AND 20
price >= 10 AND price <= 20
price > 10 AND price < 20
price BETWEEN 20 AND 10
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends and means low <= x AND x <= high. Writing the bounds in reverse order matches nothing (BETWEEN SYMMETRIC would accept that), and strict > and < leave out 10 and 20.

questions.prompt: Without ORDER BY, PostgreSQL returns rows in the order they were inserted.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Without ORDER BY the order is unspecified. Updates, VACUUM, parallel scans, synchronized scans and plan changes can all change it, so insertion order often appears in small tests but is never guaranteed.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) * FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC returns each customer's most recent order.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group in ORDER BY order, and the ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON expressions. Sorting created_at DESC inside each customer makes the latest order the first row kept.

questions.prompt: customers has 3 rows (A, B, C). orders has 2 rows for A and 1 row for B. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id return?
questions.explanation: A matches 2 orders (2 rows), B matches 1 (1 row), and C has no match but is kept with NULL order columns (1 row): 4 in total. Answering 3 assumes one row per customer, which only holds if each customer has at most one order.

questions.prompt: This query should list every customer with their paid orders, including customers with none. Customers without paid orders are missing. Why?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
options: LEFT JOIN cannot be combined with WHERE
status needs an index for the LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched rows
The WHERE filter discards the NULL-extended rows, turning it into an inner join; move the condition into the ON clause
The join condition is reversed; it should be c.id = o.customer_id
questions.explanation: For unmatched customers o.status is NULL, and NULL = 'paid' is not true, so WHERE removes them. Putting AND o.status = 'paid' in ON filters which orders match while still keeping every customer. The order of operands in the ON equality makes no difference.

questions.prompt: sizes has 5 rows and colors has 8 rows. How many rows does SELECT * FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colors return?
questions.explanation: A CROSS JOIN is the Cartesian product: every size paired with every color, 5 x 8 = 40. 13 would be a UNION ALL of the two tables, not a join.

questions.prompt: employees(id, name, manager_id) where the CEO has manager_id NULL. Which query lists every employee with their manager's name, including the CEO?
options: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e CROSS JOIN employees m WHERE e.manager_id = m.id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.id = m.manager_id
questions.explanation: A self LEFT JOIN on e.manager_id = m.id keeps the CEO with a NULL manager name. The inner join and the CROSS JOIN + WHERE drop the CEO. Reversing the condition finds each employee's direct reports instead of their manager.

questions.prompt: This report shows revenue far too high for customers whose orders have several items. What is the cause?
questions.code:
SELECT c.id, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue, COUNT(oi.id) AS items
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id;
options: COUNT(oi.id) and SUM(o.amount) cannot appear in the same SELECT
Each order row is repeated once per item before grouping, so o.amount is summed several times
GROUP BY c.id must also include o.id for SUM to be correct
SUM ignores NULLs, which inflates the total
questions.explanation: Joining one-to-many twice fans out rows: an order with 3 items appears 3 times, so its amount is counted 3 times. Aggregate items per order in a subquery (or use separate subqueries) before joining. Adding o.id to GROUP BY changes the grain but does not give per-customer revenue.

questions.prompt: You reconcile ledger(txn_id) against bank_feed(txn_id) and need every transaction that is missing from either side, in one query. Which join fits?
options: ledger LEFT JOIN bank_feed USING (txn_id) WHERE bank_feed.txn_id IS NULL
ledger CROSS JOIN bank_feed WHERE ledger.txn_id <> bank_feed.txn_id
ledger INNER JOIN bank_feed USING (txn_id)
ledger FULL OUTER JOIN bank_feed ON ledger.txn_id = bank_feed.txn_id WHERE ledger.txn_id IS NULL OR bank_feed.txn_id IS NULL
questions.explanation: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides, and the IS NULL checks keep only the mismatches. The LEFT JOIN version finds only ledger rows missing from the bank feed, not the reverse. The CROSS JOIN with <> returns almost every pair.

questions.prompt: Which query returns the same rows as orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id (ignoring column order)?
options: orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
orders o FULL JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
questions.explanation: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table, so swapping the table order and using LEFT JOIN is equivalent. Keeping orders on the left with LEFT JOIN would preserve all orders instead of all customers.

questions.prompt: customers.id is a primary key. Which queries return each customer with at least one order exactly once? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT DISTINCT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT c.* FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
questions.explanation: EXISTS is a semi-join that never duplicates outer rows, and DISTINCT removes join duplicates (safe because id is unique). The plain inner join repeats a customer once per order, and the LEFT JOIN also includes customers with no orders.

questions.prompt: Which statements about join conditions in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: For a LEFT JOIN, a filter on the right table in ON keeps unmatched left rows, while the same filter in WHERE removes them
NATURAL JOIN matches on every column with the same name, so adding updated_at to both tables can silently change the results
For an INNER JOIN, putting a filter in ON or in WHERE gives the same result
CROSS JOIN requires an ON clause
JOIN ... USING (customer_id) outputs customer_id twice, once per table
questions.explanation: Inner joins are commutative with respect to filters, but outer joins are not. NATURAL JOIN is fragile because its join columns depend on the schema. USING outputs one merged column, and CROSS JOIN takes no ON clause at all.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a self join needs a table alias for at least one copy, because the same table name cannot appear twice in FROM without one.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Without aliases PostgreSQL raises "table name specified more than once", and column references would be ambiguous anyway. Aliases such as e and m tell the two roles apart.

questions.prompt: An INNER JOIN between a 1,000-row table and a 10-row table can never return more than 1,000 rows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: If the join key is not unique on either side (many-to-many), each row can match many rows, up to 1,000 x 10 = 10,000. The 1,000 cap only holds when every left row matches at most one right row.

questions.prompt: You need departments whose average salary is above 100,000. Which query is correct?
options: SELECT dept_id FROM employees WHERE AVG(salary) > 100000 GROUP BY dept_id
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS a FROM employees WHERE a > 100000 GROUP BY dept_id
SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id, AVG(salary) > 100000
SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 100000
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Aggregates in WHERE are an error, and so is referencing the alias a there.

questions.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL reject this query?
options: dept_id must be wrapped in an aggregate such as MAX
GROUP BY columns must appear last in the SELECT list
COUNT(*) cannot be used together with GROUP BY
name is neither grouped nor aggregated, so there is no single value for it per department
questions.explanation: Each output row is a department, but one department has many names, so PostgreSQL errors with "must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function". MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off would pick an arbitrary name, which is the habit this error prevents.

questions.prompt: e.id is the primary key of employees. Does this run in PostgreSQL 16?
questions.code:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.email, COUNT(o.id)
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.sales_rep_id = e.id
GROUP BY e.id;
options: Yes, but name and email come from an arbitrary row in each group
No: LEFT JOIN cannot be combined with GROUP BY
No: name and email must be listed in GROUP BY
Yes: other columns of e are functionally dependent on its primary key, so they may be selected
questions.explanation: Since 9.1, PostgreSQL allows ungrouped columns of a table when that table's primary key is in GROUP BY, because they are determined by it. The values are not arbitrary; there is only one possible value per group.

questions.prompt: Column v holds the values 1, 1, NULL, 2. What do COUNT(*), COUNT(v) and COUNT(DISTINCT v) return?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows (4). COUNT(v) skips NULL (3). COUNT(DISTINCT v) counts distinct non-NULL values {1, 2} (2). Answering 3 for the last one wrongly treats NULL as a distinct value.

questions.prompt: scores has three rows: 10, NULL, 20. What does SELECT AVG(score) FROM scores return?
options: An error, because the column contains a NULL
NULL
questions.explanation: AVG ignores NULL inputs, so it computes (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. To treat missing scores as 0 you would write AVG(COALESCE(score, 0)), which gives 10.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you want daily paid and refunded counts from payments in a single pass. Which expression correctly counts paid rows?
options: COUNT(*) WHERE status = 'paid' AS paid
SUM(status = 'paid') AS paid
COUNT(status = 'paid') AS paid
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid
questions.explanation: The FILTER clause restricts which rows reach that aggregate. COUNT(status = 'paid') counts every non-NULL boolean, true or false, so it counts nearly all rows. SUM over a boolean has no PostgreSQL overload, and WHERE cannot follow an aggregate like that.

questions.prompt: Customer 999 has no orders. What does SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 999 return?
options: One row containing NULL
An error, because there is nothing to sum
Zero rows
One row containing 0
questions.explanation: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, and SUM over no input is NULL (COUNT would be 0). Use COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) if the API must return 0.

questions.prompt: Which of these aggregates skip NULL input values? Select all that apply.
options: MAX(score)
AVG(score)
COUNT(*)
COUNT(email)
questions.explanation: Aggregates over an expression ignore NULL inputs, so COUNT(email), AVG and MAX skip NULLs. COUNT(*) counts rows, not values, so rows that are entirely NULL still count.

questions.prompt: Which groupings does GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product) produce? Select all that apply.
options: (region)
(region, product)
(product)
() — the grand total
questions.explanation: ROLLUP produces hierarchical prefixes: (region, product), (region) and (). A per-product subtotal across regions needs CUBE or an explicit GROUPING SETS entry.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, HAVING can be used without GROUP BY; the whole result set is then treated as a single group.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 is valid: with no GROUP BY there is one implicit group, and HAVING decides whether that single row is returned.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, GROUP BY guarantees that the output is sorted by the grouping columns.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The planner often uses HashAggregate, which returns groups in no particular order. Sorted output with a GroupAggregate plan is a side effect, so add ORDER BY when order matters.

questions.prompt: SELECT * FROM coupons WHERE discount = NULL returns no rows, even though some discounts are NULL. Why?
options: Comparing anything with = NULL yields NULL (unknown), which WHERE treats as not true; use discount IS NULL
The literal NULL must be quoted as 'NULL'
PostgreSQL requires a cast such as NULL::numeric before comparing
NULL values are not stored in indexed columns
questions.explanation: NULL means unknown, so = NULL is never true, even for NULL rows. IS NULL is the predicate that tests for NULL. Quoting it compares against the four-letter string 'NULL', and a cast does not change the logic.

questions.prompt: orders.customer_id is nullable, and one order has customer_id NULL. What does this query return?
questions.code:
SELECT id FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
options: Every customer
An error, because the subquery contains NULL
Customers without orders, as intended
No rows at all
questions.explanation: x NOT IN (..., NULL) evaluates to NULL whenever x matches none of the other values, so no row ever passes. Use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL anti-join, which behave as expected with NULLs.

questions.prompt: tickets.status is nullable. WHERE status <> 'cancelled' also drops tickets whose status is NULL. Which predicate keeps them?
options: status != 'cancelled'
NOT (status = 'cancelled')
status IS DISTINCT FROM 'cancelled'
status NOT IN ('cancelled')
questions.explanation: IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as an ordinary comparable value, so NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 'cancelled' is true. The other three forms all evaluate to NULL for NULL status and filter those rows out.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, first_name = 'Ada', middle_name = NULL, last_name = 'Lovelace'. Which expression returns 'Ada Lovelace'?
options: concat(first_name, ' ', middle_name, ' ', last_name)
concat_ws(' ', first_name, middle_name, last_name)
COALESCE(first_name || middle_name || last_name, '')
first_name || ' ' || middle_name || ' ' || last_name
questions.explanation: concat_ws skips NULL arguments and puts the separator only between non-NULL values. The || operator returns NULL if any operand is NULL, and concat treats NULL as an empty string but keeps both spaces ('Ada  Lovelace').

questions.prompt: Under SQL three-valued logic, which expression evaluates to FALSE?
options: NULL = NULL
NULL OR FALSE
NULL AND FALSE
NOT NULL
questions.explanation: FALSE AND anything is FALSE, whatever the unknown value is. NULL OR FALSE depends on the unknown, so it is NULL. NULL = NULL and NOT NULL are also NULL.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) still allows duplicate emails for rows where tenant_id IS NULL. How do you prevent that?
options: Declare the constraint as UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (tenant_id, email)
Add a CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) constraint
Wrap the columns in UNIQUE (COALESCE(tenant_id), email)
Recreate the index as a hash index
questions.explanation: By default, unique constraints treat NULLs as distinct, so rows with a NULL tenant_id never conflict. PostgreSQL 15+ supports NULLS NOT DISTINCT to treat NULLs as equal (a unique index on COALESCE(tenant_id, 0) is the older workaround). A CHECK on email does nothing about the NULL tenant.

questions.prompt: A metrics query computes revenue / order_count and crashes with "division by zero" for days with no orders. What is the idiomatic PostgreSQL fix if you want NULL for those days?
options: revenue / NULLIF(order_count, 0)
revenue / (order_count IS NOT NULL)
COALESCE(revenue / order_count, 0)
revenue / COALESCE(order_count, 0)
questions.explanation: NULLIF(order_count, 0) turns 0 into NULL, and division by NULL returns NULL instead of raising an error. COALESCE(order_count, 0) still divides by zero, and wrapping the division in COALESCE does not help because the error is raised first.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which expressions evaluate to TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: NULL = NULL
NULL IS NULL
NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL
1 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL
NULL <> 1
questions.explanation: IS NULL and IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM are null-safe and always return true or false. Ordinary comparisons such as = and <> with a NULL operand return NULL, not TRUE.

questions.prompt: Which SQL operations treat all NULLs as equal to each other? Select all that apply.
options: UNION removes rows that are duplicates, including rows with NULL in the same columns
SELECT DISTINCT collapses repeated NULLs into one row
GROUP BY puts all NULL keys into a single group
A join ON a.x = b.x matches a NULL to a NULL
questions.explanation: Grouping, DISTINCT and set operations use "not distinct" semantics, so NULLs count as duplicates. Join conditions use ordinary =, where NULL = NULL is unknown, so NULL keys never match.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, CHECK (price > 0) rejects a row where price is NULL.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A CHECK constraint fails only when its expression is FALSE; NULL > 0 is NULL, so the row is accepted. Add NOT NULL if missing prices must be rejected.

questions.prompt: After a LEFT JOIN, a NULL in the right table's primary-key column reliably shows that the left row had no match.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A primary key can never be NULL in stored rows, so a NULL there must come from NULL-extension of an unmatched row. Testing a nullable non-key column would be unreliable, because a matched row could legitimately hold NULL.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING fails with "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification". What is missing?
options: A unique constraint or unique index on users.email
A primary key on users.id
A RETURNING clause
An explicit BEGIN/COMMIT around the insert
questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT (email) needs a unique index or constraint on exactly that column to detect conflicts. A primary key on id does not cover email, and transactions or RETURNING are unrelated to conflict detection.

questions.prompt: In this PostgreSQL upsert, what does EXCLUDED.views refer to?
options: The number of rows that conflicted
The value from the row that was proposed for insertion (here 1)
The value already stored in the existing row
The views value from before the last UPDATE
questions.explanation: EXCLUDED is the row that would have been inserted; the existing row is referenced by the table name (page_views.views). So this adds 1 to the stored count.

questions.prompt: A Node handler does SELECT by email and then INSERT if no row was found. Under load you get unique-violation errors. Why does INSERT ... ON CONFLICT fix this?
options: It checks and inserts atomically, so two concurrent requests cannot both pass the existence check
It disables the unique index while the statement runs
It retries the SELECT until no conflicting row is found
It runs at SERIALIZABLE isolation automatically
questions.explanation: With check-then-insert, two requests can both see no row and both insert. ON CONFLICT resolves the conflict inside one statement using the unique index, with no window between the check and the insert. It does not change the isolation level.

questions.prompt: After inserting an order whose id is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, how does a Node service get the new id in the same round trip in PostgreSQL?
options: Append RETURNING id to the INSERT
Read the id from the driver's rowCount
Run SELECT lastval() in a separate request without a transaction
Call SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders right after the insert
questions.explanation: RETURNING sends back columns of the inserted rows, including generated ids, in one statement. MAX(id) races with concurrent inserts, and rowCount is only the number of affected rows.

questions.prompt: staging has two rows for SKU 'X1' with different prices. What happens to product X1 in PostgreSQL?
questions.code:
UPDATE products p
SET price = s.price
FROM staging s
WHERE s.sku = p.sku;
options: The statement fails because a row would be updated twice
X1 is updated twice and ends with the last price in staging order
X1 gets the average of the two prices
X1 is updated once, using one of the two staging prices, and which one is unpredictable
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL docs warn that when the FROM join yields several matches for a target row, only one is used to update it, and which one is not predictable. De-duplicate staging first, for example with DISTINCT ON. The "affect row a second time" error belongs to ON CONFLICT and MERGE.

questions.prompt: You must purge 50 million expired rows from a busy PostgreSQL events table. What is the safest approach?
options: Delete in batches (for example 10,000 rows by primary-key range per transaction) and let autovacuum keep up
One DELETE ... WHERE expires_at < now() so it is atomic
TRUNCATE the table during peak traffic
UPDATE the rows to NULL first, then DELETE them
questions.explanation: A single huge DELETE holds row locks and a long transaction, generates a burst of WAL and replication lag, and stops VACUUM from cleaning up until it ends. Batching keeps each transaction short. TRUNCATE would remove the rows you want to keep.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what happens when you run this statement?
questions.code:
INSERT INTO kv (k, v) VALUES ('a', 1), ('a', 2)
ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET v = EXCLUDED.v;
options: kv ends with ('a', 1), the first value wins
Error: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
Both rows are inserted because the conflict check runs after the statement
kv ends with ('a', 2), the last value wins
questions.explanation: A single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE may not update the same row twice, so duplicate keys within one batch raise an error. De-duplicate the input (for example in the Node layer or with DISTINCT ON) before upserting.

questions.prompt: Which statements about RETURNING in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: It works with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
It only works with single-row statements
It returns values filled in by column defaults, such as a generated id or created_at
With ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, rows that were skipped are not returned
questions.explanation: RETURNING reports the final stored rows for all three DML commands, including defaults, and works for multi-row statements. Rows skipped by DO NOTHING are not returned, which surprises people who expect the existing row back.

questions.prompt: orders.customer_id references customers(id). Which statements are true in PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: ON DELETE SET NULL works even if orders.customer_id is declared NOT NULL
With ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a customer also deletes their orders
PostgreSQL automatically creates an index on orders.customer_id for the foreign key
With the default (NO ACTION), deleting a customer who still has orders fails
questions.explanation: CASCADE propagates the delete, and NO ACTION rejects it while children exist. SET NULL would violate NOT NULL and fail. PostgreSQL indexes only the referenced key, not the referencing column, so add that index yourself or deletes and joins will scan orders.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING without a conflict target skips rows that would violate any unique constraint on the table.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For DO NOTHING the conflict target is optional; leaving it out handles conflicts against any unique or exclusion constraint. DO UPDATE, by contrast, requires a conflict target.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, UPDATE rewrites rows in place, so updating every row of a table does not increase its on-disk size.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Under MVCC, an UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one dead, so a full-table update can roughly double the table until VACUUM reclaims space. HOT updates reuse space within a page but only when there is room and no indexed column changes.

questions.prompt: You need to add a `user` property to Express's Request type across your whole codebase. Which TypeScript feature makes this possible?
options: Declaration merging: re-declaring the library's interface in a module augmentation adds the field
Intersection types: writing type Request = Request & { user: User } in a global .d.ts file
Type assertions: casting req as any wherever the user field is read inside handlers
Generic defaults: passing the user type as a type argument to express() when creating the app
questions.explanation: Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge, which is how libraries let you augment their types (declare global / declare module 'express-serve-static-core' { interface Request { user?: User } }). Re-declaring a type alias is a 'Duplicate identifier' error, so the intersection trick doesn't work.

questions.prompt: What is the type of C['id']?
options: string
string | number
never
It's a compile error on the line that declares C
questions.explanation: An intersection requires a value to satisfy both members, so id must be string & number, which is impossible and reduces to never. Declaring C isn't an error; you only find out when you try to create a value. string | number would be the answer for a union A | B.

questions.prompt: Which part of this code is a compile error?
options: The type declarations, because Cat and Dog can't both declare a name property
Nothing: TypeScript lets you call any member's method on a union-typed value
p.meow(), because meow doesn't exist on Dog, so it isn't available on Cat | Dog
p.name, because a union only exposes properties that are unique to one member
questions.explanation: On a union you can only access members that exist on every constituent. name is shared, so p.name is fine; meow only exists on Cat, so you have to narrow first (e.g. 'meow' in p).

questions.prompt: Why do many teams prefer interface B extends A { ... } over type B = A & { ... } for object type hierarchies?
options: extends makes the compiled JavaScript smaller, because intersections emit helper code
extends reports conflicting property types at the declaration, while & silently produces never
Intersections can't include methods, only data properties, so services need extends
extends is the only way to reuse fields; intersections copy properties at runtime
questions.explanation: If B redeclares id: number while A has id: string, interface extends fails with 'incorrectly extends interface A'. The intersection compiles and quietly makes id never. The TypeScript team also notes that interfaces are cached and check faster. Neither form emits any JavaScript.

questions.prompt: An order service models status as type Status = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'failed' instead of string. What's the main benefit?
options: It lets the status be reassigned to any string later without needing a type assertion
The union is converted to a runtime enum, so invalid values are rejected from the DB too
String literal unions use less memory at runtime than plain strings do in V8
The compiler rejects typos like 'payed' and can check switch statements for exhaustiveness
questions.explanation: Literal unions narrow the set of allowed values at compile time: typos fail, editors autocomplete, and a never check catches missing cases. They're erased at runtime, so you still need validation (e.g. zod) for data coming from a DB or HTTP.

questions.prompt: Which call is a compile error?
options: (2), because o has a property that Opts doesn't declare
Neither, because assignability in TypeScript is purely structural
(1), because excess property checks apply to fresh object literals
Both, because retries isn't part of the Opts interface
questions.explanation: Object literals passed directly are 'fresh' and get excess property checking, which catches typos like retires. Once the literal is stored in a variable, normal structural assignability applies, and extra properties are allowed.

questions.prompt: Does this compile under strict mode?
questions.code:
type U = { a: string } | { b: number };
const x: U = { a: 'x', b: 1 };
options: Yes: excess property checks on a union allow any property that exists on some member
No: TypeScript treats object unions as exclusive, so a and b can't both be set
No: the literal must match exactly one member of the union, so b is an excess property
Yes, but only because both properties are optional in their own member types
questions.explanation: Unions of object types aren't exclusive (XOR). The literal is assignable to { a: string }, and b exists on another member, so it isn't flagged as excess. To forbid it, add a discriminant or use { a: string; b?: never } | { b: number; a?: never }.

questions.prompt: Given type A = { a: string; c: number } and type B = { b: string; c: number }, what is keyof (A | B)?
options: never
questions.explanation: From a union you can only safely access keys present in every member, so keyof (A | B) is the common keys: 'c'. keyof (A & B) is all the keys, 'a' | 'b' | 'c'. This duality trips up a lot of people.

questions.prompt: Given let v: string | number, which expressions compile without narrowing? Select all that apply.
options: String(v)
v.toString()
v.toFixed(2)
v.valueOf()
v.length
questions.explanation: Only members common to string and number are available: toString and valueOf exist on both, and String() accepts any value. toFixed exists only on number and length only on string, so they need a typeof check first.

questions.prompt: Which statements about intersection types are correct? Select all that apply.
options: string & number reduces to never
They're handy for adding fields, e.g. User & { token: string }
A & B only keeps the properties that A and B share
A value of type A & B must have all the properties of both A and B
questions.explanation: An intersection combines requirements, so the result has every property of both types. Incompatible primitives give never. 'Only the shared properties' describes what you can access on a union, not an intersection.

questions.prompt: Type aliases can't be extended at all; only interfaces support reuse through extends.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Type aliases are extended with intersections (type B = A & { x: number }), and an interface can extend an object-type alias (interface B extends A {}). What aliases can't do is declaration merging.

questions.prompt: Someone adds the 'tri' member to Shape but forgets to update area(). What happens?
options: Compile error in the default branch: the 'tri' member isn't assignable to never
Runtime TypeError thrown by the never assignment the first time a triangle is passed
It compiles, but TypeScript prints a warning about the unhandled 'tri' case
It compiles, and area() returns undefined at runtime for triangles
questions.explanation: In the default branch s has been narrowed to whatever cases are left. With 'tri' unhandled, that's the triangle type, which can't be assigned to never, so the build fails right where the case is missing. That's the point of the exhaustiveness check.

questions.prompt: Why does x.length error inside the if block?
options: typeof x === 'object' doesn't narrow at all; only instanceof narrows array types
The check narrows x to object, and object has no length property
typeof null is 'object', so x is narrowed to string[] | null and may still be null
Arrays aren't objects in TypeScript, so x is narrowed to never inside the block
questions.explanation: typeof narrowing follows JavaScript semantics, where typeof null === 'object'. Inside the block x is string[] | null, so strictNullChecks complains. Write if (x !== null && typeof x === 'object') or use Array.isArray(x).

questions.prompt: With type Fish = { swim(): void } and type Bird = { fly(): void }, what does if ('swim' in animal) do for animal: Fish | Bird?
options: Nothing at compile time; the in operator only checks at runtime
Narrows animal to Fish inside the block (and to Bird in the else branch)
Narrows animal to Fish & Bird, because both could have a swim property
Causes a compile error, because in can't be used on union types
questions.explanation: The in operator is a narrowing construct: the true branch keeps members that have (or may have) the property and the false branch keeps the rest. It's a handy way to tell union members apart when there's no shared discriminant field.

questions.prompt: What does the return type x is string give callers of isString(value) that a plain boolean return type wouldn't?
options: Callers can pass only values whose static type is already string
The compiler checks that the function body really tests for a string
In if (isString(v)) { ... }, v is narrowed to string inside the block
The check is moved to compile time, so no runtime typeof check runs
questions.explanation: A type predicate tells the compiler what a true result means, so the caller's variable is narrowed. TypeScript trusts you: it doesn't verify the body, so a wrong predicate leads to unsound narrowing. The function still runs at runtime as normal.

questions.prompt: What does an assertion function declared as function assertUser(x: unknown): asserts x is User do for the code after a call to it?
options: It converts v to a User object by copying across the matching properties
It makes TypeScript generate a runtime check of User's shape automatically
It narrows v only inside a following if block, like a type predicate does
After assertUser(v) returns, v is treated as User for the rest of the scope
questions.explanation: asserts x is T means 'if this function returns normally, x is T', so narrowing applies to every statement after the call. The function must throw when the check fails, and you write that check yourself; TypeScript doesn't generate validation.

questions.prompt: What's the bug?
options: qty is narrowed to never after the if, so the second return is unreachable
The ! operator doesn't narrow number | undefined, so it's a compile error
A quantity of 0 is falsy, so a valid 0 is reported as 'missing'
Template literals can't contain number values without calling toString()
questions.explanation: Truthiness narrowing removes undefined, but it also treats 0 (and NaN) as falsy. For optional numbers or strings where 0 or '' are valid, check qty === undefined (or qty == null) instead.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't switch (res.status) narrow res to the success or error shape?
options: Narrowing only works when the union has exactly two members
Discriminants have to be named kind or type for TypeScript to use them
switch statements never narrow; only if/else chains narrow unions
status is typed string in both members, so it isn't a literal discriminant
questions.explanation: A discriminated union needs a common property whose types are distinct literals, e.g. status: 'ok' and status: 'error'. With string in both members, checking the value tells the compiler nothing. switch works fine, and the property can have any name.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 5.5+, what is the type of ids?
questions.code: const ids = [1, undefined, 3].filter((x) => x !== undefined);
options: (number | undefined)[]
number[]
unknown[]
never[]
questions.explanation: TypeScript 5.5 added inferred type predicates: the arrow function x => x !== undefined is inferred as (x) => x is number, so filter returns number[]. In older versions you got (number | undefined)[] unless you wrote the predicate yourself.

questions.prompt: Which of these narrow a value of type string | number | Date? Select all that apply.
options: x as string
typeof x === 'number'
Calling a function whose return type is x is Date inside an if
Putting // @ts-ignore above the line that uses x
x instanceof Date
questions.explanation: typeof, instanceof and user-defined type predicates are narrowing constructs that affect the following code. as string is an unchecked assertion for a single expression, and @ts-ignore just hides an error; neither narrows anything.

questions.prompt: Which are good practices for modelling API results as a discriminated union? Select all that apply.
options: Use an in check on a property unique to one member when there's no tag
Add a never-typed default branch so new members cause a compile error
Use one type where every field is optional instead of separate members
Give every member a shared, literal-typed tag field such as status: 'ok' | 'error'
questions.explanation: A literal tag plus an exhaustiveness check makes impossible states unrepresentable and keeps switches complete. One all-optional type allows nonsense like both data and error being set, and forces checks everywhere. in narrowing is a valid fallback.

questions.prompt: With let x: string | number, writing x = 5 inside if (typeof x === 'string') { ... } is a compile error.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Narrowing changes the type TypeScript tracks at each point, not the declared type. Assigning any string | number value is allowed, and after the assignment TypeScript narrows x to number for the following lines.

questions.prompt: What is the type of v?
options: 'name'
string | number
string
unknown
questions.explanation: K is inferred as the literal 'name', and the return type T[K] is an indexed access type, so v is typeof u['name'], which is string. This is the classic type-safe property getter. 'name' is the type of the key, not of the value.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 5.x, what does the const modifier on the type parameter change about routes?
options: The function body is evaluated at compile time, like a C++ constexpr
routes is inferred as readonly ['/users', '/orders'] instead of string[]
T must be a primitive type, so passing an array is a compile error
The argument can't be mutated inside the function, but the type is still string[]
questions.explanation: const type parameters (TS 5.0) make inference behave as if the caller had written as const, keeping literal and tuple types. Without it, T would be inferred as string[], and the specific route strings would be lost.

questions.prompt: What's the fix for the compile error 'Property length does not exist on type T'?
options: Replace the generic with any so that every property access is allowed
Constrain T: function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T)
Add a default type: function longest<T = string>(a: T, b: T)
Annotate the return type as T & { length: number } so length is known
questions.explanation: An unconstrained T could be anything (including number), so TypeScript won't let you read length. A constraint says which shape T must have, and the function then works for strings, arrays and any object with length while keeping the precise type. A default doesn't constrain anything.

questions.prompt: Given interface ApiResponse<T = unknown> { data: T; status: number }, what is the type of data in a value annotated as ApiResponse?
options: any
never
It's a compile error: generic types always need explicit type arguments
unknown
questions.explanation: A default type parameter is used when no argument is given, so ApiResponse means ApiResponse<unknown>. Without a default, writing ApiResponse alone would be an error ('Generic type requires 1 type argument').

questions.prompt: Given interface Repo<T extends { id: string }> { findById(id: string): Promise<T | null> }, what happens with let r: Repo<{ name: string }>?
options: It compiles, but r.findById is typed as returning Promise<never>
Compile error: { name: string } doesn't satisfy the constraint { id: string }
It compiles, because constraints are only checked when a method is called
It compiles, and findById returns Promise<{ name: string; id: string } | null>
questions.explanation: Constraints are checked wherever the generic is instantiated. { name: string } has no id, so the type argument is rejected right there ('Type does not satisfy the constraint'). TypeScript never merges the constraint into your argument.

questions.prompt: What is R?
questions.code:
type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type R = ToArray<string | number>;
options: string[] & number[]
(string | number)[]
string[] | number[]
never
questions.explanation: Conditional types distribute over unions when the checked type is a naked type parameter: ToArray<string | number> becomes ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>. To get (string | number)[] instead, turn distribution off by wrapping: [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never.

questions.prompt: What is X?
questions.code:
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;
type X = Unwrap<Promise<number>>;
options: number
never
unknown
Promise<number>
questions.explanation: infer U declares a type variable that captures whatever sits in that position when the match succeeds. Promise<number> matches Promise<infer U> with U = number. For non-promises the false branch returns T unchanged. The built-in Awaited<T> works this way and also unwraps nested promises.

questions.prompt: Which generic signature adds nothing over a non-generic one?
options: function log<T>(x: T): void, where T is used only once
function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]
function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined
function wrap<T>(x: T): { value: T }
questions.explanation: A type parameter is worth having when it links two or more positions (an input to an output, or two inputs). In log it appears once, so it's equivalent to (x: unknown): void and just adds noise. The others all relate their inputs to their output types.

questions.prompt: Which calls compile? Select all that apply.
options: merge(1, { b: 2 })
merge(null, {})
merge([], {})
questions.explanation: The object type means any non-primitive, so plain objects and arrays satisfy it, but 1 (a number) doesn't. Under strictNullChecks, null isn't assignable to object, so merge(null, {}) is an error too.

questions.prompt: Which statements about TypeScript generics are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Generic type parameters are available at runtime through reflection by default
Type arguments are erased, so a check like x instanceof T can't work at runtime
Classes, interfaces and type aliases can be generic, not just functions
You can pass type arguments explicitly, as in parse<User>(raw)
questions.explanation: TypeScript erases all types when emitting JavaScript, so T has no runtime presence. If you need runtime behaviour, pass a value such as a class constructor or a zod schema. Explicit type arguments and generic classes, interfaces and aliases are all supported.

questions.prompt: Array<string> and string[] are the same type in TypeScript.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: string[] is shorthand for the generic Array<string>; the two are interchangeable. In the same way, readonly string[] is equivalent to ReadonlyArray<string>.

questions.prompt: Which call is a compile error?
questions.code:
type User = { id: string; name: string; email: string };
function update(id: string, patch: Partial<Omit<User, 'id'>>) {}
options: update('1', {})
update('1', { id: '2' })
update('1', { email: 'e', name: 'n' })
update('1', { name: 'x' })
questions.explanation: Omit removes id and Partial makes the rest optional, so the patch type is { name?: string; email?: string }. An empty object or any subset is fine, but id is an excess property. That's exactly the protection you want for PATCH endpoints.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't this compile?
questions.code:
type Role = 'admin' | 'user';
const perms: Record<Role, string[]> = { admin: [] };
options: Record values must be primitives; arrays need Map<Role, string[]> instead
Record keys must be string, not a union of string literals like Role
Empty arrays can't be assigned to string[] without a type assertion
Record<Role, ...> requires a key for every member of Role, and 'user' is missing
questions.explanation: Record<K, V> is a mapped type { [P in K]: V }, so every literal in K becomes a required property. That makes it great for exhaustive lookup tables. Use Partial<Record<Role, string[]>> if some keys are optional.

questions.prompt: Given function makeUser() { return { id: 1, name: 'a' }; }, how do you get its return type without writing it out?
options: ReturnType<typeof makeUser()>
typeof makeUser()
ReturnType<typeof makeUser>
ReturnType<makeUser>
questions.explanation: ReturnType takes a function type, and typeof turns the value makeUser into its type. ReturnType<makeUser> is an error because makeUser is a value, not a type, and typeof can't be applied to a call expression.

questions.prompt: For async function fetchUser(id: string) { ... return user; } returning a User, which type gives you User?
options: ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>
InstanceType<typeof fetchUser>
Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>
Awaited<Parameters<typeof fetchUser>>
questions.explanation: An async function's return type is Promise<User>, so ReturnType gives Promise<User>, and Awaited unwraps it (recursively, for nested promises) to User. Parameters gives the argument tuple, and InstanceType is for constructors.

questions.prompt: Why is this a compile error?
questions.code:
type Config = { db: { host: string; port: number }; debug: boolean };
const c: Partial<Config> = { db: { host: 'x' } };
options: debug is required, because Partial only affects object-typed properties
Partial can't be applied to types that contain nested objects
Partial is shallow: db is optional, but if present it still needs host and port
Partial makes all properties readonly, so the object literal can't be built
questions.explanation: Partial<T> only adds ? to T's top-level properties. A provided db must still be a full { host; port }. For nested patches, write a recursive DeepPartial type or use Partial on the nested type explicitly.

questions.prompt: A developer writes type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'pasword'> (note the typo). What happens?
options: Compile error: 'pasword' isn't a key of User
It compiles silently, and PublicUser still includes password
It compiles, but PublicUser becomes never
It compiles and removes password anyway, by fuzzy-matching the key
questions.explanation: Omit's key parameter is declared as K extends keyof any, so any string is accepted and omitting a nonexistent key does nothing. Pick<User, 'pasword'> would error, because Pick requires K extends keyof T. Some teams define a stricter Omit for this reason.

questions.prompt: What does Readonly<Config> do at runtime?
options: It deep-freezes the object, including every nested property and array
It wraps the object in a Proxy that throws a TypeError on any write
It calls Object.freeze on the object when it's assigned to the variable
Nothing: it only makes the compiler reject writes to top-level properties
questions.explanation: Utility types are compile-time only and are erased. Readonly is also shallow: nested objects stay mutable even at the type level. If you need runtime immutability, call Object.freeze yourself (and type it with as const or Readonly).

questions.prompt: Given function send(to: string, retries?: number) {}, what is Parameters<typeof send>?
options: [to: string, retries?: number]
(string | number)[]
string | number | undefined
{ to: string; retries?: number }
questions.explanation: Parameters returns a tuple of the parameter types, keeping names as labels and optional markers. It's commonly used to write wrappers with the same arguments: (...args: Parameters<typeof send>) => send(...args).

questions.prompt: Which statements about built-in utility types are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Pick<T, K> requires every K to be a key of T
NonNullable<string | null | undefined> is string
ReturnType<myFn> works directly on a function value named myFn
Extract<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'a' | 'z'> is 'a'
Partial<T> makes nested object properties optional too
questions.explanation: NonNullable removes null and undefined, and Extract keeps the union members assignable to the second argument. Partial is shallow. ReturnType needs a type, so you write ReturnType<typeof myFn>.

questions.prompt: Given type User = { id: string; name: string; email: string }, which types are equivalent to { name: string; email: string }? Select all that apply.
options: Exclude<User, 'id'>
Partial<User>
Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>
Omit<User, 'id'>
questions.explanation: Pick keeps the listed keys and Omit drops the listed ones, so both give { name; email }. Partial makes everything optional and keeps id. Exclude works on union members, not object keys: Exclude<User, 'id'> is just User, a common mix-up with Omit.

questions.prompt: Under default strict settings, indexing a Record<string, number> with a missing key, as in counts['nope'], is typed as number rather than number | undefined unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is enabled.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Index signatures promise a value for every key, so lookups are typed as number even though they're undefined at runtime. noUncheckedIndexedAccess (not part of strict) adds | undefined to index-signature and array-index reads.

questions.prompt: How do you fix the compile error in this function?
options: Change the parameter type to never so that every method is allowed
Add a non-null assertion: return input!.toUpperCase();
Wrap the call in try/catch so that the type error is handled
Narrow first: if (typeof input === 'string') return input.toUpperCase();
questions.explanation: unknown accepts any value but allows almost no operations until you narrow it. A typeof check proves it's a string. never means 'no value', and ! only removes null and undefined from a type, so neither fixes it. try/catch has nothing to do with compile-time types.

questions.prompt: What's the risk in this code?
questions.code:
const data: any = JSON.parse(body);
const n: number = data.count.total;
options: TypeScript infers data.count.total as never and removes the line from the output
Assigning any to a number variable converts the value with Number() at runtime
JSON.parse returns unknown, so this line doesn't compile without an assertion
data is any, so the wrong path data.count.total type-checks and only fails at runtime
questions.explanation: JSON.parse returns any, which turns off checking for every expression derived from it, and any flows silently into typed variables. A wrong field name or shape is only found at runtime. Annotate the result as unknown and validate it (e.g. with zod).

questions.prompt: What is type X = string | never?
options: never
string
unknown
string | never (it can't be simplified)
questions.explanation: never is the empty set, so adding it to a union contributes nothing: X is string. That's why conditional types return never to filter members out (as Exclude does). In an intersection, by contrast, never absorbs everything: string & never is never.

questions.prompt: Given let nev: never, let anyVal: any and let unk: unknown, which assignment compiles?
options: let n: never = unk;
let n: never = undefined;
let s: string = nev;
let n: never = anyVal;
questions.explanation: never is the bottom type: it's assignable to every type, but nothing except never is assignable to it. Even any can't be assigned to never, which is one of the few places any doesn't bypass checking.

questions.prompt: A webhook handler receives a raw JSON body. Which approach is safest?
options: const body: WebhookEvent = JSON.parse(raw), relying on TypeScript to check it
const body: any = JSON.parse(raw), then use optional chaining on every field
const body: unknown = JSON.parse(raw), then validate it with a schema before use
const body = JSON.parse(raw) as WebhookEvent, so the rest of the code is typed
questions.explanation: Typing the result as unknown forces you to validate before use, and a schema (zod) narrows it to a trusted type. as WebhookEvent and a direct annotation are unchecked claims, since JSON.parse returns any. Optional chaining prevents some crashes but doesn't validate types.

questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between a function returning void and one returning never?
options: void returns normally with no useful value; never doesn't return (it throws or loops)
void functions can't throw errors, while never functions are required to throw
They're interchangeable; never is just the strict-mode spelling of void
void means it returns undefined; never means it returns null
questions.explanation: void means callers shouldn't use the result, but control comes back. never means control never comes back, which lets TypeScript treat the code after a call (e.g. fail('x')) as unreachable and narrow types. void functions can throw too.

questions.prompt: What are keyof any and keyof unknown?
options: never, and string | number | symbol
string for both
string | number | symbol, and never
string | number | symbol for both
questions.explanation: any can be indexed with any key, so keyof any is every possible key type, string | number | symbol, which is why Omit's K is declared as K extends keyof any. unknown promises nothing, so it has no known keys: keyof unknown is never.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 4.9+, what is the inferred return type of getId?
options: string | number
any
Compile error: property 'id' doesn't exist on type 'object'
unknown
questions.explanation: Since 4.9, 'id' in x narrows x to object & Record<'id', unknown>, so x.id is unknown. The implicit undefined from the other path merges into unknown, since unknown | undefined is unknown. Before 4.9 the property access was an error.

questions.prompt: Given let u: unknown, which of these compile? Select all that apply.
options: let s: string = u;
if (typeof u === 'string') u.length;
u.foo
String(u)
questions.explanation: unknown allows equality checks and being passed where any or unknown is accepted (String(value?: any)). It can't be assigned to a specific type or have members read until it's narrowed, which is exactly what makes it safe.

questions.prompt: Which are legitimate uses of the never type? Select all that apply.
options: Filtering union members in conditional types, e.g. T extends X ? never : T
The return type of a function that always throws
A parameter type meaning 'accept any value'
Exhaustiveness checks in the default branch of a switch
The type of an optional field that may be missing
questions.explanation: never represents impossibility: unreachable branches, removed union members, and functions that never return. To accept any value, use unknown. A missing optional field is undefined (or ?), not never.

questions.prompt: A value typed any lets you call any method on it without a compile error, and it can be assigned to a string variable without any check.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: any switches off type checking in both directions: anything can go in, and it can come out as any type. That's why one any (often from JSON.parse or an untyped library) can quietly spread unsoundness. Prefer unknown at boundaries.

questions.prompt: This is the JavaScript tsc emits for enum Dir { Up, Down }. What does it print?
options: 0,1,Up,Down 1
Up,Down Down
Up,Down,0,1 Down
0,1,Up,Down Down
questions.explanation: This is what tsc emits for enum Dir { Up, Down }. Numeric enums get a reverse mapping (Dir[0] === 'Up'), so the object has both name and number keys. Integer-like keys come first in key order. That's why Object.keys or Object.values on a numeric enum returns twice as many entries as you might expect.

questions.prompt: Why is this an error?
questions.code:
enum Status { Active = 'active', Banned = 'banned' }
const s: Status = 'active';
options: The enum has to be declared as a const enum before it can be used as a type
Enum members have to be uppercase, so the value should be 'ACTIVE' rather than 'active'
String enums can't be used as variable types, only as namespaces of constants
String enum types only accept their own members, so you have to write Status.Active
questions.explanation: Unlike unions of string literals, string enum types only accept their own members, even when the underlying string is identical. Some teams like that strictness; others find it awkward when values come from JSON, which is one reason for preferring const objects with a union type.

questions.prompt: What is the type Role?
questions.code:
const Role = { Admin: 'admin', User: 'user' } as const;
type Role = (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role];
options: 'admin' | 'user'
string
'Admin' | 'User'
{ Admin: string; User: string }
questions.explanation: as const keeps the literal values, typeof Role is the object's type, and indexing it with keyof typeof Role gives the union of its values. Without as const the values would widen to string. keyof typeof Role alone would give the keys 'Admin' | 'User'.

questions.prompt: Why do many codebases avoid const enum, especially in libraries?
options: const enums can't have string values, only auto-incremented numeric members
const enums are deprecated and produce a compile error in TypeScript 5.x
const enums are slower at runtime, because each use is a property lookup on a frozen object
Per-file transpilers (isolatedModules: esbuild, swc, Babel) can't inline const enums from other files
questions.explanation: const enums are erased and their values inlined at use sites, which needs whole-program type information. Tools that compile one file at a time can't do that, so isolatedModules flags it, and a const enum shipped in a .d.ts creates version-skew problems. Performance isn't the issue.

questions.prompt: A team runs .ts files directly with Node's built-in type stripping (strip-only mode, no transform). Which construct fails?
options: function f(x: unknown): x is string
enum Color { Red, Green }
type Id = string | number
interface User { id: string }
questions.explanation: Strip-only mode just deletes type syntax, so it only supports erasable TypeScript. Enums (along with namespaces with runtime code and constructor parameter properties) generate JavaScript, so they need a transform. TypeScript 5.8's erasableSyntaxOnly flag reports these at compile time.

questions.prompt: How do you fix this so the call compiles while cfg stays an ordinary object?
options: Change Mode to plain string, because unions can't be used for function parameter types
Add as const to the literal (or satisfies { mode: Mode }) so mode keeps the literal type 'prod'
Annotate cfg as const cfg: any = { mode: 'prod' } to skip the check on this assignment
Declare cfg with let instead of const, so that TypeScript infers the narrower literal type
questions.explanation: Object properties are mutable, so TypeScript widens 'prod' to string in { mode: 'prod' }, and string isn't assignable to Mode. as const keeps the literal (and makes it readonly). Annotating or using satisfies against a type that contains Mode also works. let widens even more.

questions.prompt: What's the advantage of satisfies here over annotating routes: Record<string, Route>?
options: It skips type checking for routes entirely, which noticeably speeds up compiling a large project
It allows the values to be any type while only checking that all of the keys are strings
It converts routes into a frozen object at runtime, so none of the routes can be changed later
It checks each value against Route but keeps the literal keys, so routes.typo is an error
questions.explanation: With an annotation, the variable's type becomes Record<string, Route>, which forgets which keys exist (any string key is allowed). satisfies validates the expression against the type but keeps the inferred, more specific type. It's purely compile-time.

questions.prompt: What happens on the last line?
questions.code:
const c = { db: { port: 5432 } } as const;
c.db.port = 6543;
options: It compiles, but the assignment is ignored because the object is frozen
It compiles: as const only makes top-level properties readonly
Runtime TypeError, because as const calls Object.freeze on the object
Compile error: as const makes properties readonly at every depth
questions.explanation: as const applies recursively: c.db.port is readonly 5432 at the type level, so the assignment fails to compile. It's still purely compile-time; the emitted object isn't frozen, so JavaScript code without types could still change it.

questions.prompt: Which are real advantages of a const object plus a derived union type over a TypeScript enum? Select all that apply.
options: It's plain JavaScript, so it works with strip-only type stripping and erasableSyntaxOnly
Plain string literals like 'admin' can be passed wherever the union type is expected
Object.values() gives exactly the values, with no reverse-mapping entries
Enums can't be used as types in function parameters, while unions can
Const objects are nominally typed, so a raw string can never be passed by mistake
questions.explanation: The const-object pattern is erasable, iterates cleanly and accepts literals (handy for JSON input). Nominal typing is actually a property of enums, not unions, and enums can of course be used as parameter types.

questions.prompt: Given enum Color { Red, Green = 5, Blue }, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Object.keys(Color).length === 3
Color[5] === 'Green'
Color.Red === 0
Color.Blue === 6
questions.explanation: Numeric enum members auto-increment from the previous member, so Red is 0 and Blue follows Green = 5 to become 6. The reverse mapping gives Color[5] === 'Green'. Because of the reverse entries, Object.keys returns 6 keys, not 3.

questions.prompt: String enums get a reverse mapping at runtime, just like numeric enums.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Only numeric members get reverse mappings. tsc emits Status['Active'] = 'active' for string members without the value-to-name entry, so Status['active'] is undefined and Object.keys(Status) returns only the member names.

questions.prompt: Your project sets "strict": true and you upgrade to a newer TypeScript minor version that adds a new strict-family check. What should you expect?
options: The new check is enabled automatically, so the upgrade may surface new errors
TypeScript refuses to compile until you add the new flag either on or off
Nothing changes until you list the new flag explicitly in tsconfig.json
The new check runs only as a warning until you set strict to "latest"
questions.explanation: strict is an umbrella that turns on the whole strict family, and the docs warn that future versions may add stricter checks under it. Upgrades can therefore break builds. To opt out of a specific check, set that individual flag to false.

questions.prompt: What does noImplicitAny report here?
options: The function's return type must be written out
Nothing, because simple functions like this one are exempt
Parameters a and b implicitly have an any type
a + b may be a string, so the function must be generic
questions.explanation: With no annotation and nothing to infer from, parameters would silently become any. noImplicitAny makes that an error so you annotate them (a: number, b: number). Return types are still inferred; that flag is only about implicit any.

questions.prompt: Under strict mode, why is this class a compile error, and which fix keeps the type honest?
options: Class properties must have an initial value at the declaration, so write private db: Db = {} as Db
Private fields have to be declared with # instead of private, so the field must be renamed to #db
Constructors can't be empty under strict mode, so add a call to super() before anything else
db isn't definitely assigned in the constructor; assign it there or inject it as a parameter
questions.explanation: strictPropertyInitialization requires non-optional fields to be assigned in the constructor. The honest fix is to do that, e.g. constructor(private db: Db) {}. The ! definite-assignment assertion or {} as Db silence the error but can leave undefined at runtime.

questions.prompt: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled, what is the type of first?
questions.code:
const arr: string[] = loadNames();
const first = arr[0];
options: string | null
string | undefined
string[] | undefined
string
questions.explanation: The flag adds | undefined to element reads via index signatures and array indexes, because arr[0] can be past the end. You then narrow (if (first !== undefined)) before use. It's not part of strict, but it catches a lot of real bugs.

questions.prompt: Under strictFunctionTypes, why is f = g an error?
options: Dog is wider than Animal, so g's parameter type is incompatible the other way round
Function types can never be assigned to one another under strict mode
Parameters are checked contravariantly: g needs a Dog, but f may be called with any Animal
Arrow functions and function types must match by name as well as by shape
questions.explanation: f promises it can handle any Animal. Assigning g, which calls d.bark(), would let f({ name: 'cat' }) crash. strictFunctionTypes enforces contravariant parameter checks for function-type properties; method-syntax parameters stay bivariant for compatibility.

questions.prompt: With exactOptionalPropertyTypes enabled and type Opts = { label?: string }, which assignment errors?
options: const o: Opts = { label: String(1) };
const o: Opts = { label: 'x' };
const o: Opts = {};
const o: Opts = { label: undefined };
questions.explanation: Normally label?: string means string | undefined. With exactOptionalPropertyTypes, ? means 'may be missing' but not 'may be explicitly undefined', which matters for 'label' in o checks and for spreads that overwrite values. Write label?: string | undefined if you want both.

questions.prompt: A large legacy JavaScript codebase is being moved to strict TypeScript. Which approach usually works best?
options: Annotate every value as any first, then remove the annotations at the end of the migration
Turn strict mode off permanently and rely on the integration tests to catch any type problems
Enable strict flags one by one (e.g. noImplicitAny, then strictNullChecks), fixing errors module by module
Add // @ts-ignore above every reported error so the build passes, then turn on every flag at once
questions.explanation: Turning flags on one at a time keeps the error count manageable and every step shippable. Blanket ts-ignore or any just hides the problems the migration was meant to find. Per-line @ts-expect-error with a tracking ticket is fine for leftovers, because it errors once the problem is fixed.

questions.prompt: What does "skipLibCheck": true do?
options: Disables the standard lib (lib.d.ts), so globals like Promise and Map must be declared yourself
Stops TypeScript from resolving types from node_modules, so every import of a package becomes any
Skips type-checking all .d.ts files, which speeds up builds but can hide conflicts between library types
Skips type-checking your own source files and only emits the JavaScript output as fast as possible
questions.explanation: Your code is still fully checked against library types; only the declaration files themselves aren't checked internally. Most projects enable it for speed and to avoid errors in third-party typings. noLib, not skipLibCheck, is the flag that removes the standard lib.

questions.prompt: Which compiler options are turned on by "strict": true? Select all that apply.
options: exactOptionalPropertyTypes
strictNullChecks
useUnknownInCatchVariables
noUncheckedIndexedAccess
noImplicitAny
questions.explanation: The strict family includes strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, alwaysStrict and useUnknownInCatchVariables. noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes have to be enabled separately.

questions.prompt: For a Node 22 ESM backend, which tsconfig statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Setting "strict": false makes the compiled JavaScript run faster
module/moduleResolution "nodenext" requires file extensions in relative ESM imports (e.g. './db.js')
target controls which newer syntax gets down-levelled in the emitted JavaScript
lib adds runtime polyfills for the APIs it lists
verbatimModuleSyntax requires import type for imports that are only used as types
questions.explanation: nodenext copies Node's real resolution rules, including mandatory extensions for ESM. verbatimModuleSyntax emits imports exactly as written, so type-only ones must be marked. strict affects only checking, and lib only declares types; it never adds polyfills.

questions.prompt: Enabling strictNullChecks doesn't add any runtime null checks to the emitted JavaScript; it only affects type checking.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: TypeScript's checks are erased. strictNullChecks makes null and undefined separate types the compiler tracks, but the output is the same JavaScript. Data from outside (HTTP, DB) can still be null at runtime, which is why you validate at the boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why is async function getCount(): number { return 1; } a compile error?
options: An async function always returns a Promise, so the annotation must be Promise<number>
Async functions can't have return type annotations; the type is always inferred
The return statement needs to be written as return await 1 in an async function
Async functions can't return primitives; they have to resolve with an object
questions.explanation: Whatever an async function returns is wrapped in a Promise, so TypeScript requires the declared return type to be Promise<T> ('The return type of an async function must be the global Promise<T> type'). Returning a plain value inside is fine.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here, and what typically catches it?
options: save() isn't awaited, so failures become unhandled rejections; no-floating-promises flags it
Nothing is wrong: TypeScript reports every unawaited promise as a compile error by default
handler must be declared async or tsc refuses to compile any call to an async function from it
save() returns Promise<void>, which can't be called from a function whose return type is string
questions.explanation: Calling an async function without await or .catch() is legal TypeScript, so tsc says nothing. The response is sent before the save finishes, and a rejection is unhandled (which crashes Node 15+ by default). Lint rules like no-floating-promises catch it.

questions.prompt: Given getUser(): Promise<User> and getOrders(): Promise<Order[]>, what's the type of [u, o] in const [u, o] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getOrders()])?
options: [User, Order[]]
[Promise<User>, Promise<Order[]>]
any[]
(User | Order[])[]
questions.explanation: Promise.all is typed with a mapped tuple type, so an array literal of promises keeps each position's resolved type. Destructuring gives u: User and o: Order[]. You'd get a union array only if you passed in an existing array variable instead of a tuple literal.

questions.prompt: With useUnknownInCatchVariables on, what's the type-safe way to log an error message in catch (e)?
options: const msg = typeof e === 'object' ? e.message : String(e);
const msg = e!.message ?? 'unknown error';
const msg = (e as Error).message ?? String(e);
const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e);
questions.explanation: e is unknown, because anything can be thrown. instanceof narrows to Error, and String(e) handles everything else. The as Error cast is an unchecked claim that crashes if null or undefined is thrown. typeof e === 'object' still leaves object | null with no message property, and ! doesn't narrow unknown.

questions.prompt: What's the main benefit of returning type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E } instead of throwing?
options: TypeScript can't type thrown errors at all, so Result is the only way to type failures
Returning objects is much faster than throwing, so it's the only option for hot code paths
It removes the need for try/catch entirely, including around bugs like TypeErrors
Expected failures show up in the signature, and callers must narrow on ok before reading value
questions.explanation: TypeScript has no checked exceptions, so a signature never tells you what it throws. A Result union makes expected failures (not found, validation) explicit, and the discriminant forces handling. Unexpected bugs still throw, so you still need error boundaries.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 5.x with strict on, what's the type of err in fetchUser(id).catch((err) => { ... })?
options: any, because the lib types the rejection reason as any
unknown, the same as a catch clause variable
Error, because promises can only be rejected with Error
never, because the promise is already rejected
questions.explanation: useUnknownInCatchVariables only affects try/catch clauses. Promise.prototype.catch and then's onrejected are declared with reason: any in the standard lib, so err is any unless you annotate it (err: unknown), which typescript-eslint's use-unknown-in-catch-callback-variable rule enforces.

questions.prompt: What is the type of users, and what's the likely bug?
questions.code: const users = ids.map(async (id) => getUser(id));
options: never[]: async callbacks aren't allowed inside Array.prototype.map, so the whole line fails to compile
User[]: TypeScript unwraps promises returned by map callbacks automatically, so nothing is wrong
Promise<User>[]: the promises are never awaited together, so wrap the map in await Promise.all(...)
Promise<User[]>: map collects the results into one promise, so it just needs a single await
questions.explanation: An async callback returns a Promise, so map produces an array of promises. Code expecting User[] would break (users[0].name is an error). await Promise.all(ids.map(...)) gives User[] and runs the lookups concurrently.

questions.prompt: Why does 'done' print before the saves finish, and why doesn't TypeScript complain?
options: forEach ignores the callback's returned promise, and a Promise-returning function fits a void callback type
await inside forEach is silently ignored at runtime, and TypeScript treats it as a no-op expression
